considered as preventing the operator from driving entries or removing pillar
stumps as rapidly as the emergency may demand.
BURIAL FUND
SEC. 39. A burial fund may be established by each mine or local, to which
fund each miner shall contribute 25 cents a month until a sum of not less than
$100 and not more than $500 shall have been created, when collections shall cease
until the fund is reduced by death, when a collection of 25 cents per month per
man, shall again be made until the amount reaches the maximum agreed upon
and so on. On the day that death by accident to any employee occurs, in or
around the mine, for that day only the miners shall cease working; but under no
circumstances shall the mine be made idle for any funeral. And in consideration
of the mine continuing to work on the day of a funeral of one of its employees
is held, the operators agree to contribute to the bereaved family one-third the
amount paid by the miners, said amount not to exceed $25 provided the deceased
was not entitled to compensation fund of the State. In case the funeral occurs
on Sunday or any day the mine is idle through no fault of the employees, the
company shall contribute as above. This does not prohibit friends from attend-
ing funeral.
Where greater amounts are needed than those stipulated for burial purposes,
collection of such amounts may be arranged locally by mutual consent.
SEC. 40. There shall be a burial fund committee at each mine consisting of
three members, one of whom shall represent the operators, the other two the
mine workers, known as the burial fund committee, to take charge of these funds
and to make all necessary funeral arrangements in case of any death, and said
committee shall be paid for such duties as may be agreed upon locally. This com-
mittee shall render a report quarterly showing the amount of money collected,
amount expended, and the balance in the treasury.
CONSTRUCTION AND REPAIR WORK DURING SUSPENSION
SEC. 41. It is understood that in the event of a disagreement between operators
and mine workers, steam and electrical engineers, firemen, and pumpers are
required to continue to perform such work as is in line with their duties.
During any strike or suspension it is hereby understood and agreed that all
men on all kinds of outside construction and repair work, together with all kinds
of work inside the mine that is not producing coal, must continue at work. It
is further understood and agreed that such miners as are necessary are to be per-
mitted to mine coal for the boilers and consumption of employees of the com-
pany, but this is not to be construed to mean to mine coal for shipment.
ENTRY GOB AND DEAD WORK
SEC. 42. Where there is not sufficient room to gob the dirt and draw slate in
entries with ordinary conditions of the seam, the loader or miner shall load it
in mine cars without compensation, and the company shall unload it.
SEC. 43. For dead work, where unusual conditions exist, the price to be paid
for same shall be a question of local adjustment. Failing to agree, the company
shall have the right to remove the same and give the miner another place, but
all agreements entered into for abnormal conditions shall continue only as long
as such conditions exist.
EXPLOSIVES
SEC. 44. The miner shall purchase all explosives and detonators of all kinds,
including fuses and squibs for blasting coal. If explosives and detonators are
sold by the operators, they shall be sold at cost, which is to include handling,
transportation and insurance. The operator reserves the sole right to designate
the kind of explosives that shall be used in the mines; provided all explosives
shall be of standard grade.
SMITHING
SEC. 45. A uniform charge of one-half cent per ton for smithing shall be made
on all coal mined by the miner and loaded for pick and machine coal throughout


===== [扫描序号 73] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1095
NO DISCRIMINATION
SEC. 46. There shall be no discrimination against any mine worker on account
of activity in the affairs of the organization.
OTHER CONDITIONS NOT SPECIFIED
SEC. 47. All terms and conditions not specified under this contract to con-
tinue as they now exist during the life of this contract, except where changed by
mutual consent.
NO INVALID RULES TO BE ENFORCED
SEC. 48. All local rules in violation of this contract shall be null and void,
and no local union or group of local unions shall pass any rules in violation, neither
shall any company enforce any rules in violation of this contract, and all scale
contract provisions shall have precedent over any rules or provisions of the
district, or national, constitition of the United Mine Workers of America.
EXEMPTION UNDER THIS CONTRACT
SEC. 49. This scale shall not affect mine foreman, mine foreman's assistants,
fire bosses, machine bosses, shot firers, weighmen, dock boss, stable boss, boss
hauler, electricians, watchmen, and teamsters.
The company shall have the right to transfer contract men temporarily to
exempted work without affecting their membership in the union, by notifying
the mine committee.
LOADING MINE CARS
SEC. 50. No limit of weight shall be placed on loading mine cars. In case of
loss in transit, the company shall be held responsible, except where a wreck
occurs the average weight shall be made good by the company. In order that
miners can not take advantage of this clause, the mine management and com-
mittee of any mine where complaint is made of loading cars over their capacity,
shall mutually agree on a standard height for loading cars.
WET PLACES
SEC. 51. When it has been determined a place is a wet place, the operator
shall pay 5 cents per ton in excess of the regular rate, one cent of which goes to the
cutter and four cents to the loader.
Places shall not be classified as wet, when by ordinary method of workmanship
a mine worker can keep dry.
SAFETY LAMPS
SEC. 52. In mines where closed lights, either electric or others, are used, a
charge to the user of five cents per shift per lamp shall be made. An additional
safety lamp where required by the cutter to comply with the mining laws, will
be furnished free. The miner shall be responsible for taking care of his lamp,
and no extra charge shall be made unless he deliberately or carelessly breaks any
part of same. Where electric or other closed lights are substituted voluntarily
on the part of an operator for an open light, a charge of 5 cents per shift, per
amp, shall be made. The rate per lamp herein provided may be changed if a
more efficient lamp is placed in service.
HOUSE COAL
SEC. 53. Where coal is used for fuel in dwellings, it will be furnished to em-
ployees for their own use at $2 per ton, plus delivering cost. Where coal is not
delivered by the company, and employees carry it, they shall pay $2 per month
per house of four rooms or less. If the company does not or can not deliver the
coal, the employee shall have the right to get it hauled by outside terms.

The CHAIRMAN. I will ask Mr. Brackett to read the authority that our scale
committee was clothed with in coming down here.
Mr. Brackett read the following:
Whereas the wage agreement entered into by the membership of the United
Mine Workers of America and the membership of this association expires on
March 31, 1924, and this association has been requested to meet the United Mine
Workers in joint conference for the purpose of negotiating a new wage agreement
to take the place of the one expiring March 31, 1924; now, therefore be it
Ordered, That the scale committee of this association do meet the scale com-
mittee of district No. 17 of the said United Mine Workers of America in joint
conference in the city of Baltimore, Md., on Tuesday, March 11, 1924, or any
adjourned meeting thereof, for the purpose of negotiating or endeavoring to
negotiate a new wage agreement to affect labor rates and mining conditions in
the 12½ counties of northern West Virginia, comprising the territory covered by
this association; and be it further
Ordered, That any new wage agreement negotiated and executed hereunder
shall be returned to this association for ratification and approved before it becomes
effective and binding.
The CHAIRMAN. This is the authority, gentlemen, that the association has
clothed its committee with. I presume the miners are clothed with authority to
negotiate.
Mr. TETLOW. Yes, Mr. Chairman; the miners are here with full authority to
enter into negotiations for the purpose of arranging a new wage agreement to be
effective April 1, this year, and for such term and under such conditions as they
may negotiate. I think, though, the miners' position on that matter can be put
clearly into the record later, and I am now simply making the statement that we
are here with full authority to enter into the arranging of a wage agreement in
compliance with instructions.
Mr. MCCULLOUGH. Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of this conference, before
starting in with our negotiations there are a few things we ought to consider and
reflect upon as a representative body of men gathered here for the purpose of
negotiating a wage contract and perpetuating our relationship as coal producers
in this northern West Virginia territory covered by our scale contract.
We have met in this conference in, I think, the proper spirit. We have come
in here as the representatives of the two forces essential in the production of coal.
I have attended a good many wage conferences of this character. Sometimes,
oftentimes, we have met in a spirit other that that of cooperation and mutual
helpfulness. I have been in many conferences where we have gathered in the
spirit that might makes right. Each of these conferences have developed no
good to either side. I trust that we have met here to-day in that same spirit
of tolerance and mutual consideration for the rights and interests of each other
that has characterized our former meetings.
In fact, this organization of the United Mine Workers and cooperators was
born in the spirit of frindship and cooperation. A great many of the organized
fields of the United Mine Workers were born in a conflict and they dealt with
each other in a spirit of subjection or dominance, as the case might be.
Here from the beginning we have met in the spirit of friendliness and coopera-
tion. I trust that that same spirit will manifest itself throughout the negotiations
of this conference. No doubt on many of the questions that arise we will become
very much in earnest and very determined in our positions. But that should not
be taken as any indication of our intolerance or our desire to dominate in any way.
We are here in the spirit of mutual helpfulness to work out for this field what
each of is believes to be the best interests for the coal industry of Northern West
Virginia.
We are differently situated in this coal territory from many others. This
scale agreement under which we are now working was born in war time and has
been continued during the aftermath of the war. As everyone realizes there
has been a general unreast and a peculiar psychology of labor as the result of the
war conflict that we have not quite yet reached the normal conditions that existed
prior to the war. We are approaching that now, and all of the feverish excite-
ment of the past must subside and we must negotiate with that vision of the future.
We must recognize that the war is over, that war conditions are done away with,
and that we are approaching the pre-war normality of production.
This district as it is situated is handicapped by certain natural barriers. We
have the mountains to the east that make difficult our entrance into the markets.
We have other natural barriers not peculiar to many of the competitive fields


===== [扫描序号 79] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1101
into which we enter. These natural barriers neither the miners nor the operators
nor the public are responsible for. Neither can we change them. We must
meet them as they are and endure them.
I take it for granted that we have a mutual interest in the development of this
coal field. I have never been one to claim that the interests of the employer and
employee were indentical, but I do believe that our interests oftentimes if not
always become mutual, and I feel that our interests are mutual in the natural
development of the coal fields of northern West Virginia.
Unless this coal finds a market in competition with the coals of other fields
these mines will remain idle, and that means as much to the coal miners as it
does to this coal operators in this region. If we were here to construct an agree-
ment based upon our desires, without any reference to the natural and the arti-
ficial barriers that confront us, I imagine that we could get tagether in separate
groups and build a wonderful contract, one that would meet with the hearty.
approval of all of our associates back home.
But that has never been done, and never will be done. We meet conflicting
forces that have ever and must ever determine our position in these matters.
You are here to fight for all that you believe can be secured and still permit the
mines to continue in operation. The operators are here endeavoring to secure
such consideration at your hands as will permit them to operate these mines,
to employ men to work in them, and sell their coal at a fair profit.
Those of you who are acquainted with the coal industry I think will not argue
for one moment that the coal operators of West Virginia are to-day receiving an
excess profit upon their coal. The two or three idle coal mines that stare us
in the face each day, the number of mines that are working from one to two
and three days a week, is evidence sufficient to justify the statement that the
coal industry in West Virginia is not as lucrative as we could hope it to be.
Since the wartime prices, and with the amount of coal that is on the market
to-day, we find that prices have gone down to where there is no profit in the selling
of coal. It is a buyers market. This no doubt is the condition that is met with
in many fields. But we have in this field natural barriers that absolutely prohibit
us from fair competition with other coal fields.
We can not change those natural barriers, but we have artificial barriers
which you, ourselves, and the war-time conditions have builded up. They are
children of our own creation. We meet them to-day as formidable foes in the
production and sale of coal.
We are gathered together to-day to use our reasoning power in an endeavor
to rectify some of these creations of our own hands. I am certain if we meet
them in the proper spirit that we can in large measure rectify these wrongs that
are strangling the coal industry of northern West Virginia, which are a detri-
ment to the miners as well as the operators, and that we can unloose the bands
that are binding us, and set ourselves in a measure free to cooperate and compete
in the markets of this country.
West Virginia is a producing State. She must find a market throughout the
length and breadth of this country for the sale of her coal. She has not, like
many of the districts, large industries that consume great quantities of coal.
We must go out into other markets to find a sale for our product. Into every
market which West Virginia enters she meets coal of like quality to that we
produce here. And in every market into which we go we find these barriers
raised against our entrance-freight rates and differentials.
Every effort has been made by the operators' associations, who own and oper-
ste these mines, hundreds of thousands of dollars have been expended on hear-
ings before the Interstate Commerce Commission, in the endeavor to equalize
freight rate, so that we may have equal advantages in the markets. Up to the
present time we have not received that redress, and the future is not bright toward
rectifying that wrong.
You men are not responsible for the freight rates; neither are we. Influences
of the competitive fields, in which we sell our coal, have had sufficient political
power to hold these freight rates on. When we will get justice we know not,
but until these things are equalized, until these barriers are torn down, the
miners and operators of West Virginia must suffer.
We have other barriers of a local character, which are our own creations, and
many of these barriers have crept in and fastened themselves upon the coal
industry of northern West Virginia like barnacles on a ship.
Since the union invaded this field, since the first agreement was signed, the
differentials have been widened, we have had handicap after handicap, and
increases increases due to war-time conditions have been greater in West Virginia
than in any other district in the United States.

We have many rules governing our working conditions which have militated
against deficiency. The operators in the production of coal have been handi-
capped by many of our local rules in our scale contracts. When we entered
into those scale provisions we could not foresee what influence and effect they
would have upon the production of coal. None of us can see through a stone wall.
We learn in these things, as in everything else, by experience, by butting up
against practical propositions.
Speaking as the commissioner in this field, coming in close contact with the
officials of the miners' organization, settling these labor disputes, I can say that
we have had excellent cooperation from the officers elected by the miners. Each
one of them that sits here in front of me knows just as well as I know, the spirit
that has manifested itself in the local unions, it being a newly organized territory,
many, of them unacquainted with the real, fundamental principles of the trade-
union movement, and they believed that this organization was a sort of Santa
Claus, a big Christmas tree, where they could reach out on the lower limbs and
get what they wanted. They believed that by their economic force they were
able to extract from the companies the last penny and that, like the widow's
cruse of oil, there would always be more coming.
But, gentlemen, we have come to the bottom of the barrel. There is neither
oil nor meal. We have come down to the point where we have got to meet that
situation. It is in our power to do it. It is in our power to so build our future
destinies here, which are so indirectly woven together that you can not separate
the woof from the warp-you can not injure the coal operators without injuring
yourselves, and the coal operators can not injure you without injuring themselves.
We are here in the interest of the industry, as I see it, and not in the interest
of any one individual factor in the production of coal. When we go out under
the scale contract that we have signed there is nothing that can be done by the
official representatives of the mine workers and myself but to enforce the letter
of the agreement. We must do that.
When I was selected as commissioner for this field the operators who sit in
this meeting now said to me, "Here is your scale contract; we want you to
live up to it, we want you to pay to the miners all that the scale contract calls
for, and not a penny more." That has been my endeavor. Oftentimes I have
realized that the spirit of the contract was not being lived up to in as much as
there were retarding influences put in the way of the production of coal. Yes,
gentlemen, there stood the cold facts in black and white, and what was I to
do and say?
The officials of the mine workers were in the same position. They knew on
more occasions than one that the best of cooperation was not being given by
the men-local strikes, interference in operation, committees or other men
assuming dictatorial power and authority whereby they attempted to usurp
the right of management of the mines-saying to this fellow and that fellow,
"Don't you do this" and "Don't do that"-reducing the productive ability of
the operation, and thereby increasing the cost of the coal-when that operator
was sweating blood and doing everything in his power to find a market for his
coal and to provide work for the men employed in the mines-we have had men
to the disgrace and degredation of the entire industry-and they are no more
appreciated I will say by the miners organization than they are by us-but
they are a part, they are the fly in the ointment, men who have no other desire
than to roam around over the country, seeking local official positions, where
they can make themselves prominent, get into some official position, or to
carry out the ideas of red Russia, or something of that kind.
These are all detrimental factors in the production of coal in Northern West
Virginia. They are unwelcome to the miners' trade movement and to the gen-
eral trade movement of the country These are issues that must be met in a
cooperative spirit by the operators and the union. We must by contract so
curtail the influence and power of these fellows that they will not be a barnacle
on the ship.
We are here to meet these issues. For every statement I have made we have
the facts and figures to back them up. We are coming to you men not with
theory, not with sentiment, we are coming to you in a spirit of cooperation,
bringing to you the actual conditions, with which you are no doubt only too
familiar; and I trust and hope that you are in position to meet us in this broad
platform of mutual helpfulness and constructive legislation, and if it is neces-
sary by the knife to cut out the sore and festering spots that are standing in the
way of the regular and normal production of coal in northern West Virginia.
It is a mutual proposition. You men have your homes in this field, you are
rearing your families, educating your children. There is pride of State and pride

Mr. TETLOW. Mr. Chairman, I do not want to go at any great length into a
discussion of this motion, but I want to present the situation as I understand it,
and the reasons for the presentation of this motion.
In the first place this district of the United Mine Workers for a number of
years has been negotiating wage agreement with the United Mine Workers of
America. The basis upon which all of these wage negotiations have been deter-
mined was the initial contract made in the field. In that contract they established
certain differentials as against other districts.
I was not present when that agreement was made. The representatives of
the two sides in laying down the initial and basic contract in the Fairmount


===== [扫描序号 83] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1105
feld established prices for pick-mining machine men, for day-labor work and
dead work, and also established rules to govern the joint action of miners and
operators in their relationship with each other. They adopted that contract as a
basic contract.
They did not follow the prices for day labor and tonnage rates that were estab-
lished in the old and well-developed district where wage negotiations had been
carried on for a great number of years. I think the differentials are well known
in the tonnage rate, in the day-labor rates, and so forth. I assume that the basic
rates as established at that time were fundamentally sound and that they were
recognized by both sides as being equitable and just to all parties concerned.
Since that time wage agreements have been made in keeping with the rise and
fall of wages in the bituminous districts of the country. We have conformed in
the Fairmount field, as well as the other outlying districts, with the basic wage
agreements made in the central field. As wages have increased and advances have
been made in the wage schedules, like advances have been added in the Fair-
mount field. Consequently there has been no disturbance of the differentials
first established.
This year we are confronted with this situation: In the central field the deter-
mination there forms the basis upon which all wage negotiations are made, as
a matter of form and as a matter of economic necessity, because the central com-
petitive field being the first in which wage negotiations were conducted, became
the basis for other districts.
The central competitive field as I have stated established the basis upon which
other wage agreements have been predicated. The mine workers at their last
convention in Indianapolis instructed their representatives to proceed with wage-
making matters, and laid down a basis that the miners' representatives should
immediately proceed in joint conference with the operators for the purpose of
arranging wage schedules without any reduction in wages; that they were author-
ized to proceed along that basis.
The meeting of the central field operators was called first. They met at
Jacksonville, Fla., in pursuance of an arrangement between the representatives
of the United Mine Workers and representatives of the operators in the central
competitive field.
They reaffirmed the wages and conditions in full without change for a period
of three years. Their agreement provided that local matters, matters affecting
the respective district in the central field, should not be reopened, and they were
required to go back into their respective districts under the terms of the Jackson-
ville agreement and sign up their schedule of wages and working conditions with-
out change. Consequently the signing of wage agreements in the central com-
petitive field by the respective districts was only a matter of form and in com-
pliance with the Jacksonville arrangement. They have proceeded along that
line and so carried out the provisions of the Jacksonville agreement.
For the outlying districts outside of the central competitive field the miners
position was and is that we are authorized to go out, meet with the representatives
of the operators in the outlying districts, and arrange wage schedules upon the
same basis as was arrived at in Jacksonville for the central competitive field.
That is essential for the miners. Of course, from your side it is different. The
United Mine Workers is one organization, and it is Nation wide. They deal
with the operators in the respective districts who have their separate and distinct
organizations. That must be so and it can not be changed. It would be of
vast importance and benefit to the miners of the country if they were dealing with
a National Coal Operators Association that represented the mining industry as a
whole from the operators' standpoint.
But as I stated there are things which prevent that. There is law, and there
are other matters that are economic which will prevent that being brought about.
However, with us it is different. We represent one big organization. We repre-
sent ideas that are concrete and that are uniform. Our contention as a union
has been that wages and working conditions of miners in one district should be
the same in other districts, that labor performed in one section of the country
should receive the same merit and the same reward that it receives in another.
There enter, of course, into this situation the problems that arise from the mining
and marketing of coal. Districts that are remote from markets, districts that
have different freight rates where transportation materially and vitally affects
the marketing of coal, of course, must be considered. They have been recognized
and the United Mine Workers organization in all of its work has never attempted,
nor will it attempt, to establish wage scales that will prevent the natural flow of
coal into the market where it properly belongs, by the fixing of wage schedules or

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
artificial barriers. That has been our position, recognizing that differentials
have been established that will permit these districts to develop mines and pro-
duce coal and send it into their natural markets.
Now, we are bound here without question by this arrangement, and in speaking
of "we" I am speaking of the miners side--we are bound by these instructions
from the International Union which goes on record and declares for the reaffirma-
tion of present wage schedules for three years. That is the reason that this
motion is made.
Under the terms of our arrangement, gentlemen, speaking for the miners' side.
we have set up in our organization what is known as a policy committee, to direct
the affairs of the organization in the absence of its functioning. This policy
committee is the miners' international executive board, with one representative
thereon from each district. And if in any of these outlying districts there should
be any attempt to change the basic wage scales, before it can be approved it must
go to our international executive board for approval.
The same position has been taken, as I understand, by your association. Your
secretary has read a resolution adopted by your association in which it is provided
that before any agreement can be binding and you authorized to sign it, it must
be referred back to your association for ratification.
We are not in that position entirely. We are only in that position when there
is a change in the agreement which disturbs the basic rates. Then if that is done
we can not sign, and have no authority to do so. That is the position of
the miners here on this question.
Coming down now to the real merit of this proposition, of this motion, let me
say this, gentlemen, and I say it with all candor to your side. Every person who is
familiar with the mining industry knows full well that the reaffirming of wage
scales for a period of three years uniformly throughout the country, no matter
what the wage scales may be, under this provision many of the high cost mines
in this country are not going to operate. It is immaterial what the wage scales
are, unless there is some peculiar advantage that some district has over another in
wage making. Even if they are uniformly correct, if their differentials are
correct and their bases right and logical-and wage schedules are built upon that
principle I say to you that the mining industry, and especially the high-cost
mines, during the coming three years are going to meet with serious conditions
of operation.
We have in this country as every one of us knows mines that will produce
50 per cent more coal than the country will consume. It is a condition which is
the outgrowth beginning possibly with the war, when there was an abnormal
demand for coal, when these high-cost mines could be developed, and when low-
cost mines could be developed to an extraordinary degree. It is only in recent
years that per capita productivity has increased by leaps and bounds through the
introduction of modern machinery. All of these factors have entered into the
question of production, which is far in excess of the consumption of fuel.
Every tendency on the consuming end has been to conserve the heat units and
develop greater energy. Every attempt on the producing end has been to pro-
duce the greatest production possible. All of these factors entering into the coal
industry have created a great problem. As I see it wage schedules can not solve
that problem. Reductions in wages and the lowering of the standards of living
of the men in the mines will not solve it. It can only be solved in two ways,
either by some governmental action which will restrain and prevent over-develop-
ment, or by the economic forces, the natural forces, that come into this industry
or any other industry—and the survival of the fittest will be the solution. One
of the two must be put into practice.
Of course it is quite late now for any governmental agency to be established to
regulate developments to keep pace with the requirements of the country.
Those things are quite difficult, we all understand, because of the ownership of
these natural resources, and all of that.
Now, how can this question be met? From the miners' standpoint, we say
that we recognize this condition in the industry, and for that reason we have de-
clared in favor of a long term contract of three years, of continued peace in the
industry without the interruption of dislocation of the industry, that will permit
the natural forces to work out some solution.
We are asking the reaffirmation of this wage scale. We all recognize that
this wage scale in effect with the possibility of the working time does not give to
the men who work in the mines an adequate wage. It does not give to them
sufficient money in order to save.

A reduction in wages will not solve the coal problem that you gentlemen have
to deal with. Your problem of course is the selling of this coal, the producing
and the selling of it. Our problem of course is to assist you in producing. Our
problem is a question of wages that will permit us to live.
We are asking for our wages to be reaffirmed for a period of three years, feeling
that in doing that it is to your best interest as well as ours. You gentlemen will
be required to go out and sell your coals that these mines can run and that the
men in this district can have work. Without that we recognize that the scale
of wages is immaterial, if there is no work and men can not earn. We realize
that, too.
We have studied all these factors and we are of the opinion that if these wage
scales and schedules are approved and reaffirmed that you in your district will
have the same opportunity to go out into the markets and get your share of the
business on an equal basis with your competitors.
West Virginia, as I understand it, last year produced over 100,000,000 tons of
coal. Your production in the Fairmont field compared as favorably as any other
district in the country. In my judgment until these forces are put to work and the
problem is solved neither you in your district nor the operators in any other
will be able to operate anywhere near full time.
Our contention is that these conditions can not be changed; that is, we can not
change them by accepting wage reductions. That will not help to solve this coal
problem that you have to deal with as well as us. Therefore we are making this
motion.
I am just giving the reasons why we take this position. We can not, gentlemen,
under any circumstances in this conference, so far as the miners are concerned,
yield from that position. These basic rates must be reaffirmed for a period of
three years-recognizing, of course, in this motion, as we feel, that it would be to
your own best interests to have these wage schedules renewed for a period of
three years; and recognizing that in every district where wage schedules have been
made and will be made many operators will not be able to operate to any degree,
because of the fact there is not a market for all the coal that can be produced.
It means that many of our miners will have to go from place to place where
work can be had. That condition will come about during these three years unless
there is some extraordinary demand for fuel which arises, and we can not see it
at this distance. It is going to be a question of those who can produce coal and
meet the market conditions and market requirements, and those that can not do
it will not be able to get their share of the business. That is my judgment of the
matter, speaking plainly about it, viewing the coal situation as I see it.
That is our position, taking all of these things into consideration. We have
analyzed it and discussed it, as to what would be best for the miners' interests,
and we have come to the conclusion, judging by experience, that wage reductions
of the miners have never helped the employers of the men who worked in the
mines.
The mining industry itself has been more prosperous as a whole under the
higher standard of wage schedules than it was under the low standards. So it
all reverts back to the operators having an equal opportunity to get into the
markets to sell their coal, without any artificial barriers to prevent them doing so.
That is our position. That is the reason this motion is made, Mr. Chairman.
We say to you with all the power that we can say it and with all of the earnest-
Less that we can say it, in presenting this resolution, that this is our position,
speaking plainly, and throwing aside any restraint. This basis is laid down as
the basis upon which we must negotiate our wage agreements. We are going to
be honorable, and we are going to insist that that be the basis; and we trust that
you can see your way clear to vote with us in favor of this motion. If you can
will mean that we can close up this conference in short time, renew our agree-
ments, and go home to our work. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I ask that the
cperators support this motion.
The CHAIRMAN. Are there any further remarks?
Mr. MCCULLOUGH. Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, I am somewhat surprised

I also take the position that the miner is not largely benefited by advances.
The purchasing power of the_dollar constitutes the determining factor of the
earning power of the miner. I can remember when we got advances that really
meant reductions, because the purchasing power of the dollar was reduced.
However, the purchasing power of the dollar, while not as great as it was a
few years ago the extra number of dollars does make the condition of the miner
better, and the fact of these extra number of dollars is one of the reasons for the
overdevelopment of coal mines to-day. When a man can leave the farm, the
mill, and the factory, where he is working 8 or 10 hours and making from $2
to $4 a day, and enter a coal mine where in 6 or 8 hours he will make from
$7.50 to $10 or $15 a day, it is going to cause and it has caused an influx of
labor from the different industries of our country into the coal mines.
Naturally the fact that the number of miners working and making a living in
the coal mines is far in excess of the number required to produce coal to meet the
existing demand brings about short-time work for all concerned.
It should be apparent to the casual observer that to hold wages at the present
price or to increase them is only intensifying the situation. Give the miners $1
more on the day or $2 or $5, and in proportion to the increase in the wages of the
miner you will draw from the surrounding industries of the country, and fill, to
overflowing the mines, which in turn brings about a condition where this extra
accumulated number of men is going to produce all of the coal necessary in less
time than they have been producing it.
The same argument will hold good in connection with the request that the
miner should have an increase in wages based on the fact that he has so much
idle time. Give him another advance in wages and you draw into the mines
again an extra amount of men, and so it goes on.
There is but one real solution to it, and that is when you make the earning
power of the men in the mines on a fair comparative basis with the men in other
industries; when there is no undue incentive for men to leave the farm, the mill, and
the factory and come into the coal mines. Then we will have a hundred thousand
coal miners burning coal instead of digging it, as they are to-day.
The fault of the coal industry to-day is the high rate of miners' wages in excess
of the amount in other industries in this country. And you only intensify the
situation. It really does not matter so much whether a man gets $1 or $2 a day
if it costs him under $1 a day a dollar for a sack of flour and in the case of $2 a
day costs him $2 for the sack of flour. It is the purchasing power of the dollar.
As wages come down, prices of commodities will come down. But there is no
chance in the world for the commodity of labor to come down as long as labor
stays up at the peak price. That is sound economics, not only in theory but in
practice. We can remember back in the old days when a chicken was a chicken
25 cents. It made no difference what the size of it was, nor its age-25 cents.
It is different to-day. So it is with everything else. We are only fooling ourselves
when we believe we are building a sound economic superstructure on a sandy
foundation.
It is neither here nor there, so far as we are concerned, to say that the price
for the coal miners of the four competitive States has been settled. The men who
produce coal in Ohio, Kentucky, Illinois, and Pennsylvania have for years and
years, like the terrapin who draws his head back into his shell, closed themselves
in their holy of holies, and said to the coal-producing operators of this country,
"We will determine the price of mining coal," while one of the largest States in
the industry, West Virginia, is denied admission into this holy of holies.
They have said, "No, we will make these agreements," and the mine workers
of this country have joined with them in that, and they have made these con-
tracts. At the Indianapolis convention the miners took the position that there
would be a policy committee which would permit the negotiations of contracts
in the outlying fields, subject to the ratification of the policy committee.
But when they reached the conference and made the agreement down in
Florida they abandoned that and turned over their functioning power to the
national executive board and constituted them a policy committee; and all agree-
ments must be based upon what the men in the holy of holies have said, ignoring
the rights of all of the competitive relations of these other fields.
There was a war in this country back in 1776 over that same thing, when
George III believed that he could, across 3,000 miles of water, regulate the
American Colonies and tax them without representation. The spirit of resistance
is inherent in every human heart, and the time comes at some stage of the game
when those barriers that restrict and restrain, and those chains that bind and
shackle, whether it be the limb of the black slave or the intellect of the white,

will be broken. Men will rise in rebellion against encroachment upon their

How long this is going on, I don't know. As a representative from Michigan
years ago, along with representatives from other outlying districts, we used to
appear before these international conferences and knock upon the door for
admittance, but we were always turned back. West Virginia a year ago sought
admission into the confines of this sanctum sanctorum to give to the coal industry
the benefit of their influence, support, and advice, but they were ignored.
Now we come along, and here are conditions, barriers, natural barriers, and
artificial barriers that have been reared since the time that the United Mine
Workers came into this district-the widening of the differentials, rendering it
more difficult for the operators of this field to enter these competitive markets.
These accumulated wrongs were brought about by the conditions of war, when
coal companies could afford to pay them. But now that the time has come
when they can no longer enter these markets, when their investments, the accumu-
lation of years and years of effort and honest toil, must be destroyed, mines
abandoned, to be filled up with water and falls of slate, when mirers who have
builded their little homes, where their families have been reared, must go into

approached that stage, gentlemen, when we are willing to submit to the dictatorial
power of a few coal companies, because of their position, saying to everybody
else that you must do this and you must do that? Are the mine workers of West
Virginia going to submit to this power that takes them and their families away
from the State of West Virginia in order that they may live?
Is the national organization of United Mine Workers going to come into this
field and say that you miners must seek these other fields, going to where they can
sell the coal, going to these advantageous districts, giving up your location, your
habitation, and your associations? I don't believe, gentlemen, that we are going
to do that.
It is one of those things that strikes deep into the very heart and core of human
resistance. We are here as coal companies claiming our right to go into the

the possession of these other districts. We are not claiming immunity; we are
not claiming advantages. The only thing we ask is to be given the same chance.

It is just as well, gentlemen, for the coal operators here to understand this, and
I am speaking now without authority, but from my point of view it is just as well,
even better, for the coal operators of northern West Virginia to close down their
mines without an agreement than it is to close them down for three years with an

If they sign an agreement to be shackled for three years they can not with honor
and dignity go out and resist the chains that they have bound upon themselves.
You operators have a right to repudiate that statement if you want to. That is
my opinion.
You men in West Virginia can not succeed and thrive unless the mines operate,
and that is all we are asking for, that they operate. We are not expecting every
mine in West Virginia to operate to full capacity. We know they won't we know
they won't in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, or any other State. They
will not be able to cooperate until the wages of the miners of this country are
on a part with the earning power of the other industries of the country. That will
not be while men who as barbers, factory men, professors, and school-teachers-I
know that in some places during the war they could not get school teachers be-
cause the school-teachers were digging coal; they were getting $100 a month
teaching school and they could go into the mines and earn two and three hundred
dollars digging coal. I know some of them personally who did that. You can
not bring one industry up to a peak point and keep the others down. It is not
economics.
I want to say so far as I am personally concerned it is my belief that the man
who goes in the mine is entitled to all he can get. I would like to see every coal
miner in this country be in a position to earn not only a living wage but a saving
wage, where he can save from the fruits of his labor a sufficient amount to protect
him against the rainy day. I would like to see that. But no one industry can
go so far ahead of the others and prosper.

West Virginia is asking no advantage over any other fields. We are asking for
no reduction in wages and no conditions that the other fields are not heir to.
We are asking that some of the shackles that bind us be broken; that we may
not be the victims of the intellectual organization, and the connivance-I use
that word with everything that it means-of the coal operators of the four com-
petitive States.
We presented to you to-day our claims, which we were able to prove, that we
have natural and artificial handicaps, and that the mine workers digging coal in
West Virginia have the same right to consideration from the national organization,
they have the right to be protected from the selfishness and the greed of the other
coal fields. They have a right to be given a chance to earn their living. The
operators have a right to their consideration, and that is all we are asking. If
we can not prove out claims then we are not entitled to have them considered.
We talked this morning of our freight rates, over which we have no control.
The differentials have been widened since you men entered into this field. The
operators have taken from their profits hundreds of thousands of dollars to help
fight the battle which is for you men as well as for themselves. Your organiza-
tion has never assisted nor been called upon for $1 in this fight on these differ-
entials and freight rates. You men are just as much interested as are the coal
companies. But the operators have fought that battle alone.
We have not won our fight, and we don't know when we will. Because of the
political entrenchments and the economic power of these other coal States they
have been able to hold and to gain widened differentials.
What we want you fellows to feel is that we are here dead in earnest. We
are like the man out in the river who can not swim and he is grasping at a straw.
We have got to do something. It is not a question of going along in a quiet,
submissive way, accepting what somebody else has said. It is not a question of
fighting or of desiring to fight the miners' organization or you men.
We are
fighting your battles the same as we are fighting our own.
We are fighting for the life of West Virginia. The biggest coward in the
world, when you shove him into a corner with his back against the wall, will
fight-and you are driving us to that. We have got to fight if we are to live.
We don't want you to feel that this is any threat, or that we are in here with a
chip on our shoulder, or that we are trying to batter anybody down or do any-
thing by force.
We are rather in here desirous of appealing to your reason, your cooperation,
and your spirit of self-preservation. I can't understand why you men should
have to leave West Virginia and go to Pennsylvania, Illinois, Indiana, or some
other place to make your living, when you have the coal and the opportunity of
earning a better living than you can in many of those places.
The miner's earnings in northern West Virginia and his conditions of employ-
ment are far superior to what they are in many of the places where the miners
in those four States are working. I know that, because I have worked in them.
The miners are getting paid for things to-day that they never dreamed of getting
in some of these four States. They are getting conditions and considerations
that they never dreamed of getting in those places.
But the time has come, gentlemen, when there must be a change. I don't
know how far you men are tied up, I don't know what you can do in this.
But there is a law that ignores every other law, and that is the law of self-preserva-
tion. We are fighting now for our right to live-not only our right to live but
your right to live. I hope you men will consider the seriousness of this situation.
I want all of you to consider it in the spirit in which it is given, too.
We are
asking no favors, and we are not here to take any kicks, but we want to be
treated right.
There is a growing feeling among the outlying districts of this country as to
the wisdom and the right of a few operators in these central competitive States
saying to a district that produces one-fifth of the bituminous coal of the United
States, that "We will make your agreement for you; we will tell you what you
are to work for; we will set your basis."
The parent can often say to the child: You must do this, go here, and go there,
and the child obeys. But finally that child becomes a man; he gets wisdom of
his own, he gets power of his own, and he demands recognition in accordance
with his knowledge and with his power. West Virginia was once a baby in the
coal industry. To-day it is a full-grown, matured man; and it is demanding the
rights and the respect that is due it because of its size and its significance.
We are grown up now, we have got 100,000 coal miners in the State of West
Virginia who produce one-fifth of the coal that is consumed in the United States.

sprung into existence, and logically it became the basis, as does any movement;
the basis is arrived at at its fountain head. Changes and diversions may be
made from that original basis, but nevertheless the fountain, the beginning,
always is the basis upon which the thing revolves.
That is the reason why the central field became the basic point. I presume
if coal had first been developed in West Virginia it would have been there that
the first negotiations were made. The United Mine Workers have always
welcomed the outlying districts of the miners or operators into any general

Again, we consume double the amount of coal that we produce. Take Ohio,

40,000,000, which means that about 20,000,000 tons of coal produced in Ohio

produce the coal that it needs, and coal must enter into these markets from
West Virginia, Kentucky, and western Pennsylvania.
Pennsylvania is about the only State in the central competitive fields that
produces more coal than it consumes. Indiana consumes more than it produces;
Ohio does, and so does Illinois. Consequently coal must be shipped into those
States to take care of the market requirements.
I do not know whether it is possible to work out some general scheme for the
proper development of markets in connection with proper mining districts.
That is a question for the coal companies to handle and not for the United Mine
Workers. The United Mine Workers have tried during all of their existence to
hold themselves aloof from dealing with that question. They are organized
specifically for the sole purpose of raising the standards of living of the men who
work in the mines. They have never been able, nor do they desire, to enter into
the attempt to solve questions of transporting coal or marketing coal, and all

going to interfere if we can help it.
We have joined with the operators at times, and I think it is entirely proper
for the West Virginia miners and operators to join hands together if there is some
inequality in freight rates, in the endeavor to have them readjusted so that they
will be upon a fair basis. That is your right. The United Mine Workers'
organization as a whole can not interfere in that, nor will they interfere. It is
not their purpose.
They have miners in Ohio, in Indiana. It is true that the West Virginia
miners and the West Virginia operators should be more concerned about their
own house than the miners of Ohio or Indiana. That is their inherent right, and
it is their duty to do so. But the United Mine Workers as a whole deal with the
general situation, and their whole interest is in the question of wages and standards
of living.
Another thing with which I can not agree as stated by Mr. McCullough is
this, that we should be governed by our requirements, that standards of living
should be regulated and wages should be regulated upon that basis. We do
not agree with that. I believe wages should be predicated upon the require-
ments of the men who work, and not wages based upon standards of living.
We know full well that the requirements of men have been constantly changing,
and it is because of the demand for higher and better living, that has resulted
in the granting of increased wages.

We would not want to go back, nor would you wnat to go back, to the day

Ohio that was making interest on its investment, 6 per cent interest on its

The coal industry, as I have stated at the outset, has been more prosperous
under high wages than it ever was before. The present trouble with the coal
industry is due to over-development and over-production, and that has been
caused by conditions that were brought about during the war when coal could
be sold at any price, when any kind of coal could be sold; the quality was not
considered nor was price considered. They were bidding for the coal. That
permitted this over-development and over-production, Our potential pro-
duction now is double what is required.
That is the condition which exists. Of course, every operator is holding on.
He is employing men with the hope that there will come a change. But it will
not come it will not come in any great degree because he has to meet these
conditions.
Just one word more and then I am through. There is not to-day in any coal
district conditions that compare to those existing in Ohio, my own State, and
there they have reaffirmed their present wage agreement for three years. In the
Hocking district, the heart of Ohio's coal-mining industry, at the present time and
during this entire winter, these people have been existing upon charity. The
governor of our State appealed to the people of Ohio in public appeals to con-
tribute clothing and food to take care of the suffering and destitute in the Hocking
district.
These men, both miners and operators, realized that reductions in wages would
not bring markets to them. If nobody else was reduced but them it would help
individually, of course. But they recognized, and these miners recognize, if
it is done here it must be done not only here, but there, and other places; and they
would not be benefited if the change was made. It is an economic condition
over which they have no control, and the natural forces of economics must deal
with the problem.
Those mines are shut down and cheaper coal or better coal is going into the
markets. In the city of Columbus, my home town, to-day people are willing to
pay a dollar a ton more for West Virginia splint domestic coal than they will for
Hocking. Why? Because it is a better quality of coal, and they will pay the
dollar a ton extra to get this West Virginia coal. Those things are facts, they are
matters of record, and can not be denied.
Mr. McCULLOUGH. But that does not come from northern West Virginia.
Mr. TETLOW. No, practically all of that comes from southern West Virginia
and eastern Kentucky. You have a condition of course that is different. I
recognize that full well. But I do not think that any of these problems can be
met by reductions in wages or by reducing the standards of living of the men who
work in the mines. That is my judgment about it.
Mr. McCULLOUGH. Just a few words. They have here in the miners' agree-
ment a clause that has always been very sacred to the coal miner. He has stood"
on this clause ever since I have known anything about mine workers. It reads
as follows:
"The operator will see that an equal turn is offered each miner, that he is
given a fair chance to obtain the same."
If that applies to a man in the mine, why should it not apply to all the miners
in the district? If that is a fair proposition for a coal miner why is it not a fair
proposition for an operator? It must apply to the operator before it can apply
to the miner.
I agree with Mr. Tetlow that there will not be a pound more of coal dug
because of a reduction. I do not think anyone will deny this statement, however,
that if there was an industry developed to-morrow that paid a higher rate of
wages than the mine workers are paid, there would be thousands of mine workers
who would seek that vocation.
This overdevelopment came about during war times, as Mr. Tetlow has said,
when fabulous prices were paid for coal in some quarters. The mine workers
now are trying to hold on to a war condition. We are back to a normal condi-
tion of industry. The time of those fabulous prices that built up this industry
is over.
But the mine workers don't know that the show is out; they are linger-
ing around, they think there is another act yet, when the curtain has fallen. It
is time that we were waking up to the fact that we can not keep this great army
of men in the coal mines on a bonus basis, and that is what they are on.

Put the coal industry on the same basis with other industries, and many
miners will be leaving and going back to their barber shops, to their mills, to the
factories, and to the farm. There is no question about that.
None of us want to go back to the old conditions. I am one that has always
advocated and believed, and do to-day, in the improvement of the working con-
ditions of the working man. I think every man should have good home quarters
I never lived in a coal company house in my life; they never built a house and
painted it red for me I wouldn't live in it. I have often said that the coal
companies never asked the mule or the miner in what kind of a place he wanted
to live. But we have a whole lot of miners that will live in one of those hovels
because it saves two or three dollars extra on the month.
Mr. Tetlow has said our wages should be according to our requirements. Our
requirements mean a mental attitude toward things. One fellow requires more
than another; and our requirements come about through education. No man
ever fought for a thing until he first wanted it. There was a time when bathtubs
were as unpopular as Fords are popular now. It is a question of what we think
we need. One fellow thinks he needs one car, another two cars, and another
three or four. Some man thinks one woman is enough, and another thinks he
has got to have three or four. It is all a question of taste and mental attitude
toward these things-the interpretation we put upon it.
Every man should be given an opportunity to develop and to realize his desires
toward higher intellectual and civic attainments. But these things must be
general, gentlemen; they can not be specific in one industry. The human race is
developing and advancing. We have come a long ways from the old log cabin.
Instead of getting on the old mule, the camel, or the horse, and riding across the
country, we travel by lightning express trains and lavishly equipped steamships;
we talk by telegraph and telephone, with and without wires; after a while mental
telepathy, and we don't know what.
We are advancing, but it must be done in a general way, and West Virginia
can not be made specific. We say to you adopt the turn, the clause you have got
in your agreement which you ask the operators to use the operator will see that
an equal turn is offered to each miner. We say to you that the operators be
given an equal turn with the operators of Indiana, Illinois, Pennsylvania, and
Ohio, and other competitive fields, that go into competitive markets. That is
what we are asking. Isn't that fair? What is fair for the goose is fair for the
gander.

I desire to say again, so that there will be no misunderstanding, that the
United Mine Workers of America entered into no secret or open agreement with
the operators of the cenral competitive field relative to what the wage scale
would be in any other coal mining district in this country except the districts
represented in the central competitive field, when the Jacksonville agreement
was made.
The United Mine Workers of America arrived at their policy not due to the
particular fact that they made an agreement in the central competitive field
carrying with it for a period of three years their old agreement, but because of the
fact that the policy committee of the United Mine Workers of America decided,
in is wisdom or otherwise, that the present wage agreement be renewed in the
outlying districts for a period of three years.
As I understand the motion we are not here to-day asking that the wage
agreement arrived at, in which the operators and miners of northern West Vir-
ginia took no part, be adopted as the wages and working conditions for northern
West Virginia for a period of three years. Neither do I understand the motion
to be that we are asking for an advance in wages at this time in northern West
Virginia.
The thing we are doing or seeking to do, and asking the operators to support
us in our position, is that we renew for a period of three years the present agree-
ment in northern West Virginia, an agreement that was made between the repre-
sentatives of the United Mine Workers of America and the representatives of the
coal operators of northern West Virginia.
If I remember rightly, when the basic agreement was made in northern West
Virginia, it was not made at a time when it was generally influenced by any other
conference except the conference that actually negotiated the wage agreement.
As to the differentials that were recognized at that time, the mine workers are
not attempting to have them reopened at this time. There might be, Mr. Chair-
man, volumes of argument made why the same day wage scale should be paid
in this section of our country as was agreed upon in the central competitive
field. But the mine workers' union is not, as I said a moment ago, seeking to
even reopen that question.
The proposition that is before the conference, as I understand it, is that the
present agreement be renewed for a period of three years. Let us then consider
for a moment what a basic agreement really is, and the influence of the central
competitive field upon the basic agreements in the coal mining fields of this
country.
If I remember rightly, at Cleveland in 1922, after the central competitive field
basic wage agreement was disrupted, one of the representatives of the coal opera-
tors from northern West Virginia in that conference and I think it is a matter
of record-made the statement that if one operating company signed an agree-
ment with the United Mine Workers of America, he recognizes the fact from an
economic standpoint that that would be a basic wage agreement.
There can be no question about the fact that it would be and was at that time,
and the only basic wage agreement that is being considered here in this conference,
so that the record may be kept clear, is the basic wage agreement that is already
in effect here in this field, negotiated between the representatives of the miners
of northern West Virginia and the operators who are now taking part in this
conference.
The agreement made in the central competitive fields, my friends, is not the
agreement we are considering here now, and when we ask for a renewal for three
years of the present agreement we mean, as you well understand, the agreement
that you now have in effect in this field negotiated by the contending parties
who are present here in this conference.
So that the action taken in the central competitive field finally, Mr. Chairman,
has nothing whatever to do with what has been done in this conference. Many
a time, at least several times to my knowledge, and I know Mr. McCullough
will bear me out in this statement, when no agreements were arrived at in any
of the basic coal fields in this country the mine workers' policy committee laid
down the policy that they would follow, and they did exactly that very same
thing relative to the outlying districts in setting forth our policy in these
instances.
The mine workers' organization believe that it is for the best interests of the
coal-mining industry in every district in this country to renew the present wage
scale for a period of three years. For that reason, and no other reason, are we
asking that you gentlemen here agree with us, or concur with us, in the motion
that is now pending before this joint conference.

The CHAIRMAN. Gentlemen, the meeting is open and we are ready to transact

Mr. TARLETON. Mr. Chairman, I believe we have had about enough speech
making for a while. I have in mind to make a motion. However before making
that motion I would like to call to the attention of the conference an under-
standing arrived at at Fairmount in 1918 when the first agreement was made
with the United Mine Workers.
It was called to your attention yesterday in connection with the barriers
between the operators of northern West Virginia and the competitive fields.
It is a matter of common knowledge that the mine workers were kept out of
northern West Virginia for years and years, but it is not common knowledge why.
The main reason for barring them was the fear of the operators that if they
ever did business with them as they did in other fields that they would not only
have the operators of the competitive fields to combat but the mine workers as
well. In other words, they were afraid that the other fields would dictate wage
contracts in northern West Virginia. We were assured at that time that that
would not be permitted, that if the mine workers were in position to make
contracts with the operators that the contracts would be made by the miners of
West Virginia and the operators of West Virginia.
We never had any reason to doubt but what that was the basis on which we
were operating until 1922, when all the mines in that section were closed down
because the operators in the central competitive field had refused to meet the
mine workers in convention.
The operators in northern West Virginia were not consulted in any way,
shape, or form as to the closing of their mines. In fact, they endeavored in every
possible way to meet with the mine workers and prevent the closing of the mines.
But it was not permitted because the operators and the mine workers in other
fields were not able to agree.
In Mr. Tetlow's remarks yesterday he called attention to the prosperous
conditions in West Virginia for the past year, but he failed to state that more than
65 per cent of the tonnage produced was from nonunion mines. To-day there
are 26,000 tons being produced daily in northern West Virginia at a wage rate
very much below the one you have asked us to agree to.
In order to test out thoroughly whether or not the operators in northern West
Virginia and the miners are permitted to make their wage contract, I move you
that a subcommittee be appointed to go into session and see whether or not
there are any grounds on which they can get together.
Mr. TETLOw. I second the motion.
The CHAIRMAN. You have heard the motion; are there any remarks?
(Calls for "question.")

Mr. BITTNER. Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned we were speaking
of the action of the Bethlehem Mines Corporation in abrogating its
contract and the methods used in carrying out the abrogation and
repudiation. I stated that our people were served with house notices,
mine guards were employed in great numbers; large searchlights were
installed; fences were built around the mining community shutting it
off entirely, and we were denied any contact with the people who
lived in the company houses, although many of them were members
of our organization, and this matter was brought to the attention of
Mr. Charles M. Schwab. I sent him a telegram, a copy of which I
will furnish to the committee. I have not it here with me. I told
him that they were evicting our people in furtherance of their plan to
abrogate the wage agreement. I received no reply whatever to that
telegram to Mr. Schwab.
The only defense that the Bethlehem Mines Corporation ever gave
for repudiating their contract was that they were members of the
association but had withdrawn. But, so that the committee will
understand, the facts in the case are that that defense is absolutely
destroyed by the fact that the company accepted the agreement at
its mines, worked under its terms, and paid its wage schedule, collected
the dues from our membership in accordance with the agreement,
and put into effect the contract from the 1st of April, 1924, up until
the time of the repudiation and abrogation. Now, that is the Bethle-
hem Mines Corporation.
The Consolidation Coal Co., as I have shown, through their repre-
sentatives, signed the contract. They signed an individual contract
with us for their coking operations; the officers of the Consolidation
Coal Co.; including their attorney, Mr. Tusca Morris; Mr. Brooks
Flemming, the vice president of the Consolidation Coal Co.; and Mr.
Frank D. Lyons, the vice president of operations of the Consolidation
Coal Co., called our representatives to their office early in 1925 and
informed us that they were no longer going to operate their mines

DEAR MR. ROCKEFELLER: I wish to acknowledge your letter of July 1, with

When the Consolidation Coal Co. found that its cost of producing coal was far
in excess of the best price obtainable, it notified Mr. Lewis and his representatives
that its mines would have to be closed indefinitely. This action was taken only
after months of effort on the part of the management to avoid it.
A state of widespread suffering, due to idle mines and idle men, did not dis-

allowed to work at all.

COMMUNICATIONS BETWEEN MR. LEWIS AND MR. WATSON
[Telegram]
Hon. C. W. WATSON,
President Consolidation Coal Co.,
67 Wall Street, New York, N. Y.:
INDIANAPOLIS, IND., May 27, 1925.
I am advised from Fairmont that Consolidation Coal Co. is considering
abrogation of existing wage contracts June 1. I can not conceive that such
policy would be adopted by your company. Will you please wire me and advise
as to the authenticity of the report.
Mr. JOHN L. LEWIS,
[Telegram]
JOHN L. LEWIS.
NEW YORK, N. Y., May 29, 1925.
President United Mine Workers, Indianapolis, Ind.:
Replying your telegram. For over a year and at an appalling cost the Con-
solidation Coal Co. worked under the existing wage contract in good faith till
further operation became impossible in the face of heavy losses. Its Fairmont
mines were then shut down and will remain closed indefinitely under these
conditions. Practically the entire production of the Fairmont field, averaging
1,100 cars daily, is now being produced chiefly by former members of the United
Mine Workers under wage rates over 30 per cent less than the union scale contract.
Eleven hundred employees have left the Consolidation Coal Co., of whom a
large number are now working for its competitors on these reduced wages, while
still continuing to occupy our houses. In addition numbers of Consolidation
employees, who have been either unemployed or only partially employed for
many months, are continually appealing to us for work under the same terms
which are offered by our competitors and accepted by other former union
employees.
As an actual economic fact, from lack of enforcement in that field, the Fair-
mont union wage scale has disappeared. Our company, as always, will abrogate
no contract, labor or otherwise. If and when, however, the best interests of
both parties demand a cancellation by mutual consent of this or any other
contract, the company will cooperate and not obstruct. In other words, the
dissolution of the existing wage contract must be decided by the Consolidation
employees, in whose interest it was negotiated and whose interest it was designed
to protect.
C. W. WATSON.
Senator WHEELER. Did they open up the mines afterwards on a
nonunion basis?
Mr. BITTNER. Yes, sir.

It is headed "Collapse of the Baltimore agreement. The reason
I am taking so much time in explaining this in detail, Mr. Chairman,

COLLAPSE OF THE BALTIMORE AGREEMENT
The collapse of the so-called Baltimore agreement, entered into between
the Northern West Virginia Coal Operators' Association and the subdistrict
organizations of district No. 17 of the United Mine Workers, may be briefly
summarized as follows:
1) At the time of the negotiations, it was informally agreed between repre-
sentatives of the two parties that at least 20 per cent of the production in the
region was being produced under nonunion conditions. Subsequent investiga-
ton showed that this was, if anything, an underestimate. It was also agreed
that this situation offered a distinct menace to the stability of the union agree-
ent, and that its spread, to any appreciable extent, could only destroy it.

(2) During subsequent months, regular and careful surveys of the situation
revealed the following steady growth of nonunion production, and an equally
steady decline of tonnage produced under the Baltimore agreement:

NOTE. Since the above table of carloadings was originally prepared the statistics for the last week in
June, 1925, have been made available. The percentages were: Union, 14.1; nonunion, 85.9. This completes
the record for 1 year, viz, from June, 1924, to June, 1925. These figures throw additional light on the pres-
ent working strength of the United Mine Workers in northern West Virginia.
(3) When the sales contracts secured prior to the Baltimore agreement expired
with the beginning of the new coal year, April 1, 1925, practically every union
operation of any size, with one exception, suspended. The exception was the
Consolidation Coal Co., which, with a greatly reduced number of mines, con-
tinued its efforts to operate for another month or more. This company then
likewise came to a practically complete shutdown, forced by heavy losses and by
its practical isolation in the matter of labor costs.
(4) In recent weeks, almost the entire output of the region, totalling nearly
1,200 cars daily, has been produced by operators and mine employees working
together under nonunion conditions of wages and employment. From whatever
motive or cause,
the essential fact is now the almost complete repudiation of the
Baltimore wage contract by both sides. As a working reality, it no longer exists.
(5) During these months, the affairs of district No. 17 of the United Mine
Workers had been put into a state equivalent to a receivership. The duly elected
district officials were supplanted by personal representatives of the president of
the national organization, and local autonomy and control were suspended.
Thousands of the union members openly withdrew from the wage contract as
individuals by seeking employment wherever it could be obtained under the
terms available. Briefly, the situation now consists of outside officials, neither
chosen by nor accountable to the rank and file of the district membership, and
who supervise a body that is only a fraction of the original organization in this
field. In other words, so far as their individual economic action is concerned,
the union contract relationship has been specifically repudiated by an over-
whelming majority of the union members. As for the officials, there are none
who can speak for the district but only for the national body.
Now I think I should explain just here, so that the committee can
follow this proposition, that the international officials were originally
placed in northern West Virginia at the request of the Northern
West Virginia Coal Operators' Association, of which the Consolidation
Coal Co. was a member, due to this fact, that in the contract the
international organization stood sponsor for the enforcement of the
agreement. The coal operators insisted upon that. They stated
that unless the international union stood sponsor for the enforce-
ment of the agreement they would make no contract with the United
Mine Workers of America. And for that reason they stated that the


===== [扫描序号 107] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1129
local officials had not been trained as the international officials were
in carrying out contracts, and that the international union must
continuously have some representative in northern West Virginia to
see that the contract made with the northern West Virginia coal
operators was carried out in all of its terms and provisions. That
is why the international representatives were in northern West
Virginia at that time, at the request of the northern West Virginia
coal operators themselves. And no one requested that with more
earnestness than the officers of the Consolidated Coal Co., being the
largest operators in that field. [Continuing reading:]
(6) The alternatives now facing both the union operator and the union employee
are, therefore, not the choice between both working under the contract and
either breaking it. The contract, being in its essence a collective agreement, is
already broken and gone. Neither side has been able to cope with the forces which
brought this about. The present alternatives, and the only ones, are those
between sharing idle mines and unemployment on the one hand, and sharing
competitive production and prevailing wages on the other.
(7) Essentially this is a choice which now rests solely upon the individual
employee, just as it has already been decided by thousands of them. If an em-
ployee of a company, both hitherto bound by the union contract, prefers to en-
dure months of unemployment throughout the remaining term of the contract
in order to maintain his union membership, that is his privilege. If, on the con-
trary, he prefers not to assess this penalty upon himself and his family, as the
price of his union affiliation, but decides rather to exchange a printed scale for
actual earnings, that also is his right. The company can neither compel the one
nor deny the other.
(8) Under such conditions the issue to be decided is not the technicalities of a
document which exists only in the files of the operator and employee, but their
mutual decision on the obligations which they owe to the families and to the
properties entrusted to their care. These obligations existed prior to and in-
dependent of the relationship to the third party of the union.

Coal Co. would only extend to a far greater degree through the
business and social life of the Nation if such a policy was pursued.
