here with a petition signed at some mines, and their methods of having

man into signing a petition. Why, they would not think of coercing
a man into signing a petition. All they did was told him, "You will
either sign this petition or move. We are going to throw you out of
your home." He not only was required to accept a reduction in
wages, but if he did not do it he had no home.
Senator WHEELER. That was peaceful picketing.
Mr. BITTNER. Yes; that was peaceful picketing.
Senator GOODING (presiding). Peaceful intimidation, you mean, do
you not?
Mr. BITTNER. I would not want to dignify it by using the word
"peaceful" because it is not a very peaceful proposition. But it is
about the worst sort of an intimidation that you can conceive of.
Then they say, "These people voluntarily agreed to repudiate the
contract." Notwithstanding that hundreds upon hundreds of fami-
lies were evicted from their homes. Why? Because they would not
become parties to abrogating a wage agreement that their organiza-
tion had made in good faith. And I do not believe that this com-
mittee or the people of the United States think that men and women
and children should be thrown out of their homes by the Consolida-
tion Coal Co. headed by Mr. Rockefeller or anybody else, simply
because they want to faithfully comply with a wage agreement
they have made with their employer.
And that is the exact position of the Consolidation Coal Co. in
northern West Virginia. They threw these people out. They not
only evicted them by court order, but they had their mine guards go
out to these houses and summarily dispossess these people and
throw them out on the county road. That is the voluntary method
used by the Consolidation Coal Co. in repudiating and abrogating the
wage agreement in northern West Virginia. That is the breaking
down of the agreement. If there could be any greater degree of
industrial warfare than that, gentlemen, I can not conceive of it.
The United Mine Workers of America have spent nearly a million
dollars for northern West Vriginia. We have erected not a barracks,
but barracks and towns of barracks at 44 different mining centers in
northern West Virginia. Our people, as I said, were evicted, they
were intimidated, coerced, and brow-beaten by gunmen and thugs
that were brought in there by the Consolidation Coal Co., and then
the company has the temerity to say to the American people that the
agreement was voluntarily set aside.
I say to you that I doubt if anything has ever equaled, and I am
sure has not surpassed, the conduct of the Consolidation Coal Co. in
northern West Virginia in abrogating its wage agreement.

Senator GOODING. I suppose the explosion was investigated.
What was the cause of the explosion?
Mr. BITTNER. The same cause was decided upon by a coroner's jury
in West Virginia, Mr. Chairman, that has been decided, I think, in
every explosion that has ever occurred in West Virginia. The cause
of explosion unknown, regardless of what the testimony is.
Senator WHEELER. They have had the same coroner's jury, I sup-
pose, the same group sitting and hearing all these cases of explosions?
Mr. BITTNER. Well, I would not say that, but they control them—
it seems as though they control their verdicts. At least to some
degree. Because there have been many explosions since I have been
there that there has not been any evidence offered except that which
was unanimous as to the cause of the explosion, and still the same
verdict is always rendered. That is the reason they have so many
explosions.
Senator WHEELER. The coroner generally collects a lot of cripples

the coroner's jury? Is that not the fact of the matter?
Mr. BITTNER. Well, I don't know just exactly how he calls them.
But the last explosion we had there, after the coroner's jury rendered
its verdict of not knowing the cause of the explosion, the chief
attorney for the coal company was presented by the company with a
fine Packard automobile.
Now, this question of abrogation of contracts was something entirely
new with us. During our 35 years of collective bargaining we had
never dreamed that the contract would be abrogated in this manner.
We had not any court decisions that dealt on the question, at least so
far as the mining industry was concerned.
About the time that President Lewis wrote to President Coolidge
relative to the question of contract abrogation I visited the Secretary
of Labor Davis, as well as Secretary of Commerce Hoover, and laid
the situation before them. We thought in northern West Virginia
that the Government at that time could do something in the matter
of preventing these coal companies from abrogating their contracts.
Our reason for that was probably brought about by what the Govern-
ment did in 1919 against the United Mine Workers of America. And
I am not criticizing the Government for what it did in 1919.

And I

am not criticising them for their inactivity in 1925. But I did think
that what was good for the goose was good for the gander.
The Attorney General of the United States in 1919 secured an
injunction in the Federal courts compelling the officers of the Mine
Workers Union to recall the strike called, due to the fact that the
contract had not expired in the mind of the Government, and our
organization acceded to that authority without question. I did
think I was probably wrong, but you can not stop us from thinking
at times that the Government could at least make some sort of a
gesture along that line when these companies first began their abro-
gating of contracts.
Senator WHEELER. Do you know upon what theory they got out
an injunction? To keep you from abrogating?
Mr. BITTNER. Well, I think the injunction in 1919 was really
secured under the authority of the Lever Act, but as I understand it,
in the disposition of the cases some time afterwards the Lever Act was
declared unconstitutional by the same court. But that was the act,
as I recall it, that the injunction was secured under. But I talked
to Secretary Hoover, and, understanding the coal industry as he does,
he sort of advised that we go into the local courts and see what we
could do. And when we went back to northern West Virginia we
decided we would try it. So, after taking the matter up with our
attorneys, Mr. Townsend-
Senator WHEELER. Did Mr. Hoover advise you to go into the local

Mr. BITTNER. Well, he said we should go into court.
Senator WHEELER. Did he examine the contract?
Mr. BITTNER. Yes; he examined the contract and was very-said
plainly that there was no question about the contract being abro-
gated in his mind. That they had abrogated the contract. The fact

is evidence of that.
But what I am about to say relative to this court procedure, I do
not want the committee to think that I am saying it disrespectfully
of the courts, because I am not. I have had a lot of experience in
strikes with courts, and all that, but I still think that our system
is the best in the world. And we decided, as I said, after taking the
matter up with our attorneys, to go into the courts.
Senator WHEELER. The fault is not with the law and with the

2. Defendant is a corporation, created and existing under the laws of the State
of West Virginia, and is engaged in the business of mining coal in Monongalia
County, W. Va.

Workers of America, a labor union, which said labor union is an unincorporated
association of affiliated mine laborers, organized and existing for their mutual
benefit in securing proper wage; and working conditions, and that they and each
of them reside in Monongalia County, W. Va., and have been until recently
employed by the said defendant in mining and producing coal at its said mines in

read as a part of this bill of complaint.

about the 1st day of April, 1926, employees of the defendant company, who en-
gaged in the mining of coal in the several mines operated by the defendant com-
pany, in Monongalia County, W. Va., and had observed and carried out, each
and every provision of the contract aforesaid, covering employment of the
plaintiffs by the defendant, in the mining and production of coal in its coal
mines, aforesaid.
7. Plaintiffs further aver that they were at the time of the making of the con-
tract aforesaid, and now are members of the United Mine Workers of America
and were and are practical mine workers, trained in such avocation, and depend-

ica, and interested in the maintenance of the said contract and the wage scale,
and working conditions provided for therein.

County, W. Va., aforesaid, proceeded to work the same by and through members
of the United Mine Workers of America, including plaintiffs, and carried out the
contract in accordance with the terms, until, or about, the 1st day of April, 1926.

inter alia that-

Mr. BITTNER. This injunction was asked for against the Paisley
coal interests of northern West Virginia who had repudiated their
contract, their mines being situated in that county.
Now, as I told you this morning, that is quite a story.
Senator WHEELER. Let me interrupt you there a minute. You
went over this contract situation with both the Secretary of Labor
and the Secretary of Commerce, Mr. Davis and Mr. Hoover?
Mr. BITTNER. Secretary of Labor Davis has always been doing
what we thought was everything that was possible for a man to do
to assist us in this situation.
Senator WHEELER. And the coal operators refused to confer with
him, did they not?
Mr. BITTNER. Yes, sir.
Senator WHEELER. Did you talk it over with Mr. Hoover? Did
he examine the Consolidation Coal Co.'s contract that they entered
into with you?
Mr. BITTNER. Yes, sir.
Senator WHEELER. And the Bethlehem Mines Co.'s contract?
Mr. BITTNER. Well, it was the same contract.
Senator WHEELER. That was the same contract?
Mr. BITTNER. Yes, sir.
Senator WHEELER. That was the one that he said in his judgment
there had been an abrogation of?
Mr. BITTNER. He said there wasn't any question about it. He
was very emphatic about it.
Senator WHEELER. Did you have with you the contract that was
signed at Jacksonville?
Mr. BITTNER. No, due to the fact that the operators and miners
in northern West Virginia had signed the Baltimore and New York
agreements, I did not take the Jacksonville matter up at that time.
Senator GOODING (presiding). All right, you may go ahead with
your statement.
Mr. BITTNER. Now, we applied for this injunction to compel the
coal companies, if they operated their mines at all, to operate under
the agreement. It was immediately denied.
Senator COUZENS. In denying it did the court hand down an
opinion?
Mr. BITTNER. Yes, sir; and our attorney has the opinion and will
be glad to file it, with the statement made by the judge. But we
afterwards learned that we had applied in the circuit court of that
county, for an injunction, to the judge who has a lease with the coal
company, of which lease I will file a certified copy with the committee
attested March 17, 1928. This judge and his family had a lease
with this company for a minimum of $60,000 a year in royalties, and
20 cents a ton on all over this amount. In other words, they were to
take a minimum of 300,000 tons annually, which would mean $60,000,
and then were to pay 20 cents a ton for all taken out over that.
Senator WHEELER. Do you mean to say that this man sat and
heard this case under those circumstances?

that this is the most remarkable contract according to my understanding that I

able counsel, and I do not understand why they should not have an able contract,

1155
(The opinion of Judge I. Grant Lazzelle is here made a part of the
record, as follows:)
ANGELO DE MARK ET AL., PLAINTIFFS, v. ARK WRIGHT COAL Co., A CORPORA-
TION, ET AL., DEFENDANTS. MONONGALIA COUNTY. IN CHANCERY. I.
GRANT LAZZELle, Judge
OPINION
Gentlemen, the court has before it for consideration four separate bills asking
for injunction, all of which are based upon this little pamphlet, the contract
which is set forth in this little pamphlet which is filed as exhibit, "Exhibit A"
with each case. Upon the merits or demerits of that contract a great deal
depends in this case. Before entering into a consideration of the contract I
want to say this, that there is one thing in connection with these suits which
is very pleasing to the court, for this reason, that it is the opinion of the court,
not only of this court but all courts, and I think all good citizens, that the place
for a redress of wrongs and to obtain remedies for all grievances is in the courts
of the country. The courts are going to endeavor to give prompt, equal, and
exact justice to all people. That is not always an easy thing to do: not nearly
as easy as many people think. Courts are required to consider not only the
law as laid down in the books of the text writers and the legislative enactments
but to consider the peculiar circumstances and conditions under which many
things are done.
It is the opinion of this court, and likewise the opinion of all courts, that every
contract properly and fairly entered into for a proper consideration should be
enforced, but questions arise as to whether or not the particular contract under
consideration in any case is a proper contract to be enforced. Whether it has
proper parties, whether it is properly executed, whether it has a proper considera-
tion, whether there is mutuality between the parties, and a great many other
things. Now, reading from the brief of the counsel for plaintiffs, I find this, it
is a statement of the purpose of the suits, and it treats it as one suit and the
court will treat this as one suit because they all involve the same principles.
There are some conditions to which I shall call attention later, but they involve
generally the same principles.

Now I will refer to the case of Gregg against Starks (188 Ky., 834, 224 S. W.
459), which is rather a peculiar and interesting case arising out of employment
of conductors. A conductor on a railroad train, a passenger train, who received
exactly the same pay as a conductor on a freight train, was ordered transferred
and was transferred from a position of conductor on a passenger train to con-
ductor on a freight train, and he brings a suit for injunction and the injunc-
tion is granted and is sustained. But it is sustained upon this theory, that he
had no remedy at law. He received the same wages in either case so that he
was losing no money. But, as the court very properly stated, there was a great
difference in the two positions. While he got as much pay in one place as the
other, there was a certain difference between being a conductor on a passenger
train and on a freight train, and it also had reference to his preferment there-
after; that is, as to his promotion afterwards. Therefore, the injunction would
be the only remedy in the world that could possibly give him his rights. The
injunction was proper, because he was a conductor in his first position which
was a higher, or considered a higher position, although it paid no higher salary
or wages, and they granted the injunction refusing to permit the railroad com-
pany to demote him, at the same pay. There are other cases in connection
with that.

"The International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union, an organization of

soldiering on the job,' while, on the other hand, employees sought an increase

of the collective agreement. Acrimonious discussions, both in conversations
and through the press, indicated and developed a spirit of controversy, but a
supplemental agreement was at length arrived at on June 3, 1921, providing
for a joint commission representing equally employers and employees, to investi-
gate and report upon conditions claimed to call for a readjustment of the agree-
ment of May 29, 1919. This June agreement was regarded by the court as
being supplemental to that of May 29, 1919,' so that 'no recommendaiton
under the former could override or make nugatory the fundamental benefits
secured to the plaintiffs under the latter,' i. e., the earlier agreement.
"On October 25, 1921, during the term of the agreed activities of the joint
commission, the employers' association declared that it was necessary to return
the piecework system, to increase the number of working hours, and to reduce
the wages. This, of course, was a complete departure from the terms of the

Again, this is one association suing the other association.
Judge Wagner, speaking for the court, stated the facts as above, reaching the
conclusion that-
"Out of the mass of affidavits submitted by both sides, with denials and some
conflict of facts, there survives clearly a preponderance of evidence in favor of
plaintiff establishing its right to the extraordinary relief sought. While this
application is novel, it is novel only in the respect that for the first time an
.

employees' organization is seeking to restrain their employers' organization
from violating a contractural obligation.'
On the assumption of novelty, Judge Wagner laid down the following prin-
ciples as warranting the granting of the injunction even though a direct precedent
was not at hand.
"It is elementary, and yet sometimes requires emphasis, that the door of a
court of equity is open to employer and employee alike. It is no respector of
persons-it is keen to protect the legal rights of all. Heretofore the employer
alone has prayed the protection of a court of equity against threatened irreparable
illegal acts of the employee. But mutuality of obligation compels a mutuality
of remedy. The fact that the employees have entered equity's threshold by a
hitherto untraveled path does not lessen their right to the law's decree."
With which this court agrees absolutely and unequivocally.
"Precedent is not our only guide in deciding these disputes, for many are worn
out by time, and made useless by the more enlightened and humane conception
of social justice. That progressive sentiment of advanced civilization, which has
compelled legislative action to correct and improve conditions which a proper
regard for humanity would no longer tolerate, can not be ignored by the courts.
Our decisions should be in harmony with that modern conception, and not in
defiance of it."
There is one wide difference between that case and the instant case. The
above case is a case of one organization against another organization. Outside
of that fact, there is a very great similarity in the two cases. Now the general
principles of law and equity as applicable to a case of this character are so well
understood by members of the bench and the bar that I do not intend to under-
take to elucidate very much upon them. This case, of course, is a clear departure
from the general rule and trend of the decisions of the country, and is an entire
departure from anything that can be found in the State of West Virginia. Just
what will be done along that line in the future this court can not know. As
stated here in that opinion, every case must stand upon the peculiar conditions
and the merits of that particular case. No two cases are or can be exactlyalike.
The contract in that case was clear and unequivocal. There is no question
about that. The only remarkable thing about that case at all is that the injunc-
tion was granted to prevent them from violating a contract which ordinarily
would be considered unenforceable in equity. It looked like there would be a
remedy in some other way. And the other, and for the additional reason that it
was apparently a direction to carry out a contract which might be impossible
of performing.
Now, as I have said, the general principle is of course, as laid down, that if a
contract can be enforced in the first place it has got to be a proper contract, and if
that contract can be enforced at law, the general principle is that you can not come
into equity for the enforcement of it. And the principles under which you can
come into a court of equity are very well understood. Now, there are two things
asked to be done in these injunctions: One is that they shall be enjoined from

Now, in the first place, the question that the court has to determine and upon

This contract can not be remade by the court. The court can only construe a

conclusion, that that contract never did contemplate a condition such as has arisen

know that papers are generally prepared before they are signed.
That is an allegation of this agreement, which amounts to an allegation I

that was not authorized and there was nothing in it to show that they authorized

either in law or equity, on account of the well-known prinicples that the contract
can only bind the parties to it. Now there is no privity shown between these
parties and the parties defendant and principal to these suits.
As to the second proposition, I believe that if it isn't too broad, so as to include
the whole portion of the coal business, that a contract like that for a proper con-
sideration could be made. In other words, collective bargaining could be done
provided it could be carried out. But I want to say this, that the time has not
come, and I know that every man in this house, whatever he thinks about it
now will agree with me, that it never will come, when two or three or four or
half a dozen men can sit down with that many other people around a table
some place and sell the labor of hundreds or even thousands of people without
their consent and compel them to carry it out. They can make an agreement
and they can use all proper persuasion to have it done, but who says that they
can enforce it, says that the days of slavery have returned; and I do not believe
that the American people anywhere want to be bought and sold. Now I do not
believe that is the intention of this organization. The purpose is to better the
conditions, the wage conditions, and the conditions generally. They ought to
have the best conditions possible under which to live. Every good citizen wants
them to have such conditions, but I don't believe that anybody feels that it
would be right, and I am sure that it is not law, that a man can sit down and simply
say that he has a few men whom he will hire for you to work and if they do
Lot do it he will compel them to do it and that no power under Heaven can stop
it. If a man agrees to work and gets tired of the job, he can quit. He may be
sued for damages for breach of the contract. He has the right to quit just as
he has the right to start if he has a better opportunity to go some place else.
He can not be handled like a machine. He is still a man with all the rights that
God endowed him with. God gave him such rights and man can not take them
away from him.

the injunction, which I have to do, that the defendants in these cases have been
entirely free from blame. They have entered into a contract of the character
that it is, and a very peculiar one, as I have set out. They have so acted and
conducted themselves as to give many of these other parties the idea that they
would carry it out, not only what was in the contract but more than was in the
contract. I think that these men in good faith, most of them, believe that. Of
course the men, the plaintiffs in this case, are not versed in law. They are just
ordinary laymen and naturally might be easily misled in that way, although
they have men who are versed in law to explain it. But these things are some-
times not examined as carefully as they might be. But I do not understand why
they did not make a contract that was clear and simple so that everybody could
understand it. I haven't much patience with contracts that are drawn up with
great big loop holes in them. They cause trouble for everybody. I have seen
a great many contracts in my time. I have drawn a great many, and I am going
to say right here now that this is the most remarkable contract, according to my
understanding, that I have ever seen in my life. Now I happen to know that
most of these people have able counsel, and I don't understand why they should
not have an able contract, a clear contract; and I hope that that contract will be
embodied in any report of this opinion. That contract is to my mind-I won't
say one of the wonders of the world, but it comes pretty close to it.
Gentlemen, this is the opinion of the court, without going further, that the
injunction should be refused

OPINION
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
This suit is brought by the United Mine Workers of America, a voluntary
unincorporated association, and Charles Sage, Steve Maxwell, Joe Locare,
Daniel Kodak, Natalie Spanial, Gus Myers, and Joe Girimont, who sue on behalf
of themselves and all other members of Local Union No. 2311, United Mine
Workers of America, against the Simpson Creek Collieries Co., a corporation, and
asking for an injunction to prevent the defendant from operating its mines, con-
trary to the provisions of an alleged contract with the plaintiffs, called the
"Baltimore agreement."
The plaintiffs aver that on the 18th day of April, 1924, by what is called a
"supplemental agreement," the plaintiffs as members of Local Union No. 2311
at Galloway, W. Va., entered into an agreement with the defendant, the Simpson
Creek Collieries Co., whereby the terms, provisions, and conditions of what is
known as the "Baltimore agreement" were accepted, ratified, and confirmed,
the parties agreeing to carry out the provisions of said contract both in letter and
in spirit, and that afterwards a supplementary agreement was entered into
between the same parties respecting section 23 of the Baltimore agreement in
relation to grievances.
The Baltimore agreement, as averred in the bill, was the outcome of a confer-
ence between the mine workers and coal operators, and was entered into on the
12th day of March, 1924, and was to be effective from the 1st day of April, 1924,
until the 31st day of March, 1927, and, as averred, was ratified by the Northern
West Virginia Coal Operators' Association at Fairmont, W. Va., on the 1st day
of April, 1924, and was likewise ratified by the United Mine Workers of Northern
West Virginia on the 11th day of April, 1924, and that the plaintiffs named in the
bill were members of such organization and ratified the same.
It is further averred that on or about the 18th day of April, 1924, the defendant
began operating its said coal mines Nos. 2 and 3 at Galloway, in Barbour County,
under the terms of said Baltimore agreement, and continued to so operate the
mines until the first day of November, 1925, employing in the mines members of
Local Union No. 2311, United Mine Workers of America, and complying strictly


===== [扫描序号 143] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1165
with all the conditions and provisions of said agreement, which provides a wage
scale, together with numerous other provisions, and also that "all workmen
eligible for membership, employed in and around the coal mines or coke ovens,
shall be members of the United Mine Workers of America."
The bill further avers that while the mines were so working the defendant
employed about 500 of such workmen in its mines, who were members of the
United Mine Workers of America, that in accordance with the provisions of
said Baltimore agreement the defendant collected the sum of $2,000 as fines from
the said workmen, and still retains the same, and that on or about the 24th of
October, 1925, the defendant repudiated said contract and supplemental agree-
ments, and declined to carry out the same, and shut down their mines on the 1st
day of November, 1925; that defendant gave notice, shortly after the 1st day of
November, 1925, to the plaintiffs, of its intention to resume the operation of its
mines on January 4, 1926, upon a different and lower wage scale than that pro-
vided for in the Baltimore agreement, and is now operating, or attempting to
operate its said mines with workmen not members of the United Mine Workers
of America (though the number of workmen employed is not named) and in
violation of its said contract and agreement with the plaintiffs, whereby plain-
tiffs have been deprived, since the 4th day of January, 1926, of their livelihood
and of the benefits to which they are entitled under the provisions of said Balti-
more agreement.
The plaintiffs further aver that an action for damages on their behalf against
the defendants for the violation of said contract would be wholly inadequate and
incomplete, that plaintiffs are skilled mine workers, and to permit defendant to
repudiate its said agreement would cause plaintiffs to suffer irreparable damage
and loss; that plaintiffs' only vocation is mine working by which each obtains his
living, and that violation of said contract by the defendant deprives them of
their means of livelihood.
That this suit is brought, among other things, to prevent a multiplicity of suits,"
though it does not mention the number of mine workers belonging to Local
Union No. 2311 at Galloway, and prays that the defendant may be required to
answer this bill; that a temporary injunction may be issued, that the same may be
made final after a hearing, restraining and enjoining the defendants:
1. From operating or attempting to operate its coal mine at Galloway upon a
different and lower scale of mining and labor rates than set forth in the Baltimore
contract and supplemental agreement had with the defendant, until the expira-
tion of said contract on the 31st of March, 1927; and
2. From employing in and around its coal mines, workmen who were not
members of the United Mine Workers of America, except as provided in said
contract, and there is a prayer for general relief.
THE DEMURRER TO THE BILL-PARTIES
To this bill the defendant, by counsel, appeared on the day the same was pre-
sented to the court in vacation, and afterwards filed its written demurrer, by
counsel, assigning 30 grounds. The first ground of demurrer is for want of
proper parties, and for misjoiner of plaintiffs.
Upon this ground of demurrer it is to be observed that as a general rule, and
unless modified by statute, the law only recognizes two classes of persons who may
be parties to any action or suit. These persons are natural or artificial. Arti-
ficial persons are, of course, corporations, the State alone having power to create
artificial persons. No involuntary association or collection of persons can sue in
their assumed or trade name, because "artificial persons" in the meaning of the
law can not be created voluntarily. In such cases the persons composing the
voluntary association must sue. (30 Cyc. 28; 22 Inc. Pl. and Prac. 230-231;
20 R. C. L. 622; Neblack, Benefit Societies pl. 83 (2d); Bacon, Benefit Societies
441.) A case in point is that of St. Paul Typothetae et al v. St. Paul Book Binder's
Union (94 Minn. 351 (3 Ann. Cas. 695).) In this case the enforcement of a con-
tract was sought to be made which had been executed in the name of an unincor-
porated association as one of the parties, and another, and it was held that the
action would not lie, because the unincorporated association was neither a natural
or artificial person, and could therefore have no standing in a court. Such an
action is a nullity (30 Cyc. 27 et seq.). (On this subject see the opinion of the
court in the case last cited on p. 697 of 3 Ann. Cas. and the note on p. 699;
Western, etc., Ry. Co. v. Dalton Marble Works, 122 Ga. 744; 50 S. E. 978.)
When there is a misjoiner of plaintiffs it is proper to demur, though the joiner of
an improper plaintiff having interest in the suit, will not effect the rights of the


===== [扫描序号 144] =====
1166
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
parties having a real interest to maintain it. (Fletcher, Eq. Pl. and Prac. 59;
Story Eq. Pl. 237; 1 Hogg Eq. Prac. 95 (3 ed.); Beckwith v. Seborn, 31 W. Va. 1.)
The seven plaintiffs, who are natural persons, have a right to bring any proper
suit or action in any court, not because they are members of the United Mine
Workers of America, or any other unincorporated involuntary association, but
because the law gives them a status as natural persons who are entitled to litigate
a claim. They sue on behalf of themselves and all other members of Local Union
No. 2311, similarly situated and having a common interest in this cause. This
manner of pleading is frequently resorted to: 1 Hogg Eq. Pl. 40 (3 ed); Fletcher
Eq. P. and Prac. P. 42; Story Eq. Pl. 97; Lile. Eq. Pl. and Prac. 91 (2 ed).
OTHER GROUNDS OF DEMURRER
The next ground of demurrer is, in substance, that the bill does not show any
legal contract existing between the parties; that the same is void for want of
consideration, and lack of mutuality; that the services to be performed there-
under is not of that peculiar kind which requires particular skill or talent, and
for that reason is not enforcable.
It is fundamental that upon a demurrer to a bill all facts well pleaded are to be
taken as true. (Allen v. South Penn Coal Co., 58 W. Va. 197; 1 Hogg Eq. Prac.
317 (Carlin's Edition); 1 Barton Chy. Prac. 317 (3 ed.); Watson v. Brunner, 128
Va. 600.) And looking to the bill we find that it states and exhibits an agreement
in printed pamphlet form known as the Baltimore agreement and avers that
the plaintiffs and the defendant expressly accepted and ratified that agreement,
and in this respect, on behalf of the defendant, acceptance is shown by exhibits
Nos. 3 and 4 filed with the bill; and also avers in that pursuance of said contract the
defendant from some time in April, 1924, until the 1st day of November, 1925,
operated its mines at Galloway in accordance with said Baltimore agreement,
paying the wage scale therein provided and collecting fines from the workmen in
accordance therewith to the amount of $2,000, which fines the defendant still
retains. From all which it is apparent that the parties to said agreement thought
they had a contract which both parties sought to carry out. From April, 1924, to
November 1, 1925, only members of United Mine Workers of Local Union No.
2311 were employed by the defendant in its mine, according to the allegations
of the bill.
Was the contract mutual? By the demurrer it is insisted that it is not. The
agreement purports to be entered into by the membership of the organization
mentioned as parties, and provided the wage rate to be paid, and by section 6
the workmen to be employed, and by section 7 the time to begin work, and by
section 4 an eight-hour day, and by section 12 a committee on grievances, and by
section 28 that no strike or stoppage of work shall occur at any time, and by
section 29 a fine of $2 per day is imposed on every workman who refuses to work
or causes the mine or any part of it to shut down in violation of the rules pro-
mulgated, and section 30 provides a fine of $2 in favor of each employee per day
against the operator for shutting down his mine in violation of said rules, and
section 36 prohibits the operator from recognizing or treating with any repre-
sentatives of the United Mine Workers of America during the suspension of
work, contrary to the agreement, and by paragraph 10 of the bill it is averred
that the plaintiffs are now and always have been ready and willing to carry out
all of the provisions of said contract and supplemental agreements on their part
to be performed.
True, there is no direct and positive statement in so many words in the bill or
the Baltimore agreement that the plaintiff or members of Local Union No. 2311
at Galloway promised to work for the defendant any particular length of time,
and it is true that by section 13 of said agreement the defendant has the right
to hire and discharge its workmen. But reading the agreement as a whole we
find that it state that it is to be effective from April 1, 1924, and to continue for
a period of three years, or until March 31, 1927, and that the workmen who are
employed at the mines, according to section 6 of said agreement, "shall be
members of the United Mine Workers of America, and strikes and stoppage of
work on the part of the miners is prohibited." (See 6 R. C. L. 686; C. C. Blake
Co. v. W. R. Smith & Sons 133 S. E. 685.)
Rightly interpreted we think this means that while the defendant had the
right to both employ and discharge workmen, those employed should be members
of the United Mine Workers of America. In other words, section 13 of the agree-
ment gave the defendant the right to discharge an unsatisfactory man, but that
section 6 prohibited the employment of persons other than United Mine. Workers


===== [扫描序号 145] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1167
The whole object of the Baltimore agreement, as it seems, was to fix a scale of
wages between the workmen and the employer, and to provide certain rules and
regulations regarding such work therein mentioned for a period of three years.
But if the agreement is said to be ambiguous and uncertain, how are we to
interpret it? In the late case of Blue Creek Development Co. v. Howell et al.
(133 S. E. 699) the court held:
"If the language of an instrument leaves the meaning of the parties in doubt,
the court will take into consideration the occasion which gave rise to it, the
obvious design of the parties, and the object to be attained, as well as the language
of the instrument itself, and gives effect to that construction which will best
effectuate the real intent and meaning of the parties.' (Southern Ry. Co. v.
Franklin, etc. Ry. Co., 96 Va. 693, 32 S. E. 485.)
""
And in the case of Piercy v. Louisville & N. Ry. Co. (198 Ky. 477, 53 R. L. R.
322) it is said:
"When the language of a contract is so remote, uncertain, and ambiguous as
that its meaning may not be readily discerned, the courts in interpreting it will
give it such meaning as the parties themselves have given it in operating or acting
under it." (6 R. C. L. 852, par. 241.)
Upon the face of the bill and exhibits we think that plaintiffs have shown the
existence of a contract or agreement between the parties to this suit. It is un-
necessary to repeat that the plaintiffs and the defendant acted upon this contract
from April, 1924, until November 1, 1925, or for a year and a half, apparently
treating it as valid. On the last-named date the defendant stopped work, having
given written notice on the 24th day of October, 1925, that it would so do and
assigning as a reason therefor that under present conditions the defendant could
not operate in competition with other mines producing similar coal in this dis-
trict; that for a long time the mine had been operated contrary to defendant's
interests; that competing mines were operating under a long wage scale and were
able to sell coal below defendant's cost of production. And it may be asked did
the defendant have the right under said Baltimore agreement to close down its
mine when it found that it could not sell coal at a profit; there is nothing in the
agreement to prevent this. Defendant ceased to operate when it began to lose
money. The spirit of the Baltimore agreement did not prevent this, or require
defendant to run its mines at a loss. But if the defendant did operate its mine,
it must pay the scale wage provided in said agreement, and employ United Mine
Workers, according to the contract. On this point the agreement appears to
mean, that if the mines are operated before March 31, 1927, they are to be
worked by union men and on the union pay scale.
What other facts are presented by the plaintiffs' bill? Clearly it is to be
gathered from the allegations of the bill; that the defendant has been operating
its mines since January 4, 1926, upon the changed scale specified in exhibit 6 filed
with the bill, which is a lower wage than that of the Baltimore agreement. How
many employees have been working for defendant under the new scale, the bill
does not disclose.
Notwithstanding something like eight or nine months have elapsed since the
plaintiffs have had written notice from the defendant of its intention to change
the wage scale, and that nearly seven months have passed since defendant began
operations under the new wage scale, yet plaintiffs did not take any legal steps
by way of suit to prevent a breach of the Baltimore agreement until this bill
was presented to the court in vacation, on July 20, 1926; nor do we know what
has become of a majority of the members of Local Union No. 2311. Just what
legal effect this lapse of time has had, we are unable to say. If, in the interval,
new rights have attached, or the rights of third persons have arisen, these are
matters to be brought forward by way of answer or petition.
We have been unable to find any precedent in this State, or in the State of
Virginia, applicable to the particular facts in this case. The plaintiffs do not
pray for specific performance in their bill, and it is insisted in the brief filed on
behalf of the plaintiffs that this is not a suit to compel specific performance of a
contract. The plaintiffs ask only that an injunction may be awarded preventing
the defendant from operating its mine upon a different and lower scale of mining
and labor rates than that set forth in the "Baltimore agreement" and from
employing miners who are not members of the United Mine Workers of America.
We are cited in the case of Schesinger et al. v. Quinto et al. (192 N. Y. Supp.
564). But the facts in that case were quite different from the facts in the present
case, and upon these facts we approve the remarks of the judge to be found on
page 559 of the opinion and quoted by counsel for the plaintiffs in their brief.
That was a suit for injunction by the president of the International Ladies


===== [扫描序号 146] =====
1168
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Garment Workers' Union and others against Phillip Quinto, individually, and as
treasurer of the Cloak, Suit, and Skirt Manufacturers' Protective Association
and others. What other parties were named as plaintiffs or defendants in this
suit does not appear from the opinion of the court as reported. At any rate,
"The plaintiffs moved to continue pendente lite a preliminary injunction enjoin-
ing the defendant from combining and conspiring to order, direct, instigate,
counsel, advise, or encourage members of the defendant association to violate
a certain agreement between the association and plaintiffs' union, and from doing
any act in furtherance of such conspiracy." There is no allegation of a conspiracy
in the present bill. In the case last cited an agreement as to wages and certain
conditions between the plaintiff and defendants associations had been entered
into on May 29, 1919, and to continue operating up to June 1, 1922, and had been
acted upon. Afterwards, trouble arose between the association and their work-
men, and a conference was had between them, and on June 3, 1921, the parties
entered into a further agreement which was adjudged to be in addition to the
first agreement, and supplemental thereto. On October 25, 1921, the defendant
association adopted a resolution, which changed the original agreement, by
substituting the "piece work" system for the "week work" system, and establish-
ing an increase of the number of working hours in the week, and fixed a reduction
of the wages for the workers, who continued to work under the week work system,
which change it was declared should go into effect on Monday, November 14,
1921. These changes were without consent of the workers and they refused to
accept them, and apparently brought suit at once. Under this state of facts the
court said on page 569 of the opinion:
"It is elementary, and yet sometimes requires emphasis, that the door of a
court of equity is open to employer and employee alike; it is no respecter of
persons-it is keen to protect the legal rights of all. Heretofore the employer
alone has prayed the protection of a court of equity against threatened irreparable
illegal acts of the employee. But mutuality of obligations compels a mutuality
of remedy. The fact that the employees have entered equity's threshold by a
hitherto untraveled path does not lessen their right to the law's decree."
And on page 570 the court further said:
"It can not be seriously contended that the plaintiffs have an adequate remedy
at law. That the damages resulting from the alleged violation of the agreement
would be irremedial at law is too patent for discussion. There are over 40,000
workers, whose rights are involved, and over 300 members of defendant organi-
zation. The contract expires within six months, and a trial of the issues can
hardly be had within that time. It is unthinkable that the court would force
the litigants into a court of law. A court of equity looks to the substance and
essence of things and disregards matters of form and technical niceties."
Under the conditions above set forth the injunction was granted.
And in Goyette v. C. V. Watts & Co.; Lively et al. v. Gill et al.; Knight Bros.
(Inc.) v. White et al. (140 N. E. 285), under similar circumstances it was held:
"Labor union would ordinarily be entitled to maintain a bill to enjoin another
union which has by solicitation, intimidation, and show of force sought to cause
manufacturers under contract with plaintiff to repudiate their contracts with
manufacturers, and has induced or coerced one of such manufacturers to join
the conspiracy and notify plaintiff of its intention to repudiate its contract."
The decision last cited was in fact three cases, the first of which was styled
Joseph U. Goyette v. C. V. Watte & Co. In this case there was a decree dismiss-
ing the bill on demurrer, which was affirmed on appeal. The second case was
styled Collis Lovely and another, general president, and secretary-treasurer of
the Boot and Shoe Workers Union v. Austin E. Gill and others. In this suit the
plaintiff sought to enjoin members of the Shoe Workers Protective Union from
interfering with contracts of the Boot and Shoe Workers Union by threats,
intimidation, etc., and from interfering with members of such union desirous of
entering or continuing employment, or having entered employment, in manu-
facturing establishments in Haverhill, and from obstructing, threatening, intimi-
dating, or interfering with such members in entering or leaving the premises of
such establishment, etc., and restraining the defendant George Newburg and
others doing business as the Triangle Shoe Co., from violating and terminating
their contract with the Boot and Shoe Workers Union. The court overruled a
demurrer to the bill in this suit, holding that there was no adequate remedy at
law, that the bill was not multifarious, and that the plaintiffs were entitled to an
injunction to prevent the defendant from coercing plaintiffs by threats and intimi-
dation to join the "conspiracy" to ruin the union of the plaintiffs, etc.


===== [扫描序号 147] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1169
In the third suit the bill sought to enjoin members of both the Shoe Workers
Protective Union and the Boot and Shoe Workers Union from interfering with
its business by threats, parades, picketing, or other acts of intimidation, from
interfering with persons in its employ or desirous of entering the same, and from
obstructing, threatening or intimidating, or interfering with any persons on
entering or leaving plaintiffs' premises, etc. And the court held, under the
circumstances stated that an injunction would lie.
Under the facts stated in these cases, which contained many elements not
presented in the case at bar, it would seem clear that there could be no adequate
and complete remedy at law, and that equity ought to lend its aid; that so many
persons were involved as members of the union litigating that it would be endless,
if not impossible, to obtain redress if each litigant was driven to his remedy at
law.
Defandant's reason for refusing to go on with the "Baltimore agreement" is
stated in Exhibit 5 filed with the bill, which is in substance, that defendant can
not compete in the sale of coal with other mines in the district which are operat-
ing on a lower wage scale. Ordinarily a contract can not be repudiated simply
because of subsequent events or change of circumstances whereby the enforce-
ment of a contract may become a hardship. (Marble Co. v. Ripley, 10 Wall.
356, 19 Law ed. 955.) In Southern Ry. Co. v. Franklin & C. R. Co. (96 Va. 693),
on page 709, the court said:
"The element of risk enters more or less into every contract, and the obliga-
tion to perform it can not be allowed to depend upon the question whether it
has proved to be advantageous of disadvantageous. It would be a travesty
upon justice, and the reputed sanctity of contracts would be of little avail, if
parties could refuse the performance of contracts having some years to run, which
were fairly entered into, and believed to be just and equal when made, merely
because from contingencies, whose possibility might have been foreseen, they
had turned out, in the course of execution to be a losing interest of a profitable
bargain."
And in the case last cited it was held that "A court of equity will not refuse
the specific performance of a contract on the sole ground of hardship where it
appears that the contract, in its inception, was fairly and justly made and that
the hardship is the result of miscalculation or is caused by subsequent events or
a change of circumstances, and the party seeking performance is wholly without
fault." And in the case of Marble Co. v. Ripley (10 Wall. 356) Mr. Justice
Strong, in speaking of contracts that were supposed to be fair and equal when
made, but in the lapse of time have become bad bargains, said: "Besides, it is by
no means clear that a court of equity will refuse to decree the specific performance
of a contract, fair when it was made, but has become a hard one by the force of
subsequent circumstances and changing events."
Of course, it is well established that it is not every breach of a contract that will
be enjoined by a court of equity, because in most instances the law affords an
adequate remedy by an action. And it is also the rule that a contract for labor
or services with a single individual will not be specifically enforced unless the labor
or services are of that kind which requires particular skill or training or qualifica-
tions, such, for instance, as a singer. (Waterman, Spec. Perf. 33; Pomroy Spec.
Perf. 22, 24 (1 ed.).) Nor will all courts enjoin the breach of a labor contract.
Thus in Schwartz v. Priscell (186 N. W. 522), in granting a writ of mandamus to
stay proceedings on appeal, under a decree permanently enjoining an employer
from violating his agreement with the union to employ members of the union only
during a stated period, a majority of the Michigan Supreme Court concurred in
the opinion that such decree was improper.
Being without a precedent in this State, and feeling that the main question
involved in this litigation is new with us, and having a conscientious fear of com-
mitting error, I have concluded to certify this case to the supreme court of
appeals for their decision upon the demurrer to the plaintiff's bill, and the
questions of law and the interests involved in this litigation I do not think it
expedient or proper that the injunction prayed for should issue at once, nor until
the supreme court of appeals has passed upon and settled the law of the case,
which presents questions of no little doubt and difficulty, especially as to the valid-
ity of the contract sued on, of the presence or absence of an adequate remedy at
law-such doubts and difficulties as ought to cause anyone to be exceedingly
careful and cautious.

A recent investigation has startled me beyond measure and I want to tell you
about it. West Virginia has an area of approximately 24,000 square miles;
reduced to acreage it amounts to 15,360,000 acres. Two hundred and ten cor-

6,035,936 acres.
Add to this a million acres owned by corporations in less than 10,000-acre
tracts, and you have in round numbers one-half the State owned by corporations,
the great majority of whose stockholders reside outside the State.

FORMER TAX COMMISSIONER BARES TAX EVASION OF FOREIGN COMPANIES-

T. C. Townsend, former State tax commissioner and active in the political
life of Kanawha County, who was one of the counsel for the armed march defend-
ants in the trials at Charles Town a year ago, voiced a burning indictment of
the State administration in his Clarksburg Labor Day address to an audience
of several thousand men and women.
Assailing the coal, oil, and gas trinity, he declared foreign corporations own
virtually 50 per cent of the State natural resources and pay less taxes than the
other half, which is made up of merchants, farmers, and workers, although the
corporations' holdings are five times more valuable.
Political treachery was charged to a group of State senators by Townsend
when he asserted vehemently that the controlled Democrats and Republicans in
the upper chamber joined hands to put favorites of the foreign despoilers of West
Vriginia's natural wealth into State offices where they could continue to trick
the people.
Mr. Townsend's address follows:
"I am here to-day at the suggestion of your friends and my friends. I hope,
therefore, it may be our pleasure to have an old-fashioned, friendly, common-
sense talk together. The workers of this States, men and women who eat
bread by the sweat of their brow-whether organized or unorganized, whether
farmer, miner, mechanic, or otherwise should have a better understanding of the
problems that confront them in this State.
I
"I shall confine my remarks, therefore, to conditions in West Virginia. It is a
pleasure to me to talk about West Virginia, because it is my native State.
have lived in the State since birth and expect to live in it the remainder of my life.
Every interest I have in the world is wrapped up in the welfare of the people of
my native State.
"So far the better part of my life has been spent fighting the battles of the
common people, that class of people of whom Abraham Lincoln said, 'God must
have loved, or he would not have created so many of them.' I shall continue to
do battle along the same line.
HITS FOREIGN INTERESTS
· West Virginia is a great State. It is rich beyond the dreams of the fabled
Monte Cristo. Because of its coal and other minerals, it has become a battle
ground between forces that are contending bitterly rather than endeavoring to
live with due regard for the rights of each other.
"The big question in this State to-day is whether or not it is to be controlled
by the people who inhabit it, its affairs conducted by the people, of the people,
and for the people, or shall it be controlled and conducted by, of, and for the
privileged few.
"The constitution of this State provides that no law abridging the freedom
of speech or of the press shall be passed.' Also, the right of the people to assemble
in a peaceable manner * * * shall be held inviolate.' These are provisions
of the Bill of Rights-freedom of speech and of the press, and freedom of assem-
blage, for centuries have been recognized as inherent rights of the people.
No government can long survive without them. This State to-day is in
more danger from suppression than from violence, because suppression breeds
violence; indeed violence is the child of suppression. People should have the
right everywhere to express their honest convictions, and alas, their folly also by
printed or spoken speech through the press, by posted card, or otherwise. When-
ever people are free to express themselves, their wisdom will survive and their
folly die.

CONSTITUTION FLOUTED
"In portions of West Virginia to-day there is no such thing as free speech and
free assemblage. In Logan County no person can express himself freely upon
all subjects, without danger of personal violence. Conditions, as they exist in
that county, have become a stench in the nostrils of the people of the Nation.
"There is great danger that the conditions in Logan County, and the system
that prevails there of suppressing free speech and freedom of assembly, will
spread to other counties. It is inevitable that conditions in Logan County must
be corrected, or the people in other counties of the State must prepare themselves
to suffer like conditions.
"I am sure the people of West Virginia do not appreciate and do not realize
that a person can not travel in that county without his business being inquired
into, his purpose for being there disclosed, his personal effects examined, and,
if he is there on any mission which has anything to do with organized labor, he
will find it convenient, as well as better for his personal safety, to leave the county
in the shortest and quickest possible way.
As one person expressed it to me, he was given three minutes to get away,
with two minutes yet coming to him.
CONDITIONS EXPOSED
"During the last few years much has been said and written about conditions
in Logan County-more will be said and written until those conditions cease to
exist. It is within the power of the people of this State, through the elective
franchise, to remedy those conditions, and the people will have the opportunity
of doing so next year.
"What are the conditions in that county? Every department of government
in Logan county to-day is dominated and controlled by the Logan Coal Oper-
ators' Association. In that county there exists a complete industrial autocracy.
"For a number of years, in fact, since about the year 1912, the coal operators
of that county have employed and maintained a deputy sheriff system, the whole
purpose of which is to keep out of the county all persons who have any associa-
tion or connection with the United Mine Workers of America, or any other labor
organization.
"6
'At present these deputy sheriffs number more than 200-a small army.
Kanawha County, with three times the population of Logan, has only 20 deputies.
"For the year 1920 the Logan Coal Operators' Association paid $46,630 to
sustain this sytem, and for the first nine months of 1921 the sum of $61,517.
God knows how much money they have expended since that time, but it runs
into the hundreds of thousands of dollars.
"These deputies prevent all persons from talking unionism in that county.
No person can remain in that county who, by persuasion, argument, education,
or other peaceable means undertakes to organize the people into labor organization.
SPY SYSTEM PREVAILS
"The coal companies of that county have inaugurated and have in effect a
spy system, and if any person is even suspected of sympathizing with organized
labor, he is immediately driven out of the county. This system in 1920 had
become so notorious that the Republican Party in its platform declared as follows:
"In a republic the enforcement of laws made by the people should be and
must always be in the hands of public servants elected by the people.
deplore the abuses that have grown up under the so-called private-guard or detec-
tive systems in this State, and we pledge a Republican legislature to enact laws
that will correct those abuses, and at the same time maintain and protect all
lawful property and personal rights.'
We
"The present governor was elected upon that platform. In his inaugural
address on the 4th of March, 1921, he said:
"Another disturbing factor in some sections of the State is what is commonly
called the "private-guard system." The party of which I have the honor to be
a member, through its legally constituted representatives, recently declared that—
"""In a republic the enforcement of laws must be made by the people, should

CORNWELL DEPLORED OUTRAGES
"Not only has the Republican Party condemned the situation, but Hon.

to the legislature with reference to the situation, spoke as follows:
"The Republican State platform contained the following declaration:
""In a republic the enforcement of laws made by the people should be and
must always be in the hands of public servants elected by the people. We

"Upon the assumption that this declaration was made in good faith and with
the knowledge that the party has ample power to carry it out, I conceive it to be
my duty to discuss the questions in a frank manner, presenting the situation as
I see it.
"Let me say, first, that I am now and have always been opposed to vesting
the employees of a private company, whether a detective agency or coal com-
pany, with police power.
"It is almost certain to be abused.
The platform declaration, therefore, is one
that can be quite generally commended. However, the practice of employing
private guards and detectives, in the capacity mentioned, is no longer general in
this State.
"It is confined to comparatively few places. There is another practice, how-
ever, which prevails in one or two counties not covered by the declaration noted,
which is condemned by union officials and the officers are classed as guards and
gunmen' and they are confused in the public mind with private guards, and that
is the practice of the sheriff appointing a number of special or extra deputies and
the coal companies paying them, for the purpose of policing the mining towns.
"For instance, in one of the counties referred to, there are neraly a hundred
mining towns with several hundred, or several thousand population, each, as the
case may be. They are unincorporated. There are no mayors or police in the
towns. There are only two justices in a magisterial district where there may be
a number of towns and several thousand population.
"For each of these towns or mining camps, the sheriff of the county will per-
haps appoint two special deputy sheriffs. The county being without funds
to pay them, the operators contribute the money. Those deputies act as peace
officers. They are county officers, paid by private companies.
UNIVERSALLY CONDEMNED
"Notwithstanding the fact that both the leading political parties in West
Virginia have condemned the situation, it still exists. The present governor has
done nothing to correct the situation except talk. The law-making body of the
State, the lower house of which in 1921 was Democratic, likewise has done noth-
ing.
64
'As a matter of fact, neither the Democratic Party nor the Republican Party
has taken one single active step toward remedying the situation which has been
universally condemned as an outrage upon public decency, and wholly contrary
to both the letter and spirit of American institutions.
"Not only have the two leading political parties of the State condemned the
situation that exists in that county, but Senator Kenyon, chairman of the com-
mittee appointed to investigate conditions therein, in his report to the United
States Senate used the following strong and unmistakable language:
"The operators have been guilty of practices also in portions of this region that
can not be justified. The system of paying deputy sheriffs out of funds con-
tributed by the operators, as the testimony shows has been done in Logan County,
where a large number of deputy sheriffs were paid not out of the public treasury,
but out of funds of the operators, is a vicious and un-American policy and a
practice that should cease.

"Public officers should be paid out of the public treasury. It is rather freely

who attempted so to do. It would be difficult to imagine how any industrial

CHAFIN IS SCORED
'Apparently there is not as many Baldwin-Felts detectives in the troubled

"Mr. Chafin, sheriff, Logan County, testified there were 42 deputy sheriffs to

"Moreover, the magazine writers and newspapers, statesmen, and publicists

"The situation in that county has grown so intolerable that in the summer of
1921 it resulted in what the whole State knows as the 'armed march' of the miners.
No one undertakes to defend the armed march. As between the armed march
and the Logan situation, the armed march is the most defensible, the difference

"No one undertakes to defend the march, even those who engaged in it con-

under color of law-it is lawlessness in the name of the law.
"The armed march is not and never has been defended from any standpoint
as being lawful; however, one was as lawful as the other, and if there is any
distinction, the odds are in favor of the marchers.
CAUSED ARMED MARCH
"That the Logan situation was responsible for the armed march, no one who
is conversant with the facts will undertake to deny. In August and September,
1921, a body of men, variously estimated at from two to ten thousand, gathered
at Marmet, in Kanawha County, and marched toward Logan County, with the
avowed purpose of ridding that county of the armed-guard system.
"But for the fact that West Virginia's chief executive at time, as well as at
the present time, was completely dominated and controlled by the coal interests,
the march never would have taken place, and this for two reasons: First, the
governor of the State in 24 hours could rid the State of the Logan County situa-
tion, and, second, a governor with courage could have stopped the march in its
incipiency.

"After the marchers had started at Marmet and reached as far as Madison,
in Boone County, they were halted and turned back through the cooperation
and influence of Gen. H. H. Bandholz, of the United States Army, and the
officials of the United Mine Workers' organization.
"While they were on their way home in fact, after the great majority of them

"The men were turned back at Madison in the afternoon of August 26, 1921.
During the night of the 26th and during the day of the 27th they were on their

OPERATORS INSPIRED UPRISING
"General Bandholz returned to Washington on the evening of the 27th, after
going over the line followed by the marchers from Charleston to Madison, and
satisfying himself that the men in good faith were returning to their homes.
Major Thompson, another United States Army officer, left the same evening
for Indianapolis.
"Right here was born the most diabolical conspiracy that was hatched to
destroy a labor union, or an inexcusable, unexplainable, and an irreparable
official blunder was committed. Take your choice-one is as bad as the other.
"On the night of August 27, with the approval of the governor of the State,
Don Chapin sent 90 State police and 140 deputy sheriffs across the mountain
from the town of Logan to Coal River into union territory, in the nighttime,
and they shot down, without justification or excuse, two coal miners and
wounded three others. As soon as the shooting took place the State police and
deputy sheriffs retreated back across the mountain.
The news of this shooting, much magnified, was immediately spread through-
out the whole of southern West Virginka, and the men who had returned to their
homes, together with many additional ones, reassembled at the town of Blair, in
Logan County.
"It was after the men reassembled the second time, and because of the killing
of two coal miners, and the wounding of others, that all the violence in con-
nection with the armed march occurred.
MORGAN ASSAILED
44
During the succeeding days there was considerable violence in and around
Blair. Three alleged deputy sheriffs of Logan County were killed, and the
Federal troops, under General Bandholz, came back again.
"General Bandholz in a public statement, said that Governor Morgan 'had
made but a feeble attempt to cope with the situation,' and further stated that
he had not used the resources at his command' to stop the armed march before
it left Marmet.
"In his report to the War Department, made after a thorough and complete
investigation of the causes of the second assemblage of men, he stated that it was
the shooting of the miners by the deputy sheriffs and State police that caused
the second assemblage of men. To use his own language 'it was the untimely and
ill-advised effort on the part of the State police and deputy sheriffs to arrest
people in the trouble zone, resulting in the killing of two coal miners and the
wounding of others that caused the men to reassemble, after they had once
abandoned the march.'
"Immediately after the arrival of Federal troops, the miners returned to their
homes. A special grand jury convened in Logan County in September, 1921.
This grand jury returned indictments against four or five hundred men; then, in
October, 1921, there was a regular grand jury, and more indictments were
returned; and then in January, 1922, there was another session of the grand jury,
and more indictments were returned.
"At each succeeding grand jury from that time to the present, additional
indictments have been returned. Logan County grand juries have not been
particular about whom they indicted.
"Some men have been indicted who were dead; others indicted for murder who
were in jail in Logan County at the time the offense for which they were indicted
was committed.
"One man, whom I recall, was indicted five times for the same offense. As
the indictments were returned from time to time, wholesale arrests were made.

LAWS VIOLATED
"Men were arrested who were not in the march; men who were out of the
State at the time the march took place; men who were at home with their families.
"Not a single preliminary examination has ever been held in Logan County,
notwithstanding the law provides that everyone arrested upon a warrant is
entitled to a preliminary hearing. Every man arrested was taken to Logan
County and lodged in jail.
"If they would talk and tell what they knew, or tell something, whether they
knew it or not, they got their liberty.
'If they refused to talk and stood up for their legal rights, which they had the
right to do, they were placed in jail and denied bond. Men have been denied
bond in Logan County for months, and then released without bond.
"Almost every sort of torture possible has been inflicted upon innocent men
because they refused to make statements implicating men in the armed march,
whom the coal operators of Logan County sought to convict.
"Several months after the armed march had taken place, some ingenious mind
made the great discovery that all these men had committed treason, and then
they were indicted for treason. Its treason in West Virginia to undertake to
organize Logan County.
"In January, 1922, more than 100 cases were changed from Logan County to

a distance of more than 400 miles, where it was thought the coal miners could
not reach, and where it cost at least $100 to take each witness.
"Then began the legal battle in earnest. William Blizzard was tried for trea-

the acquittal of Blizzard, something had to be done.

STATE DERELICT
"In this connection, I desire to be clearly understood. Anyone who commits
crime should be prosecuted. The Government can not live unless its citizens
respect the law, neither can it live unless the violator of the law is brought to
justice.
"It is the duty of the State to prosecute any person who violates her laws.
But the prosecutions growing out of the armed march are not by the State.
The machinery of the State for the prosecution of crime has been literally turned
over, sold out, and delivered to the Logan Coal operators. The state has nothing
to do with it, further than lending its name.
"The cases are conducted entirely by attorneys employed by the coal operators.
The jurors in Jefferson County were paid by the coal operators. How would
you like to be tried for your life by a jury paid by the person who wanted you
convicted?

LAW-AND-ORDER BAIT
"You hear a great deal said in West Virginia by public speakers and in the
newspapers about 'law and order.' Law and order is a generic term that covers
everything and touches nothing.
"It can be applied to any situation or any condition. I have little sympathy
and little respect for the official or person who proclaims to the world that he is in
favor of law and order, and at the same time practices oppression and suppression.
"We all favor, or should favor at least, law and order based upon justice. I
desire, however, to register my protest against the use of the term 'law and order'
as a smoke screen behind which to hide tyranny, oppression, lawlessness and the
invasion of those personal rights guaranteed by the Constitution.
"The situation in Logan County to-day is maintained in the name of 'law and
order.' I have found no one outside of Logan County who favors that kind of
law and order.
"Nero accused Peter and Paul of spreading a pestilential superstition which
they called the Gospel.
"He killed them in the name of law and order. He also tried the whole
Christian church in a body, convicted them, and threw their bodies to the wild
beasts, and did it in the name of law and order, and for the preservation of his
empire.
"Herod saw fit for the good of his kingdom to put to death all the children
under 2 years of age, to preserve law and order. King George III stationed
soldiers in the homes of the Colonists to eat out their substance and destroy their
liberty in the name of law and order.
"Instances could be multiplied without number of tyranny and oppression
buttressed behind the generic term of law and order. There can be no law and
order in West Virginia or any place else, until there is a restoration in all parts
of the State of those rights of mankind guaranteed by the Constitution, and no
power has ever been strong enough, or ever will be strong enough to stifle the
voice of the freeman.
"In this connection also I do not want to be misunderstood. I have no per-
sonal grievance against the present chief executive, who belongs to the same
political party to which I do; I helped to elect him; I expect to remain a Repub-
lican, but the Republican Party doesn't stand for what the present chief executive
stands for.
ABSOLUTE LANDLORDISM RAPPED
"A recent investigation has startled me beyond measure, and I want to tell
you about it. West Virginia has an area of approximately 24,000 square miles;
reduced to acreage it amounts to 15,300,000 acres; 210 corporations, none of
which owns less than 10,000 acres, own in the aggregate 6,035,936 acres.
"Add to this a million acres owned by corporations in less than 10,000-acre
tracts and you have in round numbers one-half the State owned by corporations,
the great majority of whose stockholders reside outside the State.
"This half of West Virginia, owned and controlled by nonresidents who do not
have any interest in the world in this State, or the welfare of its people and its
institutions, except to exploit it, is worth in dollars and cents five times as much
as the remaining half of West Virginia; yet the remaining half, which is owned
by the small property owner, the farmer, the small business man, the crossroads
merchant, pays twice the amount of taxes to support the State, county, schools,
municipalities, etc., as do the 7,500,000 acres owned by nonresidents.

"One-fifth the value of the State owned by the people who live in it, is paying
twice the amount of taxes of the other four-fifths owned by nonresidents. The
nonresidents who own approximately half the State in acres, and approximately
four-fifths of the State in value can well afford to spend a half million dollars
every four years to control the executive department of the State government.
"They are preparing now to spend that much next year, while the laboring
people of the State are fighting among themselves, disagreeing about insignifi-
cant matters. The landed aristocracy is carefully laying its plans to continue
its strangle hold upon the State and its people.
THE LEGISLATURE'S COMBINES
"May I refer for a moment to the last session of the legislature? The heads
of all departments appointed by the governor must be confirmed by the senate.
The senate is composed of 11 Democrats and 19 Republicans, making a total
of 30. Some of the Republican senators indicated their intention of voting
against the confirmation of the governor's recommendations, so it became
necessary for the Democrats and Republicans favorable to his appointments
to combine.
"The head of the tax system of the State is important to the landed interests
and tax dodgers. The public service commission is important to the public
utilities. A few of the coal people who have no politics except their own selfish
interests, it is said, dictated the appointment of the State tax commissioner.
"The public utilities (that is, such utilities as furnish the people with water,
light, natural gas, telephone service, etc.), it is said, dictated the appointment of
the new public-service commissioner, and the Democrats dictated the appoint-
ment of a Republican commissioner.
"In order to bring about a confirmation by the State senate of the appointment
recommended by the governor, the Democrats combined with the Republicans
in the senate, because the Democrats are to-day getting 90 per cent of the patron-
age of the road department, which amounts to more than $500,000 annually.
DEALS EXPOSED
"The public utilities joined hands with a few of the coal crowd that financed
the campaign of the present governor, and this made the organization_complete.
The public utilities named the new public-service commissioner, the Democrats
named the road commissioner, and the tax-dodging crowd named the tax com-
missioner.
"Result: The coal people, and the nonresident land owners, who own four-
fifths of the value of West Virginia, will pay less taxes in the future than they
have paid in the past. The rates for all kinds of public-utility service, such as
gas, water, electricity, telephone, etc., will be increased. The farmer and the
laborer will bear increased burdens.
"The public-service commission has a record for fixing rates that should com-
mend itself to the people of the State. It was created in 1913, I believe.
"Since that time of the hundreds of cases considered there has never been a
substantial rate decrease. They have always been increased. Of course, you
stand for it, or it wouldn't exist, and yet the remedy is in your hands. Politics
in West Virginia has become purely a business matter. Why not make it your
business?
COMPENSATION REFORM SEEN
"The workers of this State are interested in another law that affects them very
materially, and that is the workmen's compensation act.
"If a workman is killed or crippled, or incapacitated in any way from earning
a livelihood, he is entitled to compensation. My opinion is that this is a good law
in theory. In practice, in West Virginia, it is detrimental to the welfare of the
workers. He must take what the law provides; he can secure no more.
"The rates were fixed in 1913. Since that time there has been only a slight
increase, yet it is not necessary to say to you that the cost of living has increased
since that time more than 100 per cent. This law as it stands to-day operates to
the advantage of the landed aristocracy, and is detrimental in every respect
to the welfare of the worker who happens to be injured in the hazardous employ-
ment in which he is engaged. The rates should be very materially increased
In fact, they should be increased in the same proportion as the cost of living has
increased since the law was enacted.
