CALL TO DUTY SOUNDED
"There are many other questions that could be discussed with interest to the
people of this State, and to the welfare of the worker, but time forbids. I would
like to suggest that each and every individual who earns his bread by the sweat
of his brow-farmer, laborer, mechanic or otherwise get ready for the coming
conflict next year.
"Not only get ready but get together. There can be nothing effectively done
without organization. If the coal miners of this State alone would organize
politically as effectively as they have organized their unions, the whole of West
Virginia could be organized in 12 months. All the unions of West Virginia
should get together politically.
"You should use the same weapon to promote your interests and welfare as
the exploiters use to promote theirs. They use the political machinery of the
State to promote and to protect their interests. Why don't you take it over to
promote yours?
"They not only use the political machinery of the State to protect their
interests, but they use you along with it. They vote you to support their cause.
"The one sure, complete and effective remedy for the laborers of West Virginia
is through the ballot box. You must organize and vote your sentiments col-
lectively, if you expect to get anywhere. If the opposition can continue to dis-
organize you, as they have in the past, your efforts will be as futile in the future as
they have been in the past.
"If conditions in Logan County are to be remedied—yes, more—if conditions
in Logan County are to be prevented from spreading into other sections of the
State, the people must do it, you must do it, and if you allow next year to pass
without making the power of your collective action felt in West Virginia, and
without wresting the control of the State from the plunderers who now have it,
then conditions will grow worse instead of better.
"Further, I do not want to be misunderstood. Politically I do not have an
ambition in the world. As I said, I am a Republican, but I have no sympathy
with the way the Republican Party to-day is conducting things in this State.
I am interested in West Virginia. I am interested in its welfare, and in its
future, and I would like to see the people of this State control the State.
"I would like to see the nonresident landowners compelled to pay their just
share of the taxes. I would like to see the burdens made a little lighter for the
man who toils. I would like to see the gleam of hope brighten the faces of men,
women, and children who toil in the mines, in the shops, and in the fields.
would like to see them assert themselves and take back the reins of government.
This is my only purpose and my only hope. It is up to you.'

Mr. BITTNER. Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of the committee, we
have living in barracks at this time, erected by the United Mine
Workers of America, in northern West Virginia approximately 1,000
families. They have lived there on an average of practically three
years. As I have said, the strike has been in effect for nearly four
years, and those families that were evicted, 1,000 of them at least,
are at the present time living in barracks erected by the United
Mine Workers of America.
Evictions to my mind are cruel under the best of circumstances. I
really can not give a picture to this committee of the situation that


===== [扫描序号 166] =====
1188
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
exists there. Words are inadequate to describe what that means;
when 1,000 families are not only out of work because they will not
become parties to abrogating their wage agreement, when they are
not only subject to the process of starvation, but when they are
thrown out of the only home that they know I say, that condition
is bad enough under the best of circumstances. But when mine
guards and mine owners deliberately throw people out of their
homes, on the hillsides of that State, without any court order of
any kind, then it becomes nothing less than barbarism, a relic of
the Dark Ages.
Some of the things that we can describe to you which have taken
place in this process of eviction are unbelievable to the outsider, to
one who is not on the ground, and who does not really understand
those conditions. For instance, in June, 1924, the Brady-Warner Co.,
an Ohio concern, and that is competing with itself, evicted its miners
without any court order whatsoever. In other words they hired a
bunch of gunmen and thugs, and sent them down to their mining
camp at Brady, and simply threw the people out in wholesale order.
There is one particular case that I want to refer to, and that is the
case of Mrs. J. H. Norton. Mrs. Norton was in a delicate condition
the day that they began throwing families out of their homes. She
had a letter from her familiy physician, Doctor Coombs, stating the
condition she was in. When those mine guards, with one of the
owners of the mine, Samuel Brady himself, came to her house to throw
out the furniture, she handed Mr. Brady this letter from Doctor
Coombs telling of her delicate condition. Mr. Brady, in the usual
gunman style, although he is not a gunman himself, but he employed
gunmen and was there with them, and please pardon the language,
simply told her after she handed him this letter, "To hell with your
condition. You are going out of this house." And she was thrown
out of the house and as a result of that the child was born dead.
Doctor Coombs and his assistant both declared that there was no
question in their minds that that action was the cause of the death
of the child. That case is now pending in the Federal court, where
for some reason or other, we have been unable to get a hearing, since
June, 1924. Something has always happened.
The CHAIRMAN. What is the nature of the case?
Mr. BITTNER. It is a damage suit against the company for their
action in that particular case. I do not want to summons Mrs.
Morton and the doctors here before your committee, but if the com-
mittee desires it we can easily accommodate you.
But that case just shows the method used, that humanity was not
taken into consideration at all. The matter of a court order was not
taken into consideration. Law and order were brushed aside, the
civil law as well as the moral law, in the eviction of those people.
While that is more or less an extraordinary case, yet there are other
cases of which that is typical. The committee can find many cases
more or less of that nature in West Virginia if they desire to go into
that matter.

[On letterhead of Local Union No. 4040 of the United Mine Workers of America, Brady, W. Va.]
On the 2d day of January, 1924, was the time that Mrs. J. H. Morton became
pregnant; first felt life on the 13th day of May, 42 months, and felt life con-
tinually until the 19th day of May; was being attended by Dr. F. B. Coombs and
she was subject to attacks of gallstone colic, owing to her condition. Prior to
May 19 Doctor Coombs wrote a letter to whom it may concern stating, and
warning anyone, that Mrs. Morton should not be excited or exerted in any way.
The condition she was in made it very dangerous for her to be excited, and over
my protests to Samuel D. Brady, representing the Brady-Warner Coal Corpora-
tion, my wife and six children were forcibly evicted from the house at Brady.
In protecting her as far as I could to prevent eviction I locked all of the doors and
by Sam Brady's orders my door was smashed open by three of Sam Brady's mine
guards and my furniture thrown out by Sam Brady and his son, Dunlap Brady,
and five colored men employed by him. All of this mentioned was done without
the process of law. When told of the condition of my wife at that time Sam Brady
said she looked as healthy as he. As a result of his actions, on the morning of the
2d day of August, 1924, my wife gave birth to a dead girl baby that had been dead
since the 19th of May, the day she was evicted from her home. Owing to the
condition of the dead child, my wife at this time is in very grave danger.
My wife was attended by Doctor Cox, of Shinston, and later was examined by
Dr. F. B. Coombs, of Morgantown. The dead baby is now in the possession of
Dr. F. B. Coombs.
This is a list of the names of people who seen the condition of Mrs. J. H.
Morton on May 19, 1924, the day that she was removed from her house at
Brady: Mrs. Schuller and Mr. Schuller, Mrs. Charles Rickard, Sheriff Yost,
Mrs. Leon Antrim, Mrs, Henry Howell, Mrs. James Gillespie, Mr. William
Thompson, R. M. Williams, James McLeary, J. L. Studdard, Mrs. John Moreau,
and Mrs. Anton Moreau.

Mr. TOWNSEND. I can answer that question, Senator. After this
order was entered the question was taken under consideration by
counsel representing the United Mine Workers of America, counsel
at Pittsburgh and counsel at Indianapolis. This hearing was had
on the 4th of December, 1927, and the order was entered on the 17th
of December. In that order Judge Hough allowed the miners to
occupy the houses until the 1st of April, 1928. That perhaps was as
long as they could have occupied the houses if they had proceeded
under the law regulating landlord and tenant. The United Mine
Workers' organization had so many appeals of different kinds on
hand from so many different sources-they were not as flush alto-
gether at that time as they had been at other times, and they decided,
after fully considering the matter, that Judge Hough had been liberal
as to time, and they would drop the matter at that and would not
take the appeal, because in the end it meant very little to them so
far as the occupancy of the houses was concerned.

FOUR TESTIFY IN MINE CASE ON SECOND DAY
SANFORD SNYDER AND ISH BARNES, UNITED MINE WORKERS' LEADERS ON WITNESS
STAND IN CONTEMPT CASE ENGENDERED BY RECENT INJUNCTION-ARGUMENTS
PRESENTED JUDGE GIVES ADDRESS-DECISION IN THE CASE EXPECTED LATE
THIS AFTERNOON-JUDGE EXPLAINS ALL PHASES OF CONTROVERSY IN HIS
ADDRESS
Attorney Charles Goodwin, one of the members of counsel for the plaintiffs
in the case against union mine leaders and individuals charged with violating
the terms of an injunction issued by Judge Lazzelle against persons restraining
them from interfering with the mine, concluded his argument at 2 o'clock this
afternoon. Judge Lazzelle then began an address in which he covered all phases
of the situation. It was expected that a decision would be given late this after-
Loon.
The second day of trial of seven persons charged with violating an injunction
issued by Judge I. Grant Lazzelle, July 17, restraining officials of the United
Mine Workers of America, employees of the Monongahela Valley Coal Co. of
Scotts Run and other persons from interfering with the operation of the com-
pany's mine, was begun this morning. At 11 o'clock both sides rested, and the
argument of the conusel was begun. A feature of the trial this morning was the
statement of Judge Lazzelle threatening to send Attorney Eugene H. Long to jail
for contempt of court.
Attorney T. C. Townsend, of Charleston, chief counsel for the United Mine
Workers of America, was not present this morning, having had a previous engage-
ment, as he explained to the court yesterday afternoon. His place was taken by
Attorney Walter R. Haggerty, of Fairmont, who assisted Attorney Long in the
conduct of the case for the defendants. Attorneys Charles A. Goodwin, Robert
E. Guy, of Morgantown, and Judge E. M. Showalter, represented the coal
company.
FOUR WITNESSES
Only four witnesses for the defense were put on the stand, including Sanford
Snyder, in charge of union activities for the United Mine Workers of America,
and Ish Barnes, international representative. The examination of these two
witnesses consumed almost two hours. Henry Berkhammer, an official of the
mine workers union and George Devers, a member, were the others.


===== [扫描序号 188] =====
1210
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Snyder denied that he had instructed women to oil up guns and prepare
boiling water to prevent evictions, or that he had stated "they would wade
through blood to win this strike."
On cross-examination by Attorney Goodwin, Snyder stated that he has been
in the county for the past three and a half months, and again reiterated his
statement that he did not advise any persons to oil up guns or to provide boiling
water to prevent evictions. His business, he admitted, is partly to induce
nonunion miners to join the United Mine Workers of America. He denied
saying in a speech that "we will close down these mines, then go up the Monon-
gahela River."
RECEIVED PROMISES
On April 12, he stated, he was promised by both the sheriff and the prosecut-
ing attorney that there would be no illegal evictions. He denied having done
anything since the issuance of the injunction, July 17, which could be con-
strued as a violation of that law. He did admit, however, that he was present
every morning since that date in front of the mine which the Monongahela Coal
Co. leases from the Gilbert-Davis Coal Co., but stated that he merely circulated
among the people assembled, and assisted the sheriff's officers in keeping the
road clear for traffic.
The sensation of the morning came when Attorney Long was examining Ish
Barnes. The attorney asked the witness if it was not the policy of the United
Mine Workers of America to prevent the coal operators from abrogating their
agreements with the union. At this point the attorney was interrupted by Judge
Lazzelle, who warned him that another attempt to elicit an answer to such a ques-
tion would cause his incarceration in the jail.

in said county on the charge of driving an automobile while intoxicated, was
placed in the town jail at Monongah and not allowed to give bond; that affiant
was kept in said jail overnight and all the following day and late in the evening
brought to Fairmont by an officer of the Consolidation Coal Co. and two State


===== [扫描序号 190] =====
1212
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
police; that said two State police wanted to take affiant before a justice of the
peace to give bond for affiant's appearance for trial, but said Consolidation Coal
Co. officer, whose right name is to affiant unknown, but who went by the name
of "Pistol Pete," insisted that affiant be placed in jail, but the jailer of said
county refused to accept affiant as a prisoner under such circumstances, and
affiant was taken before a justice of the peace where he gave bond for trial at a
future date. Affiant says he was not guilty of the charge preferred against him
by the officer of the Consolidation Coal Co., and that affiant appeared before
said justice of the peace several times ready for trial, but the State was never
ready for trial, and after several appearances on the part of affiant ready for
trial, the said case against him was finally dismissed.
Affiant further says that he was arrested at Watson in said county and State by
Deputy Sheriffs Digman and Charles Bartholow, two well-known officers opposed
to organized labor; that affiant was never given trial in said case and he does
not know with what he was charged and never could find out, although he was
required to give bond in the penalty of $1,000 to appear before the grand jury to
answer an indictment which the officers claimed would be for passing union litera-
ture, whatever offense that may be.
Affiant further says that while attending a union meeting at Shinnston in
Harrison County, W. Va., affiant was kicked by a State policeman; that said
Captain Brown of the State police was present and affiant made complaint to
him about said treatment on the part of one of his police officers, but without any
results.
Affiant further says that he was arrested at Kilarm in Harrison County by State
police and taken to Clarksburg, where he was required to give bond for his appear-
ance before a justice of the peace for trial or hearing; that affiant does not know
why he was arrested, but on the return day affiant appeared before said justice
of the peace and could find no one to prosecute him, so said justice directed
affiant to return home as there was no charge against affiant.
Affiant further says that all these arrests were made after said C. W. Brown
proposed to affiant that he join the forces of the Consolidation Coal Co. and at
the same time remain a member of the United Mine Workers of America and
secure information for said coal company, and preach violence to members of the
United Mine Workers of America and in their local unions, and after affiant
refused to accept said employment, and after said Brown told affiant that he,
affiant, would be arrested and placed in jail.
Affiant further says that he was never convicted or even tried for any of said
alleged violations of the law, but believes that said C. W. Brown, chief of police
officers for said Consolidation Coal Co. caused the arrest of affiant in each instance,
because affiant refused to accept employment from said Consolidation Co. as
aforesaid.
Affiant further says that he knows of many assaults being committed and
insults heaped upon men belonging to the United Mine Workers of America in
and around Fairmont in said county and State, which he has not here related, all
because they belonged to said organization and refused to take employment from
the said Consolidation Coal Co. and take a stand against union labor.
FRED STUBBS.

Mr. BITTNER. To show you just how these mine guards work, here
is an affidavit from a mine guard that I want to make a part of the
record and would like to read the affidavit [reading]:
STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA,
County of Monongalia, to wit:
W. E. Bailes, being by the undersigned authority first duly sworn, deposes and
says in answer to interrogatories propounded to him by Sanford Snyder:
Q. What is your name?-A. W. E. Bailes.
Q. What is your business?-A. Merchant at Mona, Monongalia County,
W. Va.
Q. When did you come to Monongalia County?-A. 1923.
Q. By whom were you first employed?-A. William Yost.
Q. Who was William Yost?-A. Sheriff of Monongalia County.
Q. What did he employ you to do?-A. To guard Shriver mine, and the houses
there who were employed by the Continental Coal Co.
Q. Who paid you for the work?-A. The Continental Coal Co.
Q. How long did you work there?-A. Six or seven months.
Q. Where did you go from there?-A. To the Brady-Warner Coal Co. at
Osage, Monongalia County.


===== [扫描序号 196] =====
1218
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Q. What did you do there?-A. Guarded mine.
Q. Were there any evictions there during the time you were so employed?—A.
Yes.
Q. How many families were evicted?—A. Sixty-one.
Q. Tell me in your own words what happened during these evictions.-A. We
went to the company boarding house; knocked on the door. People occupying
it told us that they were getting ready to move, and would be out in a short time;
Superintendent Rucker asked Sheriff William Yost what to do, but Yost refused to
advise him; Rucker told us to go ahead and kick down door and move furniture
out; we did so, and placed it out on the county road. We had 20 or 30 men to
carry the furniture. We were armed with revolvers and blackjacks. I had a
license to carry a gun. Company got it for me as soon as I went to work.
Q. Was there any disorder; if so, state what happened.-A. There was no
disorder at that time. We were armed and there were so many of us that the
people were afraid to say anything. The next day, however, we were getting
ready to evict some people who lived in the bottom, a man said something to us,
and Superintendent Rucker told Claude Conaway, our chief guard, to go ahead
and whip him. We drew our guns and held the crowd back, while Conaway
whipped the man. The superintendent then sent Conaway to Morgantown where
he paid a small fine. The sheriff was notified about, the matter, but when he
reached the scene he told us that it was the best thing that could have happened.
Q. You say you and the other guards were always armed.
Where did you get
the weapons?-A. They were furnished by the company. Warren Cook, the
company clerk, delivered them, together with the shells.
Q. What kind of weapons were you armed with?-A. We had revolvers,
sawed-off shotguns, rifles, and submachine guns.
Q. How many machine guns did you have?-A. Ten or twelve.
Q. Do you recall any other trouble?-A. Yes. I was sent to Morgantown to
meet a truck loaded with a strike breaker's furniture. When I met him I gave
him a 30-30 rifle and told him to use it if anyone tried to make him turn back.
When we got to the bridge in Osage a Studebaker car was stalled on the bridge.
The truck driver jumped from the truck and ran to the car, and struck the
driver over the hands and arms with the rifle. We pushed the car off the bridge.
I fired two shots, and the other guards rushed to the road with machine guns.
No one attempted to interfere with us. Sheriff Yost arrested the man who had
the Studebaker car, but the court turned him loose.
Q. Did you consult any attorney about this trouble?-A. Yes. Claude
Conaway and I went to Morgantown to see Charles Goodwin, attorney for the
company, and he told us that the company was getting an injunction, and for
us to stay with the company even if we had to shoot the union men down and
pile them up like crossties.
Q. Why did you leave Osage?-A. Because Superintendent Rucker would fire
his gun in the dark and then spread the report that the union men were shooting
at him, and in this way kept trouble stirred up.
Q. After you left there where did you go?-A. I went guarding for a company
at Barricksville.
Q. Did you have any trouble there?-A. Well, I whipped one of the leading
union men there, and the chief guard and the company each gave me $10, and
told me to do it again if I had a chance. The company also paid my fine which
amounted to $14.60. When the deputy sheriff came after me with the warrant
he did not arrest me, but merely told me to come in when I had time.
And further deponent saith nothing.
W. E. BAILES.
Taken, subscribed, and sworn to before me this 1st day of March, 1928.
[SEAL.]
EUGENE H. LONG,
Notary public in and for Monongalia County, W. Va.
My commission expires May 8, 1933.

at that time was used also as a justice of the peace office when J. K. Murray,
chief mine guard for the said coal company and other mine guards employed by

Harry Grimm fell back into the office of the affiant; and affiant further states
on oath that he called the sheriff of Monongalia County, W. Va., and the said
sheriff, together with his deputies and in company with State police officers, came
out to the town of Osage, in the county and State aforesaid, and proceeded upon
the property of the said Brady-Warner Coal Co., and found the chief guard, J. K.
Murray, and talked to him, and the said J. K. Murray told the said sheriff that
he and the guards were shooting down toward the State highway, believing that
there was some one trespassing or encroaching on the property of the said Brady-
Warner Coal Co.; and affiant further states on oath that the sheriff and other
officers found all the mine guards had been drinking or were under the influence
of intoxicating liquor, and that no one was arrested for the aforesaid violations
of the law.

Tuesday evening, September 13, 1927, and which I should like to

OFFICERS NAB 13 FOR MANY CRIMES-INCEST IS CHARGED AGAINST TWO MEN;
LIQUOR IS FOUND POLICE CLEAN UP BEAR MOUNTAIN-DISGUSTING AND
REVOLTING CONDITIONS FOUND IN CAMP
""
Bear Mountain, characterized by State Trooper O. E. Banks, as the "
"Hell
hole of West Virginia, was the scene of a series of raids Sunday that landed 13
persons in the police dragnet, for crimes ranging from the beastly and revolting
one of incest to mere possession of home brew.
With Trooper Banks in the raiding party were Trooper A. G. Brown and Con-
stable Victor Menear. Leaving Flemington before noon Sunday with warrants
for several houses in the Bear Mountain settlement where revelry and drinking
had produced innumerable fights Saturday night, the officers went to a home
where on the previous Sunday they were informed a barrel of mash had been
consumed, and numerous disorders had been reported.
In the house they found George Snider and Frank Orba in a bedroom with
Letha Snider, a sister of George. There was evidence to cause the officers to
arrest the trio, and they later were taken to jail. As a result, the girl, who is
17 years of age, was brought to the office of Prosecuting Attorney W. Merle
Watkins to-day, and after a medical examination had been made by a physician,
she told the prosecutor, so the trooper said, that her brother George and another
brother-Ed Snider-had both been guilty of incest with her, and that Frank
Orba had had unlawful relations with her. She also named another man, an
Italian, who has not yet been apprehended for a similar crime.
Going to two other miners' shanties, the officers found Alex Howard, Howard
Henderson, Sarah Washington, Esther Adams, and Earl Nicholson all engaged
in unlawful acts. The quintette admitted their guilt before Justice of the Peace
Laco Corder at Galloway yesterday and were taken to the Barbour County
Jail to serve sentences of varying length.
In another house, according to officers, they found a Cruikshank girl, unmarried,
with a 5-months-old baby. Living with her was Earl Roy, who, the officers
say, had previously lived with a Mrs. Gentry, but tiring of her, had "kicked her
out and taken the Cruikshank girl to live with him. Because of the infant
the girl was not arrested, but the man was put in custody and will be held for
further examination.
In one house, just as, the officers arrived, a woman poured out most of the
contents of a 10-gallon jar of home brew, but the State police succeeded in saving
enough for evidence against her.
The mining section just over the Taylor County line in Barbour County is
without exception the most degenerate and lawless camp in the State, State
Trooper Banks believes. He has worked in Scotts Run and other mining com-
munities having unsavory reputations, but without qualifying his remarks said
Bear Mountain was a "Hell hole" and the worst place he had ever been in on
police duty.
Many times, according to the officers, there is so much drunkenness in the
camp that it is practically impossible to drive along the road through the mass of
fighting and intoxicated persons swarming along the highway. Saturday night,
residents of a better class reported many flagrant disorders and law violations
to the police, the latter said. Sunday morning a hurried trip was made to the
section from headquarters in Flemington, and the revolting and beastly condi-
tions mentioned above were found.
For a time, there were 13 persons landed in the Flemington jail from Bear
Mountain. The jail was quickly emptied, however, when Constable Victor
Menear picked up a runaway boy from the Pruyntytown Industrial School,
who was broken out with smallpox. The constable did not apparently know of
the boy's diseased condition, and put him in the Flemington lockup with the
Bear Mountain prisoners. He was there only a short time when his condition
was known to many of the prisoners, who made a complaint. The boy was
returned to the school, and the exposed persons taken to Philippi and Grafton
for vaccination.
George and Ed Snider, their sister, Letha, George Baxter, and Frank Orba are
all held in the Taylor County Jail for the action of the grand jury. The remaining
number of the original group are in the Barbour County Jail serving time.
The raid is one of the biggest pulled off in this section in a long time.

To the Strike Investigating Committee of the United States Senate.
GENTLEMEN: We desire to inform you that, as elected officers of the town of
Monongah, which is a coal-mining center in northern West Virginia, that the
Consolidation Coal Co., whose president is Mr. C. W. Watson, and Mr. John
D. Rockefeller, jr., is a heavy stockholder, did everything in their power to
control our actions as town officials during the time we served in office, when
this company abrogated its contract with the United Mine Workers of America,
and evicted the miners and their wives and children from their homes.
Mr. Tusca Morris, attorney for the Consolidation Coal Co., as well as Mr.
Wolf, who was superintendent of the Consolidation Coal Co.'s mines at that
time, made offers to pay us a stipulated monthly salary and insured us we would
be reelected if we would carry on our various offices according to the mandates of
of the Consolidation Coal Co. and would assist in every way possible to destroy
the United Mine Workers of America. We spurned every effort made by the
representatives of the Consolidation Coal Co. and informed these men that we
would conduct these offices according to our oath and hand out equal handed
justice to all.
Owing to the large number of nonunion men imported into Monongah by the
coal company, we were defeated for office at a subsequent election. At the
present time, although Monongah is an incorporated town, every policeman in
the town is being paid by the Consolidation Coal Co. and are acting as mine
guards and nothing more.
This statement is made to the Senate investigating committee to show just what
methods are being used by the Consolidation Coal Co. to control the officers who
administer local government, in order that organized labor at the mines might
destroyed.
Taken, subscribed and sworn to before me this 29th day of February, 1928.

Senator WHEELER. What do the coal companies do down there in
the elections, with reference to controlling elections generally, State
and national?
Mr. BITTNER. Senator Wheeler, in these nonunion camps they con-
trol the votes of the miners the same as they control their wages and
working conditions. If the men do not vote the way the superin-
tendent orders them to vote, why they are immediately discharged;
and very few of them are discharged, because they have not the
manhood to assert themselves and vote any way other than the way
that the superintendent asks them to vote. That is the general
condition in these nonunion mining camps.
Senator GOODING. Do they have the secret ballot down in West
Virginia?
Mr. BITTNER. Yes, sir; but they have a way of finding out even
under those circumstances. In fact, so far as the legal ballot is con-
cerned it is secret, but so far as the process of voting is concerned there
is a method by which the coal companies know just exactly how their
men vote.

Senator WHEELER. How do they find that out if the ballot is

Mr. BITTNER. Well, they find it out when they count the votes. If

way of their own of finding out who it was that voted against the
dictates of the coal company.
Senator WHEELER. Do they control the personnel of the election

Mr. BITTNER. Oh, absolutely. They really understand their busi-

system that they have.

Mr. BITTNER. Mr. Chairman, there are a number of affidavits
and statements here relative to the case of Pasquale Loria, of Gallo-
way, W. Va. I think this case is the most brutal crime ever com-
mitted in the United States. Pasquale Loria was one of the strikers,
an Italian, a citizen of the United States, and was arrested on Janu-
ary 3, 1926, for some altercation he had had with one of the men
who was working at the mine of the Simpson Creek Collieries Co.
The man was arrested by the State police, who took him down to
a justice of the peace; and it was on Sunday, I think, and he did not
want to hold a trial that day and the man was only charged with a
misdemeanor, so the justice of the peace, knowing the man well,
and he says in his affidavit here that he had known him for 12 years,
told him to go home and come back at 10 o'clock Monday morning
to be tried. That was the arrangement. Thereafter the two State
police who had arrested him and taken him before the justice went
to another justice of the peace and secured another warrant for the
same occurrence. They then went to his home in the mining camp
at Galloway, W. Va., the camp of the Simpson Creek Collieries Co.,
between 12 and 1 o'clock on Monday morning. They broke into
his house, and the record will show that he was shot in the back by
these policemen. His dying statement is here, the statement of his
wife, and shows that he fell over on the bed shot in the back by the
two State policemen, who shot him in that dead hour of the morning
after breaking into his house, on a warrant gotten after the original
warrant had already been attended to Sunday afternoon. The mat-
ter was taken to the grand jury in Barbour County twice, and we
failed to get any indictment against these State police. The matter
was referred to Gov. Howard Gore, and my understanding is that
these two men are still serving on the State police force of West
Virginia. That case is in substance what I have told you, but I
now furnish you the record.
(The record in the Pasquale Loria case is here made a part of the

REPORT OF THE CASE OF PASQUALE LORIA, GALLOWAY, W. Va.
My name is W. P. Samples, attorney at law, practicing in the circuit courts,
Supreme Court, and the District Court of the United States for the Northern
District of West Virginia.
On the morning of January 4, 1926, I was called by telephone and informed of
the shooting of Pasquale Loria at Galloway, Barbour County, W. Va. I im-
mediately called the prosecuting attorney at Philippi, Barbour County, W. Va.,
and informed him what I had learned about this shooting, advising him that he

had better come to Grafton and we would both make an investigation of the case,
which the prosecuting attorney of Barbour County graciously consented to, and
came with his stenographer. On their arrival at Grafton we immediately went
to the Grafton City Hospital to see Pasquale Loria, and found him in such a
condition and from the information obtained from the physician and surgeon that
he could not live but a short time, we considered it necessary to get his dying
declaration, which is herewith attached and self-explanatory. After obtaining
the statement of Pasquale Loria I got in the automobile of the prosecuting
attorney of Barbour County, and we went immediately to Galloway to his home,
where this shooting occured, investigating his home, and obtained all information
that we could from his neighbors and his little girl. We found two doors broken
down, the back door and the front door. After our investigation I made a
diagram of the rooms of his house, which is herewith attached, showing the
doors which the officers entered getting inside of the house, and the doors that
they went through in getting to the bedroom, which Pasquale Loria and his wife
were occupying, with notations thereon in explanation of our investigation,
We also found that on the evening of the 3d of January, 1926, the day prior to the
shooting, that being Sunday, near the union hall at Galloway, some nonunion
men passing along the public highway in front of the union hall some difficulty
arose there between the nonunion men and Pasquale Loria, Gus Myers, L. D.
Philipps, Kirk Cleavenger, George Skidmore, and E. Z. Marple, all being union
men. Pasquale Loria struck a nonunion man by the name of C. M. Robinson in
the face with his hand, being the only lick struck by anyone in that controversy.
The State police who were present went to the office of Laco Corder, justice of the
peace of Barbour County, W. Va., located near Galloway, and asked him for a
warrant for assault and battery for Pasquale Loria, and that the justice informed
him after ascertaining that he had seen the difficulty he did not need a warrant,
and that the State police made arrangements with him then to bring Pasquale
Loria before him at 10 o'clock a. m. on the next day, Monday, being January 4,
1926, but instead the State police went to Philippi, 18 miles away, and obtained a
warrant from Ben. M. Wilson, a justice of the peace of Barbour County, W. Va.,
against Pasquale Loria, Gus Myers, L. D. Philipps, Kirk Cleavenger, George
Skidmore, and E. Z. Marple, charging them with conspiracy, a copy of which is
herewith attached, and that this was the warrant they were executing the night of
the shooting. After said investigation I advised a warrant to be sworn out for the
two State policemen, S. B. Murphy and Troy Alkire, who committed this crime.
A warrant was sworn out before Ben. M. Wilson, justice of the peace of Barbour
County, and they were held to answer the action of the next grand jury convening
at Philippi, Barbour County, W. Va., at which term of court Pasquale's wife and
daughter and other witnesses that had any knowledge of this offense were sum-
moned to appear before the grand jury and no indictment was returned against
the two policemen, but instead thereof two indictments were returned against
Pasquale Loria, copies of which are herewith attached. Immediately after the
grand jury reported I moved the judge of the circuit court to hold the two police-
men under bond to answer the action of the next grand jury, which motion the
court granted, and the men were placed under bond. The same witnesses
appeared again before the grand jury and no indictment was returned. The
reason for not returning indictments against these men I am unable to say,
but I have come to the conclusion that an indictment against these men could not
be obtained in Barbour County, W. Va.
I also obtained statements from Dr. S. D. Hays and Laco B. Corder, justice of

Question asked by W. P. Samples, attorney for the United Mine Workers
of America, at Grafton, W. Va.
Q. Mr. Corder, I believe you are a justice of the peace in Barbour County,
and was such at the time that Pasquale Loria had some little trouble with non-
union men at Galloway on Sunday, in which it was alleged that Pasquale Loria
slapped C. M. Robinson in the face, and that afterwards he surrendered himself
to you, I will have you state what you know about that trouble, if anything.-
A. I was.
I had been in Taylor County visiting, my wife and I, and as I came
back through Galloway I heard of a fight between Pasquale Loria and C. M.
Robinson, and I met the State police on the road and they asked me if I would
issue a warrant on Sunday, and I told them that it was according to the circum-
stances. I asked them what kind of a warrant they wanted and they said just
for a little assault and battery. I asked them if they had seen the fight and they
said they had, and I told the State police that they didn't need no warrant, and
the State police made arrangements with me to bring Pasquale Loria to my place
on Monday at 10 o'clock. After I went home Pasquale Loria came to my place
and wanted to confess to assault and battery, and I told him the State police had
made arrangements with me to deliver him there on Monday morning at 10 o'clock
and he went home satisfied. When I got up next morning I heard that Pasquale
Loria had been shot by the State police between 12 and 1 o'clock at night. I
went down to Galloway and made an investigation and found that he had been
brutally murdered, and arriving at his home I found that the panels in the back
door and front door had been kicked out and that the door latches had been
bursted off, and Pasquale's daughter told me after her father had been shot that
the State police had taken his revolver from his holster and shot directly through
the wall, to make it appear that Pasquale had done so, and his daughter further
stated that Pasquale was putting his pants on, and had his back to the State
police when he was shot.
Now, I had known Pasquale Loria for 20 years and had never known him to
be in trouble in no way, shape or form, and always found him to be a clean and
honest man in all of his duties.
After hearing that he had been shot and investigating the case I did not issue
no warrant for the arrest of Pasquale Loria.
LACO B. CORDER.
QUESTION ASKED DR. S. D. HAYS BY W. P. SAMPLES, ATTORNEYS FOR THE UNITED
MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA, AT GRAFTON, W. VA.
Question. Doctor Hays, as I understand, you are familiar with and know
something about the trouble of Pasquale Loria at Galloway, Barbour County,
W. Va., and that you were called to administer medical service to Pasquale Loria,
the night that he was shot, to wit: January 4, 1926. I will ask you to state in
detail what you know about that affair?
Answer. I was mine physician for the Simpson Creek Collieries Co., Barbour
County, W. Va., at Galloway, also justice of the peace, being duly elected of
Pleasant district, Barbour County, W. Va., to that office. On the afternoon of
January 3, 1926, Pasquale Loria came to my office, and asked to have one man
arrested for calling him a "hunky
-." I asked him what had


===== [扫描序号 205] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1227
occurred and he told me that he struck a man with his left fist for calling him this
name. I advised him not to have any warrant issued for this man, but to wait
for further development. He left my office later, not less than 10 minutes after-
wards, stating that the State police had accosted him and notified him to go before
Laco Corder for trial on Monday morning, January 4, 1926. I told him to go
with me, as I was going to Squire Corder's office at that time, which he did.
Squire Corder placed him under his own recognizance, and told him to return at
10 o'clock Monday morning, January 4, 1926. I took Pasquale Loria back to
his residence and advised him to not leave his house during that evening and
night. I advised him that I believed the State police and the company were
going to frame some trouble, and that if he left the house he was likely to be
injured or arrested in some way, as I felt something was going to happen, as that
mine was going to open up on an open-shop basis on January 4, 1926. The State
police had held him, Pasquale Loria, under a misdemeanor charge. He had
given himself up as stated to Squire Corder and was waiting trial. Troy Alkire
came that evening, January 3, 1926, went to the home of the man whom Pasquale
Loria had difficulty with, and took this man before another justice, at Philippi,
Barbour County, W. Va., about 18 miles away, and framed a "red mans warrant'
against this man, Pasquale Loria, at the instance of the coal company's request,
and after midnight raiding the home of Ezekiel Marple, arrested him on this
warrant, went to the home of Pasquale Loria and broke his doors, two of them,
breaking the hinges, splitting the doors from top to bottom, at 1 o'clock a. m.,
January 4, 1926, in the night time, and shot Pasquale Loria through the abdomen
from his back, piercing his intestines seven times. As soon as Pasquale Loria
was shot the police notified me at my residence in Galloway, W. Va. I, at once,
went to Pasquale's home, in about 15 or 20 minutes from the time he was shot.
I went into his bedroom and finding no one that appeared to be injured, I asked
for the wounded man and was pointed to one corner of the room, where a man lay
unattended, apparently dead. After hurriedly examining him I turned to the
policeman and said: "You have shot this man in the back. What right did you
have here?" And Troy Alkire replied, We have a felony warrant." I said,
"Produce the warrant. You had no right to come here. This man was under
arrest for a misdemeanor charge." He produced his warrant, stating that he had
secured a "red mens warrant" for this man, and as he entered the room he
stated that Pasquale Loria had fired a shot at them, the State police, showing me
where the shot had hit the wall. I told him that "You have no right here at all
for a trifling offense as a misdemeanor charge." He said, "We have secured a
felony warrant against him, and attempted to make an arrest. I stated that,
"You have shot this man in the back and his wounds are evidently fatal,
" and
it so proved. I learned at once that Troy Alkire, a police, and Murphy, State
policemen, had broken into his room, and when he offered to defend his home and
bedroom against these men breaking into his home, not knowing who was enter-
ing the house. He stated to me that when he saw that they were going to shoot
him he had turned his back and they had shot him, the bullet had entered at the
small of his back on the left side of the spine, just below the stomach, piercing the
intestines seven times, and came out in the region of the abdomen not far from
the umbilicus or navel. I at once removed Pasquale Loria to a local hospital at
Grafton, W. Va., a distance of about 17 miles, securing help of local physicians
and operated upon him at once, the operation being performed about 4 o'clock
a. m., January 4, 1926. Later Pasquale Loria died from this gunshot wound.
State Police Murphy fired the shot at Pasquale Loria, while State Police Alkire
was entering the room just in front of him. I found Pasquale Loria in his night
clothes, and that they had gone into his bedroom before he had time to place his
clothes on, and had shot him in the back, wounding him seriously, which later
caused his death.
66
""
I have known Pasquale Loria for the past 10 or 12 years. He was known to
be a good law-abiding citizen. I have talked before and since to a great many
citizens of the neighborhood and county, and they have all stated that they knew
Pasquale Loria to be one of the best Italians and one of the best men of that
community, and as I have stated before, being justice of the peace of Pleasant
district, Barbour County, W. Va., and know the habits of the State police of
framing warrants in cases against these men, I had advised him to stay at home
fearing that they might frame a warrant against him, which they did; yet to be
intruded upon in his own home, in his bedroom at the hour of 1 o'clock in the
morning, and shot to death by West Virginia State police at the instance of the
coal company.
S. D. HAYS, M. D.,
Former Justice of Peace.

STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA,
County of Marion, to wit:
This day personally appeared before the undersigned authority, one William
Slaughter, who, being by me first duly sworn, upon his oath deposes and says,
that he is 63 years of age and has lived and resided in said county and State for
the past 45 years; that affiant has been working in and around coal mines for the
past 50 years; that affiant worked some 12 or 14 years at the Dakota mines of
the Bethlehem Mines Corporation, and was working at said mines when said
Bethlehem Mines Corporation abrogated its contract with the United Mine
Workers of America in 1924.
Affiant further says that during the month of November, 1924, and while
affiant lived at Dakota, affiant was going from his home to the United States
post office at Dakota for the purpose of receiving his mail; that while on the road
from his said home affiant met one Charles Hauns whom affiant afterwards
learned to be a mine guard for said Bethlehem Mines Corporation, but whom
affiant did not know at that time. Said Hauns inquired of affiant if he, affiant,
was William Slaughter and affiant replied in the affirmative, whereupon said
Hauns attacked affiant and assaulted and beat him with something on his hand,
which affiant believes to have been a pair of steel knuckles, although affiant did
not see exactly what weapon said Hauns had in his hands. Said Hauns hit
affiant three times in the face and around the head and knocked affiant to the
ground. Affiant says he never before saw said Hauns and does not know why
he asaulted affiant because affiant had done nothing whatever to said Hauns,
nor did he do anything to any other person that would cause a mine guard to
attack him. Affiant further says that said Hauns was arrested for said assault
and fined by J. L. Blocher, justice of the peace; but affiant is advised and believes
that said fine was never collected by said justice of the peace from said Hauns
and was never paid by said Hauns, and that no attempt whatever was made to
inforce the collection of said fine, although said Hauns was in the court of said
justice of the peace when said fine was imposed. Affiant says that he is informed
that the docket of said justice of the peace shows that said fine was never paid.
WILL SLAUGhter.

he was informed by mine guards in the employ of the said various coal companies
that if he had any business on their property that he should first come to the
offices of the said various coal companies and obtain permission from officials
of said companies before proceeding upon their property. Further the affiant
states under oath that on numerous occasions he had search and seizure warrants,
properly issued by the proper authorities, and that in executing the said search
and seizure warrants, mine guards employed by the coal companies aforesaid,
as aforesaid, would halt him in the execution of the said warrants, and so hinder
said execution of the same by pretext, etc., until other mine guards had sufficient
time to go through the camps, or to go to the premises for which he had search and
seizure warrants and advise the occupants of the houses in which search was to be
made that the law was coming, and would help said occupants to clean up and de-
stroy such evidence as may have been in their possession constituting a violation of
the law. Further the affiant states under oath that in making legal attachments
of property situate on property belonging to the coal companies that officials of
the various companies would advise him and did advise him that the property
belonging to the individual for which attachment was had was the property of the
coal companies, and affiant further states under oath that in discharging his lawful
duties the officials of the various coal companies on numerous occasions hindered
him in so doing, and misrepresented and concealed material facts so that the ends
of justice were defeated. Further the affiant states under oath that in one in-
stance he went upon the premises of one of the coal companies into one of their
camps to repossess some property and that he was advised by the mine guard
on duty that unless he, the affiant had proper papers he could not come upon the
premises, and gave as his only reason for refusing admittance otherwise that he,
the mine guard intended to keep everyone from trespassing upon the property
he was guarding, and that on several other occasions he, the affiant, was called
into different and various mining camps of the various coal companies to stop
fights and other violations of the law, and that upon such occasions he was ad-
vised by the mine guards that he had no business there. Further the affiant
saith not.
WILLIAM L. PHILLIPS.

Coal Co., the Arkwright Coal Co., and the Gilbert-Davis Coal Co., all of whom
had been operating under the Jacksonville agreement, closed down; that on the
1st day of April, 1926, all of the said companies posted notices at their mines that
they would resume work on the 1917 scale of wages, and that all of their em-
ployees who did not intend to return to work under this scale would be evicted
on the 12th day of April, 1926; that all of the aforesaid companies employed pri-
vate guard and armed them, and commenced operations at a scale of wages which
reduced the wages of daymen $2.50 per day, and the pay of loaders 20 cents per
ton; that the armed guards of these companies abused and intimidated the
striking miners on every occasion an opportunity would afford itself, and in many
instances went to the homes of the striking miners and evicted them, placing
their household goods on the roadside; that on or about May 5, 1927, one G. C.
Dodrill and another mine guard, both being armed with revolvers and black-
jacks, went to the home of James Himes, a miner, and assaulted him and his
wife; that Mrs. Himes was in a family way, and that said assault caused a mis-
carriage and placed her under the care of a doctor for several weeks; that the said
guards were arrested and placed under bond to await the action of the grand jury,
but were never tried; that on or about October 25, 1927, seven armed guards
employed by the Purseglove Coal Mining Co. went to the home of Tony Cress,
a striking miner, just before noon when his wife was preparing dinner, and, throw-
ing the food she was preparing from the stove, removed all of his household goods
from the house and loaded it on a moving van, and hauled it to the city of Morgan-
town, W. Va., a distance of 6 miles, and placed it in the storage room of the Ma-
deria Transfer Co.; that the guards refused to tell this man where his goods had
been taken for several days, and he and his family, consisting of himself, his wife
and four small children, were compelled to seek food and shelter from his friends
and the United Mine Workers of America; that on or about the 22d day of July,
1926, this affiant and 26 other members of the United Mine Workers of America
and their wives were arrested and charged with violating an injunction order
of the circuit court of Monongalia County, W. Va., and this affiant and six

Charley McLush in an unconscious condition, and that this affiant then went

was made upon the said McLush by the said mine guard, and that neither the
said McLush nor this affiant had had any trouble with the said mine guard or
with anyone else that day, and that the said attack was entirely unprovoked
by either this affiant or the said McLush.

Affiant further states that on the morning of August 19, 1925, at about the
hour of 6.05 a. m., affiant in company with one Joe Bish, was lawfully and peace-
ably on his way to a point near Rachale mine of the Bertha Consumers Co., at
Downs, Marion County, W. Va., when one A. L. Core, a mine guard in the
employ of the said company approached affiant and asked his name; that affiant
courteously gave the information requested; that said mine guard Core then
asked where affiant lived; that affiant again courteously replied "I live in house
No. 25"; that said Mine Guard Core then used vile and abusive language toward
affiant and accused him of having thrown a rock at said Core on a preceding
morning; that said mine guard Core then immediately and before affiant had an
opportunity to answer, brutally assaulted affiant, striking him a number of times
about the head and face with such force that affiant was knocked to the grounds
that said mine guard Core then continued his murderous and brutal assault;
by kicking affiant on the legs, arms, and body; that while affiant lay prostrate

STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA,

abrogated its contract with the United Mine Workers of America in 1924.
Affiant further says that he is personally acquainted with one William Sank-
bell, chief mine guard for said Bethlehem Mines Corporation; that previous to
March 11, 1927, affiant received word from affiant's son that said Sankbell
desired to see affiant, and on said last-mentioned affiant met said Sankbell on

affiant, would not like to take employment with the Bethlehem Mines Cor-
poration and at the same time remain with the United Mine Workers of America.
Affiant asked said Sankbell what he wanted affiant to do and said Sankbell said
he wanted affiant to furnish him with the names of all the nonunion miners who
joined the union from mines of said corporation, and that affiant could make
some easy money if he, affiant, would follow said Sankbell's instructions. Affiant
asked him what he meant and he said that he, Sankbell, would furnish affiant

Affiant further says that he is personally acquainted with one William Sankbell,

Mines Corporation, with coal mines and operations at Barrackville and Dakota
in said county; that during the month of July, 1926, affiant met said Sankbell in
front of the National Bank of Fairmont, in Fairmont, W. Va., when and where
said Sankbell said to this affiant that "you," meaning affiant, "look all right,
can I talk with you." Affiant told him that he could, whereupon said Sankbell
told affiant that he did not like Mr. Bittner, who was then and is now chief repre-
sentative of the International Union United Mine Workers of America in northern
West Virginia, and that he (Sankbell) wanted to employ affiant and would furnish
him (affiant) with explosives and give him a good opportunity to blow up some
property in and around the mines of the Bethlehem Mines Corporation, so that
said corporation could get Mr. Bittner in trouble and get rid of him in this section
of the State. Affiant told said Sankbell that he would accept said employment,
and immediately reported the matter to Mr. Bittner, who told affiant not to
accept such employment as it would give the union miners in this field a bad
name and cause them trouble, whereupon affiant dismissed the matter from his
mind and did not report to said Sankbell for further instructions or to take the
employment.
Affiant further says that immediately after said Sankbell offered affiant said
employment and said affiant reported the matter to Mr. Bittner, said Sankbell,
as such chief mine guard gave instructions to the mine guards at Barrackville
and Dakota to prohibit affiant from entering the colored Baptist churches in
each of said towns and there doing his work in the Sunday schools of said re-
spective churches; that affiant went to said churches as usual on Sunday and was
prohibited from entering the same by mine guards of the Bethlehem Mines Cor-
poration who then and there advised affiant that it was the order of said Sankbell
to prohibit affiant from going into said churches, and affiant has ever since been
excluded from said churches by said mine guards and said Bethlehem Mines
Corporation.
J. H. JONES.

One of the specific cases that we have a clear record of is that of
Tony Biardo. He was arrested, found guilty of violating the prohi-
bition law, sentenced to two years in the penitentiary. He appealed
his case to the supreme court. The supreme court sustained the de-
cision of the lower court. This was about two years ago. This man
has been working at the nonunion camp of the Consolidation Coal
Co. at Monongah since that time. No bond has been forfeited, he
has not served a day in prison for the offense of which he was con-
victed, and this shows what he was allowed to do.
Senator GOODING. Is the record there?
Mr. BITTNER. Yes, sir.
Senator WHEELER. Why is that, do you know, by whose permis-
sion?
Mr. BITTNER. By the permission of the prosecuting attorney and
the criminal judge of Marion County. There has been no capias
issued for him since the supreme court handed down its decision.
And these men making the affidavits state that Biardo told them the
reason he got out of trouble was that he was told he could either go to
the penitentiary or scab, and that he would sooner scab than be in the
penitentiary. I will read it [reading]:
STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA,

This day personally appeared before the undersigned authority, a notary

That affiant is 31 years of age and has lived in the town of Monongah, in said
county and State for about eight years, and that during that time he has worked
in and around the mines of the Consolidation Coal Co. up until said coal company
abrogated its contract with the United Mine Workers of America in the year
1925.
Affiant further says that he is personally acquainted with one Tony Biardo
who is and was a coal miner for the above-named coal company and lived in
said town of Monongah, and that affiant has known him for about eight years.
Affiant further says that during the Christmas season of 1923 said Tony Biardo
was arrested at his home in Monongah by State and county officers charged
with owning and possessing a moonshine still, said moonshine still being found in
the dwelling house of said Tony Biardo. That this affiant arranged with the
proper officials of said county to take bond for said Biardo's release from jail and
his appearance to answer any indictment that might be returned against him by
the grand jury of the criminal court of said county at its January term, 1924, and
said Biardo was released from jail and allowed to go on bond as above mentioned.
Affiant further says that he knows that said Biardo was indicted by said
criminal court grand jury at its January term, 1924, charging said Biardo with
being the owner and operator of a moonshine still, which was and is a felony;
this being on January 10, 1924, as affiant is advised.
Affiant further says that he personally knows that said Tony Biardo was put
upon trial in said criminal court of said county under said felony charge, and affiant
is advised that the court records show that said trial was had upon January
18, 1924; that said Biardo was convicted by a jury on the same date of the felony
charge contained in said indictment, and said Tony Biardo was then and there
sentenced by the criminal court to serve two years in the penitentiary at Mounds-
ville; that said Biardo gave bond in the penalty of $2,500 to suspend said sentence
in order to take his case to the appellate court; that affiant is told all the above
matters appear of record in the criminal court of said county and are recorded in
law order book of said court, No. 3; that said record further shows that on March
18, 1924, said criminal court, or the judge thereof, signed certain bills of excep-
tions and said case was appealed or presented to the circuit court of Marion
County, W. Va., which said last named court refused to grant said Biardo a writ
of error and supersedeas, and that from said last named decision said Biardo
attempted to take his case to the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia;
that affiant is told that said Biardo did present his case to said last named court

themselves recognize the agreement made by the coal operators'
association with the United Mine Workers of America. This "yellow-
dog" contract says, among other things:
And for the consideration aforesaid I hereby waive any and all rights that I
may have under and by virtue of a certain agreement between the membership
of the United Mine Workers of America and the membership of the Northern
West Virginia Coal Operators' Association dated March 28, 1924.
So you will see that first they abrogate their contract and then
compel a man to sign a "yellow-dog" contract waiving his rights to
all the benefits under the contract between the United Mine Workers
of America and the Northern West Virginia Coal Operators' Associa-
tion.

Mr. BITTNER. Now Mr. Chairman, the statement was made here
as to conditions in the nonunion camps, and I have a report from a
poor director of one of the districts in northern West Virginia, which
I should like to read. But first I want to say this about the situation:
The men in the nonunion mining camps of northern West Virginia
and their families are in worse condition than our own people, although
our people have been out on strike for four years, and have gone


===== [扫描序号 233] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1255
through hell, we might say, during those four years. In other words
in spite of that fact our people are not to-day as bad off as the non-
union workman in these mining camps in northern West Virginia.
I want to read this statement made by David H. Jarrett, one of the
poor directors of the county.
Senator GOODING. What county is that?
Mr. BITTNER. Marion County, W. Va. This is one poor district
of that county-well, while it is known in the county organization as
a poor district, yet you might take it any way you choose, for it is
poor in more ways than one, but as a matter of fact it is the poor
district under this director. I will read it [reading]:
STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA,
County of Marion, to wit:
This day, David H. Jarrett personally appeared before me, Ulysses A. Knapp,
a notary public in and for the county and State aforesaid and being by me first
duly sworn, says:
That he is overseer of the poor in Grant district, Marion County, W. Va.;
that the principal industry in said district is coal mining; that said district in-
cludes a territory in which is located several mines of the Consolidation Coal
Co. and numerous other smaller mines, all of which are or were operating non-
union; that affiant has been such overseer since approximately the 9th day of
January, 1925; that at the time affiant entered upon his duties as such overseer
there were about 20 families from his district drawing relief from said county;
that at the present time there are about 75 families from his district drawing
relief from said county; that the majority of those now drawing such relief were
formerly employed in nonunion mines; that many of them were imported into
affiant's district as strike breakers and that affiant is informed that as the com-
panies were able to secure experienced miners these men were let go and there-
fore it became necessary for some of them to be placed on the relief list of his
said district; that affiant has turned down numerous applications for relief from
men who were at the time employed in nonunion mines and working one and
two days a week; that the following is a typical example of one of these cases:
John Bredwell: That said Bredwell is one of the committeemen of the company
union at New England mine of the Consolidation Coal Co., which is operating
nonunion and which said mine is located at Watson, Marion County, W. Va.;
that in response to questions propounded by affiant said Bredwell stated that
the company was stealing his weight; that he started with 12 checks and that
he then had but 4 left; that they not only stole his weight but his checks as well;
that affiant asked him if the company would not trust him for something to eat,
and that affiant's wife then answered that she had told the superintendent that
morning that she only had one loaf of bread in the house to eat, and that the
superintendent replied that he didn't give a damn if she only had one bucket
of water in the house, she could have nothing from the company store until her
old man had worked it out; that affiant refused said Bredwell county aid.
Affiant further states that the following are a few typical cases which he is now
taking care of with county funds; that he has investigated each of the cases set
out herein and that the descriptions of conditions given therein are truly set out
as he found them at the time of his investigations:
Mrs. Flora Demarco: Lives at Hutchinson mine of the Consolidation Coal Co.,
which is operating nonunion; that her husband formerly worked at Carolina
mine of said company, where he was injured; that when he had recovered from
said injuries he returned to work and contracted pneumonia, and shortly thereafter
died; that said Mrs. Demarco never received any compensation as a result of her
said husband's injuries; that shortly after her said husband's death she was
evicted from the company house in which she was living, and that she is now
living in a house at Hutchinson as aforesaid with an uncle; that repeated efforts
have been made to evict her from her present place of residence; that said Mrs.
Demarco has six children, ranging in age from 1 to 10 years; that she is now
receiving relief through his district from said Marion County.
Mrs. Eliza Waters: Lives at Watson, Marion County, W. Va., in House No.
26, which is owned by the Consolidation Coal Co., which company is now operat-
ing nonunion; that her husband was formerly employed by said company at its
New England mine; that he is now confined in the State penitentiary; that very


===== [扫描序号 234] =====

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS

to vacate said company house, but that she is now occupying said house; that
she and her family are now drawing relief through affiant's district, from said
Marion County.
Chester Carlin: That he is approximately 70 years of age and formerly worked
at the Carolina mine of the said Consolidation Coal Co., which is operating non-
union; that he was then transferred to the Monongah mine of the same company,

L. E. Malone: Worked for the Consolidation Coal Co. at the Hutchinson

Mr. BITTNER. That statement shows this, gentlemen of the com-
mittee, that among other things these coal companies bring in
inexperienced men, into these nonunion mines, and then when they
can get hold of experienced miners they discharge the inexperienced
men, and they become a charge on the citizens of the county in
which these nonunion mines are located in West Virginia. In other
words, they become a public charge. These men, with no experience,
are brought in by the operators, and they know nothing about coal
mining, and then are discharged and put upon the county to live.
I want to read for the benefit of the committee, and I think it is
well that you should have some sort of idea of what the conditions
were in northern West Virginia prior to the advent of the United
Mine Workers of America in 1917. It is our contention, and I
think there is no question about its being a fact, that the coal oper-
ators are trying to bring back exactly the same conditions that
prevailed prior to the coming of the union. At least that is the

SHALL WE GO BACK TO INDUSTRIAL BARBARISM, OR PROGRESS AS FREE MEN?
West Virginia is regarded as one of the industrial States in the Nation. The
growth of her leading communities has been along industrial lines. Fairmont
in 1905 was a one-corporation, one-family, and almost one-man town, whereas
to-day New York and Baltimore and Pittsburgh are sharing in the control of
Fairmont's industrial development. In these 20 years millions upon millions of


===== [扫描序号 235] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1257
dollars have been invested in new industries in Fairmont, as well as in the enlarge-
ment of industries already here. Instead of one coal company, a multitude has
grown up among us. Instead of three factories, we now have a substantial list.
Great as is the contrast in the number and capitalization of our industries of
to-day with that of 1903, the contrast in attitude between capital and labor is
even greater. When I came to Fairmont in 1905 this was a nonunion region,
and in order to keep it so the big stick policy on the part of capital was in force.
If all was told that could be told about the operations of this brutal, ungodly,
and un-American policy, it would cause the blush of shame and the fire of indig-
nation to appear on the cheek and in the eye of every honest man.
Those were
the days of the blackjack and handy billy and murderous slugging even in public
places on our main street. Thank God that such days are in the past, and let
every lover of his fellow man dedicate himself to the task of keeping them in
the past. To-day this is a unionized region industrially. Conditions are bet-
ter by far than they were. To-day the appeal to labor and capital is to apply
the golden rule in the spirit of the sermon on the mount to all of their activities
and relationships.
I will say that this was written on March 18, 1923, when the mines
were operating 100 per cent union, under contract with the United
Mine Workers of America. It shows the conditions as seen by one
of the chief clergymen of the community prior to the time when the
union came in there and during the days when the union was in
there.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we will present the scales that are paid in
that field: They range from $4.60 per day down to $1.50 per day.
As far as hours of labor are concerned the mines generally operate
on the eight-hour-day basis. The wages were cut from $7.26 to the
rates that now apply.
One company in northern West Virginia, the Victor Fuel Co., I
think, in Marion County, has taken the position that they will not
hire anybody but single men, paying them $1.50 a day and board,
boarding them in the company boarding house. That condition
exists, as I say, in mines within a distance of 7 miles from Fairmont,
the county seat of Marion County. It is a demonstration of how
low wages can go when there is no protection on the part of the men
who work in the mines.

RIVESVILLE, W. Va., March 3, 1968.
GENTLEMEN: During the month of February, 1925, certain reports were cir-
culated through the press and otherwise that the United Mine Workers of Amer-
ica had erected forts on a parcel of land overlooking the tipple and mining camp
of the New England Fuel & Transportation Co., at Grant Town, W. Va. I
desire to inform you that during that time and for some time previous and
thereafter, I was a regular constable of Paw Paw district, Marion County, sta-

tioned at Grant Town, W. Va., and working from the office of Justice of the
Peace Thomas Ashcraft, who was also in the employ of the New England Fuel
Transportation Co. This company was operating its mines nonunion.
I am familiar with the so-called forts, their location and general structural lines.
It is true, there was a net work of logs on the lower side of those buildings which I
presume were placed there as a foundation for barracks which I understand the
United Mine Workers of America intended building on this ground until they
secured level ground closer to the camp. In fact one of these barracks was com-
pleted and one of the members of the United Mine Workers of America lived
there for some time. The buildings were also used for storing garden tools of the
strikers who had planted gardens on the hillside and on the same tract on which
the buildings stood. I have also noticed on different occasions children of the
striking miners playing around said buildings.
I am of the belief that the fort story was broadcasted for the purpose of preju-
dicing the public against the United Mine Workers of America and in order to
justify the action of the New England Fuel & Transportation Co. in erecting
powerful searchlights and articles of warfare on their property.
