Mr. BITTNER. Now, Mr. Chairman, that is a fair picture as we see
it of conditions in northern West Virginia.
The question has been asked, and the newspapers, especially the
operators' newspapers in northern West Virginia, have been saying
that "If these miners are not satisfied why don't they go into some
other industry?" This theory of a man having a right to work when
and where he pleases and under what conditions he pleases, that is
just an idle thing, because a man can not work when he pleases
because he first has to have a job. He can not work where he pleases
because he also has to have a job. If a lot of men worked where they
pleased why, I understand that there are other men who would
be pleased to work in the United States Senate. I just say that as a
matter of illustration. But they can not work there. And it is
just as true about working in any industry.
Senator WHEELER. You know what Champ Clark said about that,
do you not? He said the reason that they did not was because of
the fact that their constituents would not send them there.
Mr. BITTNER. Well, I suppose Champ knew exactly what he was
talking about. But that is an idle theory. Why don't these miners
go into some other industry? What other industry are they going
into? That is the question. You can not go into the steel industry
or on the railroads or anywhere else just because you want to go on.
A man can not start to work until he gets a job, and there are no
jobs there.
And secondly, a man who follows coal mining, it becomes his
trade, the same as any other calling in life. He can not be a coal
miner for 10, 15, or 20 years and then branch out on some other
calling. And that is why we do not go into other industries on a
large scale. And frankly I say to you that I do not believe in the
theory of men who have worked in the coal mines for 10, 20, 30, or 40
years giving up their calling in the industry and turning it over to
somebody that is shipped in that knows nothing about coal mining.
I haven't anything personally against the negroes from the South,
but I do say this to you, gentlemen, that I am not in favor of our
people giving up their calling as coal miners and turning it over to
the boll-weevil negroes of the South who are being shipped into the
nonunion coal mining camps in northern West Virginia or anywhere
else in this country.
As I said yesterday, we are full of this thing. Our people are
hoping and praying to God that this committee can do something
with the cooperation of all the other American citizens that should
be interested-something that will alleviate this situation and place.
the coal-mining industry, one of the two basic industries of this coun-
try, on that solid industrial plane that it should occupy in the indus-
trial life of our Nation. These men and women and children who
are in these barracks have their eyes here. This is their Government.
And I say to you there is no set of men and women in America
that love this Government any more than do the coal miner and
their wives and little children that are on strike. It is because
they love American traditions, it is because they love American
institutions and American ideals and American standards, that
they are fighting.


===== [扫描序号 244] =====
1266
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
These operators will come here and tell you-I have heard them
say it "Go back to ork. Why don't these men go back to work?"
They do not go back to work for the same reasons that Washington's
men at Valley Forge did not quit the fight. They are fighting for
what they think are American ideals and American conditions.
That is the position occupied by the men and women and children
in northern West Virginia that have been in this battle for four
years. It is a long time to strike-four years. It is a long time to
suffer privations and hardships and make sacrifices. Four years is
a long time to live in one and two and three rooms in shacks on those
hillsides in northern West Virginia. But, gentlemen, can you not see
with me that the position of those people is that it is better to fight
four years or five years, if necessary, for American standards and
American ideals, than to see their children suffer the results of the
destruction of our Union in those coal fields in northern West Virginia?
I say that to you earnestly, and I hope that something can be done
here, and I say this to the committee from the very bottom of my
heart, that if there is anything that I can do in my humble way, if
my experience amounts to anything, there is nothing that I will not
do to assist this committee or any other body of Americans to settle
this mining proposition. That is just exactly how we feel about it,
gentlemen.
It is our life! It is our life, I say to you. And that is why we are
so earnestly hoping and praying.
The operators can not settle this question. The miners can not
settle it. The industry has tried to settle if for years, and they have
failed. And I say to you that as I see the situation it is only with
the assistance of the Government of the United States that this
question can be settled in a manner that will mean living standards
for the miners, fair profits for the coal operators, who have their
money invested, and the protection of the American people as they
should be protected.
I told you yesterday that if the mines were organized 100 per cent
in the United States I would not be in favor of such a condition being
brought about without Government regulation to protect the indus-
try and the public, and I mean that very thing. That is the position
the United Mine Workers of America occupy. We do not want to
destroy the coal mining industry in northern West Virginia. No; but
we do say this, that West Virginia men and women and little children
are entitled to just as high standards of living as are the men and
women and children in any other section of this great country of ours.
And our United States is the greatest country in the world. We
recognize that fact. We know it. We are willing to fight for the
things that we think are right along those lines. That is why the
United Mine Workers of America have been fighting in northern West
Virginia for four years. That is why we are hoping and praying.
I say to you men who are gathered here on this committee that if
you can do something to bring this situation out of the demoraliza-
tion, out of the morass that it is in, you will have done more for
American industry, for the American people, than any other set of
men that have lived since the inception of this Government. That
is what I have to say to the committee.
And I want to thank the committee for giving me this opportunity
of laying this proposition before them.

was at night; that if they were seen talking to anybody in the day-

in jail and beaten up. That is what the miners of Logan County told
me when I visited Logan County. I was followed there-all of us
were we were followed around by from 30 to 30 mine guards armed
with revolvers and blackjacks.
The Chamber of Commerce of Logan called a meeting or asked us
to appear before the committee of the chamber of commerce, and
they said they did not want us in Logan County. Of course, they
are controlled absolutely by the coal operators of Logan County.

relative to Mr. Tetlow could not go down there at least-if anybody is
killed in Logan County who represents the mine workers' union he
will be killed by somebody that Judge Wildermuth and these operators
are paying, because they all employ these mine guards. The records
here will show that they all paid into a jack pot to employ this most
murderous gang of thugs and blackguards that is to be found anywhere
in the United States. Those are the conditions in Logan County of
West Virginia.

Mr. SCHWAB. My belief is that all these great economic questions
of labor are but the old theory of supply and demand. The creation
of any artificial condition, either with reference to labor or industry,
can not be sound and lasting. I believe the true condition between


===== [扫描序号 274] =====
1296
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
labor and its employers should be a complete and thorough under-
standing with each other directly. As a result of that I have
adopted-we have adopted in most of our works the plan of having all
of our laborers elect their own delegates to confer with the manage-
ment of our various concerns, sometimes called a modification of the
collective bargaining, by which all conditions of labor and working
conditions are thoroughly discussed and settled.
Now in our plan each 300 workmen in the works or shop elect their
representative. They meet every month. And then when occasion
arrives, or at stated intervals, they meet with the management of the
company, and we have the freest and fullest discussion of everything
pertaining to their conditions.
If a question arises that can not be settled between these two
bodies, it is specified that we leave it to arbitration. It is but fair
to say that in 10,000 or more cases that have arisen not one of them
has ever gone to arbitration. They have all been settled by direct
contact with these men and the sympathetic feeling that ought to
exist between employers and employees. But if such a condition did
arise it was left to arbitration to decide, and that arbitrator is the
Secretary of Labor of the United States.
Now the result of that is that we take our employees completely
into our confidence in everything. When we meet with them semi-
annually or annually we give them all the information with reference
to the business of our company, its earnings, its costs, their earnings,
our difficulties, our volumes. The same report is made to the labor-
ing men of the Bethlehem Steel Co. as is made to the stockholders of
the Bethlehem Steel Co. at their annual meeting.
We have had reductions of wages in the Bethlehem Steel Co., and
when the workmen understood these reductions, understood the
necessity for these reductions, they were made without the slightest
difficulty. On the other hand, we have had advances. We have had
many more advances than we have had reductions, because we have
had very prosperous times. But the company has freely made these
advances when the business and conditions justified it, and each year
has seen an increase in the hourly earnings of our employees, until
in the year just ended the average earnings of the sixty or seventy
odd thousand employees of my companies-of the Bethlehem Steel
Co.-have been about 62 cents an hour. That is the average of
everybody in the company. I am very proud of that average be-
cause it is very high when you consider the great number of men,
unskilled and otherwise, in the industry.
Now, I am a firm believer in the fact that the only way to have
happy and efficient results is by understanding and direct contact
with the men. I do know that in the employment of labor, as in
almost every other walk of life, every other business in life, this sit-
uation has been taken advantage of to the detriment of men. But
as president of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers last
year I selected as the basis of my presidential address "Human
engineering," as being a much more important factor than the me-
chanical engineer. That with all of our devices for labor saving and
improvement of quality, it was of small importance to the develop-
ment of industry as compared with having the heart of the men who
operated these machines in the business.


===== [扫描序号 275] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1297
Now you can not have the heart of men in the business unless they
are a part of it. And it will probably surprise you if I tell you that
under this plan which we have now been working for 10 or 12 years,
that the most important stockholder by long odds of the Bethlehem
Steel Co. is its workmen. One-third or one-fourth-over one-fourth
of all the preferred stock of the Bethlehem Steel Co. is owned by its
workmen. And that is true even in our mines.
Now we have not made the same progress with this development
in our mines as we have in our steel work, because the difficulties
have been more difficult to surmount. And secondly, because we
have acquired mines within recent years that we have not been able
yet to bring into this same line of working as we have our other
industries. But I have every hope and I have every belief that the
best condition for the miners in the mines is to work under the sam
conditions as we work in our other branches of our industries.
I do not mind saying at this point that if it were possible for us
to run the steel industry so as to secure our supplies regularly and
of the qualities that we want, that nobody would be happier to be out
of the mining business altogether than the Bethlehem Steel Co.
would be. It has been the most troublesome, it has been the most
difficult and it has been the most unsatisfactory branch of our great
business.
Now I believe, and I am pressing constantly in every direction,
mines and elsewhere, to have the workmen select their representatives.
When we started 10 years ago we had great difficulty getting the
workmen to take the slightest interest in it. They would not even
vote for a delegate. It was not a matter that interested them.
They had not learned about it. I am glad to tell you that last year,
unsolicited, except in a clerical way to help the workmen vote---we
supplied the machinery for doing it-but in the year 1927, 93 per
cent of all the men employed in the Bethlehem Steel Co. voted for a
representative that should take care of their interests in the company.
Now I think that is very significant, because the 7 or 8 per cent
that did not vote were probably workmen of foreign extraction that
had not learned much about our methods of doing these things.
And each year has seen an increase in the number of men who actually
take an interest in it and vote.
Now I go to their meetings once a year. Our president, Mr. Grace,
end our vice presidents go more frequently. But I am not able to
do so. But when I do go I do not mind saying to you that I have
never attended a meeting in which I have seen such a complete
harmony, such complete happiness, such complete understanding, as
I have seen in ours. And I do say to you that some of the newspapers
reported that I have gone over this country and talked about this
situation. I have. And I shall never lose an opportunity of talking
about it, because I know of nothing that to my mind, and after my
40 years' management of men, has convinced me is so good for the
benefit of the working people of the United States and the industry
of the United States as this direct contact and common human
understanding between the workmen and the people who employ
them. And I reiterate that I shall always preach that because it is
the truth, sir.
Now those are the methods that I believe in.

I believe, if the good chairman will permit me to say it-and I
speak bluntly about these things-that agitation such as this does
not help working conditions. It hurts the working condition of the
people of this country. If people would devote themselves to that
common understanding with their people as to conditions and
ability to do things you will do far more than you will do by the
bringing up of sensational charges against employer and employee.
Let us be together. I have been a working man myself the greater
part of my life, and I know and understand their conditions.
I do not need money. I am finished now-pardon me if I am too
long.
The CHAIRMAN. No; go right on with it.
Mr. SCHWAB. I do not need money. I am not working for money.
And you will be surprised if I tell you that I have never made $1
out of the Bethlehem Steel Co. It has been a work of love. It has
been the work of building up a great industry that I should leave
as a monument to my industrial career in this country, and I have
never made $1 out of it, and I never hope to make $1 out of it. But
the one thing I do hope to do is to leave it a peg forward in the
treatment of its employees.
Now these questions of strikes at mines or individual things, indi-
vidual departments, or labor conditions will occur. You have diffi-
culties in this great Senate of yours and you are not working always
together, and you are intelligent people, but you have differences of
opinions. And these little things will occur all the time. But suffice
it for me to say that to-day, upon inquiry yesterday-I just returned

things, but I did ask: "Are there any striking people in the Bethlehem
Steel Co.?" and my management tell me decidedly not in their
mines, workshops, or anywhere else. And it does seem to me that
it is an exemplification in these times of the soundness of the theory
on which we are endeavoring to build.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
The CHAIRMAN. You believe then generally in the policy of collec-

Mr. SCHWAB. Well, I do not call it entirely collective bargaining.
The CHAIRMAN. Well, you said a moment ago "modified."
Mr. SCHWAB. Yes; modified.
The CHAIRMAN. What do you mean by that, Mr. Schwab?
Mr. SCHWAB. Well, I think "collective bargaining" is a dead
term. It is not bargaining. It is understanding each other. It is
knowing the conditions of each other. That the management of
works in years gone by have never known some of the conditions.
The great autocrat in industry in the days gone by has been what I
call the subforeman, the man who was immediately in contact with
the workmen-Mr. Lewis, you understand-and those fellows were
autocrats of the worst kind in the days gone by, and they would
discharge a man because they did not like his family or did not like
his looks, or some other reason, and the workman was afraid to
complain because he would surely be discharged.
Now, by this method of mutual understanding any workman, no
matter what his position or what the conditions are, can come for-
ward with his grievances and his difficulties and have them aired

Mr. SCHWAB. We were largely the pioneers in this line, yes. I

my first experience in this matter was during the great Homestead
strike in 1892. I was not manager of Homestead at that time, but
I went to settle the results of that most disastrous strike of modern
times, and became manager of that works. And I decided that the
only way that peace and happiness would prevail there would be to
have a mutual understanding between the workmen and ourselves—
myself, as manager. And I devoted my time to that, and I think if
you read the history of industry you will find that from that day on
Homestead, with its great works, has been exceedingly prosperous.
and happy, and they have never had a strike.
Now that is the beginning of this. I felt the importance of it at the
beginning. And I have developed it and practiced it and gone on and
on and on, and I do not mean to say that we are by any means per-
fect yet, but it is the only hopeful solution that I see to this.
You can apply palliative remedies for this by consolidations, and
that will help from an economic point of view. The bigger business
is done the more economically it is done, and therefore if you make
consolidations of these mines and cut down their overhead, managerial
and other expenses, of course it is to the good of industry, and I am
in favor of it. I do not even say that I am not in favor of anything
that will permit these operators, of which there is such a great
number, to work better together and get a better price. I do not say

problems, whether sociological, business, technical, or whatever they
may be. Being a layman the only way I can get at things of that sort
is to seek the best technical advice on the subject that I can get, and
then use my own judgment of course so far as it is worth anything
but based on technical advice. I am simply saying in taking up the
question point by point, it seems to me that primarily it needs to be
dealt with by those who know the business, but in any way that I
can be helpful in solving any of our great national problem, I stand
on the side of progress in the desire to be cooperative and helpful.
Senator WHEELER. You believe in collective bargaining as a general
proposition, do you not?
Mr. ROCKEFELLER. I believe in the fullest cooperation between
labor and capital. I believe their interests are common interests.
I do not believe that either of them can gain for himself except as he
works with the other, that they must work together. But the term
"collective bargaining" is a broad term. If you speak of it in the
broad sense in which I have it in mind, I may say that decidedly I
do believe in it, and that I believe in it in that broad sense, feeling
that there are many ways in which collective bargaining can be car-
ried out, and that in each group, or in each industry, or in each plant,

the method that is best adapted to bring about results in that par-

Senator WHEELER. Mr. Rockefeller, you have given some thought,

Mr. ROCKEFELLER. To the general question of industrial relations;

Senator WHEELER. And you believe in labor organizations, do you
not?
Mr. ROCKEFELLER. I believe in labor organizations as one of the

there are various means or methods in collective bargaining, and my
view is that that plan or means best adapted to bring about successful
results in each specific instance should be used, rather than to decide
that there is one and only one means, and then to measure everything
by that.
Senator WHEELER. Mr. Rockefeller, you believe generally, do you

deal to better labor conditions in the country?
Mr. ROCKEFELLER. I think that the country at large owes a great
duty to labor organizations. I take off my hat to them for what
they have done. But they are no more perfect than any other
business organizations, and they are constantly making mistakes
just as other business men are.
Senator WHEELER. Of course.
Mr. ROCKEFELLER. But I think they have made a great combina-

Mr. ROCKEFELLER. I think they have made large contributions;

Mr. ROCKEFELLER. I am very glad to make that tribute to them.

Senator WHEELER. And would you be perfectly willing to meet with

Mr. ROCKEFELLER. If I were to take any part in the solution,
Senator, I should obviously not be able to do so except in the method
of approach which seemed to me to meet with or bring promise of
success. Now I can not see promise of success in the bringing of all
the factors together to consider the various problems. I think that is
where the difficulty has happened that has been met with so often in
the past. Therefore, the method I suggest is the taking of one
problem at a time and dealing with that.

Mr. ANDERSON. Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of the committee:

The CHAIRMAN. Very well, you may proceed and make such

Mr. ANDERSON. The first thing I want to say is this: When a
stranger is appearing before a committee the members of which do
not know him, a great deal of what he says depends on what he
thinks and his position to know the situation, but we have not the
time this morning, nor would I have the discourtesy to attempt to
give you an autobiography, and yet there is one thing that I want to
say; I want at the outset to dissociate myself, and in doing that I
am sure I represent my company, from any spirit of antiunionism.
As far as I am personally concerned there is nothing of that
philosophy in me. I can talk about unions and union leaders and
union policies and not get hot under the collar or red in the face.
I have dealt with unions not only in mining but in manufacturing
and transportation and other industries, and am thoroughly familiar
with the negotiation and administration and adjudication of collective
labor agreements. They are not a particular mystery with me; I
have worked under them and with great satisfaction.
That I feel needs to be stressed at the outset, because I do not
intend to mince words in some of the things I shall say, but there is
no sting in the words, and I will appreciate it, Mr. Chairman, as the
third man in the ring if you will warn me if you think my blows are
getting a little low; on the other hand, I am not going to "pull" any
punches.
The problem that is before this committee as I see it, whether it
applies to the Consolidation Coal Co. or to other companies, is a
problem in management; and I do not know anybody that ought to
understand a problem in management in principle better than the
representatives of the Federal Government, because the problems of
management and the problems of government, as I understand it,
are practically the same, in this: That all the decisions you make and


===== [扫描序号 349] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1371
all the results that you try to arrive at are based on a reconciliation
of conflicting interests, in order that you may arrive at some results.
that will be for the greatest good to the greatest number, knowing
perfectly well at the start that at the finish not everyone will be
satisfied.
What is the problem that faces any management, in any company,
on any problem? And I stress the word "management"; I represent
management. Management sits at the center of four big interests,
all of which conflict at some points, and some of which conflict at all
points.
1. You first have your financial interests, the people, sometimes
many thousands in number, who have put their money into the cor-
poration, either as bondholders or stockholders or as bankers giving
you your working capital as the credit with which you carry on
currently. In that group you have a group without which you would
not have the company at all.
2. Then you come to the great body of labor, your producing labor,
thousands of men in many of these large units. Without labor you
would not get your product out, and, therefore, they are great in
importance.
3. You then come to the people who buy your product, the con-
suming group, a large and diverse body usually with a great corpora-
tion, widely scattered, with their definite interests in what you do,
very greatly affected by your actions, and within certain limits having
many rights and obligations which you must face.
4. And then you have at the fourth corner the public interest in a
corporation, and when I say "the public interest" I mean not only
the local public interest, the community which is directly affected
economically by the acts of the corporation, but the larger public
interest which maybe affected socially and morally by the import of
your actions. And it is that last group of course that you gentlemen
of the committee represent, and we are here, perfectly frankly and
unashamed to tell you our story.
Now, gentlemen of the committee, that is the background of general
decision in management. Next we come to a concrete decision, in a
concrete company, on a concrete question.
Three years ago the management and directors of the Consolida-
tion Coal Co. faced a problem. They faced that problem like they
had faced many problems. It was one of many but a very important
one, and they made a certain decision after long consideration. They
considered many factors; to my own knowledge they considered all
those which I have sketched, and doubtless many besides, and they
arrived at a certain decision, and they laid down a certain policy,
and the management carried out that policy
Fortunately in this case to my way of thinking three years have
elapsed, and the fundamental test in a policy is its results. In other
words, the homely proverb, "the proof of any pudding is in the eat-
ing," is here before us. Before I start to analyze the policy, to describe
to you the elements which entered into it and the arguments upon
which it was based, I want to give you a small sample of the pudding.
It is not going to be a meal, but it is a sample, and you can decide
somewhat the significance of my later statements by this sample.
I have in front of me a statement of facts about our mines in the
Fairmont region covering a period of seven years; four of those years


===== [扫描序号 350] =====

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
being complete years under one policy, one is a broken year divided
between two policies, and then there are two full years under a
different policy. And when I use the word "policy" of course in my
mind I am thinking of a number of elements other than the one to
which we are going to particularly address ourselves.
I am not going to read a lot of statistics from this statement, but
am going to use two years here for this sample of the pudding. In
the year 1924 the Consolidation Coal Co. produced in its Fairmont
mines a tonnage slightly less than 3,360,000 tons. That was the
last full year under the other policy. Then last year, the year just
closed, 1927, we produced in excess of 5,590,000 tons.
Now, before I leave those two figures, which represent an increase
of over 66 per cent, I want to take up two groups who would be
interested in that result: One group would be the financial interests
in the company, who would naturally be gratified to see the expan-
sion in the company's business. The other group are the consumers
of the Consolidation Coal Co., who by this record would seem to be
growing in numbers, and certainly not decreasing in satisfaction.
It would seem to indicate that they were receiving good coal, without
interruption, at a price which they believed to be fair with relation
to market conditions. Otherwise I do not think that this comparison
would be other than the reverse.
We now come to the labor group: In the year 1924 we averaged
approximately in number of employees, 4,180 men. In the year
1927 we employed just three under 4,500 men. And I pause again
to say this; for labor as a group, not talking of the individual work-
man but for labor as a group, the Consolidation Coal Co. apparently
under the latter policy has offered as much and even more employ-
ment to men willing and able to work.
And then switching again to another group, the local community,
it apparently has not suffered by any acts of ours in the way of increas-
ing the amount of idleness in the community.
Now, I come to work time per man in the year 1924: Of these
4,180 men employed in that year they averaged 131 days' work—a
rather sad picture from the point of view of everybody, but more
especially of the men who work. On the other hand, in the year
1927 all of the 4,500 men averaged 256 days' work-not a perfect
picture, but contrasted with 131 days is certainly an important
improvement in the condition of the men who worked.
Now, I come to a factor which I am going only to touch with regard
to the community; in the year 1924 the Consolidation Coal Co.
put into the community via pay-roll envelopes just a little over
$4,990,000. I am looking at that now as a community fund, in
which the life of Fairmont and the surrounding regions naturally
have a great stake. In the year 1927 the same fund was almost
exactly $6,825,000.
Now, of course, anybody who has an active mind and has been
following these figures at all will be making some rapid conclusions
as to what this meant to the individual. I can save your pencils
and paper by this: Summing up all these factors, the men numbered
among the 4,180 employed in 1924, and those are the men who
worked in the mines, and it does not include any of our many other
activities which are in that region, averaged $1,195 for their year's
work. In the year 1927 they averaged $1,517 for their year's work.

Increase in number of employees every day that the mines worked,

Now, gentlemen of the committee, there seems to be, and I say

it by process of elimination, a grievance against the results of this
policy from some quarter, and I wish for the moment to talk to the

me to condense very rapidly many of the factors which we had
in mind and which did not have to be told to them. In order to
make that clear to you, I want to sketch some of these things very
briefly:
Now, the first thing to remember is something that you gentlemen
put in a statement that your subcommittee issued from Pittsburgh;
and the same thought is in the language of Senator Johnson who intro-
duced the resolution under which this committee is investigating.
All of these gentlemen used substantially this phrase: What you were
confronted with was industrial war.
I want to say that I agree fully with that characterization. I do
not see how any honest man can dissent from it. And when I say
I agree with it, I mean that I agree with it as war and not as battle.
This war has already lasted twice as long as the World War. And
the major battles of the war I should like to read to you, omitting
minor skirmishes:
The national bituminous strike of 1919.
The central competitive field and anthracite "vacation" strikes.
of 1920.
The combined national bituminous and anthracite strikes of 1922.
The anthracite strike of 1923.
The outlying bituminous district strikes of 1924 and 1925.
The anthracite strike of 1925 and 1926.
The central competitive field bituminous strike of 1927, continuing
in part to this hour, and with a part of it remobilizing for this summer
as we sit here.

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Now, that requires an army that is called to battle. I have before
me, secured from the Bureau of Mines, the troops that have had to be
thrown into that fight. In one year the army was in service for 122
working days, making a total loss in mine days of just short of 75,-
000,000 and the army mobilized under the colors was 603,000 men.
I am not reading individual years, but I should like to call atten-
tion to this: The Government has given figures out only up to 1925;
but I think you will grant that the events of 1926, 1927, and 1928, will
not decrease this average. The average for the years covered by those
battles constantly in the field is 286,000 men-a number of men, if I
am correctly informed, twice the strength of the standing Army of the
United States, constantly in the field during those years. And the
loss of time is three times what it was in the same period prior, al-
though I grant you that the loss of time due to this cause is not
the great loss in the industry.
Now, I think the questions that the public wants to know out of
that record are these:
Where are the merits of this war?
What are its causes?
How did it start?
Is it a defensive army or is it an offensive army?
I want to say this: That I do not think there is any man who can
understand the present problem of the president of the United Mine
Workers of America, outside of his organization, better than an
officer of the Consolidation Coal Co., and for this reason: We are
both in the industry. We both have large interests to protect-
and we happen to be a most diversified company, and therefore have
to see things somewhat on the same scale as the president of the
United Mine Workers of America. Neither he nor we can make
any decision based on the welfare or the destiny of a single district.
We have to consider many. He considers more than we, but we
have at least a faint understanding of the problem which confronts
the man in that position.
The adoption of this war method is obviously something that we
ought to be able to dig up. That list of battles shows that during
those eight or nine years every single union bituminous district in
this country, and the anthracite field as well, have been involved.
Now, on the operators' side, everyone knows that they are not an
army-they are a mob. There is no connecting link between these
districts; and there certainly is no connecting link between the bitů-
minous operators and the anthracite operators. There is no common
meeting ground; there is no common focusing point. And I
think what can be said of this particular record in general, without
attempting to meet the issues of any particular scrap, is to say that
the operators may be criticized for not offering a peace policy. And
yet to say that they have a war policy is to fly in the face of every
economic factor in the industry.
Now, what do we have on the other side? We have that without
which no war can be fought. We have a great general. The United
Mine Workers of America some years ago dug up one man that I
suppose when the history of labor is written will be given a very high
rank as a labor man. He is a two-fisted fighting man. He is not a
diplomat, is not a statesman, does not claim to be. I understand that
he has been called by magazine writers "the Jack Dempsey of labor."


===== [扫描序号 353] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1375
Well, I admire Mr. Dempsey, but I do not think that is compliment
enough for Mr. John L. Lewis. I suspect that if we had Mr. Lewis's
psychoanalysis we would find that in his reading of history the
characters which attracted him were the Cæsars, the Alexanders,
and the Napoleons. And I give him very much higher rank in his
own field than merely a champion prize fighter.
Now, a general is helpless without an army. But this general is
fortunate in having not only the largest but one of the best disciplined
armies in the American labor movement. And he has something
that no other labor general has, he has a conscript army. He has
not got a volunteer army, he has a conscript army. And by that I
mean this: That in so far as it affects the machinery of the union,
according to my judgment, and in so far as it affects the psychology
of the rank and file of the army, the check-off system, which unionizes
the mine and not the men, puts the men subject to mobilization over-
night, and in my judgment warrants the outsider in calling it a con-
script army. I would not want that term to imply that Mr. Lewis,
as the general of the United Mine Workers of America, could hold
600,000 men out of work for five months on the basis of conscription;
he had to have a fighting army as well as a conscript army.
And now the question is: If the operators have no war policy, has
the other side a war policy? Personally I think they have, and I am
not going to debate the merits of that policy. I have already con-
ceded the great difficulties that surround the decisions of the head of
this army. He is there to protect the interests and to advance the
cause as he sees it of hundreds of thousands of men, and I am going
to confine myself to facts and not to adjudications, but I am going to
examine that policy.
Now, what are the characteristics of a war policy on the part of
anybody, a nation, or any group? Well, you have three ways of
working out the difficulty:
1. You can agree by mutual consent. And if you can not agree it is
a perfectly hopeless deadlock; and
2. If neither side will give way, you can arbitrate in some form.
Individuals have to arbitrate, they can not fight it out. Nations
pretty soon are going to have to arbitrate and are not going to be
allowed to fight it out.
But in relations between parties in industry, the question of
arbitration is a very serious one for both sides. I do not believe in
compulsory arbitration, and I do not believe in it because I am on
the side of management. And I can certainly understand why the
side of labor does not want it.
I have been a party to the making of labor arbitrations, and I
have never known one yet in which the decision satisfied them both,
and I have known many where the parties would have arrived at
better results by agreement if some hot-heads on both sides could
have been put in a cooler.
3. But if you do not agree by mutual consent, and if you do not

And when I as an outside observer look through the window

I see the union run, not as a deliberative assembly as I understand

Now externally what is the manifestation of this war policy?
Again we find something, which, like the check-off, which exists no-

I do not know any industry where war on a national scale has been

Now, I referred to this situation as a series of battles, and the
assumption is that the first battle was preceded by a declaration of

Sometimes in the United States we have had to declare war in order

I would rather take that occasion which startled the people of this

This is one of the gravest steps ever proposed in this country affecting the
economic welfare and the domestic comfort and health of the people. It is
proposed to abrogate an agreement as to wages which was made with the sanction
of the United States Fuel Administration * * * It is recognized that the
strike would practically shut off the country's supply of its principal fuels at a
time when interference with that supply is calculated to create a disastrous fuel
famine.
* * *
All interests would be affected alike by a strike of this character, and its victims
would be not the rich only, but the poor and the needy as well, those least able
to provide in advance a fuel supply for domestic use. It would involve the
shutting down of countless industries and the throwing out of employment of a
large part of the workers of the country.
From whatever angle the
subject may be viewed, it is apparent that such a strike in such circumstances
would be the most far-reaching plan ever presented in this country to limit the
facilities of production and distribution of a necessity of life and thus indirectly
to restrict the production and distribution of all the necessities of life. A strike
under these circumstances is not only unjustifiable, it is unlawful.
* I
can not believe that any right of any American worker needs for its protection
the taking of this extraordinary step, and I am convinced that when the time
and manner are considered, it constitutes a fundamental attack, which is wrong
both morally and legally, upon the rights of society and upon the welfare of our
country.

It is time for plain speaking. These matters with which we now deal touch
not only the welfare of a class, but vitally concern the well-being, the com-
fort, and the very life of all of the people. I feel it my duty in the public in-

Memorandum for President C. W. Watson:
FEBRUARY 29, 1924.
In response to your request for comment on the Jacksonville agreement, it
may be wise to distinguish between the contract as a three-year peace treaty
and as an economic fact.
To have avoided another nation-wide strike at this time and to provide for
uninterrupted production for three years was clearly to the advantage of the
industry as well as of the public. The latter is assured of a continuous supply
of coal and is, therefore, without any just cause for complaint. The industry
benefits by the fact that those portions of it which can live and prosper only by
strikes, shortage, and public panic are given no chance to profit at the expense of
established enterprises. As a peace measure, therefore, the three-year contract
has its undoubted benefits.
So far as the economics of the industry are concerned, however, an agreement
to maintain the status quo not only means little but probably can not be made
effective. Peace between operators and labor does not necessarily guarantee a
prosperous industry. On the contrary, it is obvious that the bituminous coal
industry has merely agreed to undergo a major operation, with a three-year scale
contract as anaesthetic.
That this operation is to be a painful one for all concerned needs no prophet to
predict. Up to a certain point, all elements in the industry will feel the knife
while the law of supply and demand acts as surgeon. The surplus mines and the
surplus miners, selected not by an individual but by a ruthless market, will have
to go. During that process, profits and employment will be reduced by the
amount necessary to eliminate the present excess production and excess labor.
If this shakedown is as drastic, as in my judgment it will be, it will be simply
a question both as between companies and between producing districts of cheap
coal. The difference of a few cents per ton here and there will not mean much
in the present situation. Every method of economy, efficiency, and improved
machinery will be necessary. Those companies and those districts which are
so sitiated as to put these measures most fully into effect will survive. Those
who for any reason can not reduce their costs or improve their output will go
down.
During the months ahead the buyers of coal will select the fittest from the
industry. Their fitness will be determined by the cheapest coal that can be pro-
duced under the most improved mining and management.
Now, that was a rather dark outlook and it has been a dark fulfil-
ment. Bear in mind that I am talking there to a man who wanted
my outlook on the industry as a whole. This in no way attempts to
decide or to intimate the policy or the attitude of our company in
connection with that picture, but, as business consists of about two-
thirds foresight and one-third hindsight, we have to look ahead.

Now, I pause here to say this, that I do not think any man on the

a picture of these men kneeling in prayer and imploring divine aid

A little later on, however, he introduces in evidence a letter

Now, both of those explanations, in my judgment, are wrong,
because it was the act of the international to preserve what it could
out of the wreck as it stood at the moment. And that is all that
needs to be said about it.
Now, we come to the problem of the Consolidation Coal Co.
And what did we face three years ago? We had taken business in
the spring of 1924 which lasted throughout what is known as the
coal year. The coal year, as a matter of trade practice, generally
begins around April 1.
Senator GOODING. To get clear at this point, please. Was your

alone except for some insignificant, scattered holes in the ground in a
district producing at the rate of 30,000,000 tons per year, one com-
pany sat there facing lost business, idle mines, idle men, huge losses,
and a contract.

policy a large number of mines closed, some of which have been

not you gentlemen, but some of them-in the use of the word
"wages," and when they mean one thing they are obviously saying
another.
Now, there are three entirely distinct things that may be included
with the word "wage." There is the wage scale. That is the same
as the price of anything, and by using that definition I am not
committing myself to the fact that labor is a commodity; but it is
the price as paralleled with the market.
Then there is the wage earning, which is what a man actually gets
out of that price, and that is the price times the days worked, just as
the company gets revenues, which is the price times tons sold. We
could sell coal at $100 a ton and go into bankruptcy in 10 days.
Senator WHEELER. Of course. I am looking at wages as the
purchasing power.
Mr. ANDERSON. That is what I assumed from your later statement.
Then you have something distinct from either, affected by both, and
yet never moving in any strictly connected way, because other
factors enter into it; you have wage costs.
Of those three things, wage cost is the only thing that interests an
employer. If the wage cost is based upon a high wage scale and high
earnings and is a low cost, he as one of the three parties does not care.
Fundamentally-and this is where I think a great mistake is made
sometimes by people whose hearts are in the right place-they do
not realize sufficiently, as I see it, that the great mass of men who
labor, whether they be union men or any other men, are intensely
interested in the wage earnings. The wage scale dangles before
them like the price scale before the producer. But the earnings they
must have and they must have annual earnings because they live all
the year through; and, therefore, to say that they have $50 a day and
10 days work per year means nothing to them.


===== [扫描序号 383] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1405
Then you have the third thing, the wage scale, which is of interest
to the other two parties, to a certain extent, a secondary interest,
but there is where another party comes in to whom it is of primary
interest, because it is involved in great political questions of organiza-
tion, where it is natural that it should be so.
Mr. Lewis or anybody else finds it very hard to stand in front of
hundreds of thousands of men and get them to agree on a reduction
in the price when he has no control over the volume, which is the days
worked. Therefore, he stands on the only thing that he knows where
to stand, and the volume has to come from somebody else.
This morning, unfortunately, you missed my comparison off the
records of our company. I do not attempt to speak for anybody
else. I took off the records of our company facts that are subject
to the check of certified public accountants, that under this policy,
which has offended some people so deeply, the earnings of these men,
which is what the man is interested in and which gives the key to his
actions, have increased 27 per cent.

Mr. ANDERSON. Yes.

(The witness was duly sworn by Senator Gooding.)

(Direct examination by Mr. Townsend, counsel for the United

===== [扫描序号 397] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1419
Mr. TETLOW. Well, I think it advisable that I set forth why and
how I became a party to the Baltimore wage agreement first.
In 1923 the mine workers of West Virginia, acting through their
officers, requested the International Union to assign me to that
district for work and to assist them in the affairs of the organization
in West Virginia. At that time the entire northern and southern
fields of West Virginia were in one district known as district 17,
United Mine Workers of America, for the union purposes.
I participated in all the wage agreements that took place in West
Virginia from 1917 until 1924. I participated in the wage agree-
ments in West Virginia from 1917 on. There were no agreements
made during the war. At that time, during the war period I was in
the Army. And the wages, of course, during that period were fixed
by the Fuel Administration. I participated in the wage agreements
in the northern and southern fields in 1923 and 1924. I did not
go to Baltimore as a representative of the international union be-
cause of instructions from the international union office, but because
of the request of the district itself, because of the experience I had
had in the field in negotiating wage agreements.
The Baltimore
agreement was negotiated between the United Mine Workers of
America and the northern West Virginia Coal Operators' Associa-
tion as such.
The United Mine Workers' policy was laid down in the beginning
in a convention of that union. The policies of the union were laid
down by delegates representing different local unions throughout the
entire country. The wage policies, the laws enacted, were drafted
by these delegates. The officers of the union were bound by those
laws and those instructions.
The Jacksonville wage base was made in conformity to and with
the policy of the international union. It was not the policy of its
officers. It was the policy of the men who worked in the mines, who
attended the convention and made the policy into law.
The Jacksonville wage scale, of course, reaffirmed the then existing
wage, which was the result, of course, of the Bituminous Coal Com-
mission's award of 1920.
The policy laid down by our union was that outlying districts were
authorized to negotiate wage contracts predicated upon the Jackson-
ville wage scale. That was not a new policy. It has been the
policy in the union ever since it was formed. The basic wage agree-
ments in the industry naturally originated in the central competitive
field, in the States of western Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana and
Illinois. That was natural because it was there that the wage
agreements were first negotiated. It was there that coal was first
produced in any great quantities. It was there where the United
Mine Workers was born, where the organization was formed, where
collective bargaining was first introduced into the industry, and it
became the basis upon which wage agreements were made throughout
the entire mining States and districts.
We went to Baltimore, the officers of the United Mine Workers
under direct instructions from its membership and upon a wage
agreement negotiated at Jacksonville to carry out those instructions
of that agreement.


===== [扫描序号 398] =====
1420
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
The coal operators went there, representing an association, the
same as we did. We were not representing individuals. We were
representing associations, speaking through legally selected, auth-
orized representatives. And such had been the plan in years gone.
by. There was no change.
We met at Baltimore, and the convention was organized by selec-
tion of a credentials committee. Those representing the different
organizations were accredited and given a seat in the convention
with authority to act, and negotiations began. Of course the mine
workers, because of their policy at Jacksonville, were committed
upon the premise of negotiating a wage scale in harmony with that
agreement; it would have been unfair for them to have acted otherwise.
Senator WHEELER. It would have been unfair to whom?
Mr. TETLOW. The mine workers and the coal companies through-
out the country. We could not act differently with honor to our
organization and its membership, nor could we act differently in
honor to those who had been dealing with us through all these years
of collective bargaining.
The question of renewing the contract was debated, and the only
questions which were fixed in our mind under our policy and under
the Jacksonville wage agreement were the basic wages involved.
The working conditions, the internal conditions of the district were
open for readjustment or modification or change.
A wage agreement was finally negotiated. On this premise the
operators who attended that conference were concerned in having a
majority of the tonnage of the northern West Virginia field agree to
that contract before they would sign it. And it was ascertained by
Mr. Anderson and the other representatives of the operators who were
there that a majority of the tonnage of the field, and a considerable
majority of it, were in favor of renewing the wage agreement. The
operators seemed to be concerned more with that particular fact than
any other entering into the contract; whether there would be suf-
ficient tonnage to warrant the signing of a contract, and a consider-
able majority entered into that wage agreement.
The operators who attended that conference were able to secure
modifications to this contract. They were not required to sign on the
dotted line. The negotiations were open. The working conditions
were freely discussed in every item. Modifications were made in the
contract from the preceding one. Modifications affecting the pro-
duction and cost of production were taken into consideration.
In the northern West Virginia coal field the basic wage agreement
carried certain differentials. Eighteen cents a ton on pick mining,
15.6 cents per ton machine mining, and a differential in the day
wage below the central competitive field.
Senator WHEELER. Why was that?
Mr. TETLOW. Because when the first wage agreement was made in
the northern West Virginia field, it, like every other wage agreement
made by the United Mine Workers and operators, was based upon
the competitive relationship between that district and other districts
whom they met in competition. The basic wage in the northern
field carried these differentials because of the fact that that district.
was removed from the markets and required greater cost in getting
that coal to the market, and it was for that reason, that question and
that reason of competition were responsible for that differential in


===== [扫描序号 399] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1421
the beginning. Those differentials remained constant all through
the life of the negotiations, with one or two exceptions.
In this contract in 1924 we made a change in the cutting rates.
There had been introduced in 1923 arc-wall cutters which increased
the production of the cutters, and it was a labor-saving device which
was successful. Under the terms of the Bituminous Coal Commis-
sion award both miners and operators were committed to the principle
that in the introduction of modern mining devices or methods of
mining commissions or tribunals should be set up between the miners
and operators to determine the labor savings of these new methods
or equipment and the benefits derived in the labor savings were to
be prorated between the worker and the employer. The Bituminous
Coal Commission award did not set up the percentage that would
go to either side. Under that award we made a test in 1923, and I
represented the mine workers and supervised the tests with repre-
sentatives of the men affected who were operating these new devices.
We finally agreed upon a reduction of the cutting prices averaging
three to three and a half cents a ton, knowing full well that our men's
wages were protected, that they could receive a higher wage than
the other cutting machine because of their ability to produce greater
tonnage. They received their share and benefits of that improved
machinery. The company received its share.
The result of that commission was written into the Baltimore agree-
ment of 1924, giving all companies the right to install this machine
and to have those rates effective. In the Baltimore agreement we
modified the agreement, reducing the cost of coal in gaseous mines
two cents a ton. There had been in the beginning a rate established,
a differential of 2 cents a ton, for men working in gaseous mines
where they used locked lamps. In the beginning, in the early days
under that contract the locked lamps were naphtha lamps. These
lamps are locked. If they go out during the working hours the lamps
are taken to a station where a safety foreman relights the lamp or
recharges it as the case may be. New lamps have been introduced,
modern electric lamps with batteries that give greater candlepower
than the old lights, and the men were not handicapped by the use of
the locked electric lamp, and the companies contended for a reduc-
tion of this two cents a ton. That was written into the contract.
Another question that came before this Baltimore conference of
vital effect on this issue was that the operators insisted that there be
written into the terms of the agreement itself a provision which would
commit the International Union of the United Mine Workers to the
fulfillment of the contract. And that was essential, because in the
last analysis the United Mine Workers, of which these men were
a part that worked in the mine-it was the duty of the United Mine
Workers to see that its membership complied strictly with the terms
of the contract, and every time a wage agreement would be violated
by the men, through lack of understanding of the agreement or by a
demand upon the employer which was not in line with the contract,
invariably that question went to the officers of the union for adjust-
ment. Our contract agreement provided for that very method of
dealing with the dispute.
First, when a dispute arises under the terms of this contract be-
tween the employee and the mine boss, it must go to the mine com-
mittee of that particular mine and the mine management on the


===== [扫描序号 400] =====
1422
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
ground. If they fail to adjust it then it goes to the district officers
and the commissioner of the coal companies and last, the International
Union, the United Mine Workers of America, is called in and finally
adjust that dispute before any suspension of mining can take place
at that mine or mines. That is the method by which these agree-
ments are carried out. They are not a contract based upon an indi-
vidual company, an individual mine. They are based upon the
association representing those men.
I was listening here to the statement made by Mr. Anderson upon
the question we have just been discussing, and this thought came to
me: He stated that the men who worked in the mines and for whom
the contract was made, themselves wanted this contract set aside.
That is far-fetched to say the least. The Consolidation Coal Co.
does not permit their mine bosses, superintendents, general managers
to set aside the provisions of this contract, or to deal with the men
locally upon this vital issue. They decide the question themselves
in New York. Then why assume that those men who worked in the
mines had authorized to abrogate or set aside the terms of this con-
tract, which was negotiated between the two associations? These
contracts are made in the interest of the men and the companies
involved. That is the fundamental-
Senator WHEELER. Made in the interest not only of the men work-
ing in the West Virginia coal fields but made in the interest of men
throughout the country working in the coal industry.
Mr. TETLOW. Correct.
Senator WAGNER. Is not there another advantage? Suppose the
price of coal went up so that the profits of the companies were much

would not you be obligated nevertheless to work under that scale of
wages?
Mr. TETLOW. Certainly. I have been connected with this industry
for 40 years.
It has been over 40 years since I started working in
mines, and I know something about them. I know the ills of the
industry. I have experienced them like every other man who has
been a part of the industry. If these contracts so entered into were
not vital, if they were not predicated upon the custom of years and
years of practical experience and of practice, if they were not the
outgrowth of the experience of men who have dealt with the prob-
lems on both sides, if they were not binding obligations resting upon
both sides, then no agreement or contract of a binding nature was
ever entered into by anyone.
Senator WAGNER. What I can not understand is why all these
negotiations, why this meeting at Baltimore, why this entry into a

Mr. TETLOW. Yes; and to make it more binding, Senator Wagner,
those operators who negotiated that contract at Baltimore went back
to their own association, and they asked for that right, to submit the

they notified us in writing, and it is a part of the record, that they had
affirmed the acts of their delegates to that conference. That is, that
the Northern West Virginia Coal Operators' Association affirmed the
action of the joint conference. The mine workers were not required
to submit back the question to their membership for ratification.

We had conducted our negotiations and passed upon our policy and

the international union to take over the affairs of the district, and
upon their request I was sent to West Virginia in 1924 to assume
charge of the affairs of the union in that field. And I have been
there ever since.
Mr. TOWNSEND. You are familiar with the situation as it has
existed for several years in the coal industry of southern West
Virginia?
Mr. TETLOW. Yes, sir.
Mr. TOWNSEND. And in order to distinguish the coal fields of West
Virginia, the northern field from the southern field, I will ask you to
state what railroads enter into the coal fields in the southern section
of the State?
Mr. TETLOW. The Chesapeake & Ohio, the Norfolk & Western, the
New York Central, and the Virginian.
Senator GOODING (presiding). At this point the committee will
stand adjourned until 10.15 o'clock to-morrow morning.
(Whereupon at 4.40 p. m., Monday, March 26, 1928, the committee
adjourned to meet the following morning, Tuesday, March 27, 1928,
at 10.15 o'clock.)

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS OF PENNSYLVANIA,
WEST VIRGINIA, AND OHIO
TUESDAY, MARCH 27, 1928
UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE ON INTERSTATE COMMERCE,
Washington, D. C.
The committee met at 10.15 o'clock a. m., pursuant to adjourn-
ment on yesterday, in room 212, Senate Office Building, Senator
James E. Watson presiding.
Present: Senators Watson (chairman), Gooding, Couzens, Fess,
Goff, Pine, Sackett, Metcalf, Bruce, Wheeler, and Wagner.
The CHAIRMAN. The committee will come to order. Who is the
next witness?
Mr. TOWNSEND. Mr. Tetlow may proceed.
TESTIMONY OF PERCY TETLOW-Resumed
Mr. TOWNSEND. Mr. Tetlow, you may proceed with your state-
ment, if you remember just about the point where you left off
yesterday.
Mr. TETLOW. I think you asked me in relation to the railroads
that served the southern West Virginia fields.
Mr. TOWNSEND. That is right.
Mr. TETLOW. The C. & O., the Norfolk & Western, the Virginian,
and the K. & M. Division of the New York Central; the four railroads
that enter into the field.
Out of a total production in the States in 1926 of about 143,000,000
tons approximately 90,000,000 to 100,000,000 of that is produced
in the southern field. And about 90,000 out of a total of 117,000
men-there are possibly about 85,000 of them in the southern field.
The great coal areas of the State the greatest production is in
the west and east counties bordering Kentucky and Virginia. The
growth in production of coal in these fields has been constant for
many, many years. There are many different grades of coal pro-
duced in the southern field. In the counties of Raleigh, Mercer,
Wyoming, and McDowell, those are low volatile coal fields, low in
volatile matter and high in carbons. An excellent grade of coal.
Practically has no competition from any source whatsoever, except-
ing the internal competition that may exist within the field itself.
It is just as distinctive as anthracite, and has its own particular
markets.
Senator GOODING. What percentage of that class of coal is in
West Virginia?
1425


===== [扫描序号 410] =====
1426
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Mr. TETLOw. In the southern field?
Senator GOODING. In the southern field of West Virginia; yes.
Mr. TETLOW. In the southern field of West Virginia-well, I
could not give you an accurate percentage of the total production
of the southern field, but I would say, including all of the low volatile
coals, there is possibly a production of 40,000,000 to 45,000,000 tons
annually. This coal moves to the seaboard, a great percentage of
it-not the majority of it but a great deal of it-and largely west
into the Chicago markets. It receives the highest price for f. o. b.
mine of coal in the State. Most of it is sold for-it moves west
for domestic purposes, and that which goes east goes to the seaboard
for ocean and seaboard trade.
any
The CHAIRMAN. That is the grade that we laymen ordinarily call
Pocahontas?
Mr. TETLOW. Yes, sir. In discussing this Pocahontas and other
low volatile coal I pointed out that most of the competition that
this coal had was internal competition in the field itself. And that
the reason of that is because of its high quality. Of course it meets
competition in domestic coals moving west and northwest, and
some competition from the low volatile coals in central Pennsylvania
and Maryland, but not to any great extent. Because of its su-
periority quality, it really has very little competition.
There is a great deal of gas coal produced in the southern field used
for by-product purposes, of a high quality, and then there is a great
percentage of splint coal produced in the State, hard, blocky coal
that is used largely for domestic purposes. Stands shipping well.
The State is exceedingly fortunate in its resources in that respect.
The quality of coal, of course, enters largely into the increased ton-
nage which came from this State.
Of course the question of their ability to produce coal cheaper,
because of the lower production costs have enabled them to get into
the markets of all of the producers of bituminous coal in the central
field and central west irregardless of the freight rates that may have
been against it in entering these markets, and those two factors,
quality and cheap production, have enabled this field to increase its
tonnage constantly, steadily upward.
The mine workers union were able in this field to increase their
membership shortly after the war period to about 55,000 members.
Wage agreements were made in these fields for that number of men,
which reached its peak in about 1921. In 1922 the union started to
decline in membership, wages began to decline correspondingly, until
1924, when there were no further wage agreements between the union
and the companies in that field.
The first wage agreement made in the southern field was way back
in 1902, at Huntington. The basic wage agreement was made that
was carried on from 1902 until 1924; it carried certain fixed differ-
entials in mining and day labor. The differentials established in the
mining were about 18 cents a ton on pick and machine mining, and
about 50 cents a day on day labor.
The CHAIRMAN. Why the differential?
Mr. TETLOW. The differential was arranged by reason of the min-
ers and operators in that field getting together and arranging a wage
that would permit that coal to flow in competition with other coals
in northern markets.


===== [扫描序号 411] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1427
The CHAIRMAN. The differential had to do with railroad rates?
Mr. TETLOW. That was a consideration, sir, when the basic agree-
ment was made. You must understand that in this State, out of
all that great population which last year reached approximately
150,000,000 tons, that over 95 per cent of that tonnage leaves the
State, is shipped into markets north and northwest and east. None
of it goes south. It all goes and enters into the markets north, east,
and northwest.
The CHAIRMAN. So that the question of freightage is a big ques-
tion?
Mr. TETLOW. A great question.
The CHAIRMAN. Yes.
Mr. TETLOW. The transportation problem enters into it without
question.
Senator FESS. And your contracts on the cost basis would be lower
in cost determined by this differential?
Mr. TETLOW. Correct, sir.
The day wage, to illustrate, under the Jacksonville wage basis, if
it had been continued in that field, would have been $6.95 for inside
day labor maximum rate for drivers, $7.12 for truck men and timber
men, with the scale sliding downward to about a dollar a day differ-
ential between that and the central field day wage rate.
There was about 20 cents a ton differential on machine mining,
and 8 cents a ton on pick mining.
So when you take into consideration that about 90 per cent of the
tonnage is machine mined coal the majority of the tonnage carried
the differential of 20 cents a ton.
Under this rate that was fixed in 1902 the production in these
fields gradually grew, steadily. It was not a bar or a handicap to
the successful operation of these mines south of the Ohio River in
West Virginia. And I can not understand-never have been able to
understand the attitude of the operators in that field in wanting to
destroy collective bargaining, to reduce wages to lower levels when
they were amply able to produce their coal, ship it into competition
with any other coals that were produced in the great consuming cen-
ters of the country.
The CHAIRMAN. Regardless of the railroad differential?
Mr. TETLOW. Regardless of that, sir. The tonnage increase dis-
closes that year by year.
I want to just draw this picture of southern West Virginia as I
see it. In this great area lies these great natural resources far
removed from markets. The coal areas are largely operated by great
corporations. While there are a lot of individual operating mines
they are operating under lease or under royalty basis. Many of
these coal areas are controlled by corporations operating 75,000 or
100,000 acres, owning surface rights as well as the coal, the minerals.
They are inaccessible territories in many respects, many of these
operations, the railroad being the only means of inlet and outlet to
the territories. It has only been in the last two or three years that
highways or roads have been built into these mining fields.
There is very little local self-government in the fields. Very few
of the towns are incorporated. Take Logan County as an illustra-
tion, has one incorporated town in the county. The police force
of the communities are operating from the sheriff's office as deputies


===== [扫描序号 412] =====
1428
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
or as guards appointed by the coal companies. The deputies are
paid by the coal companies. They supervise the law enforcement
to a great degree, more so than any place in the United States.
In these coal fields practically all of the trading is done in the com-
pany stores. Necessarily in many places without question because
of the ownership of the land resting in the hands of this company.
In the communities surrounding these mining fields prior to the organi-
zation losing its force the miners' union losing its force in the field,
the men were permitted to go to these mining towns and purchase
their supplies and commodities and take them home. Since the fall
of the organization things have changed. All of the dealing is done
in the company stores. The men are prohibited to deal outside of
the company stores. The scrip system has come into effect with
startling results.
The CHAIRMAN. When you say "prohibited," what do you mean
by that, Mr. Tetlow? You say the men are prohibited.
Mr. TETLOW. They are not allowed to deal outside of the company
stores.
The CHAIRMAN. Is there some sort of an order issued to them to
that effect?
Mr. TETLOW. Well, the orders have been issued in many instances
that outside merchants can not deliver merchandise or groceries
upon the company property, and men would not be permitted to
work if they bought outside of the company's store. That is the
general system throughout the field and recognized without question.
Senator GoFF. Has any one been discharged who bought outside
of the field?
Mr. TETLOW. Oh, that has happened, no question about that.
Senator GoFF. That is true, is it?
Mr. TETLOW. Oh, yes; no question about that.
The CHAIRMAN. What prices do they charge in these company

Mr. TETLOW. I would say that the prices in these company stores-
at least they were in 1924 when I made the last check of prices, com-
paring prices of the company stores against the prices of the stores
in Charleston and elsewhere the prices ranged from 20 to 35 per cent
higher. From an actual check of commodities based upon the same
article in the other stores.
Senator FESS. And, Mr. Tetlow, what is the argument for main-
taining the company stores on the part of the operators? Is there
any advantage?
Mr. TETLOW. Well, in the first place, Senator, many of these min-
ing towns are isolated. There are no other stores excepting the com-
pany stores.
Senator FESS. Well, that is what I wanted to get at. Whether they
might be left without any service in case the company stores were not
established.
Mr. TETLOW. That is true. That is true largely in the field.
Senator GOFF. Well, the company stores are really a necessity to
the employees, are they not?
Mr. TETLOW. In many places, yes, sir. I pointed that out-the
fact that the companies owned the coal lands as well as the resources,
and the mining town is built near the mine, the companies build all
stores, they build the churches and take care of all of the activities

The CHAIRMAN. Certainly.
Mr. TETLOW. The system of allowing and placing the police power
in the hands of appointed officers paid by any corporation to my mind
can not be justified from any standpoint. It is not necessary, to begin
with, and if it were it should only be temporary, to say the least. I
can not understand why these mining comunities in which hundreds
of men are employed-I can not understand why these communities
can not be incorporated. The fact that the companies own all of
the property and all of the real estate is no reason why they should
deny the incorporation of these villages, which prevents the activities
that citizens will enjoy in their affairs of local self-government. That
seems to me to be more important than any other factor in these fields.
Under this system you are denied two fundamentals. The right
of citizens to participate in the affairs of local government, and the
right of workers to enjoy their own homes. If there are any two
things that are essential to home life and community life they are
the right to participate in local self-government and home owning.
There you find the best workmen. There you find the best citizens.


===== [扫描序号 414] =====
1430
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
And it should be the desire of corporations and the communities and
the State to foster those two things. And under a system where those
things are denied you can readily understand that the exercise of
police power will be abused. And it has been abused in this State to
a degree that is possibly greater than any other State in the Union,
largely because of many of the employers being opposed to trades-
unions and collective bargaining. They have set up their police
force to prevent men from exercising this right of joining a labor
union and participating in collective bargaining. The police force
is used to prevent these fundamental rights. And you have that
condition existing throughout the field, more so now than in the other
day, because of the fact that this tremendous struggle has been going
on in the last few years for markets to take care of this surplus coal.
Let us analyze this situation. There are too many mines and too
many miners-yes. The increase in the number of mines developed
during the war, largely, and shortly after the war, to take care of the
peak load that was placed on the industry. But there are other
factors entering into this over-production that are more vital than
this, when you consider that the productivity of the miners increased
over 100 per cent in the last few years because of the introduction
of mine machinery and efficiency, and that is growing by leaps and
bounds. We used to produce about 2½ tons per day a few years
back. Now we are producing about 5 tons per day per employee
in the industry. You compare that with the production of other
countries. Here is Great Britain producing about 1,800 pounds per
worker. Germany, the most advanced nation in Europe in the pro-
duction of coal is only producing approximately a ton per worker.
And we are producing five, and I predict within the next 10 years
our production will almost be doubled again, per capita production.
The introduction of machinery and devices in this industry is more
pronounced than any other industry in the country. Loading
devices are coming into the mines in addition to the undercutting
devices that have been installed.
The CHAIRMAN. And demand is not growing that rapidly at all?
Mr. TETLOW. And on the other hand, another force is running
contrary. Every effort is being made to extract the greatest number
of heat units from the coal. Modern devices are being employed to
increase the efficiency of heat units and the use of them.
sumption has remained practically stationary for the last 10 years.

Mr. TETLOW. The consumption of coal is remaining practically
stationary, and I do not think the uses of other fuels have much to do
with it. The use of fuel oil is only temporary. It can never be
permanent. And it will change in different sections of the country
from time to time. But we are going to reduce the amount of coal
used per capita, while there will be some increase possibly in the
tonnage. But these two forces are running toward the center.
One to reduce the amount of coal, and the other constantly increasing

the ability to produce. We will be producing 8 or 10 tons per man

There is no other end. With this system of under-
