Mr. TETLOW. I think it would be well that I bring out one point
I have in mind. And I want to make it as clear to the committee
as I can. I think the position of the mine worker in this country
has been misunderstood, more so than any movement in the country.
I have been connected with it since its beginning. I have watched
the growth of the miners' union, and I saw what it accomplished.
I know that it took me out of the mines when I was working 12 and
14 hours a day. I used to go to work before daylight and come home
at dark, and the only time we ever saw the sun was on Sunday.
I went to work when I was just about 12 years of age, in the mine.
And I saw it change those conditions. It has been responsible for
the enactment of the child labor laws, laws in all the States regarding
sanitation and safety in the mines, and inspection. It has reduced
their hours of employment, it has increased their wages, it has given
them broader opportunities, made better men of them. And it has
been fighting for those things all these years.
I just want to go back a year or two, if you please. I think this is
important or I would not say it. But I want to correct, if there is
any wrong impression in the minds of this committee as to the atti-
tude of this union. During the war you know there was a Fuel
Administration, and that there was war-time legislation such as the
Lever Act, etc. The mine workers' wages during the war did not keep
pace with the increased cost of living. The Fuel Administrator did
increase wages. The wages were increased by agreement, etc.,
during the war, but not in keeping with the increased cost of living.
And the miners worked on during the war, they produced the tonnage,
they worked their working time, the amount of labor to be performed
to produce the tonnage for the country was not taken into considera-
tion. They abided their time and the question of wages. There
was no interruption with the production of coal until 1919 came, and
what happened?
There was a strike took place in the fall of 1919. It never should
have taken place, but it did. The responsibility for that strike of
course was placed upon the shoulders of the miners by the Govern-
ment itself, and I think the Government erred without question.
The strike was declared, and the Government set up the fact that the
war was not over, and you were required to work under the orders of
the Government, through its Fuel Administration, until the war
was finally declared ended. It grasped a technical proposition.
Everybody knew the war was over in the fall of 1919. I was home
working with the organization again, and I had served two years in
the Army. I knew the war was over. The men wanted redress.


===== [扫描序号 419] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1435
Their wages had not kept pace with other wages. They went on
strike. The Government stepped in. Injunctions were granted
in behalf of the Government, and the Mine Workers' leaders were
instructed to order the men back, to withdraw the strike order, which
they did. And the men refused to go to work. Finally the President,
President Wilson, proposed submitting the entire matter to a com-
mission.
I want to tell you just what happened in that matter. I was at
Indianapolis when the policy committee of the United Mine Workers
met. And the question was whether or not we would accept the
mandates of the Government. And, of course, there was discussion
upon this policy committee by men with firm convictions, men who
had opinions that were formed. Many of them were unchangeable.
Discussion went back and forth, pro and con, until finally recognizing
that the issue was one between us and the Government, and not one
between the mine workers and the coal operators, the president of
the United Mine Workers made this statement: "We are not going to
fight the Government of the United States. We are Americans."
And we accepted the Government's proposition to arbitrate.
The CHAIRMAN. Who was the president of the United Mine
Workers at that time? Mr. Lewis?
Mr. TETLOW. Mr. Lewis. And since that time, as before, it only
strengthened my opinion of Mr. Lewis, of his character and strength.
An outstanding American, without question. And leading men who
were Americans, and who believed in America's institutions without
question. And that commission found that the mine workers were
entitled to an increase in wages based upon the increased cost of
living. The factors of the selling price of coal and the ability of the
operators to pay was not considered by the Bituminous Coal Com-
mission. The factors involved were purely the increased cost of
living. And, of course, it only gave the miners increase to take care
of the increased cost of living. And no one will agree that wages
should be based upon that premise. But it did. And they accepted
it. And it became the basis-
Senator WHEELER. Is that the Hammond commission?
Mr. TETLOW. No, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. No; that was later.
Mr. TETLOW. That is the Bituminous Coal Commission of 1920.
Mr. Robinson, of California, Mr. Peale, of Pennsylvania, and Mr.
White, of Iowa, were the three representatives. I served with Mr.
White as his statistician on that commission. And the entire propo-
sition was based upon the increased cost of living. And that
became the basic wage of the industry. It was accepted through-
out the country, practically speaking.
The CHAIRMAN. By both the operators and miners?
Mr. TETLOW. By both the operators and miners. They were all
pledged to it. They accepted it, and they put its terms into opera-
tion in all the districts.
Senator FESS. Do you remember the percentage of increase?
Mr. TETLOW. Twenty-seven per cent was the total percentage of
increase that was allowed by the commission.
Senator FESS. When we increased the salaries of Government
employees for the same reason it was $20 a month, $240 a year on
the salaries here.

Senator WHEELER. What do you think they should have done?

Senator WHEELER. Do you think it was too low or too high?

for pick mining throughout the central fields. Then, with the differ-

matically applied to them and the differentials remained constant.
To illustrate, in your State, Senator Wheeler, in Montana, the basic
inside day wage to-day is $8.30. In Ohio it is $7.50.

TESTIMONY OF PERCY TETLOW, ACTING PRESIDENT OF DISTRICT
NO. 17, UNITED MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA, RESIDENCE,
COLUMBUS, OHIO-Resumed
Mr. TETLOW. Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned I was presenting
the situation in the southern West Virginia coal fields, and I want
to make this statement in connection with the one I made this
morning in reference to the Logan County field: In the southern
West Virginia field there are the counties of Mercer, Wyoming,
McDowell, and Logan. These four great producing counties were


===== [扫描序号 430] =====
1446
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
never organized. In other words, they were always operated on the
nonunion basis.
A part of the smokeless or semismokeless fields, the New River
fields, were organized up until 1922. They take in the counties of
Fayette and Raleigh largely. But the other counties were never
organized; and in these counties the production, with the exception of
Logan, was practically all what is known as Pocahontas coal.
As I have already stated they had a production of about 50,000,000
tons annually, between 40,000,000 and 50,000,000 tons. The wages
paid in these counties were never on par with the other union
districts in West Virginia; they always had a wage differential in their
favor. And it was this situation largely that brought about the
condition in the Kanawha district in 1924, I mean which brought
those operators to the position where they could not compete with
the other nonunion districts in West Virginia, and that they could
not reaffirm the wage agreement in that field, By reason of the
wage differentials in the nonunion districts of southern West Virginia,
or at least that was the basic condition that brought about deflation in
wages that crept into the Kanawha district, and then in turn to the
northern West Virginia fields, and then to the central fields, this
deflation in wages all arising from the low wage districts of southern
West Virginia.
The operators in the Kanawha district, when we failed to renew
the agreement there in 1924, set about to nonunionize their mines;
and as I have stated there were about 50,000 people evicted in that
southern field. I want to make that clear, that was between 1922
and 1925, and not only included the Kanawha field but the little and
the big Coal River fields; 50,000 people, or approximately 10,000
miners, were evicted.
And the astounding part of the whole thing is that in those fields
in southern West Virginia were large operations owned and managed
by operators in the union districts of the North. And I think if
they would have thrown their weight into the balance to prevent a
deflation of wages, they could have stabilized and maintained the
stabilized condition that existed in the industry. What caused them
to take the other course I do not know. But I do know that their
policy was injurious to the wage that was established and resulted
injuriously to them as well.
In this field were operating the Kanawha-Hocking Coal Co.,
owned by the New York Central Railroad, and being a subsidiary of
the New York Central, that had four large mines. Those four large
mines were operated under an operating company known as the
Kanawha-Hocking Coal Co. And there was the M. A. Hanna
interests operating at Boomer on Paint Creek. And there was the
John H. Jones Co., the Bertha Consumers Co., operating in that
field. And there was the Y. & O. Co., or the Youghiogheny & Ohio
Co., and the Lorain Coal & Dock Co., had operations of course in
Logan County and not in the Kanawha district. And then there
was the Essex Coal Co. of Columbus, Ohio, that operated mines in
that district, and a large number of other operators who were operat-
ing in that district, who advanced this deflation policy in their wage
negotiations, claiming that they could not compete.
But when you trace it all back you will find it all originated in
this tier of southern West Virginia counties, and that it had crept


===== [扫描序号 431] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1447
north, and it is going farther and farther, and further aggravating
the entire situation.
In 1924 the Kanawha operators, well organized, started upon a
campaign of evictions. Vast sums of money were expended in the
employment of guards, detectives, spies, etc. The first knowledge
that we had of evictions in the Kanawha district came like a bolt
out of a clear sky. A large number of mine guards set out from
Charleston in automobiles armed with high-powered rifles and shot-
guns, and had with them bloodhounds-for what reason I do not
know-and without resorting to any process of law they went into
the little town of Coalburg, on the Kanawha River, a few miles above
the capital of the State, Charleston, and those detectives or mine
guards were organized by a detective agency operated by a man.
named Howard Smith. They proceeded into this little village of
Coalburg without notice and started evicting the miners from their
homes immediately by force of arms. The miners could not resist.
They appealed to the officers of the law, but there was no redress,
and these forcible evictions took place.
Then they went to a number of other towns in the valley, this same
armed force, and evicted, without process, by force. I appealed to
the representatives of the local government, the sheriff of the county,
but without securing any redress against this unlawful invasion of the
homes, the setting aside of the duly constituted law.
And we finally appealed to the governor of the State against this
system of invasion and unlawful evictions
Senator WHEELER. When was this?
Mr. TETLOW. In the fall of 1924. Governor Morgan told us that
he could not prevent it, that he had no authority, no power to prevent
it, that he was informed they were acting within their rights in
securing possession of their houses.
We met the governor on one or two occasions, and we had already
written him, and he finally referred us to the attorney general of the
State. Attorney General England gave an opinion upon the question
of evictions in the manner pursued there, and he declared in the
opinion that the method of evictions was clearly unlawful, and that
it was an illegal invasion of the homes of those people, and that they
had a right to arm themselves in defense of their homes, and that if
evictions of this kind went on they could only go on and be dispos-
sessed legally when there was no breach of the peace.
Well, it brought out the situation that the only way those men
could prevent unlawful evictions was by recourse to arms. And
I realized immediately that that meant war.
Senator WHEELER. What coal company did that?
Mr. TETLOW. What coal company?
Senator WHEELER. Yes.
Mr. TETLOW. I am trying to think of the name of the company
now.
Senator GOFF. Where was it located?
Mr. TETLOW. At Coalburg, on the Kanawha River.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Was it the Coalburg Collieries Co.-is that the
name?
Mr. TETLOW. Yes; I think that is the name. It is a Cincinnati
company.

Mr. TOWNSEND. I am not just sure that that is the name, but it
seems so to me.
Mr. TETLOW. They operate a mine at Plymouth. It was a Cin-
cinnati company that was operating those mines. But the mine
guards were not employed by this particular company; they were
employed, as I understand it, by the operators generally, by the asso-
ciation of operators, and they were employed through a detective
agency operated by a man named Howard Smith.
Senator WHEELER. What was the name of the association?
Mr. TETLOW. The Kanawha Coal Operators' Association. Now,
who employed those detectives I can not say. From what informa-
tion I could get upon the matter it was to the effect that they were
employed by the association, and where the money came from I do
not know. But a large number of mine guards were employed, and
finally, after the governor took the matter up with the operators'
association, they discontinued the practice of forcible evictions.
And then they resorted to the courts under the laws of the State of
West Virginia, and secured possession of their houses by due process.
At all these mines there were stationed a large number of mine.
guards, and eventually the mines began operation upon a nonunion
basis, on the 1917 wage scale, which was about a 35 per cent reduc-
tion in wages.
It was a slow process, a long and bitter struggle, but finally the
mines were completely deunionized. The operators of course at-
tempted to maintain the 1917 wage scale, but the competition among
themselves finally broke down that wage, and the wage went on
down, slowly but surely, until it reached a level of 50 per cent reduc-
tion from the former union wage. And I know many companies in
there to-day that are operating at a wage around $3 a day.
But the wages in these nonunion fields, or earnings, do not tell the
story. A man may earn something, or his gross earnings may be
fairly a good wage apparently, but on pay day when he draws his
envelope he draws no money, or very little. It is all deducted in
living costs store, rent, lights, taxes, minister, doctor, hospital, and
the various deductions take practically all of his earnings.
Mr. TOWNSEND. How about mine-guard protection?
Mr. TETLOW. Well, I do not know whether they are actually
checking off for mine guards or not.

Mr. TETLOW. Yes, sir.

Mr. TETLOW. I would not say that they make a man join a church.
Senator GoFF. Do they make a man pay for the upkeep of a church

Mr. TETLOW. No; I think the deductions are to pay the minister.
Senator GOFF. Well, that means a church, does it not?
Mr. TETLOW. I thought you meant the maintenance of the building.
Senator GOFF. No; I mean the general plan of religious worship;
they pay for that, do they?
Mr. TETLOW. Oh, yes; at some places they do.

Mr. TETLOW. That is my understanding.

Mr. TETLOW. It all depends on the size of the car. These cars
hold 2 or 3 tons, and they vary at the different mines. I judge that
this man was working at loading a 90-cent car-well, it must have
been about a 3-ton wagon.
Senator GoFF. Can you estimate how long it would take him in
time to load that car?
Mr. TETLOW. Well, I could not say. But a miner has more to do
than to shovel coal. A miner is required to drill holes and blast
coal or at least that is true in practically all mines. Some of these
mines they have to do that, and at some mines they have shot firers
who shoot the coal, but as a general rule and almost unanimously so,
the miner is required to drill, shoot, load the coal, timber his working
place, furnish his own tools, buy all of his explosives out of his earnings.
Under practically all mining laws of the country in the different
States the miner is required to timber, and to take care of the working
place for so many feet back from the working face, which is usually
15 feet as a rule. That means that he has to timber there, and has
to take care of his own safety in the working place. The miner is
not always engaged in loading coal. He has the other work to do
in reference to the loading. He has blasting, and cleaning of coal,
all of which goes with the work.
Senator GOODING. And he is paid for all of it on a tonnage basis?
Mr. TETLOW. On a ton or car basis.
Senator GOODING. And this other work would be called dead work
in a sense, I suppose?
Mr. TETLOW. Dead work; yes. And one of the things that brings
more complaint in these mining fields of West Virginia at the present
time than any other, is the fact that men are paid by the car measure-
ment instead of by weight. I have pay statements here from one
man where the man loaded a 3-ton car for 90 cents, that is, 30 cents
a ton. Some men claim that the cars hold 4 tons, while the com-
pany claims they hold 3 tons. A measurement of the car disclosed
that it holds nearer 4 tons than 3 tons.
The men are required to fill a car to a certain level, if not they are
docked.
At the present time so far as I know, and I have made a careful
examination of the entire southern West Virginia field, I do not know
of a check weighman at a single mine tipple in that field, whereas
the law of West Virginia clearly states the right of the workmen to
employ check weighmen, to see that they get correct weights or
measurements.

===== [扫描序号 451] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1467
WHY NOT FEDERAL CONTROL?
United States Senator Gooding, Republican Senator from Idaho, has tenta-
tively suggested Federal supervision of the coal industry. Immediately a roar
of opposition is heard from the industry itself which makes us pause for a moment
to analyze this situation, as we see it. Government control of, regulation of,
and interference in the conduct of the business of producing and distributing
coal is the one bogy of the coal operator. He is against it in any measure or form.
Opposition to it, apparently, occupies a great portion of his working hours.
So opposed is the average coal producer to any measure of governmental
interference with his rights and risks that he flatly and consistently refuses to even
consider what form such interference, if any, should be permitted to take. Dis-
daining logic and compromise alike he has but one answer to all who would con-
sider the subject with him-he is "agin it."
Such is the idea gained from conversation with many executives and from a
careful reading of some trade papers. But we wonder, first, if this is really the
attitude of a majority of the men in the industry and second, if it really is their
attitude, we wonder if it is not a narrow minded and highly prejudiced one.
Why should coal men be so violently opposed to governmental regulations?
Because it is an invasion of their constitutional rights? The veriest rot. Their
opposition is grounded, if at all, in the belief that interference by the Govern-
ment would work harm-financial harm-to them and to their interests. More
often it has no grounding, being merely a parrot voicing of a sentiment that has
been driven into their ears and implanted in their brains so often that they have
come to believe it.
What has the coal operator to fear from governmental "interference" as it is
usually termed? Lessened profits? It is to laugh! Where in these United
States is the region where coal producers make profits so high that they are
afraid to let the people know the whole ghastly story? Where is one producer
who feels that his profits in the past 20 years have been inordinate and that it
would be possible, by any kind of governmental meddling, interference, or control
to cut them down?
Do they resent surrender of private control of enterprise through pride in the
conduct of their affairs? Pshaw, they surrendered that long ago, to their em-
ployees. Even in the boastful "nonunion" fields the employees are a factor
to be reckoned with. The only difference between "union" and "nonunion
fields is that the men in the nonunion fields are a little less rapacious and a little
more wise economically than are those in the union fields. When it comes to
dictating wages, hours, and details of mine management they have brains enough
to let the owners make sufficient money to keep the mines open, and Lewis and
his organization have not. That is the only difference.
The bituminous coal industry could not possibly be worse off under govern-
mental regulations than it is to-day, financially, mentally, or ethically. Its
performance in the past decade, were it not tragic in that it has brought about
the near bankruptcy of the Nation's greatest industry, would be comic. Its
steadfast adherents to its policy of always doing the wrong thing has piled tragedy
on top of tragedy.
And now, after many years of successfully fighting off this hydraheaded monster
of governmental "interference," it faces a coming crisis in a position as weak
or weaker than that which it has ever occupied before.
How will the industry suffer from governmental regulations? Maximum
proces? The Government has never yet set a maximum that the coal operator
had intelligence enough to live up to. Minimum profits? The railroads' 5½
per cent of allowed profit would look like the mint to most of the coal producers
we know. Unintelligent and wasteful regulation? Possibly. And there the
coal operator has the remedy in his own hands.
The way for the coal industry to insure to itself that governmental regulation
will be intelligent is for the thinkers in the industry to stop swearing at the
Congress and start working with it. Secretary Hoover has pleaded for years for
intelligent cooperation. Not getting it, he has assayed one or two moves on his
own initiative and has been damned into a million eternities by the coal industry
because he erred in his judgment. Secretary Davis said that if the coal pro-
ducers did not put their house in order the American public would do the job
without them. Both the great political parties, in their formal plan, have made
similar declarations. Four out of the last five Presidents of the United States
have made parallel demands of the industry.
We do not believe that the coal producers, as individuals, are either afraid of
or opposed to Government regulation. We think they fear the union and each


===== [扫描序号 452] =====
1468
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
other much more than they fear Congress. We believe they would welcome a wisely
devised plan of Federal regulation and the resultant stability and security that,
judging by the experience of the railroads and public utilities, would come from it.
Samuel Insull will shortly be a factor to be reckoned with in the bituminous
industry. The Insull fortunes, prestige, and power have gained steadily under
governmental supervision. If the supervision of the Government will do for the
bituminous industry what it has done for public utilities and the railroads why
not at least give this invitation from Washington serious consideration? Perhaps
we are looking at this situation through smoke-colored glasses. If so, we would
like out operating friends to tell us where we are wrong. On the other hand, if
our readers think we are right in our views on this important subject, a word of
approval would help us in shaping our future editorial policy.
Let loose the heavy artillery. A barrage of bullets or bouquets will tell just
where the industry stands on this matter of Federal regulation. If the shooting
is not too deadly, future issues will divulge myriad views which are bound to be
illuminating, to say the least.

You can not suppress and destroy in America the men who work.
The logical thing to do is to meet this problem from a standpoint of
righteousness. Here is an industry that is overdeveloped. It has
got a competitive condition that is ruinous and destructive of every-
thing worth while. Why allow it to go on? The employers will not
join with us to save it. Their interests are selfish. They are looking
at their own individual company and their own individual investment.
The mine workers are looking at it also from a selfish standpoint, but
they are looking at it from the standpoint of all the men who work in
the industry and who they want to see benefited. They know that
they can not benefit one without benefiting the other, and they are
struggling to help all of them who are engaged in the industry.
The reason why we are fighting against reductions of wages in
Ohio and Pennsylvania is to help the miner in West Virginia and
Kentucky. It is his interest that we are fighting for just as much
as it is the interest of the miner working in these other States.
We know that in the natural course of events we can not hold a
wage beyond reason in one State and beyond a rightful basis, and we
know that if wages are depressed in another State to a low standard
under this condition it is a menace to us. We must either bring it
up or go down with it. It appears that we are all going back and
downward, meaning losses in wages and making that the standard of
the industry. That is what I am opposed to.
Let us look at another phase of it. Here are great natural re-
sources, Senators. We are producing a little over 500,000,000 tons a
year. But under the methods of operation and mining every year
we are losing at least 250,000,000 tons of this valuable resource.
Over one-third of it is lost in methods of mining.
I have been in the mining districts and in the mines in foreign
countries.
The CHAIRMAN. That is a very startling statement. You say
that 250,000,000 tons are a dead loss?
Mr. TETLOW. Every year.
The CHAIRMAN. That never can be gotten out?
Mr. TETLOW. That never can be recovered. Here are Germany
and England and France and Belgium all recovering from 90 to 98
per cent of their natural resources because of their methods of min-
ing, and under our methods we are losing at least one-third, and
some estimate it at 40 per cent. If we are producing over 500,000,000
tons we are losing over 250,000,000.
The CHAIRMAN. You speak of our methods of mining. You do
not mean by that, machinery?
Mr. TETLOW. I mean methods of mining.
The CHAIRMAN. What do you mean by that?
Mr. TETLOW. Under our methods of mining we are taking out
coal as we are advancing. Necessarily we are leaving large pillars
of coal for support of the roadways and airways and haulage roads.
As we go back into the mines there are 10, 20, 30, or 40 miles of under-
ground traveling ways and passages. These are supported by pillars
of coal. We lose these pillars to a great extent.
The CHAIRMAN. How do they do that in Germany or England?
Mr. TETLOW. Most of the coal is worked on what is known as the
"long wall" retreating system. They go to the boundaries of their
territory and draw the coal back, and as they bring it back they


===== [扫描序号 455] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1471
recover practically all of the coal. The excavated areas close up
with the stratas falling in. There is no place for the accumulation
of gas and coal dust.
Under our methods we go ahead developing as we go, working out
the coal as we are advancing, and leaving in these large pillars and
blocks of coal for the protection of the mine. After this mine has
been in operation for years and years it is impossible to get back to
these pillars and blocks of coal to take them out and they are left in
the mine. This again costs from 5 to 10 cents a ton in the mining
of the coal because it is left in the hill and it is never taken out.
Many are leaving valuable coal because it costs 5 or 10 cents a ton
more to take it out.
You can not meet that situation on any other basis than Govern-
ment control. I have thought it over. How else are you going to
deal with it?
Then, again, our methods of mining are responsible for the great
death and accident rates in our mines. Both of them run hand in
hand. The reason that England, Belgium, and Germany have a
death rate only about one-fourth of ours is due to their methods of
mining. If we are to reduce the death and accident rate of our
workers we must change the methods of mining and the system.
In the long run it would save money.
Mr. STANLEY. What would be the difference in cost per ton between
our system and the "long wall" system?
Mr. TETLOW. I think the recovery under the other plan would be
greater and the cost of the recovery would be less.
Mr. STANLEY. You mean the cost per ton?
Mr. TETLOW. The cost per ton would be less. Our initial outlay
would be greater, of course, but, considering the area covered and
the tonnage recovered, it would be less in total.
Senator GoFF. Could you state in this connection the rate of wages,
relatively speaking, paid in England and Germany, as compared with
the average rate here in the coal industry? I think it would illu-
minate what you are saying if you would state it right in this con-
nection.
Mr. TETLOW. I think there have been some modifications during
the last year in the wages in Belgium and in Germany. In 1926 I
visited the mining fields of England, France, Belgium, Germany, and
Austria, and at that time the minimum wage as applied under the
British plan was $2.25 in our money. In Germany it was about $1.75.
Senator PINE. Per ton or per day?
Mr. TETLOW. Per day; $1.75 in Germany, $2.25 in Britain, and
I think about 95 cents in our money in France, with the same relative
rate in Belgium.
Senator WHEELER. What is the difference in purchasing power?
Mr. TETLOW. Of course, there is a great difference in that.
Senator WHEELER. So that, as a matter of fact, those figures that
you have given us do not mean very much unless we take into con-
sideration the purchasing power of the $1.75 and the $2.25 and the 95
cents there and compare it with what that purchasing power is here.
Mr. TETLOW. There is a great difference.
Senator WHEELER. As a matter of fact, the cost of living in this
country is practically twice as high as it is there?


===== [扫描序号 456] =====
1472
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Mr. TETLOW. It is more than that. Then, you must remember that
in addition to the wage in Germany there are many other considera-
tions. In other words, they have what they call a family wage in
Germany in addition to the basic wage. A man who has a family
gets additional pay. Then they have different sorts of pension
arrangements. They have housing arrangements. To me it was a
revelation when I went to Germany and found the type of homes that
the miners lived in and the manner in which they were maintained;
beautiful homes, homes that would be a credit for anyone to live in;
stone and brick homes; gardens; flowers, beautiful homes maintained
under their plan. In other words, they have gone into the care and
the housing of workmen to an extent that aids them materially in that
life.
Senator WAGNER. To what extent is the Government itself in-
volved in that in Germany?
Mr. TETLOW. In Germany they have what is called a Government
syndicate through which all coal is sold. They first set up a national
syndicate. Then they have dsitrict syndicates. The coal origi-
nating in any district is sold through this syndicate and in the district
under instructions from the national syndicate as to the allocation
and markets. Then, their national syndicate looks after the exports.
They are in different countries; Denmark, Sweden and Norway,
Scandinavian countries, seeking markets for their coal. In other
words, they are meeting the situation scientifically.
Of course, everybody knows that since the war there has been a
competitive situation in Europe with coal that is just as deadly as
we have it internally here. The Versailles treaty upset the situation
generally. Here was Great Britain that had been sending 25,000,000
tons of coal to France annually. Under the Versailles treaty France
was getting coal from the Germans from the Saar Valley Basin.
That coal was lost to England. France was able to produce, and is
producing, more coal now than she did before the war; she has
rehabilitated her mines and is producing more coal than she did
before the war.
Senator HAWES. Mr. Tetlow, before you conclude there is a matter
that I would like to inquire about. Senator Gooding called atten-
tion to some figures here awhile ago that possibly you could assist
in throwing some light upon. He has a table here which has been
put in the record showing the coal output between 1913 and 1927.
That shows that in all that period of 14 years Illinois lost approxi-
mately 16,000,000 tons, Kansas 5,000,000, Missouri 1,600,000, Ohio
22,000,000 and Pennsylvania 42,000,000. West Virginia increased
its output 80,000,000 tons and Kentucky 52,000,000 tons. In other
words, these five States showed a loss of 86,600,000 tons and these
two States an increase in that period of 132,000,000 tons. Now,
what is that occasioned by? Of course, the reduction was brought
about by the increased sales in these two States.
Mr. TETLOw. That is true.
Senator HAWES. It naturally upset all conditions in the other
States?
Mr. TETLOW. That is correct.
Senator HAWES. How are you going to change that?
Mr. TETLOW. Well, of course, if the mine workers were organized
in these States and if the legal barriers which have been built up

against it in the courts were removed and organizations established in
the fields, if wages were made upon a competitive basis, that met
reasonable and free competition, in my judgment much of this ton-
nage would come back to the original States that were producing it;
but on the whole the sales realization would be stabilized to such an
extent that all would be better off.
The thing that I am afraid of is that if it is allowed to go these

Senator HAWES. Let us analyze that for a moment. What per-

Mr. TETLOW. Well, some is due to that.
Senator HAWES. Well, I know you can not say exactly, but you can

Senator HAWES. Twenty-five per cent on quality?

Senator HAWES. In the competitive markets?
Mr. TETLOW. Without question; but I think the reason that these
States have increased production and the northern States have lost

the southern fields.
Senator HAWES. Now, what percentage of the labor cost is due to

Mr. TETLOW. Of course, that would vary as to the wage. Labor
costs may be responsible for 80 per cent of the total cost in some
districts.
Senator HAWES. Do they all use the same method of mining, the
same equipment?
Mr. TETLOW. Yes; practically all.
Senator HAWES. Then, according to you, this enormous increase
and this enormous loss are due 75 per cent to labor conditions?
Mr. TETLOW. That is my judgment.

UNITED STATES SENATE,

The committee met, pursuant to adjournment, at 10.15 o'clock
a. m., in room 212, Senate Office Building, Senator James E. Watson
presiding.
Present: Senators Watson (chairman), Gooding, Fess, Goff,

The CHAIRMAN. The committee will please be in order. Did you
finish your testimony, Mr. Tetlow?
Mr. TETLOW. I was on the stand when we adjourned.
TESTIMONY OF PERCY TETLOW-Resumed
The CHAIRMAN. Have you any other points that you desire to
bring out that you have not touched on?
Mr. TETLOW. No, sir; except that I had in mind to answer the
inquiry of Senator Fess. I said that I had certain opinons on the
matters about which he inquired.
The CHAIRMAN. What was that inquiry?
Mr. TETLOW. He inquired what in my judgment was necessary to
solve the problems of this industry, and I told him I would answer
when I concluded my statement.
My judgment is that the things that are essential for the industry,
for peace in the industry, are the recognition of the right of col-
lective bargaining; the right of men to choose of their own volition
as to the method of collective bargaining; relief from injunctions that
have interfered with the rights of collective bargaining and shackled
the progress in this industry.
I believe that consolidations in the industry are inevitable and
should come. I believe that more essential than consolidations are
the creation of sales organizations and the selling of the commodity;
and if amendments to the laws are necessary to permit that, they
should be made.
I think that for the well-being and permanency of this trade in-
dustry, if these powers are given by Congress they must set up some
regulatory board or tribunal to supervise them. I think that is
inevitable and must be done.
I think they should have the power also to determine and to assist
in working out methods of mining that will conserve the fuel and
prevent the waste and also conserve life and limb and health.

I think they ought to have the authority to regulate the selling
prices of coal, in order that the cost of the fuel will be equalized and
the burden spread equally. A system where the great users are
getting fuel below production cost and the smaller users of coal are
paying the burden is wrong; and with the purchasing power such as
it is in the hands of a few that can direct and control it, there must
be some regulatory board to administer those features in this industry.
It is essential, in my judgment, that such action be taken by Congress.
That, in my judgment, is necessary to cure the ills of the industry.

1477
Mr. TETLOW. And yesterday, Senator.
Senator FESS. I shall be glad to read it in the record. That is my
chief concern; that is, my concern extends to the entire industry,
but especially that particular section of the country that once sup-
plied a real production and now is so depleted that it does not look
very promising. Something ought to be done if it can be done.
Mr. TETLOW. The conclusion that I drew on that, Senator, is this:
That the trouble began in the deflation of wages south of the Ohio
River to such a marked degree that their production cost was reduced
so greatly as compared to the other producers that they naturally
took the markets that were formerly enjoyed by these other states.
In that process, of course, the miners were objecting to the deflation
of the wage that was spreading north. The Ohio miners have been
standing against it because they said-and all the miners say that
that will not solve the problem; that we may reduce the wages in
Ohio in order to recover our share of the markets which were naturally
ours; that it will only further depress the whole situation because
those who have already depressed wages to the low standard are
suffering just as keenly and intensely as we are who are not pro-
ducing any. That is the sad feature of the whole thing.
Bankruptcy and receivership are sweeping through these districts
that have deflated wages, because the price of coal has gone con-
stantly down and down, and the industry has been at the mercy, you
might say, of the great purchasers of fuel, and they have made such
inroads that even those who have reduced wages have suffered
just as keenly and more so than those who have not.
I pointed out yesterday that West Virginia had increased its
tonnage from 101,000,000 to 143,000,000 in the years 1923 to 1926,
and their sales realization, even though they had increased between
30,000,000 and 40,000,000 tons, had dropped $20,000,000. In
other words, they sold 143,000,000 tons for $20,000,000 less than
they did 100,000,000. These reports of sales realizations and
production are on file at the Department of Commerce.
I think that instead of allowing this industry to go into the jungle
deeper with this cutthroat competitive condition and permitting the
laws of supply and demand, which, in this instance is reverting to
the Stone Age, the reasonable thing to do is for Congress to regulate
this industry to a degree where it will permit the payment of a decent
wage to the men who are in the industry, a fair return to the men
who have invested money in the industry, and to equalize the burden
of cost of the fuel to the people, because under the present system
those who are less able to pay must pay the most for the fuel, and it
is wrong.
Again, as I pointed out yesterday, I think if you will refer to the
Bureau of Mines or any of the mine inspectors of the different States,
or any mining engineers or any producers who are familiar with the
methods of mining coal, you will find that we are losing approximately
for the entire country 250,000,000 tons of coal annually by our
wasteful method of mining and those methods are responsible for the
great death and accident rates in our mines.
We have not kept pace with other countries in that respect, and
the only way that we can conserve the fuel and conserve life, give
a fair wage to those working in the industry, and deal justly with all
citizens, would be through a regulatory power set up by the
Government.

productivity. In other words, men are able to produce more year
after year.
Now, it can not be consumed. In other words, your production is
going to run beyond your consumption power. I do not care how
equally you distribute that, in order for people to consume the

Senator GOODING. And cheap coal does not increase the use of it

Mr. TETLOW. They were charged with that, Senator, but what
labor was really trying to do was this: Labor was working half-time
on an 8-hour basis in the mines, and they recommended that instead

Senator FESS. That was misunderstood by the public.
Mr. TETLOW. And they were trying to bring about that by reducing

Now, just let me again go back to the production of coal. When
I worked in the mines as a boy, working with a pick, the hand picked
methods, undercutting with a pick, using an old-fashioned churn
drill to drill holes and blast the coal, our production per day was
about two to two and a half tons per man in the large veins. First
we got the compressed air undercutting machines, then the electric
machines to undercut the coal. We had the old-fashioned breast
machine. Then we changed that to the short wall and the long-wall
machines. It was constantly increasing the productivity.
Now we have drifted into the loading of the coal by mechanical
devices and our productivity has increased 100 per cent, without
the use of mechanical loaders to any great degree. They are coming
in. And instead of loading 5 tons per day, or getting out 5 tons
per day for an average of all employed in the industry, within 10
years we will be producing 8 and 9. It is just as certain as we are
here. Now, how are we going to meet that problem? In my judg

ment, without question, it is going to mean a shorter workday for

Mr. TETLOW. And producing more. We worked 12 hours in the

Senator FESS. Mr. Tetlow, I would like to have you state whether

Mr. TETLOW. It certainly is to this degree: Under my plan that I

and a voice in their hours of employment and wages. Let them
have a voice so that they can protect their own interests and their
rights that are involved, and allow the coal operators to do likewise.
Permit them to consolidate to more economically work out the
problems of production from their end. Permit the establishment
of selling agencies so that the coal can be distributed economically
from a selling standpoint and to eliminate the internal competition

Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Tetlow, you have stated that there is a con-
sumption of coal in the United States amounting to 500,000,000 tons
per annum. Is that about correct?
Mr. TETLOW. I was using approximate figures. It has been higher
and lower, of course.
Mr. BELCHER. You also stated yesterday that the consumption of
coal had been at a standstill for a number of years; in other words, it
has been stationary; it was not increasing to any considerable ex-
tent?
Mr. TETLOW. No.
Mr. BELCHER. You also stated that there were too many men
engaged in the industry?
Mr. TETLOW. On its present basis; yes.
Mr. BELCHER. And that there is an overproduction of coal?
Mr. TETLOW. Well, there is a potential production, of course, there
that enters more vitally than the overproduction.
Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Lewis stated while he was on the stand that
there were two-fifths more miners than were needed in the industry
to mine sufficient coal to take care of the public. Do you agree with
that statement?
Mr. TETLOW. Well, I would put it in another way. If three-fifths
of the men who are in the industry were working overtime they
could produce all the coal that the country would need.
Mr. BELCHER. Can you give the approximate number of men who
are engaged in the mining industry in the United States? Coal
mining, I mean.
Mr. TETLOW. About 725,000, I judge.
Mr. BELCHER. Then, if two-fifths of that number were considered,
that would mean about 300,000 miners more than are needed to
produce the coal that is needed by the country?
Mr. TETLOW. Well, you are including anthracite miners in that,
which is not included in the problem.
Mr. BELCHER. It has been stated a number of times that there are
about 250,000 more men engaged in the industry than are needed to
produce sufficient coal for the needs of the country. Do you agree
with that statement?
Mr. TETLOW. No; I think that is a little high.

sell 500 tons a day.

Mr. TETLOW. I want to tell you another incident that came to my

Armstrong Creek, advised me that the company had proposed a fur-
ther reduction in their wages, and they stated that their wages
were so low that they were ashamed to offer them another reduction,
in order to get the work, and the men and the company agreed that
the tonnage workers were to pay the day workers' wages, and they
made an agreement to check off from the loader and miner so many
pounds of coal a day to pay the day workers' wages.

[From Fairmont (W. Va.) Times, of March 1, 1928. Referred to by Mr. Van A. Bittner in
his testimony before committee]
We see by the papers that the Senate committee, investigating the bitumi-
nous coal business in northern West Virginia et al., will hold its first session
in Washington on next Tuesday morning. John L. Lewis will be the first
witness. From reading the reports of the activities of the Senate subcommit-
tee which spent last week in Pittsburgh and vicinity, it wouldn't surprise us
much if John L. Lewis would not only be the first but the only witness.
However, it is worthy of comment, this activity of the mine union in setting
the stage for the Senate investigation. The circulation of a false and mis-
leading petition which many miners are believed to have signed without an
understanding of its text or purport, is only in keeping with mine union
methods in this field since our labor troubles first began.
For instance we heard yesterday of the little son of a working miner who
came home with a sack of candy and upon being asked by his father where
he obtained the sweets declared that the "red-necks" from the barracks gave
them to him for "writing his father's name on a piece of paper."
More striking still was a story from a near-by mine of the discovery of a
"petition" addressed to the Senate committee demanding that northern West
Virginia again be unionized. This petition contained the signatures of 20 of
the company's best known and highest paid miners. A subsequent investiga-
tion showed that every name had been forged.
It is conceivably possible that some of the members of the Senate committee
will be hoodwinked by the bunkum of the mine union, but the people of West
Virginia will not be, and these include the 25,000 working miners, who, in
spite of hard times know that their condition is better than under the old
tyrannical system.
MINUTES OF MEETING OF MARKETING COMMITTEE OF NATIONAL COAL ASSOCIATION
AT PITTSBURGH, PA., OCTOBER 14, 1927
The marketing committee of the National Coal Association met at the Wil-
liam Penn Hotel, in Pittsburgh, Pa., on Friday, October 14, at 10.30 o'clock
in the forenoon, with Chairman Glover presiding, and Messrs. Booth, Bradin,
and Lockhart of the committee present, along with W. H. Cunningham, vice
president of the West Virginia Southern Coal Co., of Huntington, W. Va., and
J. A. Teegardin, vice president of the New York Coal Co., of Columbus, Ohic.
who had been invited by the chairman.
The committee discussed at length the advisability of holding one or more
regional meetings of bituminous coal sales managers and agents, in line with
the recommendation of last year's marketing committee, as authorized by
the board of directors, but decided to defer action thereon until a later meet-
ing. The executive secretary of the association was directed to make informal
inquiry of officials of the Cincinnati Coal Exchange as to whether such a
meeting would be desirable in Cincinnati; and if so, whether that organiza-
tion would sponsor same in cooperation with this committee; also to make
similar inquiry of other places where such a meeting might be held.
A communication from Ira C. Cochran, commissioner of the American
Wholesale Coal Association, under date of June 7, 1927, was read, the same


===== [扫描序号 509] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1525
having been presented at a meeting of the board of directors on June 15,
and referred to this committee. The letter follows:
"The question of marketing being one in which every wholesaler is inter-
ested, was actively discussed at our convention, and later at the meeting of
the executive committee.
"The executive committee have instructed me to communicate to you the
appreciation of this association of the work your association has done, and
is carrying on in this field, and to suggest to you that we shall welcome the
opportunity fully to cooperate with you in this undertaking.
"We are prepared to create a special committee for that purpose if and
when we can be of assistance in solving the problem."
Chairman Glover was authorized to in his discretion appoint a subcommittee
to make contact with officials or a similar subcommittee of the American
Wholesale Coal Association for a discussion of common problems of the market-
ing of coal and report back to this committee.
The standard forms for the purchase of coal prepared by the National Asso-
ciation of Purchasing Agents were considered at length. Several exceptions
were raised thereto. Executive Secretary Gandy was directed to procure
several copies of those forms and to submit same for criticism and suggestions
to members of this committee, those who had been invited by Chairman Glover
to attend this meeting, and to secretaries of coal operators' local associations.
Thereafter a statement of exceptions and suggested amendments to said con-
tract forms is to be prepared, at which time the chairman is authorized to
appoint a subcommittee to confer with representatives of the National Associa-
tion of Purchasing Agents and report back to this committee.
The above action of the committee was taken upon motion regularly made,
seconded, put and carried.
There were submitted to the committee certain suggestions for consideration,
together with tentative drafts of a statement of unfair practices and of trade
terms and trade rules, copies of which are attached to and made part of these
minutes. The committee decided that the fourth and fifth subjects under
general subjects, the first subject under sales practices, the second subject under
educational work, and the second subject under research should be dropped;
that all other subjects on said list should be carried over for future considera-
tion.
The above action of the committee with relation to subjects was taken under
unanimous consent procedure, coincident with a reading of the subjects
paragraph by paragraph.
There being no further business, the committee adjourned at 5.15 p. m., to
meet at the call of the chairman.
Attest:
H. A. GLOVER, Chairman.
HARRY L. GANDY, Secretary.
SUGGESTIONS FOR CONSIDERATION OF THE MARKETING COMMITTEE
GENERAL SUBJECTS
The marketing committee should plan and arrange for one or more sectional
sales meetings, as suggested by the former marketing committee and author-
ized by the board of directors of the National Coal Association. It has been
suggested that in addition to the sales managers, the executive heads of
bituminous companies be invited, especially in small companies having no sales
organizations of their own and no financial interest in the selling company
handling their outputs.
Advisability of having the chairman, on behalf of the committee, meet with
local associations during the year with a view to coordination of activities
with those of the marketing committee.
Shall the marketing committee urge that the producer and seller of all
coal have mutual interests, both in production and sale?
Shall the committee consider and approve forms for acknowledging orders
and contracts?
Should the marketing committee consider the compilation and dissemination
of a statement of unfair practices in rejecting coal or making claims for
adjustments?


===== [扫描序号 510] =====
1526
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Possibility of adoption of trade ethics, rules, and terms.
Cooperation with public officials and others in the drawing up of specifica-
tions for coal requirements.
It is suggested that the marketing committee present the subjects it selects
for consideration to the various local associations with the request that they
make a simultaneous study and a report thereon.
SALES PRACTICES
Should an effort be made to define and secure adherence thereto of the
respective sale fields of the producer, the wholesaler, and the retailer?
Consideration of the general question of contracts for coal, the period of
time, the nature of the contracts, and especially the matter of contracting
over any period of time at fixed prices with nonconsumers, such as retail
dealers.
The advisability of the adoption by local associations of plans for clearing
surplus sizes.
The need for consolidation of sales efforts.
The question of the use of trade-marks for both domestic and steam coals,
methods of their registration, a reference book of such trade-marks, and
whether they should be applied by the producer, the sales agency, or the
retailer.
Should producers of coal retain absolute control over the sale of their product
and stipulate a price which provides at least cost of production and a rea-
sonable margin of profit?
It is suggested that consideration be given to the matter of sales not war-
ranted by credit rating, the extension of credit beyond printed terms, the
advance dating of invoices, and the desirability of the exchange of credit
information in local associations or bureaus.
ADVERTISING
Consideration of the question of joint advertising under a particular trade
name of coal from any certain seam.
That a study be made of advertising of both steam and domestic coal, as to
whether same is more effective through magazines, newspapers, or direct mail.
It is suggested there is a large field for what might be called "demonstra-
tive advertising" in various cities, such as is done by the anthracite operators.
It is suggested that considerable local district publicity can be secured
through the railroads. These possibilities should be brought to the attention
of the local associations.
EDUCATIONAL
WORK
Should an educational effort be made in opposition to the production and
shipment of coal before it is sold?
Should this committee undertake the preparation of instruction cards for
burning bituminous coal, that said cards might be available for purchase by
operators with their individual imprint thereon?
Consideration of ways and means of bringing about a condition where
every sales manager and salesman really knows his own coal, what it is good
for, what it is not good for, for what types of equipment it is efficient, how
coal is sampled, the variations in chemical analyses, etc. In other words, every
salesman should make it bis business to find out what his coal will do to the
best advantage, and where they need such a coal.
Cooperation is suggested with architects, heating engineers, retail coal as-
sociations, individual retailers, manufacturers of domestic furnaces, etc., to
promote the installation of proper combustion equipment, the elimination of
smoke, and in general to develop more efficient, more economical, and more
desirable methods of using domestic coal.
The need for educating road salesmen in the use of coal in various types of
equipment and the chemical analyses and physical characteristics of different
coals.
The question of the use of combustion engineers in sales organizations, and
the service rendered by coal sales companies in this respect.


===== [扫描序号 511] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1527
It is suggested that we heartily approve the policy of the officers of the Na-
tional Code Association in accepting every invitation possible to speak before
meetings of coal consumers. It is also suggested local associations and indi-
vidual operators miss no opportunity of addressing representative groups
in their respective localities on the subject of coal. Selling the coal industry
to the public is a very great step in the direction of modern merchandizing of
the product.
RESEARCH
A suggestion has been made that a thorough sudy be made of the market-
ing of coal on a B. t. u. basis, from which conclusions and recommendations
might be drawn. Further, that associations in other lines might be interested
in such a study.
A study of the buying habits and needs of various lines, such as ice plants,
automobile factories, and retail coal dealers, might result in recommendations
for solicitation only at such times as would meet the needs of the various voca-
tional lines.
The question of encouraging and fostering scientific research in coal and its
use, through local associations and technical institutions. Further, tha this
committee cooperate therefor with the research committee.
TRADE INFORMATION
Consideration of the question of sales budgets with a view to more nearly
equalizing production schedules with the demand, and the need for a study of
the coal-buying habits of the American people, with especial relation to the
seasonal factors.
The matter of indorsing a most comprehensive trade-information program
for the collection and dissemination of information with respect to produc-
tion, sales, markets, surplus coal, etc., by local associations or bureaus but
leaving the details thereof to the trade information committee.
STATEMENT OF UNFAIR PRACTICES
Said practices, even if indulged in by a comparatively few producers, have
a tendency to cause criticism of the industry as a whole, and it is with the
thought of emphasizing the importance of a high code of ethics that the
following suggestions are set forth for consideration. The proposed suggestions
are recognized as being possible of adoption generally by all branches of the
industry:
I. The intentional overtesting, undertesting, incorrect grading, misdescrip-
tion of coal or coke as regards analysis, quality, preparation, or origin or in
any manner making or declaring a false return or report on the test of
the quality or grade of any coal or coke or any constituent thereof, purchased
or sold, is hereby declared unfair.
II. The making, causing, or permitting to be made, any false or deceptive
statements, either written or oral, of or concerning the business policy of a
competitor. his products, selling price, financial or personal standing, is hereby
declared unfair.
III. The use either in written or oral form of trade-marks, trade names,
slogans, advertising matter, or descriptive terms of a competitor is hereby
declared unfair.
IV. The paying or rendering, directly or indirectly, to any employee or
agent of a common carrier, any consideration or reward for the purpose or
with the effect of influencing such agent or employee to render any dis-
criminatory or unequal service between shippers, or receivers of coal or
coke, or to give any information concerning a competitor's shipments or business
is hereby declared unfair.
V. The paying or giving to competitors' or customers' employees or their
agents any money, rewards, premiums, or excessive treats or anything of
value, in order to secure business or information concerning a competitor's
or customer's business, is hereby declared to be unfair.
VI. The cancellation of orders, or suffering their cancellation by customers,
except by mutual consent, is an unfair practice.


===== [扫描序号 512] =====
1528
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
VII. The practice of allowing to customers unusual or long terms of credit,
excessive entertainment, or allowing unearned discounts for the purpose of
securing or retaining business, is declared unfair.
VIII. Obtaining any information from a competitor by making any false
or misleading statements or misrepresentations, or by false impersonation of
anyone in authority, or by any method of espionage, is hereby declared
unfair.
IX. Failure to pay or render in accordance with an offer, verbal or other-
wise, or an advertisement, the full price for coal or coke purchased, or failure
to ship coal in accordance with such offers, is hereby declared unfair.
X. The sale of any coal or coke short in weight or measure is taking unlawful
advantage of honest competitors and is hereby declared unfair.
XI. The cost of transportation by rail, water, truck, or in any other form
shall be taken into account in the settlement with customers when freight is
prepaid by shippers or sold on a delivered basis, and the practice of ignoring
the cost of transportation in such instances, is declared unfair.
XII. The interference by any person, association, company, or corporation by
any means or device whatsoever with any existing contract between a com-
petitor and his employees, or agent of such employer or employees, or inducing
competitor's employees to leave in sufficient numbers as to disorganize, impede,
or embarrass his business in any way, is hereby declared unfair.
XIII. It shall be deemed unfair, either directly or indirectly, to discriminate
in the price of coal or coke offered to different customers or different localities,
providing nothing herein shall prevent discrimination in prices to customers
based on legitimate costs, difference in grades, quality, or quantity of com-
modity offered or discrimination in price in the same or different communities
made in good faith to meet competition.
XIV. The practice of selling or offering for sale coal or coke at prices which
do not yield to the producer or seller a fair return of profit is unethical. (In
this connection it is recommended that there should be established a scientific
system of cost accounting in the coal undustry, that producers and sellers of
coal and coke may know accurately the cost of their product and the relation
of prices thereto. Without a standard system of cost accounting, practices
that may be unfair may be indulged in without the knowledge or consent of
the responsible officers of the company involved. Legitimate cost differentials
warrant different prices and tend to avoid even the appearance of a monopoly;
hence the necessity for a system of cost accounting that will reflect the funda-
mental cost items and principles.)
XV. The consigning of unordered coal to a possible buyer, in the hope that
it will be accepted, has a tendency to create an unstable condition in the
market and is considered unfair.
XVI. Threatening to withdraw advertising unless one's competitor's matter
is excluded or certain discriminations or favors are granted, is hereby declared
unfair.
The following is recognized as being applicable only to the producers of coal
or mine operators:
XVII. Failure to prorate shipments on contracts during car-shortage periods
on a basis equivalent to the percentage of cars secured against mine rating,
will be considered an unfair practice. However, nothing shall prevent a pro-
ducer from entering into a preferential contract, provided all other persons with
whom he makes contracts are informed of the existence of this preferential
contract.
The following suggestions are recognized as being more especially directed
toward the wholesale and retail branches of the bituminous coal industry:
XVIII. The false or misleading statements, either written or oral, as to prices,
advertisers' status as a mine operator or otherwise, is considered an unfair
practice.
XIX. The accepting for disposition of coal or coke consigned to a dealer
without having been ordered, has a tendecy to disrupt markets and supplies
and is considered an unfair practice.
XX. Threats to withdraw patronage from an operator if he supplies coal
to a competitor except in the case of exclusive sales agreement, is considered
unfair.

TRADE RULES
1. Both the buyer and the seller should include in the original offer and
acceptance, whether by telephone, telegraph, mail, or personal conversation,
the following specifications: (1) Number of cars; (2) kind of cars; (3) quan-
tity, kind, and grade of coal; (4) price; (5) point of shipment or rate point;
(6) time of shipment.
2. All orders taken by personal solicitation should be reduced to writing and
should be signed or acknowledged by both the buyer and seller or the author-
ized agent of each. All oral or telephone orders or conversations relative to
such orders should be promptly acknowledged or confirmed in writing.
The original order received from a buyer in response to an offer from the
seller by mail or telegraph should be considered the contract, and all settle-
ments made upon this basis. Any changes or additions should be agreed to by
both the buyer and the seller. Acknowledgment should be sent the buyer imme-
diately upon receipt of an order and in due course by mail. Failure to ac-
knowledge should release the buyer from his order obligations.
3. All spot sales should be made on the basis of freight rates in effect at
time of sales. All coal contracts should provide protection for both shipper
and buyer relative possible changes in freight rates.
4. Unless the buyer is rated and in good standing, as shown by the well-
known credit agencies, no order should be binding upon the seller until such
credit and good standing is determined to the satisfaction of the seller; investi.
gation of credit standing should be completed in a reasonable time.
5. The seller should not be held responsible for delays incident to trans-
portation beyond his control.
6. The party in possession of necessary papers for use in filing a claim of
any character against a carrier, being unable or refusing to deliver papers,
when requested to do so, to other interested parties before the time for filing
claims has expired, shall be responsible for any loss incurred as a result of
his failure.
7. When a definite time for shipment is specified, failure to ship within that
time should permit the buyer to cancel the order by telegram or mail.
8. No order should be canceled after it has been shipped provided it shall
have been filled in accordance with contract between the buyer and the seller,
except as to date of shipment.
9. Senders of telegrams or telephone messages shall prepay the charges due
thereon, and be responsible for their correct transmission, unless written
confirmation shall have been deposited in the mail to the addressee in time
for forwarding in the mail next following the transmission of the message.
10. Transit shipments should be subject to the same rules as apply to direct
shipments, except as otherwise agreed at the time the order is given and
accepted. The buyer should be given all information in the possession of the
seller as to location and movement of the cars, to avoid misunderstandings.
11. In any dispute as to meaning of trade terms, the definition given by the
association's standard trade terms will prevail.
12. Differences between members of this association, and between members
and nonmembers, which can not be amicably adjusted, should be submitted to
arbitration.
TRADE TERMS
To-day's shipments: Shipments on date of order acknowledgment.
To-morrow's shipments: Shipments on date following date of order acknowl-
edgment.
Immedate shipments: Shipments within three days of acknowledgment of
order.
Prompt shipments: Shipments within week following acknowledgment of
order.
First or early part of week: Shipments Monday or Tuesday following order
acknowledgment.
Middle of week: Shipments Wednesday or Thursday following order acknowl-
edgment.
Last of week: Friday or Saturday following acknowledgment of order.


===== [扫描序号 514] =====
1530
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Soon as cars can be obtained: Within two weeks of order acknowledgment,
unless time is extended by mutual agreement.
Shipment: Shipment means car has been loaded and necessary billing instruc-
tions furnished the carrier. A bill of lading or other transportation receipt shall
be conclusive evidence as to date of shipment.
F. O. B. Free on board cars at any designated place.
C. I. F. Charges, insurance, and freight.
Diversion: A change in the consignee and/or destination while in transit
or at destination prior to placement for delivery to original consignee and within
twenty-four hours after arrival.
Reconsignment: A change in the consignee and/or destination after arrival
of car at billed destination, and placement for unloading by original consignee.
Circulars: A circular describing available coal and naming prices is not an
offer to sell, but is a solicitation for bids and inquiries.
Limited offer: An offer to sell subject to prompt acceptance and prior sale.
Open offer: An offer to sell subject to prompt acceptance or for a specified
time to be named in the offer.

mittee adjourned to meet the following day, Thursday, March 29,
1928, at 10.15 a. m.)

Collective bargaining has been carried on in Wyoming for about 25 years.
In the beginning agreements were entered into for 1-year periods, later fol-
lowed by signing agreements for two years until on March 19, 1924, our agree-
ments were made for a period of 3 years beginning April 1, 1924, and ending
March 31, 1927.
On March 7, 1927, the representatives of the northern and southern Wyoming
coal operators associations and the representatives of the United Mine Workers
of America, district No. 22, met in the city of Cheyenne and agreed to extend
the then existing agreement until a new basic wage agreement is arrived at
and made effective in the central competitive bituminous-coal fields.
The basic inside wage scale for Wyoming under the Jacksonville agreement
is $7.92 against $7.50 for the eastern fields. Montana also is receiving a higher
rate than that paid in the East. The States of Montana and the union sections

In the District Court of the United States for the Northern District of West
Virginia at Elkins, W. Va. Lorain Steel Co., a corporation, plaintiff, v.
Brady-Warner Coal Corporation, a corporation; the Union Trust Co., a cor-
poration, as trustee; Richard Inglis, as trustee; John J. Cornwell and John
C. Rice, as trustees; and New England Fuel & Transportation Co., defend.
ants. In equity, order appointing receiver, etc.
On this July 29, 1927, this cause came on to be further heard upon the bill
of complaint, the answer of defendant, Brady-Warner Coal Corporation, the
motion of plaintiff for the appointment of a receiver of said defendant and
for a preliminary injunction, as prayed for by the bill of complaint; upon
order of this court entered on July 23, 1927, setting said motion for hearing
on July 29, 1927; upon notice in pursuance of said order only served upon
defendants New England Fuel & Transportation Co. and John J. Cornwell,
trustee; upon appearance herein by defendant Richard Inglis, trustee, by
Austin V. Cannon and Charles A. Goodwin, his solicitors, who tendered his
cross bill, duly verified, which is ordered filed herein; upon appearance by
defendant New England Fuel & Transportation Co., by Frank R. Amos, its
attorney, and leave is given said New England Fuel & Transportation Co. to
file its answer and intervening petition herein within five days, and this cause
was argued by counsel.
Whereupon it appears to the court it is proper and necessary for the pro-
tection and preservation of the rights and equities of the parties that a
receiver of the properties, assets, and business of defendant Brady-Warner
Coal Corporation should be appointed by this court, it is therefore adjudged,
ordered, and decreed that W. H. Conaway, of Fairmount, W. Va., and A.

Spates Brady, of Elkins, W. Va., be, and they hereby are, appointed receivers

purchase such new materials, supplies, and equipment and employ such agents,
servants, and attorneys, by and with the consent of the court as to attorneys,
and others as may be, from time to time, necessary or proper in conducting any
business of said defendant until the further order of this court; to collect and
receive all rents, profits, and income from the properties of said defendant and
from the conduct of its business by such receiver or otherwise and to apply
the same under the orders of this court for such period of time as this court
shall determine, and do any and all other acts which may be necessary and
proper, within the general intent of this order, to protect and preserve the
rights and property and all of the same of defendant corporation and other-
wise in all respects to exercise all incidental powers ordinarily invested in a
receiver or in receivers in like cases.
And temporarily and pending this suit and until further order of this court,
defendant Brady-Warner Coal Corporation and all of its officers, agents,
servants, attorneys, unsecured creditors and all other persons, except lien
creditors and their trustees and representatives, are hereby restrained and
enjoined and each of them hereby is restrained and enjoined from interfering
with such receiver in his possession, control management and conduct of any
and all of the business, property and assets of said defendant; and they and
vach of them are restrained and enjoined from instituting or prosecuting in
any court or enforcing any separate actions, executions or any other processes
or proceedings of any kind instituted or issuing from or in any court against
said defendant or in respect to or against any of the property and assets of
said defendant and from bringing about loss, injury, damage, destruction or
forfeiture of any of the property of said defendant on account of defaults by it
in payment or payments and on any other accounts, and from intermeddling
with or taking possession of any of the property or assets of said defendant;
and said defendant and any and all of its officers, agents, servants, attorneys
are hereby restrained and enjoined from selling, transferring, giving away
or otherwise disposing of any of the property or assets of said defendant, and
said defendant and all of its officers, agents, servants, employees, attorneys
and others, except lien creditors and their trustees and representatives, are
required to transfer, convey, assign, set over and deliver to such receiver or to
duly authorize representatives any and all of the property and assets of said
defendant corporation; all until the further order of this court.
And it is further adjudged, ordered, and decreed that said receivers are
hereby directed to file with the clerk of this court a bond to be approved by
said clerk in the penalty of $100,000 conditioned that they will well and truly
perform the duties of such receiver under this order and abide by the further
directions of this court, such bend to be with sufficient surety or sureties.
And said receiver shall file in the clerk's office of this court within 30
days from this date a first report as such, showing a full and complete inventory
(without appraisement, the right to require such appraisement being subject
to the further order of this court) of all the property of said defendant Brady-
Warner Coal Corporation taken into possession and control under this order;
and shall thereafter likewise file monthly reports of actions and proceedings in
