taxes. We pay into that fund, according to my recollection, $1,462.50
per month. We lay that aside for that contingency.
Senator GOODING. You are selling some of your coal to some rail-
roads for less than cost of production at the present time?
Mr. CONAWAY. Yes, sir.
Senator GoFF. Mr. Conaway, have these matters to which you have
referred in answer to the several questions propounded, been sub-
mitted to the United States court by you and your coreceiver as
officers of the court?


===== [扫描序号 531] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1547
Mr. CONAWAY. Yes, sir. We personally keep in touch with the
court and ask his advice as to what to do, and he usually replies,
"Use your judgment."
Senator GoFF. Has the court at any time during the period covered
by the questions and your answers approved of what you have done?
Mr. CONAWAY. Yes, sir. We monthly file at Elkins, W. Va., a
detailed monthly report addressed to the court showing our opera-
tions. That is a matter of public record at Elkins, W. Va.
Senator GOFF. When does the court approve of the reports which
you submit?
Mr. CONAWAY. We file them as of the 15th of each month. They
are immediately submitted to the court for the court's information
to keep in touch with what we are doing.
Senator GOFF. Has the court set a day for hearing, or does the
court approve of your reports without giving notice to the creditors
to give them an opportunity to object?
Mr. CONAWAY. We file a report with the clerk of the court; and I
can not say how soon, but, as I understand, the court immediately
after its inspection of our report approves it.
Senator GOODING. Mr. Conaway, what percentage of your coal
is sold to the railroads on an average running through one month
after another?
Mr. CONAWAY. I think the most of it.
Senator GOODING. Then, you are either forced to take what the
brokers offer you or close the mines?
Mr. CONAWAY. That is true.
The CHAIRMAN. Do you lose money on all you sell?
Mr. CONAWAY. Yes, sir.
The CHAIRMAN. How long are you going to keep that up?
Mr. CONAWAY. Well, we have only been at it eight months, and I
can not say; but the records disclose this fact, that according to the
indebtedness of this corporation and what you might call overhead
charges of all kinds, we must receive at least $1.95 to meet that.
Senator FESS. What proportion do you sell to get only $1.30? Is
that just a small portion, or it it any considerable quantity?
The CHAIRMAN. What is that, Senator Fess?
Senator FESS. He spoke about getting $1.30 for coal. I was won-
dering whether that was representative or whether it is just inci-
dental.
Mr. CONAWAY. It is representative throughout the mines.
Senator FEss. I do not see how you run.
The CHAIRMAN. Of course, you do not know what is in the mind
of the United States district judge.
Mr. CONAWAY. No.
The CHAIRMAN. But how can a court continue to approve a policy
of that kind? Is it better for the mine to continue to operate and
suffer that loss than it is to close the mine, from the standpoint of
expense and wastefulness?
Mr. CONAWAY. My information is, as I hear the matter discussed
in the courts and before the judge, that it is better to keep a mine in
operation than to close it down. It quickly deteriorates in value
when it is closed down.
The CHAIRMAN. Are there any other questions?

Mr. CONAWAY. I think they are yearly contracts.

Mr. CONAWAY. Yes; they tell us what they have to accept.
Mr. McVANN. And the yearly contracts that they make are made

Mr. CONAWAY. Yes.
Mr. McVANN. And they expect when they make them to obtain
the coal to fill these contracts from you and other producers? Is
that correct?
Mr. CONAWAY. Yes.

Mr. McVANN. That is the only method they have of obtaining

Mr. CONAWAY. Personally, I do not know, but I would think that

Mr. CONAWAY. Yes.

Mr. CONAWAY. No; we have tried to eliminate the broker and deal

Senator FESS. Mr. Conaway, is your case a representative case, or
an exception, in selling coal at a loss?
Mr. CONAWAY. I think it is a condition prevailing in northern
West Virginia throughout the coal business.

TESTIMONY OF W. H. CONAWAY, ESQ., RECEIVER OF THE BRADY-

TESTIMONY OF D. W. BOONE, GENERAL MANAGER OF THE NEW
RIVER EXPORT SMOKELESS COAL CO., LOOKOUT, W. VA.—
Resumed
(The witness was duly sworn by the chairman when called at
the morning session.)
(Further examination by Mr. Charles E. Townsend, attorney for
United Mine Workers of America :)
Mr. TOWNSEND. Mr. Boone, you had gotten down to the point
in your testimony where you gave the scale of wages, I think,
from January 1, 1920, to November 1, 1927. That is where you quit,
was it not?
Mr. BOONE. Down to the present time.
Mr. TOWNSEND. In the scale of wages that you gave beginning
with 1920, and that you paid your employees down to the present
time, there is quite a variation. It goes down and then goes up
and then goes down again.
Mr. BOONE. Yes, sir.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Will you tell the committee why that is?
Mr. BOONE. On account of the price of coal going up and coming
down on the market.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Have you ever operated your mine union?
Mr. BOONE. I never have.
Mr. TOWNSEND. It has always been nonunion?
Mr. BOONE. Yes, sir.
Mr. TOWNSEND. How do you go about reducing the scale of
wages?
Mr. BOONE. I talk it over with my men, and then I prepare a
price going up and coming down and present it to them for their
consideration.
Mr. TOWNSEND. And they accept it?
Mr. BOONE. Yes, sir; they always have.
Mr. TOWNSEND. You deal with them individually?
Mr. BOONE. Yes, sir.
Mr. TOWNSEND. And have individual contracts of employment
with them?
Mr. BOONE. I have a contract that we have had in effect since
1902.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Will you produce a copy of that contract? Have
you a copy of it here with you?
Mr. BOONE. Yes, sir.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Will you produce it, if you please?
Mr. BOONE. Here it is. Shall I read this contract?
Mr. TOWNSEND. Suppose you just read it to the committee.
Senator GOODING (presiding). Do you want the contract read,
Mr. Townsend?
Mr. TOWNSEND. Yes, sir.
Senator GOODING (presiding). All rigfht, you may proceed to
read it. Mr. Boone.
Mr. BOONE. It is as follows [reading]:
This contract, made and entered into this 1st day of September, 1919, between
New River Export Smokeless Coal Co., party of the first part, and hereinafter
called the employer, and the employees of the said company who sign this
contract, parties of the second part, and hereinafter called the employees;
1


===== [扫描序号 558] =====
1574
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Witnesseth: That whereas the employer is engaged in mining and selling
coal at Lookout, W. Va., and has spent large sums of money in developing its
mine and making extensive improvements thereon for the purpose of getting
out the largest quantities of coal; and
Whereas the said employer has sold and contracted and agreed to sell through
its agents and others engaged in the coal-selling business large quantities of
coal for the present coal year, and for the year next ensuing, and said coal
agents of the employer having in turn contracted to sell large quantities of
coal to be mined and shipped from the mines of the employer during said year;
and
Whereas said employer is exceedingly anxious to fulfill of its obligations in
respect to supplying the coal sold and to be delivered during the next ensuing
year, and during the length of time this contract is kept in force; and
Whereas there has heretofore existed between the employer and the employee.
a satisfactory contract and working agreement continuing since April 1, 1902,
which has worked to the satisfaction and advancement of both employer and
employees, and on account of the changed conditions in the New River field
and the changes in the scale of labor, it has become desirable to make a new
contract, and the employees of the party of the first part are willing and
anxious to continue in the employment of the party of the first part for the
coming year upon the conditions and for the consideration hereinafter named,
and are willing to engage their services for the said period of one year upon
the conditions and considerations to be paid to them as hereinafter set out:
Now, therefore, it is
Mutually agreed between the employer and the employees, That the employees
of the party of the first part agree and do hereby bind themselves to continue
to perform and to do the necessary manual labor and work for the employer
in mining and removing coal from its mine, and any and all other work in con-
nection with running the coal mine and preparing the coal ready for shipment,
and during the year beginning September 1, 1919, in consideration that they
be paid by the employer the following stipulated wages for the various work
necessary in mining and removing the coal from said mine situated as afore-
said and making the same ready for shipping.
First. The prices to be paid by the employer to the employees for the differ-
ent classes of work to be performed shall be as follows, the price to the said
employees shall be equal to and not less than the prices paid by other mine
owners in the New River field for pick and machine mining; also the prices
for all other classes of work and day labor, both in, outside, and around said
mine, to be equal to and not less than prices paid for similar work throughout
the said New River field; and we further agree that the wages shall be graded
and based upon the experience, proficiency, and capacity of the employee
performing the same, but not to be arbitrarily determined by any artificial
basis known as the Union Mine Workers' scale, the said scale of wages to be
paid based upon the experience, proficiency, and capacity aforesaid, when any
dispute arises thereover to be determined by arbitration; that is to say, when
any scale of prices has been fixed by the employer for any class of labor or for
any employee who may deem the same not commensurate with the price paid
for similar labor in the New River field, and complaint made to the employer,
the same shall be settled by arbitration in the following manner: The employer
will appoint a competent, practical, fair man, well posted in mining and mining
wages, and the employee will likewise appoint a man equally well posted in
mining and mining wages, and after the two shall have heard all evidence and
statements of facts presented they shall either increase or decrease the price to
be paid for such labor about which complaint has been made according to the
facts and based upon the fair valuation of such wages being paid in the New
River field; but in the event the two arbitrators so appointed shall fail to
agree, then the said arbitrators shall select another employee of the party of
the first part as umpire, who shall be equally well posted in mining and mining
wages, and the decision of the three so appointed shall be final. And the
parties hereto agree and bind themselves to accept such final decision and abide
by the same without appeal.
Second. It is further agreed that married employees or those having families
will be furnished houses at reasonable prices per month, to be paid monthly, the
use and occupancy of said houses to be incident to the employment, and to be
surrendered whenever the employee ceases to be the employee of the party of
the first part.


===== [扫描序号 559] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1575
Third. It is hereby mutually agreed between the employer and employee that
in consideration of the premises and the payments to be made by the employer
to the employees, that the said employees will, and they hereby agree and
bind themselves to work for the employer for a period of at least 12 months
from the date hereof at such work as the employer may have for them to do
at the prices hereinbefore set out, and that the employees will not strike or in
any way cause others to strike, or give the employer any trouble, but will use
their influence in every reasonable way in order to keep the employer's mine
running every day possible for the life of this contract, and that they will also
discourage any interference by others who are not employees of the party of the
first part, or who may undertake to interfere or give trouble or bring about
dissatisfaction between the employer and the employees.
Fourth. It is hereby further agreed that should there be an advance paid the
miners generally in the New River field for any of the different kinds of work
mentioned above, or which may be required to be performed by the employer,
that the employer will agree to make an advance in the price of all laborers
around and about the mine so that the wages to be paid by the employer to the
employees will be equal to and never less than the wages paid throughout said
New River district, thus insuring to the employees at least a wage scale equal
to and never less than that paid throughout the entire New River field.
Fifth. It is further agreed and understood that this is a contract entered
into for the mutual benefit of both the employer and employees, and that all
the parties hereto agree and bind themselves to carry out in good faith and
perform the several obligations hereunder for the mutual benefit of all the
parties hereto; and it is further agreed that this contract may be automatically
renewed from year to year in the following manner: That is to say, it shall
be renewed automatically from year to year after the same has been signed by
both employer and employees and remain and continue a contract from year to
year unless any party hereto desires to no longer be bound thereunder, where-
upon he shall give notice for at least 10 days before the end of any one year'
of his desire to no longer be bound thereby, and when such notice is given, then
such party shall have the right to release therefrom at the end of any one year,
without being further obligated thereunder; and it is further agreed that any
new employee who has not heretofore been a party to this contract may become
a party by signing the same at any time during the year and thereafter he
shall become a party to the contract as though he originally signed the same
for the whole year.

In witness whereof the said party of the first part and the parties of the
second part have hereunto signed their respective names,
NEW RIVER EXPORT SMOKELESS COAL Co.,
By D. W. BOONE, General Manager.

ARGUMENT OF A. M. BELCHER FOR THE WEST VIRGINIA
WITNESSES IN THE SOUTHERN FIELD
Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, this
question that is now before the committee is more important than the
price of coal or the conditions under which a ton of coal is mined.
It is a fundamental proposition that concerns the right of a citizen
of this country under the Constitution and laws of the country which
bind all of us.
So that I may not be misunderstood, I have reduced to writing
some of the things that I want to say in arguing this constitutional
question.
While each and all of these witnesses are willing to give the com-
mittee any and all information within their knowledge of that char-
acter as may be needed by the committee or the Senate as to enable
Congress to efficiently exercise a legislative function in the passage of
valid legislation, yet it must be understood that the information
sought, and especially under questions 2, 3, and 4, can not be of any
possible aid to the committee or to the Senate in the passage or con-
templated passage of any legislation within the power of Congress to
enact. There is no pending legislation to which these questions
relate. Resolution No. 105, under the provisions of which this hear-
ing is being had, does not point out or contain any suggestion of
contemplated legislation.
These witnesses who have been summoned by your committee and
required to bring with them certain information in the way of con-

tracts, sales of coal, prices received by them for coal sold, the names

sought by the committee, and especially under the following para.
graphs of the telegraphic communications sent by the committee to

Total tonnage cost of production, show labor cost separately, and sales reali-

In the case of Hitchman Coal & Coke Co. v. Mitchell (245 U. S.

This court repeatedly has held that the employer is as free to make nonmem-
bership in a union a condition of employment as a working man is free to join
the union, and that this-
And I want this committee to think on this proposition-
and that this is a part of the constitutional rights of personal liberty in private

exercise of a paramount police power.
Such as martial law when the country is at war, the Government
in order to protect its sovereignty may do it, and in no other way.
In the present case, needless to say, there is no act of legislation to which
defendants may resort for justification.
And in that case the United Mine Workers' organization, its offi-
cials, and members were defendants.
This case was decided in 1917, and there has been no legislation
concerning this matter subsequent to that decision. Congress can
no more-and I want to say this with all deference and with all
respect, because I am an American citizen-Congress can no more,
by legislation, compel an employer to employ only union labor than
it can compel such employer to join the Methodist Church or the
Ku Klux Klan. Therefore this subject is beyond the power or
authority of the Senate to enact into valid legislation, because it is
not the subject of valid legislation.

As above stated, practically all the information sought by the
committee from these witnesses relates solely to private affairs, pri-
vate contracts, and private undertakings. Neither branch of Con-
gress is invested with general power, or with any power, to inquire
into private affairs and to compel evidence of and concerning pri-
vate affairs in which the Federal Government or any of its depart-
ments are directly or indirectly involved in no manner whatsoever.
As stated by the Supreme Court in McGrain v. Daugherty (273 U. S.
173):
neither House is invested with 'general' power to inquire into
private affairs and compel disclosures, but only with such limited power of
inquiry as is shown to exist when the rule of constitutional interpretation just
stated is rightfully applied. The latter proposition has found support in Har-
riman v. Interstate Commerce Commission (211 U. S. 407) and others.
And it is a necessary deduction from the decision in Kilbourn v. Thompson,
and re Chapman, that a witness rightfully may refuse to answer where the
bounds of power are exceeded or the questions are not pertinent to the matter
under inquiry.
The questions propounded by the committee to these witnesses,
and especially the matters referred to in questions 2, 3, and 4, involve
matters"in which the bounds (of the Federal Government) are
exceeded;" and in no way "pertinent to the matter under inquiry."
Again, as stated in Kilbourn v. Thompson (103 U. S. 190):
We are sure that no person can be punished for contumacy before either
House, unless his testimony is required in a matter into which that House has
jurisdiction to inquire, and we feel cqually sure that neither of these bodies
possess a general power of making inquiry into the private affairs of the citizen.
In Federal Trade Commission v. American Tobacco Company (264
U. S. 298) the court said:
The Senate resolution may be laid on one side, as it is not based on any
alleged violation of the antitrust acts, within the requirement of section 6 (d)
of the act.
Not a witness summoned here is charged with any violation of
law. Federal or State, and, of course, State law would take care of
itself.
The complaints, as to which the commission refused definite infor-
mation to the respondents, and one, at least, of which, we understand, has been
dismissed, also may be disregarded for the moment, since the commission claims
an unlimited right of access to the respondents' papers with reference to the
possible existence of practices in violation of section 5.
Here was a charge of a violation of a Federal law, and yet the court
says this:
The mere facts of carrying on a commerce not confined within State lines.
Our business is confined within the State of West Virginia, and
the State of West Virginia or its citizens owns every pound of coal
within its borders, and yet not a pound of it owned or controlled by
the National Government.
The mere fact of carrying on a commerce not confined within State lines and
of being organized as a corporation do not make men's affairs public, as those
of the railroad company now may be.
Of course, it does have control of the railroads, because the States
of this country have delegated to the Federal Government the power
to regulate interstate commerce, and no State or Government can
exercise any power over interstate commerce.

In Smith v. Interstate Commerce Commission (245 U. S. 33) the
Supreme Court said:
Anyone who respects the spirit as well as the letter of the fourth amendment
would be loath to believe that Congress intended to authorize one of its sub-
ordinate agencies to sweep all our traditions into the fire and to direct fishing
expeditions into private papers on the possibility that they may disclose evidence
of crime.
There is not a remote possibility here in this instance, and none is
sought and none charged.
The interruption of business, the possible revelation of trade secrets,
and expense that compliance with the commission's wholesale demands would
cause are the least considerations.
The fact that one man may mine coal for $1.50 and another for $2
are the least of the considerations here, because the great fundamental
question is a constitutional right that this Congress can not afford
to step outside the bounds of.
It is contrary to the first principles of justice to allow a search through all
the respondents' records, relevant or irrelevant, in the hope that something will
turn up.
And what is that something in this case? That the committee may
answer itself.
The unwillingness of this court to sustain such a claim is shown in Harri-
man v. Interstate Commerce Commission (211 U. S. 407), and as to correspond-
ence, even in a case of a common carrier, in United States v. Louisville & Nash-
ville Railroad Co. (236 U. S. 318).
In Harriman v. Interstate Commerce Commission (211 U. S. 421)
the court said:
If by virtue of section 21 the power exists to summon witnesses for the pur-
pose of recommending legislation, we hardly see why, under the same section,
it should not extend to summoning them for the still vaguer reason that their
testimony might furnish data considered by the commission of value in the
determination of questions connected with the regulation of commerce. If
we did not think, as we do, that the act clearly showed that the power to
compel the attendance of witnesses was to be exercised only in connection with
the quasi judicial duties of the commission, we still should be unable to suppose
that such an unprecedented grant was to be drawn from the counsels of per-
fection that have been quoted from sections 12 and 21. We could not believe
on the strength of other than explicit and unmistakable words that such auto-
cratic power was given for any less specific object of inquiry than a breach of
existing law in which, and in which alone, as we have said, there is any need
that personal matters should be revealed.
In re Pacific Railway Commission (32 Fed. 241), it was said:
Congress can not compel the production of private books and papers of citi-
zens for its inspection, except in course of judicial proceedings, or in suits
instituted for that purpose.
The United Mine Workers have instituted no suit against these
witnesses. The court continues:
and then only upon averments that its rights in some way depend upon evi-
dence therein contained.
Congress can not empower a commission to investigate the private affairs,
books, and papers of the officers and employees of corporations indebted to the
Government, as to their relations to other companies with which such corpora-
tions have had dealings, except in so far as such officers and employees are
willing to submit the same for inspection; and the investigation of the Pacific
Railway Commission into the affairs of officers and employees of the Pacific
Railway Companies, under the act of March 3, 1887, is limited to that extent.

1593
As I said a few moments ago, of course, there are no charges or
complaints against these witnesses involving any Federal law. Their
business is not the subject of Federal control nor legislative regula-
tion. All the information sought and the papers, the production of
which are requested, concerns only the production of coal and the cost
and sale thereof.
Now, I take it, that if the production of coal is not interstate com-
merce, then this committee is absolutely powerless to exercise any
regulation over it, because we must not forget that sovereign States
of this Union still have some rights not delegated to the National
Government.
While they have delegated the power, as I said a moment ago, to
regulate interstate commerce, they have retained to themselves sover-
eignty in respect to those things that in this phase of it are not in-
terstate commerce, and that has been decided time and time again
by the Supreme Court of the United States.
In Hammer v. Dagenhart (247 U. S. 251), the court said:
The making of goods and the mining of coal are not commerce, nor does
the fact that these things are to be afterwards shipped or used in interstate
commerce, make their production a part thereof.
In United Mine Workers v. Colorado Company (259 U. S. 407),
the court said:
Coal mining is not interstate commerce, and the power of Congress does not
extend to its regulation as such.
That being the law then we naturally inquire why are we here?
The same holding is found in Delaware, Lackawanna & Western
Railroad Company . Yurkones (238 U. S. 439).
Again, in the old case of the United States v. E. C. Knight Com-
pany (U. S. 14), the court said:
No distinction is more popular to the common mind, or more clearly expressed
in economic and political literature, than that between manufacture and com-
merce. Manufacture is transformation-the fashioning of raw materials into
a change of form for use. The buying and selling and the transportation inci-
dental thereto constitute commerce; and the regulation of commerce in the
constitutional sense embraces the regulation at least of such transportation.
If it be held that the term includes the regulation of all such manufactures as
are intended to be the subject of commercial transactions in the future, it is
impossible to deny that it would also include all productive industries that con-
template the same thing. The result would be that Congress would be invested,
to the exclusion of the States, with the power to regulate, not only manufac-
tures, but also agriculture, horticulture, stock raising, domestic fisheries, min-
ing-in short, every branch of human industry.
As Senator Bruce asked Mr. Tetlow yesterday, if you can regulate
mining, why can not you regulate the making of shoes? If you can
do one, you can do the other; and if you can do one, you can control
all the industries in the United States. Then what would become of
the rights of sovereign States? The question has been asked here a
time or two, Where are we going? Whenever the downfall of this
country comes-and I hope it never will-that downfall will not be
written in terms of coal; but I say this on my own responsibility, with
all deference to Congress and all the constituted powers of Govern-
ment: That when that time comes it will be written and used in
terms of usurpation of power.

In conclusion, we cite for the serious consideration of the com-
mittee the case of Boyd v. United States (116 U. S. pp. 634-635),
wherein the court said:
* And we are further of opinion that a compulsory production of the
private books and papers of the owners of goods sought to be forfeited in such
a suit is compelling him to be a witness against himself, within the meaning of
the fifth amendment to the Constitution, and is the equivalent of a search and
seizure and an unreasonable search and seizure-within the meaning of the
fourth amendment.
That amendment, as you all know, is where a man is secure in his
paper. The court continues:
Though the proceeding in question is divested of many of the aggravating
incidents of actual search and seizure, yet, as before said, it contains their
substance and essence, and effects their substantial purpose. It may be that
it is the obnoxious thing in its mildest and least repulsive form; but illegiti-
mate and unconstitutional practices get their first footing in that way, namely,
by silent approaches and slight deviations from legal modes of procedure. This
can only be obviated by adhering to the rule that constitutional provisions for
the security of person and property should be liberally construed. A close and
literal construction deprives them of half their efficiency and leads to gradual
depreciation of the right, as if it consisted more in sound than in substance. It
is the duty of the courts to be watchful for the constitutional rights of the
citizen, and against any stealthy encroachmetns thereon. Their motto should
be obsta principiis. We have no doubt that the legislative body is actuated by
the same motives-
the Supreme Court still speaking by one of the four greatest judges
that ever adorned that bench, perhaps one of the two greatest-
but the vast accumulation of public business brought before it sometimes pre-
vents it, on a first presentation, from noticing objections which become devel-
oped by time and the practicable application of the objectionable law.
What I have said has been with deference to this committee and
to the power of Congress, but I say to you that it is the duty of every

Mr. WARRUM. If the committee please, the problem that confronts

of the resolution as to whether or not it is broad enough to author-

pertinent facts.

Resolved, That the Senate Committee on Interstate Commerce be, and it

While I am not familiar with the rules and the practice in investi-

mittee has the power to report legislation that any inquiry may sug-

Simply because a bill has not been introduced and a particular bill
is not under discussion does not indicate, as Mr. Belcher suggests,

mended by this committee.
The situation that calls for this resolution is one that in its very
nature requires an investigation before the committee will be enabled
to prudently or judiciously recommend the form of legislation that
they may think proper and effective in curing any ills that they may
discover in the industry.
Take the question of the investigation into the railroads, the con-
duct of the railroads, whether in collusion or otherwise, in depressing
the cost of the wages of coal miners, the production cost of coal. The
committee has been sitting here for some time investigating the rela-
tion of the railroads to the coal industry in Ohio, Indiana, Pennsyl-
vania, and northern West Virginia. The operators in those sections
have freely come on the stand and submitted to the committee the
exact character of data that is asked from the witnesses represented
by these gentlemen; and if anything has been made plain in this in-
vestigation, it seems to me it is that the railroads have been at least
exercising the powerful influence that they have as purchasers of 29
per cent of the bituminous coal of this country in depressing prices,
in wrecking union standards north of the Ohio River, and in exploit-
ing the industry that they confess themselves is hopelessly disor-
ganized. The broad trail that the committee has pursued upon that
point leads, and has led, to southern West Virginia. Is it possible
that in an investigation of that character you can go to the line of
southern West Virginia and be debarred from making any further
inquiries there? Has Congress a right to regulate the railroads in the
attitude that they may take toward the fuel service that they require?
Is Congress without power to say that they are dissatisfied with the
practice by railroads in disorganizing this industry? Is Congress
powerless to govern this governmental agency?
Why, if the committee please, the present transportation act would
almost seem to justify a complaint lodged before the Interstate Com-
merce Commission against the practices followed by the railroads in
buying their coal. Let me read you a part of the third section of the
transportation act.

thing that can not be done now. Why? Because Congress in the
Sherman Act and the Clayton Act has said that that could not be
done. But what Congress has said in the Sherman Act is not deter-
minative on what Congress may say now.

In some of the suits there would be as many as 60 companies.
Take the Winding Gulf district and all of the companies there

These are 12 suits instituted by various owners and operators of coal mines
in West Virginia, against the international organization, United Mine Work-
ers of America, the district and local unions of that organization in West
Virginia, and various of its international, district, and local officers and mem-

Complainants are 316 in number, embracing most of the coal companies
operating on a nonunion basis in what is known as the southern West Vir-
ginia field. The suits are instituted to restrain interference with business
of complainants by the union and its members, on the ground that such inter-
ference constitutes a restraint of interstate trade and commerce in violation
of the Sherman Act.
Now we took the position-and we cited all these cases, the first
Coronado case, the child-labor case, the Yurkones case, the Knight
case, and all these cases we cited on the proposition-that coal min-
ing was not interstate commerce and that interference with coal
mining was not interference with interstate commerce. There was
no charge there, no proof there, that we were interfering with the
operation of railroads; that we were stopping the shipment of coal,
or that we were going into other States and interfering with the
sale of coal in other States by a boycott or any other process.
The proposition was that we were trying to organize the labor
forces of these 316 companies, producing about 40,000,000 tons of
coal a year in southern West Virginia, and that our activities, in
view of the fact that they had employed their men under these
"yellow dog" contracts, that our activities in trying to organize
these labor forces, though it did not deal directly with interstate
commerce, though it did not directly impinge upon or affect the facil-
ities or instrumentalities of commerce, were nevertheless a restraint
of interstate commerce under the Sherman Act, because of the vol-
ume of coal produced, the volume being sufficient, the court said,
under the Second Coronado case, to create the presumption that our
interference with production was intended to be an interference with
commerce in the shipment of it.
We fought that proposition as bitterly as we knew how, and upon
the proposition that these gentlemen are relying upon here, the
decisions upon which they based their argument on yesterday, that
coal mining is not interstate commerce, and that interference with
coal mining is not an interference with interstate commerce.
But let me read to you what was said by the court at the instance

Defendants say, however-
And we were the defendants there-
and this seems to be their chief contention on this point, that the mining of
coal is not interstate commerce and that a conspiracy to interfere with the


===== [扫描序号 589] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1605
operation of coal mines is not a conspiracy to restrain or interfere with inter-
state commerce.
In this connection they rely chiefly upon the decisions of the Supreme Court
in the First Coronado case (259 U. S. 344), and in United Leather Workers v.
Herkert (265 U. S. 457). But we do not think that either of these decisions
is in point. The leather workers case involved a strike by laborers in trunk
factories, and it was held that the fact that the trunks, when manufactured,
were to be shipped or sold in interstate commerce did not make their produc-
tion a part thereof. The Coronado case, it is true, involved the mining of coal;
but the court, being under the impression that the coal produced by plaintiff
amounted to only 5,000 tons a week, held that a conspiracy directed against
production of so small an amount could not be said to be a conspiracy to re-
strain interstate commerce, even though the coal was intended, if produced,
for shipment in such commerce.
When the Coronado case went to the Supreme Court the second time, how-
ever (268 U. S. 295), the court adverted to this basis of its former decision and
stated that upon the second trial it had been shown that the capacity of plain-
tiff's mines was substantially more than 5,000 tons per day. It held that this,
with other evidence as to intent, made a case for the jury as to conspiracy
to restrain interstate commerce.
We think there can be no question that the case at bar falls within the rule
just quoted from the second Coronado decision. Here it appears that the
total production of the mines of complainants is in excess of 40,000,000 tons
per year, more than 90 per cent of which is shipped in interstate commerce.
Interference with the production of these mines as contemplated by defendants
would necessarily interfere with interstate commerce in coal to a substantial
degree. Moreover, it is perfectly clear that the purpose of defendants in inter-
fering with production was to stop the shipments in interstate commerce. It
was only as the coal entered into interstate commerce that it became a factor
in the price and affected defendants in their wage negotiations with the union
operators.
In other words, while our activities thus restrained by the Federal
court under an act passed by the Congress, when the jurisdiction of
the court was invoked solely upon that ground, or at least could be
predicated solely upon that ground, then our activities in trying to
organize the labor forces in these 316 mining companies, with their
40.000.000 tons of production, was a matter within Federal jurisdic-
tion and had been dealt with, the court said, by the Sherman Act, and
that they would restrain and enjoin us in perpetuity, us and our suc-
cessors in membership.

REPLY ARGUMENT OF HON. A. OWSLEY STANLEY, FOR WEST
VIRGINIA WITNESSES IN THE SOUTHERN FIELD
Mr. STANLEY. Mr. Chairman, I note in the statement of my brother
that he continually refers to the right of a court or of Congress to
do this, that or the other. There is a common impression, built upon
a reasoning by analogy-that is, the English Parliament, for in-
stance, in all probability has the same power as a court of judicature
to punish for contempt, and to compel the compulsory attendance
and testimony of witnesses, and the production of papers in answer
to any injury that the court may consider pertinent. But the Con
gress of the United States has no such power.
I was very much impressed with the pertinent inquiry of the
chairman of this committee. He displayed that rare power which
he possesses of getting at the heart of a question in a few words,
and few men possess that power more peculiarly than the chairman
of this committee. And you asked the question of Mr. Belcher,
in substance this: We want to know whether or not mining-pro-
duction of coal-is interstate commerce. If it is, then we have a
right to ask this question. If it is not, we have not. Now, if this
is not interstate commerce it goes without saying that you have no
right to ask this question, because you have no more control over the
processes of the production of a commodity than you have over the
setting of a hen; not a bit. You have got as much right to ask
how we were baptized, as to whether we believe in purgatory, as
you have to ask us about any activity in which we are engaged,
which is confined to the State, which is not related with commerce


===== [扫描序号 595] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1611
between the States, because it is beyond your ken. And, of course,
your power to ask these questions, being predicated upon your
power to exercise the legislative function, you can not ask a ques-
tion about the right to exercise an unconstitutional function, a func-
tion that is categorically denied you by the Constitution.
But, Mr. Chairman, the converse of that proposition is not true.
You can not ask any question you like of any witness you please
because you happen to be investigating some question over which
you have jurisdiction. Your jurisdiction over the subject matter of
the inquiry does not warrant you in the exercise of any such a
plenary and unlimited power, and the Supreme Court of the United
States has explicitly so stated.
It is most fortunate for us, most fortunate for the committee,
most fortunate for the stability of these institutions and the pres-
ervation of the spirit, the spirit as well as the letter, of the Consti-
tution of the United States, that this very question 40 years ago
and more, way back yonder in the One hundred and third United
States, was exhaustively reviewed by the greatest Associate Justice
that ever adorned the bench of the Supreme Court of the United
States. Congress had in that case absolute power over the subject
matter. It concerned the conduct of a Secretary of the Treasury.
The United States had loaned vast sums and placed them with Jay
Cooke & Co. as depositor. They were inquiring into the malfeas-
ance of a Federal officer in the disposition of a Federal fund, and
they asked this man in the Kilbourn case certain questions about his
private affairs. The court said: "No; it is none of your business.
You can not ask it." You are not, this Federal Congress, this Senate
is not, though it seems in many quarters to think it is, a court
of judicature. You never have been invested with the power to
punish for contempt that is inherent in a court, and you have no
constitutional warrant for the exercise of any such a power. If
you possess it at all-and for a long time it was doubted whether
you did or not-it is incidental to the right to legislate upon cer-
tain matters, and purely incidental.
This whole matter, this whole question of your right was reviewed
by Justice Miller. He said:
While there is, in the adjudged cases in the English courts, little agreement
of opinion as to the extent of this power, and the liability of its exercise to be
inquired into by the courts, there is no difference of opinion as to its origin.
This goes back to the period when the bishops, the lords, and the knights and
burgesses met in one body, and were, when so assembled, called the High Court
of Parliament.
Law officers, lords, and commons, and priests sat as a court, and
they subsequently were divided into two houses and sat as a law-
making body. But the English House of Commons was a court of
judicature before it ever was a lawmaking body at all.
In this Government the legislative and judicial were distinctly
separated by the Constitution. The legislative, the executive, and
the judicial are coordinate, independent, and separate branches, and
this right that you propose to exercise now was never incident to the
right to legislate. It is incident to a judicial body. And, as Justice


===== [扫描序号 596] =====

Miller says in this case, there is no question about your right to exer-
cise that plenary power if you sat as a court of impeachment. But
you have no such right in a case of this kind. Says the court:
But we do not concede that the Houses of Congress possess this general power
[possessed by an English Parliament] of punishing for contempt. The cases
in which they can do this are very limited, as we have already attempted to
show.
Now, your power to punish for contempt was not questioned at all
in this case, and it was never determined that you had such power at
all outside of the intimation in In re Chapman, until very recently,
and then in the recent case of McGrain v. Daugherty (273 U. S. 173).
In that case the Supreme Court held that you did have the power
under certain circumstances to punish for contempt and to force a
witness to answer question. But in that case they reaffirmed the
limitations placed upon the exercise of such a power in this great
case of Kilbourn v. Thompson.

UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE ON INTERSTATE COMMERCE,
Washington, D. C.
The committee met, pursuant to adjournment, at 10.15 o'clock
a. m., March 30, 1928, no hearing having been held on March 31,
1928, in room 212, Senate Office Building, Senator James E. Watson
presiding.
Present: Senators Watson (chairman), Gooding, Fess, Goff, Pine,

REPLY ARGUMENT OF HON. A. OWSLEY STANLEY, FOR WEST
VIRGINIA WITNESSES IN THE SOUTHERN FIELD-Resumed
Mr. STANLEY. Mr. Chairman, I realize that you have been for
some weeks on this question, and for that reason I shall conserve
the time of this committee as much as possible. It is well, however,
in the very beginning to understand just what this committee pro-
poses to do before making inquiry as to its power in the premises.
Here is a unique situation. A great number of men at the head
and in control of large concerns are brought here under the com-
pulsory process of this committee, and are kept here for weeks, to
answer certain questions concerning the most intimate details of their
business.
In much of this coal field for more than 100 years there has been
no serious labor trouble. The relations between employer and em-

ployee for some time past have been amicable. There is no charge
that the men engaged in the production of coal are engaged in any
combination in restraint of trade. On the other hand, it is admitted
that the severest competition exists; that only the most efficient can
live in this business; that coal is being produced at the lowest pos-
sible cost consistent with any profit at all. They are not officers of
the law; they hold no position of trust or honor under either State
or Federal Government, and they are not charged with a violation
of any law. The committee, however, is interested in a study of
conditions in coal fields generally, and in order to obtain information
and in aid of possible legislation, and just what that legislation is
we are not advised, you propose to ask and to compel answers to
these quetsions with the idea that they may possibly throw some light
on some legislation that you may possibly recommend to the
Congress.
The first and most pertinent inquiry is, of course, whether the
Constitution of the United States contains any such grant of power,
whether the States ever conferred upon the Congress the right in
pursuance of such an inquiry to make such a demand. All Federal
powers

Senator PITTMAN. Very well. I shall be glad to hear that.
Mr. STANLEY. This being a Government of delegated powers, as
Chief Justice Marshall said way back yonder in McCullough v.
State of Maryland:
All Federal power is admittedly delegated. This Government can exercise
no power-
And that goes without saying-
unless it is vested with that right by the Constitution or the exercise of that
power is necessarily incident to some power which has been so delegated. The
powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution or prohibited by
it to the States are reserved to the States respectively and to the people.
Has the Constitution in express terms vested in either House of
Congress the power to compel the attendance or the testimony of
witnesses or the production of books and papers? There is nowhere
in that instrument any such grant.


===== [扫描序号 607] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1617
In the latest case, McGrain v. Daugherty (273 U. S. 173), the
court says:
But there is no provision in the Constitution expressly vesting either House
with the power to make investigations and exact testimony to the end that
it may exercise its legislative function advisedly and effectively.
There is in the language of Justice Miller in the great csae of
Kilbourn v. Thompson:
No express power in that instrument conferred upon either House of Congress
to punish for contempt or to compel the attendance and testimony of witnesses.
It contains another provision:
No person shall be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process
of law.
The strongest implication against punishment by order of a legis-
lative body. Such power, then, if it exists at all, must necessarily
exist by implication. The advocates of this power, says the justice
in Kilbourn v. Thompson-
have hitherto resorted to the implication of its existence as founded on two
principal arguments-first, its exercise by the House of Commons of England,
from which country we it is said have derived our system of parliamentary
law; and, secondly, the necessity of such power to enable the two Houses of
Congress to perform the duties and exercise the powers which the Constitution
has conferred on it.
In passing I wish to say that there is the general impression that
Congress exercises a sort of common law right by analogy to the
House of Commons and our legislative and our judicial traditions
necessarily run back to the English customs. But upon mature
thought you will readily see that Congress as such can exercise no
common law right, and the fact that the English Parliament has the
broadest powers to punish for contempt, is, as Justice Miller has well
observed, no precedent for the American Houses of Congress.
It is important to understand on what principle this power in the
House of Commons rests, in order that we may see whether it is
applicable to the two Houses of Congress; and if, by the way, there
are limitations to its exercise, while there is little agreement of
opinion as to the extent of the power there is no difference of opinion
as to its origin in the House of Commons.
This goes back to the period when the Bishops and Lords and
Knights and Burgesses met in one body and were when so assembled,
called the High Court of Parliament. It is upon this idea that the
two Houses of Parliament were each courts of judicature originally,
and which though divested by usage and by statute of many of their
judicial functions, yet have retained so much of that power as en-
ables them, like any other court, to punish for contempt of those
privileges.
The House of Commons and the House of Lords, when they were
one body, and before they were a legislative body at all, were the
high court. But the reason why the House of Commons has this
power is not because it is a representative body with legislative func-
tions, but by virtue of ancient usage and proscription.
We are of opinion that the right of the House of Representatives to punish
the citizens for a contempt of its authority or a breach of its privileges can
derive no support from the precedents and practices of the two Houses of the
English Parliament, nor from the adjudged cases in which the English courts
have upheld these practices.


===== [扫描序号 608] =====
1618
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
The House of Representatives was never a court and does not derive
its power by analogy.
It was expressly decided in the case of Marshall v. Gordon (243
U. S. 521) and in McGrain v. Daugherty (103 U. S. 190).
Now, if this power is not conferred by the express terms of the
instrument, and if we can not by precedent or analogy exercise the
powers vested in the House of Commons, if this power is merely
incidental, it is well to study these limitations, and if it is incident
at all it is incident for two purposes:
1. For its own preservation, which is a very different thing from
its exercise as a mere aid to legislation.
Way back yonder just after the Civil War, Charles Sumner spoke
of the difference between the exercise of this power to compel the
attendance of witnesses and to force their testimony, especially con-
cerning their own private affairs, and the power exercised by the
Congress to prevent contempts in its presence or interference with
its orderly procedure.
In December, 1859, the Senate adopted a resolution for the ap-
pointment of a committee to inquire into the facts "attending the
late invasion and seizure of the armory and arsenal at Harpers
Ferry."

Mr. STANLEY. No, sir; I have not the full case. It is in 103
United States. I have the synopsis of the case here, which I will

to take up too much time of the committee. In this Kilbourn case,
as you will recall-it is directly in point-J. Cooke & Co. were
creditors of the United States and they went into bankruptcy. In
the Kilbourn case the alleged contempt consisted of a refusal to
give testimony and to produce documents pursuant to a resolution
of the House providing for the appointment of a committee "to
inquire into the nature and history of said real-estate pool and the
character of said settlement with the amount paid or to be paid in
said settlement, with power to send for persons or papers and report
to this House."
J. Cooke & Co. was indebted to the United States and had gone into
bankruptcy. The trustee in bankruptcy, under the settlement re-
ferred to, had received some interest or assets in a partnership oper-
ating a so-called real estate pool. The plaintiff, Kilbourn, was
thought to be a member of the partnership. The Supreme Court
held that the House had no power to make the investigation and that
its order adjudging Kilbourn guilty of contempt was void.
Here was a case where the conduct of a treasurer was investigated
and the rights of the United States as a creditor were being investi-
gated. It said the fact that you have control over a treasurer does
not give you the right to ask whether Kilbourn or anybody else is
engaged in this, that or the other business, or to inquire into his
private business.
Now, to return to the Kilbourn case. I will read you one or two
of these cases and then I will hurry on, because there are other
matters to which I want to call your attention. In the Federal
Trade Commission v. American Tobacco Co. this right to inquire is
identical with your right.
The act makes plain the duty of the commission to gather, compile, and
publish for use in its proceedings what may be voluntarily offered or submitted
in response to request or demand.
You have a perfect right, just as the Federal Trade Commission
has, to make any inquiries you please about agriculture, mining,
manufactures, or individuals, but if you inquire into the private
affairs of a citizen, he has an equal right to refuse to answer.
It may also make investigations independently, but the exercise of visitorial
power over private corporations must keep within restrictions of the fourth
amendment. "Neither branch of the legislative department, still less any
merely administrative body, established by the Congress, possesses, or can be
vested with, a general power of making inquiry into the private affairs of the
citizen."
It was not intended to grant an unlimited power of inquisition or an unlim-
ited right of access to books and papers of private parties not engaged in any
public service or a search without basis of some facts tending to establish a
charge of wrongdoing.
In sustaining this case the Supreme Court said:
Anyone who respects the spirit as well as the letter of the fourth amendment
would be loath to believe that Congress intended to authorize one of its sub-
ordinate agencies to sweep all our traditions into the fire and to direct fishing
expeditions into private papers on the possibility that they may disclose evidence
of crime. We do not discuss the question whether it could do so if it tried, as
nothing short of the most explicit language would induce us to attribute to

UNITED STATES SENATE,

The committee met at 10.15 o'clock a. m., pursuant to adjournment
on yesterday, in room 212, Senate Office Building, Senator James E.
Watson presiding.
Present: Senators Watson (chairman), Gooding, Fess, Goff, Pine,

The CHAIRMAN. The committee will be in order.

REPLY ARGUMENT OF HON. A. OWSLEY STANLEY, FOR WEST
VIRGINIA WITNESSES IN THE SOUTHERN FIELD-Resumed
Mr. STANLEY. Mr. Chairman, as briefly as possible, I shall conclude
this argument without imposing upon the patience of the committee.
In order to properly apply the law applicable to this case it is
highly important that we understand the facts. They are few and
simple.
Citizens of the States of West Virginia, Virginia, and Kentucky,
owning in great part in fee simple title to the coal lands under inves-
tigation here, under the laws of those States the absolute owners of
everything from the center of the earth to the zenith-the soil, the
coal, the mineral deposits, all that is there; and they proceed to till
that soil, to fell the timber upon the mountain side, and to extract
the veins of ore and coal that lace those hills.
Just what control the Federal Government has over that land and
over the productive processes of those people is the question here, but
there can be no question, gentlemen of the committee, that whatever
power you have, whatever control you possess, by direct grant or by
necessary implication over the processes of removing a ton of coal
from the mountainside, you have the same identical power over the
right to remove a cord of wood from the hills or shovel of dirt from
the surface of the soil,
This resolution proposes, and this committee is now inquiring into
its right to investigate the most minute personal details of the proc-
esses of production. You have nothing to do, your resolution makes
no reference, and these questions have not the remotest application
to the transportation of that coal.
You are asking the cost of removing coal from the mountains.
You are asking to whom it was sold before it was transported, and
1637


===== [扫描序号 628] =====
1638
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
for how much. You are asking for every detail of overhead involved,
not in the movement but in the production of this commodity.
If the Federal Government has a right to control in any manner
such activities, it is bound to possess it under the interstate-commerce
clause of the Constitution. It will not be seriously contended that
nowhere else in that instrument is there the remotest warrant for
the exercise of this unique, unprecidented inquisitorial power which
it is proposed to exert in this instance. It was some great justice and
I forget who it was now who said in a similar case the interstate-
commerce clause could be stretched like india rubber.
It is most fortunate, most fortunate for the proper solution of this
case, most fortunate for the autonomy of the States, for the institution
and the preservation of the institution of local self-government, Mr.
Chairman, for the preservation of those institutions as they were
handed down to us by the fathers, for as Chief Justice Chase has
well said and as I shall further call to your attention his great de-
cision, the preservation of indestructible States, is just as binding
upon you and just as necessary as the preservation of an indestruet-
ible Union. In fact, the Union, says he, is unthinkable, is inconceiv-
able, except as an association of indestructible States.
Now, under the old Articles of Confederation, as you well know,
all the industrial activities of the citizens were confined to the States;
none of them was surrendered; the taxing power and the power over
interstate commerce was absolutely in the control of the States. But
experience showed that the control of interstate commerce was more
essential to the preservation of the Union, the exclusive control, mind
you, of interstate commerce was more essential to the preservation of
a Union than the centralizing of the taxing power even in the Fed-
eral Government. And it was in order to place in the Federal Gov-
ernment this power that the Constitution had its genesis.
It is fortunate that this question was first determined in a case
that put in issue every vital point that you are called upon to de-
termine to-day-the nature of commerce, the extent of the power, the
possibility of concurrent jurisdiction in the exercise of the control
over interstate commerce. And the whole question was elucidated
as it has never been elucidated since, by John Marshall himself;
and before the rendering of that decision, in Gibbons v. Ogden, the
whole question was illumined by the transcendent genius of Daniel
Webster.
It is necessary that we should understand just what is commerce,
for if this operation is commerce or is so indissolubly associated
with commerce that the Federal Government is warranted in exer-
cising some control, or in part control-and it does not matter, for
if you exercise any you take all-in part the control that you
exercise now over the railroad systems, then if you can take one
step, if you can exercise any control, if that is settled, the right of
this committee to make this inquiry is determined, the control of the
Federal Government is absolute, the whole question is solved.
If, on the other hand, this operation is not commerce, then you have
no control over it whatsoever, and-
The CHAIRMAN. Have you a decision of the Supreme Court of

Mr. STANLEY. The first decision that was ever rendered is on that
point.

to restrain, to regulate, to punish a man who is mining coal or tilling

We are now arrived at the inquiry, What is this power? It is the power
to regulate; that is, to prescribe the rule by which commerce is to be governed.
This power, like all others, vested in Congress is complete in itself, indivisible,
may be exercised to its utmost extent and acknowledges no limitations other
than that ascribed to the Constitution.
This power, like all other powers, like the power to coin money,
make treaties, to grant letters of mark and reprisal; the State has no
more power to regulate interstate commerce in any degree than it has
to make a treaty or levy import duties or to coin money. And if you
have any power over the production of coal, over the payment of
wages, over the collective bargaining, over the prices you charge,
over any other thing done by these people prior to the time they have
engaged in commerce, you have all power. The States have none,
and the Supreme Court of the United States has repeatedly so
decided. Said Justice Johnson in Gibbons v. Ogden:
And since the power to prescribe the limits to its freedom, necessarily im-
plies the power to determine what shall remain unrestrained, it follows that the
power must be exclusive, it can reside in but one potentate; and hence, the
grant of this power carries with it the whole subject, leaving nothing for the
State to act upon.
And if the State controls the production of coal, it controls the
whole subject, leaving nothing for the State to act upon.
In Kidd v. Pearson, Justice Lamar says the same thing:
The power being vested in Congress and denied to the States, it would follow
as an inevitable result that the duty would devolve on Congress to regulate all
these delicate multiform and vital interests--
Referring to agriculture, etc.—
interests which in their nature are and must be local and in all the details of
their successful management.

As Justice Lamar remarked in Kidd v. Pearson:
Does not the grower of wheat in the Northwest, or the cotton planter of the

pool, New York, and Chicago?

A situation more penalizing to the State governments, and more provocative
of conflicts between the General Government and the States, and less likely to
have been what the framers of the Constitution intended, it would be difficult
to imagine.
In Hooper v. California, the Supreme Court said, touching the
question of this power:
If the power to regulate interstate commerce applied to all incidents to which
said commerce might give rise and to all contracts which might be made in the
course of its transaction, that power would embrace the entire sphere of mer-
cantile activity in any way connected with trade between the States; and would
exclude State control over many contracts purely domestic in their nature.
In Dartmouth College v. Woodward (4 Wheat. 518), Chief Justice
Marshall says:
That the framers of the Constitution did not intend to restrain the States
in the regulation of their civil institutions, adopted for internal government,
and that the instrument they have given us was not to be so construed may be
admitted.
And again, says that great judge in McCullough v. The State of
Maryland:
No political dreamer was ever wild enough to think of breaking down the
lines which separate the States, and of compounding the American people into
one common mass.
Yet, that, says the Supreme Court, is what impends as a result of
such legislation.
In Hammer v. Dagenhart, the court said:
The far-reaching result of upholding the act can not be more plainly indicated
than by pointing out that if Congress can thus regulate matters intrusted to
local authorities, by prohibition of the movement of commodities in interstate
commerce, all freedom of commerce will be at an end, and the power of States
over local matters may be eliminated, and thus our system of government be
practically destroyed.
Gentlemen, you have something more, and, may I add with all
respect, something finer and something higher to do, than to relieve
every ill and to cure every malady to which your attention is called
by an ingenious extension of Federal power.
I regret with you that in many places the production of coal is
wasteful. I regret with you that there are 100 or 2,000 men in cer-
tain parts of the United States that are receiving less wage than the
union scale provides. But you can not cure those evils by tearing
down the plain barriers imposed by the Constitution of your country,
as said in Hammer v. Dagenhart, without destroying our system of
government. It is your duty to preserve the autonomy of the State
as sacredly as to preserve the Union. The duty is imposed upon you
to preserve local self-government as well as National Government,
and I wish to call your attention to a pathetic and sublime statement
of Chief Justice Chase, and then I am through:
The States disunited might continue to exist; without the States in union
there could be no such political body as the United States.

Mr. TOWNSEND. Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of the committee, I
hope with profit we may again refer to this resolution. I understand
that this resolution passed the United States Senate without a dis-
senting vote, and it authorized this committee to do certain things.
Paragraphed, the Senate authorized the committee to-
First. Make a thorough and complete investigation of the condi-
tions existing in the coal fields of central Pennsylvania, western
Pennsylvania, West Virginia, and Ohio.
Second. To ascertain whether the railroad companies and their
officials have been or are, by agreement or otherwise, endeavoring to
depress the labor cost of coal produced by union mine labor.
Third. Whether in the said coal fields wage contracts have been
abrogated or repudiated.
Fourth. Whether defenseless men, women, and children, without
cause, have been evicted from their homes.
Fifth. And generally what has transpired in the said coal fields and
the reasons for conditions and happenings therein.

It is a broad and sweeping resolution. Pursuant to the mandates
of this resolution this committee issued subpoenas for a number of

2. The total tonnage, cost of production (show labor costs sep-

3. Amount of tonnage sold and delivered to railroads, prices re-

That is the information sought by the committee and here are
the reasons assigned by the recalcitrant witnesses, through their
counsel, for refusing to furnish this information. They are sub-
stantially two:
1. That the resolution contains no avowal of the purposes for which
this information is sought. In other words, there is no legislation
involved. That position, however, I take it from the course of the
argument has been more or less abandoned.
2. The mining of coal is a subject over which Congress has no con-
trol, and therefore the information if furnished can serve no pur-
pose. In other words, that the mining of coal is purely and exclu-
sively intrastate business, and Congress therefore having no control
over it, any information that might be furnished in connection with
the mining of coal would be of no value to Congress.
Now, it seems to me, gentlemen of the committee, that it might not
be time wasted if we should refer first to the conditions now existing
in the coal fields, such as have been presented to this committee, and
to conditions existing prior to present conditions.
I want to refer to a statement made by the United States Coal
Commission in 1925, pages 259-262, Part I, of the report, wherein it
said:
* **
Food and water alone outrank coal among the necessaries of life. An unin-
terrupted supply of these three is a requirement of urban life as we know it
to-day.
* Of the 43 articles of food, from meat to fruit, the only ones
into the production of which coal does not directly enter are "strictly-fresh"
eggs and fresh milk, and even those reach the market behind the steam-driven
locomotive. * * * Yet the 40,000 tons or more of bituminous coal that
invisibly reaches our tables every day is of little moment compared with the
coal that makes up the staff of life of our industries. The distribution of the
year's output of the bituminous mines tells the story: Out of an annual produc-
tion of 500,000,000 tons, 28 per cent goes to the railroads, 25 per cent to the
boiler houses of factories and mills of all kinds, 15 per cent to the coke ovens
and gas plants, 10 per cent to the homes, 7 per cent to steel plants, 7 per cent to
power plants and steel railways, 4 per cent is exported to Canada or overseas,
2 per cent is used at the coal mines for necessary power, and the remaining 2
per cent goes to the seaboard for steamship fuel. In those proportions
bituminous coal is the driving force of modern industrial and commercial
activity.
* *


===== [扫描序号 649] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1659
Every one of the 45 major coal-producing districts in the United States, except
the Michigan and Texas districts, ship coal outside the State in which it is
mined.
Three hundred miles of cars, loaded high with coal, is the
measure of the daily output of the bituminous mines of the United States, and
with that volume of traffic it is obvious that the uninterrupted flow of coal
from mine to boiler room is a prime requisite to the general welfare.
Therefore, the mining of coal in 29 States, its interstate transportation, and
its country-wide distribution together make up a service indispensable to the
general public. * *
*
*
A failure of the gas and electric plants of a great city to function would
result in a public catastrophe of almost inconceivable extent. This is one of
the reasons why these utilities have been put under public control, and the
practical logic that half a century ago clothed with a public interest the steam
locomotive and in later years the electric-power station must recognize a large
element of public service in the coal mines that furnishes the necessary energy to
both locomotive and power plant. It is this indispensable service which the coal
mine performs that gives the large social value both to the property and to its
product, and in turn this social value in effect grants to the public an interest
in that use and creates a compelling reason for public control.

Thus the position of the miners in company-owned houses is anomalous.
They are not tenants and have no more rights than a domestic servant who
occupies a room in the household of the employer. The documents which pass

Under existing laws the miners have a legal right to sign and the companies
have a right to require them to sign such leases as a condition of obtaining
employment. That they are ill-advised, obnoxious, and inconsistent with the
spirit of free local communities hardly requires argument. Self-respecting
American citizens will find a way to put an end to them. In the case of a
helpless, submerged, working population, the legis atures of the several States
might well consider making such "leases" illegal, like any other contract which
is contrary to the public interest. Self-respecting American miners who have
on other occasions shown themselves by no means contemptible defenders of
their own interests, may prefer to take the remedy into their own hands and by
insisting on reasonable leases, on the incorporation of their villages, and other-
wise, win for themselves those elementary civil liberties which must always be
won and held by free peoples for themselves rather than thrust upon them by
external benevolence.

The presumption is that this investigation is for the purpose of

No one will undertake to dispute that.
You have the unquestioned right to summon representatives of the

you not have the right and power to get such information from one

A court of justice in order to ascertain a fact, to establish a certain

It might be found necessary to amend the Sherman Act in order
to allow the coal companies to merge and combine. You would
want to know something about the price they received for coal, and
cost of production, in order to make a necessary and proper recom-
mendation. And strange as it may seem the Congress of the United
States has already put itself on record by an act passed by both
Houses of Congress and signed by the President, declaring that they
are entitled to this identical information.
The United States Coal Commission says that Congress is entitled
to this information after an exhaustive investigation. And Con-
gress itself which says they are entitled to it. Let us see what this
act is. It is found in volume 42, Part I, United States Statutes at
Large, an act passed in 1922, the title of which is as follows:
An act to declare a national emergency to exist in the production, transporta-
tion, and distribution of coal and other fuel, granting additional powers to the
Interstate Commerce Commission, providing for the appointment of a Federal
fuel distributor, providing for the declaration of car service priorties during
the present emergency, and to prevent the sale of fuel at unjust and unrea-
sonably high prices.
Congress could not declare an emergency to exist unless they had
constitutional authority to so declare. This act creates a fuel dis-
tributor and vests in that fuel distributor this power:
It shall be the duty of the fuel distributor to ascertain—
(a) Whether there exists in the United States, or any part thereof, a short-
age of coal or other fuel, and the extent of such shortage.
(b) The failures of production of coal and other fuel, and the principal
markets to which such production is or may be transported and distributed,
and the means and methods of distribution.
(c) The prices normally and usually charged for such coal and other fuel,
and whether current prices considering the costs of production and distribution
are just and reasonable.
This act, passed by both Houses of Congress and signed by the
President, declares that Congress had the right to vest in a fuel
distributor the power to acquire almost the identical information
asked for in this subpoena.
If the Congress had power to vest in another, authority to get that
information, does not this committee, acting under the direction of
the United States Senate, have the right to go get this information?
Distinguished lawyers discussed that identical bill in the House,
and Senate among whom was the present Secretary of State, who
defended the bill. The late Senator Cummins defended the bill.
And it was passed after much debate and mature consideration, and
with only seven votes registered against it. And investigation of the
record will show that the chairman of this committee not only dis-
cussed the bill but voted for it, and that the Senator who now occu-
pies the chair voted for the bill.
The United States Coal Commission is on record, the Congress of
the United States is on record as saying you have the right to this
information, through a bill enacted into law with only seven dis-
senting votes, and yet these gentlemen say that you are invading their
constitutional rights if you dare ask them to produce their cost sheets
for the purpose of making recommendations in connection with this
sick patient.

intrastate business; and, therefore, Congress is powerless to compel

If the practices indulged in are likely to restrain, obstruct, or

Following this case is the Leather Workers case to which the

The case of Stafford v. Wallace and other cases are also supposed in some

The mining of coal, for example-
threatened to obstruct or unduly to burden the freedom of interstate commerce,

The reasonable fear by Congress that such acts, usually lawful and affecting

Mr. TOWNSEND. Here is the reason: The livestock broker and

living in Kansas would ship their livestock to a broker in Chicago.
When the stock was delivered and unloaded into the cattle pens the

Indiana, reload them into railroad cars, and start them on toward
their final destination. The livestock broker occupied the same posi-

​What do we next find? The second Coronado case. I am going to

The mere reduction in the supply of an article to be shipped in interstate
commerce by the illegal or tortuous prevention of its manufacture or produc-
tion is ordinarily an indirect and remote obstruction to that commerce. Bur
when the intent of those unlawfully preventing the manufacture or production

We find a remarkable case bearing upon this question which arose
from an act of the West Virginia Legislature passed in 1919. That
act, in effect, provided that natural gas, yet in the ground when
hereafter produced, the users and consumers thereof in West Vir-
ginia were entitled to the preference. Justice Holmes, of the Su-
preme Court of the United States, in his dissenting opinion stated
the purpose of the act as follows:
The statute seeks to reach natural gas before it has begun to move in
commerce of any kind. It addresses itself to gas hereafter to be collected and
states to what use it first must be applied.
The Supreme Court of the United States struck down the act
passed by the West Virginia Legislature by a 5 to 4 vote. We won-
der why sometimes the question of what does or does not consti-
tute interstate commerce is not clear. When the Supreme Court of
the United States can not get closer to it than 5 to 4, it is not diffi-
cult to understand why others might differ about it.

===== [扫描序号 664] =====

and mills of all kinds, 15 per cent to the coke ovens and gas plants, 10 per
cent to the homes, 7 per cent to the steel plants, 7 per cent to power plants and
street railways, 4 per cent is exported to Canada or overseas, 2 per cent is
