to the seaboard for stemship fuel. In those proportions bituminous coal is the
driving force of modern industrial and commercial activity. Every one of the
45 major coal-producing districts in the United States, except the Michigan and
Texas districts, ship coal outside the State in which it is mined-300 miles
of cars loaded high with coal is the measure of the daily output of the bitumi-
nous mines of the United States, and with that volume of traffic it is obvious
that the uninterrupted flow of coal from mine to boiler room is a prime requisite
to the general welfare.
Therefore the mining of coal in 29 States, its interstate transportation, and
its country-wide distribution together make up a service indispensable to the
general public.
A failure of the gas and electric plants of a great city to function would
result in a public catastrophe of almost inconceivable extent. This is one of
the reasons why these utilities have been put under public control, and the
practical logic that half a century ago clothed with a public interest the steam
locomotive and in later years the electric-power station must recognize a large
element of public service in the coal mine that furnishes the necessary energy
to both locomotive and power plant.
It is this indispensable service which the coal mine performs that gives
the largest social value both to the property and to its product, and in turn
this social value in effect grants to the public an interest in that use and
creates a compelling reason for public control.

Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of the committee, under Senate Resolution No.
105, passed, as I understand it, without a dissenting vote, the Committee on
Interstate Commerce is authorized and directed immediately:
First. To make a thorough and complete investigation of the conditions
existing in the coal fields of central and western Pennsylvania, West Virginia,
and Ohio.
Second. To ascertain whether the railroad companies and their officials have
been or are by agreement or otherwise endeavoring to depress the labor cost of
coal produced by union mine labor.
Third. Whether wage contracts in said coal fields have been abrogated or
repudiated.
Fourth. Whether defenseless men, women, and children, without cause, have
been evicted from their homes.
Fifth. And generally what has transpired in the said coal fields and the
reasons for the conditions and happenings therein.
Sixth. Whether in industrial disputes or strikes in said coal fields injunctions
have been issued in violation of constitutional rights.

Seventh. Whether in said coal fields by injunction or otherwise the rights
granted by the Constitution of the United States have been abrogated and

Pursuant to this mandate of the United States Senate, the committee issued
subpoenas for a number of witnesses. These witnesses appeared, but refused to
disclose certain information asked for in paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 of the
2 subpoenas, which are as follows:
"2. Total tonnage, cost of production (show labor cost separately), and
sales realization of all coal produced, mined, and marketed from 1923 to
1927, both inclusive.
"3. Amount of tonnage sold and delivered to railroads, the prices received
therefor, from 1923 to 1927, both inclusive.
"4. The names of railroads to whom coal was sold and the amounts sold
to each."
Two grounds are assigned in justification of the refusal to furnish this
information:
First. That the resolution contains no avowal of the purposes for which
this information is sought; in other words, that no legislation is involved.
Second. That the mining of coal is a subject over which Congress has no
control, and therefore the information, if furnished, can serve no purpose.
Before undertaking a discussion of the legal objections to furnishing the
information asked for under paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 of the subpoenas, it
might be profitable to look at the facts which have already been disclosed to
this committee, and to consider whether or not these facts disclose the situation
over which or in connection with which the Congress of the United States
should legislate, if it has the legal authority to do so. This resolution is
broad and comprehensive and directs the committee to investigate exhaus-
tively and searchingly the bituminous-coal industry of Ohio, Pennsylvania, and
West Virginia.
The United States Coal Commission in 1925, at pages 259 to 262, part 3 of
the report, said:
66
"Food and water alone outrank coal among the necessaries of life. Of the
43 articles of food, from meat to fruit, the only ones into the production of
which coal does not directly enter are strictly fresh" eggs and fresh milk,
and even those reach the market behind the steam-driven locomotive.
66
Yet the 40,000 tons or more of bituminous coal that invisibly reaches our
tables every day is of little moment compared with the coal that makes up
the staff of life of our industries. The distribution of the year's output of
the bituminous mines tells the story; out of an annual production of 500,-
000.000 tons, 28 per cent goes to the railroads, 25 per cent to the boiler houses
of factories and mills of all kinds, 15 per cent to the coke ovens and gas
plants, 10 per cent to the homes, 7 per cent to the steel plants, 7 per cent to
power plants and street railways, 4 per cent is exported to Canada or over-
seas, 2 per cent is used at the coal mines for necessary power, and the remain-
ing 2 per cent goes to the seaboard for steamship fuel. In those proportions bi-
tuminous coal is the driving force of modern industrial and commercial activ-
ity. Every one of the 45 major coal-producing districts in the United States,
except the Michigan and Texas districts, ship coal outside the State in which
it is mined. Three hundred miles of cars loaded high with coal is the measure
of the daily output of the bituminous mines of the United States, and with
that volume of traffic it is obvious that the uninterrupted flow of coal from
mine to boiler room is a prime requisite to the general welfare.
"Therefore the mining of coal in 29 States, its interstate transportation, and
its country-wide distribution together make up a service indispensable to the
general public.
"A failure of the gas and electric plants of a great city to function would
result in a public catastrophe of almost inconveivable extent. That is one of
the reasons why these utilities have been put under public control, and the
practical logic that half a century ago clothed with a public interest the steam
locomotive and in later year the electric-power station must recognize a large
element of public service in the coal mine that furnishes the necessary energy
to both locomotive and power plant.
"It is this indispensable service which the coal mine performs that gives
the largest social value both to the property and to its product, and in turn
this social value in effect grants to the public an interest in that use and
creates a compelling reason for public control."

Since the Coal Commission made its report, the bituminous coal industry
of the United States, and particulraly in the States involved in this investi-
gation, has undergone many changes. As a business it has steadly gone from
bad to worse until to-day, as this investigation has disclosed, the business,
from the standpoint of both the coal operator and the coal miner, is completely
and wholly demoralized. The coal miners and their families, including in-
nocent and helpless children, in Central and Western Pennsylvania, Ohio, and
northern West Virginia, by the thousands, have been driven from their homes
like cattle; homes where they had lived, may of them, for more than a score
of years, reduced to scant rations and few clothes, housed in barracks unfit
for human habitation and without the ordinary conveniences, to say nothing of
the comforts of life. One disinterested and distinguished witness described
the conditions existing in Western Pennsylvania as worse than any she had
encountered in her travels throughout Russia. Their places in the mines have

1677
been filled by incompetent, inexperienced, and irregular workmen. Communities,
heretofore peaceable and law-abiding, are now infested with a lawless and
vicious element which has been followed by the commission of unspeakable
crimes. A fertile field has been prepared for the spread of Communism, Bol-
shevism, and every form of doctrine and creed which, if allowed to flourish and
spread, in the end will spell destruction for American institutions and dur
present form of civilization.
Looking further into the condition of the miners as disclosed by the testimony
before you, we find in central and western Pennsylvania, northern West Vir-
ginia, and Ohio the most vicious injunctions ever issued by the courts-
injunctions under which are denied to American citizens rights guaranteed by
the Federal and the State Constitutions. Under these injunctions the union
miners are restrained from marching or parading on the public highways, from
establishing pickets, from making speeches to nonunion miners, or singing
hymns. The union is restrained from contributing the necessaries of life in
some instances to union strikers. In fact, under some of these injunctions, the
strikers can not peaceably assemble, peaceably persuade, advertise their cause
in the newspapers, upon billboards, upon signboards, or otherwise. Under some
of these injunctions the union miner can not "speak, look, or listen." They are
as effectively deprived of all human activities in so far as the promotion of
their craft organization is concerned as if they were instantly paralyzed.
Turning to southern West Virginia, what do we find? In portions of this field
there has never been a union. We find the wages of the miners in some
instances reduced, according to the testimony, to $2.61 a day for 10 hours, and
50 cents a ton of 2,240 pounds for loading coal, and when the same coal is
sold in the market, 2,000 pounds constitute a ton. Reference has already been
made to the injunction in the Red Jacket case. This case involved 312 separate
and distinct coal operations in the smokeless coal fields of southern West
Virginia. At the time the case was before the courts the tonnage involved was
40,000,000. The same territory now produces 50,000,000 tons annually. Two
hundred thousand people, at a low estimate, have their homes in this terri-
tory. This vast number of people are as effectively insulated by the terms of
this injunction as if they resided in Siberia. Under the decision of the
Supreme Court of the United States in the Hitchman case members of the
United Mine Workers of America can not persuade persons under contract with
a coal company not to join the union to join the union and continue to work for
the company. Under the Red Jacket case a miner under contract with a coal
company not to join a union can not be approached and asked to join while
under contract. The result of the two cases is that he can not be reached at
all. While under contract he can not be talked to in his own home, on the public
highway, in the home of another, or any other place. With the injunction, the
contract of employment, which may more appropriately be termed, if the con-
tract furnished in evidence is a fair sample, "contract of ownership," the
"house lease," which makes the place in which the miner lives a mere incident
to the business of producing coal, and the "mine guard," is it any wonder that
you find one judge of the Supreme. Court of the United States using the
language that these conditions “remind of involuntary servitude?"
These are the conditions of the miner. What can be said for the operator?
His business has gone from bad to worse. If we are to believe press reports,
coal is now selling at the mines in some portions of southern West Virginia
as low as 93 cents a ton. Page after page of testimony in this record show
conclusively that much coal is being sold at less than cost of production. The
capital assets of the coal companies in many instances have almost, if not
altogether, disappeared. Failures, bankruptcies, receiverships, trustees' sales,
constables' sales, sheriffs' sales, sale under executions are the order of the
day. Ask the operator in regard to his financial condition, and the usual answer
is "Two jumps ahead of the sheriff." The commission of wrongs, crimes,
outrages, and deprivation of constitutional rights have brought disaster to the
industry.
The crowning infamy of these conditions was the repudiation by the coal
operators of wage contracts, most solemnly entered into, for which not a single
legal or moral excuse has been or can be offered to this committee or to anyone
else.
With such condition existing in the industry it seems perfectly obvious and
clear that if there is any remedy within the power of Congress, that remedy
should be immediately forthcoming.

The Constitution of the United States and the laws of Congress passed in
pursuance thereof have been invoked in support of the injunction, the "yellow
dog" contract, the house lease, and the mine guard. That deplorable, inexcus-
able and unlawful conditions now exist, no one can deny; yet this committee
is now told that under the Constitution of the United States, Congress is power-
less to reach and remedy these conditions.
Let us turn to the legal aspect of the situation. That this committee has
the right to investigate this subject preliminary to recommending legislation
which Congress has authority to enact and which would remedy existing condi-
tions seems to be under the authorities undebatable. The Supreme Court of
the United States in the case of McGrain v. Daugherty (273 Ū. S. 135, 71 L.
ed. 580) said:
"The first of the principal questions-the one which the witness particularly
presses on our attention-is, as before shown, whether the Senate or the
House of Representatives, both being on the same plane in this regard-has
power, through its own process, to compel a private individual to appear before
it or one of its committees and give testimony needed to enable it efficiently
to exercise a legislative function belonging to it under the Constitution.
66
The Constitution provides for a Congress consisting of a Senate and House
of Representatives and invests it with all legislative powers' granted to the
United States, and with power to make all laws which shall be necessary and
proper' for carrying into execution these powers and all other powers' vested
by the Constitution in the United States or in any department or officer thereof.
(Art. 1, secs. 1, 8.) Other provisions show that, while bills can become laws
only after being considered and passed by both Houses of Congress, each House
is to be distinct from the other, to have its own officers and rules, and to
exercise its legislative function independently. (Art. 1, secs. 2, 3, 5, 7.) But
there is no provision expressly investing either House with power to make
investigations and exact testimony to the end that it may exercise its legis-
lative function advisedly and effectively. So the question arises whether this
power is so far incidental to the legislative function as to be implied.
'In actual legislative practice power to secure needed information by such
means has long been treated as an attribute of the power to legislate. It was
so regarded in the British Parliament and in the Colonial legislatures before
the American Revolution; and a like view has prevailed and been carried into
effect in both Houses of Congress and in most.of the State legislatures.
"This power was both asserted and exerted by the House of Representatives
in 1792, when it appointed a select committee to inquire into the St. Clair expe-
dition and authorized the committee to send for necessary persons, papers, and
records. Mr. Madison, who had taken an important part in framing the Con-
stitution only five years before, and four of his associates in that work, were
Members of the House of Representatives at the time, and all voted for the
inquiry. (3 Cong. Ann. 494.) Other exertions of the power by the House of
Representatives, as also by the Senate, are shown in the citations already made.
Among those by the Senate, the inquiry ordered in 1859 respecting the raid by
John Brown and his adherents on the armory and arsenal of the United States
at Harper's Ferry is of special significance. The resolution directing the
inquiry authorized the committee to send for persons and papers, to inquire
into the facts pertaining to the raid and the means by which it was organized
and supported, and to report what legislation, if any, was necessary to preserve
the peace of the country and protect the public property. The resolution was
briefly discussed and adopted without opposition. (Cong. Globe, 36th Cong., 1st
sess., pp. 141, 152.) Later on the committee reported that Thaddeus Hyatt,
although subpoenaed to appear as a witness, had refused to do so; whereupon
the Senate ordered that he be attached and brought before it to answer for his
refusal. When he was brought in he answered by challenging the power of the
Senate to direct the inquiry and exact testimony to aid it in exercising its
legislative function. The question of power thus presented was thoroughly
discussed by several Senators-Mr. Sumner, of Massachusetts, taking the lead
in denying the power, and Mr. Fessenden, of Maine, in sppporting it. Sectional
and party lines were put aside and the question was debated and determined
with special regard to principle and precedent. The vote was taken on a reso
lution pronouncing the witness's answer insufficient and directing that he be
committed until he should signify that he was ready and willing to testify.
The resolution was adopted-44 Senators voting for it and 10 against. (Cong.
Globe, 36th Cong., 1st sess., pp. 1100-1109, 3006–3007.) The arguments advanced

were created; and these purposes are defined in the Constitution. What are
they? The great purpose is legislation. There are some other things, but I

"The deliberate solution of the question on that occasion has been accepted
and followed on other eccasions by both Houses of Congress and never has been
rejected or questioned by either.
"The State courts quite generally have held that the power to legislate carries
with it by necessary implication ample authority to obtain information needed
in the rightful exercise of that power and to employ compulsory process for the
purpose.
"In Burnham v. Morrisey (14 Gray, 226, 239, 74 Am. Dec. 676) the supreme
judicial court of Massachusetts in sustaining the exertion of this power by one
branch of the legislature of that Commonwealth said:
"The house of representatives has many duties to perform, which necessarily
requires it to receive evidence and examine witnesses.

occasion to acquire a certain knowledge of facts in order to the proper perform-
ance of legislative duties. We therefore think it clear that it has the constitu-
tional right to take evidence, to summon witnesses, and to compel them to appear
and to testify. This power to summon and examine witnesses it may
exercise by means of committees.'
"In Wilckens v. Willet (1 Keyes. 521, 525), a case which presented the
question whether the House of Representatives of the United States possess
this power, the court of appeals of New York said:
"That the power exists there admits of no doubt whatever. It is a
necessary incident to the sovereign power of making laws; and its exercise is
often indispensable to the great end of enlightened, judicious, and whole-

"In People ex rel. McDonald v. Keeler (99 N. Y. 463, 482, 483, 52 Am.
Rep. 49, 2 N. E. 615), where the validity of a statute of New York recog-
nizing and giving effect to this power was drawn in question, the court
of appeals approvingly quoted what it had said in Wilckens v. Willet
and added:
"It is difficult to conceive any constitutional objection which can be
raised to the provision authorizing legislative committees to take testimony
and to summon witnesses. In many cases it may be indispensable to intelli-
gent and effectual legislation to ascertain the facts which are claimed to
give rise to the necessity for such legislation and the remedy required,
and irrespective of the question whether in the absence of a statute to that
effect either house would have the power to imprison a recusant witness,
I can not yield to the claim that a statute authorizing it to enforce its
process in that manner is in excise of the legislative power. To await
the slow process of indictment and prosecution for a misdemeanor might
prove quite ineffectual, and necessary legislation might be obstructed and
perhaps defeated if the legislative body had no other and more summary
means of enforcing its right to obtain the required information. That
the power may be abused is no ground for denying its existence. It is a
limited power and should be kept within its proper bounds, and when
these are exceeded a jurisdictional question is presented which is cog-
nizable in the courts. *
Throughout this Union the practice of
legislative bodies and in this State the statutes existing at the time the
present constitution was adopted. and whose validity has never before been
questioned by our courts, afford strong arguments in favor of the recog
nition of the right of either house to compel the attendance of witnesses
for legislative purposes, as one which has been generally conceded to be
an appropriate adjunct to the power of legislation, and one which, to say
the least, the State legislature has constitutional authority to regulate and
enforce by statute.'
"Other decisions by State courts recognizing and sustaining the legislative
practice are found In re Falvey (7 Wis. 630, 635-638); State ex rel. Rosenhein
r. Frear (138 Wis. 173, 119 N. W. 894); Ex parte Parker (74 S. C. 466. 470.
114 Am. St. Rep. 1011, 55 S. E. 122, 7 Ann. Cas. 874); Sullivan v. Hill (73
W. Va. 49, 53, 79 S. E. 670, Ann. Cas. 1916B, 1115); Lowe v Summers (69 Mo.
App. 637, 649, 650). An instructive decision on the question is also found in
Ex parte Dansereau (1875) (19 Lower Can. Jur. 210), where the legislative
assembly of the province of Quebec was held to possess this power as a neces-
sary incident of its power to legislate.
"We have referred to the practice of the two Houses of Congress; and we
now shall notice some significant congressional enactments. May 3, 1798
(ch. 36. 1 Stat. at L. 554. Comp. Stat. sec. 155, 2 Fed. Stat. Anno. 2d ed. p. 532).
Congress provided that oaths or affirmations might be administered to witnesses

pertinent to the inquiry, should, in addition to the pains and penalties then

an inquiry, which otherwise could not be obtained, by exempting witnesses
required to give evidence therein from criminal and penal prosecution in respect
of matters disclosed by their evidence.
"Four decisions of this court are cited and more or less relied on, and we
now turn to them.
"The first decision was in Anderson v. Dunn (6 Wheat. 204, 5 L. ed. 242).
The question there was whether, under the Constitution, the House of Repre-
sentatives has power to attach and punish a person other than a Member for
contempt of its authority-in fact, an attempt to bribe one of its Members.
The court regarded the power as essential to the effective exertion of other
powers expressly granted, and therefore as implied. The argument advanced
to the contrary was that as the Constitution expressly grants to each House
power to punish or expel its own Members and says nothing about punishing
others, the implication or inference, if any, is that power to punish one who
is not a Member is neither given nor intended. The court answered this by
saying:
6
"(P. 225:) There is not in the whole of that admirable instrument, a
grant of powers which does not draw after it others, not expressed, but vital
to their exercise; not substantive and independent, indeed, but auxiliary and
subordinate.'
"(P. 233): This argument proves too much; for its direct application would
lead to annihilation of almost every power of Congress. To enforce its laws
upon any subject without the sanction of punishment is obviously impossible.
Yet there is an express grant of power to punish in one class of cases and one
only, and all the punishing power exercised by Congress in any cases, except
those which relate to piracy and offenses against the laws of nations, is de-
rived from implication. Nor did the idea ever occur to anyone, that the ex-
press grant in one class of cases repelled the assumption of the punishing
power in any other. The truth is, that the exercise of the powers given over
their own Members, was of such a delicate nature, that a constitutional pro-
vision became necessary to assert or communicate it. Constituted, as that
body is, of the delegates of confederated States, some such provision was neces-
sary to guard against their mutual jealousy, since every proceeding against
a Representative would indirectly affect the honor or interests of the State
which sent him.'
"The next decision was in Kilbourn v. Thompson (103 U. S. 168, 26 L. ed. 377).
The question there was whether the House of Representatives had exceeded its
power in directing one of its committees to make a particular investigation.
The decision was that it had. The principles announced and applied in the
case are, that neither House of Congress possesses a 'general power of making
inquiry into the private affairs of the citizen'; that the power actually possessed
is limited to inquiries relating to matters of which the particular House has
jurisdiction,' and in respect of which it rightfully may take other action; that
if the inquiry relates to a matter wherein relief or redress could be had only
by a judicial proceeding' it is not within the range of this power, but must be
left to the courts, conformably to the constitutional separation of governmental
powers; and that for the purpose of determining the essential character of the
inquiry recourse may be had to the resolution or order under which it is made.
The court examined the resolution which was the basis of the particular in-
quiry, and ascertained therefrom that the inquiry related to a private real-


===== [扫描序号 672] =====
1682
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
estate pool or partnership in the District of Columbia. Jay Cook & Co. had had
an interest in the pool but had become bankrupts, and their estate was in
course of administration in a Federal bankruptcy court in Pennsylvania. The
United States was one of their creditors. The trustee in the bankruptcy pro-
ceeding had effected a settlement of the bankrupts' interest in the pool, and.
of course, his action was subject to examination and approval or disapproval
by the bankruptcy court. Some of the creditors, including the United States,
were dissatisfied with the settlement. In these circumstances, disclosed in the
preamble, the resolution directed the committee to inquire into the matter
and history of said real-estate pool and the character of said settlement, with
the amount of property involved in which Jay Cook & Co. were interested, and
the amount paid or to be paid in said settlement with power to send for persons
and papers and report to the House.' The court pointed out that the resolu-
tion contained no suggestion of contemplated legislation; that the matter was
one in respect to which no valid legislation could be had; that the bankrupts
estate and the trustee's settlement were still pending in the bankruptcy court;
and that the United States and other creditors were free to press their claims
in that proceeding. And on these grounds the court held that in undertaking
the investigation the House of Representatives not only exceeded the limit
of its own authority, but assumed power which could only be properly exercised
by another branch of the Government, because it was in its nature clearly
judicial.'
"The case has been cited at times, and is cited to us now, as strongly inti-
mating, if not holding, that neither House of Congress has power to make
inquiries and exact evidence in aid of contemplated legislation. There are
expressions in the opinion which, separately considered, might bear such an
interpretation; but that this was not intended is shown by the immediately
succeeding statement (p. 189) that this latter proposition is one which we
do not propose to decide in the present case, because we are able to decide the
case without passing upon the existence or nonexistence of such a power in
aid of the legislative function.'
"Next in order is Re Chapman (166 U. S. 661, 41 L. ed. 1154, 17 Sup. Ct.
Rep. 677). The inquiry there in question was conducted under a resolution
of the Senate and related to charges, published in the press, that Senators
were yielding to corrupt influences in considering a tariff bill then before the
Senate and were speculating in stocks the value of which would be affected
by pending amendments to the bill. Chapman appeared before the committee
in response to a subpoena, but refused to answer questions pertinent to the
inquiry, and was indicted and convicted under the act of 1857 for his refusal.
The court sustained the constitutional validity of the act of 1857, and, after
referring to the constitutional provision empowering either House to punish
its members for disorderly behavior and by a vote of two-thirds to expel a
member, held that the inquiry related to the integrity and fidelity of Senators
in the discharge of their duties, and therefore to a matter within the range
of the constitutional powers of the Senate,' and in respect of which it could
compel witnesses to appear and testify. In overruling an objection that the
inquiry was without any defined or admissible purpose, in that the preamble
and resolution made no reference to any contemplated expulsion, censure, or
other action by the Senate, the court held that they adequately disclosed a
subject matter of which the Senate had jurisdiction, that it was not essential
that the Senate declare in advance what it meditated doing, and that the
assumption could not be indulged that the Senate was making the inquiry
without a legitimate object.
"The case is relied on here as fully sustaining the power of either House
to conduct investigations and exact testimony from witnesses for legislative
purposes. In the course of the opinion (p. 671) it is said that disclosures by
witnesses may be compelled constitutionally to enable the respective bodies to
discharge their legitimate functions, and that it was to effect this that the act
of 1857 was passed;' and also 'We grant that Congress could not divest itself,
or either of its Houses, of the essential and inherent power to punish for con-
tempt, in cases to which the power of either House properly extended; but.
because Congress by the act of 1857, sought to aid each of the Houses in the
discharge of its constitutional functions, it does not follow that any delega-
tion of the power in each to punish for contempt was involved.' The terms
'legitimate functions and constitutional functions' are broad and might well
be regarded as including the legislative function, but as the case in hand did


===== [扫描序号 673] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1683
not call for any expression respecting that function, it hardly can be said
that these terms were purposely used as including it.
"The latest case is Marshall v. Gordon (243 U. S. 521, 61 L. ed. 881, L. R. A.
1917F, 279, 37 Sup. Ct. Rep. 448, Ann. Cas. 1918B, 371). The question there
was whether the House of Representatives exceeded its power in punishing,
as for a contempt of its authority, a person-not a Member-who had written,
published, and sent to the chairman of one of its committees an ill-tempered
and irritating letter respecting the action and purposes of the committee.
Power to make inquiries and obtain evidence by compulsory process was
not involved. The court recognized distinctly that the House of Repre-
sentatives has implied power to punish a person not a Member for contempt,
as was ruled in Anderson v. Dunn, supra, but held that its action in this
instance was without constitutional justification. The decision was put
on the ground that the letter, while offensive and vexatious, was not cal-
culated or likely to affect the House in any of its proceedings or in the
exercise of any of its functions-in short, that the act which was punished
as a contempt was not of such a character as to bring it within the rule
that an express power draws after it others which are necessary and
appropriate to give effect to it.
While these cases are not decisive of the question we are considering, they
definitely settle two propositions which we recognize as entirely sound and hav-
ing a bearing on its solution: One, that the two Houses of Congress, in their
seperate relations, possess not only such powers as are expressly granted to
them by the Constitution, but such auxiliary powers as are necessary and appro-
priate to make the express powers effective; and the other, that neither House
is invested with 'general' power to inquire into private affairs and compel
disclosures, but only with such limited power of inquiry as is shown to exist
when the rule of constitutional interpretation just stated is rightly applied. The
latter proposition has further support in Harriman v. Interstate Commerce Com-
mission (211 U. S. 407, 417-419, 53 L. ed. 253, 262, 263, 29 Sup. Ct. Rep. 115),
and Federal Trade Commission v. American Tobacco Co. (264 U. S. 298, 305,
306, 68 L. ed. 696, 700, 701, 32 A. L. R. 786, 44 Sup. Ct. Rep. 336).
“With this review of the legislative practice, congressional enactments and
court decisions, we proceed to a statement of our conclusions on the question.
We are of opinion that the power of inquiry-with process to enforce it—is an
essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function. It was so re-
garded and employed in American legislatures before the Constitution was
framed and ratified. Both Houses of Congress took this view of it early in their
history-the House of Representatives with the approving votes of Mr. Madison
and other members whose service in the convention which framed the Consti-
tution gives special significance to their action—and both Houses have employed
the power accordingly up to the present time. The acts of 1798 and 1857,
judged by their comprehensive terms, were intended to recognize the existence
of this power in both Houses and to enable them to employ it more effectually'
than before. So, when their practice in the matter is appraised according to the
circumstances in which it was begun and to whose in which it has been con-
tinued, it falls nothing short of a practical construction, long continued, of
the constitutional provisions respecting their powers, and therefore should be
taken as fixing the meaning of those provisions, if otherwise doubtful.
We are further of opinion that the provisions are not of doubtful meaning.
but as was held by this court in the cases we have reviewed, are intended to
be effectively exercised, and therefore to carry with them such auxiliary powers
as are necessary and appropriate to that end. While the power to exact infor-
mation in aid of the legislative function was not involved in those cases, the
rule of interpretation applied there is applicable here. A legislative body
can not legislate wisely or effectively in the absence of information respecting
the conditions which the legislation is intended to affect or change; and where
the legslative body does not itself possess the requisite information-which not
infrequently is true-recourse must be had to others who do possess it. Ex-
perience has taught that more requests for such information often are unavail-
ing, and also that information which is volunteered is not always accurate or
complete; so some means of compulsion are essential to obtain what is needed.
All this was true before and when the Constitution was framed and adopted.
In that period the power of inquiry-with enforcing process--was regarded
and employed as a necessary and appropriate attribute of the power to legis-
late-indeed, was treated as inhering in it. Thus there is ample warrant
for thinking, as we do, that the constitutional provisions which commit the legis-


===== [扫描序号 674] =====
1684
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
lative function to the two Houses are intended to include this attribute to the
end that the function may be effectively exercised.
"The contention is earnestly made on behalf of the witness that this power
of inquiry, if sustained, may be abusively and oppressively exerted. If this
be so, it affords no ground for denying the power. The same contention might
be directed against the power to legislate, and of course would be unavailing.
We must assume, for present purposes, that neither House will be disposed to
exert the power beyond its proper bounds, or without due regard to the rights
of witnesses. But if, contrary to this assumption, controlling limitations or
restrictions are disregarded, the decisions in Kilbourn v. Thompson and Mar-
shall v. Gordon point to admissible measures of relief. And it is a necessary
deduction from the decisions in Kilbourn v. Thompson and re Chapman that
witness rightfully may refuse to answer where the bounds of the power are
exceeded or the questions are not pertinent to the matter under inquiry.
"We come now to the question whether it sufficiently appears that the purpose
for which the witness's testimony was sought was to obtain information in aid
of the legislative function. The court below answered the question in the
negative, and put its decision largely on this ground, as is shown by the fol-
lowing excerpts from its opinion (299 Fed. 638-640):
"It will be noted that in the second resolution the Senate has expressly
avowed that the investigation is in aid of other action than legislation. Its
purpose is to "obtain information necessary as a basis for such legislative and
other action as the Senate may deem necessary and proper." This indicates
that the Senate is contemplating the taking of action other than legislative as
the outcome of the investigation, at least the possibility of so doing. The
extreme personal cast of the original resolutions; the spirit of hostility toward
the then Attorney General which they breathe; that it was not avowed that
legislative action was had in view until after the action of the Senate had been
challenged; and that the avowal then was coupled with an avowal that other
action was had in view are calculated to create the impression that the idea
of legislative action being in contemplation was an afterthought. *
"That the Senate has in contemplation the possibility of taking action other
than legislation as an outcome of the investigation, as thus expressly avowed,
would seem of itself to invalidate the entire proceeding. But, whether so or not,
the Senate's action is invalid and absolutely void in that in ordering and con-
ducting the investigation it is exercising the judical function and power to
exercise that function, in such a case as we have here has not been conferred
upon it expressly or by fair implication. What it is proposing to do is to deter-
mine the guilt of the Attorney General of the shortcomings and wrongdoings
set forth in the resoultions. It is "to hear, adjudge, and condemn." In so
doing it is exercising the judicial function * *
"What the Senate is engaged in doing is not investigating the Attorney
General's office; it is investigating the former Attorney General. What it has
done is to put him on trial before it. In so doing it is exercising the judicial
function. This it has no power to do.'
"We are of opinion that the court's ruling on this question was wrong, and
that it sufficiently appears, when the proceedings are rightly interpreted, that
the object of the investigation and of the effort to secure the witness's testimony
was to obtain information for gislative purposes.
"It is quite true that the resolution directing the investigation does not in
terms avow that it is intended to be in aid of legislation; but it does show that
the subject to be vestigated was the administration of the Department of
Justice whether is functions were being properly discharged or were being
neglected or misdirected, and particularly whether the Attorney General and
his assistants were performing or neglecting their duties in respect of the insti-
tution and prosecution of proceedings to punish crimes and enforce appropriate
remedies against the wrongdoers-specific instances of alleged neglect being
recited. Plainly the subject was one on which legislation could be had and
would be materially aided by the information which the investigation was calcu-
lated to elicit. This becomes manifest when it is reflected that the functions of
the Department of Justice, the powers and duties of the Attorney General, and
the duties of his assistants are all subject to regulation by congressional legis-
lation, and that the department is maintained and its activities are carried on
under such appropriations as in the judgment of Congress are needed from year
to year.
The only legitimate object the Senate could have in ordering the investiga-
tion was to aid it in legislating; and we think the subject matter was such

An
that the presumption should be indulged that this was the real object.
express avowal of the object would have been better; but in view of the par-
ticular subject matter was not indispensable. In the Chapman case, where the
resoiution contained no avowal, this court pointed out that it plainly related
to a subject matter of which the Senate had jurisdiction, and said, 'We can
not assume on this record that the action of the Senate was without a legitimate
object'; and also that it was certainly not necessary that the resolutions
should declare in advance what the Senate meditated doing when the investi-
gation was concluded' (166 U. S. 669, 670). In People ex rel. McDonald v.
Keeler (99 N. Y. 463, 52 Am. Rep. 49, 2 N. E. 615), where the Court of Appeals
of New York sustained an investigation ordered by the House of Representa-
tives of that State where the resolution contained no avowal, but disclosed that
it definitely related to the administration of a public office the duties of which
were subject to legisiative regulation, the court said (pp. 485, 487): 'Where
public institutions under control of the State are ordered to be investigated it
is generally with the view of some legislative action respecting them, and the
same may be said in respect of public officers.' And again, We are bound to
presume that the action of the legislative body was with a legitimate object if
it is capable of being so construed, and we have no right to assume that the
contrary was intended.'
"While we rest our conclusion respecting the object of the investigation on
the grounds just stated, it is well to observe that this view of what was in-
tended is not new, but was shown in the debate on the resolution.
"Of course, our concern is with the substance of the resolution and not with
any nice questions of propriety respecting its direct reference to the then
Attorney General by name. The resolution, like the charges which prompted
its adoption, related to the activities of the department while he was its super-
vising officer, and the reference to him by name served to designate the period
to which the investigation was directed.
"We think the resolution and proceedings give no warrant for thinking the
Senate was attempting or intending to try the Attorney General at its bar or
before its committee for any crime or wrongdoing. Nor do we think it a valid
objection to the investigation that it might possibly disclose crime or wrong-
doing on his part.
"The second resolution--the one directing that the witness be attached-
declares that his testimony is sought with the purpose of obtaining informa-
tion necessary as a basis for such legislative and other action as the Senate
may deem necessary and proper.' The avowal of contemplated legislation is in
accord with what we think is the right interpretation of the earlier resolution
directing the investigation. The suggested possibility of other action' if
deemed necessary or proper' is, of course, open to criticism, in that there is
no other action in the matter which would be within the power of the Senate.
But we do not assent to the view that this indefinite and untenable suggestion
invalidates the entire proceeding. The right view, in our opinion, is that it
takes nothing from the lawful object avowed in the same resolution and rightly
inferable from the earlier one. It is not as if an inadmissible or unlawful
object were affirmatively and definitely avowed.
"We conclude that the investigation was ordered for a legitimate object;
that the witness wrongfully refused to appear and testify before the committee
and was lawfully attached; that the Senate is entitled to have him give testi-
money pertinent to the inquiry, either at its bar or before the committee; and
that the district court erred in discharging him from custody under the
attachment."
The right to make the investigation being established, how far can the com-
mittee go? Will the specific information asked for by the subpoena. and which
has been denied. aid the committee in framing or recommending legislation
which Congress has authority to enact? The United States Coal Commission,
upon which were distinguished lawyers, made this recommendation:
"The Congress of the United States is by the Constitution authorized to
' regulate commerce among the several States'
* *.
*
"The regulation of commerce in coal among the several States involves the
right to know the cost of its production, whether the investment on which a
return is claimed is fairly estimated or inflated, what profits are made by
owner, operator, and dealer, and what are the earnings and working conditions
of the miners."
I am not a constitutional lawyer. I do find, however, some provisions in the
Federal Constitution which seem to me entirely clear and applicable to this


===== [扫描序号 676] =====
1686
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
situation. The preamble to the Constitution of the United States declares that
this Constitution is established, among other things, for the purpose of promot-
ing "the general welfare." To promote the general welfare Congress is vested
with exclusive authority to regulate commerce among the several States and
to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execu-
tion this provision of the Constitution as well as all other provisions thereof.
Let us assume that Congress as a result of this investigation and as a result of
the report of this committee found it advisable to establish a commission, or
tribunal similar to the Interstate Commerce Commission for the purpose of
regulating commerce in coal. Would they not find it very essential to have
and to know the information asked for in the subpoena, to wit: The tonnage
produced, cost of production, sales realization? And would not this informa-
tion be desirable in regard to each particular coal mine? In this same con-
nection would they not find it desirable and in fact indispensable to any
proposed legislation to know the tonnage sold to the railroads and the prices
received therefor, as well as the names of the railroads to whom sold? I can
think of many distinct reasons why the information called for in this subpoena
would be valuable to this committee and to Congress in connection with any
proposed legislation affecting the shipment of coal in interstate commerce, a
subject over which Congress has exclusive jurisdiction and control. I shall
only mention a few.
First. The United States Coal Commission declared that coal is as essential
to the welfare of the people of the United States as is foodstuff. A parallel
may be drawn. Under the pure food law the Department of Agriculture of the
United States has the right to send its agents into slaughtering houses, cattle
pens, and food factories before such cattle are slaughtered or foods are prepared
for interstate commerce and before they are invested with a single attribute
of interstate commerce and examine the cattle or inspect the foods. They may
examine the cattle before slaughtered; they may examine them after slaugh-
tered; and then stamp the meat "Inspected." They go further than this. They
make inspections for the purpose of seeing that no foodstuffs are improperly
branded or marked in order that the consumer may not be deceived and misled
as to the article purchased. Oleomargarine may not be stamped as butter, or
butter as oleomargarine. Wheat and corn may be burned or destroyed in the
field of the farmer to prevent the spread of pests; whole forests of chestnut
trees may be cut down in order to stamp out the blight. All this is done to
promote the "general welfare" and to protect the citizens of the United States
against impure foods and the spread of disease. It is done under the commerce
clause of the Constitution.
As to coal, there are many different kinds. There are the two general
classes-anthracite and bituminous. Of the bituminous there are many grades
and kinds, some valuable for one purpose and some for another. Some is
superior for steam purposes, other for domestic purposes, others for by-product
purposes, all as necessary to the welfare of the people of the United States as
food products. For the welfare of the American public, present and future, is
it not just as necessary that the Government of the United States, through its
designated agencies, shall inspect, analyze, grade, and recommend the different
classes and kinds of coal that may be used and consumed by the public for
different purposes as it is for the Government to inspect the food supplies of its
citizens? And may not this be done under the commerce clause of the Con-
stitution? Would not the Government have the right, through its agents and
representatives, to go into the mines where the coal is produced, even before
it enters interstate commerce if designed for interstate commerce, and mark it
or brand it as to kinds; designate and classify it as to quality and purposes
for which best adapted, all for the general welfare of the public. This is not
far-fetched or extreme. The same objections were made to the passage of the
pure food law as are made now with reference to this question. As was said
here the other day, it is a crime to use anthracite coal for steam purposes.
The smokeless-coal fields of southern West Virginia furnish the highest quality
of bituminous coal in the world, and it is a crime against the people of the
United States and future generations yet unborn to allow these coal fields
to be depleted, exhausted, and wasted without the public realizing therefrom
the full advantages to which it is entitled. Suppose it were possible to scoop
up the productive soil of Iowa, Idaho, or Montana and sell it in vast quantities
to farmers of distant States. How long would such a wholesale denuding of
the soil be permitted? Congress would soon find a way to stop the outrage.
In a modified degree, this is precisely what is going on in the removal of natural


===== [扫描序号 677] =====

1687
resources. For these purposes and to accomplish these ends, would not the
Congress of the United States have the right and the authority under the
commerce clause of the Constitution to know the cost of production, the sales
price, to whom sold, and every kind and character of information asked for in
this subpoena?
Second. Let us assume that this committee should determine that because o
existing conditions in the coal fields, that because of the "injunctions," the
“contract of employment," the "house lease," the "mine guard," the insulation
of 50,000,000 tons of coal and 200,000 people, coal was being produced in viola-
tion of the right of free speech, freedom of assembly, freedom of locomotion,
freedom of the press, and that a condition existed that "reminds of involuntary
servitude." Would not Congress have the right to regulate in interstate com-
merce coal produced under such conditions and under such circumstances, and
if it does have the right to regulate in interstate commerce coal thus produced,
how could it intelligently legislate in regard to the subject unless it knew the
cost of production, sales realization, names of consumers, etc.?
Coal mines located in the New River territory, the Winding Gulf territory,
the Pocahontas territory, and the Tug River territory comprise the smokeless
coal fields of southern West Virginia. Practically all the producers of this terri-
tory, more than 300 in number, were plaintiffs in the Red Jacket case. The
United Mine Workers' organization, their officers, and membership were the
defendants. The plaintiff's alleged that defendants were engaged in a criminal
conspiracy in violation of the Sherman antitrust law and the Clayton Act to
prevent the shipment of coal produced from these coal fields in interstate com-
merce. The evidence in the case fails to show interference with any instrumen-
tality of interstate commerce directly or indirectly. The court held that intent
to interfere with the shipment of coal in interstate commerce could be inferred
from the fact that 40,000,000 tons' production was involved even though the
activities of the mine workers' organization were directed toward the stopping of
production at the mouth of the mine, and the injunction was accordingly issued.
The defendants then said, and undertook to support their position by citing the
first Coronado case and other cases, the same cases which are relied upon here
to sustain the position of the recusant witnesses, that the "mining of coal" was
not interstate commerce and that the activities of the mine workers' organiza-
tion did not constitute an interference directly or indirectly with interstate
commerce. The court held otherwise. The defendants in that case may properly
be designated as the proponents in this hearing.
The proponents now here say that one illegal condition after another has been
established in rapid succession in the smokeless coal fields of southern West
Virginia until coal is now being produced, which is intended and designed for
interstate commerce in violation of the constitutional rights of the coal miner;
that proponents believe that the injunctions issued and sustained are unwise, to
say the least; that the contract of employment is in reality and to all intents
and purposes, and was so designed to be, a contract of ownership of the miner's
labor; that it is un-American, against public policy, and, as recently said by the
courts of New York State, of similar contracts, is inequitable, and unenforceable;
that the house lease is unwise; that the mine guard and secret spy are an “abom-
ination"; that these different questionable activities, all directed toward the
same end, create a status for labor which deprives it of its constitutional
guaranties, and that the product so produced is produced in violation of and in
disregard of established rights of the citizens, and therefore the Congress of the
United States has authority to regulate in interstate commerce any product so
produced and designed for interstate shipments; that the barbed-wire entangle-
ments surrounding this "No man's land" are not bombproof against the Congress
of the United States. I ask the question, Would not Congress have the legal
right to declare contracts like those produced in evidence here against public
policy, in deprivation of constitutional rights and privileges, and to say that no
coal produced under such contracts shall be shipped in interstate commerce?
Third. If we are to give credence to published reports, some of which emanate
from high authority in the coal business, the housewife pays little less for coal
now than at the peak war-time prices. According to the statements of George
Wolfe, a distinguished ex-coal operator, who until recently was connected with
the smokeless coal fields of southern West Virginia, appearing in a published
article in the Charleston Gazette, the domestic consumer is receiving very little
benefit, if any, from the present low price of coal. Coal in the city of Norfolk
is selling for $10.50 a ton, with a freight rate of $2.85 a ton. Is not this a sub-

Finally, if this commitee has no right to go into these questions, we have

ATTORNEY REPRESENTING WEST VIRGINIA WITNESSES
Mr. GREEVER. Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of the committee, the
discussion of the questions before the committee by Mr. Warrum and
Mr. Townsend has taken a rather broad turn. The real question, as
I understand it, which we have before us is whether or not those
witnesses who have been subpoenaed shall be required to answer
certain questions set out in the subpoena. However, these gentlemen
have deemed it proper to leave that question and to discuss at some
length other questions before the committee.
When the original resolution under which you are acting was
adopted by the Senate we of southern West Virginia construed it as
leaving us out of the investigation altogether. The matters referred
to on the face of the resolution seemed particularly confined to west-
ern Pennsylvania, eastern Ohio, and northern West Virginia. The
matters referred to were things growing out of labor troubles and
strikes. But for those troubles and the things growing out of those
troubles this investigation, I take it, would never have been directed.
We have no labor troubles in southern West Virginia. We have
no strikes. We have no difficulties. I believe that I am warranted
in saying nowhere in the United States, in no industry in the United
States, does there exist a condition more satisfactory to all concerned,
to employers and employees alike.
However, when the subpoenas were issued, directed to certain indi-
viduals in southern West Virginia, they, as all good American cit-
izens should, immediately responded to the summons, and they are
here.
1689


===== [扫描序号 680] =====
1690
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
We made specific objection the other day to certain questions, to
being required to answer certain questions; and upon that objection
we are now being heard.
I want to say in the beginning that I shall take the position before
I am through, and I should like for the committee to understand it
now, that there is no power in this committee to compel an answer
to any of these questions. I shall develop that idea later, but I want
you to know now what my position is.
A careful examination of the cases which have been cited to you
and from which copious extracts have been read, I think, conclusively
lead to certain conclusions. I find no conflict in these authorities.
The principles laid down are without question, I believe. The only
questions that arise arise in the application of the principles recog-
nized by the courts in all these cases to particular instances.
I think that these cases establish these conclusions:
1. The subject of inquiry must be a proper one for Federal legis-
lation.
That is, it must be one over which the Congress of the United
States has the power to legislate. It could not be otherwise. And
I want to say to you gentlemen of the committee-
Senator WHEELER. Do you think that the Congress has not the
power to amend the Sherman antitrust law so that we might, if we
saw fit, permit the coal producers of the United States to enter into a
combination?
Mr. GREEVER. Senator Wheeler, you have asked my opinion as to
a special legal proposition. That may or may not be a proper sub-
ject of legislation. I am laying down the proposition that an inquiry
must be confined to some subject which is proper for Federal
legislation.
Senator WHEELER. I understand that correctly; but I am asking
you a specific question; if you do not think the Congress has the
right, for instance, to repeal the provisions of the Sherman antitrust
law relating to the production and transportation of coal.
Mr. GREEVER. Oh, well, if you had not added the concluding clause
to your question, I should have known exactly what you meant.
The CHAIRMAN. Yes; or the repeal of the law altogether.
Mr. GREEVER. Congress having the right to enact it in the begin-
ning, I certainly should not question their right to repeal it, whether
the original action was proper or improper.
Now, your inquiry being tested and being found to be with refer-
ence to some subject proper for Federal legislation, you come to
the question of evidence. The second conclusion that I draw from
these cases is:
2. That the evidence called for in such an inquiry must be in aid of
legislation.
It could not be otherwise in that case either, because that is the
sole public function of the Congress-legislation. So any evidence
that you might desire or might call for must be evidence in aid of
your constitutional function.
Senator WHEELER. I do not think there is a question of doubt about
that proposition in the mind of anybody in the committee, but
Mr. GREEVER (interposing). Senator Wheeler, you have practiced
law for, well, not anything like as long as I have, of course, but you
have practiced law fong enough to know that a great deal of loose

1691
thinking and loose talk is attributable to the losing sight of the
fundamental question.
Senator WHEELER. I think the members of the committee have the
fundamental principles pretty well in mind. But what we should
like is to have those fundamental principles applied to this specific
case.
Mr. GREEVER. That is what I am trying to do now, but I want to
lay my foundation first.
Senator WHEELER. I think the foundation has been laid here re-
peatedly.
Mr. GREEVER. I have only one other stone to add to it, and with
your permission I will now put it down:
3. The evidence called for must be pertinent to said lawful inquiry.
Now, if we keep these three fundamental propositions in mind all
the time and do not wander away from them, we will avoid a good
deal of difficulty.
I discovered from these cases that a court in determining whether
or not legislation is contemplated will look to the resolution itself
and to nothing else.
Senator WHEELER. Well, let me interrupt you right there.
Mr. GREEVER. All right.
Senator WHEELER. In the Daugherty case you do not find that,
do you?
Mr. GREEVER. Yes, sir.
Senator WHEELER. Do you mean to say that the Daugherty reso-
lution had anything of that kind in it?
Mr. GREEVER. I do; and I will show you presently. I am going to
discuss that case.
Senator WHEELER. All right.
Mr. GREEVER. In determining whether or not legislation is con-
templated by a resolution of this kind, the courts will look to the
resolution and to nothing else. Now, the resolution may on its face
state what the contemplated legislation is. In that event the courts
have no trouble in determining the question. But if the resolution
does not state on its face what the contemplated legislation is, or
that legislation at all is contemplated, the courts will do as it did in
the Daugherty case-look to the subject matter of the resolution and
determine from that-
Senator WHEELER (interposing). It went further than that. It
looked to the debates in Congress and the statements made by
Senators.
Mr. GREEVER. I think, Senator Wheeler, that that was only a
makeweight. The court really only reached its conclusion on the
face of the resolution itself.
Senator WHEELER. Let me say to you that I think you are entirely
in error with reference to that, because of the fact that even the
counsel who argued the proposition in the Supreme Court of the
United States, Mr. Wickersham, expressly took that very proposi-
tion up with me and suggested that, perhaps, the resolution ought to
be amended, as suggested by you here, but I disagreed with him, and
when the matter went to the Supreme Court it was argued and
presented.

Mr. WARRUM. In this section that you have just read, Mr. Greever,
the miners were charged with conspiring to interfere with interstate
commerce by increasing the cost of production by strikes and the
activities connected with strikes, and the court inquired then into
our activities relating to the processes of production and the cost
of production for the purpose of determining whether or not we
were under the Sherman Act. Is not that true?
Mr. GREEVER. That question is very easily and conclusively an-
swered. There is no difficulty about it. When you establish a con-
spiracy to do an unlawful thing, then any act or thing done, no
matter what its character per se, is unlawful.
Wr. WARRUM. But this related to interstate commerce, did it not,
Mr. Greever?
Mr. GREEVER. The conspiracy charged, and which the court said
we proved, was to prevent the movement of our coal in interstate
commerce. The means that you adopted were immaterial as to their
character per se. It did not make any difference whether you stopped
production at a mine or blew up a railroad bridge. The character
of the thing itself is of no moment. It is unlawful whenever it is
made the instrument or the step in the accomplishment of an unlaw-
ful conspiracy, and the object of the conspiracy is unlawful; every-
thing done to accomplish that object, no matter what its character
per se, becomes unlawful in that respect.

Mr. WARRUM. Then, Congress has jurisdiction over the activities

whether or not interstate commerce os burdened, restrained, or
interfered with, but not over your activities in the process of produc-

Mr. GREEVER. No; that is not right. That is not what I said.
Congress has jurisdiction over a conspiracy to restrain interstate
commerce; it makes no difference who enters into it. If the oper-
ators in a vast section of this country were to get together and
agree that they would not ship any coal in interstate commerce for
three months in order that they might get a better price, they could
at once be prosecuted under the Sherman antitrust law. So far
as I know, there is no exception to the proposition that anyone,
or any set of people, engaged in an unlawful conspiracy can be
reached by the courts. Now, we charged the unlawful conspiracy
had as its object the prevention of the movement of our coal in
interstate commerce in competition with coal produced north of the
Ohio River by union labor. Now, that was the charge, and that is
what the court said we proved. Anything that they did to bring
about that object, that unlawful end, became in and of itself thereby
unlawful, although the acts done had to do directly with the pre-
vention of the production of coal. But there is a vast difference
between that and undertaking as a primary proposition to regulate
the production of coal. There is no kinship between the two propo-
sitions.

From this findings of fact you observed that the court, found as a fact,

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
