You also observed from the finding of fact that the methods
adopted by the conspirators to accomplish the end of the conspiracy
was to stop the production of coal in West Virginia, and I took the
position, which I hope you understand fully, that the contention
made by us in that case, and approved by the court, was that while
the mining of coal is not interstate commerce, the stopping of the
mining of coal when done as a means to accomplish the end of the
conspiracy, namely, to prevent the movement of coal in interstate
commerce, then, that fact rendered what was in and of itself a
perfectly lawful thing, an unlawful means to accomplish an unlawful
end. Therefore, the jurisdiction of the court, having been based
upon the conspiracy charge and the interference with the movement
of coal in interstate commerce, all of the means used, no matter what
the character per se, toward accomplishing that conspiracy at once
came under the jurisdiction and control of the court.
And I stated to you that this incidental, accidental character con-
ferred upon the mining of coal by the acts of the conspirators is a
far different matter from the mining of coal and any attempted
Federal regulation of the mining of coal in and of itself.
Now, that case was appealed to the Circuit Court of Appeals and
decided by that court at Richmond, Va. I want to read rather
copiously from that opinion so that this record will have in con-
venient form for the use of the committee and anyone else interested
what that court said about this case. The court said:
The first question for our consideration is whether the evidence establishes
a conspiracy in restraint of interstate trade and commerce in violation of the
Sherman Act. This inquiry goes not merely to the propriety of the granting
of the injunction, but to the very existence of the power to grant it; for
except in the case of the Red Jacket Coal Co., the jurisdiction of the court in
all of the cases rests not upon diversity of citizenship, but upon the fact that
they arise under the laws of the United States. Complainants ask an injunc-
tion under the Clayton Act to prevent injuries threatened in the carrying out
of a conspiracy violative of the Sherman Act. Unless, therefore, there is
shown a conspiracy violative of the Sherman Act, no case is shown arising
under the laws of the United States, and the jurisdiction of the court is at
an end.
Now, there is a very fundamental principle laid down and it
answers conclusively all of the criticisms that have been made of the
Red Jacket case. The court continues:
With the importance of the question in mind, we have given the most care-
ful consideration to the evidence bearing thereon, and we should say in the
outset that we do not think that the evidence sustains some of the conclusions
which counsel for complainants seek to draw therefrom, or the interpretation
they would have us place upon certain of the findings of the learned district
judge with regard to this matter. In the first place. we do not think that the
international organization, United Mine Workers of America, constitutes of
itself an unlawful conspiracy in restraint of interstate trade and commerce
because it embraces a large percentage of the mine workers of this country or
because its purpose is to extend its membership so as to embrace all of the
workers in the mines of the continent. It may be conceded that the purposes
of the union, if realized, would affect wages, hours of labor, and living condi-
tions, and that the power of its organization would be used in furtherance of
collective bargaining and that these things would incidentally affect the pro-
duction and price of coal sold in interstate commerce. And it may be con-


===== [扫描序号 697] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1707
ceded further that by such an extension of membership the union would ac-
quire a great measure of control over the labor involved in labor production.
But this does not mean that the organization is unlawful. Section 6 of the
Clayton Act (38 Stat. 731) provides:
Which I will not read as it is not material here. Then the court
goes on as follows:
As pointed out in Duplex Printing Press Co. v. Deering et al. (254 U. S. 443),
this section does not exempt a labor union or its members from accountability
where it or they depart from its normal and legitimate objects and engage in an
actual combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade, as, in that case, the
I carrying on of a secondary boycott; but the section does declare the normal
objects of labor unions to be legitimate, and forbids their being held to be
combinations or conspiracies in restraint of trade because they are organized
or because the normal effect of such organization on interstate commerce.
said by the Supreme Court in the case just cited (254 U. S. 469):
As
"The section assumes the normal objects of a labor organization to be legiti-
mate, and declares that nothing in the antitrust laws shall be construed to
forbid the existence and operation of such organizations or to forbid their
members from lawfully carrying out their legitimate objects; and that such an
organization shall not be held in itself-merely because of its existence and
operation-to be an illegal combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade."
Again the court says:
As pointed out in the case of the Duplex Printing Press Co. v. Deering, supra,
however, when the union turns aside from its normal and legitimate objects
and purposes and engages in an actual combination or conspiracy in restraint
of trade it is accountable therefor in the same manner as any other organiza-
tion; and we think that the evidence adduced in this case justifies the conclusion
that the defendants have engaged in an actual combination and conspiracy in
restraint of trade in a manner quite foreign to the normal and legitimate objects
of the union. In this connection it is not necessary that we consider whether
complainants have established a conspiracy between the United Mine Workers
and the operators of the central competitive field or whether the acts of which
complaint is made were done in furtherance of such conspiracy, for we think
that the evidence sustains the finding of the district judge that a combination
or conspiracy existed among the defendants themselves, without regard to par-
ticipation by the central operators, to restrain and interfere with the interstate
business of complainants. By this we do not mean, of course, that the union
was unlawful of itself, but that defendants as officers of the union had combined
and conspired to interfere with the production and shipment of coal by the
nonunion operators of West Virginia in order to force the unionization of the
West Virginia mines and to make effective the strikes declared pursuant to the
policy of the union. The presence of this nonunion field in West Virginia has
been a hindrance to the union in its every contest with the operators. It has
furnished arguments to the operators in wage negotiations and in time of strike
has furnished coal which has supplied in part the needs of the country and
weakened the effect of the strike. Since 1898 the union officials have recognized
the importance of unionizing this field and, with the exception of an interim
during the World War, have been engaged in an almost continuous struggle to
force its unionization through interference with the business of the nonunion
operators. They have called strikes from time to time for this express purpose
and have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in interfering with their
business.
And there can be no question that the strikes called by the union in the
nonunion fields of West Virginia in 1920 and 1922, and the campaign of violence
and intimidation incident thereto, were merely the carrying out of the plan
and policy upon which the defendants had been engaged for a number of years.
In May. 1920, at a time when there was no general strike, union organizers
were sent into the nonunion Williamson-Thacker field, and in July following a
strike was called for the avowed purpose of organizing the field. The armed
march of the succeeding year was made by union miners for the purpose, among
other things, of organiznig nonunion territory. The nation-wide strike of 1922
was made applicable to the nonunion field of West Virginia by proclamation of
union officials, and representatives of the union began interfering with the
92214-28-PT 7-7


===== [扫描序号 698] =====
1708
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
employees of nonunion operators for the purpose of forcing the closing down of
nonunion mines. When the strike of 1922 was settled by the Cleveland wage
agreement the interference with these nonunion operators was continued. The
district judge has found that the conspiracy existed and that the acts com-
plained of were done pursuant thereto. We think that these findings are sus-
tained by the evidence; and the rule is well settled that the findings of the
trial judge should not be disturbed unless it clearly appears either that he
misapprehended the evidence or has gone against the clear weight thereof, or,
in other words, unless we are satisfied that his findings were clearly wrong.
(Wolf Mineral Process Corporation v. Minerals Separation North American
Corporation (C. C. A. 4th) decided this term; McKeithan Lumber Co. v.
Fidelity Trust Co. (C. C. A. 4th) 223 Fed. 773; U. S. v. U. S. Shoe Machinery
Co. 247 U. S. 32, 41; Adamson v. Gilliland 242 U. S. 350.)
Defendants say, however, and this seems to be their chief contention on this
point, that the mining of coal is not interstate commerce and that a conspiracy
to interfere with the operation of coal mines is not a conspiracy to restrain or
interfere with interstate commerce. In this connection, they rely chiefly upon
the decision of the Supreme Court in the first Coronado case (259 U. S. 344)
and in United Leather Workers v. Herkert (265 U. S. 457). But we do not
think that either of these decisions is in point. The Leather Workers case
involved a strike by laborers in trunk factories, and it was held that the fact
that the trunks, when manufactured, were to be shipped or sold in interstate
commerce did not make their production a part thereof. The Coronado case,
it is true, involved the mining of coal; but the court, being under the impression
that the coal produced by plaintiff amounted to only 5.000 tons a week, held
that a conspiracy directed against production of so small an amount could not
be said to be a conspiracy to restrain interstate commerce, even though the
coal was intended, if produced, for shipment in such commerce. When the
Coronado case went to the Supreme Court the second time, however (268 U. S.
295), the court adverted to this basis of its former decision and stated that
upon the second trial it had been shown that the capacity of plaintiff's mines
was substantially more than 5,000 tons per day. It held that this, with other
evidence as to intent, made a case for the jury as to conspiracy to restrain
interstate commerce. The court then proceeded to lay down the rule which we
think is applicable here, as follows:
"The mere reduction in the supply of an article to be shipped in interstate
commerce by the illegal or tortuous prevention of its manufacture or production
is ordinarily an indirect and remote obstruction to that commerce. But when
the intent of those unlawfully preventing the manufacture or production is
shown to be to restrain or control the supply entering and moving in interstate
commerce, or the price of it in interstate markets, their action is a direct viola-
tion of the antitrust act. (United Mine Workers v. Coronado Co., 259 U. S. 344,
409; United Leather Workers v. Herbert, 265 U. S. 457, 471; Industrial Associa-
tion v. United States, ante, p. 64.) We think there was substantial evidence at
the second trial in this case tending to show that the purpose of the destruction
of the mines was to stop the production of nonunion coal and prevent its ship-
ment in markets of other States than Arkansas, where it would by competition
tend to reduce the price of the commodity and effect injuriously the mainte-
nance of wages for union labor in competing mines."
This court goes on as follows:
We think there can be no question that the case at bar falls within the rule
just quoted from the second Coronado decision. Here it appears that the total
production of the mines of complainants is in excess of 40,000,000 tons per year,
more than 90 per cent of which is shipped in interstate commerce. Interference
with the production of these mines as contemplated by defendants would neces-
sarily interfere with interstate commerce in coal to a substantial degree. More
over, it is perfectly clear that the purpose of defendants in interfering with
production was to stop the shipments in interstate commerce. It was only as
the coal entered into interstate commerce that it became a factor in the price
and affected defendants in their wage negotiations with the union operators.
And, in time of strike, it was only as it moved in interstate commerce that it
relieved the coal scarcity and interfered with the strike. A conspiracy is in
violation of the statute where there exist an intent to restrain trade and com-
merce and a scheme appropriate for that purpose, even though it does not act
directly upon the instrumentalities of commerce. (Loewe v. Lawlor, 208 U. S.
274; U. S. v. Reading Co. 226, U. S. 324; Duplex Printing Press Co. v. Deering,


===== [扫描序号 699] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1709
254 U. S. 443; United States v. Brims, 47 Sup. Ct. Rep. 169.) And where the
necessary result of the things done pursuant to or contemplated by the con-
spiracy is to restrain trade between the States, the intent is presumed. (United
States v. Reading Co., supra, at p. 370.) Defendants must be held "to have in-
tended the necessary and direct consequences of their acts, and can not be
heard to say the contrary. In other words, by purposely engaging in a con-
spiracy wihch necessarily and directly produces the result which the statute
is designed to prevent, they are, in legal contemplation, chargeable with intend-
ing that result." (U. S. v. Patten, 226 U. S. 525, 543; Addyston Pipe & Steel
Co. v. United States, 175 U. S. 211, 243.)
In the very recent case of U. S.. v. Brims, cited above, the Supreme Court,
dealt with an indictment for a conspiracy between manufacturers, contractors,
and laborers pursuant to which the manufacturers and contractors agreed to
employ only union carpenters and these in turn agreed not to install nonunion-
made millwork. The circuit court of appeals reversed a conviction in the case,
saying: "The restriction was not against the shipment of millwork into Illinois.
It was against the nonunion-made millwork produced in or out of Illinois."
This decision, however, was reversed in turn by the Supreme Court and the
conviction was sustained on the ground that all parties intended that the out-
side competition should be cut down and interstate commerce thereby impeded.
The court said:
"They wished to eliminate the competition of Wisconsin and other nonunion
mills, which were paying lower wages and consequently could undersell them.
Obviously, it would tend to bring about the desired result if a general com-
bination could be secured under which the manufacturers and contractors
would employ only union carpenters with the understanding that the latter
would refuse to install nonunion-made millwork. And we think there is evi-
dence reasonably tending to show that such a combination was brought about,
and that, as intended by all the parties, the so-called outside competition was
cut down, and thereby interstate commerce directly and materially impeded."
The Brims case is directly in point. There the conspiracy affected interstate
commerce by its effect upon consumption, here by its effect upon production;
but in both cases the conspiracy was intended to operate upon matters not
directly connected with transportation or sale in interstate commerce, and in
both cases interstate commerce was intended to be affected and was necessarily
affected by what was done. We think, therefore, that in the light of this recent
decision, there can be no doubt that the conspiracy established by the testimony
was one in restraint of interstate trade and commerce in violation of the
Sherman Act. See also Bedford Cut Stone Co. et al. v. Journeymen Stone
Cutters Association of North America et al, decided by the Supreme Court
April 11, 1927.
There, may it please the committee, we have the clean-cut, clear
decision of the United States Circuit Court of Appeals establishing
the proposition for which we then and now contend, that where a
conspiracy is proven and the intent is shown to interfere with inter-
state trade and commerce any act done in pursuance of that con-
spiracy becomes unlawful.
The CHAIRMAN. How do you apply that now to this question at
issue?
Mr. GREEVER. I apply it in this way, Senator, that the mining of
coal is not interstate commerce and never has been held to be inter-
state commerce; and there is no control over it by Federal authorities
except where the obstruction of the mining of coal is a step toward
carrying into effect an unlawful conspiracy.
Mr. TOWNSEND. May I ask you a question, Mr. Greever?
Mr. GREEVER. Yes, sir.
Mr. TOWNSEND. There was not any conspiracy involved in the case
of Stafford v. Wallace, was there, which operated upon the plant
by the broker in the stockyards?
Mr. GREEVER. Is that the case to which you referred yesterday?
Mr. TOWNSEND. Yes.

An attempt has been made here upon the employment contracts,

contracts. To a man who lives in southern West Virginia and who
knows the facts that is the most absurd declaration ever made in
public. You can not hold thousands and thousands of independent
free-born American citizens in subjection that way and compel them

That is all.

Senator HAWES. There must be some reason why you can not mine
coal and store it. Will you tell me why that can not be done?
The CHAIRMAN. Is there danger of spontaneous combustion?
Mr. GREEVER. In some cases that is true. Most of the valleys in
which the mines are located are very, very narrow, and when you get
your tipples and your railroad tracks and the miners' houses in the
valley you have it full. You have no place to store the coal.
Mr. STANLEY. There is another thing; storing necessitates addi-
tional handling.
Mr. GREEVER. It would be the purchaser's place to store it. That
depends on him. He does not want to tie up a lot of money in the
coal and store it away and let it alone. Then it adds very greatly
to the cost if you get your coal out and dump it on the ground and
store it and reload it at some other time.
Senator HAWES. That is the cost of handling. That is one ele-
ment. Now, what is another element?
Mr. GREEVER. Another element is the deterioration of the coal. It
crushes it.
Mr. STANLEY. I had occasion to investigate that question when I
was in Congress. The economics of the handling of coal are based
upon the idea of keeping it in one continual stream. From the time
it leaves the tipple until it goes into the store, the cost of coal is so
little compared to the cost of storage that a manufacturer can not
afford to pile his coal out somewhere. He would have to haul it.
The coal goes into the car. That car goes onto the siding of the
factory or the mine or the coke oven or wherever it is to be needed,
often on hump tracks by gravity. These cars open in the bottoms.
It is dumped into the place where it is to be consumed and nobody
will risk the chance of rehandling. The only place where it is stored
in anticipation of strikes is in the yards of the railroads. It is im-
possible for manufacturers to provide coal ahead, even in the face of
an expected stringency. That is one of the great troubles.
I remember that Senator Frelinghuysen introduced a bill to equal-
ize the seasonal demand for coal and authorizing the Interstate Com-
merce Commission to charge a lower rate at such times as the coal
moves slowly and a higher rate at such times as there was congestion
in the movement of coal. I had occasion to go into that question of
the feasibility of storing cheap coal, and the only place on earth
where you can store coal is in the coal yards in the city for con-
sumption.

Senator GOODING. Thank you. You may proceed now, Mr. Boone.

TESTIMONY OF D. W. BOONE, LOOKOUT, W. VA.
(The witness had been previously sworn by the chairman.)
Mr. BOONE. When I left the stand on the 29th of March there were
some questions that I was asked that I did not get to finish, and I
have written the answers to the same. If the Chair does not object,
I will read the answers.
Senator GOODING. All right. You may proceed.
Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Chairman, in order to clear up one proposition
that the witness was last asked about. Mr. Townsend asked the
question as to whether or not the law of West Virginia provided for
a check weighman. I want to ask Mr. Boone if it is not the law that
when the majority of your miners requested the services or employ-
ment of a check weighman, then it becomes the duty of the company
to do so, and not otherwise, under the law.
Mr. BOONE. That is correct. On March 29 I was before your com-
mittee when my testimony was discontinued for the argument of
the legal questions submitted, and I, therefore, desire to complete
my testimony by furnishing you the following brief outline of my
mines, Blume, Lookout, Prosperity, and Michigan, operated under
the name of New River Export Smokeless Coal Co.
I was born and reared in Fayette County, W. Va., where my mines.
are located. I began the development of these mines in the year
1896 and have operated them continuously up to the present time,
on the open-shop basis and private contracts with my men, a copy
of which I submitted while on the stand.
I desire to further answer the question asked me by Mr. Townsend,
if I weighed my coal on the long-ton basis, or 2,240 pounds. I have
from the beginning of business in the year 1896 to the present time
weighed by the long ton by special agreement with my employees.
Mr. Townsend also asked if West Virginia did not have a State law
in reference to weights. We have a State law, and I herewith sub-
mit a written opinion from our attorneys as to this State law, that
by agreement with my men it is permissible to continue as I have
always done. There is another consideration I gave my men. Dur-
ing this long period of time I have made no change in the charge
for the houses in which they live, my rent being about $1 per month
per room for their houses. Also I have continued through this long
period of time charging my men only $1 per month for the coal used
in their houses.
I herewith submit a comparative statement taken from my records.
showing the mine weights for which my men were paid and the
return weights on which I received pay for coal mined and shipped,
which shows a loss over this period of time of 14,271.583 tons.
One reason for the loss in weights between the mine weights and
return weights is that I am mining a 3-foot seam of coal and use
1-ton cars. In the wintertime and during the entire season, if the cars
are not kept clean, there is a certain amount that sticks to the cars
and is weighed over and over, which is to the benefit of the digger.
This is especially so in the wintertime in freezing weather.


===== [扫描序号 722] =====
1732
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
All my coal leases are based on the long ton, 2,240 pounds, and some
of this coal is sold long ton and some of it is sold short ton, or 2,000
pounds. I herewith give information furnished from my coal sales
agents as to the markets in which my coal is sold on long-ton and
short-ton bases. As some of the coal is sold on long ton and some on
short ton, it is necessary that it all be reduced to either long tons
or short tons, and as a matter of convenience it is the practice to
reduce it to short tons; so that during the year's business my mines
have gained no advantage whatever by using the long ton at the
mines, and my miners are acquainted with the conditions I have
stated. I submit this statement to prove conclusively that I have
at no time desired to take advantage of my men by giving them
unfair weights.
I heard Mr. Tetlow make a statement in reference to company
stores and company houses. I wish to answer that question for my-
self that in my long experience in operating mines I have never dis-
charged a man for not dealing in my company stores, and never will.
I have never operated a mine but what I have employed some men
living in their own houses, and I have always encouraged their
owning property wherever they can, as I think it makes better men
of them.
I am now selling surface land to any or all of my men who desire
to build their own houses, and quite a number of my men do own
their own properties.
As to my wage scale, which I submitted while before your com-
mittee, I think it is conclusive proof that when the coal prices ad-
vanced I have advanced my wages at the mines without being asked
to do so, and when coal prices decline I have called my men together,
told them truthfully the market conditions, and have mutually agreed
with them as to the reductions.
On last November it was necessary to make a reduction, which my
statement to you shows, and when the market condition of coal ad-
vances sufficiently that I can advance the price of wages, I will volun-
tarily do so. This method of dealing with my men has been entirely
satisfactory to both them and to me. I have never dealt with the
United Mine Workers or any labor organization.
Senator WHEELER. How many men do you employ?
Mr. BOONE. Somewhere between 200 and 220.
Senator WHEELER. How do you call them together?
Mr. BOONE. I generally call them to my hotel. I have a small
hotel in the place. I consult them in regard to conditions of making
those changes.
Senator WHEELER. Do you call them all together in a meeting?
Mr. BOONE. We do not get them all. We get the majority. I can
not say that we get all of those people. We get the majority of them
and explain conditions, and the news soon spreads to the others.
I have never dealt with the United Mine Workers or any labor
organization, but have always worked open shop, and I have no
labor troubles at present. I have never had a strike at my mines
over the long period of time which I have operated them. I have a
number of men who have been in my employ for more than 20 years,
and it has been my pleasure to try to help them in every reasonable
and possible way that I could.

1733
I was asked by Mr. Townsend while on the stand if my present
scale of wages was equal to that paid in the New River field. I am
not a member of any coal association, but I understand there was a
time when the New River operators had a uniform wage scale, and
issued circulars setting forth the prices to be paid throughout the
field, which practice I now understand was discontinued some time
ago, and I was therefore unable to answer that question definitely
as to the comparison of my prices with the average prices of other
operators in the New River field, as I am operating independently of
any coal association. I would be glad, however, to answer this ques-
tion definitely if I had the information, but I am without the infor-
mation for the reason herein stated. I have never been requested by
my employees, nor asked, to make a comparison of the wage scale,
but would gladly do so at their request, though under the present
circumstances they are satisfied with my scale of wages and working
conditions.
Senator WHEELER. You say they are satisfied?
Mr. BOONE. Yes, sir.
Senator WHEELER. How many hours do they work?
Mr. BOONE. They work 10 hours.
Senator WHEELER. What wages do you pay them?
Mr. BOONE. The wages vary. I have submitted a scale here and I
will refer to it again.
Senator WHEELER. When do the 10 hours begin; at the face of the
mine?
Mr. BOONE. They begin at the drift mouth.
Senator WHEELER. How far is that from the face of the mine?
Mr. BOONE. Well, there are some of the mines that are new; others
where the farthest working is about 2 miles back.
Senator WHEELER. In the case of those that are 2 miles back it
would take them at least half or three-quarters of an hour to get to
them, would it?
Mr. BOONE. Those that ride motor trucks get there very quickly.
Those with mules would take some 20 minutes to get back there.
Senator WHEELER. So, as a matter of fact, they are working a
longer period than 10 hours a day?
Mr. BOONE. No; they are working a less period than 10 hours a
day. They do not work more than nine and one-half hours.
Senator WHEELER. What wages do you pay them?
Mr. BOONE. My scale of wages runs from $5 down to $2.98.
Senator WHEELER. From $5 down to $2.98?
Mr. BOONE. Yes, sir. I think $2.98 is the lowest I have on the
scale. I submitted it here and you ought to have a copy of it.
Senator WHEELER. You do not think that a man at the present
time can raise a family and live on $2.98, do you?
Mr. BOONE. There are very few men that receive $2.98. Those
are men that are not able to do a day's work, such as trappers and
people that are not able to do a day's work in loading coal, that are
paid these lower prices.
Senator WHEELER. What do you employ, colored or white men?
Mr. BOONE. There are about 10 per cent of my employees.colored
and the rest are white.

Mr. TOWNSEND. What do you mean by a small profit?

Senator GOODING. How long can you continue to operate at a loss?
How long can this go on with a big loss every year?
Mr. BOONE. It is not wise to run any business at a loss, but should
I stop, I have a loss; my organization goes to pieces and my mines go
to ruin for want of attention; and I figure that I would not lose
any more to operate than I would to stop, for my capital is invested
in the mines and all my earnings for 32 years; and I am most com-
pelled to stay with it.
Senator GOODING. Have you given any thought or consideration to
any legislation that might help in your operation down there?
Mr. BOONE. I have made it a study; and I have within my mind
something that might be helpful.
Senator GOODING. We would be very glad to hear from you.
Mr. BOONE. Now, it seems that the powder people, and we have
to use powder in the production of coal, and we also have to use
steel rails in the production of coal, it seems that the powder people
have their business so classified and so arranged that they realize
a reasonable profit upon their business; and the steel people seem
to conduct their business so that they also realize a reasonable profit
on their business. And it seems to me that the coal people should
be allowed the same right, and should be allowed to conduct their
business similar to the steel and powder people; and that by so
doing they could stop losing money and realize a profit instead of
suffering a loss.
Senator GOODING. Mr. Boone, you might mention also the railroads
in that connection.
Mr. BOONE. The railroads should haul our coal at a reasonable
freight rate, and all should be fair to each other, and matters should
be so adjusted that we might all realize some profit on our business.

I undertake to work for the J. D. Boone Coal Co. at its mine near Kanawha

and now promise that I will not become or be a member of that organization,
or obey any instructions of any of its officials while I am employed by this
company. It is understood that my employment depends on these facts. If
at any time while I am employed by this company I want to become connected
with the United Mine Workers of America, or any affiliated organization, I
agree to withdraw from the employment of the company and to give three
day's notice to the company before doing so. And I agree that while I am
in the employ of this said company, I will not make any effort among its
employees or others to unionize any mine owned or operated by it.
I will inform myself in reference to my duties under the mining laws of
West Virginia and under the rules of the company, and I will strictly observe

TESTIMONY OF J. G. BRADLEY, PRESIDENT OF THE ELK RIVER

(The witness was duly sworn by Senator Goff.)
Mr. BRADLEY. Mr. Chairman, I have come here under subpoena
to this committee to contribute what I can to the solution of the
problems of the bituminous coal industry. With that in view I
have prepared a statement, which, with your permission, I would
like to read. I would ask that I be allowed to read this without
interruption, and at the end of that time I am prepared to answer
all questions asked by the committee in their subpoena and any
questions which you see fit to be allowed to be put to me.
Senator GoFF. You may proceed.
Mr. BRADLEY. My name is J. G. Bradley, of Dundon, W. Va.,
president of the Elk River Coal & Lumber Co., a West Virginia
corporation, engaged in the mining of coal and the manufacture of
lumber in Clay County of the said State. I went to West Virginia
in 1904 after graduation from Harvard University, and since that
year have been a resident and citizen of the State.
The company of which I am president now employs about 600
men in the mining of coal and is producing more than 500,000 tons
of coal annually. Through the operation of flexible policies be-
tween the management and the employees we have been enabled to
meet changing conditions in the industry and the varying demand
for our product. We have thus been enabled to give steady em-
ployment to our employees, our mine operating 298 days last year
and 302 days in the preceding year.
While our property is located midway between the adjacent south-
ern and northern districts of West Virginia, the amicable relations
that the company has enjoyed with its employees has resulted in a
labor turnover that has been exceedingly low, and we have oper-
ated for 24 years without interruption, never losing a day because
of labor difficulties or differences.
It has been frequently stated, Mr. Chairman, that there is an over-
production of coal in this country. With that assertion I do not
entirely agree. Rather, it seems to me, there has been a temporary
displacement of coal in the consuming markets of the Nation, in
rather large measure by other forms of power-producing energy
which have enjoyed a very remarkable development in recent years,
accentuated, I believe, by demands made during the war period.
The greater development and increased production of these so-
called substitutes for coal, together with the demonstration of
greater efficiency in the generation of steam that we have witnessed
in recent years, has been responsible largely, in my opinion, for the
glutting of markets with coal and the failure of consumers to absorb
the supply.
That the situation has brought distress to many who have been
engaged in the coal industry, I concede, yet I am constrained to
believe that the depression is ephermal in character, for coal is an
important factor in the world-wide struggle for industrial su-
premacy. It may be temporarily partially supplanted, but it is the


===== [扫描序号 742] =====
1752
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
base of our industrial superiority as a nation. When other fleeting
resources have been expended or halted through the fickleness of the
goddess of fortune, coal will survive as the anchor sheet of our
industrial power. Primarily this is true for the reason that we
have coal in abundance, and its presence can be more accurately
defined than any other source of energy to which we have resort.
Reference to the statistical information provided by the Depart-
ment of Commerce discloses that in the years immediately preceding
the World War the consumption of coal (bituminous and anthracite),
petroleum, and natural gas was equivalent, approximately, to
572,000,000 tons of coal. From 1921-1925, inclusive, the correspond-
ing production was 658,000,000 tons. The increase in production of
power was 15 per cent while the increase in population was 16 per
cent. It has been asserted by these same agencies that the amount of
power utilized in industry in this period increased by more than 40
per cent.
This significant statement indicates in a very great measure the

It is reflected even more accurately in the annual report of the Inter-

While the movement of freight by the railroads increased, the con-
sumption of coal has decreased. In the 10-year period to which I
have referred, 1917-1926, the ton-miles of revenue freight carried
increased from 398,263,000,000 to 444,039,000,000. The latter per-
formance was 49 per cent greater than in 1913. The pounds of coal
consumed per 1,000 gross ton-miles decreased approximately one-
third between 1913 and 1926. In 1913 the pounds of coal consumed
per 1,000 gross ton-miles was 232; in 1920, 197 pounds; in 1926.
155 pounds; and in 1927, 148 pounds.
It is conclusive that while energy demand has increased with the
greater use of machinery in our industrial life, consumption of fuel,
especially coal, has not kept pace with the increased demand, because
of the increasing efficiency of fuel consumption.


===== [扫描序号 743] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1753
The increase in the size of boilers and engines, devices for rapid
and complete condensation of steam, improved methods of use, me-
chanical stokers, pulverized coal, high-pressure steam, and many
technical improvements have greatly increased the efficiency of steam
generation in recent years.
Bituminous coal production in the United States has not shown
any unusual increase. In 1920 it was 568,000,000 tons, and while it
fell to 415,000,000 tons in 1921 during the business depression, the
Department of Commerce gives the tonnage for 1926 at 578,000,000
tons; 1927, 520,000,000.
Contrast these figures with the increase in other forms of fuel.
The average annual petroleum production in the period of 1916-1920
was 363,000,000 barrels. In 1926 the production of oil was 767,000,000
barrels. The average annual production of natural gas in the period
of 1916-1920 was 763,000,000,000 cubic feet. In 1926 it was 1,200,-
000,000,000 cubic feet. The average annual water-power energy in
the 1916-192 period was 6,700,000 of horsepower capacity. In 1925
there was a production of 9,500,000 of horsepower capacity.
In the equivalent of coal tons the increase in the production of oil,
natural gas, and water power in 1926 over the average annual pro-
duction of the 1916-1920 period was 132,000,000 tons.
The average production of bituminous coal in the 1916-1920 period
was 533,000,000 tons. The production of bituminous coal for 1926
was only 44,658 tons greater than the average production for the
1916-1920 period as compared with the increase of 132,000,000 tons of
other fuel.
Effect of high wages and resulting high prices upon the promotion
of use of coal substitutes and search for coal economies are respon-
sible for the present anthracite situation.
Perhaps coal is a dying industry.
In looking back over this period since the war, we find that much
higher wages were paid in the coal industry than had ever been
before, and we also find it to be a period of the highest known freight
rate in this country. These two factors so increased the cost of coal
to the consumer that his attention very naturally turned toward
effecting economies of use and toward the substitution of other fuels,
with gratifying results to the consumer, but with rather disastrous
ones to an industry which was developed in the expectation of a
continually increasing coal demand, such as had been the experience
of the industry since the close of the Civil War. This situation is
most clearly in evidence in the market territory occupied by the
anthracite industry, where anthracite as a domestic fuel is being
replaced to such an extent by oil-burning apparatus as to jeopardize
the future of the industry. The possibility is presented of the disap-
pearance of anthracite from the markets because of the wage demands
of the United Mine Workers to which the anthracite operators have
been compelled to accede, which restricted the market for domestic
sizes and has put the small sizes of anthracite in a position where
they can not compete with either the bituminous coal or oil. The
same condition confronts the producer of the domestic sizes of bitu-
minous coal, but has not yet become so acute because of the lower
price level prevailing in the bituminous trade.
It may be argued that part of this high price to consumers is
due to the exactions of the retail coal trade and merchants; but that is


===== [扫描序号 744] =====
1754
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
likely to be only a temporary condition, because the retail coal mer-
chant is less able to maintain unfair prices in the face of coal sub-
stitutes than any other factor in the production or the distributive
system, as he usually has limited financial resources and can not
afford to lose business for any protracted period of time.
Many statements have been made in the record in these hearings
which are based upon misinformation, misunderstanding or which
are gross and deliberate misinterpretations of the facts. The result
is the great State of West Virginia has been slandered and a great
industry has been grossly misrepresented.
We are called here as witnesses by this committee, and we want
to take this opportunity to correct, so far as one may correct, these
erroneous statements. We want to be understood that we want to be
helpful to this committee. We are not charging this committee with
any responsibility for the misrepresentations that have been heaped
upon our State and the industry in which we are engaged; and we
believe this committee will, when a proper understanding is had,
do all that is within its power to correct the damage which has been
done and is being done in our State.
It has been charged here that West Virginia is not a free State,
and that the people are not in charge of government. This state-
ment is absolutely false. There is no place in the United States
where a citizen has greater liberty and freedom of action-no where
do the people of a State so completely have a voice in the govern-
ment of the State.
We have good roads, good schools, and all other things that govern-
ment can or should provide for its people. We have churches,
orphanages, and hospitals in proportion to our needs. For the
past three years we in the southern part of the State have been prac-
tically free of industrial disturbances. There was never a time
in the history of southern West Virginia when the people have been
more happy, contended, and prosperous. This is due in a large
measure to the fact that the United Mine Workers of America are
no longer an active part of the industrial section of the southern
West Virginia. They never had any voice in the affairs in many
parts of the southern part of the State, and in those environments
where they have been the dominating factor is labor, the consequent
trouble and turmoil characteristic of their policies have eliminated.
them from our industrial life.
The only people who are claiming that there is not freedom of
person, life, and property in the southern part of our State are a
small group of men representing the United Mine Workers organiza-
tion who desire, for their own selfish purposes, to come into our
State and create industrial strife. And these people are the people
who are responsible for the slanders against our State. The charge
has been made here that a great industry and the men engaged
therein are about to be destroyed. Let us examine into the matter
and see who are making these charges. Three-fourths of the coal
in this country to-day is being produced by nonunion operators
and nonunion employees. No nonunion operators are complaining
to the Government or asking Government aid and subsidy at the
expense of the rest of the people. To their credit, we must say that
very few of the union operators are asking anything from the Gov-
ernment. except to be allowed to go on, obey the laws of the land.


===== [扫描序号 745] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1755
and transact their business like other peaceful, law-abiding citizens,
with freedom from interference by the Government in their legiti-
mate affairs. No employees in the nonunion mines are complaining
to the Government, so far as we can learn, and the only complaint
is coming from a minority interest in the industry; and this minority
seeing that they are about to lose control of the coal industry, find-
ing that their policies are being disapproved and discredited by the
country, and anxious to save themselves and their positions, have
now come to this committee hoping through adroit, skillful, and un-
scrupulous propaganda to be able to get the assistance of the Gov-
ernment to reinstate them in the important position in the industry
which they once occupied and from which they have been displaced
by their own acts.

This information is, in my opinion, typical of the situation in the
southern part of the State of West Virginia. I do not mean to say
that there are not cases where some companies are paying a lower
wage, because this is true, but, on the other hand, other companies
are paying higher rates. The companies that are paying lower wages
are probably small companies badly financed, do not have first-class
properties, and probably are in bad financial condition. These com-
panies are doing what other companies do under similar circumstances
in any industry. They are doing their best to survive in an industry
where the production is at the moment in excess of the demand, and
it is inevitable that some of these companies in all districts must fall
by the wayside.

We do not understand that it is the province of Government to

I particularly call attention to the rate of operation of this plant:

It has been further charged that these men do not draw any cash
from the company.
In 1927, of this amount, $551,821.96, or 55 per cent of the total pay
roll, was paid to the employees in cash. The deductions were for
credits advanced these employees for rent, coal, water, lights, mer-
chandise, and other miscellaneous items, all of which were furnished
the men at their request at prices satisfactory to them. When it
comes to questioning these items which are charged the men, I want
to say positively to this committee that all these items and charges were
incurred by the men at their instance and request. Any intimation
that the men are coerced and required to buy goods at the company
stores is wholly unfounded in fact. They are free to buy as much or
as little as they desire. It is not the policy of our company to take
any note, and we do not know what men buy through the store and
what men do not. I believe this is the general custom throughout the
southern part of the State. Our stores are places where our men
can buy goods and where they do have credit which they can use
if they so desire, but no man is preferred in his job or in his pay on
account of the amount of money he spends or fails to spend in the
company store. In spite of the fact that there are three independent
stores within a radius of 2 miles, the country people came as far as 8
or 10 miles to deal at the company store.
When it comes to a question of living conditions and the cost of
living. I do not believe there is any place in the United States where


===== [扫描序号 749] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1759
men who labor can live more economically and save more money,
if they desire so to do, especially if they elect to live on the com-
pany's property in company houses. In our community there is a
savings bank account for each household. There has been no ad-
vance in the cost of rent, coal, water and lights, which constitute a
substantial part of most laboring men's cost of living, since the war.
Good, well-built, comfortable houses rent from $2 to $3 per room,
per month, depending upon the location and construction of the
house; our own renting for $2 per room.
West Virginia has excellent systems of community and rural
schools and good schools are available in every mining community,
separate schools being furnished for white and colored children in
accordance with a provision of the constitution of West Virginia.
As in other places in the South, the white and colored people do not
mix socially. Yet there is an equality of economic, opportunity. In
the mines, at times, white and colored men work together, but there
is no antagonism between them, and as workmen they have a mutual
respect for each other, but usually the working men are by them-
selves or in very small groups, but even underground the white and
colored men are not thrown together as much as they are in other
industrial work. I can not speak too highly of the capability and
efficiency of the negro miner. The foreign labor in our fields com-
pose probably not as much as 25 per cent of our mine labor. A
great many of them have been in this country for years; most of
them are naturalized American citizens, and practically all of them
speak and write the English language. So it may be said that we
do not have a race problem, from an industrial standpoint; and from
the social standpoint the various races segregate themselves in their
own communities according to their beliefs and customs. At our
operation in 1927 there were 77 foreigners, 72 negroes and 460 native
white, a total of 609.
Mr. Tetlow in testifying here attempts to leave the impression that
the coal mines are practically all located far away from towns and
communties. As a matter of fact, the contrary is largely true. Most
of them are situated on hard roads, and all of them on railroads and
a majority of them near towns and cities. In fact, each of these
coal districts is usually a well built up industrial community. There
are hundreds of independent stores scattered throughout southern
West Virginia that depend upon these men for their business and
trade, as is shown by the reports of Dunn & Bradstreet. There is
no hostility between these merchants and the coal companies, ex-
cept in isolated instances. The merchants in these towns and even
in the rural communities send their trucks to the towns and to the
houses of the employees of the coal company daily to take orders
and deliver merchandise, and from my knowledge I believe it to be
a very rare case to find that the operator of a coal mine objects to
this situation: Many of the employees of many of the coal com-
panies own property not held by the coal company, living either in
houses owned or rented by them; and many of the coal companies
encourage this system purely from a selfish standpoint. There is
no money in building and renting houses to employees, and if the
men all were to rent their own houses built away from the coal com-
pany property, the company would usually be financially better off.


===== [扫描序号 750] =====
1760
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Owing to the locations of the lands, the towns, and villages, it is
not always possible to get workmen to live in houses other than coal
company houses, and for this reason the coal companies have ex-
pended large amounts in nonprofitable houses for the purpose of
inducing men to bring their families so as to live near the work in
the mines. It would in fact be unfair to sell houses to men in towns
whose life is limited by the life of a coal mine which may be worked
out within 10 to 30 years.
In addition to this labor supply there are thousands of men
living on their own farms in southern West Virginia, native citi-
zens of the State, who spend a part of the year on the farm and the
rest of the year working at or about the coal mines.
This gives these farmers opportunity to earn money and improve
their living conditions during the season when the work is not neces
sary on the farm.
Mr. Tetlow has attempted to give the impression here that the
man who works in a coal mine is not fitted for, can not do, and will
not do other work. This does not agree with our experience. As I
have just stated, we have thousands of farmers working in our coal
mines for a part of the year. At certain seasons of the year we
have an influx of labor from industrial centers when work in
those centers is slack. At other seasons of the year we have men
in our mines who go to Dayton, Detroit, Cleveland, Akron, Pitts-
burgh, Paterson, and Newark, N. J., and practically all points
in the country where men are employed in industry, work for a
few months, and return to our mines for another period. This is
true all over the southern end of the State. Some of these men are
coal loaders, some are machine runners, and some of them from
the various classes of day labor. These men are not confined to
any class of nationality and are as capable of working in other
industries as are other men, the only reason they ever work in coal
mines being purely a matter of preference and wages. During
periods of strikes in the central competitive fields, hundreds and
often thousands of men come into southern West Virginia and eastern
Kentucky from the union mines, work until the strike is over, and
go back home. We have had many of them say to us that if it
were not for the fact they own their homes or property at the
places they come from they would much prefer to remain per-
manently, and many of them who do not happen to be so situated
when coming to us during a strike period have remained and been
employed for years.
It has been argued here that there are too many men engaged in
the coal industry. This may be and I believe is true to some extent,
but not to the extent that this committee has been informed. When
the coal industry is producing 10,000,000 tons of coal per week, there
is usually some surplus of labor, but when there is being produced
13,000.000 tons per week there is usually a shortage of labor. So, in
my opinion, there is not a great surplus of labor in the country. Be-
cause when the mines are idle or on strike, part of the men are not
lying around idle, but are in other industries and doing other work
while their names remain on the mine pay roll from the time they
quit work. I do not believe that we have any great man problem in
the coal industry. There is some to be sure, but I believe there is
enough work to be done and which should be done in this country


===== [扫描序号 751] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1761
to utilize all these men in profitable business and employment, rather
than begin to try to make the country support artificially a large
number of men in each industry who are not needed. I have not
come to the place where I believe it is good for a man, a community,
or a country, for men to loaf most of the time. I am a thorough
believer in the old adage that an idle brain is the devil's workshop;
and I believe that men and communities are happier, better off physi-
cally, mentally, and morally when they are actually engaged at work.
I do not agree with Mr. Tetlow and his organization that a life of
idleness subsidized by Government is good for any class of people.
The question has been repeatedly asked here why the southern coal
has supplanted coal from the central competitive fields in the mar-
kets, and the answer is or has invariably been that it was due to low
wages in the southern fields, although Mr. Tetlow would agree that
to some extent the quality of the southern coals was responsible for
this situation.
In my opinion the wage scales have not been responsible for a
great part in the shift in tonnage. They do, of course, affect it to
some extent. I believe the primary reason why the southern fields
have grown, and why they were forced to grow, is the fact that the
United Mine Workers organization has so interfered with the min-
ing of coal in the central competitive fields, so restricted the pro-
duction, hampered the regularity of supply, that it has forced the
consumers of coal-who must have a steady and dependable supply-
to go into the southern fields and buy their product. Ohio experi-
enced a 14-month strike in 1913 and 1914, when practically all of the
mines in that State were shutdown. The year before it had pro-
duced 40,000,000 tons of coal. Consumers of coal could not shut-
down their plants and allow their homes to grow cold waiting for
the Ohio miners to go to work. They bought coal in West Virginia
and Kentucky-they were pleased with the service, preparation, and
quality. This strike made numerous customers for West Virginia
and Kentucky coals. Every succeeding strike has made thousands
of customers for the southern coals.
Again, in my opinion, the southern coal mines are better equipped
physically and mechanically to mine, clean, and prepare coal than
are the northern mines. This is shown in the Keystone Coal Mining
Catalogue, which describes all the coal mines in the country indi-
vidually. Southern operators have spent more money to enable
them to give the consumer the product he desires. The result is
that the coal shipped by the southern producers, as a whole, contains
less ash, slate, and rock than that shipped by the northern coal mines.
Having less ash it has a greater heat value and requires less labor to
handle and burn, and there is less refuse to dispose of after burning.
As the consumer pays the freight on the coal, he has less impurities
upon which to pay freight and this has been one of the important
things that has made southern coals desirable in the market; and we
believe that this committee will agree that the advantages of these
expenditures and this initiative which has been for the general good
of the country should not be taken away from the southern coal
producer.
Mr. Anderson read to you the statements of President Wilson and
President Harding, regarding the necessity of these nonunion mines


===== [扫描序号 752] =====
1762
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
during the periods of the 1919 and 1922 miners' strikes. As we see
it and as we conceive it, we are not subject to public censure from
any member of this committee because we have and do operate non-
union mines. We feel that we have performed and are performing
a great public service; that we have protected and are protecting the
public interest; that we have saved the country from tremendous in-
dustrial losses by supplying it with fuel. We have saved the people
of the country from privation and suffering by furnishing them the
fuel when it could be obtained nowhere else.
It has been charged here that nonunion labor is inefficient. We
deny this charge on behalf of our men. We believe, on the whole,
that there is no more efficient labor than that engaged in the southern
nonunion coal mines. The records of the Kanawha Coal Operators
Association show that since they changed from union status in 1921
to the year 1927, the efficiency of the men increased 50 per cent.
I will read you again the total tonnage from that group of Kana-
wha mines. In 1921 for the group of 41 mines it was 3,821,937 tons,
and in 1926, having changed to a nonunion basis, 41 mines, in the
same group, two-thirds the number in the first group, produced
7,180,642 tons.
Mr. Tetlow charged the Kanawha operators said they would pay
20 per cent more wages than the nonunion operators of Logan paid
because their men were more efficient. My reliable information
shows that there was no district in West Virginia that was more
efficient on production and coal per man per day than in Logan
County.
Mr. Tetlow states that the average production per man in the
United States, as shown by the Bureau of Mines for the year 1925,
was 4.52 tons per day. The Island Creek Coal Co., for the year
1927, working eight hours a day, produced 10.97 tons per man per
day in their mines in Logan County. I produced 7.2 tons per man
per day at my mines in Clay County. All of these mines have always
been nonunion mines. This does not mean that these men worked
harder than men in the union fields, but it means that they were
provided with modern machinery in well planned mines under the
best care and supervision, and instead of using man power to do the
work, they are using electric power. Statistics show that each man
in my mines uses 50 horsepower of electricity per day on the aver-
age last year. I am advised that the Island Creek Coal Co. at their
mines last year consumed electricity equivalent to 55 horsepower
per man per day. Our efficiency in mining does not come from low
wages, in driving our men, or from long hours, but it comes from
mines well equipped with the most modern machinery throughout,
with practical help and supervision and intensive effort. It comes
because we have not followed union rules and method and divide
the work up between different classes of men to make it easier and
more efficient for all. I believe that our men perform less manual
labor per hour than the men in the union fields.
The whole progress of this country is based upon the use of power
in industry. Coal is the source of two-thirds of this power. The
West Virginia coal mines constitute one of the greatest consumers of
this greatest labor-saving device. West Virginia has made more
progress than most of the country in expenditures for new mining


===== [扫描序号 753] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1763
machinery. Coal operators have expended large sums of money for
this purpose. The country is interested in purchasing cheap coal to
make cheap power. We do not believe the Government of this
country has yet arrived at the point where it is ready to say to the
workers in other industries that they must work for average wages
in their industries and support men in coal mines working part time
at high wages, because if one industry is subsidized the laborers in
other industry must pay the subsidy, since it is true, after all, that
labor is the greatest consumer of all goods and commodities. I do
not believe the farmers feel that they should subsidize the coal miner;
or that they should give a six-hour day four or five days a week to
any class of people while they themselves work 10 hours a day six
days a week for much less per day.
It has always been my desire and ambition to improve the_con-
ditions of safety surrounding the work of our employees, as I be-
lieve it has been of the other operators in southern West Virginia,
by instruction, example, and discipline, and while I regret that any-
one should have lost their life while fulfilling their duties in my
employ, our record of the last eight years, 1920-27, inclusive, shows
a death rate from accidents of one man for each 366,665 tons of
coal produced. The history of these 13 deaths shows some of them
to have been the result of direct violation of rules, and some from
individual negligence, thereby reducing considerably the death-rate
application to those killed from the normal hazards peculiar to the
coal-mining industry.
Analysis would seem to indicate that our rate of death from acci-
dent in the southern coal fields is somewhat augmented by the ven-
turesome spirit of our people who assume risks in their desire for
accomplishment which on sober second thought should not have been
taken. But such is the spirit of our freedom-loving mountain
people! It is their nature to give consideration of themselves the
second place.
I am not arguing for low wages, because I believe labor is worthy
of its hire, but I do not believe men employed in other industries will
be as anxious to have the Government tell them to support the coal
miner as even I would be.
I have said that the southern operators and southern miners are
not asking anything from Congress, but we are asking fair and
proper treatment at the hands of our Government, and we are insist-
ing that our rights as citizens be protected by our Government. We
are suffering under artificial handicaps built up by one department
of the Government, i. e., freight rate differentials built up by the
Interstate Commerce Commission. Mr. Tetlow testified here that
wages of coal mining in union fields was approximately $1.25 a ton.
This was in answer to a question by Senator Fess in regard to Ohio
fields. Our freight rate handicap against Ohio ranges from 45 cents
a ton to $1, so it can readily be seen that we can not meet this kind
of handicap out of wages alone. It may be that these handicaps have
made us work harder than the Ohio operators, expend greater
amounts of money to better equip our mines and better prepare our
coal. But for these handicaps we might be drifting along mining
coal by man power instead of by electrical power, but in order to sur-
vive against these handicaps fixed by the Interstate Commerce Com-


===== [扫描序号 754] =====
1764
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
mission we have had to use every method known to engineering
science to increase the safety and efficiency of our mines and reduce
our cost of production. These freight-rate handicaps as against
Indiana and Illinois at certain points amount from $1 to $2 per ton,
and where we have these handicaps we can only ship coal during
periods of strikes or ship only special quality coal which, after all, is
only a very small percentage of our production-and when we ship
this percentage of high quality coal we must sell resulting coal at a
low price. We have these freight-rate handicaps in the East as well
as the West and North. We ship negligible amount of coal into the
South as compared with our total production.
Mr. Tetlow charges that we are wasting and destroying large
quantities of unmined coal in this country. I believe the records
will justify me in the statement that this loss is much greater in the
union than in the nonunion fields. We believe in conserving the
natural resources of the country, and also, in our opinion, it is
necessary to recover these natural resources at a cost at which they
can be used by the public and in a manner that will give the greatest
safety to our employees. Our mines are laid out and operated under
the direction of skilled engineers with the object of extracting every
possible ton of coal, and the percentage of extraction often exceeds
90 per cent.
Mr. Tetlow has charged that 50,000 people were evicted from their
homes in the Kanawha district when the Kanawha operators refused
to enter into a contract with the United Mine Workers after the
Jacksonville agreement. I am in a position, I believe, to have better
information on this subject than Mr. Tetlow, and my information
is that his statement is exaggerated at least ten times. This will
be more fully elaborated upon by other witnesses who are here under
subpœna.
Mr. Tetlow has talked a great deal about, and one or two of the
members of the committee have referred to a wage scale of $3 a day,
and the statements have been made that there is practically no com-
petition for coal mine labor, although in the next breath Mr. Tetlow
has admitted that when a man leaves one mine he is taken on at
another. If the other mine had no use for him, the man would not
be employed. There is no general surplus of labor in the southern
fields. At certain seasons there may be short working time, due to
lack of demand, but there is competition for labor from many other
industries. The statement that there is a base wage in southern West
Virginia that anywhere near approaches $3 a day is the grossest mis-
representation of the actual situation, as I have heretofore shown by
the statements I have filed.
Mr. Lewis stated that the northern operators have complained of
the southern rates. We have every reason to believe that our northern
competitors have desired to see us placed under as many disadvan-
tages as possible, from the standpoint of wage rates, freight rates,
and any other disadvantages they could have placed upon a com-
petitor. The effect of this pressure from the North, exerted through
the Interstate Commerce Commission, is shown by the following

Mr. Tetlow has stated that southern West Virginia wages are now
back to approximately the 1914 wage scale, and says this is approxi-
mately the same as 1913. The records of the Kanawha Association
show that wages in that field are now 180 per cent of the 1914 wages
in effect in that district. My own wages are in excess of 200 per cent
of the wages in effect at my mines in 1914. The cost of living in the
United States in the last period reported by the Department of Labor
was 162 per cent of the 1914 cost.
Senator Wagner in asking a question indicated that he believed
labor was the only variable item in the production of coal as between
the various districts. Mr. Tetlow agreed that this was correct. We
do not agree with this as a fact. We believe that two mines having
the same natural conditions, with different management, different
methods, and using different machinery can have a greater difference
in cost than can possibly be caused by any difference between the
wage scales; and we believe that the southern mines have spent the
most money and made the greatest effort to take advantage of all
these factors, and we believe that this same remedy to reduce costs is
open to the northern operators. We are not trying to encourage the
northern operators in making these expenditures, and all the oper-
ators in the southern fields have not made them, but the ones who
have not made them in the southern fields are suffering from their
failure to do so, just as the northern operators are suffering.

Mr. BRADLEY. These tables show merely the actual tonnage lost as

of tons more is shown by the extraordinary growth of coal mining
in the southern fields. Practically no new mines have been opened
in the union districts in the last 10 years, all of the new investment
being made in the nonunion fields.
When speaking of West Virginia, it would not be fair not to men-

A comparison of the fatalities for the years 1926-27 shows a grati-
fying reduction in fatalities from all causes except explosions, in
regard to which the chief of the department of mines, Mr. R. M.
Lambie, writes:
If it had not been for the explosion at Everettsville we would have shown
a decrease of 81 for the year instead of an increase of 16.
And Mr. Lambie further says in a letter to Mr. Harry L. Gandy,
dated January 28, 1928:
It might be news to you to learn that we have just convicted four men
for setting fire and attempting to blow up the No. 3 mine of the Simpson
Creek Collieries Co. at Galloway, W. Va. There are six indictments against
another person for placing nitro glycerin and dynamite in the Monongah mine
the day before our Morgantown State safety day. We hope within the next
few months to clear up some other things which were of a mysterious origin,
which, if brought to light, will prove that many of the fires and explosions
were caused by vandals instead of natural hazards.
I can not speak too highly of the splendid work being done by
Mr. Lambie in the mining department of West Virginia, where he
has made a national reputation.
I would call the attention of the committee to the practical elimi-
nation of the United Mine Workers of America as an industrial
factor in the State of West Virginia, and to the great change that
has come over it in the bituminous coal fields since January, 1922,
when approximately 65 per cent of the coal was being produced
by mines having contractual relationship with the union. Accord-
ing to the figures of the Bureau of Mines, by 1925, this figure had
dropped until the union mines were producing only about 34.7 per
cent of the country's tonnage of bituminous coal; and, since then,
there has been a further shifting of the figures until in December,
1927, the percentage of union-mined coal was only 23 and the non-
union was increased to 77 per cent. A study of this is outlined in
Department of Commerce Bureau of Mines Circular W. C. R. No.
497, dated January 22, 1927. At the present time-that is, since
the 1st of April, 1928, such mines as were operating under union
conditions at the end of 1927 are generally now on strike, so that
the production of union coal to-day is virtually nil, and the coun-
try again finds itself wholly dependent for its coal upon the non-
union miners and operators, who are again performing a splendid
service, which they have so often performed in the past, of saving
the country; and yet we again see the leaders of the miners' union


===== [扫描序号 758] =====
1768
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
demand that this committee assist them in restoring their power to
shut off the coal without which the wheels of industry would be
idle and the hearthstones of its citizens would be cold.
That the union, as exemplified by the United Mine Workers of
America, has failed, would seem to be obvious. It only seems to
have brought disaster to those who have entered into contracts with
it on the side of the operators; but, what is still sadder, is that it has
brought misery and poverty to the rank and file of its members who
gave it their faith and hopes. This disaster has been so stupendous
as to be an indictment of its leaders and of its inherent policies.
In the heyday of its power, its leadership was possessed of enormous
revenues and a political organization which exacted the strictest dis-
cipline upon its rank and file. Yet with both of these and virtual
control of its industry, it has dwindled to a mere obligarchy of office-
holders, raising a wail for the power and revenues that are gone.
Upon a record of failure that is the most stupendous in labor history,
to-day it asks for political help lest the remnant of its membership
that is left turn to the I. W. W. And yet what is to be feared by
the American people of the I. W. W. which it has not already suffered
at the hands of the United Mine Workers of America. Its leaders
cry out that, if their places are not saved for them, they will be re-
placed by communists, as though that were something to make the
country shudder. Judged by their records, why is one to be feared
more than the other? If the country stands in any awe of this threat
from this little band of desperate men, it is only because it has not
realized that by the change in the United Mine Workers' constitution
in 1914, when it ceased to ask for an "equitable share " of the value
of the product of its industry and demanded "the full social value "
of its labor, it had gone completely over to communism in principle;
and was only awaiting a favorable opportunity to put these prin-
ciples into effect for its own benefit, and at the expense of the other
working people of the country. If the United Mine Workers of
America, under the present leadership, has contributed anything to
the safety and welfare of the miners or the prosperity of the in-
dustry, in which its membership should have been deeply interested,
beyond lip service and empty words, the records fail to show it.
The demands which it enunciated in 1914 antedated by several years
the similar doctrine by which Lenin brought the industry and hopes
of the Russian people to despair and might well have done the same
for America under different leadership if they had not been rejected
by the good sense of the American miners themselves.
I have sat here and heard abuse poured upon West Virginia be-
cause, having rejected the communistic doctrine of the United Mine
Workers and the tyranny of the Mine Workers' leaders, the coal-
mining industry in West Virginia has grown and prospered. I heard
this with amazement, particularly when it came from the lips of
members of the Interstate Commerce Committee of the United States
Senate, but I realize that this criticism lies in the ignorance on the
part of the committeemen in question that the industrial condition
which exists between employers and employees to-day in West Vir-
ginia is a generation ahead of the obsolete rule-or-ruin unionism
which they see exemplified by the United Mine Workers. West Vir-
ginia to-day sets an example to the world for successful and prosper-
ous cooperation between employer and the employee under the skilled


===== [扫描序号 759] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1769
leadership of the employer and with the intelligent backing of the
employee. They meet their problems together and share the good
and bad with fortitude and an equitable division of the burdens and
the benefits. That any Member of Congress should rebuke them is a
reflection rather on him who casts the reproach than upon those
whose industry and good will have insured themselves a livelihood
and insured the great consuming public fuel for its industries and
homes in unlimited supply and at reasonable prices. Unwillingness
to deal with the United Mine Workers of America implies no con-
demnation of the principle of collective bargaining, because that
organization by its stupid policies and indelible record has put
itself outside of the circle of those who can claim the protection
collective bargaining affords.
A demand that 200,000 extra men should be maintained in the
bituminous coal industry at wages based on the Jacksonville scale
by some form of control which would guarantee this wage basis
to all those engaged in the industry is almost too preposterous for
consideration because it would compel the consuming public to
pay at least 50 cents a ton more than it otherwise needs for its
500,000,000 tons of bituminous coal per annum or $250,000,000 a
year. This seems a terrible price to pay in itself, in addition to
which it seems to be coupled with a stipulation that the adminis-
tration of the industry should be turned over to the leaders of the
United Mine Workers, giving them greater power over American
civilization than was ever exercised by the Czar of Russia over
his domain. The ultimate price of such a domination staggers the
imagination.
This committee was given authority to investigate certain phases
of the bituminous industry in a certain designated section of the
coal field. It seems to be the thought of some members of the com-
mittee that this implies a duty to suggest and promote Federal
legislation. I say without reservation that, if it has found abuses
or irregularities, their correction lies in the more effective enforce-
ment of the police power of the States, and that there is no place
or need for Federal legislation. The major problems of the bitumi-
nous coal industry are economic and not political, at present, a
shrinkage of demand and a shifting of what demand there is, to new
fields, and their solution is in the unrestricted operation of economic
forces, to which the industry must adjust itself without the shackles
of legislative handicap.
Much has been said about the abrogation of contracts. If a con-
tract exists, there is an obligation to carry out its terms and condi-
tions under our laws. In any one of the States of the Union, re-
dress is available in the courts to the party injured when a contract
is broken by the other. I would like to ask, if this injury has been
so obvious and so great, why appropriate suits have not been brought
and appropriate damages secured to redress the injury. But this
is a matter as to which I only make inquiry as an interested by-
stander because I have been no party to any such contract. I have,
over a long period of years, endeavored to conduct the business
which has been instructed to me with a proper respect to the rights
of the public, my employees, and my stockholders, and, in view of
the fact, that I have received no complaint from anyone of the


===== [扫描序号 760] =====
1770

three, believe that I have no cause to be ashamed of my record,
and make this statement so that the fact that I have been called before
this committee can not be taken as a reflection upon my conduct. I
categorically deny the right of this committee to inquire into my
private affairs, or the affairs of my company, and such information
as I give is given voluntarily and to assist the committee to see
conditions in the bituminous coal mining industry as they are
in West Virginia when stripped of misrepresentation.

Mr. BRADLEY. That road was built as a common carrier. The
