RESOLUTION FROM THE COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND LABOR
In order to correlate the machinery and principles enunciated by the second
industrial conference, and to bring about action through legislative enactment,
the chairman of the Senate Committee on Education and Labor, on January
22, 1920, introduced in the Senate concurrent resolution No. 24.
This resolution proposed that by action of the Congress a national labor
board should be created, composed of representatives of capital, labor, and the
public, with power to establish similar boards in all the basic industries. This
board would constitute the supreme court of industry. It would not have
original jurisdiction, but would hear appeals on questions of principle or pure
law only. The subordinate boards in the various basic industries would have
original jurisdiction as to questons of fact. Pending the calling of another
industrial conference, after the plan adopted in Great Britain, the code, or
series of principles of the National War Labor Board, would be mandatory
upon the deliberations of decisions of the national labor board and the subordi-
nate industrial labor boards. When another industrial conference had been
convened it might modify these principles, or approve them, and add new ones
for the guidance of the machinery created for the judicial settlement of labor
disputes. If the conference could not agree, or if it did not act, the system as
established would proceed to function until changed in the judicial machinery
or the code by action of the Congress.
Complete machinery for the judicial settlement of controversies, with a
mandatory code, was thus provided. Changes were left to conference and
agreement between labor and capital and, this failing, to legislative action.
The intent of the proposal was to provide for industrial self-government or an
industrial judiciary in a sound way and to develop a code of procedure which
would make for industrial peace and the acceleration of output. Unfor-
tunately, after several hearings before the Senate Committee on Education and
Labor, this proposed measure was not pushed, because of the pressure of other
legislative matters.
THE TRANSPORTATION ACT
In the early part of 1920 the beginnings of an industrial code were incorpo-
rated in the transportation act passed by the Congress. In the so-called labor
clauses of the law providing for the Railroad Labor Board seven principles or
standards were enumerated which should be mandatory upon the board in its
determination of wages. Later the board itself in its decision on national
agreements of April 14, 1921 (decision No. 119, dockets 1, 2, and 3), enunciated
16 additional principles which were made mandatory upon industrial rela-
tions and conditions throughout the transportation industry. Thus, by action
of Congress, supplemented by the decision of the Labor Board itself, a code of
23 fundamental principles has been established in this basic industry for the
determination of wages, working conditions, and industrial relations. It
affords a direct parallel and precedent for the constructive action which should
now be taken by the Congress for the coal industry.
JUDICIAL PRECEDENTS
While our industrial conferences since the war from a practical standpoint
have been disappointing in that they have failed in the. effort to secure an
agreement or a sanction for the practical application of a code for industrial
relations, on the other hand, in the practical adjustment of industrial disputes.
great pains have been made in the development of a code or set of principles
as a guide to the regulation of industrial relations and conditions. This has
necessarily been so for the reason that official agencies for the judicial settle-
ment of industrial disputes, or, arbitration boards and commissions established
to pass upon a spec al controversy, have been forced to find a basis for the
interpretation and application of the facts which have been submitted for con-
sideration by the parties to the controversy. The necessity for setting forth
the reasoning upon which their decisions rest, have caused labor adjustment
agencies to accept or reject certain basic princ ples. This procedure has been
a striking feature of the arbitration of labor disputes since the war.
Prior to the war, the established customs of agencies of this character was
to announce a decision without any discussion of the reasons which led to
ther conclusions. The advocacy of fundamental principles in the presentation
of disputes to arbitration or other labor boards has also been a significant fea-


===== [扫描序号 799] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1809
ture of such proceedings as are contrasted with the period prior to the war.
Noteworthy precedents in this connection have been established by the report
of the Federal Electric Railways Commission, and the decisions of the Bitumi-
nous Coal Commission, the Railroad Labor Board, and the various arbitration
boards established for the settlement of disputes in street railways and other
industries. In general, it may be said, that the development of an industrial
code has steadily gone forward since the war, through industrial usage and
agreement, the decision of labor adjustment boards, the pronouncements of other
official agencies, and the advocacy of the churches, and organizations of labor
and capital, until the idea has been crystallized and given an official sanction
and recommendation by President Harding in his last message to the Congress.
THE RIGHT OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
The right of collective bargaining means the right of employees, when they
so desire, to deal collectively with their employers. It likewise implies a
limitation upon the freedom of their employers to discharge employees for
membership in unions. It may be argued, as has been done in this connection
in most able briefs, that such procedure violates the fundamental rights of
the employers; that the employer, in other words, has an absolute right to
discharge an employee for any reason he may see fit, or even for no reason
at all. He may discharge an employee because he does not like the color
of his hair; because he is a Methodist or a Catholic, or for any other reason.
The case most frequently cited as sustaining this doctrine is what is known
as the Hitchman case hereinbefore referred to. (245 U. S. 250.) It was
decided in 1917. Apparently the Hitchman case supports this doctrine, but
it must be borne in mind that the language in that case would seem to permit
the limitation upon the right by legislative action. The power of the employer
to discharge at will is not supported by statutory law. The support for this
power must be sought in the constitutional provisions regarding personal
property rights. It has been held that these guaranties are not absolutely
unlimited and that the question of public welfare must be considered in con-
nection with them. We quote from the Hitchman case, as follows:
* This court repeatedly has held that the employer is as free
to make nonmembership in a union a condition of employment as the work-
ingman is free to join the union, and that this is a part of the constitutional
rights of personal liberty and private property, not to be taken away even by
legislation, unless through some proper exercise of the paramount police
power.
In the present case, needless to say, there is no act of legis-
lation to which defendants may resort for justification. (Hitchman Coal &
Coke Co. v. John Mitchell, 245 U. S.)"
The holding of the court there is apparently that the employer has a con-
stitutional right not to employ men who belong to a union, but there is a
fair inference that this right may be modified by a proper exercise of the para-
mount police power. It must be borne in mind that at the time of the decision
of the Hitchman case there had been no "act of legislation" by Congress
restricting the right of discharge. If there had been such legislation, the
court would then have been called upon to take into consideration whether that
was a proper exercise of the powers of Congress. So the question of legis-
lative enactment might have brought about an entirely different opinion of the
Supreme Court. However, be that as it may, and granting the fullest claim
that is made for the Hitchman case, the query then arises, Can this right be
restricted by positive act of Congress? It seems to me clearly it could be.
And that would depend upon whether or not the public welfare required the
principle of collective bargaining to be conceded to the workers as a legal
right. There is a wide spread between the opinions of the two sides of economic
thought on this proposition, one school claiming that collective bargaining
can be carried out only through the employees of the particular industry, and
that the employees are not entitled to have agents representing them who are
not members of the working force of the particular establishment. The opinion
of the other school has been heretofore stated. The position of the operators
may perhaps as well be shown as in any other way by quoting from the brief
of the Island Creek Coal Co., as follows:
"7. Collective bargaining, if actually collective and actual bargaining, is
recognized by law; equally individual contracts are so recognized. But col
lective bargaining, when one side or the other represents substantially all the
owners or substantially all the workmen in a basic industry, would permit


===== [扫描序号 800] =====
1810
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
extortion, is unlawful and should be prevented. In case of collective bargain-
ing it may properly be confined to the employees of a single mining operation
and operators may properly refuse to deal with any except their own employees,
whose wages, working rules, and conditions should be governed by local con-
ditions and not necessarily by the wages, working rules, and conditions of other
operations."
The President of the United States in his recent message to Congress said:
“The right of labor to organize is just as fundamental and necessary as is
the right of capital to organize. The right of labor to negotiate, to deal with,
and solve its particular problems in an organized way, through its chosen
agents is just as essential as is the right of capital to organize, to maintain
corporations, to limit the liabilities of stockholders. Indeed, we have come to
recognize that the limited liability of the citizen as a member of a labor
organization closely parallels the limitation of liability of the citizen as a
stockholder in a corporation for profit. Along this line of reasoning we shall
make the greatest progress toward solution of our problem of capital and
labor."
There is apparently some conflict between the view of the operators and the
view of the President.
In the modern large industry the individual worker is at a hopeless disad-
vantage in dealing with his employer, especially when that employer is a
huge corporation. Why should not equality of bargaining power be con-
sidered fair and just?
Secondly, the denial of the right of collective bargaining is the cause of dis-
cord, injustice, and injury to the public.
No intelligent man will hold that the present organizations of labor are
perfect or are always conducted in the interest of the public. For their
abuses remedies must be found. On the other hand, no intelligent and just
man will desire to use the imperfections of the present organizations as an
argument against granting the coal-mine workers the right of collective bar-
gaining. This is a right to which they are entitled as men and as workers in
our vast industrial enterprises. Furthermore, the granting of this right to the
workers is in the interest of sound public policy. A large industry, such as
the coal industry, is vested with a public interest hardly second in importance
to railroad transportation. The public therefore can not be indifferent to
the relations between employer and employee in that industry when conditions
arise which threaten or interrupt the supply of one of the commodities most
essential to life and industry. If direct and uncontrolled relations between
operators and labor are no longer capable of maintaining peace and insuring
a coal supply at a fair price, the State must intervene even to the extent, if
necessary, of infringing upon private rights.
As Chief Justice White said in rendering the majority opinion of the Supreme
Court in the so-called Adamson Law case:
* * The capacity to exercise the private right free from legislative
interference affords no ground for saying that legislative power does not exist
to protect the public interest from the injury resulting from a failure to
exercise the private right. (Wilson v. New, 243 U. S. 353.)"
This reasoning is as applicable to the coal industry as now organized and
conducted as it is to railroad transportation. This may be said to be a fact
of common knowledge among those who have devoted themselves to a study
of the subject of the coal industry in its various aspects-productive efficiency
of management, the relations of employer and employees, the prices charged
the public, etc.
The knowledge obtained by the increasing study of industrial conditions
and relations is the fundamental factor back of the State's policy, as expressed
by the legislature and as sustained by the courts. The legislature as well
as the courts must take and have taken notice of this growing fund of knewl-
edge. The Constitution is a live, not a dead instrument. Modern industrial
organization has brought problems which require new laws and new interpre-
tations of the Constitution. It is recognized that in the world as it exists
to-day, certain restrictions upon personal liberty, however regrettable in theory,
must be imposed in practice in order that greater damage may not otherwise
be done to the body politic. The legislatures and the courts have long recog-
nized these changed conditions. Factory inspection laws, child labor laws,
8-hour legislation for women, 10-hour legislation for men-these and innumer-
able other forms of legislation, all of which restrict in greater or less degree
the rights of persons and of property-have been passed, have been approved


===== [扫描序号 801] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1811
by the courts, and are now accepted as matters of fact in the every-day activi-
ties of the Government. In every case, however, these laws were long and
bitterly fought and with exactly the same arguments as those now advanced
against the legal sanctioning of the right of collective bargaining.
THE KANSAS INDUSTRIAL COURT
During this period there has also been much discussion of the law establish-
ing the Kansas Court of Industrial Relations. I do not want to be critical
of a State or of the effeort of its legislature to solve troublesome problems
of unrest, but personally it seems to me the Kansas Industrial Court can not be
a success because it has no underlying code of rules or principles which are
regulatory or mandatory upon the court. A labor organization, person, or cor-
poration coming under its jurisdiction has no bill of rights which can be in-
voked before the court. The matter depends entirely upon the decision of the
judge. Further, it seems to me the court is based upon a violation of previous
experience, both here and abroad, arising from legislation prohibiting strikes,
and, further, it aims to solve a problem in human adjustments with an arbi-
trary, rigid, and unrestricted judicial fiat. The tribunal which I am proposing
differs from it in that it is based upon a code of principles, sanctioned by
industrial usage and, if passed, the action of the Congress. It would not have
the defects which are apparent as a fundamental in the Kansas Industrial
Court, and not having such defects ought to meet with complete success and
approval.
THE INDUSTRIAL CODE
The principles which have heretofore been discussed are intended to be
basic principles in the determination of controversies properly coming under
Federal jurisdiction. We may well limit the matter, however, in the present
instance to the mining industry, the principal part of which is engaged in
interstate commerce, in the effort to compose difficulties with equal and exact
justice to capital, labor, and the public, and that production may be stabilized
and stimulated, and that there may be industrial peace in the coal industry,
For the carrying out of the principles hereinafter enunciated one of two
methods can be adopted: The Board of Mediation and Conciliation now exist-
ing could be enlarged and given additional powers, or a new board somewhat
similar to the Railroad Labor Board could be created consisting, as has been
suggested, of three representatives of the employees, three of the employers,
and three of the public, all of these members to be appointed by the President
of the United States. The findings of the board to be published, and enforced
by public opinion. No fines or penalties to be provided.
We recommend therefore that the following principles in substance at least
should be sanctioned by the Congress as the basis of relations between mine
operators and mine workers and all adjustments of such relations, the same to
be carried out as heretofore stated by a tripartite board consisting of repre-
sentatives of operators, mine workers, and the public, which board shall inter-
pret and apply these principles and make findings, but which shall not have
the power of compulsion or enforcing decrees or orders, that being left to an
enlightened public opinion:
"1. Coal is a public utility, and in its production and distribution the public
interest is predominant.
2. Human standards should be the constraining influence in fixing the
wages and working conditions of mine workers.
3. Capital prudently and honestly invested in the coal industry should have
an adequate return sufficient to stimulate and accelerate the production of this
essential commodity.
"4. The right of operators and miners to organize is recognized and affirmed.
This right shall not be denied, abridged, or interferred with in any manner
whatsoever, nor shall coercive measures of any kind be used by employers or
employees, or by their agents or representatives, to compel or to induce em-
ployers or employees to exercise or to refrain from exercising this right.
"5. The right of operators and of miners to bargain collectively through repre-
sentatives of their own choosing is recognized and affirmed.
The
"6. The miners who are not members of a union have the right to work
without being harassed by fellow workmen who may belong to unions.
men who belong to a union have the right to work without being harassed by

operators who do not believe in unionism. The organizations have a right to
go into nonunion fields and by peacable methods try to persuade men to join
the unions, but they have no right to try and induce employees to violate con-
tracts which they have entered into with their employers, and the operators
on the other hand have the right by peacable means to try and persuade men

"7. The right of all unskilled or common laborers to earn an adequate living
wage sufficient to maintain the worker and his family in health and reasonable

efficiency.
"8. The right of women to engage in industrial occupations is recognized and

same or equivalent service performed, they shall be accorded all the rights and
guarantees granted to male workers and the conditions of their employment
shall surround them with every safeguard of their health and strength and
guarantee them the full measure of protection which is the debt of society to
mothers and potential mothers. Few women are engaged in any way in min-
ing, but it may be as well to announce this proposition as to pass it by.
"9. Children under the age of 16 years shall not be employed in the industry
unless permits have been issued under State authority.
"10. Six days shall be the standard work week in the industry with one
day's rest in seven. The standard work day shall not exceed 8 hours a day.
"11. Punitive overtime shall be paid for hours worked each day in excess of
the standard workday.
"12. When a dispute or controversy arises between operators and mine
workers, there should be no strike or lockout, pending a conference or a hearing
and determination of the facts and principles involved."
PRINCIPLE OF THE LIVING WAGE
We desire before closing to refer to the vital question of a living wage.
It may be said that a living wage is a wage which, with due regard to time
lost from unavoidable causes, will insure the lowest paid worker an income
sufficient to maintain himself and family at a level of health and modest
comfort and with a reasonable degree of security against death, incapacity,
and the other contingencies of life, it being assumed, of course, that the wage
earner will contribute his full measure of productivity.
For the skilled or especially efficient worker there should be, of course, a
differential equitably adjusted in accordance with the degree of skill, period
of training, productive efficiency, etc. The size of these differentials need give
us no concern. Skill and efficiency should be encouraged in every way and
compensated fully and justly. They are perhaps the most valuable industrial
assets any nation can have.
The principle of the living wage, as a basis of wage adjustment, recognizes
the obligation of industry vested with a public or quasi public interest to pay
each of its employees a sufficient wage not only to permit such employee to
maintain himself in health and decency but to encourage him to marry, to
rear a family, to fit himself and them for the duties and responsibilities of
American citizenship. A bare subsistence wage is not enough, and would mean
the stagnation of our civilization. An industry which can not meet its obliga.
tion in this respect must be so organized that it will be able to do so, and there
is no doubt that the coal industry, if not already in this favorable position,
can be put there by intelligent effort and coordination.
The idea here had in mind is nowhere more clearly presented than by Presi
dent Harding in an address in New York City May 23, 1921 (as reported in
the Baltimore Sun of May 24, 1921). Touching upon this subject, the President
then said:
"In our effort at establishing industrial justice we must see that the wage
earner is placed in an economically sound position. His lowest wage must be
enough for comfort, enough to make his house a home, enough to insure that
the struggle for existence shall not crowd out the things truly worth living
for. There must be provision for education, for recreation, and a margin for
savings. There must be such freedom of action as will insure full play to the
individual's abilities."


===== [扫描序号 803] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1813
The determination of the precise amount of money necessary to constitute a
living wage as thus outlined in principle can not be attempted here. It is a
matter of detailed evidence and inquiry. Many interesting studies along this
line, however, have already been made, and the physical things necessary to
the maintenance of a family at a desirable minimum standard for American
workers have been fairly well analyzed. Part.cularly valuable on this point
is the study of the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics entitled "Tentative
quantity and cost budget necessary to maintain a family of five in Washington,
D. C., at a level of health and decency," and later revised to apply to all classes
of industrial workers. As a result of its investigations, the bureau suggested
the following as the minimum needs of a family living at a level of health and
decency:
"(1) A sufficiency of nourishing food for the maintenance of health, par-
ticularly the children's health.
"(2) Housing in low-rent neighborhoods and with the smallest possible num
ber of rooms consistent with decency, but with sufficient light, heat, and toilet
facilities for the maintenance of health and decency.
"(3) The upkeep of household equipment, such as kitchen utensils, bedding,
and linen, necessary for health, but with no provision for the purchase of addi-
tional furniture.
"(4) Clothing sufficient for warmth, of a sufficiently good quality to be eco-
nomical, but with no further regard for appearance and style than is necessary
to permit the family members to appear in public and within their rather
narrow social circle without slovenliness or loss of self-respect.
*(5) A surplus over the above expenditures which would permit of only a
minimum outlay for such necessary demands as:
"(a) Street-car fares to and from work and necessary rides to stores and
markets.
“(b) The keeping up of a modest amount of insurance.
"(c) Medical and dental care.
"(d) Contributions to churches and labor or beneficial organizations.
"(e) Simple amusements, such as the moving pictures once in a while, occa-
sional street-car rides for pleasure, some Christmas gifts for the children, etc.
"(f) Daily newspaper."
With the addition of the important items of "savings" the above list is
highly suggestive of the points which must be considered in establishing a living
wage. Nor can such a standard be regarded as extravagant. The Bureau of
Labor Statistics comments upon this point as follows:
"It needs to be emphasized that the budget level adopted in the present study
is in no way intended as an ideal budget. It was intended to establish a
bottom level of health and decency below which a family can not go without
danger of physical and moral deterioration. This budget does not include
many comforts which should be included in a proper 'American standard of
living.' Thus no provision is directly made for savings other than insurance,
nor for vacations, nor for books and other educational purposes.
"On the other hand, a family with the items listed in this budget should be
able to maintain itself in health and modest comfort. It would have a suffi-
ciency of food, respectable clothing, sanitary housing, and a minimum of the
essential sundries.'"
CONCLUSION
The report herein filed represents the individual views of the chairman of the
committee, and no other member of the committee can be charged with respon-
sibilty therefor. The work of Congress is so tremendous and the duties of
members of the various committees are so varied and urgent that there has not
been the time on the part of many of the members to give thorough and careful
study to the West Virginia situation. I mean this in no sense of criticism at
all, but it has become customary for the chairman of the committee to have
placed upon him most of the responsibility for an investigation. I have felt
that no report could be drawn that would fully meet the views of the members
of the committee, and each one is at perfect liberty to file his own report. I
believe the question of bringing about industrial peace in this country is the
most important question that confronts the American people, and, believing
that, have given considerable thought and study to it. I claim no sanctity
surrounding these opinions and no particular originality. They may be faulty,
but to my mind they offer some solution for the difficulties now confronting us
and which bid fair to confront us more acutely before another season shall

VIEWS OF SENATORS STERLING, PHIPPS, AND WARREN
In compliance with Senate Resolution 80, authorizing and directing said com-
mittee to make a thorough and complete investigation of the conditions existing
in the coal fields of West Virginia and in the territory adjacent to the border
of West Virginia and Kentucky.
The undersigned members of the Committee on Education and Labor do not
wish to take issue with the report filed by the chairman of that committee as
the result of the investigation authorized under the terms of Senate Reso-
lution 80. The chairman visited the region in question, conducted an exhaustive
investigation, and his report reveals mature study and deliberation. In this
connection it is believed that too much stress may have been laid upon the
points in which the operators were at fault, and not enough is said about the
crimes, including murder, of which the employees were guilty. Paid organizers
of labor from one State were sent into another State, where mines were being
operated in a manner entirely satisfactory to the employees, and resorted to
intimidation and violence to force the unionization of the miners as a body.
It is freely admitted that the remedy outlined in this report, the establishment
of a board of arbitration, backed by public opinion, for the purpose of settling
any future controversies, merits the closest possible attention of the Congress.
In this connection, however, the following constructive suggestion is offered:
One of the main difficulties in the attempted arbitration of labor disputes has
been the fact that there was no legally responsible body representing the
workers with which to deal. Agreements might be reached with officials of
labor unions; contracts might be signed; promises might be exacted; but there
has always been an uncertainty whether these agreements and contracts would
be lived up to, or whether these promises would be kept. The employers, on the
other hand, were unquestionably bound-in almost every case they were incor-
porated bodies, legally liable for their acts.
As a matter of fact, when conditions made it safe to do so, when wages
soared, or when men were badly needed, these contracts were broken by the
employees, and there was no redress, while, at the same time, the operators
were liable for the full performance of their contracts to deliver specified
quantities of coal at prices at which they had been sold.
This condition is un-American. It is contrary to the fundamental theories of
equality upon which our Government is based. In fact, it is a well-established
principle of law that there must be mutuality in contracts to make them
binding. Both sides, or neither, should be bound.
In order, therefore, that the proposed arbitration board should render real
service to the public, labor unions appearing before it should be incorporated.
It ought not to be necessary to compel incorporation, for their is no valid
reason which can be urged for the failure of labor unions to take such action.
Incorporation would merely mean the assumption of proper responsibility for
their own acts, and, in addition, an accounting, through required annual re-
ports, as to the funds intrusted to their officials by the individual members of
the union. The present method of voting large lump-sum appropriations for
certain purposes is most unbusinesslike, and the great body of union men never
know what becomes of the dues they pay into the general treasury. Annual
reports will give figures upon which more detailed estimates can be based; and
it can easily be made public whether or not the amounts allotted are actually
expended for the objects intended. Thus, in the end, incorporation would be
to the interest of the union members themselves.
As already stated, it ought not to be necessary to compel such action, but,
although the matter has been presented to labor leaders on a number of occa-
sions, the issue has been evaded and nothing has been done.
Some students have gone so far as to hold that there was an exercise of
corporate powers without corporate existence, an unauthorized and unconsti-


===== [扫描序号 805] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1815
tutional usurpation of rights belonging only to corporations. Be that as it may,
the Government can recognize whom it will in dealing with industrial problems,
and, in the opinion of the undersigned, it would be most salutary, should an
arbitration board be created, to write into the law a provision that only
unions which are incorporated should be recognized.
In fact, it is doubtful whether any improvement over present conditions could
be secured unless such a provision were adopted by the Congress. Much of
the difficulty in the past has been occasioned because labor unions had no
legal entity; much trouble can be avoided in the future if the plan proposed is
put into effect.

1834
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
I live in Columbus, Ohio, and our mines are in West Virginia. We
are not, however, an Ohio coal operator who has gone to West Vir-
ginia for mines. We have never been connected with coal mining in
Ohio or Pennsylvania. We have never employed any but nonunion
labor and have never had any contractual relations with the United
Mine Workers.
The circumstances under which the Red Jacket Consolidated Coal
& Coke Co. (Inc.) entered the coal business in West Virginia require
a brief reference to the early days of the coal industry in southern
West Virginia.
That industry started something more than a third of a century
ago, when a railroad, the Norfolk & Western, was projected and
built through there, connecting Virginia and the Atlantic seaboard
with Ohio and its capital city, and the great basin of the Ohio and
the Mississippi, and with the Great Lakes.
This railroad was built; adjacent and outlying coal and timber
properties bought by hundreds and thousands of persons and com-
panies, who came from many quarters, largely from Pennsylvania
and the North; sawmills were started; coal mines were opened; towns
and cities were founded, built, and expanded; and the people who did
these things had no idea that it was legally, morally, or economically
wrong for them to build the railroads, found the cities, start the saw-
mills, and open the mines.
Nor did the country generally think otherwise. The industrial and
economic transformation of southern West Virginia was hailed every-
where as a wonderful thing, a praiseworthy achievement.
The activity of the coal-mining industry in West Virginia at an
early date excited, if not the envy, at least the concern of competitors
in the Pittsburgh and Ohio sections, and as early as 1898 the northern
operators began stipulating and thereafter always stipulated as a
part of their contract with the United Mine Workers that they, the
United Mine Workers, would during the next contract period so
organize the southern fields as to limit and restrict the production
of the southern fields. Their whole effort was not to help either the
operators or the miners of the southern fields, but to destroy the
business of these operators and to deprive the laborers in those fields
of the opportunity to work. And later the operators of the northern
fields, supported by the United Mine Workers, entered upon an ener-
getic campaign to widen the freight-rate differentials so as to restrict
the output of the southern fields.
These resourceful men discovered that those mountains and valleys
of southern West Virginia ought never to have been settled and de-
veloped; that that region should have remained in a state of nature,
and that inasmuch as the mistake had been made of not preventing
its development that mistake ought to be corrected by destroying
what was already there. As there was no system of birth control
when these industries were born, they accordingly determined to
kill the thing they say should never have been brought into the
world.
And, Mr. Chairman, as stated, a part of the effort to stifle and to
kill this coal industry of the South-including southern West Vir-
ginia-has been the effort to organize that territory. The effort to
organize the coal industry in southern West Virginia did not arise
from any desire within the industry in that section-it was some-


===== [扫描序号 825] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1835
thing that was endeavored to be forced upon the industry in that
section from without. And that effort had its origin in the famous
conspiracy of 1898 between the United Mine Workers and the oper-
ators of the so-called central competitive field of Western Pennsyl-
vania, Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois.
The object was to increase the price of coal to consumers for the
joint benefit of the northern operators and the United Mine
Workers.
I have heard it stated, and I think what has transpired here tends
to support it, that a union man said he would be glad to see coal
cost the public $20 per ton-and labor get the lion's share and the
coal producers some of it. Whether or not that was a correct
report of what was said, it seems to represent the union attitude.
I think it is fair to say that the attitude disclosed here is that it is
immaterial how high the cost of coal is to the public, if only it is the
same to all, and labor is the beneficiary.
Here, with this conspiracy, is where the trouble began, and not
as Mr. Tetlow said. He stated it could all be traced to a single
county in West Virginia. I say it can be, and has been, traced posi-
tively to this agreement of 1898.
In all of these fights against southern West Virginia, the Ohio
and Pennsylvania operators have had the sympathy and support
of the United Mine Workers. This has included the matter of the
freight rates and the differentials, as well as the effort to organize
that territory.
Notwithstanding the many quarrels between themselves, the north-
ern operators and the United Mine Workers have made common
cause of a conspiracy against the coal industry of West Virginia.

Mr. TOWNSEND. Pardon me; I do not want to break in on your
testimony, but do you have an extra copy of that statement?

Now, I think I should say at this point that there are two com-
panies here that I should present data respecting because they are
associated and affiliated companies. One is the Red Jacket Consoli-
dated Coal & Coke Co. (Inc.), and the other is the Red Jacket Junior
Coal Co., and they all really own the same property and it is practi-
cally operated as one operation, but it would be practically impossible
for us to present separately the data. I do not suppose that it would
really be wanted or desired in that way.
I should mention the fact that those days referred to are 8-hour
days.
We have 417 houses for employees, about 20 per cent of them
with baths; those with baths rent for $2 per room per month, the
others for less, according to circumstances.
About one-fifth of our employees live elsewhere than on our
property-some at Matewan, some even over in Kentucky. The
company furnishes these men free transportation by auto busses to
and from Matewan. It makes three trips with two cars, morning
and evening.
And in this connection I may mention our negro employees.
Some of our best employees are negroes. We endeavor to treat
them as we do the rest, with justice. The negro is not responsible
for his position in America. It is the duty of the white man to
treat him with justice, mercy, and compassion. I do not believe
in social equality but I do believe in providing the negroes with
every economic and industrial opportunity possible.
Among the 16 per cent of our employees who are colored men
there are 9 machine men (cutters), 2 shooters, 16 crack loaders, 45
good loaders, and 4 motormen: total, 76.
These men have averaged for several years the following earnings:
Machine men, from $2,200 to $2,850; shooters, $2,500 to $3,200;


===== [扫描序号 827] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1837
crack loaders, $2,000 to $2,750; good loaders, not less than $1,500;
motormen, from $1,200 to $1,500.
Of the remainder, about 60 per cent are white, native-born Amer-
icans, 22 per cent are Hungarians, 18 per cent Spaniards, Italians, etc.
Of our employees 25 per cent of them own their own automobiles,
ranging from Ford to Cadillac; 15½ per cent of our colored em-
ployees own cars. Of our white employees, 27 per cent own auto-
mobiles. All our employees for the year 1927 earned an average of
$1,366.82 per man.
After deducting all charges for groceries and supplies, house rent,
electric light, doctor, fuel, and gasoline (no inconsiderable item),
we paid our employees in cash 65.81 per cent of their earnings in
cash through the pay envelopes. After making all these deductions,
the average man drew $73.99 in cash per month.

We have been asked to give the total tonnage we produced, total
cost of production, and total sales realizations on all coal produced,
mined and worked from 1923 to 1927, both inclusive. These figures
are as follows:


===== [扫描序号 828] =====
1838
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
For 1923, we produced 497,298 tons; the total cost of production
was $1,164,671.92; sales realization, $1,108,477.24; loss, $56,194.68.
In 1923 and up to May 1, 1924, our coal was sold to a jobber.
Since that time we have maintained our own sales department.
For 1924, we produced 750,466 tons; the total cost of production
was $1,269,038; sales realization, $1,106,937.35; loss, $162,100.65.
For 1925, we produced 1,026,133 tons; the total cost of production
was $1,576,140.28; sales realization, $1,452,994.32; loss, $123,145.96.
For 1926, we produced 1,196,584 tons; the total cost of production
was $1,894,192.05; sales realization, $1,858,296.50; loss, $35,895.55.
For 1927, we produced 1,228,474, tons; the total cost of production
was $2,169,945; sales realization, $1,941,665.63, loss, $228,279.37.
Our sales department gets 15 cents per ton for selling the coal.
In 1924 it showed a profit of 0.052 cents per ton; in 1925 it showed
a profit of 0.048 cents per ton; in 1926 it showed a profit of 0.051 per
ton; and in 1927 it showed a profit of 0.087 cents per ton.
Reducing the operating losses by the sales department profits the
result is as follows: 1924, loss 0.164 cents per ton; 1925 loss, 0.048 cents
per ton; 1926 loss, 0.051 cents per ton; 1927 loss, 0.091 cents per ton.
In other words, if we did not have our own sales department,
but paid some separate company 15 cents per ton to sell our output,
our losses would have been greater than those stated by the respective
amounts mentioned as sales department profits.
Other items of information asked for are the total amount of ton-
nage sold and delivered to the railroads by years from 1923 to 1927,
and total realizations therefrom.
For 1923 we did not sell any coal to railroads.
For 1924 we sold 24,014.35 tons of coal to the Norfolk & Western
Railway for which we received $42,278.75. This was the only sale
we made to a railroad this year.
For 1925 we sold to railroads 162,642.25 tons, for which we received
$251,516.73.
For 1926 we sold to railroads 232,743.75 tons, for which we re-
ceived $378,788.27.
For 1927 we sold to railroads 321,349.10 tons, for which we received
$489,182.44.

Wholesale criticism has been here indulged against the alleged
treatment of their employees by nonunion operators. Such state-
ments, so far as they apply to our company, our employees, and our
neighborhood, with which we are acquainted, are false, evidently
malicious, and without any, foundation whatsoever. Much that
has been said could not have been, it seems to me, more reckless and
irresponsible, if this were a forum for propaganda instead of a com-
mittee of our august Senate.
And so far as our company may have been included in this general
denunciation, I want to take sharp exception to it.
If what has been said here was intended either as a narration of
facts as to our mines and properties, or as a description of our policies,
then, Mr. Chairman, I can only say it was a perversion of the facts
and a distortion of the truth in both respects.
Mr. Chairman, we take second place to none in our sympathetic
attitude toward labor and toward our employees in all classes and
grades. We have a genuine solicitude for their well-being and we
resent the imputation that our labor has been oppressed and enslaved
and unjustly treated.
The company, in whose behalf I appear, has a capital stock out-
standing of $2,386,000 common and $715,800 preferred, or a total of
$3,101,800 of both.
This company was chartered under the laws of Virginia in June,
1924.
It had bonds outstanding: December 31, 1924, $1,097,000; Decem-
ber 31, 1927, $946,000, or in other words, it redeemed in these four
years, $151,000.
Its cash and accounts receivable were: December 31, 1923,
$82,353.58; December 31, 1927, $416,517.99.
Its notes and accounts payable were: December 31, 1923,
$275,759.81; December 31, 1927, $831,518.61.
An increase in notes and accounts payable over cash and accounts
receivable for the period of $221,594.39.
We have no surplus, but, on the contrary, a deficit of $1,753,417.88.
This company, since 1907, has never paid a penny of dividends on
its common stock. On its preferred stock, in 1917 it paid 6 per cent
and in 1918 it paid 6 per cent. With those two exceptions this com-
pany has never paid a penny of dividends to its stockholders. It has
kept its plant equipment in as good shape as possible. It has kept
its houses in good repair. It has a physical plant and layout of
which it is proud. It has paid its labor not what it would like to
have paid, but all that it could pay, reasonably, under the circum-


===== [扫描序号 830] =====
1840
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
stances. Whenever there has been a period of prosperity in the coal
industry, it has increased its wages. Whenever it has been neces-
sary it has reduced them, and generally speaking, whenever it has
reduced its wages, its men have willingly acquiesced, because they
know that Mr. Ritter and his associates, in the management of this
business, would treat them, and does treat them, just as fairly and
just as justly, as honestly, as sympathetically, as the employees of
the W. M. Ritter Lumber Co., one of the outstanding industrial con-
cerns in its field in America, and because they know, and because he
has told them, that it is and will be the policy of this company to
share a reasonable amount of any prosperity that may come to it
with them. And notwithstanding this deplorable situation from a
financial standpoint, we are not asking anything of Congress, but to
be allowed to continue our business in an orderly and legal manner;
there is no legislative nostrum that we can think of that will do the
situation any good.
But, Mr. Chairman, we have lived in the hope and expectation of
the time's coming when we would be fairly and justly dealt with as
respects freight on our coal. We are fighting for what we conceive
to be our rights in that regard, and we shall continue to do so, but
there is no prospect that this industry will ever achieve a position.
where either the men employed in digging the coal, or the men who
own the stock will ever receive what they are entitled to, unless such
iniquities be corrected.
In the course of these hearings I have heard criticism made of the
policy of the coal operators of southern West Virginia, respecting
almost everything, including stores, schools, and churches. I, there-
fore, desire to say a word on these subjects.
We run stores, located at three places on our property. We use
both a charge system and script. The charge system is the McCaskey
system, largely used, especially in retail groceries throughout the
country. Some employees prefer script. The use of script is per-
fectly proper, and is authorized and regulated by law in West Virginia.
There is no compulsion about trading at our stores. They are pro-
vided primarily as a matter of convenience for the industrial com-
munity.
Our plants are but 3 miles from Matewan, and some sales and
deliveries are made from that place; orders can be taken and deliveries
made without any molestation; and with the large number of auto-
mobiles owned by our employees, it would be an easy matter to trade
in Matewan if any one wanted to do so, as no doubt some do.
The Red Jacket school building is 66 by 42 feet, with a wing 33
by 30 feet, with 6 classrooms, office, hallway, lavatories, cloakrooms,
and basement with furnace. The building is steam heated. The
principal has an A. B. degree, and instructs "junior high school"
classes. There are 6 other instructors; 4 have normal standard
degrees, and 2 short-course certificates. Average attendance of
pupils, 240.
The grounds are fenced and equipped with playground equipment,
approved by the State department of education.
The rating of the school is a "standard graded school"; and
"approved junior high school," by the State department of education.
Children are transported to and from school by automobile buses.


===== [扫描序号 831] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1841
The colored building is frame, 27.5 by 58 feet, built according to
plan No. 2-F, standard, State of West Virginia. The present build-
ing is new, completed last month. It has two classrooms, lavator-
ies and cloakrooms. It has two instructors with standard normal
degrees. Average number of pupils is 57.
As to employment of preachers, etc., any preacher of any denomi-
nation can preach at our places. So long as they obey the law they
are very welcome. We have never, so far as I know, sought to learn
the religious affiliation of anyone seeking employment of us.
We are not so much interested in the particular brand of one's
religion, as we are pleased to find out that they have some religion,
and the more the better.
Our policy with respect to this coal property is not different from
what it is in all of our plants in our lumber business in which we have
been engaged for 30 years in five States, where such men as Rev. Dr.
Frank E. Clark and Reverend Mr. Harding of Cincinnati, come and
go. They could tell you, I am certain, if you asked them, that there
never has been a suggestion of what they shall or shall not say at our
place when they preach or visit.
Whenever any religious group at any of our places want to build a
church it is our policy to give them a site for it, and we convey it in
perpetuity for trustees for religious purposes, and we part control
with it entirely. We reserve no control as to who shall preach or
what they shall say, and the community at Red Jacket is largely
the result of the activities of Mr. Harding. He came there, we do
not know why. We did not invite him. Maybe some of the other
people did. He came there and held a revival and they have a great
deal of religious interest in the community. Just as soon as the
weather opens up they are prepared to build a church, for which
conveyances are in process of being made for the site of the building.
We have at Red Jacket a picture-show building.
Mr. Chairman, of course, I understand that you will tell me when
to stop.
Senator GoFF. Are you going to reach soon a convenient stopping
place?
Mr. BELL. I am at a good place now to stop, Mr. Chairman.

TESTIMONY OF LANGDON C. BELL, DIRECTOR OF THE RED
JACKET CONSOLIDATED COAL & COKE CO. (INC.), COLUM-
BUS, OHIO-Resumed
Mr. BELL. Mr. Chairman, yesterday afternoon I made some men-
tion toward the close of the session on the matter of religious worship
in the churches, and I have learned since adjournment on yesterday
of the most recent development in that situation, which is a desire
that our company build a church house for the use of all religious
bodies, and Mr. Ritter, one of our stockholders, has subscribed $4,000
to the building fund, and others of our stockholders have subscribed
very substantial sums, and the church will be very soon built and
will be available for public worship by all who may desire to do so.
Mr. Chairman, further I made some mention of the stores that our
company has, and I should just like to say a word further in that
regard. Our policy, both toward our labor and including all such
questions as our service, in our stores and otherwise, is no new matter
with us. Our policy in that regard is one of long standing. The
Red Jacket Co. is essentially owned by the same interests that own
the W. M. Ritter Lumber Co., and our policies in our stores and in
our commissaries toward our labor is the same in the coal end of the
business, if that expression may be permitted, as in the lumber end;
and our policies are well known and have been a matter of public
notoriety for years, so much so that a number of years ago Mr.
Ritter, then president and now chairman of the board of W. M.
Ritter Lumber Co. published a little volume in which he gave expres-
sion to our policies.
And I may say that this little volume which I hold in my hand is
furnished to all of our superintendents, store managers, and em-
ployees that want it; it is in our circulating library, and is very
widely read by all our employees. I suppose it would be difficult to
1843


===== [扫描序号 834] =====
1844
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
find anyone who had not read it in its entirety, and probably many
times. On the subject of our stores Mr. Ritter had this to say:
In the conduct of the stores and commissaries, the effort here should be true
to the company's idea of the principle of service-not a gratutious service or
one rendered without a reasonable profit, but a thoughtful, efficient service,
taking into consideration the needs and requirements of those to be served.
This
The general store manager should impress his subordinates with the desirability
of making careful analysis of the needs of his patrons in order to give them the
greatest value at the lowest reasonable cost. This involves a study and knowledge
of values. A patron should never be under the necessity of purchasing a high-
priced article that will last a short while, when his real need is for a more durable,
substantial (if less fancy) article which costs less and will last much longer.
principle should be carried through the entire business of buying and selling mer-
chandise and supplies. There is no need now to enter into minute directions or
to give numerous illustrations, one illustration will suffice: If the store is that
one which supplies loggers with shoes or boots needed in a rough, mountainous
country, for the most severe sort of service, it should be able to supply a quality
of article which is known to be able to give long wear and great satisfaction; a
shoe of equal cost, of soft texture, of light construction, with only 60 or 70 per cent
of wearing life to it, should not be sold to a man unless upon deliberate choice he
insists on buying it; certainly he should not be put to the choice of having to
accept such an article or of going elsewhere to get the proper boot to supply his
needs.
The stores and commissaries should not be run at a loss, nor should they be
conducted with a view to making more than a fair margin of profit. They should
be conducted upon scientific, business principles of efficiency, and the manage-
ment and personnel should be as courteous and as considerate of customers as if
it were in a populous center and engaged in a keenly competitive effort to please
and thereby get and keep patronage.
Now, as to the general attitude. of our company toward the mat-
ters of mutual concern that affect the company and its employees,
there was this to say:
The aim of our company has always been to square its actions with a rule of
justice; to deal fairly with everyone, whether employees or the public, customers
or competitors. Indeed, its aim has been more-it has been its purpose to
pursue this policy in a broad-minded, liberal, if not indeed benevolent spirit.
If, in actual accomplishment, it has fallen short of these ends, it has resulted
not from the lack of an ideal of service, but from the frailty and imperfection of
human agencies; from a failure to have cooperation where it should have had it,
or from opposition and criticism where it should have had aid and encouragement.
And again:
Old creeds and old faiths are being discarded; they do not conform with new
experiences; they do not satisfy the new aspirations; and just as there are new
creeds and new faiths coming into vogue, so there must be new ideals set up in
the minds of the business men-new ends sought by new methods based upon
broader, more altruistic oundations.
And again:
Not
There is no more impelling force than the power of example. It is worth while
individually and collectively to set the right example, to persuade others by the
power of example to do the wise thing, to adopt the right policy. The short-
sighted, illiberal acts of some, causing to be made rules and laws of a character
necessary to deal with such cases, bring injury and detriment to those others
who, because of broad-minded, liberal policies, are entitled to better things.
only should a company or a business have a vision, but it should persuade others
to have the same vision, the same wise and liberal attitude toward men and
events, for otherwise there is grave danger that all will be judged and rewarded
by the standards and rules made necessary by the least liberal individuals of the
group.
These aims and objects can not be attained by companies, and by industries
unless they are reflections of the minds and hearts of the men who shape and
direct their policies. An enterprise can not be bigger and broader and more
constructive in its thoughts and purposes than the men behind it. Therefore, it
becomes necessary for everyone to take measure of himself.


===== [扫描序号 835] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1845
Every man who succeeds must get down to the foundations of his business, to
the fundamentals of his personal capacity and performance, and look himself
squarely in the face to find out what he has of real value. If he does not do so,
and if he can not adjust himself, and expand and grow and think to keep pace
with marching events, he is likely to find himself sooner or later cast into the
discard.
And again:
Certain principles should govern and inform every act of the individual. No
one can live up to principles by following mere rules for doing or not doing
specific things. But the method converts the man into a mere machine. The
acts should be the results of the leavening influence of the principles-the working
of the principles in the thoughts of the individual.
The policy of this company should be a reflection of its individuality which
marks it as different from other companies.
Loyalty to its policy is necessary, for it is only through its employees that it is
known to the public-if the employee or representative is not ture to the ideals
of the company, the company is misunderstood and misjudged by the public.
It is the purpose of this company to conduct its business upon the principle of
service.
Its aim is to render efficient service.
Efficiency is "doing the right thing in the right way, at the right time, all the
time."
This policy contemplates that everyone with whom we have business rela-
tions-employees and customers-shall have the maximum of satisfaction for
this is good business.
Good service is the only thing for which one can long continue to receive a
reward.
This policy is not entirely altruistic, for he receives most who gives most. The
more perfect the service rendered by one the greater and more certain will be the
reward flowing back to him.
The patronage of customers naturally gravitate toward the merchant who
serves his customers best; the service of the employee naturally goes to the
employer who serves his employees best; the reward from the employer to the
employee is in greatest measure received by the employee who serves his employer
best.
Cooperation not competition finds its place in this policy. If you deal with a
person in the spirit of competition, you seek to get the most for the least; by
applying the spirit of cooperation, you seek to find the need, and then to render
the most perfect service in filling the need.
This policy recognizes and insists that the interest of the seller and the buyer,
of the employer and the employee, are identical, and so intimately united and
interrelated that nothing can be ultimately beneficial to the one which is injurious
to the other.
No one can live by rules alone. The state of mind in which the rules are fol-
lowed, the mental attitude toward the rules is as important as the rules themselves.
The spirit of the principles, rather than the words in which they are formulated,
is the thing to remember.
If thoroughly comprehended, and broadly applied, possibly no other rule than
this will be needed: Always do unto others as you would have them do unto you—
but do it first. Confer the benefit, do not wait to receive it. Make the other
man your debtor by a feeling that he has been benefited by you.
Our theater and picture show building, one that we constructed,
is 45 by 100 feet, with stage and dressing rooms, seating capacity of
400, with admission rates 25 cents for adults and 15 cents for children.
The pictures shown are superior, as a rule, to those shown at
Matewan and compare with those shown at Williamson, except that
Williamson has an earlier run.
The pictures are the "mine run," or entire productions of such
producers, as Paramount, First National, Metro-Goldwyn, United
Artists, and Vitagraph.

The circumstances under which the Red Jacket Consolidated Coal & Coke
Co. (Inc.) entered the coal business in West Virginia require a brief reference
to the early days of the coal industry in southern West Virginia.
That industry started something more than a third of a century ago, when a
railroad, the Norfolk & Western, was projected and built through there, con-
necting Virginia and the Atlantic seaboard with Ohio, and its capital city, and
the great basin of the Ohio, and the Mississippi, and with the Great Lakes.
This railroad was built; adjacent and outlying coal and timber properties
bought by hundreds and thousands of persons and companies, who came from
many quarters, largely from Pennsylvania and the North; sawmills were started;
coal mines were opened; towns and cities were founded, built and expanded;
and the people who did these things had no idea that it was legally, morally,
or economically wrong for them to build the railroads, towns, or cities, start
the sawmills, and open the mines.
Nor did the country generally think otherwise. The industrial and economic
transformation of southern West Virginia was hailed everywhere as a wonderful
thing, a praiseworthy achievement.

It was something that was endeavored to be forced upon the industry in that
section from without. And that effort had its origin in the famous conspiracy of
1898 between the United Mine Workers and the operators of the so-called
central competitive field of western Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois.
The object was to increase the price of coal to consumers for the joint benefit
of the northern operators and the United Mine Workers.
I have heard it stated, and I think what has transpired here tends to support
it, that a union man said he would be glad to see coal cost the public $20 per ton-
and labor get the lion's share and the coal producers some of it. Whether or not
that was a correct report of what was said, it seems to represent the union attitude.
I think it is fair to say that the attitude disclosed here is that it is immaterial
how high the cost of coal is to the public if only it is the same to all and labor is the
beneficiary.
Here, with this conspiracy, is where the trouble began, and not as Mr. Tetlow
said. He stated it could all be traced to a single county in West Virginia. I say
it can be and has been traced positively to this agreement of 1898.
It was purely a means of self-defense. No doubt many people who
have gone down there and invested their money in that territory
would never have thought of making such a contract but for the
fact that they had their investments, and these freight rates were
widened from 9 cents in 1912 to 19 cents in 1919 to 25 cents later on,
and then on up to 45 cents, with the avowed purpose as I have stated,
and as witnesses have stated of backing up the declaration that it
was an economic blunder to have opened those southern West Vir-
ginia fields, and that they now ought to be suppressed-that was
made in formal pleadings before the Interstate Commerce Commis-
sion, and one commissioner said to me, in substance, just what I have
stated, and that was Commissioner Potter. And what were we to do,
with our investments there? We had to pay the freight rates, there is
no question about that.

Now, this contract which I read, I take it, Mr. Chairman, is the
contract that I have referred to as the "yellow dog contract.'
""
Here I have heard men characterize the lawful agreements of those
who do not approve their policies as "yellow dog" contracts. We
would resent the use of that term, were it not the harmless vapor-
ings of chagrin and defeat. Here is a contract made by free Ameri-
can citizens, voters and sovereigns of a sovereign State. A contract
made under the liberty of contract guaranteed not only by the bill
of rights of the State but by the Constitution of the United States.
A contract pronounced valid by all the Federal courts up to the
United States Supreme Court-and yet, after that, these opponents
of liberty, this organization, with infamous chapters of its history
written in the blood of men who dared maintain their liberty and

1856
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
their rights a history of the acts at Herrin, at Coronada, on the
Kanawha, on Cabin Creek, and in Mingo-dare describe it as a
"yellow dog" contract.
Whatever they may have thought of such contracts, whatever
they may have called them, until the Supreme Court spoke, cer-
tainly no one-certainly no lawyer who had sworn to uphold the
Constitution can be excused in persisting in such a course of conduct.
Those who think this a "yellow dog" contract no doubt also think
the judiciary is a "yellow dog" judiciary; the Supreme Court of the
United States a "yellow dog" court; the Constitution of the United
States a "yellow dog" Constitution; and all laws which thwart their
illegal purposes "yellow dog" laws. Their iteration and reiteration
of the term is nothing but a sneer at law and order; and expression
of contempt for the judiciary; and a plain indication of a lack of
respect for the Constitution of the United States.
It is a commentary upon those who continue to use the term, and
the organization they represent.
Under the Constitution and the laws the owners of property have
certain rights and duties incident to the fact of ownership. They
have the right to conduct their business in respect thereto as they
think best so long as they obey the law.
They have the duty in the exercise of their lawful rights to decide
whether they prefer to conduct their business with nonunion labor.
They have a right to make contracts to make that policy effective.
And in doing that they ought to be free from molestation.
United States Supreme Court says this is the law.
The
What is happening here is, so far as the United Mine Workers are
concerned, the making of an attempt by indirection to subvert
constitutional rights.
It is an attempt to subvert the rights of ownership and use of
private property as these rights have been understood and assured
by the Constitution and the laws ever since this Government was
founded.
I do not think that what these people are attempting to do ought
to be done. I do not think it would be wise or beneficial to anybody.
But if I am mistaken about that then I do know it can not be
legally done without changing the Constitution. If the institution
of the ownership of private property is wrong, the Constitution must
be changed or destroyed to change our system.

Mr. TOWNSEND. I do not want to bother you, but right in that

Mr. TOWNSEND (reading):
Labor unions are recognized by the Clayton Act as legal when instituted for
mutual help and lawfully carrying out their legitimate objects. They have long
been thus recognized by the courts. They were organized of the necessities of
the situation. A single employee was helpless in dealing with an employer. He
was dependent ordinarily on his daily wage for the maintenance of himself and
family.
If the employer refused to pay him the wages that he thought fair, he was
nevertheless unable to leave the employ and to resist arbitrary and unfair treat-
ment. Union was essential to give laborers opportunity to deal on equality with
their employer. They united to exert influence upon him and to leave him in a
body, in order, by this convenience, to induce him to make better terms with
them. They were withholding their labor of economic value to make him pay
what they thought it was worth. The right to combine for such a lawful purpose
has, in many years, not been denied. The strike became a lawful instrument in
a lawful economic struggle or competition between employer and employees as
to the share or division between them of the joint product of labor and capital.
To render this combination at all effective, employees must have their combina-
tion extend beyond one shop. It is helpful to have as many as may be in the
same trade in the same community united, because, in the competition between
employers, they were bound to be affected by the standard of wages of their
trade in the neighborhood. Therefore, they may use all lawful propaganda to
enlarge their membership, and especially among those whose labor at lower
wages will injure their whole guild.
Do you agree with that doctrine?

very well under come conditions.

(The following taken from bill of complaint in the case of Carbon
Fuel Co., a corporation, et al. v. International Organization of the
United Mine Workers of America et al., in equity No. 1246, Southern
District of West Virginia, is here made a part of the record:)
That since the year 1898 it has been the primary and avowed purpose of said
United Mine Workers of America, and they have conspired to that end, to secure
the control of and to operate a monopoly of all labor in and about the coal mines
of the United States by compelling all persons working and about said mines in
the United States and on the American Continent to become members of that
organization and to abide by its rules and regulations and become obedient to it
in all matters affecting mine labor and the terms and conditions of employment
of the coal industry in the United States and on the American Continent; that,
inasmuch as the labor cost in the coal industry is from 75 to 90 per cent of the
production cost of coal, the United Mine Workers of America in the event it
completely succeeds in carrying out its objects, purposes, and policies in monopo-
lizing the mine labor as aforesaid, will be able to control absolutely both the pro-
duction and price to the consumer of all coal produced in the United States and
on the American Continent, and further by such control of the production and
price of coal it will be able to control absolutely all industries in the United States
and on the American Continent which use coal as fuel; that the United Mine
Workers of America has already succeeded in organizing or unionizing the larger
part of the coal fields of the United States, and the arbitrary use that organiza-
tion makes of its power was demonstrated in the great coal strike effective
November 1, 1919, and the nation-wide strike heretofore declared by the officials
of the United Mine Workers of America beginning April 1, 1922, and now in
effect; that the remaining nonunion coal fields of the United States, and the oper-
ators, like these plaintiffs, operating upon a nonunion or open-shop basis, alone
remain between the United Mine Workers of America and the accomplishment
of its unlawful and sinister purpose of absolutely monopolizing the coal mines,

commerce in such coal; that as a result of such monopoly of labor and the unlawful

coal industry, the said Mine Workers' organization is in a position to, and does
arbitrarily, unlawfully, and unreasonably determine and fix the production cost
and selling price of coal, and has destroyed, by virtue of such power, all compe-

"That I will not reveal to any employer or boss the name of any one member
1 of our union; that I will assist all members of our organization to obtain the

is idle for advancing the interests of the union, or asking a better remuneration
for his labor; and as the mine workers of the entire country are competitors in
the labor world, I promise to cease work at any time I am called upon by the
organization to do so.
"And I further promise to help and assist all brothers in adversity, and to
have all mine workers join our union, that we may all be able to enjoy the fruits
of our labor; that I will never knowingly wrong a brother, or see him wronged,
if I can prevent it.
"To all this I pledge my honor to observe and keep as long as life remains, or
until I am absolved by the United Mine Workers of America."

to-day you will see three or four, or more than four, wagons of West Virginia coal
to every one of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois put together on the streets of Chicago."

At another of said joint conferences held in the city of Cincinnati in 1910, Mr.
Maurer, coal operator of Ohio, said:
"The chief evil was the fact that districts which did not recognize United
Mine Workers and had no agreement with them produced coal much more
cheaply than those districts which sustained contractual relations with that
organization.
"In order to correct these most harmful conditions, a joint convention of
operators and miners of western Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana and Illinois, at the
solicitation of the miners' officials, was called to meet at Chicago, 1898. At this
convention an interestate joint agreement was established. The granting of the
eight-hour day by the operators, after making these numerous other important
concessions, was with the distinct understanding and explicit promises of the
miners to give to the operators of the four contracting States adequate protection
against the competition of the unorganized fields. From year to year they have
been called upon to fulfill that promise. The operators, parties to that agree-
ment, at the time of its execution, felt that it was absolutely necessary to the
safety of their investments that they be protected from the encroachments upon
them by the competition of the unorganized fields.
* * *
"It is evident to any candid observer that such unfair conditions should not be
imposed upon the operators and miners of the unionized territory. That the
interests of miners and operators are mutual in every respect does not admit of
controversy. Each is equally concerned in rescuing this business from its present
peril.
"Finally we ask for the fulfillment of the pledge of 1898, upon which we made
to the miners so many important and costly concessions. Though that promise
has not been kept, we have continued for 12 years to make additional conces-
sions by increasing the miners' price from 66 cents agreed upon at that time to 90
cents, and in other respects conceding demands without any compensating con-
cessions upon the part of the miners, until we now find ourselves at the limit of
our financial safety. The operators can make no further concessions. It is now,
in our view, not only to the interests of the miners, but their duty as well, to
do their share to meet these conditions.
"It has been set forth as the controlling reason for an increased price for mining
that the cost of living has increased during the past few years. Is it not fair,
equitable, or reasonable to believe that by making conditions in all competing
districts equal, the districts which are parties to this agreement will benefit by a
large number of days' employment and thus the earning capacity of the miners
of our district be largely increased?
"We believe this to be a true statement of fact, and therefore call upon you
to relieve us as well as yourselves from the unfortunate situation in which we
now find ourselves, due to the failure of the miners' organization to keep the
faith pledged at Chicago in 1898.
"We therefore insist that your organization place the districts parties to this
agreement on the same relative basis as the unorganized districts with which
we are compelled to compete."

coal in the markets belonging to you and to us because of our geographical posi-
tion, you can tell us how we are going to prevent it on this side? We can not
say to the operators of West Virginia, Get more for your coal,' because they are
forcing their coal into our markets and every ton of our coal that is displaced is
displaced by a ton of West Virginia coal. West Virginia is growing, and in order
to grow she must drive you and me out of business or she can grow no more.
And the same is true of Kentucky. There is only so much demand for coal; and
while year after year the great demand is increasing and the product is increas-
ing, yet West Virginia and Kentucky are growing and growing, and doubling
their output, while we are barely crawling along, and we are getting no benefit
from that increase, and never can get any benefit from it, until we stop this com-
petition.
"I can understand why the employers in West Virginia do not want their men
organized; and one of the chief reasons is because they see and know from public
and private sources how the employers are treated in localities where the union
is strong. And they properly conclude that it is cheaper by any method which
they may see fit to adopt, it is cheaper to adopt these methods and pay the bills
than it is to submit to the unionizing of their properties. They are properly
afraid of what might be the consequences. They will read the reports of this
meeting. They have of other meetings just like it. They see where we have
talked of a desire to unionize West Virginia, for only one purpose, namely, to
exclude them from the markets in order that we may replace their products with
ours. And hence they lay back and conclude, 'We are going to take no chances.
We have those markets, and we are going to maintain them as long as we can
and encroach as much farther as we may.'
Mr. McDonald, of the Mine Workers' organization, said:
"There is only one way I see-and I don't know that it is possible to bring it
about-and that is to in some way eliminate the cutthroat competition between
the operators in the different States and sections of States. If that were done,
you could afford to grant the miners a good, substantial increase."
Mr. J. L. Lewis, an official of the United Mine Workers' organization, said:
"The argument made against the advance [in wages] on account of competition
from West Virginia is not a new one. The burden of the responsibility for failure
to organize West Virginia and Kentucky is placed upon us by the operators. I
made the broad statement that the operators are just as much responsible for
this condition that exists in West Virginia and Kentucky as the miners are.
"The operators of West Virginia are impressed with the idea that the purpose
of this movement is to organize the miners of West Virginia to keep the operators
out of the market, or to readjust the freight-rate differential in order to make it
impossible for them to get into the market. That is the one side. The other
side of the proposition is that our own people-and when I say our own people I
mean the miners-insist that we must organize West Virginia in order to protect
the central competitive field. And you fix in the minds of the nonunion operators
