MINE RESCUE CREWS
[Effective April 27, 1927]
AN ACT To provide for the training of men in mine rescue work to be subject to call by the State
department of mines of West Virginia, in the event of an explosion or mine fire
Be it enacted by the Legislature of West Virginia:
SECTION 1. That the chief of the State department of mines is hereby author-
ized to train and employ at each of the mine rescue stations, operated by that
department within the State, two rescue crews of six members each.
SEC. 2. Each member of a rescue crew shall devote four hours twice each
month for training purposes, and shall be available at all times to assist in rescue
work at explosions and mine fires. He shall receive for his services the sum of
five dollars per month, payable on requisition approved by the chief of the
depatment of mines, and such other sums, to be paid by the operating company,
as may be agreed upon when engaged in rescue work at explosions of mine fires.
SEC. 3. The chief of the department of mines may remove any member of a
rescue crew at any time for neglect of duty, or failure to obey instructions.
OIL REGULATIONS
[Acts 1901-Chap. 31.-In effect May 15, 1901]
AN ACT To provide for the inspection of and regulation of oil used for illuminating purposes in coal mines
Be it enacted by the Legislature of West Virginia:
SECTION 1. (a) That only animal, vegetable or paraffine oil or other oil as free
from the evolution of smokes as a standard cottonseed oil, when burned in a
miner's lamp, shall be used in any open lamp or torch for illuminating purposes
in any coal mine in this State and that kerosene or blackstrap oil or a mixture
of kerosene and blackstrap shall not be used in miners' torches for illuminating
purposes in any coal mine in this State. Except that a mixture of mineral oil
(other than blackstrap oil) and vegetable oil can be used (in lamp?) upon
machinery used as motive power to haul coal in any mine in this State, and except
further, that a mixture of mineral and vegetable oil can be used for all stationary
lights.
(b) A standard cottonseed oil shall have the following test:
1. It shall be free from mineral oils or mineral oil compounds.
2. It shall be tested in a glass tube one and one-half inches in diameter by
eight inches deep, and the oil shall be at a temperature of sixty degrees Fahren-
heit when the test is made and shall not exceed twenty-four degrees Tagliabue
hydrometer.
3. If the oil to be tested is below forty-five degrees Fahrenheit temperature,
it must be slowly heated until it reaches eighty-five degrees temperature. Should
the oil be above forty-five degrees temperature and below sixty-five degrees, it
must be heated to seventy degrees, when, in either case it must be well shaken
and allowed to cool gradually to a temperature of sixty degrees, when the test
must be made.
4. In testing the gravity of oil the hydrometer must be, when possible, read
from below, and the last line which appears under the surface of the oil shall be
regarded as the true reading.
5. Where the oil is tested in difficult circumstances an allowance of one-half
of one degree may be made for error of parallax.
6. All oil sold to be used for illuminating purposes in the mines of this state
shall be contained in barrels, casks or packages branded conspicuously with th
name and address of the manufacturer of said oil, the specific gravity of the
same and the date of shipment.
SEC. 2. (a) Any person, firm or corporation, either by themselves or an agent
or employee, which shall sell or offer for sale for illuminating in any mine in this
State, any oil or any mixture or compound of oils which does not comply with
the tests as prescribed in section one of this act, shall be deemed guilty of a
misedmeanor, and upon conviction thereof, shall be fined not less than twenty-
five dollars nor more than one hundred dollars for each offense.
(b) Any miner, or employee in any mine, or employee of any mine operator
or mine owner, who shall knowingly use or permit to be used for illuminating
purposes in any mine in this State any oil other than that prescribed in section
one of this act shall, upon conviction thereof, be fined not less than five dollars
nor more than twenty-five dollars for each and every offense, and in default of
payment of such fine within twenty days from the day of conviction, shall be


===== [扫描序号 902] =====
1912
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
given a sentence in the county jail for a period of not less than ten nor more than
sixty days.
(c) It shall be the duty of the district mine inspectors whenever they have
reason to believe that oil is being used or sold or offered for sale in violation of
the provisions of this act, to take samples of the same and have them tested under
the direction of the chief of department of mines, and if they are found to be
inferior to the quality prescribed by this act, the inspector shall make complaint
to the prosecuting attorney of the county in which the offense is committed, who
shall forthwith commence proceedings against the offender in any court of com-
petent jurisdiction.
Any miner, mine employee, firm, corporation, or their agents, who shall refuse
to permit the mine inspector to examine his or their oil used for or sold for illumi-
nating purposes in the coal mines of this State shall be guilty of a violation of
this act and may be taken before any justice of the peace and fined five dollars
or imprisoned in the county jail for ten days for each offense.
(d) In all cases of prosecution where the accused stands convicted of a viola-
tion of this act the cost of such prosecution shall be borne by the person, firm,
or corporation so convicted, and in case of failure to convict the accused the State
shall pay the costs in the same manner as in other prosecutions for misdemeanors.
CHECKWEIGHMAN
[Chapter 20, Acts 1901.-In effect May 23, 1901]
AN ACT Providing for the weighing of certain products and fixing and prescribing the duties of check.
weighman or weighmaster
Be it enacted by the Legislature of West Virgnia:
SECTION 1. Whether the amount of wages paid to any of the persons employed
in any manufacturing, mining, or otherwise public enterprise employing labor,
depend upon the amount produced by weight or measure, the person so employed
may at their own cost, station or appoint at each place appointed for the weighing
or measuring of the products of their labor a checkweighman or measurer, who
shall in all cases be appointed by a majority ballot of the workmen employed
at the works where he is appointed to act as such checkweighman or measurer.
SEC. 2. Every corporation, company, or person engaged in the business of
mining coal in this State, where such checkweighman is employed by the miners
working at such mines, shall furnish such checkweighman with a check or number
and pay the said checkweighman for all coal placed to his check or number same
per ton as is paid to the miners. Each of the persons so employed to see the
weighing of said coal before entering upon the discharge of the duties of his
employment shall take and subscribe an oath before a justice of the peace or a
notary public, that he will honestly and impartially do and perform the duties
of his employment and do equal and exact justice between employers and em-
ployees to the best of his judgment, skill, and ability.
SEC. 3. This act shall apply to all weights, balances, steelyards, and weighing
machines and measures used in any factory, mine, mill, or otherwise industrial
concerns for determining the wages payable to any person employed according
to the mineral or otherwise products produced by them through their labors..
SEC. 4. Where the weighman is mutually selected by the consent of a majority
of the miners working in any mine and the operator or agent of said company it
shall not be considered necessary to employ said checkweighman, but at any
time that either of the parties to said agreement should become dissatisfied with
said weighman they may dismiss him on ten days' notice or the miners may
employ a checkweighman. Any corporation, company, or person violating any
of the provisions of this act shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and upon conviction
thereof shall be fined for each and every offense not less than ten nor more than
two hundred dollars.
It shall be the duty of every court in each country, in which any such coal
mine is operated and in which a grand jury is empaneled, to give this act in
charge to the grand jury.
I hereby certify that the foregoing is a correct copy of the State law pertaining
to mining, as printed in the acts of the Legislature of West Virginia.
R. M. LAMBIE,
Chief of Department of Mines.

CHILD LABOR LAW
[Effective May 11, 1919]
AN ACT To prohibit and regulate the employment of minors
Be it enacted by the Legislature of West Virginia:
SECTION 1. That no child under fourteen years of age shall be employed,
permitted or suffered to work in, about, or in connection with any gainful occupa-
tion except agriculture or domestic service: Provided, That boys twelve years
of age or over may be employed in mercantile establishments and business offices
outside of school hours provided that they obtain a special work permit from the
school authorities as hereinafter provided.
That is shall be unlawful for any person, firm or corporation to employ, permit,
or suffer any child under fourteen years of age to work in any business or service
whatever during any of the hours when the public schools of the school district in
which the child resides are in session.
SEC. 2. That no child under the age of sixteen years shall be employed, per-
mitted, or suffered to work in any occupation dangerous to the life or limb, or
injurious to the health or morals of such child. The State commissioner of labor,
the State commissioner of health, or the State superintendent of free schools may
from time to time, after hearing duly had, determine whether or not any particular
trade, process of manufacture, or occupation in which the employment of children
under the age of sixteen years is not already forbidden by law, or any particular
method of carrying on such trade, process of manufacture, or occupation, is
sufficiently dangerous to the lives or limbs or injurious to the health or morals of
children under sixteen years of age to justify their exclusion therefrom. No
child under sixteen years of age shall be employed, permitted or suffered to work
in occupation thus determined to be dangerous or injurious to such children.
There shall be a right of appeal to the supreme court of appeals from any deter-
mination.
No child under the age of sixteen years shall be employed, permitted, or
suffered to work in any mine, quarry, tunnel, or excavation. No child under the
age of sixteen years shall be apprenticed, given away, let out, or otherwise disposed
of to any person or company to engage in the occupation or service of rope or
wire walker, gymnast, contortionist, circus rider, acrobat, or clown, nor in any
indecent, obscene, or immoral exhibition or practice; and it shall be unlawful for
any person, firm, or corporation to take, receive, or employ such child for any of
the purposes or occupations mentioned in this paragraph.
SEC. 3. That no child between the ages of fourteen and sixteen years shall be
employed, permitted, or suffered to work in any gainful occupation, unless the
person, firm, or corporation by whom such child is employed, permitted, or suf-
fered to work obtains and keeps on file and accessible to officers charged with the
enforcement of this act, a work permit issued by the superintendent of schools of
the city or county in which such child resides, or person authorized by him in
writing. The superintendent of schools or person authorized by him in writing
shall issue such work permit only upon receipt of the following documents:
PROOF OF PROSPECTIVE EMPLOYMENT
A written statement signed by the person for whom the child expects to work,
that he intends legally to employ such child and agrees to return the work permit
to the issuing officer within two days of the termination of such child's employ-
ment.
PROOF OF AGE
(a) A birth certificate or attested transcript thereof ussued by a registrar of
vital statistics or other officer charged with the duty of recording births.
(b) Or a record of baptism or a certificate or attested transcript thereof showing
the date of birth and place of baptism of the child.
(c) Or a bona fide contemporary record of the date and place of the child's
birth kept in the Bible in which the records of the births of the family of the child
are preserved, or other documentary evidence approved by the State commis-
sioner of labor, such as passport showing the age of the child, a certificate of
arrival in the United States issued by the United States immigration officers and
showing the age of the child, or a life insurance policy: Provided, That such other
satisfactory documentary evidence has been in existence at least one year prior
to the time it is offered in evidence, and provided further, that a school record of


===== [扫描序号 904] =====
1914
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
parent's, guardian's, or custodian's affidavit, certificate, or other written state-
ment of age alone shall not be accepted.
(d) A certificate signed by the public health physician or a public school physi-
cian specifying what in the opinion of such physician is the physical age of the
child; such certificate shall show the height and weight of the child and other facts
concerning its physical development revealed by examination and upon which
the opinion of the physician as to the physical age of the child is based. In de-
termining such physical age the physician shall require that the school record or
the school census record showing the child's age be submitted as supplementary
evidence.
The issuing officer shall require first the proof specified in subdivision (a) and
shall not accept the proof designated in any subsequent subdivision until he shall
have been convinced that the proof specified in the preceding subdivision can not
be obtained.
PROOF OF SCHOOLING
A certificate signed by the principal of the school last attended showing that
the child can read and write correctly simple sentences in the English language
and that he has satisfactorily completed the studies covered in the first six yearly
grades of the elementary public schools, or their equivalent; in case such certifi-
cate can not be obtained, then the officer issuing the work permit shall examine
such child to determine whether he can meet the educational standard specified,
and shall file in his office a statement setting forth the result of such examination.
PROOF OF PHYSICAL FITNESS
A certificate signed by a medical inspector of schools or public health officer
stating that the child has been examined by him and in his opinion has reached
the normal development of a child of its age, and is in sound health and physically
able to be employed in the occupation in which the child intends to engage:
Provided, That the superintendent of schools, or person authorized by him, in
writing, shall have authority and is hereby empowered to issue a vacation-work
permit to children fourteen years of age or over without requiring a statement
that the child has completed the sixth grade of the elementary course of study, or
its equivalent, as herein before provided. Such vacation work permit shall be
different in form and color from the regular work permit and shall be valid only
during the time when the public schools of the district in which the child resides
are not in session. Every vacation work permit shall be null and void on the
day the public schools open for regular session: Provided, further, That the super-
intendent of schools or person authorized by him in writing, shall have authority
and is hereby empowered to issue a special work permit to any boy twelve years
of age or over to work in business offices and merchantile establishments outside
of school hours without requiring a statement that he has completed any school
grade whatsoever.
SEC. 4. That the work permit mentioned in the foregoing section shall set
forth the full name, the date and place of birth of the child with the name and
address of his parent, guardian, or custodian and shall certify that the child has
appeared before the officer issuing the permit and submitted the proofs of age,
physical fitness, schooling and prospective employment required in the foregoing
section. Printed forms for these permits and certificates shall be prepared and
furnished by the State commissioner of labor to the superintendent of school in
the cities and counties of the State. A copy of each permit issued shall be for-
warded to the State commissioner of labor within four days of its issuance and
there shall be kept in the office of the issuing officer a record of all permits granted
and of all applications denied as well as all certificates of age, schooling, physical
fitness and prospective employment submitted by the applicants for permits.
The State commissioner of labor may at any time revoke a permit if in his judg-
ment it was improperly issued and for this purpose he is authorized to investigate
into the true age of any child employed, to hear evidence and to require the pro-
duction of relevant books or documents; if the permit be revoked the issuing
officer and the person employing the child at the time shall be notified of such
action, and the child shall not thereafter be employed or permitted to labor until
a new permit has been legally obtained.
SEC. 5. That upon the request of any employer who is desirous of employing a
child who represents his or her age to be sixteen years or over, the local officer
charged with the issuance of work permits shall require of such child the proof
of age specified in section three of this act and upon receipt thereof if it be found
that the child is actually sixteen years of age or over, shall issue to such employer

1915
a certificate showing the age and date and place of birth of such child. Such age
certificate when filed in the office of the employer shall be accepted by the officer
charged with the enforcement of this act as evidence of the age of the child in
whose name it was issued. Any officer charged with the enforcement of this act
may inquire into the true age of a child apparently under the age of sixteen years
who is employed, permitted or suffered to work in any gainful occupation and for
whom no work permit or age certificate is on file and if the age of such child be
found to be actually under sixteen years the presence of such child in such estab-
lishment shall be deemed a violation of the provisions of this act. The State
commissioner of labor may at any time revoke any such age certificate if in his
judgment it was improperly issued and for this purpose he is authorized to inves-

The issuance of work permits and of age certificates shall be under the super-
vision of the State superintendent of free schools, who shall seek at all times to
standardize this work.
SEC. 6. That no child under the age of sixteen years shall be employed, per-
mitted or suffered to work in, about, or in connection with any gainful occupa-
tion except agriculture or domestic service for more than six days in any one
week, nor more than forty-eight hours in any one week, nor more than eight hours
in any one day; nor before the hour of six o'clock in the morning nor after the
hour of seven o'clock in the evening of any day. Every employer shall post and
keep posted in a conspicuous place in every room where any child between the
ages of fourteen and sixteen years is employed, permitted or suffered to work, a
printed notice setting forth the maximum number of hours such person may be
required or permitted to work each day of the week, the hours beginning and
ending work each day and the time allowed for meals; the printed form of such
notice shall be furnished by the State commissioner of labor and the employment
of such child for a longer time in any day than so stated or at any time other than
as stated in said printed notice, shall be deemed a violation of the provisions of
this section.
SEC. 7. That it shall be the duty of the State commissioner of labor, his assist-
ants, factory inspectors, school truancy officers, and accredited agent of the
humane society, to enforce the provisions of this act: Provided, however, That the
provisions relating to the employment of children in mines shall be enforced by
the State department of mines, said department to make complaint against any
person, firm, or corporation violating any of the provisions of this act, and to
prosecute the same before any magistrate or court of competent jurisdiction.
SEC. 8. That any person or agent or representative of any firm or corporation
who violates any of the provisions of this act, or any parent, guardian, or cus-
todian of any child who permits or suffers such child to work in violation of any
of the provisions of this act, or any uperintendent of county or city schools who
illegally issues a work permit to a child, or any person who furnishes false evi-
dence in reference to the age or birthplace or educational qualifications of a child,
shall for a first offense be punished by a fine of not less than twenty dollars or more
than fifty dollars, for a second offense by a fine of not less than fifty dollars or
more than two hundred dollars, or by imprisonment for not more than thirty
days or by both such fine and imprisonment; for a third or subsequent offense by
a fine of not less than two hundred dollars or by imprisonment for not more than
sixty days or by both such fine and imprisonment.
SEC. 9. That sections twenty-four (in so far as it relates to the employment of
children), twenty-five, seventy-one, seventy-two, seventy-three, and seventy-four,
chapter fifteen-h and section sixteen-d (two), chapter one hundred and forty-
four, code one thousand nine hundred and sixteen, and all acts or parts of acts
inconsistent herewith are hereby repealed.

Rules adopted by the
NOTICE
for the government and operation of its mines
County, West Virginia, made in compliance with the requirements
of the acts of the legislature of 1925, section 25 of the Mining Laws.
SEC. 25. There shall be adopted by the operator of every mine in this State
special rules for the government and operating of his mine or mines, covering
all the work pertaining thereto in and outside of the same, which, however, shall
not be in conflict with the provisions of the mining laws of this State. Such
rules when established shall be printed on cardboard, in the languages spoken
92214-28-PT 7—20


===== [扫描序号 906] =====

by ten or more employees, and shall be posted up in the drum house, tipple, or
some other conspicuous place about the mines where the same may be seen and
observed by all employees at such mines, and where said rules are so posted the
same shall operate as a notice to all employees at such mine of their acceptance
of the contents thereof; and it shall be the duty of each mine operator to furnish

RULES
RULE 1. It shall be the duty of each employee of this company to comply
with the mining laws of this State, and to report any violation thereof coming
under his observation to the mine foreman.
RULE 2. When "shot fires" are employed to fire all shots at a given time in
the mines, they are directed not to fire any shots until all other employees are
out of the mines, and then to begin firing farthest from the intake air current and
proceed against the air current, and this rule shall apply whether shooting is
done by shot firers or miners individually.
RULE 3. Every workman or miner in want of props, cap pieces, and timber
shall notify the mine foreman at least one day in advance, giving the length and
number of props or timbers and cap pieces; but in case of an emergency, the
timbers may be ordered immediately upon the discovery of any danger; and it
shall be the duty of each miner or workman to properly prop and secure his place
in order to make the same secure for him to work therein. Every order or
request upon the mine foreman for props, cap pieces, and timbers shall designate
the place where the same is wanted. In case the props, caps, or timbers are
not delivered the miner or workman shall cease to work in any place where
timber is needed to make the place safe, until such timber is delivered.
RULE 4. Every miner and workman shall each day before beginning work,
examine his working place and take down all dangerous slate, or otherwise make
it safe by properly timbering, and he shall always keep on hand and available
the necessary props and caps for timbering. Should a dangerous condition
arise and he be without timber, he shall immediately cease work, vacate his
working place, and report the fact to the mine foreman.
RULE 5. Miners and all employees shall observe every precaution to prevent
accidents inside, outside, or about the mines.
RULE 6. All employees are instructed and required to see that all engines,
motors, mining machines, cars, wagons, brakes, couplings, switches, ropes, wires,
tools, machinery, harness, chains, and equipment of every kind and character
used or handled by them or with which they work alone or in connection with
others inside or outside the mines, are in proper condition and provided with
the proper appliances, including sprags or other means of obstruction in operat-
ing or moving any car or cars before using them, and not to use them unless
they are safe and in the proper condition for use and operation.
KULE 7. No miner or other employee shall take into any mine in this State
any larger quantity of powder or other explosive than he may reasonably expect
to use in any one shift and all powder shall be carried into the mine in a metallic
canister, or fiber receptacle, of a capacity not to exceed five pounds, which
shall be properly closed with an approved top.
RULE 8. No shots shall be fired in any place known to liberate explosive gas
until such place has been properly examined by a competent person who is
designated for that purpose, and no shots shall be fired in any place where gas
is detected until said gas has been removed by means of ventilation.
RULE 9. No miner shall fire more than one shot at a time, and after firing
said shot he shall not return to the working place until the smoke has cleared
away; and before starting to work he shall make a careful examination as to
the condition of the roof, and do what is necessary to make himself safe before
beginning to load coal.
RULE 10. In no case shall more than one kind of explosive be used in the
same drill hole. Every blasting hole shall be tamped full from the explosive
to the mouth and no coal dust or inflammable material shall be used for tamp-
ing. No fuse shall be used unless permission is granted by the mine foreman;
and in no case shall fuse be used of less length than the drill hole, nor shall
dynamite be used in blasting coal. Where permissible explosives are used, the
detonators and explosives shall be kept separate; no black powder, high ex-
plosives or detonators shall be hauled on any trip operated by electric haulage
motors, unless inclosed in nonconducting boxes approved by the district inspector.


===== [扫描序号 907] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1917
RULE 11. Employees are warned as to the danger of handling powder or
other explosive in a rough or careless manner, and opening the same with any
kind of sharp or blunt instrument. Powder or other explosives should never
be thrown about, but should always be carried and laid down carefully, and kept
clear of electric wires, open lights, or fire of any kind. Powder or other explo-
sives must not be handled on or in motor cars propelled or controlled by electric
current unless inclosed in nonconducting boxes approved by the district inspector.
RULE 12. No powder or other explosive or oil shall be stored in any part of
the mines.
RULE 13. Every miner or other employee is forbidden to burn kerosene or
blackstrap, or mixture of kerosene and blackstrap, or any other oil forbidden
by law, in his lamp within the mine under penalty of fine and imprisonment by
the State authorities.
RULE 14. No person shall be permitted to or shall enter, work in, or about
the mine or mine buildings, tracks, or machinery connected therewith while
under the influence of intoxicants.
RULE 15. No person or persons shall go into an abandoned part of the mine
unless permission in writing be granted by the mine foreman.
RULE 16. Every employee, except those in the proper discharge of their
duties, or when necessary to escape or remove danger, is forbidden from opening
and not closing any door used for directing ventilation, tampering with, moving
or handling any rope, wire, engine, car, switch, signal, light, notice, tool, ma-
chinery, or equipment of any kind inside, outside, or about the mines.
RULE 17. All persons are forbidden to ride upon the incline or upon any car,
engine, or motor, except as provided in section 17 of the mining laws.
RULE 18. No employee shall travel to or from his work upon any slope, plane,
or motor road when another road is provided or may be used, and employees
shall also avoid as far as possible using any haulway in traveling to or from their
work, but where it becomes necessary to travel any slope, plane, or motor road,
or haulway, employees must use every precaution to prevent accident to them-
selves and others.
RULE 19. No driver or employee shall hitch or attempt to hitch his mule or
team to a mining machine or move same until the front bits are taken from the
machine.
RULE 20. In working places where gas is likely to be encountered a safety
lamp, or other suitable appratus for the detection of fire-damp, shall be provided
for use with each machine when working, and should any indication of fire-damp
appear on the flame of the safety lamp, or other appratus used for the detection
of fire-damp, the person in charge shall immediately stop the machine, cut off
the current at the nearest switch, and report the matter to the mine foreman or
fire boss, and the machine shall not again be started in such place until the mine
foreman, fire boss, or a person duly authorized by either has examined it and
pronounced it safe.
RULE 21. No coal-cutting machine shall be continued in operation in a gase-
ous portion of a mine for a longer period than half an hour without an examina-
tion as above described being made for gas, and if gas is found, the current shall
at once be switched off the machine, and the trailing cable shall forthwith be
disconnected from the power supply.
RULE 22. Machine runners must take care of their machines and all parts
thereof and cables and report promptly to the mine foreman or electrician any
repairs necessary, and they must not run a machine after the bits become too
dull to do the work with ease; and they and all others working about the machine
are cautioned to guard against the swinging of the machine when the front jack
is tightened at the time the machine starts to cutting. No employee or other
person, except those in charge of and operating a machine, shall enter any work-
ing place while such machine is in operation without the written permission of
the mine foreman or electrician.
RULE 23. Any machine runner or other person found tampering with or short-
circuiting machines, power lines, motors, or other electrical machinery will be
dealt with according to law.
RULE 24. Machine runners and helpers shall use care while operating mining
machines. They shall not permit any person to remain near the machine while
it is in operation; they shall examine the roof of the working place, and see that
it is safe before starting to operate the machine. They shall not move the
machine while the cutter chain is in motion.
RULE 25. Shooting "off the solid" is distinctly prohibited except by permis-
sion in writing from the mine foreman, and under conditions which may be
prescribed in writing by the district mine inspector.

RULE 26. Any machine runner or other person in the mine loading coal which
is not properly cleaned and prepared shall be subject to the customary “dock."
RULE 27. Any driver or person found mistreating a mule will be prosecuted.
RULE 28. Any employee of this company found taking coal from railway
cars will be charged with same at the market price in addition to the regular
monthly fuel charge.
RULE 29. No employee quitting work or discharged by the company will be
paid off until he has cleaned up and left his working place in proper condition;
nor, if occupying a house, until he has vacated the same and surrendered posses-
sion to the company.
RULE 30. Pay of all the employees shall be subject to such deductions for
doctors, fuel charge, and other charges as are now or may hereafter be in effect.
RULE 31. Persons seeking employment shall secure it outside the mine.
RULE 32. No employee of this company is required or expected to work in
any place of unnecessary danger or to do anything in conflict with the mining
laws of the State; in fact, a faithful observance of these laws is expected and
required.
RULE 33. No boy under sixteen years of age will be permitted to work in this
mine.
RULE 34. Nothing in any of the foregoing rules shall be construed to mean
that safety first shall not always be given first and greatest consideration by all
employees of this company.

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS IN PENNSYLVANIA,
WEST VIRGINIA, AND OHIO
THURSDAY, APRIL 19, 1928
UNITED STATES SENATE,
COMMITTEE ON INTERSTATE COMMERCE,
Washington, D. C.
The committee met (pursuant to adjournment on yesterday), at
10.15 o'clock a. m., in room 212, Senate Office Building, Senator Guy
D. Goff presiding.
Present: Senators Goff (presiding), Metcalf, Smith, Wheeler, and
Wagner.
Senator GoFF (presiding). The committee will be in order. Mr.
Townsend, you may call your first witness.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Mr. Coolidge.
TESTIMONY OF WILLIAM H. COOLIDGE, ATTORNEY AT LAW
AND CHAIRMAN OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF THE IS-
LAND CREEK COAL CO., MANCHESTER, MASS.
The witness was duly sworn by Senator Goff.
Senator WHEELER. I understand, Mr. Coolidge, that you have the
distinction of being a relative of the President of the United States.
Mr. COOLIDGE. Not enough to hurt him any and not enough to
do me any good.
Senator WHEELER. I was just wondering how close the relationship
was.
Mr. COOLIDGE. The first Coolidge that came to this country
arrived here in 1630. He had four boys and several girls. The
President is descended from one of those boys; I am descended from
another; so, 10 generations back, we had a common ancestor. I
think there has been no intermarriage between the two branches of
the family since.
Mr. Chairman, I have prepared a statement which I will read and
hand in various schedules from time to time, reading them if the
committee wants me to do that; otherwise; I will not take the trouble
to read them.
Mr. TOWNSEND. There is contained in that paper the information
asked for?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Everything that is asked for you will get.
This investigation of the coal industry has been ordered by the
Senate at the request of the United Mine Workers of America, who
desire that the cost of coal to 100,000,000 people in the United States
shall be increased for the benefit of 500,000 coal miners and their
1923


===== [扫描序号 920] =====
1924
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
families and possible 100,000 people who are owners and stock-
holders in coal companies; heretofore investigations have been or-
dered because the people were alleged to be paying too much for their
coal. This investigation is being held to see if some way can be
found, within the Constitution, to make coal production cost more.
We have not believed this matter was within the control of the Fed-
eral Government, but so far as possible we desire to help this com-
mittee in considering the question. There is no coal problem so far
as the company I represent is concerned
I understand I have been summoned before this committee be-
cause I am chairman of the board of directors of the Island Creek
Coal Co. and am alleged to be a nonresident with no interest in the
employees of our company, merely using them if not abusing them.
The word "nonresident" is applicable to those who have helped
to develop the natural resources of West Virginia. Men of Boston
are largely responsible for the building and development of the rail-
roads of this country; for example, the Atchison, Topeka & Santa
Fe, the Union Pacific, the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy, the Pere
Marquette, and the Chicago Junction Railway. It was Boston
capital which was largely responsible for the Moffatt tunnel, just
opened in Colorado. It was Boston men and Boston capital that
developed the copper mines in Michigan; the Boston & Montana
Copper mine in Montana; the Yuba and other gold mines in Cali-
fornia; the zinc mines of the American Zinc Co. in Tennessee, Mis-
souri, and Oklahoma; the zinc smelters in Illinois; and the zinc oxide
plant in Columbus, Ohio. It was Boston men and Boston capital
that developed the great central manufacturing district of Chicago.
Senator WHEELER. As far as I am concerned, I am perfectly
willing to admit that Massachusetts and Boston are producing great
men.
Mr. COOLIDGE. You do not have to admit it. It is a fact that the
cotton mills of the South have been largely constructed and devel-
oped by New England men and New England capital.
The people of West Virginia have been as anxious to have their
resources developed as have the people of any other State in the
Union. They recognize the advantage of such development. The
success that has resulted from the development caused the Republi-
can convention of West Virginia to put into its platform of 1920 the
following plank:
With raw materials in abundance, with stores of fuel and energy at our very
doors * * *. This glaring material fact only recently recognized by indus-
trial authorities, with the aid of a sound economic policy, will bring countless
thousands of new capital into the State. We pledge the Republican Party to
the continuation of those policies which invite sound investment.
In the Democratic State platform of 1924 we find the following
plank:
The bringing into the State of outside capital for the building of manufacturing
plants will increase the taxable property of the State, while the operation of such
plants will result in the utilization of our raw materials instead of having them
shipped outside our borders.
It has never been blameworthy in this country for the people of one
State to build and develop industries in other States.
The history of the Island Creek Coal Co. well illustrates the use of
capital from outside the State in the development of the great coal
industry in West Virginia at the request of citizens of West Virginia.


===== [扫描序号 921] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1925
Early in the spring of 1902 Mr. Taylor Vinson, of Huntington, and
other citizens of West Virginia, came to Boston and asked my associ-
ates and myself to become interested in a tract of coal land, some
30,000 acres in area, located in Logan County some 75 miles south
of the city of Huntington. Mr. Albert F. Holden, of Cleveland, Ohio,
a mining engineer without a superior, together with myself and two
or three others, went in May, 1902, to West Virginia.
We left the Norfolk & Western Railroad at a little, almost deserted
town, rode across the mountains a distance of about 15 miles into
Logan County. There were then no railroads in Logan County.
The roads were well-nigh impassable. Transportation was almost
entirely by horseback and muleback. The population of the county
was approximately 5,000-it is now 60,000-and the county seat,
Logan, the largest town, had less than 500-now 10,000 people. The
tract now know as the Island Creek property was beatuiful by nature,
mountainous with narrow ravines. There were no people living on
the tract. It contained several coal seams, since estimated by engi-
neers to contain between 300,000,000 and 400,000,000 tons of coal.
The chief seam, some 62 feet in thickness, is now known as the
Island Creek seam.
The property was purchased and development begun. Of course,
we had to build houses, provide a store, and build tipples before we
could begin to mine coal. Everything except the machinery was
obtained from the property itself. The first machinery was hauled
over the mountain a distance of 15 miles. The Guyan branch of the
Chesapeake & Ohio Railroad ran up the Guyandott River to its
terminus some 40 miles from the town of Logan. The Chesapeake
& Ohio was induced to build the 40 miles to Logan, with which our
mines were connected by a road some 4 or 5 miles in length, built
by our company. The first coal shipped by our company was in the
winter of 1904-5.
The county of Logan now has approximately 200 miles of railroad,
approximately 100 different mines producing coal, about 150 miles
of concrete and hard surface roads, and a population of about 60,000.
Upon our property are now some 10,000 people, the majority of
whom live in 1,500 houses built by our company. We have 10 stores
on our property. The production of coal from our properties has
been as follows:
From 1905 to 1920, inclusive__
From 1921 to 1927, inclusive_
Total.....
Tons
26, 012, 542
34, 676, 061
60, 688, 603
In 1922 the Chesapeake & Ohio Railroad was persuaded to spend
many millions in double tracking this road, and especially the Guyan
branch, and in buying cars and locomotives, so that in the last four
and a half years we have had a full car supply and perfect transpor-
tation service.
Mr. Holden was the president of our company until his death in
1913, and in 1912 the production was 2,225,139 tons.
In order that our mines might be continuously operated, the com-
pany, during Mr. Holden's life, acquired docks at and near Duluth
at the head of Lake Superior, and acquired steamers and barges to
transport coal on the Ohio River to the vicinity of Cincinnati.
Within the last few years the company has established a retail busi-


===== [扫描序号 922] =====
1926
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
ness in Cincinnati, known as the Queen City Coal Co., but we have
now sold our docks at the head of the lake, selling such coal as goes
over the lake to other distributors. The Island Creek Co. produces
no coal outside of Logan County.
Mr. Holden's wife was Miss Davis, a niece of ex-Senator Davis, of
West Virginia, one of the chief developers of West Virginia coal and
other resources. On Mr. Holden's death, Mr. T. B. Davis, jr., his
brother-in-law, a West Virginia boy and man, who had joined our
company in 1907, became president of the company and still remains
its president.
The committee has been told that the conditions in southern West
Virginia are deplorable-that the men do not get enough to eat that
they are underpaid and that they need the United Mine Workers for
their protection.
The pictures which I want to show the committee we believe
absolutely refute that statement. These pictures were not taken for
this hearing, but were pictures that we happened to have. This one
that I show you is a picture showing the middle of the town. That
building in the center is the store building in the town. The big house
up on the corner is the house that we built originally for the manager
of the plant.
Senator WHEELER. What is the name of the town?
Mr. COOLIDGE. The name of the town is Holden. This picture
that I now show you represents a meeting some time in 1926 when
they were having a contest between our safety-first crews for each
mine. Every man that goes into our mines is supposed at least to
learn the safety-first methods. Every mine has a safety-first crew
and this picture was taken when they were having a contest. These
automobiles are automobiles owned by our men. That is a deplor-
able condition in our property.
Senator METCALF. Has each one got an automobile?
Mr. COOLIDGE. There are about 800 cars out of about 2,000 to
2,500 men. And there are garages. But these are the deplorable
conditions, and there is a picture of the discontented men.
Senator WHEELER. These automobiles, I assume, represent the
visitors that have driven in from outside the town.
Mr. COOLIDGE. Those automobiles, 800 of them, at least, are ours;
our employees own them; and if you will notice-Mr. Couzens is
not here there are no Fords among them; they are all better than
Fords.
Senator GOFF. Mr. Coolidge, I do not know whether this story was
told in reference to your mine, but I understood that a man drove
up in a car to obtain a position at one of the mines in the southern
district and could not find any parking space. He went in to the
manager and complained that there was no parking space, and the
manager said, "Well, I am very sorry, but we have adopted a rule
to employ no miners unless they have their own chauffeurs."
Mr. COOLIDGE. Being under oath I can neither affirm nor deny
that statement.
Senator SMITH. But it sounds natural?
Mr. COOLIDGE. It sounds natural.
Mr. TOWNSEND. That was a union man that tried to get in there.
Senator GOFF. I do not care what his status was in the union.
Mr. COOLIDGE. That shows that he could get in without being hurt.


===== [扫描序号 923] =====

1927
Senator SMITH. Maybe they employed a union man as a chauffeur.
Mr. TOWNSEND. I do not think so.
Mr. COOLIDGE. No; I think that is one industry that has not
attempted as yet to unionize. Here is a picture of our central
schoolhouse.
There is no better or more healthy place in the United States than
the town of Holden and its adjoining communities. There are good
schools and schoolhouses on land owned by the county-post office in
buildings leased to the Government. In 1921 there was an investiga-
tion by the so-called Kenyon Committee of the United States Senate.
A subcommittee headed by Senator Kenyon, went to southern West
Virginia, and the chairman, Senator Kenyon, speaking of the town of
Holden, at page 918 of the record, stated: "It would be hard to
find one better.'
We have built some 20 miles of concrete roads inside our property.
Our houses are well kept and are all regularly occupied. We have
never made money from the rent of our houses. It is a necessity that
we should have houses for our employees. Our employees are not
required to live in our houses but they prefer to live in them because
they can not get as good accommodations elsewhere for anything like
the same price. Our charge for rent ($2 per room per month) has
not been advanced since 1905, when we began operations. We did
not build these houses to make money out of thein. We built these
houses because it was necessary for us to build them.
We have always used all safety devices to protect the lives of our
employees as fast as they have been discovered. The fatality rate
on our property we believe is lower than in any other coal-mining
property in the country. It has been charged here that the death
rate in the United States per million tons is greater than in other
countries. This is a mistake. The death rate in the United States
for the years 1921-1925, inclusive, was 3.67 per million tons of pro-
duction, whereas in Great Britain it was 3.98; in France, 5.68; in
Belgium, 6.54; and in Prussia, 10.30. From the statistics com-
piled by the Bureau of Mines we find that in 1927 in the United
States there was one fatality for each 299,599 tons produced. In-
stead of 3,000 fatalities per annum in the bituminous industry, as
has been stated to this committee, the records show a total of 1,830
fatalities in 1925; 2,001 in 1926, and 1,750 in 1927. In the Island
Creek property in 1925, with a total production of 6,058,317 tons,
there were 7 fatalities, or 1 for each 860,816 tons. In 1926 there
were 8 fatalities with a production of 6,638,427 tons, or 1 for each
821,116 tons, while in 1927, with a production of 7,481,570 tons,
there were 6 fatalities, or 1 for each 1,232,997 tons. In other words,
our record in 1927 was four times as good as the average in the
United States. We naturally resent the charges made by the
United Mine Workers of America that we have no thought for the
lives and welfare of our employees.
We were told by operators north of the Ohio River soon after we
opened our mines that it was an "economic crime" to open these
mines. That was stated to Mr. Holden and myself at a conference
with the officers of the Pittsburgh Coal Co. We felt otherwise. We
appreciated that there were many more consumers of coal than pro-
ducers of coal; that the consumers were entitled to the cheapest coal
that could be produced, and we now appreciate that while perhaps

500,000 men are employed and possibly 100,000 men are interested
in the ownership of coal-producing properties, there are many times

Senator WHEELER. Mr. Coolidge, who were the officers of the

Mr. COOLIDGE. I think it was a Mr. Taylor, the chairman of the

Senator WHEELER. How long ago was that?
Mr. COOLIDGE. That was soon after our mines were started, and
they were endeavoring to impress us with the fact that it was an
economic crime for us to help open up other coal properties than those
already existing in the central competitive field. We did not agree

Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Coolidge, I will ask you if in the last Lake
Cargo case the same interests took the same position in that case
before the Interstate Commerce Commission?
Mr. COOLIDGE. They did.
Mr. BELCHER. We will want to file that in the record. I have not
got it now. It shows that their attitude has not changed at all since
his statement was first made.
Mr. COOLIDGE. Neither has ours.
They, the consumers, do not desire the coal so cheap that the men
employed shall not receive a living wage or a saving wage, nor do
they desire that the coal shall be sold to them at a loss to the producers
but there is no reason why the consumers of coal shall be compelled
to pay other than a reasonable price merely in order that mines
inefficiently managed or inefficiently operated may continue to live.
The 100,000,000 people not interested in the mining of coal are
entitled to consideration as well as the 500,000 or 600,000 and
their families who are interested in the mining of coal.
This committee has been told by Mr. Lewis that only 40 per cent
of the coal is saved and that 60 per cent remains in the ground. We
have already exhausted 2 mines-we have 22 mines in our property—
from which we have extracted 90.2 and 93 per cent of the coal, and
in leasing a tract of some 5,000 acres it was provided that royalties
shall be paid on at least 85 per cent.
Senator WHEELER. Do you deny that that statement that Mr.
Lewis made is not true with reference to some of the mines that are
being operated?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I have no knowledge as to other mines, but he
referred to what is the percentage of production from the mines. I
am showing that it does not apply to ours. I do not know what other
people do. I know what we are doing.
The committee has been told by Mr. Lewis, as appears upon pages
381, 406, 426, and 432 of the record in this case, that the wages in
southern West Virginia range from $1.90 per day to a maximum of
$4.50 per day. This statement is absolutely wrong so far as our
company is concerned. Perhaps his source of information is unreli-
able. Mr. Bittner in his testimony has referred repeatedly to the
deplorable conditions in West Virginia and the inadequate wages in
the nonunion mines. He is wrong, especially so far as our company
is concerned. The committee has been told by the United Mine
Workers that through our stores, etc., nonunion miners have little or
no money left and are often in debt after pay day.

1929
The Island Creek Coal Co. does not have a wage scale in the sense
that is used by the term "Jacksonville scale." We operate upon an
eight-hour-day basis. Our employees are not compelled to work
every day or eight hours a day, but they receive pay for the time
they work. We do not use the same system of mining that is used
north of the Ohio River. Our loaders, for example, do substantially
nothing but load coal. They have no dead work to do, no timbering,
no tract work, no drilling, nor any of the other things that loaders in
the union mines are accustomed to do. We have one crew of men
who lay the tracks; another crew looks after the electrical wiring;
other men cut the coal; others drill the holes; other men take care of
the timbering, and still others look after the ventilation.
Our present rate of wages has been in force since February 1, 1924,
except for two ro three months during the British strike in 1926-27,
when we voluntarily increased the rate temporarily for 22 months.
In 1927 approximately 50 per cent of our employees worked at the
rate of $6.80 per day; 15 per cent at from $7.30 to $10.80 per day;
4 per cent at from $6 to $6.72 per day; 16 per cent at from $5.04
to $5.68 per day; 5 per cent at from $4.56 to $4.96 per day; 9 per cent
at from $4 to $4.40 per day, and only 1 per cent of our employees
receive less than 50 cents per hour. These rates are paid to men who
are practically disabled or doing some relatively unimportant work
outside the mines and are as much or more than rates paid for similar
work in other industries. From the statements already filed in
this case but a copy of which I am asking to be inserted again at
this point, it appears that the average daily wage in 27 different
industries in the United States was 45.3 cents per hour for unskilled
labor and 63.6 cents per hour for skilled labor, and it will be noted
that our average rate for both skilled and unskilled is considerably
higher than the average rate for skilled labor for the industries listed.
Our rate is about 80 cents per hour on the average. Our rates
placed upon an hourly basis are as shown in this schedule, which,
unless desired, I will not take time to read:

I have been accustomed to have them send to Boston a statement
showing what our men were making who worked sufficiently to have
their names appear on each fortnightly pay roll. We pay fortnightly.
Now, that does not mean that the men work every day unless they
want to. The list does not contain the names of men who do not work
so they were paid something on each pay day.

1931
Mr. TOWNSEND. The building trades also put out a similar state-
ment, do they not?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I should say from my knowledge of what happens
in my country, where I live, that plasterers, plumbers, carpenters,
bricklayers; in fact, those who are engaged in the building trades.
generally, get a higher wage rate per hour when they work than they
do in our mines in West Virginia. I think that is undoubtedly true,
but I am just wondering how much more they make per annum.
Mr. TOWNSEND. They are not included in this list?
Mr. COOLIDGE. No.
Mr. TOWNSEND. The highly organized industries, like bricklayers
carpenters, plasterers, and plumbers, that class of union labor, are not
included here?
Mr. COOLIDGE. The union men that have been so organized that
nobody in this country in a union territory can build a house or a
building without paying very high wages is the best organized in-
dustry in the country, I think. The garment workers are well
organized. The railroad men, as a rule, are well organized. There
are one or two others, perhaps, that have a practical monopoly, and
the cost to the people that need the houses has been jumped two or
three or four times.
I know I built a house some 10 or 15 years ago and I asked my
contractor last year, the man who built my house, how much more
he would have to charge than he contracted for in 1914 or 1915, and
he said he would not dream of bidding at less than three times what
he did. That is the union. We do not want that kind of union
down in our country. We do not want to have the cost of coal to
the public generally boosted two or three times. We would be very
glad personally with our mines to pay any rate of wage, because with
our mines as they are we can make more money, we believe, than
anybody else.
Mr. TOWNSEND. This statement would more accurately reflect the
situation if it had included those trades that you have spoken of,
would it not?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I suggest that you put those in, then they can be
compared with these and you can compare the difference between
the cost to the people of a strongly unionized industry and the cost
to the people where the people get the benefit of reasonable wages.
Nobody can suggest that the plumber's wages are reasonable.
Mr. TOWNSEND. It is your contention that the industries that
have not been included in this list are paying their labor too much?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I do not know whether they are, but I know that
the people that have to buy from the people that do pay them are
paying three and four time as much as they were, and while the
cost of living has gone up in this country, and the average wage
rate has gone up in this country, it does not compare with what
these strongly, absolutely closed-shop industries have made the
people of this country pay.
Senator WHEELER.-Mr Coolidge, do you think that the cost of
living in this country has been due to the high wages?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Not entirely, but partly.
Senator WHEELER. As a matter of fact, has it not been almost
entirely due to the tremendous amount of watered stock that has
been dumped into every great corporation in this country?

Mr. COOLIDGE. That has nothing whatever to do with it.
Senator WHEELER. Do you mean to tell me that when you increase
the capitalization by putting a lot of watered stock in, that requires
the consumers to pay dividends upon that watered stock, that it has
not increased the cost of living?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I do not believe it has increased the cost of living
one cent. There is no watered stock in our company.
Senator WHEELER. I am not contending that there is in your
company.
Mr. COOLIDGE. Mr. La Follette, when he was a Senator some years
ago, insisted upon having railroads appraised with the idea of watered
stock; and the investigation of the Interstate Commerce Commission
has shown that there is not only no watered stock but the railroads
are worth more than double the amount of bonds and stocks. There
may be incidental cases otherwise.
Senator WHEELER. Will you say to me that there was not watered
stock originally injected into many of the railroads of this country?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I have no doubt that the Union Pacific and some
others issued stock to represent the future earnings of that company
and the future value of that company.
Senator WHEELER. And then they charged the public a freight rate
that made them pay upon the watered stock that they had put into it.
Mr. COOLIDGE. No; they charged, and the Interstate Commerce
Commission is authorized and directed by the Congress to charge,
only enough to pay not exceeding 6 per cent upon the value of the
property, and it is immaterial how much bonds or how much stock
there may be.
Senator WHEELER. That was not when the railroads were first
organized.
Mr. COOLIDGE. I am not talking about 50 years ago; I am talking
about now and about 1914 and 1915.
Senator WHEELER. Do you mean to say that when you organize a
power company, for instance, in this country that they have not
injected a lot of watered stock into some of those companies and that
the public utilities commissions of this country have not permitted
those companies to charge an interest rate so that they would charge
the consumer enough money for the electricity that is furnished in
order that they could pay upon the watered stock that they pumped
in?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I do not know anything about Montana.
Senator WHEELER. I am talking about Massachusetts as well as
Montana.
Mr. COOLIDGE. I know about Massachusetts.
Senator WHEELER. I know something about it.
Mr. COOLIDGE. Yes; you and I were born within 10 miles of each
other. I know about Massachusetts, and I know that the amount
of stock and the amount of bonds has nothing to do with it. They
value the property and fix the rates upon the value of the property,
and the United States Supreme Court has stated that that is a proper
method. It is not a question of stock amount or a question of bond
amount. It is a question of the amount of property that is devoted
to the public use, and upon that amount of property they are entitled
to receive a reasonable return. That does not apply to coal com-
panies.

1933
Senator WHEELER. What is your idea as to what has increased
the cost of living in this country?
Mr. COOLIDGE. The automobiles have increased the cost of living.
Everybody now in this country-and it is right-wants as a necessity
what even at your age when you were a boy was considered a luxury
and when I was a boy was not even known. It is a necessity to-day
for practically every man to own an automobile. Ten or 15 years
ago they were few and 25 years ago there was none. Every man has
to have a telephone. Most men want-and rightly-a graphophone,
and they also want a radio. Those things have become necessities,
and, of course, they have increased the cost of living, and the wage
rate, as a rule, has kept along with it, sometimes over and sometimes.
under.
Senator WHEELER. Mr. Coolidge, you do not think, do you, that
the high wages in this country have been a detriment to the country?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I do not. I think they have been a great help to
the country.
Senator WHEELER. And you think, do you not, that organized
labor has done a great deal toward the raising of wages and the raising
of the standard of living in this country?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I do not dispute that they have, but they are so
small in number compared with all the others. Take our property.
We have no organized labor and our rates of wages are as high as the
union rates and our men make more per annum than they do in the
United Mine Workers.
Senator WHEELER. But has not that been due, to a large extent,
to the United Mine Workers because of the fact that you knew if you
did not pay them some increased wage the United Mine Workers
would be able to come in there and organize your men?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Not a particle. We run our property without any
idea of what they would or would not do. We have seen to it that
our men get just as high a rate of wage as it is possible for us to pay
in order that they may make as high an annual earning as any other
class, and although I can not prove this I believe that our men have
during the last five years, for example, made more per annum than
the men in the organized field.
Senator WHEELER. Assuming, then, that you do this out of the
goodness of your heart-
Mr. COOLIDGE. We do not. We do it out of good business.
Senator WHEELER. Well, either out of the goodness of your heart
or because you believe it is good business to do it, and I believe it is
good business to do it; you do know, do you not, that there are a
great many people engaged in industries in this country that do not
look upon it in the same way that you say you look upon it?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I do not know about others. I can only speak for
myself and our company.
Senator WHEELER. You do know that there are mines in this
country that are not paying nearly as high a wage as you are paying
down in West Virginia, do you not?
Mr. COLLIDGE. I have heard so. I understand so.
Senator WHEELER. You know it as a fact, do you not?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I have not any doubt about it any more than as I
heard a witness say here yesterday that he knew that Senator Willis
was dead and yet he could not prove it. I do not doubt that it is a
fact.

Senator WAGNER. If they were all unorganized?
Mr. COOLIDGE. No; if they were merely organized in their own

Mr. COOLIDGE. At my age, yes.
Senator WHEELER. You know, Mr. Coolidge, that is why I
differ with some of these distinguished men upon the committee
here.
Mr. COOLIDGE. Well, I have quite a respectable family of my

Senator WAGNER. Mr. Coolidge, before we get off this subject I
would like to say that I disagree with you entirely that the workers
would be better off perhaps with local company unions or no unions
at all than they are to-day. You have probably studied the subject
more carefully, than I have, that is, the question of labor legislation
in this country; but I was for 14 years a member of the State legis-
lature where I was largely interested in welfare legislation. I think
it has helped the workers of our State, and all of that legislation,
which has resulted in a boon to labor, was in a great measure resisted
by the employers. It was advocated by the labor organzations,
and I am sure that without their aid, without their arousing the
interest of public opinion, these laws probably would not have been
enacted, because there was nobody else interested. In that way I
think that organized labor, because it has been organized, has been
able to better the conditions of the workers, and without it I do not
think we would be so far advanced. I think history sustains that
point of view.
Mr. COOLIDGE. May I tell a story of something that occurred along
that line within my own knowledge? For years I was conusel for
railroads in New England. A man who was representing what he
called a labor district introduced a certain bill relative to hours of
labor, and at the end of six or seven years, after he had made that
his issue, his bill passed the House and was in the Senate, where it
had gone through all the necessary readings and was at the engross-
ment stage. He telephoned to me in my office and asked if the rail-
roads were not going to kill that bill. I said, "No." I said, "We
are not interested in the bill. If the men want it they can have it."
He exclaimed, "Do you mean to say that that is going through the
Senate without any opposition from the railroads?" I said, "It is
so far as we are concerned." He said, "If that goes through what
issue can I have to get back to the legislature on?" I said, "You
will have to make one yourself."
The man went to the Senate and personally caused the bill to be
killed at his personal request in order that he might have an issue
upon which to get reelected.
A great deal of the so-called legislation in this country has been
caused by just that kind of legislators. I do not believe that the
work of the unions has had any more to do with the passage of legiti-
mate, honest legislation for the benefit of the workers than has been
caused by civic organizations, by the churches of every denomina-
tion, who have wanted to see to it that the condition of the working
people, as they are called, was bettered. I do not believe that it is
the unions that have done it.
Senator WHEELER. That legislator did not happen to come from
the western part of the State, I hope.
Mr. COOLIDGE. He did not.

Mr. COOLIDGE. I do not think so. I think that the civic organiza-

Mr. COOLIDGE. No; I think we have-well, I am not sure, but I

Senator WAGNER. But there is quite a difference in regard to

Mr. COOLIDGE. I think we have it in our factories.
Senator WAGNER. As to hours for men?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I think so.

Senator WHEELER. Mr. Coolidge, is it your view that the men

beneficial to the laboring man, or that they would have given the

Mr. COOLIDGE. I think if the labor organizations have helped,
they have not been more than 50 per cent responsible if they have
been even as much as 50 per cent responsible; and I believe that the
organizations outside of union labor are more responsible for laws
for the benefit of women and of children and of men.
Senator WHEELER. Well, I think they have added a great deal,
but what I am asking you is: Do you think had it not been for labor
organizations and the civic organizations that you spoke of, contrib-
uting in whatever percentage they did contribute, that those engaged
in industry in this country would have voluntarily carried on the
work and bettered the conditions as they have been bettered in this
country?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I think they have, quite a great deal.
Senator WHEELER. That they have increased wages and so on?
Mr. COOLIDGE. But I doubt very much if laws would have been
passed by legislatures unless there had been that urge behind it. I
think you will agree with that proposition.
Senator WHEELER. Yes, of course; and-
Mr. COOLIDGE (continuing). And I believe that the urge has been
from the civic organizations and the churches that has caused such
legislation more than from union labor. That is simply my view of it,
you understand.

Senator WHEELER. I am not disputing that proposition at all.

Mr. COOLIDGE. I believe that employers in general are impressed

Senator WHEELER. Let me call your attention to this: When I
was in China this year I happened to attend a meeting of the Ameri-
can Chamber of Commerce, an executive meeting. One of the men
engaged in the manufacturing industry there was complaining
because of the fact that the southern Chinese group had come into
Shanghai and had insisted that he increase the wages of his men.
When I asked him how much he was paying he said: Well, we are
paying more than anybody else, but the trouble is that I employ
Chinese men to work for me, and they in turn go out and buy Chinese
kids; they give them a little food and some scanty clothes, and they
insist that I include these Chinese kids as among my employees and
pay them the same as I do other employees. Now, there was an
American manufacturer who, because of the fact that he was desirous
of making money, was willing to enslave those Chinese kids and to
make money off of them.
Mr. COOLIDGE. But that has nothing to do with this.
Senator WHEELER. No; not particularly with this, but it has to do
with the general problem.
Mr. COOLIDGE. You do not think that that is applicable to em-
ployers in this country as a rule?
Senator WHEELER. No; I do not think that it is.
Mr. COOLIDGE. You cite it then as the exception?

According to the Federal reserve bank index, the cost of living in
the United States has increased from the base of 100 per cent in
1913-14 to 176 per cent in 1927; our wages have increased from 100
per cent to 226 per cent, and the "1917 scale," so often spoken of,
has increased from 100 to 176 per cent.
Out of the cost of living of the ordinary employee engaged in
general industry, economists estimate that from 25 to 30 per cent of
wages paid are used for rent, heat, light, and water, whereas in our
mines this total cost averages less than 9 per cent of the wages paid.
Senator GOODING. That is the housing cost, you mean?
Mr. COOLIDGE. That means rent, heat, light, and water.
Senator METCALF. Are there no extra charges? Are those the
only charges that you have mentioned?
Mr. COOLIDGE. There are no extra charges. In order to make our
houses accessible to near-by towns we have built more than 20 miles
of cement concrete roads at an expense of approximately $1,000,000,
and as there are over 800 automobiles owned by our employees they
can easily to to other places to live if they so desire and they can
easily trade at other stores if they so desire. Whether our employees
buy from us at our stores or not is purely optional with them. Bus-
line service is available at low rates. Some 20 or more stores daily


===== [扫描序号 946] =====
1950
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
take orders and deliver goods to our employees living in our 1,500
houses.
There have been three stores built right on the edge of our property.
Sears, Roebuck and Montgomery Ward & Co., mail-order houses, are
constantly sending stuff to our employees.
We do not discourage their trading elsewhere as we want our em-
ployees to be satisfied and we know that while we might sell them a
better grade of merchandise at lower prices, the only way they can
know it is by having competition with other sources of supply, and
we are glad to be able to have them make this comparison by their
buying goods elsewhere.
After deducting from our employees' wages all their store accounts,
their rent, their heat, their light, their doctors' and hospital expenses,
we have paid to them in cash over 70 per cent of the entire pay roll.
Instead of our men having no money or only a little money after
deducting the above items, they received last year in cash over
$4,000,000, and in the last five years have been paid in cash
$18,720,208.52.
So that the statement that has been made relative to some people
not having any money left at the end of the year or absorbing the
pay roll from stores, etc., does not apply to the Island Creek Coal Co.
Prior to 1922 our mines were run absolutely as open-shop mines.
We made no inquiry of men about to enter our employ whether they
were Catholic or Protestant, members of the United Mine Workers,
or not, but owing to the acts of the United Mine Workers, especially
at the time of the West Virginia insurrection, when an army of
from 6,000 to 10,000 men marched from the then union mines in
Kanawha County, W. Va., for the avowed purpose of unionizing
our mines and the other mines of the Guyan field of Logan County
(with the accompanying destruction of our property), and thence
continuing their march into Mingo County, where many murders had
been committed and many mines dynamited resulting from the
attempt in 1920 by the union to unionize the mines of Mingo County,
we determined to avail ourselves of the opportunity of having our
men sign a contract similar to the contract which had been sustained
by the United States Supreme Court in the Hinchman case (245
U. S.), whereby we agreed not to recognize the union, and our
employees agreed that so long as they remained our employees they
would not belong to the union. The form of contract entered into
is as follows:
CONTRACT

for whom he pleases and the right to payment in proportion to service rendered,
to preserve the natural and constitutional right of individual contract, to preserve
to each individual the fruits of his own labor and to promote the interests of both
parties hereto.

Mr. COOLIDGE. Our mines have never been under the domination
or control of the United Mine Workers. Our experience with the
United Mine Workers, their attempts to unionize mines and the
resultant murders, etc., whenever they have attempted to unionize
mines, and our experience in other companies of which Mr. Holden
and I have been directors with the Western Federation of Miners
and the I. W. W. in California, Kansas, and elsewhere, have con-
vinced the members of our board of directors that we ought never
to permit our property either for the sake of our employees or of
our stockholders, to get under the domination of the United Mine
Workers of America. Their history in the last 10 years we believe
to be worse as to murders, etc., than even the history of the I. W. W.
or of the Western Federation of Miners. Never so far as I have
been able to learn have the officers of the United Mine Workers ever
expressed any regret at the murders, dynamiting, etc., by the United
Mine Workers.

Mr. COOLIDGE. No sympathy from the officers of the United
Mine Workers has ever been expressed for that terrible massacre.
Those indicted after the West Virginia insurrection were defended
by the United Mine Workers. Thousands of dollars have been paid
by the United Mine Workers for the damage done by them in their
attempts to unionize mining properties. Whether a man as an indi-
vidual shall belong to a given union is one thing.
There is just as little chance for a man to talk nonunion in a union
mine as they allege to be the objection to union men talking at a
nonunion mine. The history of the United Mine Workers will bear
out that statement.
A deliberate attempt to unionize a property in order that nobody
shall work on that property except members of the union, is an en-
tirely different thing.. In the latter case I have never known of such
attempt to unionize a mine to fail to cause disorder, dynamiting of
mines, destruction of property and even murder. We have, there-
fore, definitely decided that so far as we are able to do so, we shall
never recognize or confer with the officials of the United Mine
Workers. We have nothing in common with them and we do not
desire to have anything to do with them. They do not represent
our employees and there is no reason why we should confer with them.
In order to protect themselves, our men have obtained injunctions
against any attempt by the United Mine Workers to interfere with
them; and our company has likewise obtained injunctions to prevent
the United Mine Workers interfering with the company's property
or with the wage contracts. We believe our men to be fully war-
ranted in keeping the United Mine Workers away from Holden.
Bishop Donohue in the Cabin Creek investigation in 1912, testi-
fied that their then vice president stated their purpose as follows:
He said they were profoundly dissatisfied with the conditions as they were
there [Cabin Creek] and they intended to increase their demands until at last
they got possession of the mines.
Senator KENYON. To unionize the mines?
Bishop DONOHUE. They wanted first to unionize them, and then increase

Senator GOODING. Mr. Coolidge, in this cost do you figure the cost
on your investment?
Mr. COOLIDGE. No; we owe no money, and, therefore, we have
no interest to pay.
Senator GOODING. Well, you have an investment there, of course?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Yes; something like $20,000,000. In the cost we
do not figure anything on investment. Cost includes labor and every-
thing that goes into cost, depreciation, accretion, everything that
goes in in order to know whether you are making money or whether
you are not making money, and what we get over is what we have for
interest, more or less, on our investment.
In addition to that, we made sales as shown in the following table
to C. H. Sprague & Son Co., of Boston, who own ships and transported
some coal which we know went to the Boston & Maine Railroad and
to the Maine Central Railroad in New England:
