Senator GOODING. Have you any organization in Boston selling
coal?
Mr. COOLIDGE. No, sir.
Senator GOODING (presiding). You may go ahead with your state-
ment.
Mr. COOLIDGE. We believe we have the most efficiently operating
bituminous mines in the United States.
Senator GOODING (presiding). What is the thickness of the vein of
coal?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Six and a half feet.
Senator GOODING. It is a large vein, is it not?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Very.
Senator GOODING. That is a thick vein of coal?
Mr. COOLIDGE. Very thick. And we believe that we have a most
marvelous property, and we believe that it is very efficiently handled.
We believe our men average higher wages than any other men
employed anywhere in bituminous mines in the United States. We
have never had any trouble or any disorder on our property. Our
employees and our operating officials, citizens of West Virginia, all
of whom live either at Holden or at Huntington, within two hours
ride by automobile of our mines, have always lived in peace and
harmony. We have never broken any contract. We agreed with
the Secretary of Commerce, while others were charging $5 and more
for coal, that we would sell our coal at a maximum price of $3 per
ton in 1922 when the United Mine Workers tried to stop the produc-
tion of all coal in the United States.
And that was at the time when President Harding said had it not
been for the nonunion mines the people of the United States would
have been entirely at the mercy of the United Mine Workers of
America. We sold coal at not to exceed $5 a ton when we were offered
$15 and $20 a ton. That was not particularly patriotism on our part,
but we considered it good business not to profiteer to the extent to
which we might have profiteered, and that by selling at what was
deemed to be a comparatively cheap price we would be establishing
good will that could not be taken away from us, and the records since
have justified what we did.
In 1912 the United Mine Workers changed their constitution, which
theretofore had demanded an equitable share of the product of their
labor, into a demand for its full social value, which they construed
to mean that the workers should have all that the coal sold for and
that the owners should have nothing. I understand that within the
year the United Mine Workers of America have changed their con-
stitution back to the former language, saying that they no longer


===== [扫描序号 954] =====
1958
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
demand "the full social value," but "demand an equitable share."
This organization for 15 years has been trying by force as well as by
persuasion to compel the people of the United States to recognize
their demands for "the full social value," but now for political or
other reasons it demands-but I better show you the language
perhaps "an equitable share," but has it really changed its purpose?
In 1912 Mr. Bittner introduced a resolution to use words "an equit-
able share of the fruits of their labor." Thereupon another delegate
asked to have the words changed to read, "the full social value of our
product." The delegates in arguing that question stated what they
meant by "the full social value of our product."
In the debate over this change there appears on page 2008 (Paint
Creek Investigation, 1913):
Delegate Bittner moved the adoption of the preamble as read.
Delegate WILLIAMS (district No. 12). I move to amend the committee's report
by striking out, in the fifth line of the second paragraph, the words "an equitable
share of the fruits of their labor, " and inserting the words in resolution No. 151,
"the full social value of our product."
(Seconded.)
Delegate FARRINGTON. I Would like to ask the mover of the amendment what
an equitable share of the labor would be, in his judgment?
Delegate WILLIAMS. I would say, as one of the working class, that I would not
be willing to concede that any parasite has any right to any share of it. The
working class is entitled to the full social value of its product.
Delegate FINNEY (district 5). I feel that we ought to get at least as much as
we can for our labor, but at the same time I feel there is some other question
attached to this part of the preamble we must also consider. "The full social
value of our product." That sounds very well, gentlemen, and I hope we will
see the day when we will be able to command that much of the fruits of our
toil. To my mind we have not reached that period of our organization when we
can command the full value of our toil. I feel that we must have some other
system of government; or at least some other protection through law before we
reach that period. The full value of our toil would mean, to my mind, that the
man who employs us will receive no compensation for the money he has invested.
We would not under any circumstances have a clause in the preamble of that
kind, at least until the present system of government has been changed.
Delegate GERMER (district 12). The amendment, as it now reads, might be
construed to mean that the full social value of the worker's product is "an equi-
table share," yet it is susceptible of various constructions. There are men in the
labor movement to-day who contend that the present share that the workers
receive is an equitable share, and they do all in their power to perpetuate the
system that only permits the worker to get one-fifth of what his labor creates.
The amendment to the committee's report is only in keeping with the resolution
adopted here in the convention of 1909, which provided that we believed in the
collective ownership of all means of production and distribution, and that the
workers should receive the full social value of what their labor creates. After
the convention adopting that resolution three years ago, we will be perfectly
consistent if we embody the language of that resolution in the preamble of our
constitution.
I realize that inserting that language in our constitution would not necessarily
give us the full social value of what our labor creates, but this is only a declara-
tion of principle, and it is question as to whether or not we are going to declare
that we are entitled to the full social value of what our labor creates or whether
we will continue to say we shall continue to receive "an equitable share," which
can be construed in a dozen different ways. I believe the amendment should be
adopted. It is consistent with our former action, and I believe it is consistent
and in harmony with the ideas of the great majority of the delegates of the con-
vention. I am entitled to all my labor creates; you are entitled to all your labor
creates; and if that philosophy is right, then why have any hesitancy in inserting
that in our preamble? It is a declaration of our sentiment.
Delegate HEFFERLY (district 12). I want to go on record as supporting the
amendment offered by Brother Williams. It states what constitutes the full
social value of labor's toil. On the other hand, the substitute brought in by the
committee, as Brother Germer has stated, can have a dozen or more different

constructions placed on it. I take it there are no delegates here, nor are there
any of their constituents at home that do not want the full product of their toil;
and I believe that we can not afford to go on record here as voting down an
amendment which says that we are entitled to the full value of the product of
our toil.
Delegate BITTNER (district 5). Just a few words in support of the recommenda-

In 1921 at the Kenyon investigation, Mr. Murray, vice president
of the United Mine Workers, stated (Record Kenyon Investigation,
685) that he wanted nationalization of the mines and that that was
the principle of the organization.
Has it really changed its purpose? In 1912 Mr. Bittner moved
the adoption of the preamble as it then existed, that is, the demand
for an equitable share, but Delegate Williams moved to amend the
committee's report by striking out the words "an equitable share of
the fruits of their labor" and inserting the words in the resolution,
"the full social value of our product." Several delegates spoke to
the amendment. They stated what they meant.
Mr. Williams himself said:
I would say as one of the working class that I would not be willing to concede
that any parasite has any right to any share of it. The working class is entitled
to the full social value of its product.
At the end of the debate Mr. Bittner said:
Just a few words in support of the recommendation of the committee. I
think that so far as the English is concerned there is not the least difference
between the amendment and the report of the committee. Equitable means
just, and that is all that the United Mine Workers ask for, that which is just
and right. Now, we have no objection to the amendment, but so far as the
language is concerned, so far as English is concerned, the amendment and the
report of the committee mean exactly the same thing.
Therefore, I repeat, that for 15 years this organization has been
trying to enforce upon the United States their idea that the workers.
are entitled to everything and that capital is entitled to nothing.
It is plain they mean the same thing to-day that they meant in 1912.
The committee has asked, What is the remedy? Remedy for
what? Something to increase the cost of coal? Something to make
100,000,000 people pay more for coal? For whom is the Congress
to legislate, assuming it has the power to legislate, which we very
much question, and what does the Congress want to do? The child
labor cases decide that the Congress can not pass legislation requir-
ing that no coal shall be shipped in interstate commerce unless pro-
duced by union labor or by nonunion labor.
Assuming that Congress has power to legislate, will it appoint a
coal commission to control the coal industry? If so, then commission
should be appointed to control all manufacturing and all industry.
Is the Congress to establish an additional bureau in Washington?
We already have bureaus enough.
The great issue in this country is whether the Government-that
is, the officeholders-shall control the people or shall the people
control the Government. In the Declaration of Independence


===== [扫描序号 956] =====
1960
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Thomas Jefferson enumerated as one of his complaints that "He
(the Government, the king being the Government) has erected a mul-
titude of new offices and sent hither swarms of officers to harass our
people and eat out their substance."
Bureaus in Washington already are sending out questionnaires on
every subject that require the expenditure of millions of dollars per
annum to answer. The Senate some years ago created a gold and
silver commission, and that commission sent out a questionnaire
requiring the answer to 750 questions relating to each mine for each
of the preceding 20 years. Yes; I think I have one of those ques-
tionnaires here-here it is; that the gold and silver commission sent
out, but I am not going to leave it with the committee.
Senator GOODING (presiding). You do not want that put in this
record, do you?
Mr. COOLIDGE. I did not ask for it to be done, but I will do so if
you would like to have it done.
Senator GOODING. Oh, no.
Mr. COOLIDGE. And this only a part of it. This would have re-
quired of one company of which I happen to be a director, answers to
300,000 questions. It would have required years to have examined
the records, and even then a large percentage of the questions could
not have been answered.
The United States Coal Commission sent our questionnaires that
took us from six to eight months to prepare answers to. We advised
our officials that they were not obliged to answer those questions, but
in order to help so far as we could we hired a lot of extra men and did
answer the questions. Judging by the United States Coal Commis-
sion's report, however, it is perfectly evident that our answers were
not considered in making up their conclusions, and I was informed by
one member of the commission that they were not even taken out of
the box.
Is legislation desired in order that the coal industry shall support
40 per cent more miners than are needed, to support walking dele-
gates and union organizers? Saint Paul in his second letter to the
Thessalonians (2 Thes. chap. 3, verses 10 and 11), wrote:
For even when we were with you this we commanded you, if any will not work
neither let him eat, for we hear of some that walk among you disorderly that work
not at all but are busybodies.
That is what we think of the walking delegate of the United Mine
Workers.
Are there too many miners? Then let the excess go into some
other line of business. It happens in every other line of business,
why not in the coal industry? Are there too many mines? Let the
least efficient go out of business-retain only the most efficient.
Shall the law contain a proviso that collective bargaining shall
always be required? If so, let the law also contain a proviso that
individual contracts alone shall be required. One is just as much
legal as the other. And this Nation was founded upon the theory of
individual rights, not of collective rights. The Revolution was waged
in order to preserve life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. The
Constitution guards life, liberty, and property, which include the
freedom of contract.


===== [扫描序号 957] =====

1961
Shall the law attempt to fix prices? Then the Constitution must
be changed. The Supreme Court has decided that the Lever Act,
fixing prices even in time of war, was unconstitutional.
It is desired to amend the Sherman Act to permit combinations of
coal companies? If so, why not oil companies, steel companies, and
all other industries? If joint selling agencies are desirable, they are
equally desirable in other lines of business. Already under the law
as it now exists mergers and joint selling agencies are permissible so
long as they do not restrain interstate commerce. Certain strikes are
legal but national strikes to form monopolies, to freeze and starve
the people, are illegal. If the Congress has the power, let it pass a
law that no strike shall be called unless the employees, by secret
ballot, vote to call a strike.
Ballots and not bullets should be the means of settling cases in the
United States.
There is no law and there ought to be no law that gives to any
man the right if he gives up his job to refuse by force or otherwise
to let some other man, who is willing to work, go to work.
Class legislation should cease. What is illegal for one man should
be illegal for another. What is a crime when done by one man, should
be a crime when done by another. The Congress. might well strike
out the proviso in its appropriation for the Judicial Department where-
by the Attorney General may spend the appropriation in prosecuting
illegal conspiracies and combinations on the part of the owners and
eliminating the use of the money for prosecuting illegal combinations
and conspiracies on the part of labor.
I thank you. Any questions?

Senator GOODING. You have been very much more fortunate than

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1979
THE UNITED MINE WORKERS IN WEST VIRGINIA
(Submitted by the bituminous operators' special committee to the United States
Coal Commission, August, 1923)
PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
This brief is submitted in further compliance with the request issued by the
United States Coal Commission on February 14, 1923, for the facts respecting
violations of law and constitutional rights in the coal industry. It describes
such violations on the part of the United Mine Workers of America in West
Virginia during the years 1919-1922. The statements as to these violations
are based primarily on the evidence given in court or before a public investi-
gating body. In support we present herewith copies of 22 records of trials
with 15,375 pages of testimony taken thereat, which might not otherwise be
readily accessible to the commission, and also other statements and documents
bearing on these matters. Our references are to the paging of the copies we
submit. It has been impossible in this brief even to summarize much of this
material. If the commission desires amplification of any points in our state-
ment, we should be glad to go into them before the commission in any manner
which it may deem desirable.
We have not concerned ourselves here with isolated acts of violence or the
fixing of individual responsibility. It is only as part of the broad question
of labor relations in the coal industry and the relationship of Government
to these transactions that we have felt them to be of significance.
The outstanding fact in the history of labor relations in West Virginia has
been the long campaign of the organization of the United Mine Workers of
America to compel the coal operators of that State to contract with it and
collect for it from every mine worker in the State such dues and assessments
as that organization may see fit to impose. That campaign was progressively
successful down to 1919. Since that time the organization has rapidly lost
ground, and lost it, as the evidence which we shall now go into indicates, for
three reasons:
1. The arbitrary exercise of control by the central organization of the United
Mine Workers at Indianapolis in disregard of local economic needs and
conditions.
2. The policy of compelling the closed shop and the collection of the checkoff.
3. The actual violence and defiance of the authority of the Government of the
State which has accompanied its campaigns.
The bituminous operators of Utah, New Mexico, Colorado, Tennessee, Ala-
bama, the greater part of Kentucky, and almost half of Pennsylvania, after
various experiences with the United Mine Workers of America, particularly
during the strike of 1922, refuse to contract with the United Mine Workers of
America, and are firmly resolved not to deal with it in the future-certainly
not so long as the present policies and methods of that organization continue.
But it is West Virginia that is associated in the popular mind with determined
and unyielding resistance to the organization. That attitude of mind is one
of the outstanding facts of the bituminous-coal industry. That firm resistance
has led to a constant and bitter attack upon the State as stubborn, reactionary,
and un-American.
Clearing up popular misconceptions essential to peace in West Virginia.—
In this attack it is tacitly and often expressly attempted to palliate violence
and defiance of the State by painting a picture to the public of miners in non-
union fields ground down as to wages, dwelling in unspeakable living con-
ditions and held in bondage at the mines. Fortunately, the investigations of
this commission are making it possible to show up once and for all the funda-
mental falsity of these assertions.
A popular dramatist paints to the public as a contemporaneous picture West
Virginia miners working 12 hours a day without even a Sunday off for a
pittance which barely keeps the flicker of life in starved and hungry faces
that never see the light of day. A popular preacher in a public statement
declares that the West Virginia nonunion miners are forced to live in shacks
which are not fit to keep pigs in. There has been a flood of glib talk of
the "coal barons" of West Virginia and the "slavery " of their workers.
Eager young saviours of society recently journeyed into the coal fields, preach-
ing to the "slaves" in the public square of Logan the gospel of freedom, and
found in the general local ridicule to which they were subjected their worst


===== [扫描序号 976] =====
1980
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
indictment of the State-the supposed supine degradation of its citizens. Yet,
less than two years before, when over 6,000 armed United Mine Workers
of America marched from the Kanawha River 50 miles to this same Logan
County to "liberate" them, these same "slaves," arms in hand, had deplored
out into the firing line on Blair Mountain to resist their "liberators" and would
have made that resistance good even without the Federal troops who were
sent by the President into West Virginia to aid them in quelling this armed
insurrection against the State.
Nor does the popular fancy of the " enslaved" and "supine" non-union
worker quite fit in with the stubborn courage of the Willis Branch and
Mingo mine workers, who, as we shall see, kept at their work day after day
under harassing rifle fire from the United Mine Workers-the wives of some
delivered of children in houses under fire-who took arms themselves against
their "liberators." Again, the popular conception of Logan County held in
subjection by an army of thugs and gunmen in the pay of coal operators
masquerading as deputy sheriffs is dissolved into the reality of a county with
a population of 60,000 on the one side, and on the other, the sheriff and
43 deputy sheriffs, only four of them paid by operators, as the sole police
force.
The dramatist's picture of the West Virginia miners toiling in subjection
twelve hours a day every day in the week underground and never seeing
the light of day is somewhat blurred if the coal fields be visited on "Rabbit
Day." Then, in many districts, hardly a man will go into the mines, as
they desire to take full advantage of the first day of the hunting season.
The facts are the reverse of these lurid pictures, and fortunately the com-
mission has these facts.
1. The eight-hour day is universal among the nonunion miners.
2. The earnings of nonunion miners range far in advance of farm laborers
and other unskilled workers.
3. The earnings of miners in nonunion fields are at least as high as those
in union fields. In 1920, in a substantial number of mines in Winding Gulf,
in the heart of the nonunion fields, 29 per cent of the machine miners, pick
miners and loaders who worked 100 days or more earned over $2,500. In
1920 and 1921 a few such miners in Logan, Pocahontas, and Winding Gulf
earned even over $4.000. We go into this in detail in Point II.
4. The miner is more nearly his own boss as to whether he will work when
the mine is running, how long he will work and how he will work than almost
any other class of laborer.
5. The housing and living conditions of the miners are those of a progressive
industrial community and compare favorably with mine communities the country
over in union and nonunion fields. We also go into this in detail in Point II.
6. Finally, the miners of southern West Virginia, far from being held in sub-
jection and kept from unionization by force of arms, have themselves taken up
arms to resist forcible attempts of the organization of the United Mine Workers
of America to impose unionization upon them and in defense of their right to
work.
How much of the popular misconception of the independent West Virginia
mining regions has been due to the deliberate propaganda of the United Mine
Workers is difficult to estimate, but it is established, as we shall see in more
detail later, that the rank and file of the membership of the United Mine Work-
ers of America, as well as the public, have been persistently fed with stories
that would be grotesque in their absurdity if the consequence had not been that
they had done much to make it possible to create false loyalties and to lead men
into armed insurrection against the State and into violence and murder.
The West Virginia operators themselves have from the start taken the posi-
tion that the best thing that could happen to West Virginia was for the com-
mission itself to come and personally examine all the conditions of the State at
first hand and form its own impressions. This request we emphasize and
repeat. It is only by first-hand contact, we believe, that it is possible to visual-
ize physical conditions and understand the character and point of view of the
operators and independent miners of West Virginia.
It has become evident to us that the best defense of West Virginia is
acquaintance with West Virginia itself, with its rugged virtues, and its no less
rugged faults. But, as we have proceeded with our acquaintance with the
story of the struggle between the United Mine Workers' central organization on
the one hand, and operators and independent miners of West Virginia on the
other, the question has been pressed home on us by the facts: Is it West Vir-


===== [扫描序号 977] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1981
ginia that needs defense? Have not the independent miners and operators, who
kept at work amid the rattle of bullets from United Mine Workers' rifles, who
slept in beds with sheet-iron sides, who deployed into the firing line on Blair
Mountain to resist the armed march, not only been defending themselves and
their own interests, but defending America in certain of its most vital principles
of independence, self-reliance, and freedom?
We feel that the commission in its examination of the facts in West Virginia
and its presentation of them to the American public can do much to establish
peace. Just so long as the popular conception prevails that the independent
miners of West Virginia are a down-trodden, exploited class, ground down to
starvation wages, living in hovels unfit for human habitation, and held in
peonage, so long efforts will continue to be made to influence public opinion to
condone the attempts of the United Mine Workers to organize by the use of
dynamite and the high-powered rifle. But the facts are to the contrary and
nothing will so tend to establish peace as for the commission to sweep away
these popular misconceptions and with them the demoralizing plea for pallia-
tion and excuse of violent methods of attack and breach of the law. The
public, with intelligent knowledge of the facts, will not tolerate for an instant
violent methods in an attempt to compel all operators of southern West
Virginia to contract with the organization of the United Mine Workers of
America and to agree to collect their dues and assessments from every mine
worker in West Virginia.
Any survey, therefore, of acts of violence in the West Virginia field to be fully
informing to the public and helpful in ending the conditions of violence which
have there existed can not accomplish its full effect without at the same time
negativing the popular conception of the supposed misery, suffering, and oppres-
sion of the independent mine workers of West Virginia.
Further, in any consideration of the defensive methods adopted in West
Virginia against violent attack there are three considerations which it seems to
us should be dwelt on:
a. The State should furnish adequate force to defend the property of its
citizens and the right of its citizens to work without fear of intimidation or
danger from acts of violence.
b. If the State does not furnish adequate protection to these rights, it is
inevitable and it is right that operators and independent mine workers should
use methods of defense, by force if necessary, to meet violent methods of attack,
much as the necessity for such private methods of defense is to be deplored, and
even though it is inevitable that, where such private methods of defense are
necessary, occasional individual acts of hot-headedness and lack of proper
individual restraint will develop.
c. Where the force of a State to protect the rights of its citizens from vio-
lence is inadequate, the attitude of the contending parties toward the creation
and maintenance by the State of a force adequate to deal with such situations
should be examined and reported to the public.
In the State of West Virginia, for example, it will appear, as indeed generally
throughout the country, that there has been determined opposition on the
part of the Organization of the United Mine Workers of America to the creation
and maintenance of governmental forces adequate to restrain acts of violence
committed on its behalf.
In our analysis of the facts as to West Virginia we shall take up the
following points:
I. The physical and economic characteristics of Southern West Virginia
and a brief narrative of the campaign of the United Mine Workers in West
Virginia down to 1919.
II. Living conditions and earnings among the independent mine workers of
Southern West Virginia.
III. The campaign of violence of the United Mine Workers, 1919-1921, to
force the Willis Branch Co. to collect dues and assessments from every worker,
even though the company was willing to grant the wage scale and working
conditions and employ the members of the United Mine Workers of America.
IV. The campaign of intimidation and violence to compel the operators of
Mingo County to contract with the United Mine Workers' organization and
to compel the independent mine workers by intimidation and violence to cease
work-1919-1921.
V. The armed marches of the United Mine Workers of America upon Logan
County to compel the operators and independent mine workers of Logan and
Mingo Counties to contract with and pay the dues and assessments of the
United Mine Workers of America.

VII. The part played in these attacks by the "check off.”

I. HOW THE RECENT SITUATION IN SOUTHERN WEST VIRGINIA ABOSE, 1890-1919
Pursuant to the Commission's request, we are confining our statement as to
acts of violence to the period since January 1, 1919, but the events which have
occurred since January 1, 1919, we believe, can be better understood if we
run over briefly the earlier conditions and events.
A. Physical and economic characteristics.-Southern West Virginia in the
nineties was a wild and rough mountain country. The Chesapeake & Ohio
Railroad climbed over the mountains and threaded its way down the wild gorge
of the New River in Kanawha to connect the sea with the Ohio Valley. Back
to the south, mountain streams cut their way through steep-sided gulches to
ultimately flow westward with the Ohio. It was frontier country. The people
were of the old front er American stock, winning a difficult living by frontier
pursuits. Living conditions were often as primitive as in the unfloored Ken-
tucky cabin where Abraham Lincoln got his start. It was a country to breed
self-reliance, independence, the rougher virtues, and the rougher vices.
As efforts began to win the coal from the mountain hillsides the natives car-
ried into the coal business much of the same rough and ready frontier spirit,
and those who came from other States were molded and influenced by it. In
those days the step between coal miner and coal operator was a short one and
was taken again and again by the more vigorous and energetic. The railroads
pushed their way up the gulches and over the div des. Drifts pierced the hill-
sides and great inclines brought the coal down to the tipples at the rails in the
bottom of the gulch. The mountain cabins of the miners strung out along the
creek, the wilderness at their back.
In general there was little large scale investment of capital in the region.
Capital was literally created on the spot by the energy, industry, and saving of
those carrying on the enterprise. Unlike Pennsylvania, unlike Ohio, Indiana,
and Illinois, there was no local market for the coal from these mines. The
economic existence of these fields from the start rested on the structure of
railroad rates and since the function of fixing rates has been taken over from
the railroads by the Government there has been a long series of rate litigation
between these and other districts. For years, in spite of the quality of the
coal and the enterprise of the operators, most of the mines of these districts
barely kept on going, and even the largest and best managed companies ran along
on an average margin between cost and selling price of a few cents per ton.
In the late nineties the United Mine Workers' organization, originating in
the central competitive field, began its campaign to extend its organization
over all of the coal fields of the United States, southern West Virginia among
the others. In 1900 and 1901 organizers were sent all over the State, even to
the remote counties of the Pocahontas district, and late in 1901 there were
locals generally in the fields then developed. The operators offered no great
opposition to this process of organization. While they did not recognize the
locals they made no objection to their men being members of the United
Mine Workers' organization. At that time the United Mine Workers' organi-
zation proclaimed adherence to arbitration and conciliation to be its cardinal
principles.
B. The sympathetic strike in West Virginia in 1902 called by the United
Mine Workers' organization in aid of the authracite strike.-In 1902 the
anthracite strike was begun in Pennsylvania. In April the United Mine
Workers' organization called a meeting of its organizers and officials at
Huntington, W. Va., and against the views of the more conservative leaders
of the organization it was voted to call a State-wide strike in the mines of
West Virginia in order to keep West Virginia coal from going east to take
the place of anthracite coal, the production of which had been stopped by the
anthracite strike. A month after this decision a meeting was held to formu-
late formal grievances and demands on which to base the strike.


===== [扫描序号 979] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1983
This strike was financed by the international organization and was a step
in its national policy. It made a very deep and lasting impression on the
minds of the operators of West Virginia. It presented in a clear-cut way
the danger to any district, particularly to one which had no local markets of
its own, of having its operations completely shut down and its markets lost
because it seemed desirable to the nation-wide union in aid of a compaign in
other districts to cut off the supply to the public of coal from this particular
district. Further the denomination of an outside organization ran head-on
against the instincts of independence, self-reliance, and initiative of a group
of men who with frontier spirit and in frontier conditions were fighting their
way through enormous difficulties to build themselves an industry.
We should be very glad to present in any way the commission may desire
further detail of this transaction if the commission is not already fully
acquainted with what we regard as this vitally important piece of history.
The strike called under these conditions met with a vigorous resistance by
the operators. In the course of it the National Guard was called out to quell
riots. In general, as a result of the strike the Union Mine Workers lost
ground, but in the Kanawha district the United Mine Workers maintained an
effective organization.
C. The United Mine Workers' organization in West Virginia in 1904 takes
a definite stand against permitting any but members of its organization to work
in the mines and against arbitration of disputes as to the interpretation of its
contracts. In 1904 another incident occurred of significance in the building
up of that attitude of mind of the West Virginia operators toward the nation-
wide organization of the United Mine Workers of America which we have
already described as one of the important facts of the coal industry. In that
year, certain operators in Cabin Creek, a part of the Kanawha district, posted
a notice at their mines saying that no discrimination would be made between
union and nonunion men. The United Mine Workers forwith called a strike
at these mines claiming that this was a violation of their agreement with the
Cabin Creek operators. The operators in turn demanded arbitration of this
dispute, but the international organization, through its president, absolutely
refused to arbitrate, though the contract between the operators and the United
Mine Workers called for the arbitration of disputes. In view of this attitude,
the Cabin Creek operators decided to run their mines nonunion. The remainder
of the Kanawha district remained under contract with the United Mine
Workers.
D. The Paint and Cabin Creek struggle.-In 1912 the agreement between the
Paint Creek operators and the United Mine Workers expired. The operators
refused to renew it. The United Mine Workers called a strike demanding an
advance in wages and the check-off. On April 1, 1912, a body of armed United
Mine Workers marched into Paint Creek with resulting violence. The strike
spread to Cabin Creek and in July the National Guard was called out. The
situation quieted down and the troops were relieved. Disorder broke out
again and early in September the governor again called out the militia and
declared marital law. Order was restored and the troops were withdrawn.
They were called out again in November and later in February, 1913. In
July, 1913, the United Mine Workers made a contract with the Paint Creek
operators for a scale less than that in effect in the rest of the Kanawha district,
and for a check-off. The Cabin Creek agreement signed in the same month
provided that there should be no check-off.
E. The United Mine Workers secure the closed shop and check-off in Ka-
nawha.-In 1914 the United Mine Workers called a strike in the mines in the
Kanawha district in which they already had contracts making the sole issue
the securing of a check-off. There was no violence in this strike, the operators
making no attempt to operate their mines. Finally a three-year contract was
signed permitting the open shop, but the operators agreeing to check off union
dues for everyone that gave the order. This agreement expired in 1917 during
the war, and the operators, in view of the national emergency and to prevent any
decreased production of coal, acceded to the demand of the United Mine Workers
for a closed shop with a compulsory check-off of union dues and assessments
for all mine workers in the Kanawha field.
F. The United Mine Workers secure contracts in the New River district.-
The United Mine Workers, working up river from the Kanawha district, created
an organization in the New River district with which the operators of that

===== [扫描序号 980] =====

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
district finally contracted. The contracts up to 1919 did not establish the
compulsory check off of union dues and assessments.
G. Unsuccessful attempt of the United Mine Workers to organize Winding
Gulf district in 1917.-From the New River field the United Mine Workers
pushed into the Winding Gulf district, which adjoins it. In October, 1917, the
United Mine Workers called a strike at the mine of the E. E. White Coal Co.
at Glenn White to compel the company to contract with it. This was during
the war. The majority of the men stayed at work. Representatives of the
Government, called in to arbitrate the controversy, decided against the strikers.
When the strike had apparently failed, the international organizer, who was
representing the central organization, posted armed men in cover on the
mountainside and lay in wait for the workers to come up in the cage at the
end of the day's work. He furnished his followers with red handkerchiefs to
wear, saying that this was the sign of Cabin Creek. A cage came up, but had
only three passengers. The United Mine Workers waited. A second came up,
this time with 10 men. The attacking party then opened fire, but without
casualties (State v. Stafford, pp. 1254-1265). The international organizer and
the local president were apprehended and convicted of attempting to commit
murder. Four followers pleaded guilty. This ended the attempt to organize the
Winding Gulf district.
H. Northern West Virginia fields.-There are two fields of importance in
northern West Virginia, one the Fairmont field and the other the so-called
Panhandle, wedged in between the Ohio and Pennsylvania fields in the extreme
northern part of the State. Neither of these fields has the remotest of market
of the southern West Virginia fields. Both of them were in relatively old and
settled parts of the country and nearer in point of business relationship to the
Maryland and Pennsylvania fields than to those of southern West Virginia.
In the Fairmont field the United Mine Workers in 1917 took advantage of the
situation created by the war to press for the organization of this field, and by
August, 1918, had obtained a closed shop contract, including the check-off,
with over 80 per cent, of the companies in the field.
In the Panhandle the United Mine Workers early succeeded in securing
closed shop contracts. The operation of these contracts proved wholly unsatis-
factory to certain of the operators for reasons which the Supreme Court of
the United States has very clearly set forth in its opinion in Mitchman Coal &
Coke Company v. John Mitchell, 245 U. S. 229, as justifying their subsequent
action. Surrounded as these mines were by the closed union shop and faced
with the bitter opposition of the United Mine Workers to the open shop, the
Hitchman Co. made a definite contract with its workers by which they agreed
not to become members of the United Mine Workers organization while in its
employ. Under the protection of the Supreme Court this and several other
companies continued to operate without contract with the United Mine
Workers.
I. The situation in 1919.-The situation in West Virginia on January 1, 1919,
the beginning of the period during which the commission has asked us to sub-
mit facts as to acts of violence and breach of civil rights, was this:
In the Fairmont field, nearly all operators were under contract with the
United Mine Workers of America, which compelled the operators to collect its
dues and assessments from all persons working in the mines of that district.
In the Panhandle in northern West Virginia the same closed union shop pre-
vailed except in those mines which, after a bitter contest, under the protection
of the decision of the Supreme Court of the United States, refused to contract
with or employ members of the United Mine Workers of America. In the
Kanawha district the same closed shop prevailed and the check-off had been
finally established. In the New River district, the operators contracted with
the United Mine Workers, but the collection of the check-off as against all
workers, had not yet been compelled. In Clay County, in the Winding Gulf
district, in the Logan field and the Williamson field, and in the Tug River and
Pocahontas fields, the operators had maintained the position of refusing to
contract with the United Mine Workers of America, and while there were un-
doubtedly large numbers of men in their employ who had been members of
the United Mine Workers and probably some who still were such members, the
mine workers of those districts as a whole were entirely independent of that
organization.
During this period, the mines of West Virginia, particularly those of southern
West Virginia, had made tremendous strides in their development. The output
of the State had increased from 7,394,654 tons in 1890 to 79,036,553 in 1919.


===== [扫描序号 981] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1985
Their competition with the other fields of the country, particularly those in
which the United Mine Workers were organized, had grown keener and keener.
This competition was felt by the United Mine Workers in those districts .n
which they were dominant. In conventions of the United Mine Workers, again
and again there were expressions that the competition of the West Virg nia
fields must be checked. Control of the wage scale of those fields by the
national organization would put it completely in the power of that organization
to encourage or discourage the economic progress of those districts by establish-
ing or refusing to establish differentials in wage scales. During this period we
have pointed out the persistent efforts to control the Kanawha and New River
districts, and we shall point out that when control became complete the wage
scales insisted upon the national organization for those districts were such as
to make it almost impossible for them to operate. As will appear in the evi-
dence which will presently be discussed, this studied attempt by the United
Mine Workers organization to secure the organization of these fields did not
have as its cause or justification oppression or suffering of the mine workers of
those districts, but was dictated by two things-desire of the central organiza-
tion to increase its power and desire to control the competition of those districts.
II. LIVING CONDITIONS, WAGES, AND EARNINGS OF THE INDEPENDENT MINE WORKERS
OF SOUTHERN WEST VIRGINIA
A. Living conditions.-The public is often asked to excuse and condone the
methods of violence which have accompanied the campaigns of the United Mine
Workers in southern West Virginia on the asserted ground that the miners
there are working under unspeakable living conditions and at starvation wages
because the operators refuse to contract with the United Mine Workers of
America. These assertions have been so dinned into the ears of the public
that, through mere reiteration and the absence of authoritative information as
to the actual situation, which is to the contrary, they have been widely accepted
with a resulting tendency toward the perpetuation of intolerable conditions of
armed attack and necessary armed defense in the coal fields of southern West
Virginia.
In this region there are still to be seen some rough mountain cabins clinging
like eyeries to the steep cliffs of the mountainside, and there still remain some
rows of old houses strung along the V-like bottom of a gulch, similar to those
generally found in the frontier districts of this country. The coal operators in
southern West Virginia have not been less progressive than other employers in
making successful efforts to improve on older conditions. The progress of this
region from one of a purely frontier character to one of modern industrial
communities has been rapid and steady.
Older communities still survive, some merely marking worked-out abandoned
mines, others small or obsolescent properties which, whatever their will, the
owners have not had sufficient capital to improve. Such exceptional conditions
are to be found not merely in southern West Virginia, but in all the older
coal fields of the country, whether or not under contract with the United Mine
Workers of America. To treat them as characteristic of southern West Vir-
ginia, and as resulting from the refusal of the operators to contract with the
United Mine Workers of America is grossly to mislead the public. The com-
mission is in a position to inform it that such is not the fact.
A survey of the conditions in West Virginia has been made for the bituminous
operators' special committee, for the purpose of providing it with accurate and
reliable information on the subject. If the commission desires to supplement
the reports of its own investigation, the detailed reports of our investigation
are available to the commission and its experts, whenever it desires to see
them. Our investigators are also available for interview, and we ask the com-
mission to inspect their reports, and should be glad to have it examine them
personally.
The Williamson field, the Logan (or Guyan) field, and the Tug River and
Pocahontas fields have been particularly in the public mind, the first two as
scenes of United Mine Workers campaigns from 1919 to 1921, and the last
two as strongholds of the opposition to the United Mine Workers. Accordingly
these fields were selected for special study by the field agents of the committee.
The other fields of southern West Virginia we have inspected, and conditions
in them are generally similar to those in the fields named.
Other and official inquiries have been made into the conditions in these fields.
The report of a special investigating committee appointed by Governor Glass-


===== [扫描序号 982] =====
1986
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
cock to investigate the troubles in the Cabin Creek and Paint Creek districts
in 1912, submitted November 12, 1912, reads as follows:
"THE CONDITION OF THE MINERS
*
To this inquiry we have devoted special attention within the
limits of the time and opportunity at our disposal and, after careful personal
investigation, supplemented by a very great body of formal sworn testimony
sifted and tested by severe and exhaustive cross examination, this commission
has arrived at the unanimous conclusion that the general surroundings of the
miners in Paint Creek and Cabin Creek, respectively, are very good, when com-
pared with those of the miners of the few unionized plants on the right bank
of Kanawha and with those of the miners throughout the State and the Nation.
We have gone into their houses and carefully examined them. They are above
the average of miners houses in most places."
The standards of mining communities in southern West Virginia have to-day
progressed far beyond those of 1912.
The commission appointed by Governor Cornwell to investigate the armed
march of 1919 against Logan County reported on April 10, 1920:
46 * * * Your commission went largely into the welfare work, and social
and religious conditions as they obtain in the Guyan field, and whatever may
be the motive of those who are responsible for those conditions; the record
abundantly shows that the labor, industrial, and living conditions in this field
are as good as in the best coal fields in the State."
Existing standards have been brought about by the operators in the face
of almost insurmountable obstacles. The operators have had to overcome not
only the difficulties presented by the physical contour of the land, but also
the immobility of century old customs and the conservative character of the
native stock which inhabits southern West Virginia.
This region is a mountainous one, with steep and beautifully wooded hills,
whose precipitous slopes preclude easy community building. Here modern
houses can be erected and water and sewerage systems installed on the ter-
raced hillsides only at a great expense to the operators. The difficulty of
supplying adequate water should also be emphasized.
The character of the people inhabiting the widest sections of West Virginia
has already been mentioned. About 50 per cent of the mine workers are native
whites. Many of them belong to old mountaineer families of what was formerly
one of the most backward sections of the United States. Large numbers of
negroes and foreigners work beside the native whites in the mines, and live
in the mining communities, thus adding to the complexity of the racial
problem.
In spite of these disadvantages the general level of conditions in the non-
union fields of southern West Virginia is as high as, if not higher than, condi-
tions found generally in other fields, union or nonunion. Under nonunion
conditions operators often succeed in forming and maintaining a close personal
relationship with their men, which is an important factor in the improvement
of living conditions and in the steady progress of the present day.
In the Williamson field 12 representative company-owned communities
ranging in age from 2 to 25 years were visited by our investigators. Of these
communities 10 had piped water systems; 5 had partial or complete piped sew-
age systems; and 10 had regular garbage collection. Three had company
doctors devoting their entire time to employees, and 9 had from one to 3 con-
tract doctors; 4 conducted some form of welfare work for the benefit of em-
ployees. Eleven had schools for white children in or adjacent to the communi-
ties, the twelfth using the town school one mile distant. Of these, six
companies, by supplementing the teachers' salaries, made possible a longer
school term than the county provided. Five had separate schools for colored
children. All either owned church buildings or utilized the schoolhouse for
religious services. Among the recreational activities or facilities were found
5 baseball teams, 7 company-owned pool rooms, 2 basket-ball teams, 3 boy
scout and 2 girl scout clubs, 5 tennis courts; and in 7 communities moving
pictures are shown three or four times a week. Houses in the field gen-
erally are equipped with electricity, and miners' wives in the communities
were found using such conveniences as electric washing machines, irons, fans,
toasters, and ranges, generally without any charge beyond the small flat rate
charged per lamp. The living conditions illustrated by these facts were


===== [扫描序号 983] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1987
superior to those found in noncompany towns visited for the purpose of
comparison.
The investigation of company-owned communities in Logan County also
indicates progressive conditions. The operators were found to be taking an
active interest in the betterment of community conditions. It is important to
note that not only the operators but also the townspeople of Logan, the county
seat, feel that conditions in the county have been grossly misrepresented by
so-called social investigators in the past.
The mine community at Holden is situated in the foothills 4½ miles from
the town of Logan. The community is 18 years old. All houses erected in
the last eight years are built on a concrete foundation, and are plastered and
weather boarded. They contain four rooms and a washroom. The older houses
range from three to five rooms. They are all kept in good repair. Hedges and
flower and vegetable gardens around the houses furnish an attractive setting.
The community is supplied with filtered water from drilled wells. The water
is regularly analyzed by the State department of health. All the houses are
equipped with electricity for which a nominal charge is made. The company
has erected on the hillside an excellent hospital, surrounded by trees, in the
center of a well-kept lawn. It maintains men's and women's wards of 16
beds, and a well-equipped operating room. In addition a general clinic is held
every afternoon from 1 to 4. The community has a 10-grade school for white
children and an 8-grade school for colored. The former has an auditorium
seating 400 persons. It has departments of domestic science and physical edu-
cation and conducts special work in music. An evening school is conducted in
the winter at which English and mathematics are the principal subjects taught,
and stress is laid upon Americanization.
Many other communities visited in Logan showed their owners active in pro-
viding their employees with proper housing and healthful community environ-
ment. Expensive improvements in water supply have eliminated typhoid.
The Pocahontas and Tug River fields, largely in McDowell County, were also
visited by agents of the committee. As in Williamson and Logan, the operators
there were found to be making a constructive and successful effort to further
the progress of living conditions. The larger operating companies were every-
where taking the lead in building new up-to-date houses, rebuilding old ones, and
providing their communities with such advantages as better roads, better sani-
tary and water systems, medical care, and recreational facilities. Special
attention was being given to the improvement of schools. The county superin-
tendent said that it was mainly due to the operators' support and financial aid
that the nine-months school term is so nearly universally found in both urban
and rural schools. It is also noteworthy that colored children are given educa-
tional facilities in every way equal to those provided white children. McDowell
County established one of the first dental clinics for school children in the
United States.
At Crozer the houses vary in size and color. They are grouped about the
churches on the hillsides. The houses generally are fenced, and have sidewalks.
The streets are paved and have concrete gutters. Flights of concrete steps make
short cuts to the higher terraces and roads. Fine shade trees and gardens are
found throughout the town, and the company gives garden prizes. There is
always a waiting list for miners' houses here. The water supply is softened
and filtered, and 30 per cent of the houses have hot and cold running water.
The sanitation is above reproach. The company has given land for five churches,
and contributes toward their support. It aids generously the Americanization
work of the Greek Catholic priest, who teaches American civics to his Russian
parishioners through the medium of their own language.
At Exeter the company has erected 17 modern brick double houses. Above
the level ground on which these houses stand, the company has terraced the
mountainside at enormous expense, and built houses less pretentious than the
others, but equally comfortable. It has installed a central water system
supplying 40 per cent of the houses with water inside, and 60 per cent at hy-
drants near the houses. Septic tanks are used by 60 per cent of the families.
The company has equipped all of its houses with electric lights. It has also
built two churches, one of which it supports in part. Its recreation building for
white employees is duplicated for colored. There are tennis courts and a
movie theater.
B. Wages and earnings.-The commission has called for reports which for
the first time will make it possible for the public to be authoritatively informed

as to the earnings of mine workers. This information is particularly im-

starvation wages, because of the refusal of the operators to contract with the

(1) Opportunity to work and turnover: We have made an analysis of the pay
rolls of a considerable number of mines in various southern West Virginia
fields, using duplicates of the records prepared by the operators for the com-
mission in the form prescribed by it. We have considered three classes:
The miners operating cutting machines-" machine miners."
The miners undercutting by pick—“pick miners.”
The miners who load the broken-down coal into the coal cars-"loaders."
As all these classes of miners are pieceworkers and ordinarily work on their
own without the surveillance of a foreman, and often knock off before the com-
pletion of the regular eight-hour day, there is a considerable variation in the
amount of work which the various men that go into a mine on a particular day
actually perform.
The records which the commission has asked for show the earnings of a par-
ticular person only while working at the same mine. In districts where there
are a large number of mines closely grouped, as is the case in southern West
Virginia, a considerable part of the mining population frequently changes its
place of work from mine to mine. This is particularly true of the unmarried
miners who live at boarding houses and who perhaps share the boarding-house
spirit in their willingness to change their fare. The commission has already
called attention to the large proportion of men in the anthracite field who work
at the same mine only for a few days. In southern West Virginia the same
characteristic appears.
We have analyzed the records of 28 mines in the Logan field, 34 mines in the
Winding Gulf field, and 34 mines in the Pocahontas field to show this factor.
From these records, the originals of which are in the hands of the commission,
it appears that in 1921 in the Logan mines over 85 per cent of the machine
miners employed worked less than 75 per cent of the days on which the mines
were working.
In these Winding Gulf mines over 80 per cent of the machine miners employed
worked less than 75 per cent of the days on which the miners were working.
In these Pocahontas mines over 65 per cent of the machine miners employed
worked less than 75 per cent of the days on which the mines were working.
Moreover, in each of these fields even greater proportions of both the pick
miners and loaders worked less than 75 per cent of the days the mines were
working. In Logan 90 per cent of the loaders worked less than 75 per cent of
the days on which the mines were working, and in Winding Gulf over 90 per
cent of the pick miners worked less than 75 per cent of the days the mine
worked.
(2) Yearly earnings from the same mine: From what we have just shown
as to the extent of the shifting of men from mine to mine and in and out
of mining work, it is at once apparent that it is practically impossible to
ascertain from these records what the actual yearly earnings of miners are.
The most that can be ascertained is the amount of pay which they receive
while working at a particular mine. It is further evident that it is only
when a man has worked at the same mine for a considerable number of days
that his total earnings at that mine are of any significance in affording any
index as to his actual income during the year. We have, therefore, in our anal
yses of these records taken the earnings of men who worked 100 days or more at
the same mine. We have compiled these figures from duplicates of Forms I-1
which have been submitted to the commission by most of the commercial
mines of the Logan district, the Pocahontas district, the Winding Gulf district.
and the Kanawha and Fairmont districts for the year 1921. For the year
1920, we have figures covering only a substantial number of mines in the
Winding Gulf district and the Pocahontas district.
We submit below a table showing for these mines in each of these five
fields the percentage of the miners (machine, pick, and loaders) who worked
100 days or more in the same mine in 1921 and thereby earned over $1.600.

Gener-
Further the cost of living of a great majority of these miners is conspicuously
lower than that of other workers, because of the fact that the companies provide
various necessities of life to their employees at exceptionally low rates.
ally speaking, the miners live in company houses for which they pay rent of
$2 a month or less per room, which includes the use of water. They can buy
their coal in unlimited quantities from their employers at a flat rate ranging
from $1 to $2 a month, which often includes the cost of delivery. Electric
lighting is supplied at a cost of from 25 to 50 cents per month per lamp.
Various electrical appliances are frequently used, usually without extra charge.
Medical service is generally supplied by a competent company or contract
doctor who receives for his services, including medicines, from $1.25 to $2 a
month from each married worker, and 75 cents to $1 from each single worker.
Several companies carry group insurance, which entitles their workmen to
standard life policies according to their length of service to the companies, the
premiums on which are assumed by the companies. Other manual workers
living in the vicinity of the mines or in near-by towns pay at least twice as
much for rent and fuel. When electricity can be purchased from a private com-
pany it is always on the more expensive meter basis.
The commission will have, and will no doubt make public, more complete
data on earnings than we have at this time been able to work up from dupli-
cates of the reports that have been made to it. What we have is sufficient to
negative the popular conception and picture the true conditions.
III. THE WILLIS BRANCH AFFAIR-THE CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE CONDUCTED BY THE
UNITED MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA IN THE NEW RIVER FIELD IN 1919-21 ON THE
SOLE ISSUE OF WHETHER THE OPERATORS SHOULD BE COMPELLED TO FORCIBLY
DEDUCT THE UNION DUES AND ASSESSMENTS FIXED BY THE UNITED MINE WORKERS'
ORGANIZATION FROM THE PAY OF EVERY MINE WORKER BY MEANS OF THE CHECK-
OFF
In 1919-1921 there occurred a series of events in the New River field which
drew sharply the issue between the United Mine Workers and the operators
and independent mine workers of southern West Virginia, and which confirmed
and in their minds absolutely justified, if it needed any justification, the deter-
mination not to contract with the United Mine Workers of America. In 1913
the operators in the New River field, unwilling to go through the inevitable
long struggle against violence which was being enacted in the Paint Creek and


===== [扫描序号 987] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1991
Cabin Creek fields, agreed to contract with a committee of miners, members
of the United Mine Workers, and later during the war with the organization
itself, but on the condition that they should not be compelled to refuse employ-
ment to mine workers independent of that organization.
In 1919 the United Mine Workers' organization demanded not merely a
continuance of contractual relations but, what has again and again proved to be
its objective, the closed shop and the enforced collection from all mine workers
of such dues and assessments as it might from time to time fix. The New River
operators, as a whole, again were not willing to engage in a conflict with the
power of the United Mine Workers' international organization, with all that
such a conflict involved, and for the most part acceded to this contract.
A. The check-off issue at Willis branch.-One group of companies, however,
refused to accept the compu sory check off. This group was willing to pay the
scale of wages provided for in the United Mine Workers' contract and to cou-
form to the hours and working conditions provided for by that contract, and to
employ members of the United Mine Workers of America. It was also willing
to permit continuance of locals at these mines, and to furnish the members of
the union a place in which to hold their meetings free of rent. They were
unwilling, however, to agree to deduct from the pay of every mine worker in
their employ such dues and assessments as that organization might see fit to
deduct.
On this clear-cut issue in the autumn of 1919 the organization called a strike
against the Willis branch mine and six other companies.
Enough men reported at the mines of these six other companies so that they
opened up from time to time in November and December. The miners who
continued to work were intimidated and beaten up to some extent, but the
attack of the organization was centered on the Willis branch mine.
B. Living conditions at Willis Branch.-Willis Branch village and mine are
located on the border of Fayette County in the New River field. It is over
1,500 feet above sea level in a valley lying between steep hills. The living and
mining conditions were excellent. The water supply came from deep wells and
springs. House rents were $2 per room per month. The services of a doctor
were available to employees who were married upon payment of $1 a month,
and to unmarried employees upon payment of 50 cents a month. The company
did not operate any store itself, but a store was run on company property by an
outsider under the supervision of its officials. The rates at this store were
kept reasonable, and many of the farmers in the vicinity, who were in no way
connected with the mine dealt at this store.
C. Persistent attempt to prevent by violence operation of Willis Branch mine,
December, 1919-May, 1921.-On December 8, 1919, about 100 men started in to
operate Willis Branch, but, as the result of threats and intimidation, work
ceased on December 16. On the 8th of January some men again reported for
work. On the 20th several of them were stopped on their way to work and
beaten up by members of the United Mine Workers of America. On that same
day the hoist house was broken into and so badly damaged that it could not be
used until February 17. Up to this time no guards of any kind had been em-
ployed for the protection of the property of the company or the defense of its
workers. After the hoist house had been repaired and the mine resumed on
February 17, four or five employees of the Baldwin-Felts Agency were brought
to the property.
Willis Branch was particularly exposed to violence for the reason that the
plant is strung out for a long distance and coal cars have to go 2 miles in the
open from mine mouth to the tipple. To protect its property over this distance
the company never employed more than 18 guards, and this number only in
times of particular emergency. The Baldwin-Felts men were replaced as soon
as possible by a force of private watchmen.
On
When the mine resumed operation attacks upon men working in it and
shooting into the houses began, and what amounted to a state of siege con-
tinued for over a year. Many workers were frightened away. However,
enough of the men got their backs up to stick it out in a fashion, which did
more credit to their character as Americans than to their discretion.
January 4, 1921, the incline at the mine was dynamited. Robert Ratcliff,
Lee Donald, Clarence Donald, and John Kidd, all members of the United Mine
Workers of America, were convicted of this crime and sentenced to seven years
in the penitentiary. (Record of trial and convictions submitted to the com-
mission.)

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
This dynamiting opened a period of particularly violent attack. A picture
of life in that community during this period is given by the contemporaneous
weekly reports of the superintendent in charge of the mine, made up from
a daily diary kept at Willis Branch during the strike. This appears in an
affidavit of A. M. Fittro, assistant general manager of the Willis Branch Coal
Co., submitted in an injunction suit by the Willis Branch Co. against the
United Mine Workers of America in the Federal district court at Charleston.
We submit a copy herewith and should be glad to produce Mr. Fittro before
the commission.
A DIARY KEPT UNDER FIRE
"Week ending January 29: Had 55 men; 11 watchmen, worked 32 hours,
produced 1,100 tons.
“An attack was made on our camp on the night of January 28. This attack
was made from several different points and it is estimated that 40 to 50 people
participated. Heavy firing was observed from the vicinity of the Wierwood
superintendent's house, also from the Weirwood schoolhouse, which is about op-
posite Willis Branch tipple and where a barricade of large rocks had been
thrown up for the protection of the attackers, from a point in the corner of an
orchard about 300 yards from Willis Branch store and office building, from the
two ridges west of Willis Branch camp, from a long ridge just east of the
camp and from the railroad track near Weirwood tipple. The telephone wires
run over the Weirwood property and in order to insure the Willis Branch
people from calling for assistance seven of the mine wires had been cut. The
attack was commenced about 11 p. m. and continued till about 3 a. m. We
had been advised an attack was contemplated for the early morning, and Mr.
Fittro and another man went over. They reached Pax and commenced to
walk to Willis Branch but the firing was too heavy and they went back to
Pax. While waiting on the railroad track below Weirwood they were passed
by a party of women leaving Weirwood and heard a remark that indicated
the shooting would be more intense shortly; this was confirmed by the heavy
fusillade that shortly followed from the Weirwood camp. Our people at
Willis Branch had been instructed not to return the fire, and this was done with
few exceptions; one being when the attack on the superintendent's house was
worst, the attackers were fired on and dispersed.
"On Monday, February 2, Sheriff Conley with Deputy Sheriffs Crago, Blue.
and Barker visited the scene and saw the bullet holes in the houses on the
property. The superintendent's house was hit several times, two bullets enter-
ing the bathroom and several entering front and side. The superintendent's
office was shot into and one bullet entered the upstairs which was occupied by
a Mrs. Spangler and children. The sheriff and deputies went to the point
where shooting had been done from about 300 yards east of the office and
found a large number of shells of different caliber and the tracks of the
men who had been shooting. This location was in a fence corner just above
the railroad track. The same party visited the location beside the Weirwood
schoolhouse from which heavy firing had been done and found a barricade of
rocks which had been used as a shelter; they also saw the place where the
telephone wires had been cut; these had by this time been repaired by the
Weirwood superintendent. They also visited houses in the Willis Branch
camp as follows: No. 1.-House of Roscoe Jackson occupied by Jackson, his
wife, and two children. Mrs. Jackson reported that one bullet just missed
her head. Jackson had made a dugout under the floor in which the family
took shelter during these attacks. No. 2.-House of Lum Maynor. This man
owns a farm just east of Willis Branch and because he was working for the
company he was chased away from it and was obliged to come to Willis
Branch camp to live. Three or four bullet holes were seen in this house, the
shots coming from the ridge between the camp and Cirtsville. Maynor reports
the firing extended all along the ridge. Some of his children and a boarder
occupied the adjoining house, which was struck by two bullets; when the firing
commenced he called them to come to his house. An electric light is situated
close by and the attackers could see the children and knowing this the children
endeavored to circle around toward an outhouse but were observed and fired
on, two bullets entering the outhouse. The children, however, got to Maynor's
house and all descended into a dugout which Maynor had excavated under the
floor of his house-an electric wire is carried to the dugout and furnishes light

in it. No. 4-House of Mr. Bently. Bently was on duty during the shooting,
but his wife was in the house. One bullet entered near the corner of the

in the opposite wall. No. 5-Boarding house kept by Mrs. Smith, who has
two children. One bullet passed through an outer wall and a partition just
