The following extract from another weekly report describes the dynamiting
of the power substation:
..
'On Tuesday morning, February 15, about 3.45 a. m., the two watchmen,
Guy Simkins and Bill Maynor, were on duty and heard the crack of a small
pistol a short distance away. This was promptly followed by a fusillade of
shot from two directions aimed at the shanty which acted as a shelter for
them and the substation which is close alongside. Apparently about 15 men
in two parties were making the attack. One party coming down the hill
immediately behind the substation and the other party coming down the hill
at one side of it, both parties approaching the substation. A heavy fire was
kept up for about half an hour and the watchmen did not at any time return
the fire, but retreated into a tunnel in the mine for protection. During the
half hour of shooting two blasts of dynamite were heard immediately about
the substation but these did no damage. The shooting then ceased for possibly
10 minutes when a very heavy explosion was felt (this was so heavy that it
was heard at Glen Jean, 12 miles away). The substation was built close to
the hillside and much earth and rock had worked down and piled against
the wall to a height probably 8 feet. Evidently a large quantity of dynamite
had been placed against this wall and when it was exploded it damaged the
substation and machinery badly, making further operation impossible. The
rear wall was bulged in and the inside layer of the wall over a space of
3 feet square had been thrown against the switchboard and generators knock-
ing the switchboard forward and damaging the apparatus on the back of the
board. Knocking off and ruining the transformers and covering the oil switch
and starting box with rock, it also tore loose the iron frame carrying the
disconnecting switches and a large number of rocks were thrown onto and
into the two generators. It also broke out all the windows in the building."
On February 16, 1921, all the employees of the mine were paid off and
dismissed on account of this dynamiting and the consequent closing of the
mine, but a few people were left to guard the property. On February 19
an attack was made on the superintendent's house and members of the union
who have since confessed that they participated in this attack, have said
that their plan was first to shoot at the lower floors of the house, forcing
the men defending it to go upstairs, and then under cover of a rifle barrage
to set fire to the house and burn it up. Henry Lafferty, a member of the
union, was killed in trying to carry out this plan, while he was approaching
the store and office building with a bucket of gasoline.
On the same night, two men were asleep upstairs in the company office
building when the shooting started. They escaped by knotting their sheets
together and climbing down to the ground under the protection of a large
stone chimney. The office building still stands. Its walls and partitions,
as personally observed by one of the writers of this brief. are still literally
riddled with bullet holes from this and other shootings.
Mrs. L. M. Smith, who kept a boarding house at Willis Branch, in an affidavit
in the Willis Branch injunction case, a copy of which is submitted herewith,
described the somewhat dangerous and nerve-racking conditions under which
the inhabitants of that community had to live during the strike. She said
that her own house was frequently shot up by members of the United Mine
Workers and for protection her sleeping room was permanently barricaded
with sand and the windows covered with sheet iron. Two large pieces of
sheet iron were at all times kept in the corner of another room in the house
so that she and her children could take refuge quickly in case of an unex-
pected attack. On the 21st of January, 1921, while the boarders were eating
supper. the firing became so intense that they were all forced to leave the
table and take refuge in the stone basement of the adjoining house. Many.


===== [扫描序号 990] =====
1994
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
99
of the employees of the Willis Branch Coal Co. had dugouts under their houses
during most of the strike where the women and children could take refuge
when the shooting became particularly severe. These dugouts had to be
occupied so much of the time that some of them were lighted by electricity.
After the mine closed down in February, 1921, as a result of the destruction
of the power house, there was no one left to look after the property except a
local farmer, "Uncle Jimmy' Davis. A house belonging to him was burned
down. The company tried to repair the substation, but on the 22d of May,
when these repairs were almost finished, the tipple and trestle were completely
destroyed by fire about 3 a. m. There was no one in charge of the property
at this, time, except Davis. This burning was so serious that it stopped all
immediate prospect of reopening the Willis Branch mine and the trouble came
to an end.
When Willis Branch was finally abandoned it had much the same appearance
as a village in the war zone. Fire, dynamite, and bullets had made the place
practically uninhabitable, and had made mining impossible. The actual property
damage to the houses and mining equipment and the loss caused by the forced
suspension amounted to many hundreds of thousands of dollars.
The mine has since been reoponed and is being run on an open-shop basis
and a great many of the employees are those who were among the most active
of the strikers during the trouble. Although no objection by the company is
made to their belonging to the United Mine Workers, the men themselves seem
to have had enough of it and there is now no union at that mine.
D. Responsibility of the international organization of the United Mine Work-
ers of America for this campaign.—Much of the inside history of this trans-
action is now available through the court records in the case of Carbon Fuel
Co. et al, v. International Organization of the United Mine Workers, recently
tried in the United States District Court for the Southern District of West
Virginia. In this suit the secretary of the local testified that the only dispute
between the Willis Branch Co. and the United Mine Workers was the question
of the check-off. Percy Tetlow, from Columbus, Ohio, in the employ of the
central organiaztion, who stated that he was representing the president of the
international organization and addressed a convention of the United Mine
Workers of America at Beckley in 1919 before the strike, said that it was the
policy of the international organization to insist on a check-off in the New
River field, and that the international organization would back to the limit of
its power a strike against any operators who might refuse to agree to the
check-off (Carbon Fuel Co. v. United Mine Workers of America, p. 65).
Further, it was testified that David Robb was sent in by the international
organiaztion to take charge of the strike sent in, as he informed the local
leaders, by the international president (Carbon Fuel case, p. 35). David Robb
had for many years seen sent by the international organization to points of
conflict where violent methods were in use. He went through the campaign of
violence in Colorado and was indicted and convicted and sentenced to prison
for a killing which took place there, but was pardoned before completing his
sentence. Robb was the international financial agent and furnished funds,
it was testified in the Carbon Fuel case, for the purchase of supplies for
the men and for guns and ammunition. It was also testified that he him-
self brought in guns and ammunition which were delivered to the local leaders
for distribution (Carbon Fuel case, pa. 32). One way in which money was
obtained for purchasing guns and ammunition with leaving any record as to
how it had been used was, it appeared from the testimony, by cashing relief
orders made out to men who had been on strike, but who had left the field
to secure employment elsewhere. As to Robb's policy in carrying on the strike,
it was testified by the secretary of the local, as follows:
"Q. What, if anything, did Mr. Robb say, from time to time about actions
of violence there? Just tell the court what he said and how it came about.-
A. The mine got to producing about from somewhere to five to eight or nine
carloads of coal per day; that is railroad cars; then Mr. Robb threatened to take
the relief list and leave the State and talked very rough to myself and Mr.
Maynor and Mr. Kidd and Mr. Daniel and some fellows that went there to the
office to see him in regard to the relief; and he said if the men continued to
allow these nonunion men to produce coal that he would take the relief list and
leave the State and go back to Indiana; and the question came up as to how to
prevent it; and he told them that the only way to prevent it was to send them
away in a black box.
"Q. Send them away in a black box?-A. Yes, sir.


===== [扫描序号 991] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1995
"Q. What did you understand by that?-A. Wanted them murdered was the
way we understood it.
Q. Did you commit any acts of violence before that?-A. No, sir." (Car-
bon Fuel case, p. 38.)
Romine also testified that from $50,000 to $80,000 furnished by Robb passed
through his hands during the Willis Branch strike. (Carbon Fuel case, p. 36.)
During the progress of the strike, Romine talked to the manager and super-
intendent of the Willis Branch mine and ascertained that they were willing,
in addition to the other offers, to assist the union in any legitimate way they
could in collecting dues from members employed, but were unwilling to deduct
dues and assessments from the pay roll. Romine went to Beckley to take this
up with Gilmore, the president of the district. Gilmore was in favor of accept-
ing this offer and thus ending the strike, but David Robb, the representative
of the international organization, vetoed this arrangement and said he had been
sent there to fight for the terms of the check-off contract to the letter and he
expected to do that. (Carbon fuel case, pp. 60-62.)
There was another international organizer sent down by the central or-
ganization to aid this campaign at Willis Branch, one George Barrett by name.
Walter Romine testified as to Barrett's connection with transactions at Willis
Branch as follows:
"Q. What knowledge, if any, in addition to what you have stated, did George
Barrett have in the activities of the organization there at Willis Branch?-
A. Well, Mr. Barrett knew of everything that was happening there.
"Q. Did he come there from time to time?-A. He was at the scene of the
disturbance more than any other official of the organization; he visited the
mining camp more than any of their other men." (Carbon Fuel case, p. 40.)
Romine testified (in the Carbon Fuel case) that the shooting into the
Willis Branch camp by members of the United Mine Workers of America
occurred for over a year from one to a dozen times a month, and that houses
occupied by women and children were deliberately shot into. He testified
that no action had ever been taken by any part of the United Mine Workers'
organization to penalize the local union or its members who had been con-
cerned in these matters, and that the United Mine Workers' organization con-
tributed to the expense of defending the men convicted of dynamiting the
incline and power station at Willis Branch (Carbon Fuel case, pp. 82, 83.)
During this whole period of repeated acts of arson and violence extending over
nearly 18 months, there is not the slightest evidence nor, so far as we have been
able to discover, has there ever been the slightest claim made that the inter-
national organization in any way ever sought to deter or reprobate the methods
being used in the strike at Willis Branch to compel the check-off, which it
had sent its direct representatives to supervise and aid.
E. Admission of responsibility of the international organization by payment
for damages inflicted.-The actual property damages to the Willis Branch
Co. amounted to several hundred thousands of dollars. The company brought
suit against the international organization of the United Mine Workers of
America. This suit is described in the issue of the United Mine Workers'
Journal for October 1, 1922, where there appears a leading article under this
heading: "United Mine Workers will be interested in this latest suit to mulet
the union." "The suit is another union-busting attempt by a nonunion coal
company, and shows to what lengths such corporations will go in order to
smash the union." But the facts in this case were not such that the inter-
national organization was willing to stand suit and have the record go to
the American people. We have not found in the files of the United Mine
Workers' Journal any statement to their members telling what became of this
suit. The fact was that the international organization admitted its responsi-
bility for the long drawn-out attack and destruction of property at Willis
Branch by settling the suit out of court and paying the large damages which
had been sustained.
F. Loss of New River field to United Mine Workers of America.-The subse-
quent history of the organization in the New River field, where these acts of
violence had occurred, is important. The same year, 1921, which brought the
general business depression and the general fall in prices of all commodities,
created such a situation in the New River field that it was impossible to oper-
ate the mines of many of the companies and pay the wage scale contracted
for with the United Mine Workers of America. One of the largest of these
companies was compelled to close down. The records now in the hands of
the United States Coal Commission show numerous mines in this district


===== [扫描序号 992] =====
1996
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
operating at this time at an actual loss. The effect of attempting to maintain
an artificial wage scale in the face of a drop in the price of all other com-
modities and of the cost of living came forcibly home to the miners of this
district, and in the months that followed the mine workers of the district
repudicated the policy of the international organization and by an overwhelm-
ing sentiment, which the international organization was powerless to resist.
resumed work at a new wage scale more in accord with the general level of
wages in industry-a scale which with the improved conditions of 1922 was
voluntarily increased by the operators.
IV. THE CAMPAIGN OF THE UNITED MINE WORKERS' ORGANIZATION TO COMPEL
THE OPERATORS OF THE WILLIAMSON FIELD TO CONTRACT WITH IT AND DEDUCT
FROM THE PAY OF ALL MINE WORKERS EMPLOYED BY THEM SUCH DUES AND ASSESS-
MENTS AS THAT ORGANIZATION MIGHT SEE FIT TO IMPOSE
A. The international organization centers its campaign to organize southern
West Virginia on the Williamson field.—While the campaign of violence, which
we have just been describing, to impose the compulsory check-off on the Willis
Branch mine was under way, the international president of the United Mine
Workers of America went to Bluefield, in the heart of the nonunion southern
West Virginia fields, and announced that the campaign of the United Mine
Workers of America to compel those fields to contract with it would be pushed
to a finish.
The Williamson field was selected as the center of attack. It includes Mingo
County, W. Va., and part of Pike County, Ky. The two counties are separated
by the Tug River. Up the Tug River lie the nonunion fields of Tug River and
Pocahontas in McDowell and Mercer Counties and across the hills lie the non-
union fields of Logan and Winding Gulf, these being the only fields at that
time left in West Virginia which did not contract with the United Mine Workers
of America.
The campaign which began after this visit to Bluefield at the end of January,
1920, culminated in the armed march of a force of over 6,000 men in August.
1921. The organization of the United Mine Workers was unsparing in the use
of men and money. The Williamson field is not a large one. The number of
men employed in the field was normally about 5,000, scattered over a large terri-
tory and employed by a large number of organizations, most of them small in
size.
Into this field the United Mine Workers' organization sent a large number
of international and district professional organizers and, as was admitted by
the president of district No. 17, at least $2,500,000.
Among the international organizers sent in was David Robb, whose past
record of violence in Colorado and whose contemporaneous policy of violence
in directing the Willis Branch campaign have just been described.
B. Wages and living conditions in the Williamson field.—The Williamson field
is a rough country. Coal mining is the only industry in this field.
These counties had been typical Kentucky and West Virginia mountaineer
communities and had been the scene of the old Hatfield-McCoy feud. Since
coal mining had begun, there had been steady progress from the old primitive
mountaineer conditions which nevertheless still left their marks on the little
towns and the isolated cabins in the hills which had existed from premining
days.
Where mining communities had been built by the companies their conditions
showed in general marked progress over the original communities, and the
company-owned houses in general were markedly better than the privately
owned cabins of some of the miners.
Rentals were so low that in many cases houses were maintained by the com-
panies at a substantial yearly loss, as appears from the records gathered by
the commission.
Earnings for the year ending March 31, 1921, from 36 typical mines in the
Williamson field were compiled by the Williamson Operators' Association and
submitted to a senatorial investigating committee in 1921. They were com-
pared with the figures of such mines in Kanawha contracting with the United
Mine Workers of America as it was possible to obtain. The average earnings
for machine miners, pick miners, and loaders was $9.84 per day, as compared
with $7.85 in Kanawha. The average of day workers in these mines in the
Williamson field for the time actually employed was $6 per day as against
$6.10 in the Kanawha field. The 8-hour day prevailed in both fields.


===== [扫描序号 993] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
1997
The charge sometimes made against company stores that mine workers are
compelled to trade at them had no application in this field. Many company
stores were maintained in the mining communities, but the mine workers
dealt freely also with independent stores in the towns. The prices at the
company stores, however, averaged lower than in the independent stores.
Detailed evidence on this point was submitted to the senatorial investigating
committee.
C. Attitude of the operators.-Back in 1902 the Williamson field was one of
those which had been partially organized by the United Mine Workers without
much objection from the operators. But the strike which was called in that
year by the national leaders of the organization in aid of the anthracite strike
had here, as elsewhere in southern West Virginia, led to a definite determination
not to deal with the United Mine Workers' organization. From that time up
to 1920 operators and mine workers had been independent of that organiza-
tion; there had been no industrial disturbances, and no loss of time on account
of labor disputes.
During these years there was in general no objection to employing men who
were members of the United Mine Workers. In fact, many of the men who
worked in the Williamson field had come there from the union fields, preferring
independence of contract to the hard and fast control of mine committees and
union officials as to working rules and regulations, and the system of union
dues and assessments.
In the Williamson Field the operators had with the growth of the field and
improvements in its business conditions made repeated voluntary increases in
the rates of wages.
Confronted with the preparations of the organization of the United Mine
Workers to make a determined effort to force them to contract with its organi-
zation and accept the check-off and consequent closed shop, the operators de-
termined to resist this campaign and to work their mines without such con-
tract if it was possible to obtain men to do so, and with the issue thus definitely
drawn they determined not to continue in their employ any men who became
members of the United Mine Workers of America during this campaign.
D. Mine guards.-The loose charge often made as to West Virginia that op-
erators employed Baldwin-Felts guards to keep union organizers out of the
district had no application whatever to Williamson field. As a matter of
fact, it developed during the Senatorial investigation that there was not a
single Baldwin-Felts mine guard employed in the field and had not been for
five years prior to 1920. The union organizers came into the field with absolute
freedom and made their headquarters in the county seat and the town of
Matewan. Early in the spring of 1920 four or five Baldwin-Felts guards were
employed at one mine. None were employed after July 1, 1920, but four or five
secret operatives were used in getting up evidence on the murder cases.
deputy sheriffs were paid by coal companies in Mingo County in 1920.
No
E. Methods of organization.-In the early spring of 1920 organizers of the
United Mine Workers of America entered the Williamson field and began to
form local unions at several points. Miners were told that it was to their
advantage to join the United Mine Workers' organization and unquestionably
the harangues and the prospect of belonging to an organization appealed
strongly to many. They further argued that the field would soon be entirely
controlled by that organization, and that when that day came no one who
had then refused to join would be allowed to work, and that meanwhile a
strike would be called and that any who persisted in working would be
subjected to the danger of violence. They put the experiences of Cabin Creek
and of Paint Creek very forcibly before the men. In addition there was a
threat made which becomes particularly important, considered in the light of
the armed march of 1921. The organizers often said that when the strike
came there would be a march of armed union miners from the Paint and
Cabin Creek districts who would carry the strike over the top and who would
kill or drive out of the field all men who by that time had not joined the
union-a threat which in view of the history of Paint Creek and Cabin
Creek carried more weight to the men and women on the spot than to those
of us 500 miles away.
The general method of handling the organization of a particular mine, as
our investigation shows it, is: First to win over a small group of the more
irresponsible and turbulent. Organizers hold out to them the prospect of
places in the local organization, emphasize the power of the national organi-


===== [扫描序号 994] =====
1998
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
zation and the stock idea of getting in on the ground floor of the new organiza-
tion. Next, this group circulates about the mine, painting a glowing picture
of the advantages of unionism. They attract the "joiner" class and those
impressed by profuse promises of results to be obtained.
One of the most interesting results to us from our study of this situation has
been how much easier it is for organizers to make progress along these lines
with the miners of a district which has never had any experience with contracts
with the United Mine Workers than a district which has been once under con-
tract with them and has since broken away or in which there has been a cam-
paign of organization which has failed.
As the group shows, resort is made at first to covert and finally to open threat
as to the consequences of not joining. The danger of being prevented from
working when the organization is effected, the pressure on wives and children
as the movement gains in strength, and the fear of the opprobrious term “scab”
carry into the organization more and more who join to avoid trouble.
Finally, particularly in time of actual strike, the pressure is applied by enough
instances of actual violence to shake the nerve of those who have not yet
come in.
We present affidavits of miners who went through this strike, and the results
of our own investigations are at the service of the commission; but the facts
could best be learned by the commission from the first-hand evidence of the men
themselves.
Further, the United Mine Workers of America succeeded in gaining the defi-
nite support of a certain part of the community, particularly in the town of
Matewan, one of the centers of the Hatfield feud. An important ally was Sid
Hatfield, then chief of police of this town, who, as we shall presently see,
brought into this dispute the methods of feud days.
F. Matewan massacre.-In May, 1920, at Matewan, one of the operating com-
panies discharged a number of miners who had become members of the United
Mine Workers of America.
The men refused to leave the company's houses. The company gave them
ten days' notice and extended it, on their failure to get out, the Baldwin-
Felts agency was employed to send men in from outside the field to remove
them. Evictions were made from six houses and were conducted in accord-
ance with the laws of West Virginia.
Albert and Lee Felts and eleven employees went into Matewan to take the
train to leave the county. A large crowd of armed United Mine Workers
gathered. While waiting for the train in front of a store, a shooting occurred,
in which Albert Felts and Lee Felts and four of his men were killed, and others
wounded. The mayor of the town, a boy and a member of the United Mine
Workers were also killed. Another member of the United Mine Workers was
wounded. Only Albert and Lee Felts and one of their men had pistols. None
of the others had arms available. One of the wounded Baldwin-Felts men.
in trying to escape, took refuge on the porch of a house some distance away.
He was badly wounded, unarmed and begging for mercy. He was shot down
by members of the union who had followed him from town. That night the
bodies of the Baldwin-Felts men were thrown like sacks of mail on a train
going to Williamson. Hatfield and about twenty members of the United Mine
Workers of America were tried for the murder of Felts and acquitted. The
evidence was conflicting as to whether Hatfield had become a member of the
United Mine Workers of America (testimony, State v. Sid Hatfield, submitted
herewith). A number of these same defendants were tried for the murder of
Ferguson, the wounded man, and the jury disagreed.
The United Mine Workers of America paid for the defense of these trials.
One of the most important witnesses for the State before the Grand Jury had
been murdered before the trial, and it was recently testified that this murder
was planned at a meeting of members of the United Mine Workers at Black-
berry City. (Carbon Fuel Co. v U. M. W. of A. p. 149.)
G. Progress of the strike.-Up to July 1 the companies had been operating
with diminishing forces. On that day a formal strike call brought the number
of men on the pay rolls to its lowest point. At this time, instead of a normal
number (something over 5,000), the total number on the pay roll in the Wil-
liamson field for July, 1920, was 2,673; but the major part of the men who re-
mained at work were up the valleys from the Tug River in Pike County, Ky.
In that county the sheriff from the start made every effort to afford protection
to the properties and men who desired to work, and succeeded in doing so
except on the properties along Tug River, which were exposed to fire from the

The
West Virginia side. The larger number of operations in the field lay along the
1 Tug River and here the strike was effective, the number of men on the pay rolls
dropping on July 15 to 107 in Mingo County, and only rising by the end of the
month to 658 in all the mines affected in both counties. In August there was
little change, and production in the mines on strike was only 33,000 tons.
number of men employed in the mines affected by the strike steadily increased
through the fall until in January there were over 3,000 men on the pay rolls,
substantially the normal number, and production increased to 185,000 tons.
From that time, although acts of violence continued, the mines continued to run
with a normal complement. During the whole of the strike only about 350
men were brought into the district by the companies to increase their working
force. A considerable number of these were normal replacements and went to
mines not affected by the strike.
H. Attack and defense.—(1) Firing on mining villages and operations--de-
struction of property: We have just pointed out the steady building up of the
operating force of the mines affected by the strike. This was only accomplished
in the face of violent attack which might well have deterred both operators
and mine workers. The United Mine Workers early began to bring quantities
of high-powered rifles and ammunition into the Williamson field and distribute
them. The method of covering up the use of funds for this purpose was the
same as that employed by Robb, the international financial agent, at Willis
branch. A certain amount of relief scrip would be left over each week. This
was cashed and the proceeds used for guns and ammunition. (Kenyon investi-
agting committee, testimony, p. 803.)
One witness testified that he knew of at least 700 rifles in the hands of the
United Mine Workers at one time in the Williamson field. These guns were
put to work in firing on the property of the companies which attempted opera-
tions in face of the strike order. Further, there were repeated attempts to
destroy the property of the operating companies by fire and explosion. A
chronology kept by the Williamson Operators' Association gives the most strik-
ing incidents of the attempt to prevent by violence the operation of the mines.
We shall here merely illustrate conditions by briefly noting incidents extending
over two of the months detailed in this chronology.

(2) The Mohawk affair: In August, 1920, the United Mine Workers deter-
mined to carry the strike into McDowell County, and to that end attacked the
mines operated by the Mohawk Coal & Coke Co., Tug River Field, just across
the line from Mingo County. Two organizers of the United Mine Workers
arranged for the guns and ammunition for this shooting, clearing through a
restaurant in Matewan (Kenyon Investigation, pp. 370-371). The attacking
party gathered during the night and on the morning of August 21 opened fire
on the cars on the incline as they began to take men up to work in the mine.
Warning, however, had been received of the impending attack and guards were
placed to meet it during the night on the property. The attack was repulsed.
A number of members of the United Mine Workers were indicted for attempt
to commit murder by this attack. They obtained a change of venue from
McDowell County to Greenbrier, a farming county. They were convicted.
Among others indicted for this offense was Sid Hatfield, of the Matewan affair.
While visiting Welch, the McDowell County seat, on this charge, he encountered
the detective who had given the warning as to the proposed attack on Mohawk
and whom he had threatened to shoot on sight. The detective shot and killed
him, claiming to be acting in self-defense. He was tried for this and acquitted.
(3) Federal troops called in: The sheriff of Mingo County made no effort
to check the increasing violence of the mine workers. The State militia had
not been reorganized after the war. The governor called upon the Federal
Government for assistance. Troops were sent into the field August 29, 1920,
many miners returned to work, the production increased, and the troops with-
drew on November 4. Almost immediately the violence increased and the troops
were ordered back and kept in Mingo County until February, 1921. By ar-
rangement between the Governor of Kentucky and the Governor of West Vir-
ginia, the troops policed both sides of the Tug River. This helped greatly in
stopping the shooting which had previously been going on with impunity from
one side across the river on the mines and miners attempting to work on the
other. The Kentucky National Guard assisted during part of the strike on the
Kentucky side of the river. The governor had also sent the West Virginia State
police to Mingo County under the command of Captain Brockus, who had served
for many years in the Regular Army of the United States and during the war
became a major of Infantry overseas. During the course of the strike four
of the men in his command were shot, all in the back. Three were killed.
A new sheriff came into office in January, 1921, and, unlike his predecessor,
did his utmost to enforce the law.
(4) The three days of May: In the spring a fresh effort was made to close
down the mines. As has been pointed out, the working force and production had
by this time returned to normal.
On May 12, 1921, fire was opened on the White Star Mining Co.'s plant at
Merrimac, from a low wooded ridge that runs along the river on the Kentucky
side only about 200 yards away from the buildings of the coal company. Fir-
ing upon other mines which were operating spread up and down the river for
seven or eight miles. The firing was controlled by blasts from a cow horn-
one blast to open fire and three blasts to cease firing. Three detachments of
deputy sheriffs and as many State police as possible gathered in defense. Dur-
ing the first day's firing Staton, a justice of the peace, who had been an im-
portant witness for the State in the Matewan case, was killed. Calvin McCoy,
a United Mine Worker and one of the defendants in the Matewan case,
was convicted of murder as a result of his participation in this killing.
On the next day the firing spread over an even wider area, from Rawl, W. Va.,
up the river to McCarr, Ky. The Allburn Coal Co. has a mine on the Kentucky
side of the Tug River at McCarr, just across from Blackberry City in West
Virginia. In a little hollow, back of Blackberry City, was a tent colony main-
tained by the United Mine Workers. On the hill back of the colony were
trenches from which firing into the Allburn Co.'s plant across the river had
been carried on. At Merrimac the wives and children of the men at work took
refuge in the mouth of one of the mines. In McCarr they sought safety in
the cellar of the company store. The upper part of that store still stands pock-


===== [扫描序号 998] =====
2002
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
marked with bullets. A shelter was constructed there in the cellar of the
store for three women about to become mothers. One child was born under
rifle fire in a company house at McCarr with mattresses piled around the bed
to keep off the bullets. One of the employees of the company was fatally
wounded on the bridge at McCarr between Kentucky and West Virginia during
this shooting, but the firing was so heavy that no one could get out and bring
him in. He lay there during the greater part of the day until a rope was
gotten to him on a weel and he was dragged down to the company store.
On the third day, firing was carried on at Sprigg, New Howard, McCarr, and
Merrimac. Staton was buried in the yard of his home and his grave was dug
under fire. Wives and children of the working miners at Sprigg and Burn-
well took refuge in concrete cellars during the three days' firing.
During these days the miners who had been at work, as during other attacks,
fought in their own defense and acted as their own "mine guards." The State
police force gave such assistance as it could over such a wide area.
(5) Public sentiment in Mingo crystallizes: Coming as it did after nearly a
year of disorder, this three days of firing aroused the citizens of the county,
whatever their general views might be as to contracts with the United Mine
Workers, to a determination to restore the observance of the law in the county.
Among the most effective leaders in this movement was Mr. Carpenter, a Pres-
byterian minister in Williamson. A meeting was called at the county seat of
all interested in restoring law and order. Captain Brockus of the State police
addressed this meeting and told the citizens that if they desired law and order
they would have to aid in enforcing it themselves. The sheriff of Mingo
County issued a warrant to the State police, pursuant to the West Virginia
statute, calling upon that department to enforce the laws of the State. Cap-
tain Brockus then enrolled about 780 volunteer State policemen. Further,
Governor Morgan declared martial law in Mingo County on the 18th of May.
Maj. Tom Davis, acting as adjutant general of the State, was sent to take active
charge of the martial law area.
From this time on disorders decreased. There were a few outbreaks, trace-
able in the most part directly to tent colonies which the United Mine Workers
were maintaining.
These tent colonies were instituted at the beginning of the strike by the
United Mine Workers' organization. They furnished shelter for the workers
who had been induced to strike and in them that organization supported in
idleness all those who preferred to stay on the spot rather than seek work else-
where. The companies offered to pay the moving expenses to union fields of
former employees, their families and household goods.
The organization used these tent colonies as a means of securing public
sympathy and as a reason for raising a national assessment. (United Mine
Workers Journal, January 15, 1921, p. 15.)
The tent colony has come to be recognized as primarily a weapon of offense
of the United Mine Workers' organization and not a relief institution. They
were maintained in Williamson long after it had appeared that enough men
had remained at work and preferred to return to work to make the strike
entirely hopeless in the absence of successful violence. Here, as elsewhere,
they proved demoralizing to the people maintained by the organization doles.
In the middle of June, 1921, the superintendent of the White Star mine was
fired upon while passing the Lick Creek tent coloney in an automobile. Adju-
tant General Davis, the sheriff, Captain Brockus and three members of the
State police went to the Lick Creek colony to investigate the firing. They were
fired upon by rifle from the county road, but without casualties. They went
back to Williamson, called out the State police and returned to Lick Creek with
a force of 70 men and surrounded the colony. Captain Brockus with 55 State
policemen went up behind where the firing earlier in the day had come from.
When within about 800 yards of the tent colony the left of their line was
fired upon.
Advancing, they came on Alexander Breedlove, a Union miner,
gun in hand, crouching behind a tree, with ammunition and food enough with
him to last for a day or more of fighting. Called on to surrender, he raised his
gun to fire and was killed. Private Bolles of the State police was seriously
wounded. (Kenyon Committee Investigation, pp. 309, 310.) The Lick Creek
colony was searched and all guns and ammunition taken from them. Seven or
eight of the men captured in the tent colony were indicted by the Grand Jury
for offenses in connection with the strike. (Kenyon Committee Investigation.
pp. 332-346.)

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2003
The exhibition on the part of the citizens of Williamson of their determina-
tion to enforce law and order, even at personal risk, broke the backbone of the
campaign of violence and with the end of violence the strike died a natural
death and conditions returned to normal.
I. Attitude of the miners of Williamson.-On June 30, 1921, there were about
5,200 men on the pay rolls of the mines in the Williamson field. Of these,
4,931 signed a petition to the senatorial investigating committee stating that
they were satisfied with their terms of employment, that they did not wish to
become members of the United Mine Workers or to be interfered with in their
work by that organization. In one colliery. the impression was gathered by
the men that the petition was got out for the purpose of soliciting members
for the United Mine Workers, and until this was cleared up the men refused
to sign.
There was also a petition bearing the names of 912 women, wives and rela-
tives of miners, which was circulated upon the initiative of these women,
asking the Kenyon committee not to interfere with the status existing between
the employers and employees.
But of far more significance than any petition was the action of these miners
and their families in sticking to their work through this campaign of violence
and taking a hand in their own defense against the assault on their right
to work. Many of the workers who were initially induced to go on strike
went to the union fields for employment but have since returned to Williamson,
preferring individual contracting with the operator to the control of the mine
committee and officials of the United Mine Workers. The commission can
readily satisfy itself that at the present time mine workers, as well as operators
in this field, are opposed to contracting with the United Mine Workers
of America and the imposition of the check-off; that the earnings. hours of
work, living conditions, and spirit of independence and initiative of these mine
workers compare favorably with those of mine workers in the fields where the
operators contract with the United Mine Workers of America. We have con-
siderable detailed information on this matter which is at the disposal of the
commission if it desires it.
V. ARMED MARCHES OF THE UNITED MINE WORKERS
A. The 1919 march on Logan.-In the years 1912-1919 there had been a very
rapid development in the Logan field. This is situated in the valley of the
Guyandot River just over the mountain from Boone County and the Coal River
side of Logan County, which are part of the Kanawha district. In the Kanawha
district, as we have seen, the operators had for many years contracted with the
United Mine Workers' organization. The competition of the Logan field,
in the depression which immediately followed the war, made itself felt in the
unionized districts.
As a step in the general campaign of the United Mine Workers to organize
all of southern West Virginia, and in the first instance the Logan field, a letter
was sent out from the headquarters of district No. 17 at Charleston, W. Va., to
all locals throughout the district. This letter reads in part as follows:
"The miners of the Guyan River and the Norfolk & Western fields are ready
for organization. They have made up their minds to eliminate the thug system
and be free. We are going to organize those fields regardless of the opposition
and some of them are now on strike against the deplorable conditions which
compose their environment and they appeal to you through us for assistance
to obtain that degree of democracy so widely advertised for the last few years.
* * *They are now beating men up and jailing them right and left because
they have dared to ask for their constitutional rights and the piteous appeals
coming from that section leads us to believe that they mean business,
Shortly after the circulation of this letter, armed members of the United
Mine Workers began to assemble at Marmet on the Kanawha River, about 10
miles from Charleston, the State capital.
*
On September 4, 1919, Governor Cornwell went up to Lens Creek, about 10
miles above Charleston, and found a very large body of men in camp, the
president of the District estimating the number at 5,000. A large number
were carrying rifles, all high powered, so far as the governor could observe
by moonlight and the glare of the camp fires. Keeney, the president of the
district, urged by the governor to disperse the men, had told him it was
impossible to do so. The governor addressed the men, urging them to abandon


===== [扫描序号 1000] =====
2004
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
their adventure and stating that he would make an investigation of the alleged
outrages carried on in the Logan coal fields, and that if there were illegal
practices there he would do all he could to see that they were corrected. In
spite of the governor's speech, the march continued through Kanawha County
and up through Boone County toward Logan as far as Madison. Meanwhile,
Governor Cornwell asked that Federal troops be sent in. They actually en-
trained, and when this fact became known at Madison, the march was discon-
tinued. It had then proceeded about 30 miles.
B. Investigation and report by the governor's commission. The governor
directed Acting Adjt. Gen. Thomas B. Davis to make an investigation, and Col.
George S. Wallace of Huntington, former Assistant Judge Advocate General in
the War Department and later in the A. E. F., to conduct the examination of
witnesses.
The commission met, in accordance with the governor's direction, and invited
the operators and the United Mine Workers to present evidence. In scope it
went beyond the mere facts of the march and included conditions existing in
the nonunion mines in Logan County at that time.
The commission found that no armed guards were employed, but that the
Coal Operators' Association paid a sum of money each month to the sheriff,
which was used by him in employing deputy sheriffs. It examined the charges
that the "guards had beaten, slugged, and maltreated workers and other per-
sons in the Logan field and infringed upon the rights of law-abiding persons."
As to these charges the commission examined evidence presented by the United
Mine. Workers and found that there had been one assault without justification;
that there were three cases of assault as to which there was a dispute as to
justification; that two men men had been stopped and questioned, and a third
arrested and searched. The other witnesses who had been arrested charged
with offences, with the exception of one against whom the warrant had been
withdrawn, had been tried and found guilty. The commission pointed out that
in considering these cases the tension occasioned in Logan County by the
threatened invasion of an armed force was to be borne in mind and that " upon
consideration of these incidents they do not suffice to sustain this charge or to
justify the wholesale indictment of conditions in Logan County."
As to the question, "Are men kept in mines by threats and intimidation?" the
commission replied, "There is not a scintilla of evidence in this record from any
source to justify this charge."
To the question, “Do a large majority of the workmen in the Guyan field
desire to join the union, but are prevented by force from doing so?" the com-
mission replied, "The evidence under this head shows an expression of opinion
of the several witnesses who testified, and each witness was equally certain that
his opinion was correct. If the testimony of the operators is entirely disre
garded, and the opinions of the men who testified as witnesses on behalf of the
United Mine Workers of America are accepted, they do not sustain this propo-
sition."
Further, the commission "went largely into the welfare work and the social
and religious conditions as they obtained in the Guyan field (now generally
called Logan), and whatever may be the motive of those who are responsible for
these conditions, the record abundantly shows that the labor, industrial and
living conditions in this field are as good as in the best coal fields in the State."
Finally, the commission found from its examination of facts that the evi-
dence introduced by the United Mine Workers of America did not justify the
inflammatory statements contained in the letter addressed by them to the local
unions and the newspaper interviews published about the same time, and that
these statements by union officials had been the proximate cause of the march.
For example, the officials had represented to the rank and file that Forber, one
of their organizers sent into Logan County, was in danger at a time when he
was actually with them in Charleston and entirely safe.
The most important lesson, as we see it, of the 1919 march is that it was
made possible by the misrepresentation to the rank and file of the miners as to
actual conditions in the Logan field. This emphasizes the importance, as we
see it, if there is to be peace in West Virginia, of the commission, in connection
with its discussion of labor relations there, setting forth the facts as to the living
and working conditions of the miners in fields which do not contract with the
United Mine Workers of America, and ending those misconceptions which again
and again are made the incitements to violence.
C. The 1921 march on Logan and Mingo.-In the early days of the strike in
Mingo County the argument was used that, if necessary, there would be an


===== [扫描序号 1001] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2005
› armed march into that country from Paint and Cabin Creeks that would force
the unionization of the district. After the declaration of martial law by the
I Government after three days' fighting in May, 1921, and the aroused public
I opinion of the citizens of the county, disorder was practically ended and the
mines were operating with a normal force. If these conditions continued, the
attempt to organize the county, on which, according to the testimony of the
district president of the United Mine Workers of America, more than $2,500,000
had been spent, was definitely defeated.
During the past year feeling had run high. As during the weeks preceding
the march of 1919, stories of oppression and violence directed against the
members of the United Mine Workers were spread in the organized fields of
West Virginia. With the defeat of their efforts in the Williamson field staring
them in the face, the feeling of bitterness and readiness to believe any story
that circulated, and the hostility of the power of the government of the State
which had asserted itself in the declaration of martial law, grew and spread.
(1) PRELIMINARY PROPAGANDA BY OFFICERS OF THE UNITED MINE WORKERS
On Sunday, August 7, 1921, a mass meeting was called in the capitol grounds
at Charleston in Kanawha County, by the United Mine Workers for the pur-
pose of discussing the Mingo situation. This meeting was addressed by C. F.
Keeney, president of district 17; by Mother Jones, an organizer in the employ
of the international organization, and by others. It has been testified that
Keeney said at this meeting: "The only way you can get your rights is with a
high-powered rifle, and the man who has not got this equipment is not a union
man.' (Testimony of Earl Hager in Blizzard murder trial just completed.)
Keeney, in testifying at the same trial, denied having made this speech. A
committee was appointed to draft resolutions to be submitted to Governor
Morgan. The resolutions in effect called upon the governor to rescind his
martial-law proclamation in Mingo County. This he refused to do.
On August 14, 1921, at Kingmont near Fairmont in Marion County, which is
in the northern part of West Virginia, Keeney addressed a meeting of United
Mine Workers and others. A. O. Stanley, a lawyer, who lives in Fairmont
in a United Mine Worker field, testified as follows in the treason trial of Walter
Allen as to Keeney's speech:
"Mr. Keeney, without any introduction by the chairman, began his speech.
The first thing he said was that he felt glad to be in the northern part of the
State owing to the relation between the miners and the coal operators, and that
it was a pleasure to be there. He said the same conditions would exist in the
southern part of the State if they were organized and had proper protection.
He went on to say, 'There are probably persons here under the sound of my
voice that in the last fall election cast their elective franchise for the present
executive of this State, and whoever did it is a red-handed murderer, for
Governor Morgan is as much a murderer as any pirate that ever sailed the high
seas.'
He said women and children were being murdered in the southern part of the
State, and that Governor Morgan knew it and refused to give protection. He
made the remark that they were going to organize that coal field down there
if it took all the United Mine Workers of America to do it; that they had
attempted to organize it and could not do it; and he said further that there was
now 500 men under arms in the southern part of the State and others were
arming, and that they were going to organize that field, and all of Don Chafin's
hired gunmen and all of the companies' thugs and all of Governor Morgan's
Cossacks couldn't prevent them. He said if they did undertake to organize
it and were prevented he didn't know what would happen; that whatever did
happen would not be his fault, but could be laid at Governor Morgan's door.
He said: "It is my opinion that if we meet any resistance," or words to that
effect, that the Matewan affair would look like a sunbonnet parade compared
with what would happen."
(Record, pp, 582-583, State v. Wa'ter
Allen, submitted herewith.)
At the same time there had been meetings of a great many locals in Kanawha,
Fayette. Raleigh, and Boone Counties protesting against the Mingo martial law
and the governor's refusal to withdraw his proclamation. At one of these
meetings Savoy Holt, a United Mine Workers' organizer, made a speech, testi-
fied to by J. S. McKeaver, general superintendent for the Kanawha & Hocking
Coal & Coke Co., a company contracting with the United Mines Workers, in
the Walter Allen trial:

"But Savoy Holt's speech was very explicit. He told of things that were
being done over there and said that the State had taken possession of that ter-
ritory; that they had gone to Eph Morgan (he referred in that way to the
governor) and asked that martial law be revoked, and he had refused to do it;
he said: Now, it is up to us.' He went on to say there would be a place desig-
nated and the time appointed, and if you are men you will be there, prepared

Similar speeches were made at various other local meetings, and it was
understood among all union men in Paint and Cabin Creek and neighboring
fields that something was going to be done about Mingo County.
Earl Hager testified in the recent murder case of the State v. William Bliz-
zard that at a mass meeting held at Laurel City before the armed march a letter
was read from C. F. Keeney saying, "Every drop of blood and every dollar
of the union will be spent in the attempt to lift marial law in Mingo County."
This letter was greeted by loud cheers.
(2) FIRST ACTS OF VIOLENCE AND ATTACK ON CONSTITUTED AUTHORITY
Arms appeared in the hands of the members of the United Mine Workers.
There was a prevading restlessness and a sense that action was impending.
Up in Boone County, which was situated next to Logan, occurred the first
acts of violence. On August 12, 1921, Dr. W. F. Harliss, who lived at Clothier,
W. Va., which is just on the line between Boone and Logan Counties, had to
make a professional call at J. W. Swanner's house. A man named Embry,
a conductor on the Chesapeake & Ohio Railroad, offered to take him in his
automobile. While the doctor was making his call Embry took his sister-in-
law, together with another girl and a man, up the road for a ride. As the
doctor came out of the Swanner house he saw the car coming down the
road and a group of about 40 or 50 armed men coming up. These men sud-
denly opened fire on the car. Embry put on speed and got away without
anybody being injured, but with six bullet holes in the car and two bullets
through his hat. (Dr. W. F. Harliss, pp. 011-015, State v. Walter Allen.)
Josh Pauley testified in the State v. Allen case (pp. 039 and 049) that he was
forced to go along with the crowd which shot up Embry's car, and that Lewis
White, a member of the United Mine Workers and leader of the crowd, re-
marked as the car came in sight, "Here comes a lot of Baldwin thugs."
It was about dusk when this shooting occurred, and it appears that the crowd
of men who did the shooting thought that the car contained Logan County deputy
sheriffs, whom the United Mine Workers were in the habit of referring to as
'Baldwin thugs." There had, in fact, been no Baldwin-Felts guards in Logan
County since 1912.
This shooting took place in Logan County, and by the time Doctor Harliss
had walked home, he found that his wife had already called up the wife of
John Browning, at Ethel, and had told her about the attack. Mrs. Browning
told her husband, who was a deputy sheriff, and he with another Logan deputy
and two members of the State police in uniform, started out toward Clothier,
in order to apprehend the men who had done the shooting. They were stopped
between Sharples and Clothier by the same crowd that had shot Embry's car,
and were so outnumbered by armed members of the union that they were forced
to surrender and give up their guns. After they had been disarmed, they were
told to get back home, which they did. (State v. Walter Allen pp. 015-094-096.)
From that time on the roads in the eastern part of Logan County and the
western part of Boone County were patrolled continually by armed members
of the United Mine Workers. John Brown, a member of the United Mine
Workers at Blair, testified in State v. Allen (p. 657), and also in Carbon Fuel v.
International Mine Workers' Union (p. 322), that he advised against hostilities
and was consequently severely beaten by his associates. He was then told that
he must "Fight, guard, or die." He decided to guard, and patrolled the roads
in the vicinity of Blair.
(3) Organization of the march: A mass meeting was called for August 20 at
Marmet, the same little town, about 10 miles up the Kanawha River from
Charleston, from which the 1919 march had started. Before the date set for
this mass meeting officials of local unions began to gather up guns and ammuni-
tion and to procure funds for the march, which it was generally understood
was to be the upshot of the mass meeting. In a great many cases where the
local union officials in charge of the funds of a local were unwilling to turn


===== [扫描序号 1003] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2007
them over, they were forced to do so at the point of a gun. The necessity for
money was so great that even the burial funds of many locals were handed
over to buy guns, ammunition, and other supplies. (State v. Allen, pp. 108, 169,
210, 295, 337, 345, 355, 385, 462.)
On August 20, according to schedule, a large number of union members
assembled at Marmet and went into camp there on Lens Creek. The camp
was apparently well organized and under good discipline. While these men
were assembled under arms at Lens Creek various reports about the matter
came out in the Charleston papers. Two responsible citizens of Charleston
motored up to Marmet to see for themselves exactly what the conditions were
there. They were halted by a man who was walking post armed with a rifle
on the public highway and asked what their business was. They told him
that they wanted to go farther up the river; that they had some sort of busi-
ness to attend to there. The sentry told them that he would have to consult
his superior before he could let them pass. (Testimony of Patrick Kuntz in
Blizzard treason trial.) At about this time the local union at Gallagher, on
Paint Creek, sent a delegation to Charleston to interview the district president.
Henry W. Dawson, who was on this committee, testified as follows in the case
of Carbon Fuel Co. v. International Organization United Mine Workers et al.,
in June, 1923:
"A. Well, we talked to Mr. Keeney.
66
Q. What did he tell you as to the matter?-A. Well, he told us to go back
home.

Q. Did he make any statement to you at the time as to how the matter

Lawrence Dwyer was a member of the international executive board of the
United Mine Workers of America, attached to district No. 29, who had been
active in the Willis Branch matter. Dawson also testified that Dwyer sug-
gested to him that a machine gun which had been obtained for Willis Branch
by George Barrett, an international organizer, be turned over for the march,
that it was brought down and handed over with 3,000 rounds of ammunition,
and that it was subsequently taken on the march up to the firing line (Carbon
Fuel Co. v. United Mine Workers of America, pp. 41 to 45, 343, 346).
A young man named Petry, about 20 years old, was sent by members of the
union to get some guns at a company store at Cedar Grove. He went to the
store and talked to the superintendent, coming back without the guns. When
he told the men who had sent him of his failure, he was immediately shot
and killed, and his body put into an automobile in which it was carried to an
undertaker's at East Bank (State v. Walter Allen, p. 0148). The men who
had killed him knocked at the door, threw the body inside and called to Mr.
Pryor, the undertaker, saying, "Here, take charge of this damn scab."
On August 24 Mother Jones addressed a meeting of the men in camp at Lens
Creek. She urged them to disperse and go home and said that she had a tele-
gram from President Harding, ordering them to abandon the march. When
she had finished speaking, Keeney, the president of district 17, and Mooney, its
secretary-treasurer, told the men that the telegram was a fake, and that the
march had gone too far to be abandoned. Guard lines were thrown out to
prevent anyone from going home (State v. Allen, p. 171). Keeney and Mooney
went back to Charleston, called up President Harding's secretary, and found
that the telegram was in fact not authentic. Mooney at once took this word
to the Lens Creek camp (testimony of Fred Mooney, State v. Walter Allen, p.
1210), and that night the column got under way (State v. Allen, pp. 213-14).
(4) Object of march: The purpose of the march, as testified to by many
witnesses who had a part in it, and by others who heard the general conversa-
tions of the marchers, was mainly to overthrow martial law which was inter-
fering with the strike in Mingo County. The way to Mingo County from
Marmet was through an attack on nonunion Logan County. There was also
talk of disposing of the sheriff of Logan County and his deputies and of blow-
ing up Logan County courthouse. (State v. Allen, pp. 172, 212, 300, 328, 347,
348, 372, 379; Carbon Fuel Co. v. U. M. W. of A., pp. 16, 245, 255.)
(5) The march to Madison: The general line of march from Marmet was the
same as that in 1919, but the 1921 march was a much more ambitious affair
and was carried out in a much more businesslike manner. On the evening of
August 24 the column moved up Lens Creek, across the mountain, and down
to Racine on Big Coal River, a distance of 10 or 12 miles in a southwesterly


===== [扫描序号 1004] =====
2008
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
direction. After marching all night they went into camp that morning on
Indian Creek, which flows into the Coal River about a mile below Racine.
The camp at Racine was reinforced by a large number of men who had come
down Coal River from Raleigh and Fayette Counties. Part of the force in
this camp left Racine on the 25th on a train commandeered from the Chesa-
peake & Ohio Railroad. This train was sent down Big Coal River to Sproul,
then up Little Coal River to the ball ground between Madison and Danville.
which had been selected as the next camping place. (State v. Allen, p. 175.)
Another force marched over the rough country roads from Indian Creek to
Madison, a distance of 13 or 14 miles.
On the 26th of August practically the whole marching force was camped on
the ball grounds. Further up the Little Coal River at Jeffery, Sharples and
Blair the armed miners from Boone County and the union side of Logan County
had taken possession of the roads and positions in the hills.
(6) State authorities appeal to Federal Government: Meanwhile, the sheriff
of Boone County had appealed to Governor Morgan for assistance in stopping
the march. The governor had at his disposal at the time less than 100 State
police. The National Guard had never been reorganized after its demobilization
at the end of the war. He therefore directed the sheriff of Logan County to
swear in a large number of extra deputies and appealed to President Harding
for Federal assistance. In response to this appeal Major General Bandholtz
and Major Thompson, both of the United States Army, were sent to Charleston.
On August 26th General Bandholtz sent Keeney and Mooney to Madison to
order the United Mine Workers there to disperse and go home. There were
then camping in and around the baseball park between six and seven thousand
United Mine Workers, most of whom were armed (State v. Allen, p. 176).
Keeney made a speech to these men in which he advised them to go home.
Holly, a member of the local union at Leevale, gave this testimony as to
Keeney's conduct after this speech:
"Q. After he made that public statement to the men did you hear him say
anything else?-A. I did.
"Q. What was that?-A. He got down from where he made the speech and
walked over with three or four more fellows and told them he had to make
that speech in order to save district 17, but he said he had went too damn far
to turn back now.
"Q. Do you know to whom Frank Keeney was making this last statement?—A.
Well, several fellows standing there; our commander also was standing there,
Mr. Kirk.
"Q. Your leader?-A. Yes, sir." (State v. Allen, p. 460; see to same effect
testimony of Reynolds, State v. Allen, p. 177).
(7) The march goes on: Many of the marchers took a special train that night
down Little Coal River toward home, but several hundred others commandeered
a train and went on up Little Coal River to Jeffery, close to the border of Logan
County. Many others marched to Jeffery. There the expedition divided into
two parts. One under the command of Ed Reynolds went up Hewett Creek
into Logan County. The other went on to Blair, also in Logan, under the leader-
ship of William Brizzard, president of subdistrict 2, district 17, of the United
Mine Workers. The plan was for the two parties to go over the ridge to the
Guyandot Valley and meet at Logan County courthouse. Reynolds' detach-
ment went into camp on the mountain that night. (State v. Allen, pp. 179–184.)
(8) Measures of defense in Logan: While these events were taking place the
sheriff of Logan, at the direction of the governor, had organized a force of 2,000
or more men on the Guyan side of Logan County. This force was made up
largely of independent miners from Logan County augmented by volunteers
from McDowell, Mercer, and other counties. On the night of August 26 Major
Davis, in command of the martial-law area of Mingo County, at the governor's
orders, sent Capt. J. R. Brockus with 71 State policemen to Logan to the assist-
ance of the sheriff and to act under his orders. On August 27 the sheriff, acting
under the governor's previous direction (testimony of Governor Morgan, State v.
Allen, p. 247), gave Captain Brockus warrants for the arrest of the men who
had disarmed the State police on August 12, and with his State police force
and a number of Logan deputies he went up to Ethel, across the mountain, and
down Beech Creek toward Sharples, where he was informed the men were for
whom he had warrants. (State v. Allen, pp. 556–559.)
(9) The Beech Creek skirmish: It grew dark before Captain Brockus had
gone very far down Beech Creek. He and a party of about 15 State police
acted as point of the expedition with the deputy sheriffs in reserve. They


===== [扫描序号 1005] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2009
soon encountered a patrol of United Mine Workers, whom they arrested, and
proceeded down the creek. As they were coming to a mining camp belonging
to the Boone County Coal Corporation they were met by a large body of
armed miners, who asked their business, and immediately opened fire on them.
The State policemen returned the fire, killing two of the union men and
wounding three. Men in the houses of the mining camp began to fire at the
State policemen and they took to the ditches alongside the road. Captain
Brockus, not knowing the size of the force which opposed him, and being
unfamiliar with the county, decided to withdraw the State police and deputy
sheriffs to Ethel. The United Mine Workers taken prisoners had escaped in
the darkness and the excitement of the skirmish. (State v. Allen, pp. 559-565.)
(10) The firing line on Blair Mountain: After the Beech Creek skirmish the
sheriff and the State police organized their forces so as to hold a line from
Buffalo Creek, following the mountain ridges which separate the Coal River
from the Logan field for 15 or 20 miles, to the head of Big Creek (see map).
(State v. Allen, p. 258.)
Wild stories as to this skirmish were used to call back to the aid of the
United Mine Workers' forces on Blair Mountain those of the marchers who
had turned back from Madison. Rumors were freely circulated that women
and children were being murdered by the deputies in Logan County. It has
also been testified in the recent Blizzard trial that a typewritten letter bearing
the signatures of Keeney and Mooney, and certified by the district seal, tell-
ing the men to go on with the march, as it was the only way they could keep
out of jail, was circulated, and a trainload of armed men moved to Blair that
evening.
On August 30, 1921, a force of the United Mine Workers marched up Whites's
Trace Branch to attack the Logan deputies on Blair Mountain. The next
morning this force encountered three Logan deputies, John Gore, Cafalgo, and
Munsey. They shot and killed these three men. A negro who was among
the United Mine Workers was fatally wounded in the fight. (State v. Allen,
pp. 724-731 and 697-705.)
From August 27 until September 3 there was general firing along the whole
line from time to time. Doctor Milliken, of Blair, in the union side of Logan
County, testified:
"Q. To what extent was this firing?-A. It was sharp at times. I was in
the Spanish-American War in the Philippines, and I heard about as much
shooting at Blair as I did at Manila." (State v. Allen, p. 604.)
A number of prisoners were captured by the marchers and threatened and
beaten in an attempt to make them tell how many defenders there were in
Logan County. John Gore's son was one of these prisoners. He was taunted
and insulted about the death of his father, and told that he would meet a
similar fate. (State v. Allen, pp. 629, 630.)
(11) The Federal troops arrive: On August 27 General Bandholtz had gone
to Madison to investigate conditions. At that time the camp had broken up
there and the marchers had either advanced into Logan County or returned
home. The general saw no men and went back and reported that the dis-
turbance was over and left for Washington at just about the time that the
Beech Creek skirmish took place. When Governor Morgan learned that the
march had not in fact been abandoned he appealed again to the President and
seat Adjutant General Charnock to Sharples to order the United Mine Workers
to disperse, which they refused to do. General Bandholtz returned to West
Virginia and recommended that Federal troops be sent there. (State v. Allen,
235, 236.) On September 3 two companies of the Nineteenth Infantry moved
up Coal River to Madison and Blair for the purpose of disarming the United
Mine Workers assembled there. About the same time another detachment
of the Nineteenth Infantry moved into Logan County on the Guyan side.
all, about 2,400 Federal troops, Infantry, accompanied by some machine guns
and several airplanes, moved into the region. The United Mine Workers' forces
offered no resistance to the Federal troops. Many of them were disarmed,
others hid their arms and ammunition in the woods, and all of them went
home almost immediately.

(12) Attempted military organization of the marchers: The United Mine
Workers' forces maintained a remarkable degree of organization throughout
the march. The commissary department was well taken care of and mess
halls were established at various school houses near the firing line. Trains
and automobiles were commandeered whenever necessary for transportation.
On some of these trains large signs were displayed marked "Mingo bound."

The union counties were thoroughly combed for guns and ammunition for
days before the beginning of the march. The marchers were accompanied
by nurses in uniform, wearing instead of the conventional red cross the
letters of "U. M. W. of A." on their caps. Highways in Boone, Logan, and
Kanawha Counties were thoroughly patrolled by guards. When the marching
column arrived from Marmet on Hewett Creek its leader found that the Boone
and Logan County union men had organized their patrol system so well
that he had to pass through guard lines about every 200 yards going up
Hewett Creek on to the mountain (State v. Allen, p. 180.) Passwords were
required in order to move about the country. The first password employed
was "To Mingo." The uniform adopted was a blue overall suit with a red
handkerchief tied around the neck. This, it was explained to the marchers.
had been the sign of the United Mine Workers on Paint and Cabin Creeks
in 1912 and 1913. C. G. Williams, a pay roll auditor for the Boone County
Coal Corporation, a union mine, and who was in the service during the war.
testified as follows in regard to an incident which took place at Sharples:
"Q. What was this platoon doing at the time you observed it-or these
squads? A. I noticed one company march up opposite the station, face to the
front, and commanded by a man acting as a captain. He faced the men to
the front, like a captain of an army would do. He called the roll call and
started with man No. 1. He said 'Here,' he got down to 39, 39 was absent.
He called a man from the rear of the company, probably a lieutenant, to
know where the man was. Later he ordered the men to throw down their tin
cups, he said they were going into action that night and he didn't want any-
thing to rattle." (State v. Allen, p. 518.)

(13) Attitude of the international organization toward the armed march of
1921: Philip Murray, vice president of the international organization of United
Mine Workers of America, visited the "battle front" at the time of the 1921
Logan march. He admitted before the Kenyon committee that he had reported
to the convention of the United Mine Workers of America as follows:
"I visited the battle front, met with large numbers of the citizens' army,
discussed every phase of the so-called insurrection with them, and am satisfied
in my own mind that if Federal troops had not arrived in the State of West
Virginia at the time they did, that there would have been very little cause for
further complaint from anyone about further activities of Baldwin-Felts mine
guards in the State of West Virginia, as it was self-evident to any casual
observer that the outcome was inevitable, as the citizens' army was making
steady advance into the camp of its enemy." (Kenyon Committee Testimony,
p. 671.)
(14) Impression made by march on West Virginia: The armed march of
1921 made a deep impression upon the operators and independent mine workers
of southern West Virginia. From a safe distance there appeared to have been
a great deal of arming, a great deal of organization and marching, and a great
deal of firing for a very few casualties. But ineffective firing sounds very
different several hundred miles away from the way it does to those in front of
it and to whom it has not yet been demonstrated that it will consistently miss
its mark. To that body of Logan citizens, the greater number of them inde
pendent mine workers, who took arms under the leadership of the State officials
and stretched out in a thin line to defend the valley, the advance of this armed
