CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2011
force in definance of the State authority seemed anything but the grotesque and
absurd adventure which, from a safe distance, it now appears to have been.
Few have the philosophy to regard a bullet fired in their direction as only
serious if it kills or wounds.
(15) Prosecutions: It was determined in Logan to make every effort to en-
force the law against the leaders of this march. Indictments for treason and
murder were found in that county, but a change of venue was asked and
granted and the trails have proceeded in farming counties far distant from
the scene of the fight. The funds of the State available for these necessarily
expensive prosecutions proved to be wholly inadequate, and, as is the custom
in West Virginia and of old in England and many of our States, attorneys
employed by those had been attacked aided the State in the prosecution.
William Blizzard, president of subdistrict 2 of district 17, was first tried
for treason in Charles Town, W. Va. He was acquitted. Next J. E. Wilburn
was tried and convicted of second degree murder. Next Walter Allen of the
Dry Branch local was tried and convicted of treason. In all of these cases
the defense was conducted by the attorneys for the United Mine Workers of
America. In one of these cases an application for delay was made on the
ground that the defense had no funds to pay their witnesses, and as there
were no State funds available for this purpose the trial would have had to
go over except for the fact that the necessary funds were contributed by the
operators to the State to pay for the witnesses and so defeat the technical
plea of poverty raised by the United Mine Workers' attorneys. The first
trials were against the men who were in close proximity to the actual killing,
but indictments were also found against the men whom the evidence before the
grand jury had indicated to be the more responsible leaders in the movement.
Blizzard, who was acquitted of treason, has recently been tried in Greenbrier
County for murder, the jury disagreeing. Money, the secretary of district
No. 17, Keeney, its president at the time of the march, and Houston, counsel
for the district, are under indictment for murder awaiting trial.
These trials are being prosecuted under great difficulties and at a personal
risk by the participants on behalf of the State, whether as witnesses or
counsel, that makes the task that they are doing a public service which it
takes a high degree of courage to render. For example, this incident has
occurred during the life of the commission. Immediately preceding the second
trial of William Blizzard two of the most important witnesses for the prose-
cution were Ed Reynolds and J. W. Swanner, who had both been associated
with Blizzard in the attack on Logan county. Reynolds had testified for
the State in the Allen trial. (State v. Walter Allen, pp. 166-206.) J. R.
Miller, who was an old friend and associate of Reynolds and Swanner in the
United Mine Workers' organization, was among those who had been indicted
in West Virginia for the killing growing out of the armed march of 1921.
He had fied to Ohio and was living at the Vulcan mine in the Pomeroy district.
He had sent word to Reynolds and Swanner that he desired to return to
West Virginia. On the morning of May 9, 1923, Swanner and Reynolds arrived
at the little village of Rutland, looking for Miller. They bore an offer of
immunity to him from the prosecuting attorneys in West Virginia if he would
testify in the Blizzard case. Savoy Holt, a member of the United Mine
Workers and friend and associate of the men about to be brought to trial against
whom Miller was sought as a witness, apparently got wind of the trip and
after meeting Swanner and Reynolds casually in Rutland drove at top speed
to Miller's house. Swanner and Reynolds made some search for the house
and arrived shortly after Holt. They went upon the porch and while standing
there shots fired from within killed Swanner instantly. Reynolds, who was
lame, started to limp away. He fell dead, shot three times in the back. Both
bodies were unarmed. Miller was indicted and tried, and, taking the stand
in his own defense, stated that Savoy Holt had so worked on his fears that
he shot Swanner and Reynolds as described on their appearing at his house.
He was convicted of manslaughter. Holt is about to be tried as an accessory.
The State thus lost two of its important witnesses. The probable effect of
such an incident on the minds of others is evident.
Blizzard was about to be put on trial for the third time when the court, on
evidence of attempts to tamper with the panel on behalf of the defense, sus-
pended the case. The grand jury of Greenbrier County had just handed down
an indictment against the foreman of the jury of the second Blizzard trial which
disagreed for accepting a bribe on behalf of the defense and for attempting to
bribe members of the incoming panel.

It has also just handed down indictments against Clarence Hickey for at-

(16) Conclusion. We are not concerned here with the individual guilt of
Blizzard or of Mooney or of Keeney or of any other of the leaders of the United
Mine Workers of America. That is a matter which will be before the courts
and juries of the State of West Virginia; but it is apparent from the bare
facts, as to which there is no dispute, that there was a march, that the people
who participated in it were members of the United Mine Workers' organization.
that it was armed, that there was sufficient directing brains to organize and
carry forward a body of over 6,000 men over a distance of 50 miles, and sufficient
determination to proceed in defiance of State authority and only yield to the
intervention of the Federal troops; that it had as its specific, declared object
the advance of the organization across Logan County and the abolition of
martial law in Mingo County; and that when it was checked by the arrival of
2,000 Federal troops it impressed the officers of those troops with its high degree
of organization.
VI. THE 1922 STRIKE IN WEST VIRGINIA
A. United Mine Workers lose ground in Kanawha field through arbitrary
control by the central organization.-On February 24, 1922, in view of the
approaching termination of the contracts with the United Mine Workers on
April 1, the Kanawha operators wrote to President Keeney, of district 17 of the
United Mine Workers, stating that the operators were willing to meet the
United Mine Workers on or before March 11, 1922, to negotiate a new wage
scale and working agreement. The officials of the United Mine Workers refused
to meet on the ground that they were bound by the decision of the policy com-
mittee of their international organization to make no district settlements until
an agreement had been reached in the central competitive field. On March
29 the operators posted notices at their mines stating that the mines would
continue to operate under a somewhat lower wage scale and on an open-shop
basis. A strike was called by the United Mine Workers, and at first most of
the mines shut down. Thirteen, however, continued to operate without any
interruption due to the strike, and this number had been increased until, in
August, over 126 mines were in operation, and production was approaching
normal. On August 19, 1922, after the signing of the Cleveland agreement, the
operators met the United Mine Workers of the Kanawha field to negotiate a
new wage contract, and the only questions at issue were those of a check-off
and the continued employment of nonunion men who had remained at work
without discrimination. The president of the Kanawha Coal Operators Associa-
tion offered to arbitrate these issues. This was rejected by the United Mine
Workers district officers on the ground that they were compelled by the action
of their international policy committee to reject any such proposal put to them
for arbitration. Following this several operators signed individual contracts
with the United Mine Workers organization, but a majority of the mines, pro-
ducing 60 per cent of the tonnage, continued to operate without contract with
the United Mine Workers organization.
The vigorous measures taken after the armed march in 1921 to uphold the
law and the repercussion of those events upon the minds of the members of the
United Mine Workers organization themselves made it possible, with the consent
of the majority of the miners, to change over the operation of these mines from
union to nonunion.
Further, the equity proceedings brought by operators, and the fact that the
important district leaders of the United Mine Workers were all under indict-
ment for murder, undoubtedly had a moderating effect upon the situation and
also prevented any such attempts being made in the nonunion fields of southern
West Virginia to call strikes in aid of the general campaign of the United Mine
Workers, as were made in Kentucky, Colorado, Utah, Tennessee, and Pennsyl
vania. There were some minor incidents of attempted intimidation, such as the
firing upon the incline of a mine in New River when the men were going up on
the lift to work, but generally, as in that instance, the sentiment among the
mine workers themselves was so strongly resentful of interference that they
themselves promptly took care of the situation.
B. Refusal of United Mine Workers to negotiate in the Fairmont district, and
the resulting strike.-In the Fairmont field, on the approach of the termination
of the existing contract with the United Mine Workers on April 1, 1922, the


===== [扫描序号 1009] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2013
operators early in March called upon the United Mine Workers to negotiate a
new wage scale. This the president of district 17 at first promised to do, but
finally refused, on the ground that district officials of the United Mine Workers
were bound by decision of the policy committee of the international organization
to enter into no contract for this district at that time. The officials of the United
Mine Workers thereupon called a strike throughout the Fairmont district on
April 1, 1922.
A few mines, which prior to April 1 were not under contract with the
union, continued to operate thereafter. The United Mine Workers attempted
to call out the workers in these mines by notices, by picketing, and, in prac-
tically every case, by some form of intimidation or violence.
A number of the operators who had had contracts with the union, in view
of this refusal of the United Mine Workers to negotiate, opened their mines
and offered work to miners in the neighborhood on an open-shop basis. Within
six weeks the mines of the W. H. Green Coal Co., New England Fuel & Trans-
portation Co., Shamrock Fuel Co., West Virginia Coal & Coke Co., Big Chief
Coal Co., and other operators-operating in all about 100 mines-opened
with those of their employees who desired to continue to work and others
from the neighborhood seeking employment.
There were no "professional
strike breakers" imported. These attempts to operate were obstructed by
continual picketing, intimidation, and violence.
At the Hughes mine, operated by the Robinson Coal Co., near Fairmont,
W. Va., a mob of several hundred strikers forced their way upon the com-
pany property on June 23, 1922, demanding that the miners be called out
from the pit so that they might speak to them. The superintendent notified
the sheriff, who with h's deputies arrested over 100 prisoners, partly armed.
Similar marches were made against practically every mine that attempted
to operate, but the sheriff and State police acted with firmness.
Mobs gathered in the streets and about the street car lines, shouting and
threatening miners going to and from their work. For example, there was
a violent attack by strikers and the r wives on men going to work in a street
car near Clarksburg. W. Va.. on June 23, 1922, repulsed by deputy sheriffs
with loss of life to the attacking party. No deputy sheriffs in this field were
employed or paid by the operators.
The extent of the acts of violence and attempts to intimidate workers was such
that the courts were called upon for aid, and in six counties in the Fairmont
field injunctions were issued against the United Mine Workers' leaders and
rank and file, prohibiting intimidation, trespass, destruction of property, and
similar acts of violence.
Fairmont field, like the Kanawha field, forms a part of district 17 of the
United Mine Workers. the officers of which were under indictment for the
killings growing out of the armed march of the summer before.
After the settlement at Cleveland in August work was resumed throughout
this field. Most of the companies signed a new agreement with the un on.
Some of these have found that they are unable to operate under the union
scale and have been forced to close and discharge their men. Some 40 other
companies, however, which formerly had contracts with the United Mine
Workers' organization, refused again to contract with it and have continued
operating open shop.
C. Attack by United Mine Workers locals from Pennsylvania on the Clifton-
ville Mine.-In the northern part of West Virginia, in the Pittsburgh district,
there occurred an incident in July, 1922, which made a very deep impression
throughout the State. Brooke County is situated in the Panhandle of West
Virginia, a narrow strip of territory running up along the Ohio River, squeezed
in between Pennsylvania and Ohio. Wellsburg, the county seat, is the center
of a long established, conservative, and thoroughly American citizenry whose
main industry is glass manufacture. To the west of Brooke County across the
Ohio River, the Ohio districts were completely controled by the Un'ted Mine
Workers' organization, and to the east across the Pennsylvania line in the
Pittsburgh district it exercised the same control. This narrow strip of the
West Virginia Panhandle between these thoroughly organized fields had long
been a sore point to the organization. It was in the Panhandle that the United
Mine Workers in 1907 had conducted the campaign against the nonunion
companies which was condemned by the Supreme Court in the Hitchman case
(245 U. S. 229).
There were continual efforts made by United Mine Workers to bring all
operators in this district into contrac ual relations with it, and this campaign


===== [扫描序号 1010] =====
2014
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
was successful by 1920, with the exception of mines operated by the Hitchman
Coal & Coke Co., by the Richland Co., and the West Virginia-Pittsburgh Coal Co.
Cliftonville is a little mining community on Cross Creek 3 miles east of the
Ohio River. On both sides of this valley hills rise to a height of about 300
feet. The Salkeld Co. had been operating the mine under a union contract
with the organization until the United Mine Workers stopped work on April
1, 1922. After being shut down for two months, in June, 1922, the Richland
Mining Co. leased the property from the Salkeld Co. and gave notice that it
would operate the mine through its subsidiary, the Richland Brooke Coal Co.
Up to this time the former employees continued living in the company's houses.
When the Richland Co, gave notice that it would open this mine it offered to
reemploy the old men. A few of them accepted this offer and are still working
for the company.
The others refused the offer and were forced to move when
the company needed the houses they were in for new employees. The company
charged them no back rent and paid for the work they had done in their gar-
dens during the spring. These men, perhaps 50 in number, formed a tent
colony on the north side of the creek. Work began at the mine on June 25,
and the company began to ship coal immediately. The new men employed were
about 50 in number-about 35 white and 15 negroes, all coming from neigh-
boring towns, most of them from Wellsburg, 15 or 20 from the near-by mines
of the West Virginia-Pittsburgh Coal Co. They were not imported "strike
breakers "or "thugs," but the usual run of American workmen who in this
instance chose work rather than allegiance to the United Mine Workers of
America. The company paid the scale of wages which had been in force at the
mine prior to the strike.
Beginning July 1, men from the tent colony and others began to make threats
against the workers. To prevent violence on the part of the picketers the com-
pany employed guards for its property. These men were not deputized nor
were they armed until the afternoon of July 15. Five were college men who
took the jobs during their summer vacations, and the others men from the
locality, all of good character.
Rumors of impending attack grew more serious on July 15. The sheriff
deputized the 15 guards and they were armed.
(1) Attack: On Sunday night, July 16, the superintendent of a mine 5 miles
away across the Pennsylvania border telephoned the superintendent at Clifton-
ville that local miners were assembling at the ball grounds to march on the
Cliftonville mine. Learning this at Wellsburg, H. H. Duval, sheriff of Brooke
County, took four men, including his son and two college men, and went at
once to Cliftonville.
Immediately after the warning message had come through, the telephone
wires were cut. The sheriff posted the 20 guards to cover the vulnerable
points of attack and mounted guard. Meanwhile at the ball grounds just
across the State line the United Mine Workers had been gathering. At Avella.
Pa., a few miles away, several local unions had met and planned the attack on
Saturday or Sunday morning. On the night of the 16th the Avella local as-
sembled and marched to Penobscot, being joined by other locals, stopping oc
casionally at groups of houses along the road to get members to joint them.
At the ball grounds they were met by the men from the Cedar Grove locals.
In all, there assembled at the ball grounds over 400 men, coming from the fol-
lowing locals: Studa; Donahue; P. & W. (No. 1355, Avella); Cedar Grove:
Waverly; and Jefferson.
Some men had come from Ohio. Addresses were made and the march started
about midnight down the railroad track and through the tunnel of the Wabash
Railroad to the West Virginia side. Coming out of the tunnel they were met
by the president of the Cliftonville local, who distributed additional arms and
ammunition, and directed them to take a back road and attack from the north.
The marching attackers were kept in order by file closers.
The first shot was fired from a steel casing of four-inch mouth, which had
been improvised as a cannon by the attackers and filed with powder and old
iron, placed just across the creek from the company property, and aimed at the
store. The charge only damaged the roof of one of the company houses. Cries
came from the ridge calling for immediate attack on the property, but the
attacking force was not in place yet and it was too dark. The sheriff's men
on guard at the conveyor house on the top of the tipple could occasionally
see and hear the men on the ridge about 100 yards above them. A train went

The main attacking party had come down the slate track to attack the con-
veyor. The six guards protecting it retreated under cover down the conveyor
returning the fire. Finding the defense stubborn, the attackers set fire to the
upper part of the tipple and conveyor and retreated in disorder. The sheriff's

this retreat started, was advancing alone through a small patch of woods to
the rear of the attacking party. In these woods he met the retreating miners.
After the attack was over his body was found there with the bodies of two
miners lying a short distance away. His two revolvers had been taken and his
body mutilated. In all at least six of the attacking party were killed. There
may have been more who were burned in the fire which had been set in the
head house.
(2) Prosecution: The authorities of Brooke County took immediate action,
and the county grand jury returned indictments against 230 men. Four mem-
bers of the United Mine Workers were tried, found guilty by juries and sen-
tenced to 10 years. Seven plead guilty and received sentences of from four
to eight years, including one officer of a local. Thirty pleaded guilty and
received sentences of three years, including the presidents of the Donahue local
and the Cedar Grove local, the temporary president and the recording secretary
of the P. & W. (Avella) local, and two pit committeemen. The president of
the Cliftonville local is a fugitive from justice. The defense was conducted by
the United Mine Workers of America and paid for out of funds raised by the
check-off.
(3) The attack not an isolated incident, but the expression of a widespread
belief and policy opposed to fundamental conceptions of American life: The
armed attack from without the State and the death of the sheriff in the line of
duty deeply stirred this community, and the law was enforced with a vigor
which will no doubt go far toward the preservation of industrial peace in that
part of West Virginia for many years to come. Enforcement of the law will
restrain but it will not reach the fundamental cause of the Cliftonville attack.
The 500 men who took arms and marched in that attack were not ordinary law
breakers. They were acting with the same motives and with the same convic-
tions that animated the members of the United Mine Workers in seven different
counties in Ohio in their armed attacks on workers at properties attempting to
operate at New Straitsville, New Lafferty, Weems, Cadiz, Adena, New Lexing-
ton, Harmon Creek, Jobs, and Uniontown. They were acting with the same con-
victions and same motives as the United Mine Workers in Johnson County, Ky..
in their attack on the North East Coal Co.'s property and workers; with the
same motives and convictions that inspired similar attacks in Indiana, similar
attacks in the Danville district in Illinois, and the attack on the strip mine at
Herrin, Ill. In fact, it appeared from the statements of the participants in the
Cliftonville attack that they had been definitely inspired and encouraged in
this attack by what had occurred at Herrin.
In the Hitchman case (245 U. S. 258) the Supreme Court of the
United States said: "The disordered condition of a mining town in time of
strike is matter of common knowledge." Why is this so? Why do intimidation,
riots, and marches seem necessarily to accompany almost every attempt to
mine and ship coal during a strike called by the United Mine Workers
organization?
The motive and belief which is at the bottom of all of these attacks is that
in time of strike it is the moral right and duty of members of the United Mine


===== [扫描序号 1013] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2017
Workers' organization to prevent the mining of coal by men not members of
their organization; that they are morally justified in taking violent means to so
prevent this mining; that they have a moral right to wage violent warfare to
accomplish a purpose which they believe to be for their advantage and pro-
tection.
The publications of the organization, which circulate among its members,
and the speeches of its organizers are shot through with the thread of this
belief, and with a spirit of bitter, almost personal, hatred of all operators who
do not contract with its organization, and of workers who are not members
of it and who are willing to work where a strike has been called. They are
shot through with inflammatory misstatements which inevitably create false
loyalties and false beliefs as to the rights and duties of its members. Its presi-
aent uses the epithet "common strike breakers" and 20 men are killed at Herrin.
When its members are told that the organization will throw its whole weight in
support of an effort to organize a district, they know that the whole weight of
the vast resources available through the "check-off" will be used to block any
efforts of the public to punish the perpetrators of violence.
So long as it remains the belief of members of the United Mine Workers'
organization that they have the moral right to prevent the mining of coal by
other workers-a belief which they are ready to risk their own personal safety
to act on-so long will such incidents as Cliftonville and Herrin and the rest
be the inevitable accompaniments of efforts to organize new territory as in
Mingo County, or in time of general strike unless, indeed, the community is
prepared to accept and enforce the principle that there shall be no mining of
coal, except by members of United Mine Workers' organization.
The general prevalence of this belief throughout the United Mine Workers'
organization is illustrated in three ways:
(1) No disciplinary action was taken by the national organization against
the locals participating in the Cliftonville attack any more than against those
participating in the numerous attacks in Ohio, in Kentucky, in Indiana, in
Danville, or in Herrin.
(2) Every person charged with a breach of the law in these attacks was
defended by attorneys employed by the United Mine Workers of America and
paid for out of funds raised by the check-off.
(3) There is, to put it conservatively, a tolerance and tacit approval of the
principle, even in the printed material circulated by the national organization
among its members. There was never a word of reprobation for such clear-cut
acts of unprovoked and unjustifiable violence as the attacks on the strip pits
in Ohio, on the mines of the North East Coal Co. in Kentucky, the Willis
Branch mine in West Virginia, and the Cliftonville mine in northern West
Virginia. After all these instances, and in spite of the fearful lesson which
had been taught at Herrin of the inevitable consequence of the cultivation of
this belief that the United Mine Workers have a moral right to keep every
miner not a member of their organization from working, on February 15, 1923–
during the life of this commission-the United Mine Workers' Journal published,
with evident relish, an account of the driving of men from work by intimida-
tion in England under the caption: "Some Reminiscences of the Coal Strike in
Great Britain During 1921-The Raid. This article was written by a British
miner and tells in a graphic way how the union miners of three districts broke
up a nest of 'blacklegs' (as British nonunionists are called), who were pro-
ducing coal while the union men were on strike." We submit a fac-simile copy
of this article.
Common sense and law are the obvious guides in fixing responsibility. Of
such situations a Federal court, in Alaska S. S. Co. v. International Longshore-
men's Association, 236 Fed. 964, at page 972, has said:
"When persons or parties set in motion machinery for the purpose of shaping
sentiment, they can not take the benefits without also being burdened with
responsibilities. Such parties thereby assume the burden of controlling such
agency if within their power; and if, perchance, some persons unauthorized,
acting with defendants, commit unauthorized acts, it is incumbent upon the
defendants to show such fact, and, if committed by members under the control
of the association, to disavow such acts by causing such offending members to
be disciplined or expelled."
In Stevens v. Ohio State Telephone Co., 240 Fed. 759, 778-779, another
Federal court said:
"The local and defendant union set in motion machinery for the purpose
of shaping sentiment'; its responsibility is clear to control such agency within


===== [扫描序号 1014] =====

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
lawful bounds.
There is no legal excuse for disorder in a strike;
somebody is always responsible in some degree to the law for disorder."
The individual participation of organizers and officers of the United Mine
Workers in the efforts to prevent mining of coal in time of strike have been
referred to in the detailed records submitted herewith. But we are not con-
cerned with individual responsibility but with pointing out the head-on conflict
between the assertion of the moral right of the United Mine Workers of America
to prevent the mining of coal in time of strike by men not members of their
organization and the fundamental principle of freedom of individual contract
and the right to work.

VII. THE CHECK-OFF
IN WEST VIRGINIA--A BREEDER OF STRIFE AND A WAR CHEST
Throughout the history and campaigns of the United Mine Workers in West
Virginia the "check-off" has played a vitally important part.
1. In the early days in the Kanawha district the question of whether the
operators were to be compelled to collect such dues and assessments as the
organization might see fit to impose from every mine worker again and again
formed the breaking point between the operators and the organization. The
operators have again and agath been willing to employ members of the United
Mine Workers' organization, to interpose no objection to the organization of
locals and to contract with the organization, but have broken on the issue of
becoming tax collectors for the United Mine Workers' organization in such a
way that their mines became closed to independent workers.
2. The clearest cut, longest sustained, and most successful campaign of vio-
lence conducted in West Virginia by the United Mine Workers, i. e., that of
Willis Branch, was waged solely and exclusively on the single issue of the
imposition of the compulsory "check-off."
3. The campaign of violence in Williamson field, the armed marches against
the authority of the State, the defense of each and every person charged with
crime in their organization campaigns, have been financed by the United Mine
Workers' organization from the proceeds of the "check-off" obtained in West
Virginia and elsewhere; $2,500,000 from this source was thrown into William-
son field alone.
4. It has presented to operators of West Virginia this clear-cut issue-they
must either refuse to employ members of the United Mine Workers of America
or refuse to employ independent mine workers. The organization, by insisting
on discrimination against those who are not its members, has brought down
on itself exclusion of its membership.
VIII. THE USE OF THE HITCHMAN CASE CONTRACT AS A DEFENSIVE MEASURE AGAINST
THE METHODS OF ATTACK USED BY THE UNITED MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA
A frequent criticism against the nonunion fields of West Virginia is that they
contract with their employees that during the continuance of their employment
they will not belong to the organization of the United Mine Workers of America.
Such contracts are frequently loosely denounced as discriminatory and illegal.
In understanding the West Virginia situation it is essential to consider how
and why they have come into use and the views of the Supreme Court of the
United States as to their necessity and propriety as defensive measures both
to the operators and mine workers against attacks by intimidation and violence.
A. Reasons why operators do not contract with the United Mine Workers
organization. The operators of southern West Virginia have taken and take
the position that they are unwilling to contract with the organization of United
Mine Workers of America.
(1) Wisely or unwisely, they object to placing their labor relations with their
men under the absentee control of the international officers of the United Mine
Workers organization at Indianapolis. They point to strikes called by the
central organization in districts in which there was no local dispute. They point
to the fact that it was only through the existence of the fields which refused to
contract with this organization that the public, as the President told Congress.
was saved from being entirely at the mercy of that organization during the 1922
nation-wide strike.
(2) Wisely or unwisely, they are convinced that contracts with that organiza-
tion are in the interest neither of the operator nor the miner, but tend to
stifle efficiency and individual initiative, and to create a relationship based
not on mutual confidence and sense of responsibility, but on mutual hostility.


===== [扫描序号 1015] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2019
They point to a 20 per cent loss in productivity per worker in the Fairmont
field when it contracted with the organization. They point to an 18 per cent
increase in efficiency and 15 per cent increase in miners' earnings in the
Kanawha field in the mines which have changed from union to nonunion
operation.
(3) Wisely or unwisely, they are convinced that to contract with that or-
ganization is to put the economic future of their fields which have no local
markets at the mercy of wage agreements dictated by the international officers
in Indianapolis, who have a deep-rooted hostility to this field, and whose
primary interests are elsewhere. They point to the bitter complaints of the
operators in the Kanawha field and the States of the Southwest to the effect
that the central organization, through arbitrarily dictating wage scales inap-
plicable to local conditions, has in effect discriminated against those fields.
(4) Wisely or unwisely, they object to the principle of being compelled to
employ only members of that organization and to being forced to collect, by
the "check off," for that organization, such dues and assessments as it sees
fit to impose on each worker in their mines.
B. The operators insist on the right of freedom of contract and the right to
protect that freedom.-We are not concerned here with arguing whether these
convictions are right or wrong, but that they exist is one of the facts of the
bituminous coal industry. Further, it is the belief of these operators that in
refusing to contract with the United Mine Workers organization or to employ
men who desire to insist on their doing so, they are exercising the freedom
of contract in which the Constitution protects them. In this they rely on
certain clear-cut decisions of the United States Supreme Court, where there has
been an attempt by State and Federal legislatures to abridge this right.
They do not, of course, claim any obligation on the part of employees to
work for them if they prefer to belong to the United Mine Workers of America
and to work only with fellow employees who belong to that organization, but
they are convinced that their own employees prefer the contrary. There is no
doubt that they resent and oppose the efforts of the United Mine Workers to
extend their organization to their fields, for the reason that such efforts disturb
a relationship existing between them and their employees which they believe
is in the interest of both and satisfactory to both. To them the presence of an
organizer has come to be synonymous with attempted intimidation and violence
In this connection they do not, of course, dispute the right of "peaceable as-
sembly" or "free speech," but they object to the community being subjected to
intimidation and violence under the guise of those phrases. They say that
"peaceable efforts" must be looked at and interpreted in the light of the indi-
vidual history of the organizers and of all the surrounding facts. They believe
that the words of Judge Wilkerson in his recent opinion in U. S. v. Railway
Employees Department of the American Federation of Labor (not yet reported)
correctly characterize the situation:
"The peaceful words of the strikers and pickets, the peaceful exhortations
of the strike leaders, take on, by virtue of the atmosphere of lawlessness and
violence in which they are spoken a force not inhering in the words themselves,
and therefore transcending any possible right of free speech. Under such cir-
cumstances they become what have been called 'verbal acts,' and as much
subject to. injunction as the use of any other force whereby property is unlaw-
fully damaged. (Gompers v. Buck Stove & Range Co., 221 U. S. 418.) To
undertake to throw around the so-called peaceful words of those engaged in this
violent assault upon the commerce of the Nation, the protection of the doctrines
of free speech and peaceful assembly, is a perversion of those great constitu-
tional guaranties."
C. The Supreme Court of the United States in the Hitchman case upholds
freedom of contract and points the way to its effective protection by the
courts. In the past there has been a running fire of accusation and counter-
accusation with regard to the measures taken in these fields as to what were
claimed by the one side to be the lawful activities and the other side the
unlawful activities of “organizers” in these fields. Human nature being what
it is, and particularly with inadequate governmental protection, there was a
constant temptation to the use of extra-legal methods.
This whole situation and the method of dealing with it by the courts has
been clarified by the decision of the Supreme Court in the Hitchman Coal
& Coke Co. Case, 245 U. S. 229. In that case in the northern Panhandle of
West Virginia, after experiences with the United Mine Workers detailed in
the opinion of the Supreme Court, the Hitchman Co. entered into a contract


===== [扫描序号 1016] =====
2020
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
with its employees that they would not belong to the union. The Supreme
Court held that such a contract was lawful and the relationship so created was
entitled to the protection of the courts, and issued an injunction forbidding
interference with the same. Further, the Supreme Court in no uncertain
terms has held that the right to make nonmembership in a particular union a
term of a contract of employment is one which can not be abridged either
by the State or Federal Government.
The Supreme Court said at pages 250-251:
"That the plaintiff was acting within the lawful rights in employing its men
only upon terms of continuing nonmembership in the United Mine Workers of
America is not open to question. Plaintiff's repeated costly experiences of
strikes and other interferences while attempting to 'run union' were a suffi-
cient explanation of its resolve to run nonunion,' if any were needed. But
neither explanation nor justification is needed. Whatever may be the advan-
tages of collective bargaining,' it is not bargaining at all, in any just sense,
unless it is voluntary on both sides. The same liberty which enables men to
form unions, and through the union to enter into agreements with employers
willing to agree, entitles other men to remain independent of the union and
other employees to agree with them to employ no man who owes any allegiance
or obligation to the union. In the latter case, as in the former, the parties
are entitled to be protected by the law in the enjoyment of the benefits of
any lawful agreement they may make."
This doctrine was laid down by the United States Supreme Court in the case
of Adair v. U. S., 208 U. S. 161, in which the Federal statute making it a
criminal offense to discharge an employee of an interstate carrier on account
of his membership in a labor organization, was held unconstitutional under
the fifth amendment. This decision followed the current of decisions in the
State courts on similar cases:
Coffeeville Vitrified Brick Co. v. Perry, 69 Kan. 297, 76 Pac. 848; 66 L. R. A.
185.
State v. Julow, 129 Mo. 163, 31 S. W. 781; 29 L. R. A. 297.
Jackson v. Berger, 92 Ohio St 130: 110 N. E. 732.
In the case of Coppage v. Kansas (236 U. S. 1) the Supreme Court held that
not only was there no power in the Federal Government to limit the freedom of
contract between an employer and employee as to nonmembership in the union,
but that a State statute forbidding any person to contract with an employee
that he would not belong to a labor organization during the continuance of his
employment was invalid under the due process provision of the fourteenth
amendment.
The existence of the right of employers to operate on a nonunion closed shop
basis in no way conflicts with the constitutional right of employees to become
members of labor organizations. Liberty to contract simply means liberty to
enter into a contract provided another person can be found who is willing to
enter into the particular sort of contract desired. This is brought out by the
statement of Mr. Justice Pitney in Coppage v. Kansas (236 U. S. 1, pp. 19
and 21):
"Conceding the full right of the individual to join the union, he has no
inherent right to do this and still remain in the employ of one who is un-
willing to employ a union man, any more than the same individual has a right
to join the union without the consent of that organization. *
The liberty
of making contracts does not include a liberty to procure employment from an
unwilling employer, or without a fair understanding. Nor may the employer be
foreclosed by legislation from exercising the same freedom of choice that is the
right of the employee.
"To ask a man to agree, in advance, to refrain from affiliation with the
union while retaining a certain position of employment, is not to ask him to
give up any part of h's constitutional freedom. He is free to decline the em-
ployment on those terms, just as the employer may decline to offer employ-
ment on any other; for it takes two to make a bargain.'”
These decisions of the Supreme Court pointed the way to operators who were
unwilling to contract with the United Mine Workers to secure the protection of
the courts for the preservation of their lawful contractual status. A series of
injunctions obtained from the State and Federal courts in southern West Vir-
ginia from 1920 on. based on the doctrines laid down by the Supreme Court,
are doing more to stop violence than all other measures.
In order to secure the protection of the courts against violent attack, many
companies who were unwilling to contract with the United Mine Workers of


===== [扫描序号 1017] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2021
America but were formerly entirely willing to employ members of the United
Mine Workers, and who but for their experience with their violent methods
of organization would to-day be willing to employ them, have adopted the policy
of using this form of contract as an effective measure of peaceful defense.
IX. OUTLINE OF HISTORY OF GENERAL DEFENSIVE METHODS USED IN WEST VIRGINIA
AGAINST THE METHODS OF ATTACK OF THE UNITED MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA
AND THE CONDITIONS WHICH HAVE BROUGHT ABOUT SUCH MEASURES
A. West Virginia not unique in this respect.-The first thing to be said about
the history of methods of defense of law and order in West Virginia is that it
is not unique, but is merely a replica of what has taken place generally through-
out those portions of the United States which were new or frontier communi-
ties at the time when the great American industrial development of the last
century began. Writing nearly 40 years ago, and before there was any coal
problem in West Virginia, James Bryce, in the American Commonwealth, de-
scribed the way in which such communities had relegated the maintenance
of law and order to private hands:
"The want of a proper police is apparently the cause answerable for the
numerous train robberies. Even in such States as Illinois and Ohio, robberies
occur, which are detected and punished more frequently by the energy of the
railroad or express (parcel delivery) companies and their skilled detectives
than through the action of the State authorities. Brigandage is due to the
absence of a mounted gendarmerie in the vast and thinly peopled farther West,
and there is no gendarmerie because the Federal Government leaves the States
and Territories to create their own, and these unsettled communities, being well
armed, prefer to take care of themselves rather than spend their scanty cor-
porate funds on a task whose cost would, as they think, be disproportionate to
the result.
"It is a regrettable evidence of the extent to which public authorities have
seemed to abnegate the function of maintaining order that the habit has grown
up among railroad directors and the owners of other large enterprises of hiring
a private armed force to protect, at the time of a strike, not only the workmen
they bring in to replace the strikers but also their yards, works, and stock in
trade."
So the system of protecting life and property with private guardians in
labor troubles is not peculiar to the coal industry nor is it peculiar to West
Virginia. It is the result of American frontier condition in a poor and thinly
peopled State.
In West Virginia, as in other parts of the country, it has been gradually
yielding to the public opinion which feels that the preservation of law and
order is a fundamental State function which should not be delegated. But
in West Virginia the transition has come rather more rapidly than in most of
our States.
It is only 18 years since the first State force of mounted constabulary, that
of Pennsylvania, was created in this country. It was only in the year 1917
that the great State of New York authorized the creation of such a force.
West Virginia created hers in 1919. Forty-one States to-day are still without
any such State police force. Incidentally, as we shall show below, this develop-
ment of a proper State police force has been retarded everywhere by the
stubborn opposition of organized labor, headed frequently by the same United
Mine Workers of America who now criticize West Virginia for the results
of not having adopted it earlier.
B. The successive steps of defensive measures used in West Virginia.—As
already pointed out in this brief, the coal areas of West Virginia, particularly
in the southern portion of the State, are composed of wild and mountainous
country having a very scanty population until coal mining began. The advent
of the coal companies brought a sudden increase in that population which had
the usual experience of finding the local laws and government entirely inade-
quate for the new conditions. For instance, the population of Logan County
has increased from 14,000 to 60,000 in the past 10 years.
(1) The Baldwin-Felts stage: The first defensive force resorted to was the
one which has been employed under similar conditions by all of our large trans-
portation and other companies, namely, the private guard or watchman. The
southern West Virginia coal operators turned to the Baldwin-Felts Agency.
This was a well-known agency of good repute and extensively employed
throughout the country, particularly by railroads. It is employed to-day by


===== [扫描序号 1018] =====
2022
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
many of our promiment railroads, particularly in the South, and, as far as we
have been able to ascertain, neither the public nor the railroad labor unions
have ever objected to its being so employed. Its regular men have had the
reputation of high character and known bravery, many of them being ex-service
men and in several instances holders of the Congressional Medal of Honor. In
normal times these guards were effective and there was little trouble. At
times of strike they were necessarily diluted by hasty recruiting, and during
the Paint and Cabin Creek troubles of 1912 and 1913 there was trouble and
complaint of their actions on the part of the strikers. A commission appointed
by the governor to investigate those troubles and headed by Bishop Donahue
condemned in strong terms the methods of attack of the United Mine Workers
of America and also the Baldwin-Felts system of defense. The report of this
commission, however, recognized the necessity for protection of mine property in
time of strike and suggested as a substitute for the Baldwin-Felts system a
system not substantially unlike the later deputy sheriff system.
(2) Deputy sheriff stage: Under the influence of this Donahue report and the
constant pressure of the United Mine Workers, the operators graduaily abar-
doned the employment of Baldwin-Felts operatives. As a substitute for this in
some of the counties a system was adopted whereby deputy sheriffs were
appointed by the sheriff and approved by the county court, their wages being
paid, at least in part, directly by the operators. Later in most cases the pay-
ments were made to the sheriff and he paid the wages.
Most of the coal counties have discontinued this system of payments by
cperators either directly or indirectly. Nowhere in West Virginia did the
sheriff receive any fees himself for the appointment of such deputies on behalf
of the companies, as has been the system in some other States. Furthermore,
the system of privately paid wages to deputy sheriffs was never peculiar to the
coal companies, similar payments being made by railroads, electric-light com-
panies, and in at least one instance by the United Mine Workers themselves.
In view of the sweeping charges made to the commission as to the deputy
sheriff system in Logan County and the constantly reiterated allegations as to
the employment of hundreds of armed guards, Baldwin-Felts detectives and
deputy sheriffs by the operators, we will take up the situation in Logan County
in some detail.
Prior to 1912, when the mining communities were just starting, Baldwin-
Felts guards were employed by the operators for community and property pro-
tection. As the mining camps increased in number and size, the need for protec-
tion increased rapidly, but as the county developed it was conc.uded that its
policing should be under the direct supervision of its own sheriff.
In 1912 a sheriff was elected on this issue, and the Baldwin-Felts guards were
discontinued, and they never since have been reemployed in Logan County. The
deputy sheriff stage then began, the sheriff deputizing a man for each of the
various mine-community groups. These mine communities are the only con-
siderable settlements in Logan except Logan Town, the county seat. The
deputies were paid by the coal companies, in whose camps they acted as police
officers. There was usually about one deputy to two or three mining camps, and
sometimes the different companies shared in the expense. Until the armed
invasion of 1921 by the United Mine Workers of America the police force of
the county consisted of the sheriff, 3 or 4 office deputies, and 40 to 50 deputies,
most of them paid by the coal companies, who acted as police officers for the
different camps.
In 1921 the county authorities faced an invasion. Approximately 6,000 armed
men marched on the county in defiance of the State authorities. The regular
deputies were inadequate for defense, but they formed a nucleus about which a
defensive force was recruited. The sheriff gathered something over 2,000 vol-
unteers, mainly miners who were working in and were citizens of Logan County.
They were specially deputized, but in most cases no bonds were issued, under
the proviso of the law that the sheriff may call upon the citizens to aid him in
case of an emergency. The invasion repelled, the county again returned to its
normal deputy system.
As the different mining communities became more settled, however, and the
first heavy expenditures for the building of roads and the organization of
schools were met it was determined that the county itself should take over its
own police work and that the deputies should be paid by the county, not by
the coal companies. Accordingly, in the summer of 1922 the county court
passed an appropriation to provide for the payment of all deputies. This was
approved by the State tax collector, as required by law, but under the limita-

court to pay all of these deputies as soon as funds are available.
The situation in Logan County at present is as follows: One sheriff, 43
active deputies, and 67 special deputies.

rest are paid by the county.
The special deputies do not have the right to make arrests unless called upon
by the sheriff. Their commissions merely permit them to carry a pistol for the
protection of pay rolls, or in traveling at night on duty, and are issued to

The present deputy sheriffs are in no way comparable to mine guards. There

We will submit to the commission complete documentary evidence as to these
deputies, certified to by the county authorities. As will be seen, almost all of
the deputies were born and bred in the county. They are representative citizens
of it.
At the recent session of the West Virginia Legislature the representative
from Logan County, former Circuit Judge Estep, introduced a bill which was
generally supported by the citizens of Logan County, making the private pay-
ment of deputy sheriffs unlawful, and providing that where county funds were
insufficient to employ an adequate number of deputy sheriffs the county court
might lay an additional levy not exceeding 10 cents on each $100 valuation
for the purpose of paying such deputy sheriffs as might be necessary. This
bill was supported by the coal operators, but did not receive the supoort of the
United Mine Workers, though it would have done away with all that is left
of the system to which they had been vociferously objecting for years. It was
sidetracked in the fight over the bill pressed by the United Mine Workers to
repeal the State police law.
(3) State police stage: In 1919 West Virginia established a State con-
stabulary. This originally consisted of about 100 mounted men. In 1921 it
was increased to about 200. Since then it has been reduced and has now about
150. These men are under the command of a former field officer of the Amer-
ican Expeditionary Force. Practically all of them are ex-service men. They
are uniformed, disciplined, and drilled according to the best standards recog-
nized in such bodies of State constabulary, notably the original Pennsylvania
force. The bill for the original creation of this force was sponsored by Gov.
John J. Cornwell, a Democrat, to whose influence the establishment of the
constabulary was primarily due. His successor, Governor Morgan, a Repub-
lican, strongly advocated the continuance of the system and defended it vigor-
ously in 1921 when it was attacked by the United Mine Workers in the
legislature and was sought to be abolished. Thus, so far as the government
of the State is concerned, the State constabulary has received the nonpartisan

and enthusiastic support of the two chief executives who have been in office
since its establishment.
C. Thus the history of West Virginia shows-
1. That its system of defense of life and property during labor controversies
has been no different from that used in other States throughout the country
nor has it been different in the coal industry from other large American
industries.
2. That there has been rather rapid evolution in the direction of substitut-
ing public for private control and responsibility for such agencies.
3. That there is now in effect a State police force modeled on the most
approved lines of the most advanced States of our Union.
4. That this evolution has not met with any opposition from the operators,
but has met with the vigorous and uncompromising opposition of the United
Mine Workers at every stage. This last feature we will take up in the next
point.
X. THE OPPOSITION OF THE UNITED MINE WORKERS TO THE CREATION OF AN ADE
QUATE FORCE IN THE STATE TO MAINTAIN ORDER AND ENFORCE THE LAW
A. Opposition to the State police in West Virginia.-1. In 1919 when Gover-
nor Cornwell's bill for the creation of the department of public safety (which
is the official title of the constabulary) was before the legislature, a mass
meeting and parade was organized by the United Mine Workers in Charleston,
the capital, where the legislature was sitting, in protest against the passage
of such a bill. Representatives of the United Mine Workers unsuccessfully
fought the bill in the legislature.
2. In 1921 Gov. E. F. Morgan advocated the continuance of the State police
and recommended an amendment to the original act and an increased appro-
priation in order that the force might be increased 50 per cent. Representa-
tives of the United Mine Workers worked for the repeal of the act creating the
department of public safety. Failing in this, they made an unsuccessful at-
tempt to prevent the increase in the appropriation.
3. In 1923 House bill 123 was introduced by Representative Sutphin, provid-
ing for the abolition of the department of public safety. The committee on
judiciary held hearings on this bill. Percy Tetlow, sent from Indianapolis by
the central organization to take charge of district 17, as well as Harold Houston
and T. C. Townsend, attorneys for district 17 of the United Mine Workers,
appeared at these hearings in favor of the bill. In his address before the
judiciary committee on April 6, 1923, at 9.30 a. m., Mr. Houston spoke as
follows:
"I am here to represent the United Mine Workers of America, which has a
considerable membership in this State, and is in favor of House bill No. 123.
I believe that from the outset the creation of the State constabulary
was an indefensible piece of legislation, fostered by the special interests, being
the coal operators and particularly the nonunion coal operators. They were
organized for the specific purpose, and I weigh my words, to take the place of
the Baldwin-Felts detectives and to thus unload the cost of the system on the
taxpayers, and take the heavy burden of cost off the shoulders of the coal
operators."
(NOTE. The commission will contrast this argument with the frequent de-
nunciations of the United Mine Workers against the Baldwin-Felts system and
the special deputy system because their compensation did not come from the
taxpayers but from the operators themselves.)
* It is a complete system of persecution. Since you have been meet-
ing in Charleston they have been a little more mild. But as long as this
system exists there will be industrial trouble. It is a most vicious system and
there is no reason why it should exist. The civil authorities have all the
power they need and the prohibition department has its authority and it could
be enlarged. Every sheriff has back of him the Army of the United States
and the posse comitatus. Whenever State policemen get into a fight it makes
trouble. When the Federal Army comes in, there is no opposition. Then the
situation is composed and the people are satisfied. Even after thte Beach
Creek episode when the Federal Army came in it was welcomed. You could
do no more to restore the civil rights of the people of West Virginia than to
wipe out this system and carry this bill."

4. That same year the power of the United Mine Workers was exerted in

B. The opposition of the United Mine Workers to the State constabulary in
West Virginia is in harmony with their general policy of opposing the estab-
lishment of effective police forces elsewhere in the United States.-1. The
belated establishment by the various States of forces of constabulary or
State police to preserve order in situations which have gotten beyond the power
of the county sheriffs and local constables has been recognized generally as
a great step forward in American administration. Outside of the ranks of
organized labor there has been practically no dissent in the general approval
of this evolution. And the first of these forces, the State constabulary of
Pennsylvania, has been widely recognized as the model of what such a force
should be.
Thus on November 10, 1916, Theodore Roosevelt wrote:
"Year by year the efficiency of the force has increased and its usefulness
has correspondingly increased, All good citizens in Pennsylvania should
heartily support the Pennsylvania State Police. The sooner all our other
States adopt similar systems, the better it will be for the cause of law and
order, and for the upright administration of the laws in the interests of justice
throughout the Union." (Justice to All, Mayo, Introduction, p. XXVI.)
As far back as 1909 Mr. Herbert Croly wrote in his The Promise of American
Life (p. 344):
"A State government which could not escape and had the courage to meet
its responsibilities would necessarily demand from the people a police force
which was really capable of keeping the peace. It could not afford to rely
upon local 'posses' and the militia. It would need a State constabulary,
subject to its control and numerous enough for all ordinary emergencies.
When other States besides Pennsylvania establish constabularies,
it will be an indication that they really want to keep order."
2. The Pennsylvania State police was established in 1905. Since that date the
United Mine Workers, together with certain other organizations of union labor,
have not ceased to seek to abolish or emasculate that force and to prevent the
creation of similar bodies of police in other States.
For many years each meeting of the Legislature of Pennsylvania witnessed the
introduction of bills at the instance of union labor, and particularly United
Mine Workers, for the abolition of the Pennsylvania constabulary. In 1906 the
United Mine Workers in local convention in Clearfield passed a resolution de-
manding the repeal of the State police law and calling upon all miners to sup-
port only such legislative candidates as would pledge themselves to support the
repeal measure. Commenting on this the Philadelphia Press says:
"It is just this sort of thing that is injuring the mine workers' cause. In
years past the coal and iron police were denounced in unmeasured terms; the
police of every city or borough and the sheriff of every county that organized
and armed a posse to protect life and property in the coal regions was condemned
as the arch enemy of organized labor." (Justice to All, Mayo, p. 39.)
3. In 1921 an effort was made to introduce a system of State constabulary into
the State of Indiana, and a bill for that purpose was under consideration in the
Indiana Legislature, John L. Lewis, then, as now, the international president
of the United Mine Workers of America, appeared as the principal spokesman
for labor in opposition to this bill. He said:
"Organized labor in Indiana, as elsewhere in the United States, are opposed to
the enactment of a State constabularly measure, not because of any fancy or
dreams or visions they might have concerning this matter, but because of their
experience, if you please, in other States of our Union which have constabulary
police forces of this character."

The requested assistance was promptly furnished and this instance was not
an isolated one. As far back as 1909 we have a record of a request by the
United Mine Workers Union of Exeter for a detail of two State policemen
to preserve order at a meeting. Such appeals became a matter of routine..
The records of Troop B of the Pennsylvania State Police, having its head-
quarters at Wyoming, Pa., in the anthracite region, for the year 1917 show
that the assistance of the police was invoked 38 times by miners where they
were only called upon 13 times by coal operators. (See Justice to All, ap-
pendix E, p. 365.)

STATEMENT TO THE UNITED STATES COAL COMMISSION BY NON UNION OPERATORS
OF SOUTHERN WEST VIRGINIA
UNITED STATES COAL COMMISSION,
BLUEFIELD, W. Va., January 12, 1923.
Washington, D. C.
GENTLEMEN: These operators of West Virginia have no proper place before
your board. Our own labor difficulties have never deprived the people of their
coal; rather we have always supplied the Nation when there were labor dis-
turbances elsewhere. Our mines are not over-developed; instead we must
constantly expand them to meet the demand for our coal. Our business is not
seasonal; on the contrary we have the Central West throughout the year and
the lake trade to serve in summer, the industries of the East and New England
to support, and a foreign commerce to sustain, all of which keeps us constantly
engaged. Our prices, as a whole, have created no scandal; rather we have
always joined hands with the Government in every effort to control the whole
market in the interest of the public. And, on only rare occasions and then
due to outside influences-have our transportation difficulties risen to the
dignity of a public menace. On these accounts we do not belong in the throng
which crowds your anteroom to explain their misdeeds.
And yet, we men of West Virginia are here. You have drawn us in. The
public will not be satisfied unless we appear. We have come, therefore-and
gladly to say this one thing and to prove it:
West Virginia's difficulties have all been imported. They were carried into
our borders. And they originate in the fact that others having fallen into a
quagmire are and have been trying to drag us in with them.
That this may be apparent, we recite our simple story from the beginning.
The coal bearing part of southern West Virginia is extremely mountainous
and rough-a country of deep and narrow mountain gorges which afford the
only low-level routes through which the railroads and the public roads can be
driven. Only three practical passageways across the State from the seaboard
to the Ohio River Valley are available. Because of the mountain peaks, direct
rail communication between the north and south portions is so difficult as to
be next to impossible. There is little level ground.
In these gorges, the coal veins outcrop. Here is found the coal of the greatest
variety and of the best quality in any district of similar size in the world.
At the eastern outlet of these gorges is the port of Norfolk, the gateway
to the commerce of New England and the world. At the western end of these
gorges begins the great coal-consuming district of the Middle West.
The people in both directions from these mines have come to depend upon
this assortment of coal. Three great railway systems were built on, and
sustained by, the commerce which these mines create.
Prior to the opening up of the mines, the country generally was an almost
unbroken forest; practically none of it was, or is, fit for agriculture. Towns
and even hamlets were small and few, because there was nothing to sustain
community life. The tide of emigration, seeking fertile plains to the west,
flowed around this barren mountain section. Those who eked out an existence


===== [扫描序号 1024] =====
2028
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
there were descendents, generally speaking, of the trappers and hunters who
made our postcolonial days romantic with their pioneer spirit.
With the advent of the coal operator in this region came the modern com-
munity life. Coal mining demands labor in quantity. None being available,
the operator had to carry his workmen with him. He had to provide for
them all the creature comforts-houses, food, clothing, water supply, light,
medical attention, sanitation, and later, roads, schools, churches, recreation,
and amusement.
The uncertainties of any new commercial venture accompanied these early
mining operations. In addition, the pioneers were under the handicap of
having to try to introduce an unknown coal to patrons already supplied. For
years they struggled for existence. The operator and his employee ventured
together into this field. There was hope, but hardly that either would there
establish a permanent home. Even with land available, few cared to make
investment in homes. For this reason the residences of officers and employees
alike were constructed by the mining companies as parts of the plants. This
practice remains.
Under these conditions the railroads, the mining industry, and the communi-
ties grew together.
Of the group of mines here represented, the New River coal field was first
developed. Then followed Pocahontas in 1880, and the Tug River, Thacker,
Logan, and Winding Gulf fields at much later dates.
The close contact inspired by a common risk and a primitive life brought
naturally an intimate and friendly relationship between owners and employees
such as arises between captain and crew of a ship in peril from a storm.
This relationship has always existed, exists to-day, and will continue to exist.
unless ruptured-as has frequently been threatened-by outside influences.
Many of the employees of former days are the employees of to-day; relations
entered into in these fields are enduring.
This relationship developed into community action. Prior to the develop
ment of the coal mines school facilities were of the most primitive type; the
teachers were poorly qualified and poorly paid, while the school terms lasted
but two or three months a year. In their places to-day are up-to-date school
buildings which compare favorably with similar institutions of larger towns,
The teachers are well educated and well trained; in most instances they are
graduates of normal schools. Their salaries are as large as those paid in many
cities, and quite frequently their services are obtained in competition with the
larger communities.
With the development of this community spirit came frequent meetings of
a public, semipublic, and social nature for the promotion of the common wel-
fare. All communities have their churches around which center many of these
activities. These churches were erected and are maintained by joint contribu-
tions of employers and employees.
Again, the same community spirit inspired modern roads built with money
raised by bond issues directed by popular vote. So large a proportion of the
employees own their automobiles that finding suitable ground for garages is
difficult. Their children are carried to school in motor busses operated at
public expense.
In addition to assuming their share of expense for community development
each coal company provides competent physicians, whose services, including
medicines, are furnished the employees at a small fixed charge-usually $2 per
month per family. Many of the companies provide at their own expense, with-
out any charge whatever to employees, trained and certified nurses, and ade-
quate emergency hospital facilities at the mines.
House rents are usually based on a charge of $2 per room per month. Electric
power and lights are furnished at prices less than half the rates paid in cities.
Employees are permitted to use all the coal they want for culinary and heating
purposes, for which a small fixed charge is made, usually about $1 per month
per family.
These items entail a heavy fixed charge upon the coal companies for which
the only compensation is satisfied and contented employees.
The necessities from the beginning have demanded that the companies main-
tain stores. In these the prices of food, clothing, and other necessaries of
life are so low as to call forth protests and criticism from independent stofes
in neighboring small towns and to induce customers from the larger towns fre
quently to go considerable distances to patronize these company stores.


===== [扫描序号 1025] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2029
Athletics, including baseball, football, and other outdoor sports, play an im-
portant part in the life of these communities. Athletic grounds exist practically
everywhere and local and interplant contests frequently occur. Other recrea-
tion facilities include motion-picture theaters and other indoor entertainments.
We have gone fully into these details, not to boast but to depict the spirit
which has grown because employers and employees sustained the proper rela-
tions to one another. We have had from the beginning the spirit which
great corporations everywhere are trying to build by all the arts of modern
welfare work. Because of it, we employers and employees found, together, a
wilderness and caused it to blossom into an advanced community.
Up to this point, we have shown our relations among ourselves. We begin
here to show what our relations have been to the rest of the country-what our
internal accord has meant to the national community.
In her natal year, 1863, West Virginia began to contribute to the bituminous
coal needs of the Nation. She produced that year 4 per cent of the total
national consumption. The increase in production thereafter was naturally
slow, owing to the difficulties and handicaps hereinbefore described. It was
not until the coal fields, heretofore mentioned, began to be developed that its
percentage of production materially increased. But in 1889 the State produced
62 per cent of bituminous coal of the country, and by 1915 had made such
progress that it produced 17.4 per cent of the Nation's coal, In tonnage, West
Virginia produced in 1863, 444,648 tons; in 1889, 19,252,995 tons; in 1915,
77,184,069 tons; and in 1918, 89,935,839 tons.
Beginning shortly after the Civil War and down to 1915, with certain tem-
porary exceptions, the average price of West Virginia coal seldom, if ever, varied
more than 25 per cent. That is to say, from the time when West Virginia coal
first entered the market until the Great War in Europe, fluctuation in the price
of this coal was small and unimportant.
When in 1916 it became evident that this country would become involved in
the Great War-a year previously it had become involved in it in an economic
way-bituminous coal became of the first importance. By reason of the exces-
sive demand for it by the manufacturers who were struggling to fill war orders
from Europe, as well as America, and by reason of the growing shortage of
railroad transportation and the inability of the carriers to purchase equipment
to prompt delivery, all the coal which was needed could not be supplied. There-
fore the price was forced, by urgent buyers, to unheard-of heights.
Our country's entry into the Great War in 1917 brought the coal industry
under Government control. With it came the incessant demand from the United
Mine Workers of America for increased wage scales. The granting of these
demands; the increased wages conceded to other unions by manufacturers who
furnish the materials used at the mines; the consequent increase in railroad
rates; and the increases in vessel rates, so increased the prices of coal that our
American customers were, and have been, compelled to pay from two to three
times the former price for coal. They can not understand it. Nor will they be
satisfied until prices are deflated, not only on coal at the mines, but of the rail-
road rates, and all other distribution charges accruing between the mine price
and the consumer's door.
Deflation did start in promptly on armistice day, November 11, 1918. It be-
came apparent to buyers early in 1919. The downward trend was halted
sharply in the fall of 1919 when the United Mine Workers of America-de-
manding an increase rather than a decrease in wages-called a general strike,
which after six weeks again increased the price of coal. Doctor Garfield, then
United States Fuel Administrator, insisted that the United Mine Workers Union
modify its demands. It refused. And it succeeded in securing a substantial
increase effective November 1, 1919. It won a still greater increase August
16, 1920, through the United States Bituminous Coal Commission appointed by
the President.
Peace restored, after the 1919 strike, the law of supply and demand began
to reassert itself in 1920. The tendency toward lower prices was short lived.
The outlaw strike of the railways came in April. Terminal congestions and
a stoppage of coal movement resulted. Public officials and the newspapers
became alarmed and incited panic among the people. And, at the critical time,
Europe, to save itself from Bolshevism which was sweeping into western Europe
from Russia, where it was finding a ready foothold because the factories were
idle from lack of coal, began to plead with American producers for coal. We
did not have the coal to spare, but our public officials were convinced that the


===== [扫描序号 1026] =====
2030
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
peace of the world depended upon our getting coal to Europe, and we did it.
At this critical time, the gambling middlemen, at home and abroad, descended
upon this distressing situation and created panic and prices which have shamed
the industry.
This wild demand began to slacken in November, 1920. Early in 1921 it had
entirely passed. Then, again, the inexorable law of supply and demand com-
menced to work. Again deflation started. And, for the first time since 1916,
prices went back to low levels, and in many instances greatly below the then
ocst of production.
Again the United Mine Workers of America, unalterably opposed to doing
its share in this deflation, called a strike effective April 1, 1922, with the result
known to all.
