President Harding made the coal situation, in connection with the strike of
1922, the subject of a message to Congress on August 18, 1922. After discussing
the various efforts made to settle the strike and their failure by reason of the
defiance by the United Mine Workers of America of all sense of obligation to
the public and to the Government, the President says:
"The simple but significant truth was revealed that, except for such coal as
comes from the districts worked by the nonorganized miners, the country is at
the mercy of the United Mine Workers."
We have now shown our relations and their fruits. We have produced coal
in season and out of season. We have received modest prices except when a
world upheaval created conditions beyond our control. Our record is that as
soon as an abnormal situation disappeared, the normal tendency asserted itself
and prices declined. We now come to a new set of conditions which were
imposed upon us from without-and for reasons which we will recite.
From the beginning of the coal industry in West Virginia it has been the
policy of the operators to conduct the business on a nonunion basis. This pol
icy on the part of the operators is shared by a great number, if not all, of their
employees, many of whom frankly state they will not work under the union;
they will abandon mining rather than do so, and will seek other occupations.
Notwithstanding the legal right of the operator and the miner to agree upon
terms of employment satisfactory to themselves, we have, for a generation, been
interfered with almost without cessation in every way the United Mine Workers


===== [扫描序号 1027] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2031
of America could devise to accomplish the conquest of our State. They have
employed all means from noisy oratory and false representations in private
and in public, to leading armed groups, numbering many thousands of men,
across the State in open defiance of the State and Nation. Let us give you a
brief outline of the history of the United Mine Workers of America's con-
spiracy to conquer West Virginia and its consequences.
The initial conspiracy had its origin in a contract entered into at a joint
conference between the miners and operators of the central competitive field
in Chicago, January 17-28, 1898. From that contract we quote the eighth
clause, which is as follows.
"That the United Mine Workers' organization, a party to this contract,
do hereby further agree to afford all possible protection to the trade and the
other parties hereto against any unfair competition resulting from the failure
to maintain scale rates." (See hearings before the Committee on Education and
Labor, United States Senate, S. Res. 80, p. 394.)
The true meaning of the clause just quoted, as understood by the parties
thereto, appears in the minutes of the various joint conferences held after that
time, from which we give only three excerpts out of many which might be
given.
At the conference held in Pittsburgh, January 18, 1899, John Mitchell, na
tional president of the United Mine Workers of America, said:
"I want to say to the operators that an effort has been made in the past year
to curtail the West Virginia coal by preventing its sale on the market." (See
hearings before the Committee on Education and Labor, United States Senate,
S. Res. 80, p. 395.)
At the same meeting, Mr. Ratchford, whose term of office as president of that
organization had just expired, said:
"I want to make a proposition here, that the interest of the West Virginia
miners, by reason of the efforts of our organization, have been hampered and
injured more in the past year than in any year since they have been operating
in the State of West Virginia.” (See minutes of joint conference of January
17-24, 1899.)
At the joint conference of 1902 John Mitchell, then president of said organi-
zation, further said:
"We want the check-off system for several reasons; first, * * * because
the Pennsylvania operators come here this year and raise Cain with the miners,
because they do not organize West Virginia." (See hearings before the Com-
mittee on Education and Labor, United States Senate, S. Res. 80, p. 399.)
66
This conspiracy" of 1898 was referred to at practically every joint con-
ference from that year forward, as the minutes of said conferences will show.
It has been set up and proven in numerous suits in various courts of the
country. It has never been denied and the courts have uniformly held it to
exist and that it was unlawful.
That it has continued to the present is shown by the statement made by Mr.
Fred Mooney, secretary and treasurer of district No. 17, United Mine Workers
of America, and published in the United Mine Workers Journal of December 1,
1920, from which the following quotation is taken:
"For the struggle in Mingo County is an economic one
in fact it
is the continuance of a struggle begun in West Virginia some 23 years ago and
extending throughout this period."
The struggle to which he refers is of course the struggle to unionize the coal
miners of West Virginia which the United Mine Workers of America had
promised the operators and miners of the central competitive field to do, in order
to raise the cost of production of coal in West Virginia to such a point that it
could not compete with the coal produced in the central competitive territory.
This was a part of the consideration for the joint-wage scale and the check-off
which had been granted to the organization by the operators of the central com-
petitive field.
A further effect of the joint agreements in the central competitive field has
been to fix the wages of coal miners throughout the United States wherever the
union exists and has control, because wages elsewhere have been fixed by the
union with relation to the wages in the central competitive field. This control
of mine labor by one organization has materially affected the selling price of
bituminous coal everywhere.
The United Mine Workers of America is frankly and fully committed to the
theory of a monopoly of mine labor in all the coal mines of the United States

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
and has never omitted any act, lawful or unlawful, within its power to bring
about that situation.
So tremendous and menacing is its power, by reason of the very large percent-
age of coal mines in the United States as it now dominates, that when it
arbitrarily calls a strike, as in did in 1919 and again in 1922, approximately 60
per cent of the coal production of the country stops instantly and nothing
except the production of coal in the nonunion fields has saved the country from
national calamities.
This enormous and widespread curtailment in production naturally and
inevitably results in unduly high prices to the consumer for the coal being
produced, because consumers become panic-stricken and bid against each other
for the available supply. This reduced production and the panic of the buyers
are not the only things that then contributed to the high price of coal, for the
union, in order to increase the chances of making the strike a success, directed
every possible effort and attack against the nonunion fields to hamper and
reduce their production, which efforts and attacks had to be resisted, including
protection of the rights of nonunion men to work-an expense which increased
greatly the cost of production in the nonunion fields. It may fairly be said
that except as to the unusual situations heretofore referred to, the high prices
of coal during recent years have been the direct result of the actions of the
United Mine Workers of America in calling nation-wide strikes, such strikes
being made possible by its absolute control of mine labor in such a large part
of the country.
Not only does it aim at the absolute control of all mine labor in the United
States, but it has further declared its intention to secure a world-wide con-
trol. In line with this object this organization made efforts during the past
summer to influence British coal miners to prevent the shipment of any
British coal to the United States while this organization was on strike.
The history of the efforts of the United Mine Workers' organization to
organize West Virginia is made up of a series of crimes against persons and
property without any parallel, certainly in the United States. Short reference
will be given to some of the outstanding acts of violence.
In 1912 the union made a determined effort to organize the Kanawha field.
Trouble first broke out on Paint Creek and then spread to Cabin Creek and
New River, both being nonunion fields. Martial law was declared on Sep-
tember 2, 1912, and the whole of the State's militia was stationed on the two
ereeks mentioned. This trouble was made the subject of a very exhaustive
investigation by a committee of the United States Senate. The whole issue
was whether or not the union would be recognized by the operators. The
trouble continued for more than a year, during which time there was a great
deal of violence of all kinds, including the shooting up of mines by members
of the union.
On November 16, 1917, members of the United Mine Workers of America
on strike shot up the town of Glen White, W. Va., under a well-devised and
well-carried-out plan preceded by the purchase of high-power rifles for that
purpose. Six of these men were tried and convicted of attempt to commit
murder in the first degree, including Toney Stafford, international organizer
of the United Mine Workers of America, and Ed Snyder, president of Glen
White local of that organization, each of whom was sentenced to five years
in the State penitentiary, the other four pleading guilty and receiving one
year sentences. Three of them were ordered deported by the United States
Government on account of their being undesirable aliens. Four others were
not prosecuted because they turned State's evidence, and it was upon their
testimony chiefly that the above convictions were had. One of the men im-
plicated was never apprehended. It will be observed that this shooting up
of the town of Glen White occurred during the war, when all patriotic citi-
zens were straining every nerve and energy to supply the fuel needs of the
country, and had for its direct object the stopping of production of the mine
situated there, notwithstanding that a representative of the Federal Govern-
ment had made an investigation and had decided that the miners were wrong
in their contention.
Perhaps the most consistent, persistent, and typical example of the length
to which this organization will go to accomplish its purpose, is that of Willis
Branch in Fayette County, W. Va. The original difference involved six or
eight coal companies and was confined to one issue, namely, the refusal of the
companies to enforce the closed union shop (by refusing work to applicants
not members of the union) and the check off, having agreed to the union wage

cale and all other conditions imposed by the union. The village of Willis

Another man deserving special mention for his activities in connection with the
Willis branch violence is David Robb, stated, in numerous written confessions of
members of the union who participated in said violence, to have acted as
financial agent of the union in supplying guns and ammunition. He after-

is said to take him back to the Coronado Coal Co. destruction and to the Colo-

The union also made an effort to organize the miners in Mingo County,
W. Va., and the means they adopted were to make night and day attacks
on the mining camps and tipples by shooting into them and at the miners
who remained at work with high-power rifles and guns of every description.
Several tipples were dynamited and burned and a great deal of property was
ultimately destroyed and 28 lives lost. Here again the only issue was recog-
nition of the union by the operators.
The armed march on Logan County in 1921 was an effort to intimidate the
nonunion members of Logan County and to forcibly organize them. This march
was the most pretentious effort to force unionization on nonunion men that has
yet been made. The marchers, estimated to be 10,000 in number, fully armed
and equipped with all the arms, ammunition, and supplies necessary to fit out
an army, started in Kanawha County in the unionized fields, and marched
thence 50 miles, or more, across the country, commandeering arms, supplies,
and trains en route. They were met on the border of Logan County by the
nonunion miners and other supporters of law and order and their march was
stopped. The Federal Government soon after that sent United States soldiers
to maintain law and order and the marching miners finally were sent home.
Your commission is considering the industry as a whole. From others you
have received a recitation of their situations. From us you here received an
exposition of our own case. Speaking now as part of the whole industry, we

believe you will find all operators and all miners in substantial agreement on
the following facts:
The shortage of coal in no period is, or has been, due to lack of capacity in
the mines to produce coal; no one can seriously contend that this is the case.
There were in 1910, according to Geological Survey figures, 5,818 mines in the
United States, and in 1920, on the same authority, 14,766-an increase in the dec-
ade of 154 per cent. During the same period and on the same authority, the pro-
duction of coal in the country in 1910 was 416,000,000 tons and in 1920 was
569,000,000 tons-an increase of only 37 per cent. We think that production
and consumption are sufficiently close to one another for figures to be inter-
changeable for present purposes. The disparity shown above between the 37 per
cent increase in consumption and the 154 per cent increase in the number of
producing mines is, in our opinion, a complete answer to any suggestion that
the mine capacity is insufficient.
If the supply of coal is insufficient, after this show of capacity, the cause
must be sought in some other direction. To assist you in that direction we
recite:
Our mines to-day are running at less than 50 per cent capacity. This is due
solely to a lack of transportation. We can not supply our market if the rail-
roads can not carry more than half of what we can produce.
As we have shown, every period of shortage except that caused by the
war demand-has been preceded by a strike of the union miners.
This leads us to suggest: Stripped of all nonessentials, the two questions
before you are:
(1) How can the periodical interruptions of coal production be stopped?
(2) How can the wild fluctuations of coal prices be brought to an end?
Answering these questions categorically, the interruptions of production can
be stopped if you can arrange to prevent, forever, the union from calling a
nation-wide strike. In this connection your particular attention is called to
the vital distinction in the principles involved between a "local" and a "na-
tional" strike. In a 'local' strike the effects are confined to the employers
and employees directly concerned in a personal or local issue; whereas in a
"national" strike the issues are political rather than economic in character,
and bring suffering, loss, and disaster to the general public.

"9
The price fluctuations will disappear if and when the great strikes cease and
when the railways can carry our coal to market.
Your commission represents the whole people of the United States. If you
feel that the consumers should continue to pay present, or higher, prices for
coal, the miners' union should be encouraged by new concessions. If you feel
that the people are paying prices which are too high, an effective curb should
be put upon its activities by removing exceptions to the anticonspirary laws
and by protecting all American citizens in their right to work unmolested under
such conditions as they elect.

LETTER AND STATEMENT TO THE UNITED STATES COAL COMMISSION ON HERRIN
[Submitted by the Bituminous Operators' Special Committee, May 16, 1923]
To the United States Coal Commission:
MAY 15, 1923.
GENTLEMEN: Herewith, as requested in your published statement of February
14, are the charges and facts relating to the denial of rights to American citizens
at Herrin, Ill.
Herrin is no isolated mining camp, tenanted by a population of “foreign-born
radicals." It is a flourishing American city of 11,000 inhabitants. Attractive


===== [扫描序号 1031] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2035
stores line its streets. Hundreds of automobiles crowd its thoroughfares. The
writers of this letter have visited it and personally observed its well-kept char-
acteristics. It stands in an old farming region, and though mines and miners
have come, farms and farmers still remain. The population of Williamson
County, of which Herrin is one of the principal towns, is overwhelmingly Ameri-
can by birth, the percentage of foreign-born inhabitants being insignificant. Nor-
mally it would respond like any other American community to the principles of
orderly government and liberty.
Yet on June 22, 1922, in the middle of a bright, sunny morning the people of
Herrin watched six Americans, survivors of the massacre which had already
taken place a mile south of the town, forced to creep on their hands and knees
through the streets of Herrin in token of their subjection to the power of the
United Mine Workers, and then watched these same six men taken to the ceme-
tery east of the town and there slowly put to death-very much as the red sav-
ages who inhabited Illinois two centuries ago watched the tortures of their war
captives.
Later that day, when the mutilated remains of 17 of the victims of that mas-
sacre had been stripped, brought into town, and dumped upon the floor of one
of its buildings, the people of Herrin in large numbers-men, women, and
children alike passed through this morgue in procession, jeering at these help-
less bodies. The local newspaper perpetuated these jeers in the following lan-
guage, taken from its account of the occurrence:
"The faces of the men who were killed in the disturbance are horrible sights.
Uncouth, as all crooks must be at the beginning, they were doubly unattractive
as seen after justice had triumphed and the county had again resumed its normal
peace-time behavior."
The offense of which these "crooks" had been guilty was to attempt to
work at a time when a supergovernment known as the United Mine Workers
of America had forbidden work. Their work was particularly heinous, because
it was for the purpose of supplying coal to the people of the United States at
a time when this supergovernment, by a nation-wide strike, was engaged in
starving the people of the United States into submitting to a scale of wages
somewhat higher than that then prevailing in any similar industry. Sentence
of guilt had been duly pronounced upon these men by a decree of the super-
government, signed by its president, John L. Lewis, in which they were ad-
judged to be "common strike breakers," members of an "outlaw organization,"
the Steam Shovelers Union, and every man, woman, and child in Herrin knew
that this judgment meant death if the decree were resisted.
These events of last June in Herrin are not one whit more abhorrent to
American principles than the events which have taken place in Herrin and in
Marion, the neighboring county seat of Williamson County, since that date,
culminating only a few days ago. The sovereign State of Illinois has been
endeavoring to enforce the rules of American justice against the killers of last
June. The supergovernment of the United Mine Workers has been opposing this
attempt. Its representatives in open court, unrebuked, have claimed belligerent
rights for those killers-the rights of soldiers waging honorable battle against
wrong. And it has triumphed. Murder is no longer murder in southern Illinois.
The attorney general, chief law officer of Illinois, publicly announced last month
that American law could not be enforced in Williamson County. His announce-
ment apparently has been accepted by the State of Illinois. The supergovern-
ment has established its position and the former authorities have acquiesced.
This is the system which John L. Lewis and the United Mine Workers are
avowedly attempting to extend over all the thirty States of the Union where
bituminous coal is mined. What has taken place in Herrin was due to no acci-
dental, sporadic outburst of mob spirit. The events in the five different counties
of Ohio, already covered by our Ohio brief and evidence; the events in north-
eastern Kentucky, covered by our Kentucky brief; the events in Indiana, Penn-
sylvania, West Virginia, Utah, Colorado, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Kansas, and
Missouri, to be covered by our coming briefs on those regions, completely dis-
pel any such comfortable hypothesis. Mob passions were undoubtedly aroused
in Herrin eventually on that 22d day of June last year, but in Herrin, as in all
these other cases, the original homicidal attack upon men, who under the law
of the land had committed no other offense than that of trying to work, was
pursuant to a deliberate, premeditated conspiracy, conceived and carried
through to enforce the policy and monopoly of the United Mine Workers.
What took place in Herrin was the logical and inevitable result of the estab-
lishment of this Mine Workers' super-government in an American State. Such
a result will inevitably follow its establishment in any other State just so soon


===== [扫描序号 1032] =====
2036
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
as the aims and purposes of the super-government run afoul of the laws of that
State.
We do not believe that the people of the United States wish to have their
American system of laws and government thus supplanted by another sovereign
and another code. Herrin is a warning signal. We do not believe that this
commission can afford to disregard or neglect its purport.
The statements of fact in the accompanying brief and charges are based upon
the sworn testimony taken in the trials at Marion and upon the investigation

STATEMENT OF FACTS CONCERNING THE HERRIN MASSACRE
Probably the most glaring example in the history of this country of the
methods of violence used by the United Mine Workers of America in their
effort to establish and maintain their monopoly of labor in the coal industry and
to prevent every person, not a member of that organization, from laboring in
that industry, is presented by the facts concerning the organized attack on the
property of the Southern Illinois Coal Co. near Herrin, Williamson County,
Ill., on June 21 and 22, 1922, and the incidents leading up to that attack and
subsequent thereto.


===== [扫描序号 1034] =====

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
GENERAL SITUATION IN WILLIAMSON COUNTY, ILL.
Williamson County, Ill., is one of the southernmost counties of that State.
It is now distinctly a coal-mining county. Before coal was discovered it was
an old farming country and most of its land is still under cultivation.
Most of the coal mines in Williamson County are deep mines. There are,
however, a few stripping operations. In these stripping operations the coal iies
in thick veins near the surface of the ground and is mined by first removing the
earth from the veins of coal with steam shovels. The coal is then loosened by
blasts of powder and loaded directly on cars by other steam shovels.
Two of the chief towns of Williamson County are Marion, the county seat,
and Herrin, situated a few miles apart. These are not small mining com-
munities, but good sized, modern, up-to-date towns. Herrin has a population
of 10,986 and Marion a population of 9,582. Each town has all modern improve-
ments, including paved streets, water and sewer systems, gas and electricity,
churches, hospitals, libraries, banks, and schools. Williamson County itself has
a population of over 62,000 and an assessed valuation of over $16,450,000. This
population is overwhelmingly American by birth. The percentage of foreign-
born inhabitants is quite insignificant.
About midway between these two towns was the stripping operation of the
Southern Illinois Coal Co., of which W. J. Lester was president.
Williamson County is completely dominated by the local organization of the
United Mine Workers of Amer ca. A very large part of the workingmen in the
county are members of that union and many of the remaining citizens are
closely connected with the United Mine Workers of America by family ties or
otherwise. The storekeepers and business men of the county are mainly de-
pendent for their living upon the business given them by members of the
United Mine Workers of America.
The local organization of the United Mine Workers of America in Williamson
County is subdistrict No. 10 of district No. 12.
In June, 1922, the President of this subdistrict was William J. Sneed, a State
Senator of the State of Illinois. Hugh Willis, Otis Clark, and Fox Hughes
were vice presidents of this subdistrict.
The sheriff of the county, Melvin Thaxton, was a former miner and member
of the United Mine Workers of America.
On April 1, 1922, the mining of coal in Williamson County stopped, as it did
all over the country in union mines.
SPECIAL SITUATION WITH RESPECT TO THE STRIPPING OPERATION OF THE SOUTHERN
ILLINOIS COAL CO.
From April 1, 1922, to about May 15, 1922, the machinery and plant of the
Southern Illinois Coal Co. was undergoing repairs. From about May 15, 1922,
to about June 13, 1922, the company was engaged in stripping dirt from veins
of coal.
All of this work was done with the consent and permission of the officers of
subdistrict No. 10 of the United Mine Workers of America and was done par-
tially with the labor of members of that organization pursuant to an agreement
between W. J. Lester, the president of the mine, and officials of the United
Mine Workers of America.
Between April 1, 1922, and June 13, 1922, no coal was mined or shipped. By
June 13 some 65,000 to 75,000 tons of coal had been stripped of earth. The
American public was in sore need of this coal and W. J. Lester desired to
mine and ship it, but the local officials of the United Mine Workers of America
told him that he would not be allowed to do it.
W. J. Lester then determined that he would not be dictated to by the United
Mine Workers of America, but that he would exercise his constitutional rights
and mine and ship his coal by the use of labor which did not belong to their
organization. He therefore arranged with the Steam Shovel Men's Union in
Chicago to obtain men from that organization to operate his steam shovels.
In view of the hostile attitude of the United Mine Workers of America in
Williamson County he also brought from Chicago a number of guards to pro
tect the members of the Steam Shovel Men's Union while at work.


===== [扫描序号 1035] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2039
These workers started to arrive at the stripping operation about June 13,
and by the 21st of June the company had some 50 to 60 employees who were not
members of the United Mine Workers of America, including cooks, engineers,
and about 24 guards. All of these men were able, willing, and anxious to work.
Between the 13th and 21st of June, 1922, the company loaded and shipped to the
American public about 3,500 tons of coal over the tracks of the Chicago, Bur-
lington & Quincy Railroad Co.
The United Mine Workers of America have endeavored to justify their
attack on these workers on the ground that the antecedents of the men so
brought in by the Southern Illinois Coal Co. were not all that could be desired.
Perhaps the antecedents of some of these men were not of the best. But it
must be remembered that the Southern Illinois Coal Co. had the constitutional
right to work its property and to protect its property and employees. In the
face of a strike by the United Mine Workers of America to enforce their monop-
oly, such as existed in June, 1922, the exercise of such a constitutional right is
of an ultrahazardous nature. So much so was this the case that not one single
operator of a deep mine in Illinois, where United Mine Workers of America
are necessarily employed, dared even to consider the operation of his mine
during the strike. It was universally recognized by them that the supergovern-
ment of the union was supreme, and not one of such mines operated in the
State of Illinois. In a stripping operation such as the Southern Illinois Coal
Co. carried on there was no use for miners, and United Mine Workers of
America are not ordinarily employed in such operations. Nevertheless, the
hazard at such a time of producing coal was so well recognized that only men
of a type willing to take their lives in their hands were available to the South-
ern Illinois Coal Co. as workers or guards. Among such men are bound to be
found a proportion of undesirables alongside men of bold courage and high
type, such as Robert Officer, hereinafter referred to. The Southern Illinois
Coal Co. had the absolute constitutional right to operate its plant. The con-
stitution of the State of Illinois gave it the right to defend is propery. The
experience of similar stripping operations in other districts, such as Ohio, had
shown that to attempt to carry on these operations without means of self-
defense was to expose the operator to the destruction of his property and his
employees to the murderous attack of the United Mine Workers of America
before the protecting forces of the State could be brought into operation. The
men that the Southern Illinois Coal Co. employed were probably the best that
it could get under the circumstances, and that the guards were needed the facts
stated hereafter in this brief are conclusive evidence.
The stripping operation of the Southern Illinois Coal Co. was located in a
secluded spot in the country about 4 miles southeast of Herrin and about
the same distance from Marion. It was quite a distance from the main high-
way and could only be reached by a little-used country road. The workers
and guards of the company were all quartered on the company's property,
and, so far as the record shows, remained quietly on the company's property
between June 13 and June 21, and did not show themselves in the towns.
The United Mine Workers of America claimed on the murder trials that the
actions of these men provoked the attack, but the record shows that the United
Mine Workers of America themselves had to go miles out of their way into the
country in order to come into collision with these workers and guards, and
that such collisions as actually did occur prior to June 21 were of the United
Mine Workers' own seeking.
The members of the United Mine Workers of America in Williamson County
entered into a conspiracy to prevent by the use of force and arms W. J. Lester
from continuing his stripping operation in defiance of the orders of their union.
The conspiracy had its inception about the 13th of June and culminated
on the 21st of June, with an attack upon the property of the Southern Illinois
Coal Co. by a large body of armed men. This attack was thoroughly organized
and carefully prepared and was the definite result of action taken by officials
and members of subdistrict No. 10 of the United Mine Workers of America.
It is not known at just what moment the decision was reached to make the
attack, but immediately after the 13th of June the union miners in Williamson
County deliberately set themselves about the task of creating an atmosphere
which would enable them to carry through their avowed purpose of preventing


===== [扫描序号 1036] =====
2040
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
any person not a member of the United Mine Workers of America from mining
a ton of coal.
Commencing with June 16 and continuing through the 17th, 18th, 19th, and
20th of June numerous persons, many of whom were members of the United
Mine Workers of America, went purposely to this out-of-the-way stripping opera-
tion and attempted to invade the property of the company upon various
excuses. Some represented themselves to be berry pickers, some sightseers,
but the very evident object of all was to come into collision with the company
guards, to be stopped by those guards and to be turned back. The news of the
action of the guards in stopping and turning back trespassers on the company's
property was quickly spread. Stories were freely circulated, among others that
the guards were stopping citizens on the highway and otherwise interfering with
their rights. By the 19th and 20th of June the whole of Williamson County
was boiling with excitement and the union miners were ready for anything.
On the afternoon of June 17 or 18 Sheriff Thaxton and State Attorney Duty
visited the stripping operation and asked C. K. McDowell, the superintendent,
what men he was using and McDowell notified them that he was using union
men, members of the Steam Shovel Men's Union.
Following this information, Senator Sneed, the president of the subdistrict,
telegraphed John L. Lewis, international president of the United Mine Workers
of America, on June 18, asking for an official ruling on the status of the mem-
bers of the Steam Shovel Men's Union.
Lewis, under date of June 19, immediately sent to Sneed the following tele-
gram, which Sneed received on June 19:
WILLIAM J. SNEED,
INDIANAPOLIS, IND., June 19, 1922.
President subdistrict 10, district 12, U. M. W. of A.,
Herrin, Ill.:
Your wire of 18th. Steam Shovel Men's Union was suspended from affilia-
tion with American Federation of Labor some years ago. It was also ordered
suspended from the mining department of the American Federation of Labor
at the Atlantic City convention. We now find that this outlaw organization is
permitting its members to act as strike breakers at numerous strip pits in
Ohio. This organization is furnishing steam-shovel engineers to work under
armed guards with strike breakers. It is not true that any form of agreement
exists by and between this organization and the mining department or any
other branch of the American Federation of Labor permitting them to work
under such circumstances. We have, through representatives, officially taken
this question up with the officers of the Steam Shovel Men's Union and have
failed to secure any satisfaction. Representatives of our organization are
justified in treating this crowd as an outlaw organization and in viewing its
members in the same light as they do any other common strike breakers.
JOHN L. LEWIS.
The effect this telegram had on the striking miners has been tersely stated
in the following account by Thoreau Cronyn of the New York Herald:
"A veteran of Williamson County to whom the correspondent showed a copy
of this (the Lewis telegram) pushed his spectacles up his forehead after reading
it and said:
66 6
Well, you can never make me believe John Lewis intended to have any-
body go out and do some killing. I should say he was merely settling a dis-
puted point in the routine of his business. But I will say that John Lewis
was unfortunate in his choice of language. Everybody down here knows how
the union miners felt about these things and how certain words inflame them.
I should not say that the word outlaw riled them so much, but when Lewis
officially told them that those fellows out at the Lester mine were to be
treated like any other strike breakers I should say it was about the same as
saying, "Hike out there to the mine and clean 'em out."'"
John L. Lewis undoubtedly did not contemplate a wholesale massacre. but
he can not in justic say that he did not realize the effect his telegram would
have in arousing the spirit of violence in Williamson County. He well knew
the general attitude of the United Mine Workers of America toward strike
breakers. His telegram shows that he was familiar with the stripping oper-
ations which were then being attempted in Ohio, upon which murderous at-


===== [扫描序号 1037] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2041
tacks,' even as he wrote his telegram, were being made by members of the
-organization of which he was president, on the ground that the workers were
"strike breakers." He must also have been thoroughly familiar with the
many acts of violence against strike breakers of which the United Mine Workers
of America had for years been guilty. Lewis himself was an old Illinois man
and he must be deemed to have known of the armed attacks upon strike breakers
at the neighboring town of Ziegler when in previous years the operators at-
tempted to run their mines in defiance of the United Mine Workers of America.
From the moment the Lewis telegram was received the preparations for the
attack were rushed to a conclusion. With the statement of the international
president of the United Mine Workers of America that the members of the
Steam Shovel Men's Union were to be treated as common strike breakers all
check was removed from the actions of the local members of the United Mine
Workers of America.
The telegram was published conspicuously on June 20 in the Marion Daily
Republican and in the Herrin Journal, and there is no doubt that its contents
became immediately known to practically all of the union miners and their
sympathizers over the whole of the coal field.
A mass meeting of the union miners was held on Tuesday afternoon, June
20, at the Sunnyside mine. What was done or decided on at that meeting
has never been made known. A second and larger meeting was held in the
cemetery at Herrin on Wednesday morning, June 21. The Lewis telegram was
read to this meeting, and it was from this meeting that the armed body of
men moved to the attack on Wednesday afternoon, June 21.
That trouble of some kind was brewing among the union miners of William-
son County was a matter of common knowledge throughout Illinois several
days before the attack. Col. Samuel N. Hunter, the personnel officer of the
Thirty-third Division of the Illinois National Guard and the personal repre-
sentative of the adjutant general of the State, had arrived at Marion on June 18
for the purpose of observing the situation and attempting to prevent trouble.
He remained on the scene until after the massacre. During the 19th, 20th, and
21st he had numerous conferences with Sheriff Thaxton and repeatedly asked
the sheriff to call upon the governor for troops in order to prevent blood-
shed, but the sheriff, who was a former miner, continuously refused to call
for troops, even after the attack on the mine had begun, affirming that he and
his deputies had the situation well in hand.
It is a significant fact that Hugh Willis, vice president of subdistrict No. 10,
was overheard to make the statement to a group of people on a street in
Herrin on the night of June 21 to the effect that the hardest task he had
had in the whole matter was to keep the sheriff from sending for the State
troops.
ATTACK ON THE TRUCK
Early on the morning of June 21 the Southern Illinois Coal Co. sent a truck
to Carbondale, 13 miles from Marion, to meet and bring back to the stripping
operation additional workers who were coming down from Chicago. This truck
was ambushed and fired on by an armed party near Fossert Bridge. Several of
the men in the truck were wounded and the others fled. Sidney Morrison,
the driver of the truck. was mortally wounded and afterwards died. The oc-
cupants of the truck were unarmed and did not return the fire of their at-
tackers. This was a delibera'e, cold-blooded ambush and murder. The shots
fired at the truck were the opening volley of the coming battle. They were
the first shots fired on either side. Report of this attack at once reached Mc-
Dowell at the s ripping operation over the telephone. He and his men knew
of this murderous assault long before the main attack and were thereby
warned of what they themselves might have to expect.

On the morning of June 21 hardware stores in neighboring towns were
simultaneously visited and arms and ammunition taken therefrom in the name
of the United Mine Workers of America.

On June 21 Williamson County was invaded by parties of armed men in auto-
mobiles from adjoining towns, counties, and States. Automobiles were present
at the scene of the attack bearing license numbers from Kentucky, Missouri, and
Indiana.
The mine next to the operation of the Southern Illinois Coal Co. and through
which the wires bearing electric current to that company passed was visited by
an armed party and the current cut off.
Everything in fact that could help to make the attack a success seems to
have been thought of and done.
ATTACK ON THE STRIPPING OPERATION
Shortly after 12 o'clock noon on June 21 an armed body of men fired a heavy
volley at the stripping operation. These were the first shots fired by either
side at the stripping operation, and were not returned by McDowell's men.
After this opening volley by the United Mine Workers of America, no further
attack was made for an hour or so, and then an armed body of at least 500
men approached the stripping operation and opened a heavy fire on it, which
was returned for the first time by McDowell's men.
A large part of this attacking force had marched directly to the attack
from the mass meeting of the United Mine Workers of America held that
morning in the Herrin Cemetery. It was at this meeting that the telegram
from John L. Lewis, international president, had been read characterizing
the members of the Steam Shovel Men's Union as common strike breakers and
authorizing the United Mine Workers of America in treating them as an outlaw
organization. The attack was kept up all the afternoon of June 21.
McDowell's men returned the fire of the United Mine Workers of America.
and during the afternoon two union miners by the name of Henderson and
Pitchonis were shot and killed.
THE TRUCE
News of the attack reached Colonel Hunter early on the afternoon of June
21. He endeavored unsuccessfully to find the sheriff. He then had a confer-

2043
ence with Fox Hughes, subdistrict vice president of the United Mine Workers
of America, and by telephoning to Lester got him to agree to stop operations
and arrange for a truce. Fox Hughes agreed to go to the stripping operation
with Hugh Willis and William G. Davis, the latter secretary and treasurer
of the local union, and see that the truce was put through. The following is
from a statement made by Colonel Hunter shortly after the tragedy of what
he did on the afternoon of June 21:
"I told Mr. Hughes that I would instruct McDowell to put up a white flag
pending further negotiations. I would instruct Mr. Hughes to have other
union mine officials accompany him to the mine under a white flag suggesting
that they and McDowell make some sort of an agreement or arrangement
whereby further loss of life might be avoided. Secondly, that the nonunion men
be afforded protection and safety from the mine after closing. Mr. Hughes
agreed to get Davis, and with Mr. Hugh Willis and Mr. Davis would accompany
them to the mine under the white flag of truce and that they would endeavor
to have their men discontinue the attack on the mine. That is the truce under-
standing."
Later, on the evening of the 21st, Hughes and Willis told Hunter that both
sides had white flags up and that the firing had stopped.
The attackers thereupon cut the telephone wires and no more communications
could be had with McDowell from the outside.
During the night some firing occurred on both sides and in the morning the
attack was resumed.
Shortly after daylight on June 22 McDowell offered to surrender to the leader
of the attacking force provided his men would be given safe conduct out of
the county.
Robert Tracey, a locomotive engineer employed by the Southern Illinois

THE MARCH
"1
The men who had surrendered were then marched away in column of twos,
guarded by their captors, out to the highway and along the highway to a place
called Crenshaws Crossing. They were there halted and an altercation took
place between two of the leaders of the march. One of them made a speech
to the effect that the prisoners should be treated as human beings. It has not
been possible to ascertain his identity. The other leader interrupted him and
made him stop his speech. This other leader was identified by witnesses at the
murder trial as Otis Clark, a vice president of subdistrict No. 10 of the United
Mine Workers of America.

THE MURDER OF M'DOWELL AT MOAKS CROSSING
After Otis Clark's speech at Crenshaws Crossing the march was resumed and
the column proceeded about a mile along the highway to a place called Moaks
Crossing. Meanwhile the ranks of the United Mine Workers of America were
constantly increased by the arrival of additional armed men. The unarmed
prisoners were continually beaten with guns, kicked, and otherwise abused.
At Moaks Crossing the column halted at about 7 a. m. near a little house
where Mr. and Mrs. George Nelson lived. They were there at that time. Me-
Dowell gave out at this point. He had an artificial leg and was known to the
United Mine Workers by the nickname "Old Peg Leg." He could walk no
farther.
George Nelson at the first murder trial testified that some one in the crowd
called out:
"There's no use to go any farther with him."

had known Otis Clark for 30 years. Nelson testified that Clark had a revolver
and had McDowell by the arm and he saw these men lead McDowell from the
column along a side road toward the south. Another man came up to Nelson
and said:
"Go into the house so you will not know anything."
He then went into this house and heard some shots in the direction that
McDowell had been led. A few minutes afterwards he saw Otis Clark sitting

Mrs. Nelson also testified at the first murder trial that she saw the two men

Robert Officer, one of the officials of the Southern Illinois Coal Co., an engi-
neer and a graduate of the University of Pennsylvania, and the man who
had had numerous conferences with Hugh Willis during April and May, and
had made the arrangements with him whereby the company had obtained the

confer with the leader of the march. He was too far back in the column

to hear what Hugh Willis said, but he testified that three or four minutes
after Willis's conference with the leader the prisoners were marched into
the woods and the massacre occurred.
Other witnesses also testified that they heard the crowd call out-" Here
comes Hugh Willis, the president"-as Willis drove up in his automobile.
Willis thereupon left and the leader to whom Willis had spoken marched
the column of prisoners 150 to 200 yards north in the woods by the power,
house and they were lined up against a barbed-wire fence and the captors
with their rifles, revolvers, and shotguns opened a murderous fire against this
unarmed body of prisoners. In cold blood a large number were there shot
down. Those who escaped death at the barbed-wire fence by flight were hunted
and tracked over the county until the last one who could be found was shot
and killed. Some 19 bodies were eventually brought into the morgue at
Herrin.
THE MAN HUNT FOR THE FUGITIVES
When the prisoners were line up at the barbed-wire fence and the shooting
began those who could, fled. The pursuit commenced and the fugitives were
hunted down. The sworn testimony of witness after witness at both murder
trials describing this man hunt, and the subsequent murders of those who were
caught, presents a picture of cruelty, bloodshed, murder, and violence that
we do not believe has ever been equaled in the annals of American history.
Just south of Herrin was the farm of George Harrison. He and his son,
Fred Harrison, were on their farm that morning. Their testimony is that four
unarmed fugitives were murdered there and that one of these was hung to
the limb of a tree.
THE MASSACRE AT THE HERRIN CEMETERY
The last act in the tragedy occurred at the Herrin Cemetery, situated a
little over a mile east of the town of Herrin. Six of the fugitives had been
captured. They were wounded and bleeding. They were marched at about
8 o'clock in the morning through the streets of Herrin, crowded with people-
Herrin, the city of 11,000 inhabitants, with its paved streets and its modern
improvements, its banks, and its churches. These poor, tired, and wounded
prisoners were not even permitted to stagger along on their feet but, in token
of their subjection to the United Mine Workers of America, were forced to
crawl on their hands and knees with heads bowed low to the ground in the
presence of hundreds of men, women, and children.
Dr. O. F. Shipman, a reputable physician of Herrin, who has now been
driven from Herrin because of his testimony, testified at the first murder trial

Two of the men here shot down were Howard Hoffman and R. J. O'Rourke.
Hoffman did not die immediately, but died later in the Herrin Hospital.
O'Rourke, though severely wounded and his throat cut, eventually recovered
and testified at the first murder trial.
Dr. O. F. Shipman testified at the first murder trial that he followed the six
wounded prisoners to the cemetery; that he saw the rope tied around their
necks by Percy Hall and that 10 to 20 men did the shooting. He identified
four of these union miners as Jack Carnaghi, Leva Mann, Percy Hall, and
Jim Gilligan.
His testimony reads in part as follows:
66
Q. Did you notice anybody else or observe anybody else shooting Hoff-
man? A. Yes, sir-Jack Carnaghi stood in front of me, I could put my hand
on him, looking at the other fellow, took out an automatic revolver from his
right-hand pocket and began shooting around himself and shot one cylinder
full, pulled out the bottom of the cylinder, put another in and went ahead
shooting. On one occasion he shot a man in the left side through in the right
shoulder blade; the man made two shrugs of his shoulder, rolled back flat on
his back. He then shot at Hoffman and hit him first below the shoulder
blade not the shoulder blade-in the sink of the shoulder. The blood spurted
up a foot high and then he got quiet also."
This massacre in the Herrin cemetery occurred a little after 9 o'clock in the
morning of a bright, clear day. The murdered men had been marched publicly
through the streets of Herrin. The chief of police had stood on the corner and
watched the march and had made no attempt whatsoever to interfere.
Donald M. Ewing, a newspaper correspondent, who on June 22, 1922, was the
city editor of the Associated Press of Chicago, arrived at Herrin that morning.
He arrived at the cemetery shortly after the murders and testified at the first
murder trial that he saw the six men lying on the ground tied together with a
rope around their necks. At that time three were dead and three were breath-
ing. He saw a miner by the name of Bert Grace with a gun in his hand and
he testified as follows:
"Q. If this particular defendant, Bert Grace, said anything there or did any-
thing during the time you were there, tell the jury what he said and what he
did.-A. He told me to keep away from the men who were lying in the road, the
wounded men * *
He was holding the gun * * *
66
Q. What, if anything, were you doing there in connection with these men, or
either one of them?-A. I was trying to bring one of them a drink of water.
"Q. Tell the jury what you saw him do.-A. I saw him put his foot against
the body of Howard Hoffman * *
and push at it with his foot.
"Q. Tell the jury what he said.-A. He said, 'You'll get no water here.'"
And so the last act in the tragedy was completed. Not even a drink of water
could be given to a victim whose life had not quite ebbed away.
DESECRATION OF THE VICTIM'S BODIES AT THE MORGUE
Of the men who were murdered, 17 were brought to an improvised morgue at
Herrin. The disfigured and mutilated bodies were stripped and exhibited to
public view. Men, women, and children filed by and laughed and joked over
the remains of the murdered men. The reporter for the Associated Press
sending his dispatch from Herrin on June 22 described this scene as follows:
"In the morgue here to-night were 17 bodies, some riddled with buckshot and
others minus various parts. * * *
What has become of the bodies not in the morgue is not known.
The usual solemnity of death is lacking in the local morgue. Hundreds of
persons filed past the lines of bodies to-day frequently commenting on their
mutilated condition. Children laughed, women pointed and the men chuckled.”
Later the unclaimed mutilated bodies of victims were burned side by side in
the Herrin Cemetery, where to-day they are uncared for and marked only by
a small cross with the sole exception of the grave of Antonio Mulkovich, a
World War veteran, over whose grave has been placed a small wooden
monument.
The attack was not made by an uncontrolled mob but was made by a well-
organized body of union miners and as the result of careful preparation.
To prove conclusively that the attack was made after careful organization
it seems hardly necessary to do more than to quote one or two articles from
local papers describing the tragedy immediately after its occurrence.

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
The Williamson County Miner, a paper published in Herrin, contained the
following description of the attack:
"At daybreak the 3,000 armed citizens (surrounding the mine) realizing that
the future peace of their county was at stake, formed what has been termed
by many, one of the neatest columns of troops ever seen in the vicinity, worked
their way into the stronghold of the outlaws and captured those that remained
alive. Several of those that were taken from the pit alive were taken to the
woods near Herrin, where later they were found dead and dying. There were
no riots, merely the citizens of the county acting in the only way left them for
the safety of their homes. The faces of the men who were killed in the dis-
turbance are horrible sights. Uncouth, as all crooks must be at the beginning,
they were doubly unattractive as seen after justice had triumphed and the
county had again resumed its normal peace-time behavior."
The Christopher Progress, another local paper, contained the following de-
scription of the attack:
66
"The whole of Williamson and Franklin Counties was in turmoil until late
Thursday and on Wednesday afternoon the miners in Zeigler and West Frank-
fort were canvassing the business districts and homes for arms and ammunition,
and we doubt whether there was much of either one left in their towns after
the cars had left for the scene on Wednesday evening.
"We have talked to several who were near the scene of rioting and many have
reported to us that no city in the community showed their colors so much
as the city of Ziegler which is located in Franklin County. At least 300 strong
men journeyed in cars from Ziegler on Wednesday evening and almost every
car was loaded with men, guns, and ammunition."
Thoreau Cronyn of the New York Herald, who went to Williamson County
immediately after the massacre and spent days investigating the matter, has
stated, as a result of his investigation, that
"Nearly everybody in the region knew the mine was to be attacked, and
the scabs cleaned out. If they resisted the fight was to go on until they gave up.
"One story is that 25 union miners, who were ex-service men and knew
the rules of warfare, had been picked to receive the surrender and guard the
marchers."
In addition Col. Samuel N. Hunter, who was himself an eye witness to
many of the things that occurred, in a statement made shortly after the attack,
said:
"It was a seemingly well organized, remarkably sober, determined, resolute
aggregation of men and boys fighting, as they put it in their own words, 'to
preserve the unions.'"
The records of the two murder trials support Colonel Hunter's statement in
a conclusive manner.
The fact is indisputable that the attack on June 21 was carefully planned and
organized by officials and members of the United Mine Workers of America in
Williamson and adjacent counties.
THE INDICTMENTS
The entire country was roused by this terrible crime. But the local authori-
ties did nothing. No arrests were made. Thaxton, the sheriff, made no at-
tempt to apprehend the murderers. The officials and the inhabitants of the
county hoped that nothing would be done. Their sole desire was to ignore the
occurrence and to have everyone else ignore it. But the pressure of public
opinion forced their hands. Edward J. Brumdage, attorney general of the State
of Illinois, a fearless public official, seeing that the local officials would do
nothing, finally took personal charge of the grand jury investigation, and upon
the evidence produced before it a Williamson County grand jury found in-
dictments charging many members of the United Mine Workers of America
with murder.
Among those indicted were Otis Clark, Joe Carnaghi, Peter Hiller, Leva
Mann, and Bert Grace, for the murder of Howard Hoffman, killed at the
Herrin cemetery, and Hugh Willis, James Brown, Oscar Howard, Philip Fon-
tanetta, Otis Clark, and Bert Grace for the murder of Antonio Mulkovitch, a
World War veteran, killed at the barbed-wire fence.
Under the laws of the State of Illinois, the trials had to take place in Wil-
liamson County. It was not possible for the State to remove the cases to an-
other county where an impartial trial might have been held. The defendants
must be tried in the midst of a community completely dominated by the United
Mine Workers of America.


===== [扫描序号 1045] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2049
THE TRIALS
Two trials were held.
On the first trial Otis Clark, Joe Carnaghi, Peter Hiller, Lava Mann, and
Bert Grace were tried for the murder of Howard Hoffman.
On the second trial Hugh Willis, James Brown, Oscar Howard, Philip Fon-
tanetta, Otis Clark and Bert Grace were tried for the murder of Antonio
Mulkovich.
The two juries were made up of citizens of Williamson County. The ma-
jority were farmers, but some were present or former members of the United
Mine Workers of America.
So sure were counsel for the defense of obtaining verdicts of acquittal from
these juries that in both murder trials they did not even take the trouble to
sum up to the jury.
So sure were the officials that verdicts of acquittal would be rendered that the
defendants, although charged with murder, were not even confined to jail or
taken into custody during the trials. They were admitted to bail and walked
freely in and out of the court room like defendants in civil cases.
The verdicts were uniformly "Not guilty."
No other verdicts could have been expected in an atmosphere where no man
could call his soul his own without permission from the United Mine Workers
of America.
No further trials will be held. The State of Illinois has decided that it cam
not obtain a conviction in Williamson County. All the untried indictments
have been dismissed. Attorney General Brundage, in a recent letter to Crandal
Mackey, in answer to a criticism for this action, wrote as follows:
"Williamson County is exclusively devoted to coal mining, and fully 90 per
cent of the population are affiliated with the United Mine Workers of America.
It is probably a stronghold of the union miners of the United States.
Under the laws of Illinois, the trials must be conducted in the county where
the crime was committed.
In Williamson County it has been absolutely impossible to obtain a jury to
convict. I personally conducted the grand jury inquiry and obtained the indict-
ments. Before the trials were commenced, an assessment of 1 per cent upon
the wages of all union miners in this central district was levied and deducted
from their pay under the check-off system. This yielded practically $125,000
a month, which has been collected since last July. Every lawyer of prominence
in southern Illinois was retained by the defense, and an army of propagandists
was put to work upon the inhabitants to create an atmosphere favorable to
the defense. The witnesses for the State were threatened with bodily injury,
and even the prosecuting attorneys, including myself, were constant recipients
of threatening communications. Such threats, however, have no influence upon
myself and assistants, but the witnesses absolutely rebelled against testifying
further after two futile efforts to convict.
Knowing the situation, and in justice to these unwilling witnesses, I saw
no other course but to abandon further indictments."
What a commentary this is on conditions in Williamson County! What a
charge to be answered by the United Mine Workers of America! To what help-
less condition has our Government come if such an organization can absolutely
prevent the perpetrators of such a wholesale series of murders from being
brought to the bar of justice?
THE EVIDENCE PRODUCED WAS AMPLY SUFFICIENT TO CONVICT
The trials were conducted for the State of Illinois by and under the super-
vision of Assistant Attorney General C. W. Middlekauff, another fearless public
official. He and his assistants, in spite of constant threats, even against their
lives, used every effort to bring the murderers to justice. They left no stone
unturned, and the records of the trials show that the evidence produced was
amply sufficient to have warranted verdicts of guilty.
None of the defendants took the witness stand in their own defense to deny
the commission of the crimes of which they were accused.
The defense relied chiefly upon three things:
1. It tried, as far as possible, to discredit the testimony of the State's wit-
nesses, but in this an examination of the testimony shows that it miserably
failed.


===== [扫描序号 1046] =====
2050
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2. It produced witness after witness in an attempt to show that the men
who were on trial for the murders were “not present" when the murders were
committed. The great mass of this alibi testimony is inherently incredible,
and we do not believe that it would have carried the slightest weight with a
jury sitting in a different atmosphere.
3. It endeavored to create an atmosphere of justification by claiming what
amounted to belligerent rights for those who committed the murders. It
claimed that Lester's attempt to mine coal and defend his property and workers
was a justification for the armed attack.
This attitude is perhaps best shown by the opening remarks of Angus Kerr,
counsel for the defense, on the first murder trial.
After describing how the supergovernment of the United Mine Workers of
America had been permitting W. J. Lester to strip the dirt from his coal, so
that at the end of the strike he could immediately mine and load his coal, Kerr
said:
"But this man was not satisfied with that, and we will show you before we
have concluded our testimony in this case that he knew when he undertook
the mission of loading coal here that it meant in all probability killing of
human beings.
*
"Counsel in this case
has said that the act of loading coal on the
part of the Southern Illinois Coal Co. was a lawful act; that Lester and the
Southern Illinois Coal Co. were within their lawful rights. Those are the terms
he uses when he undertakes to load coal. We will show you by the law and
by the facts in this case that there was the real murder in this case, the at-
tempt to load coal, when Lester and McDowell and everybody connected with
that company not only knew down in their hearts but they had been so advised,
to do so meant breach of the peace and riot and disturbance.
*
*
*
"Did W. J. Lester know in advance that the loading of coal from that strip
pit would create riot, disturbance, and breach of the peace? We will show you
that he knew this.
"In his greed to make profits during the suspension of work, he does what
the unduly, the wilfully malicious, and wicked employer of America-and,
thank God, that does not apply to them all-he brings into your county an
army; he invades your county with a well-equipped force of the most treacher-
ous men known in all the world. Oh! the old Apache had nothing on them,
because the Apache sometimes had mercy.
*
66 Lester
went to Chicago and he recruited this army, knowing, as

"We claim here that this invading army, and I don't care who equipped
them, whether Lester or McDowell-they were all parties to this original thing
in this case and the real body of this crime. Theirs is the fault; theirs is the
criminality, born of a mad desire to wring improper prices from the consumers
of coal in this country."
In the eyes of the United Mine Workers of America the real crime is not the
murder of another human being, but the loading of coal against the orders of
the union. The exercise of such a constitutional right on the part of an oper-
ator gives the armed forces of the United Mine Workers of America the rights
of belligerents in honorable warfare. In their own estimation, the United
Mine Workers of America are above the law of the State of Illinois and have
the right to carry out their edicts with force and arms and without account-
ability to the State for their breaches of the law.
JUSTICE THWARTED IN THE STATE OF ILLINOIS
The very moment that the massacre was over the United Mine Workers of
America set themselves about the task of thwarting justice.
The United Mine Workers of America openly financed the defense of the
indicted men.


===== [扫描序号 1047] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2051
The chief counsel for the defense on both trials, Mr. Angus Kerr, in his open-
ing remarks to the jury on the first trial made the following statement:
*
*
"We are going to produce a great many witnesses to show you-we are
going to show you by nearly 100 men who stood along the line of this march-
good honorable men-most of them union coal miners, however, because that
is what there is in this county; and I am going to make a confession to you
now: We are going to pay these union miners; we are going to pay them $10
a day.
My brother, Lewis, suggests that I explain to this jury why
we are going to pay these men. I am glad to do it. There has been a strike, and
I ought to have amplified my statement. The United Mine Workers, the Illinois
Mine Workers, the organized miners in Illinois, are financing this case. They
are paying the lawyers in this case. they are paying all the investigators, and
they are paying every dollar of expense in this case; and they are going to pay
the men that give up their day's work for testifying in this case, for giving
up their days."
The money so openly stated to be used to pay counsel, investigators and
witnesses was raised by the check off.
By means of the check off the United Mine Workers of America raised the
enormous sum of nearly $900,000 for the defense of their indicted members.
The check off amounted to 1 per cent of the pay of every United Mine Worker
in the State of Illinois. It commenced September 1, 1922, and was not ter
minated until March 31, 1923. Mr. Brundage in the letter above quoted has
estimated that the amount raised was approximately $125,000 a month, which
would make the grand total nearly $900,000. This fund was administered by
Frank Farrington, president of the United Mine Workers of America for Dis-
trict No. 12, which included the State of Illinois, and by counsel employed for
the defense.
The following is the circular letter sent out by Frank Farrington under date
of April 11, 1923, discontinuing the check off because there would be no further
prosecutions:
SPRINGFIELD, ILL., April 11, 1923.
To all local unions in District 12, United Mine Workers of America, greetings:
This is to advise that the special 1 per cent assessment levied by the last
State convention, held in Peoria, Ill., will be discontinued with the pay ending
March 31, 1923.
Local unions that failed to collect the special assessment for the pay begin-
ning September 1, 1922, or any subsequent pay, are authorized to continue
the assessment after the pay ending March 31, 1923, in order to allow them
to square up their accounts with the district organization.
We have every reason to believe that there will be no more criminal suits
against any of our members. We also have reason to believe that civil suits
for heavy property damages will be filed against the district organization,
and that we will be obliged to defend against such suits. However, we feel
that we will be able to take care of such matters out of the regular revenue
that comes into the district organization, and we therefore hope and feel
that there will be no necessity to levy any special assessment against our
membership for that purpose. In conclusion, we take this means of earnestly
thanking our membership for the splendid manner in which they came to the
support of our members who were indicted because of the so-called Herrin
trouble.
The acquittal of our members is without parallel in labor circles in this
country and perhaps any other country and to know that their defense was
financed and made strictly by the Illinois mine workers without their calling for
outside help bespeaks volumes of praise for the loyalty of our members and the
power and efficiency of your district organization.
Yours fraternally,
FRANK FARRINGTON,
President.
HARRY FISWICK,
Vice President.
WALTER NESBIT,
Secretary-Treasurer.
This immense fund was used by the United Mine Workers of America in
every conceivable way to defeat the ends of justice and to obtain verdicts
of acquittal for their indicted members.


===== [扫描序号 1048] =====
2052
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
We have been informed that every lawyer of any prominence in southern
Illinois, except Senator Otis Glenn and State's Attorney Duty, was retained by
the United Mine Workers of America on behalf of the defense, so that the
prosecution could not avail itself of their services. Although many of these
attorneys are not publicly known to have taken any active part whatsoever
in the defense, they were paid large retainers by the United Mine Workers of
America-in some instances, we are informed, as high as $15,000.
A veritable army of propagandists was set to work in Williamson County
for the purpose of creating an atmosphere favorable to the defense. There
was apparently no limit to the expenditure of this fund so long as that expendi-
ture would tend to obtain the acquittal of the indicted men.
Direct evidence of how this enormous defense fund was spent can only be
obtained by a body having the power to subpoena witnesses and to ascertain
the facts.
We therefore urge the United States Coal Commission. which has this fact-
finding power, to examine to the smallest detail how this fund was expended
by the United Mine Workers of America, to the end that the American public
may know in what manner and to what extent this expenditure contributed to
the defeat of justice in Williamson County.
Thaxton and Clark have been honored by their neighbors.
Melvin Thaxton, the sheriff who would not send for State troops even after
the attack had commenced and the battle was raging, himself an ex-member
of the United Mine Workers of America and at the time of the massacre a
candidate for office, was greatly honored.
Melvin Thaxton was elected in the autumn of 1922 treasurer of Williamson
County by the largest vote said to have ever been polled in that county by any
candidate.
Otis Clark, who was one of the principal defendants, was also honored. It
is common knowledge in Williamson County that his unfinished house was
completed by the work of union labor, which, it is generally understood, cost
him nothing. This was his reward for the part that he had taken.
Such an atmosphere of terrorism was created by the United Mine Workers
of America that convictions in Williamson County were rendered impossible.
Threatening letters were sent to witnesses and to their families and to every-
body connected with the prosecution. Every effort was made to create such a
feeling of terror that a witness could only testify against a United Mine
Worker with the fear of personal danger hanging over his head.
Our investigators in Williamson County have been repeatedly told that it
was common knewledge in the county that witnesses for the prosecution, who
were business men, had been given to understand that if they testified against
the United Mine Workers of America their business would be boycotted. In a
county like Williamson County, almost entirely inhabited by union men, this
meant ruin.
In one instance that we know of a resident of the county who had been
shocked at the murders was unfortunate enough to express his opinion. This
became known. From that moment his life was in danger. A squad of United
Mine Workers started for his home with the obvious intention of killing him,
and it was only through the courage and foresight of a friend that he was able
to escape with his life. To him, to-day, Williamson County is a forbidden spot
merely for expressing an opinion that the murders were without justification.
It is impossible to-day to get an ordinary citizen of Williamson County to
speak with any freedom about the Herrin massacre. The fear of personal
violence and perhaps death hangs over the community, as it did in Pennsylvania
in the days of the " Molly McGuires."
In the midst of such an atmosphere of terrorism, and with the expenditure
of their enormous defense fund, it is not strange that the United Mine Workers
of America succeeded in their attempt to thwart justice.
Thoreau Cronyn, of the New York Herald, on July 12, said:
"No one in Williamson County will admit that he was one of those who shot
up the mine or shot down the miners, or that he was even an innocent by
stander peeking at the show from an attic window or a distant hilltop.”
The testimony at the trials showed that hundreds of people, men, women,
and children, saw the march from the strip mine to the barbed wire fence:
that hundreds of people stood on the sidewalks of Herrin, the modern up-to-
date city, and saw the six prisoners marched through its streets on the way to


===== [扫描序号 1049] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2053
their death at the Herrin cemetery. And yet witness after witness went on
the stand and testified that they did not recognize a single person among the
captors. They dared not testified to anything else.
Could any evidence be more eloquent in its condemnation of the United Mine
Workers of America? In such a community and under such circumstances
the murderers, unless they had been members of that organization and unless
that organization had by its reign of terror aided, abetted, and countenanced
the crime, could have been brought to justice on the spot.
The inevitable conclusion is that the verdicts of acquittal for the individual
defendants were in reality verdicts of guilty against the United Mine Workers
of America.
And this conclusion is amply justified by the attitude throughout of the United
Mine Workers of America.
What did they do to ascertain and bring to justice the perpetrators of the
crime?-Nothing.
'What did they do to help the State enforce its laws? Nothing.
What did they do to discipline their local unions in Williamson County for
the part played by them in this terrible affair? Nothing.
And what could they have been expected to do when John L. Lewis, presi-
dent of the International Union, had told them they could view the shovel
men as common strikebreakers?
PURPOSE OF UNITED MINE WORKERS OF AMERICA
The following facts must be borne in mind:
1. The Southern Illinois Coal Co. was and had been engaged only in stripping
operations. This was not a "mine" at all in the ordinary meaning of the
word. It was not customary for members of the United Mine Workers of
America to be employed in these stripping operations. This was work that did
not need to be, and is not usually, done by "miners," although in this case
some United Mine Workers of America had been employed at the shovel pit up
to about June 13, 1922, at which time they quit, not because of any grievance
but because the United Mine Workers of America did not propose to allow any
coal to be produced and shipped to the public during their nationwide strike.
2. At the time of the attack, the employees of the Southern Illinois Coal Co.
were either members of the International Union of Steam Shovel Men and
Dredgemen or nonunion men. There was no quarrel between the company and
its actual employees. They wanted to work. There had been no quarrel
between the company and the United Mine Workers of America as to con-
ditions of work, pay, or anything else.
3. The sole objects of the attack by the United Mine Workers of America
were (a) to aid its nation-wide strike, (b) to prevent an ounce of coal being
mined or shipped by men not members of its organization, and (c) to prevent
the people of the United States from receiving one ounce of coal while the
United Mine Workers of America chose to strike.
4. The methods of the United Mine Workers of America prevailed. The
plant of the Southern Illinois Coal Co. was destroyed and burned. Its em-
ployees were killed, wounded, and driven from their work and 75,000 tons of
coal which might otherwise have been shipped to a suffering public stayed in
the ground of Williamson County.
SUMMARY
Thus did the United Mine Workers of America-
(a) Murder at least 20 employees of the Southern Illinois Coal Co.;
(b) Assault and wound many other employees of the Southern Illinois
Coal Co.;
(c) Prevent all of the employees of the Southern Illinois Coal Co. from peace-
fully carrying on their daily work;
(d) Burn and destroy the property of the Southern Ilinois Coal Co.;
(e) Force the Southern Illinois Coal Co. to cease its operations;
(f) Prevent at least 75,000 tons of coal from reaching the American public
from stripping operations with which the United Mine Workers of America
ordinarily had nothing to do;
(g) Raise an enormous defense fund of nearly $900,000 to obtain the ac
quittal of their members indicted for the murders;


===== [扫描序号 1050] =====
2054
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
(h) Use this enormous fund and all the weight and influence of their organi.
zation to defeat the ends of justice in the State of Illinois; and
(i) By so doing obtain verdicts of acquittal for their individual members,
which they themselves have characterized as "without parallel in labor circles
in this country and perhaps in any other country," but which, in the eyes of
public opinion, have branded their organization with the word "guilty."

Mr. BRADY. I have. And I should like to read it without inter-
