Senator GOODING (presiding). You may go ahead and read your
statement.
Senator WHEELER. But we will not guarantee not to interrupt you.
Mr. BRADY. All right. This statement is made in my own defense
answering accusations made by Mr. Van A. Bittner as to eviction
proceedings at the Brady-Warner plants in 1924.
On the 1st day of September, 1922, the Brady-Warner Coal Cor-
poration, which is a West Virginia corporation, owns and operates
two bituminous coal-mining plants in Monongalia County, W. Va.,
known respectively as the Monon and Osage plants. The Monon
property consisted of about 1.260 acres of Pittsburgh coal and 1.450
acres of Sewickley coal, with the Sewickley vein lying directly over
the Pittsburgh vein, and is situated on the Monongahela Railway
at Brady Station, about 12 miles north of Morgantown. The Osage
plant of the company is situated on the Scotts Run Branch of the
Monongahela Railway, and the property consists of about 260 acres
of Pittsburgh coal and approximately the same amount of Sewickley
coal lying directly over the Pittsburgh seam. This is one of the
finest coal properties in northern West Virginia for the reason that
this is the only company which owns and operates both the Pitts-
burgh and Sewickley seams, the one supported by the other, which
enables the company to operate approximately 15 feet of coal in
thickness from the same property.
On the date aforesaid this property was capable of producing
800,000 tons of coal a year, and in order to finance the company it
negotiated a bond issue in the amount of $1,100,000 upon these prop-
erties, together with a coal property owned by the company situated
on the Western Maryland Railway and known as the Abrams Creek
plant, and the mortgage also covered 9,600 acres of coal and timber
in Clay County, W. Va.
At the time this bond issue was placed the company was operating
under an agreement with the miners' union and paying a scale of
wages which is the same scale set forth in the Jacksonville agree-
ment.
In March, 1924, due to the steadily declining price of coal and the
high-wage scale which the company was compelled to pay, it became
unable to meet the interest and sinking-fund charges on the bond
issue referred to, and the company was falling steadily behind and
was threatened with foreclosure of its mortgage.
In these circumstances the executive committee of the company,
composed of myself, Whitney Warner, and Charles A. Goodwin,
held a meeting in the office of W. H. Warner & Co. in the city of
Cleveland about the 20th of March, 1924. The contract between
the company and the miners' union expired by limitation on the 1st
day of April, 1924, and the company had been advised by W. H.
Warner & Co., its sales agents, through Whitney Warner, that it
could secure a contract from the Jersey Central Railroad of 700
tons of coal per day at $1.60 per net ton f. o. b. mine, if it could begin
shipping coal on the contract by the middle of May. W. H. Warner
& Co. became a stockholder of the Brady-Warner Coal Corporation
at the time of the execution of the mortgage in the amount of one-
fourth of its capital stock, and the company's executive committee


===== [扫描序号 1062] =====
2066
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
met for the purpose of reaching a decision upon two propositions,
(1) whether it would refuse to renew its agreement with the miners'
union after the 1st of April, and (2) whether it could afford to
take the Jersey Central contract and such other contracts as it might
be able to obtain at the very low price of $1.60 per ton and attempt
to operate its mines-open shop on a lower scale of wages.
At this meeting, after a thorough discussion of the company's
affairs, the committee decided that it would not renew its agreement
with the miners' union, and since it was the only business in sight
and the condition of the market did not justify the presumption of
a higher price, the company decided to accept the Jersey Central
contract and attempt to operate its mines and to put into effect
the 1917 scale of wages.
At this meeting we were advised by Mr. Charles A. Goodwin, of
counsel for the company, that if we did not agree to renew our
agreement with the union the courts would protect us in the oper-
ation of our mines on the open-shop basis and that under our con-
tracts of lease with our employees under which they occupied our
houses, we could give them the notice required by the lease and if
they refused to vacate within a reasonable time, we had the right
to evict them, and that this had been decided by the Supreme Court
of West Virginia, and that if they attempted to interfere with our
right to operate our mines, with employees who would be willing to
work for us, by such acts as intimidation or force, that we could
restrain them by an injunction.
With this advice and driven by the necessities of our situation,
we decide, as I have said, to adopt this policy, and the meeting
adjourned with that understanding.
Immediately after this meeting in Cleveland at which the Brady-
Warner Coal Corporation decided upon the policy to be pursued by
it, the company withdrew its membership from all coal associations
because the officials of the company did not want to be bound in
any manner by the action taken by any of the associations with
reference to renewing the scale agreement with the United Mine
Workers of America.
**33
As president of the Brady-Warner Coal Corporation, I also noti-
fied Mr. McComas, president of subdistrict No. 4 of district No. 17
of the United Mine Workers, that it was not the intention of the
company to renew the union scale agreement on April 1, and that
I was giving him notice in order that the company would be in
no way bound by the action of any coal association.
The officials of our company were furthermore requested to notify
the men that while the company would not sign the union agreement,
that the company would give them work commencing on the 1st
day of April on an open-shop basis and paying the 1917 scale, and
that no distinction would be made as between union and nonunion
men.

Mr. TOWNSEND. Not altogether. So far as he stated it, it was

that the relationship of landlord and tenant did exist in so far as the
occupancy of the house was concerned, but that was a tenancy at will.
The supreme court further held that under the agreement where he
had agreed to vacate in five days upon receiving notice, that if at
the expiration of the notice he refused to vacate the house, the land-
lord had the right to take his goods and possessions and put them
out of the house, provided that in doing so he created no breach of
the peace. In other words, if there was resistance of any kind, or if
there was a show of force on either side, then it became a question of
a breach of the peace, and the landlord was then required to resort to
his regular court proceedings of unlawful entry and detainer. And
I want to say, since the chairman asked that question, that during
the industrial conflict in West Virginia, extending over a long period
of time, a number of years, the coal companies, except in isolated
cases, have resorted to the action of unlawful entry and detainer in
the regular way to gain possession of their houses, and they did it
throughout the territory where this particular property is located.
The attorney general of the State in that connection delivered an
opinion to the effect that where there was any sort of a breach of the
peace or an appearance of use of force, that they must resort to their

right of unlawful entry and detainer, and the State police of that

On the night of the 21st of May, large numbers of men, many of
whom were afterward shown, in a contempt proceeding tried in
the Circuit Court of Monongalia County, to be members of the
United Mine Workers of America, assembled on the hills on three
sides of the company's mining village and fired repeated volleys,
estimated at from 300 to 500 shots with high-powered rifles, into the
dwelling houses of the company, which were then occupied by its
employees, including its club and boarding house, which was then
being conducted by a woman. A large number of bullets of large
calibre, among them steel-jacketed bullets, were found on the com-
pany's property the next morning. Fifty bullets were fired into one
house. The firing was wholly directed toward the dwelling houses
occupied by the company's employees and the dwelling houses occu-
pied by two of its former employees and their families, who had
agreed to voluntarily vacate the houses they occupied. These bullets
were fired at close range and penetrated the windows and window
casings, and doors, and walls, and roofs, and floors of the houses.
This firing by volleys continued from one-half to three-quarters of
an hour. I herewith exhibit some of the bullets that were fired into
the dwelling houses. I picked those up myself in the houses.

On account of the shooting up of the company's plant and the
numerous acts of intimidation and terror practiced against its em-
ployees in an effort to compel it to cease the operation of its mines,
the company applied to the Circuit Court of Monongalia County,
W. Va., for an injunction which is obtained on the 23d day of May,
1924, and which is similar to the injunction order which was sus-
tained by the United States Supreme Court in the case of American
Steel Foundries v. Tri-City Central Trades Council (257 U. S.
184), except that it did not in express terms enjoin picketing.
From the 20th day of May, 1924, until the 17th day of June,
1924, large numbers of persons affiliated with the United Mine
Workers of America met daily at its union hall adjoining the
Brady-Warner mining plant. About midnight of June 18, 1924,
lights appeared up against the hillside above the plant of the com-
pany and several shots were fired, and about the same time a fiery
cross was lighted on the hilltop; and immediately thereafter a
couple of charges of dynamite were exploded, and following that
shots were fired into the mining village and plant of the company
from the direction of the lights and fiery cross and from the sur-
rounding hills and localities between a schoolhouse and the union
hall and from down the Monongahela River on both sides.
The CHAIRMAN. How do you know who did that?
Mr. BRADY. We arrested them, and they proved to be our former
employees. We knew them all personally and they all belonged
to the union. They were convicted.
The CHAIRMAN. Of this offense?
Mr. BRADY. Of this offense, and were not sentenced because the
attorneys made an agreement that if we would not have them sen-
tenced they would let us alone; and after that time they never
bothered us.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Mr. Brady, just to clear up one question about
which I think there was some confusion here-

The foregoing facts were alleged and proved in a proceeding for
contempt of the court's injunction brought against E. E. Coulter
and 18 other members of Local No. 4040 of the United Mine Workers
of America, and on the trial of said proceeding the company intro-
duced testimony which directly connected these 19 defendants with

by the court, the court took time to consider of its judgment and
from that time on the company was permitted to operate its prop-
erty without further molestation.
During this time and thereafter Mr. Van A. Bittner was com-
mander in chief of the army of the United Mine Workers and had
direct charge of their activities in the field.
My attention has been called to parts of the testimony given before
this committee by Van A. Bittner and with especial reference to that
part of his testimony which relates to the Brady-Warner Coal Cor-
poration and its activities, and my personal actions, I desire to say
that the Brady-Warner Coal Corporation has at all times proceeded
within the limits of the law of the State of West Virginia. The
court records in relation to its affairs and troubles with the United
Mine Workers of America and its officials are very full and complete.
As an aftermath of the trouble we had with the United Mine
Workers of America at Monon mine diverse and sundry suits were
instituted by members of the United Mine Workers against the
Brady-Warner Coal Corporation and against some of its officers
personally. Three of these suits were instituted in Monongalia
County, W. Va., and after being continued from term to term with-
out any attempt or effort on the part of the plaintiffs to prosecute
them, were dismissed from the docket of the court. Two suits are
now pending in Marion County, W. Va., one charging the officials of
the company with having burned the union hall owned by the United


===== [扫描序号 1081] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2085
Mine Workers and situated at Brady Station near the Monon plant
of the company. Although these cases have been pending since
early in the year 1924, no effort has been made on the part of plain-
tiffs to prosecute them to a conclusion.
On page 1921 of the transcript of the testimony of Van A. Bittner,
he makes especial reference to inhuman treatment on the part of
myself and my son and other employees, to one Mrs. J. H. Morton-
it is Morton, M-o-r-t-o-n, here. I think they had it Martin in the
proceedings during the eviction proceedings at the Monon plant
of the Brady-Warner Coal Corporation. I want to deny specifically
each and every allegation of the testimony of Van A. Bittner in
this particular matter.
On Sunday afternoon of the 18th day of May, 1924. I had a
conference, by request, with Sheriff William Yost, of Monongalia
County. His attorney, ex-Governor William E. Glasscock, was pres-
ent. My attorneys, Charles A. Goodwin and David C. Reay, were
also present. We advised the sheriff that we were going to evict
the ex-employees at the Monon Mine from the houses, pursuant to
notice and agreements and that we would commence to move them
out on Monday morning, May 19. At that conference Attorney
Glasscock, who represented the sheriff, advised the sheriff as to his
duties and told the sheriff to permit no violence, either by the com-
pany's officials or any of the members of the union or anyone else, and
instructed the sheriff to be present, preserve the peace, and to arrest
anyone who violated the law.
I made arrangements with the sheriff to meet him and his deputies
at the property on Monday morning, May 19. I proceeded on that
date with several trucks and had employed six men to do the
moving. When we arrived at the property we found a number
of people congregated on the hill near the mining plant, and the
sheriff ordered them to disperse, and he told them he was there to
see that no violence would be permitted on either side and that he
was advised by his counsel that the coal company had the right to
the possession of its houses.
I went first to the house of E. E. Coulter. Mr. Coulter told me
his wife was in a delicate condition and after seeing her I was
convinced beyond any doubt that this statement was true and that
no effort should be made to dispossess the Coulters, and I offered
to send for an ambulance and send his wife to a hospital and pay
all the expenses for the delivery of the child. Coulter refused
this offer in vile terms and tried to shoot me with a high-powered
rifle and was prevented from so doing by the prompt action of two
of the mine watchmen.
We left his premises and proceeded to house No. 8, occupied by
J. H. Morton and his wife, The same Morton purchased the cotton
and oil used in burning the fiery cross on the premises. When we
got there Mr. Morton was sitting on his porch, and I advised him
that I came there to move him off the property and asked him where
he wanted his furniture and effects moved to. He said he didn't
give a damn where I moved him to and that he didn't think I
could move him out, that he had been advised by the attorneys
of the United Mine Workers that I could not move him. I talked
with him for quite a while, as he had been one of our employees
for a number of years and had seemed very friendly to the company.


===== [扫描序号 1082] =====
2086
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
It was then about noon, and we decided to get our lunch at the
boarding house, and about 1.30 in the afternoon we returned to the
Morton house to move him.
We found the door locked and nailed, and I went around to one
of the windows and looked in and saw Morton and his wife in
the house. I instructed one of the mine watchmen to break down
the door, having been advised by our attorney before I went there
that day that if they locked themselves in we had the right to
break down the door of our own property, but to be careful and
not offer the tenants or their families any violence. The door was
broken down, and I entered with two of the watchmen and found
Morton standing in the front room, and I said to him, "Joe, where
do you want your furniture moved to?"
Senator WHEELER. You were advised by your lawyers, were you,
that you could knock down their house?
Mr. BRADY. Could knock down the door, so long as I did not
disturb the tenant.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Isn't that violence?
Mr. BRADY. No, sir; breaking a door is not violence. The door
is a door. Violence is to a human being. I had advice from my
attorney.
Senator WHEELER. If you tried that in Montana they would put
you in jail for it.
Mr. BRADY. I was working under the laws of West Virginia.
I was there at that time.
Senator WHEELER. I do not believe you have any laws in West
Virginia that will permit you to do that.
Mr. BRADY. I was working under the instructions I got from my
attorney. When I need a doctor I go to him, and take his medicine.
I think I had said that I said to him, "Joe, where do you want
your furniture moved to?" He said, "I don't give a damn where
you move it to." I then called the men I had on the premises to
move the furniture, to load it up on the trucks and to be careful
and not break any of their furniture, and haul it to the county road.
about a half mile distant. Morton then said, "You can't move me,
my wife is sick." I said, "What is the matter with your wife?"
He said, "She has gallstones." I said, "Have you got a doctor's
certificate stating that I can not move you out of the house on
account of danger to your wife?" He said he didn't have one nor
did he need any. At that time Mrs. Morton appeared in the kitchen
door carrying a baby on her hip. The child looked to be about
six months old. During the time that we were moving out the fur-
niture, Mrs. Morton did not say a word to anyone nor did she act
like she was ill, but before we completely moved the furniture out
of the house Mrs. Morton went out into the crowd which had by
this time congregated and spent the rest of the afternoon running
around in the mud, cursing and damning the company and calling
me very vile names.
Just before the truck started to the county road with the furniture,
Mr. Morton told me he would like me to haul the furniture to Union
Hall, which was just over the property line about a thousand feet
from house No. 8 which was occupied by him. The furniture was
loaded and unloaded carefully and I took particular notice that
nothing was broken.


===== [扫描序号 1083] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2087
The next morning we found that the house out of which we had
moved the Morton family had been entered in the night by some-
one who had taken a pickaxe and vertibly wrecked the entire in-
terior of the house, breaking out all windows and tearing the plaster
from the walls. While I have no personal knowledge of the person
guilty of this act, I am reliably informed that this destruction was
committed by Mrs. Morton.
Under this statement of facts, J. H. Morton and his wife Annie
Morton instituted a suit in the Federal district court for the northern
district of West Virginia.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Do you mean to say it was upon that statement

Senator GOODING (presiding). The committee is very anxious to
clean up the work of West Virginia this afternoon. Can we do so?
Mr. TOWNSEND. I think so, Mr. Chairman.
Senator GOODING (presiding). All right. Go ahead, Mr. Brady.
Mr. BRADY. Instituted a suit in the Federal district court for the
northern district of West Virginia against the Brady-Warner Coal
Corporation and against myself, two sons, and one mine watchman,
claiming damages in the amount of $30,000. This suit is still pend-
ing in the United States court. It has been continued once or twice
at the request of counsel for Mr. Morton and his wife, once or twice
by request of counsel for the company, and once at the instance of
the judge of the court. The matter is still pending and undeter-
mined, but the company expects to make a proper defense when the
case is finally called for trial.
In the month of September, 1924, the company determined to start
operation at its Osage mine on Scotts Run, which was closed down on
April 1, 1924, when the scale agreement with the union terminated.
The company followed the same procedure at this mine-posted a
notice and a scale of wages, which was the 1917 scale, and requested
those who did not want to work to vacate the houses in which they
lived and move from the property. No one offered to work; and
after due legal notice in accordance with the terms of the leases,
the company evicted its former employees and started the plant on
an open-shop basis with new employees.
Putting this plant in operation was attended with the usual dis-
order and lawlessness. On two separate occasions the boarding house
of the company situated along the line of the Scotts Run Railway
was dynamited, the explosive being thrown from passing coal trains.
At the times the attempts were made to blow up the boarding house
it was occupied by from 15 to 20 boarders. The porch was blown
down, windows and doors blown out, and the furniture and dishes
were destroyed, but fortunately no lives lost.


===== [扫描序号 1084] =====
2088
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Shooting into the camp of the company at Osage was a nightly
occurrence and the company was compelled for months to maintain
a large force of watchmen to protect the property and the lives of
the men and their families who desired to work for wages under
the 1917 scale.
I have read the testimony.of Van A. Bittner before this commit-
tee in reference to the trouble at Osage plant, and desire to say that
except for an outbreak of lawlessness caused by the members of the
union interfering with the company in its effort to operate this mine
very little trouble occurred.
No action was taken by the company that was not strictly in
accordance with the law. After the union had started its efforts to
prevent the operation of the mine and committed the usual number
of lawless acts, the company promptly applied for and secured an
injunction.
With this injunction order (which has not been dissolved) and
the efficient assistance of the State police, a company of which was
stationed at Osage, the company has since been enabled to operate its
mine continuously until this time with very little additional inter-
ference, except that in the month of March, 1927, one section of the
interior of the mine was set on fire in three different places in an
effort to destroy the property and prevent production.

HOUSE-LEASE AGREEMENT-BRADY-WARNER COAL CORPORATION, MONON MINES
This agreement made this 28th day of March, 1924, between Brady-Warne?
Coal Corporation, a corporation, of the first part, and Joe Griffin of the second
part, witnesseth: That the said party of the first part does hereby lease and
let to the said party of the second part, from the 16th day of March, 1924, for
and during the good will of said party of the first and no longer, the follow-
ing described premises, owned by the party of the first part, in the condition
the same may be at the date of this lease, situate at Brady in Grant district.
Monongalia County, W. Va., and known as house No. 502, block No. ——, and
the said party of the second part hereby covenants and agrees to pay to said
party of the first part rent for said premises at the rate of ($2) two dollars
per month, payable on the first day of each month, and to be deducted from
said lessee's pay due him by the said company. No charges less than one-half
month's rent will be made.
That he will not relet or sublet, the said premises. or any part thereof, to
boarders, lodgers, or others, or he shall not harbor on, or permit the transient
use of, or permit to be on said premises, any person objectionable to said com-
pany, or who might be injurious or detrimental to the conduct of the said
company's business or anything which might be dangerous to the premises, the
property, or the business of said company, or assign this lease without the
written consent of the said party of the first part, under the penalty of im-
mediate and absolute forfeiture of this lease and damages.

That he will not under a like penalty use or occupy the said premises, or

or pretense whatsoever; and it is further agreed that should the said party

upon the failure of the party of the second part to pay the rent at the time

the employment of said party of the first part or being dismissed therefrom,

mination of this lease or retaking possession of said premises shall deprive
said party of the first part of any action against said party of the second part

And he further agrees that any moneys that may at any time be due him

retained by it from time to time and applied to the payment of any rent that
may at such times be due under the lease or any damages that the said party
of the first part may have sustained by the nonperformance by the said party
of the second part of the stipulations or conditions contained in the lease.
The superintendent or manager of the said company, at said mining plant is
authorized to execute this agreement for and in the name of the said company.

Mr. TOWNSEND. The amount expended for watchmen?
Mr. KEELY. We have none.
Mr. TOWNSEND. You have none?
Mr. KEELY. We have never employed a watchman or guard or spy,
or detective, or deputy sheriff since I have been on the job.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Is that a statement you desire to file?
Mr. KEELY. Yes; I had a five-page statement there, like the others,
that I would like to have in.
Senator WHEELER. You say you have a five-page statement there?
Mr. KEELY. Yes; to file with this.
Senator WHEELER. What is the nature of the statement?
Mr. KEELY. It is a short history, Senator, of the time I was on
Cabin Creek. I was hindered by having a Harvard degree and
10 years' experience teaching school, and I thought collective bar-
gaining would work.
Senator WHEELER. And you say you do not think it would now?
Mr. KEELY. I did not.
Senator WHEELER. Well, do you still think it would not work?
Mr. KEELY. That was the nature of my-in the light of the experi-
ence I had, I was afraid it would not.
(The statement presented by Mr. Keely is as follows:)
My name is Josiah Keely. I am general manager and president of the
Carbin Creek Consolidated Coal Co., a company formed in 1907 entirely by
West Virginians. Nearly 80 per cent of the stock is now held in Kanawha
County. All the directors are actively engaged in the conduct of the company's
business. We employ a little over 1,000 men in and about the mines, and
maintain our own selling agency.
In January, 1914, when I took charge of the company's operations, Cabin
Creek was just recovering from a two years' struggle with the United Mine
Workers of America. I had been a school-teacher for 10 years before entering
mining in 1907, with a particular interest in economics and sociology, so, natur-
ally, was not averse to trying out collective bargaining. In fact, I thought it
might work. Being in the enthusiastic mood of an experimenter, I thought
colored people had some rights, and one of my first duties was to investigate
why it was that no colored people could live in one of our mining towns. At
that time our employees on Cabin Creek were about half native white Amer-
icans, one-fourth native black American, and one-fourth foreigners. In talking
it over with the men they agreed as to the brotherhood of the workers, and
that the negroes were their fellow craftsmen, but when we sent good "union
niggers" in there, one night was about as long as they would stay, and I was
never able to overcome this while the union lasted, though I took it to a negro
board member in Charleston.
Another instance in which I failed to have the brotherhood of man recog-
nized was the case of an Italian foreman. This man was naturalized and had
worked his way up in our mines from miner, tracklayer, motor runner, and
assistant boss. He was mine foreman when the union came into Cabin Creek,
and they used Italians for the presidents of some of their locals. I did not
consent at once to the demands of the men to give them a native American
foreman, but could readily see the distinction between working for an Italian
boss and using one for a president in order to hold the Italians in union line,
and, before I could work out the change in justice to the Italian he was
called out of his house on Sunday morning and shot down by an official of the
union mine workers. Less than one year's sentence was served for this second
act in collective bargaining, union sentiment being used effectively at the trial.
At another mine dead work was outrageously expensive, and, instead of
confining myself to cost sheets, I went in the mine and stayed there until I
found out what was the matter. The foreman and superintendent were paying
an illegal bonus of $1 per yard in the entries and covering it up with extra
time turned in on slate. They had yielded to the pressure of what we call
"bushwhacking," and, instead of standing on the contract, or calling in some
collective bargainers, had taken the easiest way to keep the mine going. I


===== [扫描序号 1096] =====
2100
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
had to get rid of them and take off the illegal bonus. The local union called a
strike. The president of district 17 came to aid in the collective bargaining.
At the hearing an entry worker thought he was helping the cause by testifying
that the superintendent still owed him $50, but had promised to turn it in as
soon as the row was over, the slate cost and the manager had quit checking
the time. It was then that I began to learn things about collective bargaining.
The president of district 17, the position now held by Mr. Tetlow, held that
the illegal bonus had been established. I agreed that the $50 should be paid
and all obligations made by the superintendent up to date, but that a new rate
could not be written into the contract by fraud. It was stoutly maintained
that a rate could be established even by fraud, and that if I did not concur.
all the other 20 mines would be closed. This was becoming collective with
a vengeance, so I asked if I did not have the right to stop all entries in the
mine in question. This right was conceded, and, after about a year of room
driving, the working places began to be scarce. I had two men start an entry
and work several days before it was discovered, claiming that I had then re-
established the correct rate. This was grudgingly admitted and the entries
allowed to proceed, but the two establishers were expelled from the union
for 99 years.
The right to hire and discharge was granted to the management on paper,
but we had various warnings not to attempt discharges. At the Shamrock Mine
a foreman discharged a relative of one of the union officials for refusing to
lay a certain turn in the track before that of another loader who had been
last served. The trackman went home, changed his clothes, and returned to
the pit mouth where he waited until the boss came out and shot him dead
without argument. This murderer for several months did not even leave
Kanawha County, and it was after the union had left southern West Virginia
before any attempt was made to arrest him.
By the terms of collective bargaining, our weighmen were not eligible to
join the union, but were supposed to belong to the operating organization.
However, in a year or two, all had to join the union to enjoy the rights of
citizens, and, in a single year we lost 16,000 tons of coal at the tipple scales.
We were getting the worst of it from either our men or the railroads, and
I put on a special scale expert to see every ton weighed and sworn to, “for
use in a suit" if the fault was the railroads. The losses stopped wherever he
went, but it was quite an extra expense, having three men setting down every
weight. Here I would like to interpolate, in view of the fact that it has
been charged that coal has been measured and weighed improperly in the
absence of a union, that, in the past years wherever we have found mines
losing weight through an improper tare weight on cars the cars have been
reweighed and the proper adjustment made. Likewise at mines where the
mine scales have shown a less weight than the railroad weights returned we
have reduced the tare weights on the mine cars so that neither company nor
men would lose coal.
The checkweighmen were paid by the miners according to State law, but
were union officials chosen with a view of dominating every activity on the
tipples. For awhile after we found that our own weighmen were simply acting
as bookkeepers for the checkweighmen, we proposed to just let the checkweigh-
men do the weighing and cut off our own men, but this was collectively
decided against us. The checkweighman told the tipple boss when to start
the tipple in the morning, but several times, when the cars were blocked up.
and we tried to start a few minutes early so the empties could get back to
the loaders on time, the mine was ordered shut down for the day. I recall
that this happened once when a car dropper released a brake three minutes
before the whistle blew.
From 1914 to 1922 there were murders, robberies, gambling on the porches
of the company buildings, drunken brawls in public places, beatings, blackmail,
and disturbance of public worship. Lodges of the regular secret orders dis-
appeared, and Boy Scout organization was prevented. I was a good while
finding out why we could make no headway in the Boy Scout movement
during union days, but I have learned since that there was at that time a
constitutional prohibition against scouts. This used to perplex me not a
little, as my idea of community work was for officials and men who lived
together on the job to do their own uplifting instead of hiring some one to
do it. The union movement on Cabin Creek always seemed to me like a
revolutionary party within a regularly constituted government.


===== [扫描序号 1097] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2101
I have always liked to have an intimate acquaintance with my friends
and neighbors, and, during union days, my men shunned me like a leper. It
is only since the thing subsided that I have been accepted as a human being.
If the mining class really become self-conscious and wants to band together for
perpetual isolation, I would rather it stay in Ohio, as it is hard for moun-
taineers to get used to classes which are self-conscious.
The union oath was a protection for criminals in every resort to law. The
climax was in 1921 when thousands of good citizens were terrorized into
participating in the "armed march." Masked bands went from house to house
and ordered, in the name of the United Mine Workers of America, to arm for
war and report to Marmet, the mobilizing point. Enough, were shot down for
refusal to put fear into the rest. Many hid in the woods. Few refused the
call. Old mother Jones, who had led many a band in acts of violence on
Cabin Creek in the years of 1912 and 1913, plead with them at Marmet to
turn back, only to be slapped in the face by an official high up in district 17.
Our collective bargaining contract did not expire until 1922, and I had sub-
mitted to every ultimatum, yet, instead of presenting a solid front for the
alleged industrial slaves of Logan County, the army divided up into masked
bands and looted and robbed and abused those of us who had been doing
business with them. It is no wonder that, when the contract expired in 1922,
we had little trouble starting up our mines on an open-shop basis, especially
as our men were told that they would not be permitted to make a contract
until one was handed down to them from the central competitive States, and
were just sitting around with no chance for a collective bargain.
Mr. Tetlow spoke of 50.000 evictions in Kanawha district with guards,
deputy sheriffs, strike breakers, and bloodhounds. Kayford was probably the
union stronghold on Cabin Creek, and I can speak firsthand only for the
1,000 men we employed. We first ascertained that practically all of our
men wanted to go to work regardless of the attitude of the mine workers,
but were afraid. We served about 200 houses notices with a view of eviction,
and a great many more with the idea of not slighting anyone. One man
came to me to get a notice because, he said, he did not want the others to
know that he was figuring on staying and going to work. I served many
personally and unattended, and chatted and talked more freely with the men
than I had been able to since 1914. We never had a guard, a deputy sheriff,
a detective, a spy, nor a strike breaker. Though we contended that we had
the right to take summary possession of our houses-and we still claim that
right--we never exercised it. I think we averaged about three months to
the house in getting possession through the courts.
Not many of our families went to the tents, and there is considerable
mystery as to just who many of the tent dwellers were. As staying in the
tents was a condition of union relief they changed occupants a good many
times. I counted the tents and barracks often and, as I recall, there were
never much over 100 on Cabin Creek, and in the. three years this gesture
continued I rarely ever saw people that I knew--and I know Cabin Creek men
pretty well.
In the fall of 1924 we were subjected to one more attempt at absentee
collective bargaining. An organizer from Ohio came to Kayford and made
several speeches at meetings held on the railroad tracks at the tunnel. At
the end of each speech names were called for to be placed on a list. Sometimes
a man gave his own name and sometimes he called for some one else. They
were supposed to have had 80 or 100 names, and these men did not come to
work. When it was apparent that numbers were falling off instead of in-
creasing, a final meeting was held and a speaker, pointing to the hills over-
looking Kayford, said, "In the days of our victorious union we shot our way
to victory from those mountain tops (which was literally true), and those
old mountain tops are still there.' After the meeting this organized stopped
in a certain house in "Shamrock Hollow." In a few days two young men
staying at this house ambushed a hoist of 10 men being drawn up to work
in the darkness of early morning. One miner was killed and four wounded.
In three hours the assassins were taken and, together with another con-
spirator, were sentenced to the penitentiary; one being made a "trusty
violated his parole and escaped. The other two are now serving time in the
State penitentiary. I presume the organizer escaped to Ohio. This dastardly
attempt to intimidate-in the absence of guards, strike breakers, or any
other resistance-was the death blow to unionism on Cabin Creek and to


===== [扫描序号 1098] =====
2102
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
my cherished theories of collective bargaining. Maybe both operators and
union started wrong down here, but if you ask me if I favor a union and
collective bargaining I will have to answer in the negative.
It has been charged here before the committee that Cabin Creek, since the
union died a natural death, has been guilty of certain unfairness, dishonesty,
and oppression as touching its employees, and, I take it that this same Cabin
Creek was pointed out as typical, at least it is fair to suppose that our critics
would choose for an example a place of average nonunion iniquity. I will
summarize quickly some of the points covered:
Since 1920 the coal companies on Cabin Creek have spent over $150,000
improving the regular county roads running through the properties. There are
independent stores all up and down this 12 miles of road, depending on the
trade of the miners for a living. They depend almost entirely on a trucking
business to the mining towns. Charleston and Montgomery also send in trucks
both to the company stores and to the miners. By automobile, Kayford is dis-
tant from Charleston, two hours; Montgomery, one and one-half hours;
Chelyan and Cabin Creek Junction, one hour; Miami, 30 minutes; and Eskdale
but 20 minutes. The following trucks make daily, weekly, or occasional deliver-
ies, most of them daily: August Saber, A. Joseph, Frank Harris, Frank
Palmer & Co., Kanawha Cash Grocery, Dan Scott, Mike Shibley, Best Meat
Market, Eskdale Meat Market, and others I can not recall, but 35 separate
trucking concerns do business on Cabin Creek. In season there are trucks of
apples, melons, potatoes, and vegetables from clear out of Kanawha County.
The company in the last three years has built over 300 garages to house the
machines of the miners purchased with earnings made on the 1917 wage
scale. In two hours at the most these machines may be driven to the best
markets in the State.
At the mine where one company was charged with collecting a dollar over
the pay roll for a minister, August Saber worked in the mine, and sold meat
to the miners on the side, until he saved enough to be able to quit mining and
put up a meat market of his own, not 40 feet from the company store. Several
of our miners have trucks and peddle their garden produce to the company
stores and to the miners. Most of the population live next to the hillsides.
Every pay day peddlers open their wares right under the pay windows. Our
company club house buys much stuff from trucks and order houses. George
Ort, the same mentioned as supplying the United Mine Workers, has been
doing quite a nice business with the nonunion miners on Cabin Creek. We
have never even made a check to see what our miners are spending in the
company stores, and, as to discharging, or in any manner discriminating
against an employee for not patronizing our stores, there is not only no ground
for the criticism, but the facts demonstrate the contrary. Every mail brings
me letters from credit companies asking for recommendations as to the ability
of our men to run accounts with them. Some I approve and some I do not.
but I would not receive these letters if it were generally understood in the
business world that we tried to prevent our employees from mail-order busi-
ness. Cars of melons and potatoes have been shipped and placed on our sidings
by outsiders and distribution made to the employees.
Testimony has been introduced to show that scrip is used to pay off the
employees instead of money, and that it is a means of taking advantage of the
miners' earnings. I can not believe this was offered seriously, as the scrip sys-
tem obtains uniformly in West Virginia both under union and nonunion con-
ditions, and State laws govern its use. When a miner comes into a company store
to purchase he does one of three things: (1) He applies to the scrip clerk
for an evidence of credit; (2) he pays cash; or (3) he goes to the store
manager and opens a book account, the same as he would at any other store.
The scrip clerk is the credit man and issues these evidences of credit in con-
venient sizes from $1 to $10. This saves the store clerks the delay and em-
barrassment of having to ascertain every purchaser's ability to pay. If the
holder of a $10 scrip wishes to spend $5, this amount is punched ou, and the
rest is used as needed, or passed on by him to some member of his family.
Legally it can be redeemed in cash by the rightful owner at the first pay day.
but as it has a cash value in the community I have never heard of an employee
presenting any of his unused scrip for cash redemption. It is true that a man
will sometimes discount this for cash between pays, but we do not permit the
stores or any office or the company in any way to discount scrip. Miners have
many advantages which other employees do not enjoy. The expensive, pre-


===== [扫描序号 1099] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2103
pared sizes of coal are delivered to the employee for $1 per ton. Elec-
tricity is furnished for lights, washing machines, electric irons, battery chargers,
radios, and Frigidaires at less than 5 cents per kilowatt-hour. Rentals will
hardly average $1.50 per room per month. In no other business is so much
latitude given to credits. This may well be a doubtful service, but our over-
drafts frequently reach $30,000. Certain miners have these overdrafts at many
different mines, and are allowed to make easy payments any time they come
back to work, or they may escape payment entirely if they go to a mine where
they have never worked.
The isolation of many of these company stores and this liberal credit system
may account for some excess in price, if it exists, but, as company stores will
not exceed a net profit of 12 per cent, and since Mr. George Ort's store must
make some profit to stay in the business, the company store could hardly over-
charge more than 5 per cent as compared with this store, and a 35 per cent
overcharge, as stated by Mr. Tetlow, seems an unauthorized statement. With
our improved roads have come school buses free to the children of Cabin Creek.
The Cabin Creek High School has 487 pupils, and in junior high schools are a
somewhat larger number.
I have refrained from abusive language and I appeal to the fairness of the
committee as to the properiety of the implication made at this hearing that the
nonunion operators and their employees are "yellow dogs." Our contractural
relations are, in many cases, more or less gentlemen's agreements, but the Cabin
Creek Consolidated has always considered these sacred and legally binding.
In 1924, when we contracted with our men for a reduced scale, we neglected
to include the cutting price on arcwall machines. By reason of this over-
sight, the contract provided for 10% cents per ton instead of 7½ cents. One
man made $7,000 and three others over six thousand in a year. The company
thus lost 3 cents on every ton of coal. There were other cases where I had to
rule against the company's interests to satisfy the guaranty that rates would
not be reduced during the contract period.
It seems to me that we should not discredit the negro as a coal miner. I
will grant that he is not always a good union man, for he naturally has loyal
instinct toward his employer, but when you class the southern negro as cheap,
undesirable labor, you have overlooked something. During the war a Cabin
Creek negro named " Bumpus loaded 60 tons of coal at 44 cents per ton in
one shift of eight hours, believing he was winning the war. Much of the coal
hauled in the mines of the southern fields is moved by mules. A darkey and a
mule is a combination which is industrially perfect. I have been somewhat
surprised at the slurs heard against the negro workman since this investigation
started. There seems so little ground for it.
As to the practice of checking off fixed charges from the miners' wages.
I can speak positively only for our own company, but I believe it the general
practice. The doctor, hospital, insurance, burial fund, and donations of various
kinds for churches, etc., are all absolutely voluntary. All may, and many
do decline to participate in one or more of these funds, and anyone can stop
or begin at the end of any two weeks' period. We simply notify the various
services when a man leaves the list, and then, if he requires a doctor, a hospital,
etc., he is taken care of at the regular rate, which is of course higher than
the list rates.. I think this is a general practice in large pay rolls of many
businesses. We never charge any commission for any of the collections, but
we do insist on having a voice in the choice of a company doctor, as no re-
putable physician will contract with a floating constituency without some guar-
anty from the company. Our doctors were likewise employed by the union
to attend to the tent colonies.
The company has always borne a part in the maintenance of churches,
but when I first came on the job it was paying a fixed monthly amount and the
miners were paying little or nothing. When I noted this, I declined to pay
for the company.
This gave rise to a practice which has been quite satisfactory; the minister,
or his people, solicit a list to be checked off through the office. The company
contributes dollar for dollar. When the men stop paying the minister, the com-
pany stops. There is no denominational favoritism. The Cabin Creek Consoli-
dated Coal Co. participated in building and maintaining on Cabin Creek the
first miner's Y. M. C. A. in the United States.

Senator WHEELER. Has your company prospered down there?

month was $122.47, and the average for the year per man was
$1,469.64. I think under the highest wage paid that probably would

Mr. TOWNSEND. Mr. Gross, your mines are all located in Fayette
and Raleigh Counties, are they not?
Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir.
Mr. TOWNSEND. And you mine what is known as the New River
smokeless?
Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Fire Creek and Sewall seam?
Mr. GROSS. Only Sewall seam.
Mr. TOWNSEND. That is a very high quality of coal, is it not?
Mr. GROSS. We believe it is.
Mr. TOWNSEND. For what purpose is it largely used? Do you
know?
Mr. GROSS. Steam and domestic.
Mr. TOWNSEND. By-product?
Mr. GROSS. No by-product. The Sewall seam is not very well
suited for by-product purposes. We are not mining the Buckley,
although we have some of it.
Mr. TOWNSEND. The major portion of your coal is used, then, for
steam and domestic purposes?
Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir.
Mr. LEWIS. Have you any bunker coal at all, Mr. Gross?
Mr. GROSS. Yes; we do sell a good deal of bunker coal.
Mr. LEWIS. Have you any Navy contracts?
Mr. GROSS. We have in the past enjoyed some Navy business, but
unfortunately, we have not been able to get any Navy business lately.
They want to buy it too low to suit me.
Mr. LEWIS. Does your fuel meet the Nevy test?
Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir.
Mr. TOWNSEND. You did not bid on this last contract that was let
for 93 cents.
Mr. GROSS. No, sir; we did not.

Mr. BELCHER. I will ask you whether or not the Government does
not try to get coal just as cheaply as it can?
Mr. GROSS. They certainly do.
Mr. TOWNSEND. I guess everybody will admit that.
Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Gross, have you hard roads in the vicinity of
your mines?
Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir.
Mr. BELCHER. I will ask you whether or not you compel your
employees to deal at your company stores?
Mr. GROSS. We do not.
Mr. BELCHER. Do you have competition with other stores?
Then,
Mr. GROSS. The way our mines and towns are located we have a
lot of competition. Take the Loop Creek Mine, for instance; they
are all available on these hard roads to Mount Hope and to Ther-
mont or White Oak Branch; all are adjacent to Oak Hill, which is a
thriving center and which has plenty of independent stores.
over in the Cranberry field or the Buckley field our mines are adja-
cent to the city of Buckley, which is a thriving city. All of our
mines can be reached from our central warehouse and our central
machine shop on hard roads in about 20 minutes, and they extend over
a distance of 20 miles; that is, the warehouse and machine shop are
practically in the middle.
Mr. BELCHER. Do you publish a magazine for the benefit of your
employees?
Mr. GROSS. We do.
Mr. BELCHER. Have you a copy of that magazine?
Mr. GROSS. I have.
Mr. BELCHER. Will you file a copy of that magazine for the in-
spection of the committee, if it so desires?
Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir. I would like to say in connection with that,
if I may just take a minute or two, that this magazine was gotten up
with an idea of seeing what we could do to help better the condition
of our men. I have been a stickler in this respect, that I felt that
whatever we could do for a man to help him be more orderly, to have
a more orderly mind, a more orderly house, and be more orderly
in his personal tastes, etc., made him a better workman and a better
citizen. In getting up this magazine we had two things in mind:
first, we wanted to stress, if we could, the value of first-aid and
mind-safety work. We have stressed that in every one of these
magazines. In fact, in the back of the magazine we carry a yellow
sheet of this kind [illustrating], which is a suggestion sheet to be
used for safety-first suggestions, and we ask the men to help us to
help themselves and so we carry that. This magazine, which we will
file, shows one of our first-aid meets of the New River Coal Co. teams
exclusively. Also I may say that our teams competed in international
contests and have succeeded in winning first and second prizes at
Denver and first at other international meets.
I am told, but can not vouch for the correctness of it, that at a
public statement made in Pittsburgh, I think, by a man who ought
to know, our company was the first company in the United States to
have all of its men 100 per cent instructed to render first aid. We are
proud of that distinction.
Mr. BELCHER. Have you any other exhibits that you care to
file?

Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir. In this connection, I may say that we started
out on a campaign a few years ago to endeavor to help the men to
raise more in the gardens. We have about 1,700 houses in our differ-
ent towns, and most of the houses have around them about half an
acre or possibly more. We felt that if there was anything that we
could do to help the men raise more stuff in the gardens it would be
a good thing, and, at the same time, if we could help them to beautify
their yards by growing some rambler roses over the doors, etc., it
would all be helpful.
When we put that system in we thought it would be well to offer
some prizes, which we did, first and second for the first and second
garden, and first and second for the first and second best yards in
each of our 15 towns, making 60 prizes in all. I think you will be
interested to know that last year our vice president told me that
while we awarded and paid the 60 prizes, there were 400 of our em-
ployees whose yards and gardens were so good that he had to write
them a letter because they deserved special mention.
I would like to file for your inspection, if you like, a few of these
photographs of yards and gardens in that district to show what is
being accomplished. I am proud of what this little work is doing.
In addition, something has been said here about automobiles. I
do not want to be in the back stretch on this thing. I do not know
how many of our 2,500 men have got automobiles, but there is a little
picture taken at one of the ball games. I will say that our general
manager, who was here in Washington last week, told me that we
had already built 800 garages and we are not through building them
yet.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Who is your general manager?
Mr. GROSS. Mr. M. L. Garvey. Mr. Scott has been our general
manager and vice president, but we had to give him some assistance.
Here is a picture of one of the hospitals. This one is at Beckley
where our men are taken care of at, I think, $1.25 per month, and that
includes all of the hospital attention for themselves and their entire
families.
Senator GOFF. You may file all of these memoranda and photo-
graphs with the committee for inspection when they come to con-
sider the case.
Mr. LEWIS. Do your employees have the right to buy the homes
in which they live?
Mr. GROSS. Yes. We tried that out a few years ago. We thought
it would be a good idea to get these men working for us and in
whom we have a great interest to buy their own homes. We made
them the most liberal kind of propositions, but we were surprised
to find that they did not avail themselves of that. There were only
one or two that did so. I do not know why they did not avail them-
selves of the offer unless it was that they could rent these places of
ours so much less than they could afford to own them for that they
elected to rent the houses and buy automobiles.
Mr. LEWIS. Can you give me an idea of the approximate value of
one of those houses?
Mr. GROSS. Those houses are costing us in the neighborhood of
$2,000. Of course, that is considerably more than it was before the
war, but the building values did not go down to what they were pre-
war. It is substantially $2,000 for the houses.

Mr. LEWIS. How is you town run down there?

Mr. LEWIS. Do they elect their own constables, justices of the

Mr. GROSS. I really do not know.
Mr. LEWIS. I was wondering whether the people elected them
or not.
Mr. BELCHER. The officials are all elected by the people.
Senator GOFF. Then they are municipal corporations.
Mr. BELCHER. Several towns, such as Mount Hope, Oak Hill, Ther-
mont, and places of that kind.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Those are not mining towns?
Mr. GROSS. In addition to the hospital at Beckley, which serves the
people over in that field, there has been recently built a hospital at
Oak Hill, and we were very largely instrumental in building these
hospitals. We built them and very largely financed them and then
turned them over to private interests who are now running them.
We did it for the purpose of getting things of that sort into the
community.
I want to take just a moment to say that we are proud as a com-
pany, and I can say this without being termed egotistical because I
live in Boston, we are proud of what our West Virginia organization
has done in that country. I think without doubt it can not be dis-
puted that the New River Coal Co. has done more than any other one
company; or, put it this way, that there is nobody that has done any
more than the New River Co. to improve conditions in the New River
field of West Virginia, and we hope to continue and do better as
time goes on, but we are proud of what we have been able to do.
Senator GoFF. In other words, you believe in mental, moral, and
aesthetic education and its maintenance?
Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir; we believe in treating men as men; and we are
all brothers, to a certain extent.

Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir.

maintain it and distribute it free.

Mr. LEWIS. How much per ton would that be?
Mr. JONES. Our average mining rate is about 36 to 40 cents a ton
at the different collieries.
Mr. LEWIS. Do you lay that coal on the carpet?
Mr. JONES. That only means that the men work at machine work.
The company
undercuts the coal, the men drill it and shoot it and load
it. If there is any slate, they are paid extra for it.
Mr. LEWIS. They pay for their own explosives?
Mr. JONES. Yes, sir.
Mr. LEWIS. Do you know how much explosive they use?
Mr. JONES. I believe it amounts to about 3 cents a ton.
Mr. LEWIS. What is the height of that coal?
Mr. JONES. The coal varies from 4 feet to 9 feet and 10 feet at
different collieries.

I am not now a member of the United Mine Workers of America, the I. W. W.,
or any other organization of mine workers, and will not during this employ-
ment join or affiliate with any such mine-labor organization, because I believe
the preservation of the right of individual contract, free from interference or
regulation by others, and payment in proportion to service rendered to be to
my best interest, to the best interest of the public, and of all industry, and I

POCAHONTAS FUEL Co. (INC.),
Mr. LEWIS. How many mines are you operating now?
Mr. JONES. The Pocahontas Fuel Co. operates 16 mines.
Mr. LEWIS. What is the approximate number of your employees?
Mr. JONES. About 3,800.
Mr. LEWIS. Would you mind saying what your total acreage is
there?
Mr. JONES. Under the Fuel Co. we have about 25,000 acres. We
have 16,000 acres of coal land left with about 185,000,000 tons of coal.
Mr. LEWIS. Does the Fuel Co. own all the coal companies?
Mr. JONES. They own the Pocahontas Corporation and the Pulasky
Iron Co.-I am giving this for the Fuel Co. alone-and the Poca-
hontas Navigation Co.
Mr. LEWIS. Do you do a considerable bunker business?
Mr. JONES. I believe we do. That is in the sales department and
I can not tell you difinitely about that.
Mr. LEWIS. Have you a sales organization of your own?
Mr. JONES. Yes, sir.
Mr. LEWIS. And you go into New England rather heavily?
Mr. JONES. We go into New England and sell a great deal of coal.
Mr. LEWIS. Do you furnish some Navy coal?
Mr. JONES. Yes, sir.
Mr. LEWIS. Substantial amounts at the present time?
Mr. JONES. No, sir; not very much. It is not very attractive in
price.
Mr. TOWNSEND. You did not want to get in on this last contract?
Mr. JONES. I do not think we did.

2121
Mr. TOWNSEND. For what purpose is the major portion of your
coal used, Mr. Jones?
Mr. JONES. For steam, domestic, by-product, and coking purposes.
We use it for all purposes. We ship about 50 per cent East and
50 per cent West, something like that; I am giving you approximate
proportions.
Mr. TOWNSEND. Can you state approximately the amount that is
used for by-product purposes?
Mr. JONES. I can not. It is not within my department. I have
not the information.
Mr. TOWNSEND. You have a very fine quality of coal?
Mr. JONES. We believe so.
Mr. TOWNSEND. And the natural conditions for mining opera-
tions are favorable?
Mr. JONES. Fairly favorable.
Mr. BELCHER. Do you compel your employees to deal at the com-
pany stores?
Mr. JONES. No, sir. We never have.
Mr. BELCHER. Do you have competition with independent stores?
Mr. JONES. At some of the mines the outside stores are located
within half a mile or 2 or 3 miles of the property. In others they are
located right in the town. We are in competition with towns. One
of the offices is Pocahontas. That is an incorporated town. There
are half a dozen or more independent stores there of all kinds,
Piggly Wiggly and everything else.
Mr. BELCHER. Have you hard roads to run into and from your
mines?
Mr. JONES. We have hard roads to every mine except one, and
that is only three-quarters of a mile from the end of the hard road to
the drift mouth.
Mr. BELCHER. Do your employees or a considerable number of
them own automobiles?
Mr. JONES. About one-sixth or one-seventh of our employees own
their own automobiles.
Mr. BELCHER. How many houses have you?
Mr. JONES. A little over 2,250 houses.
Mr. BELCHER. How many garages have you for your employees?
Mr. JONES. I have forgotten how many garages we have, but I
believe it is between 600 and 700.
Mr. LEWIS. The garages are at the mines?
Mr. JONES. Yes, sir.
Mr. LEWIS. Do the employees have the right to purchase the
houses in which they live?
Mr. JONES. Mr. Lewis, the land that we are operating there now,
which I was speaking of, is leased from the Pocahontas Coal &
Coke Co. We have no right to purchase on that, but we encourage
and assist them in buying homes in Virginia and around on the
property. A great many of our men come in from the outside
and do not live on our property.

questions of Mr. Jones.

Mr. TOWNSEND. Did you state how many different operations you
had?

Northern District of West Virginia:
The petitioner in amendment of its petition filed in open court at Elkins on
July 15, 1922, respectfully represents that it is the plaintiff in a certain suit
in equity, now pending in this court, entitled Hitchman Coal & Coke Co.,
plaintiff, v. John Mitchell and others, defendants, and that in said suit a
decree of injunction duly entered by said court, as modified and affirmed
by the Supreme Court of the United States, enjoins the defendants named
therein and all persons combining and conspiring with them and all other
persons whomsoever-
(1) From interfering and from combining, conspiring, or attempting to
interfere with the employees of the plaintiff for the purpose of unionizing
plaintiff's mine without plaintiff's consent, by representing or causing to be
represented in express or implied terms, to any of plaintiff's employees, or
to any person who might become an employee of plaintiff, that such person
will suffer or is likely to suffer from loss or trouble in continuing in or in

mine.
(2) From interfering and from combining, conspiring, or attempting to
interfere with employees of plaintiff for the purpose of unionizing plaintiff's
mine, without plaintiff's consent, and in aid of such purpose knowingly and

Mr. BELCHER. Mr. Chairman, the committee this morning asked
that the case of Watt Angel v. Black Band Consolidated Coal Co.,
decided by the Circuit Court of Appeals for West Virginia, be copied
into the record of this hearing. We now submit the decision to be

(The decision above referred to is as follows:)
Charleston. Watt Angel v. Black Band Consolidated Coal Co.
Submitted March 11, 1924. Decided March 18, 1924.
1. Landlord and tenant." Estate of will" defined.
An estate at will in lands is that which a tenant has an entry made thereon
under a demise to hold during the joint wills of the parties (p. 53).


===== [扫描序号 1130] =====
2134
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2. Same. Right to occupy premises leased to miner by coal company held to
cease when services terminated.
A coal mining company owns a number of dwelling houses for the use of
those employed in and about its mines; they form a part of its plant and are
necessary to the successful conduct of its business. They are rented to its
miners at a nominal charge, hardly sufficient to cover repairs and insurance.
The rent or charge is calculated at so much per month, but it is paid every
two weeks by deductions from the miners' wages as they are earned. Miners
are not required to live in the houses and those who do not are paid the same
wages as those who do, all being paid at so much per ton. The houses are not
kept for rent generally, but are occupied only by the company's employees, and
then only by its consent. Under these conditions a miner is employed, is
furnished a house, he moves in, continues his employment for a number of
years, and the deductions for rent are regularly made from his wages every
two weeks; he then voluntarily quits work and and pays no rent thereafter.
There being no agreement that he should occupy the house for any definite
period, when he ceased work for the company his right to occupy the house
also ceased.
3. Same. Relationships between miners and employer as landlord and tenant
and employer and employee held not necessarily inconsistent.
The miner was an employee in respect to his mining coal, but a tenant as
respects his occupancy of the house, the two relations of employer and em-
ployee and landlord and tenant not being necessarily inconsistent with each
other.
4. Same.-Tenant held tenant at will.
The contract being terminable at the will of either party, the miner had only
an estate at will in the house and occupied it as a tenant at will.
5. Same.-Landlord may reenter and remove goods of tenant at will without
legal process, where it was done without violence or breach of the peace.
Where he held over for a period of six months or more after he quit work,
it may be inferred that his holding over was with the landlord's consent, thus
creating a new tenancy at will; and upon refusing to vacate and remove his
goods from the premises after notice to do so, he thereafter became a tres-
passer and his landlord had a right to reenter and remove his goods, without
legal process, where it was done without violence or breach of the peace.
6. Same.-Landlord held not liable for damages to removed goods.
Where the company removed his goods to the open, covered them with tar-
paulins, and they remained there for four days and nights, without any care of
them on the part of the owner although he was present and knew their con
dition, the company is not liable for damage done thereto by frosts.
7. Insufficiency of evidence.
A verdict which clearly has not sufficient evidence to support it should be
set aside.
Error to circuit court, Kanawha County.
Act on by Watt Angel against the Black Band Consolidated Coal Co. Judg.
ment for plaintiff, and defendant brings error.
Reversed and remanded.
S. B. Avis, for plaintiff in error.
Stewart & Whitt and J. Howard Hundley, for defendant in error.
Meredith, president:
Plaintiff recovered judgment for $300 in an action of trespass on the case for
damages alleged to have been done by the company's employees in evicting
plaintiff and removing his household goods and effects from one of its houses.
Defendant assigns error.
Defendant operates a coal-mining plant at Oclott, Kanawha County. It owns
and maintains there about 90 dwelling houses for the exclusive use of its
employees. It does not rent them to nor permit them to be occupied by anyone
who is not an employee of the company. But its employees are not compelled
to live in its houses to secure employment in its mines. At the time of the
injury complained of the company employed about 155 men, about half of
which number lived in company houses, and the remainder lived in homes of
their own or homes rented from persons other than the defendant. It is
claimed by the defendant that it is absolutely necessary that it own these
houses in order to enable it to carry on its business; this is probably true; its
mining operations could probably not be carried on without them.
The plaintiff is a coal miner and had been employed by the company for
about six years and had lived in the house from which he was ejected about


===== [扫描序号 1131] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2135
three years. He was employed at mining coal, for which he received so much
per ton.
He received the same rate per ton that was paid those miners who
mined coal there but who did not live in the company's houses, so that the
rate of pay per ton in nowise depended upon whether the miner did or did not
live in a company house. At the time plaintiff was employed he was furnished
a house by defendant, and for its use there was deducted from his wages as
they were earned $3 every two weeks; there was also deducted at the same time
50 cents for electric current for lighting purposes. The houses were not owned
and maintained by the company to be rented at a profit; the cost of repairs
and insurance exceeded the deductions from the wages of those who occupied
them.
On March 15, 1922, plaintiff voluntarily quit work and about April 1 with a
number of other employees went on strike and refused thereafter to work for
the company upon the terms offered. From the time he quit work no more
wages accrued; thereafter he neither paid nor offered to pay rent, though he
continued to occupy the house until he was evicted on October 26, 1922, a period
of more than six months. Defendant notified plaintiff on October 1 to vacate;
it contends that he then agreed to do so, but this is denied by him, though he
admits that he received such notice. On October 20 defendant gave him a
written notice to vacate on or before October 26, stating that the company
wished "to take possession on that date"; refusing to vacate, on the 26th
defendant evicted him, placing his household goods out in the open about 50
feet distant from the dwelling house, where it covered them with tarpaulins and
placed a guard over them. They remained there four days until plaintiff found
a place of storage. Plaintiff claims that his property was damaged by improper
handling and by the night frosts.
There are but two main questions arising on the record: (1) The character
of the relation between the company and the plaintiff that is, whether it was
that of landlord and tenant-and if so for what period, or employer and
employee; and (2) whether the verdict is excessive.
Plaintiff claims he was a tenant from month to month; and, therefore, was
entitled to a month's notice of the termination of his tenancy before he could be
lawfully evicted; it is conceded that no such notice was given. On the other
hand, the defendant claims that plaintiff was only an employee, both as
respects his services as a miner and also as respects his occupancy of the
house; that when he ceased to work on March 15, his right to occupy the house
ceased, he became a trespasser and could be lawfully evicted by the company
without legal process. There is no proof of any special contract of lease
between plaintiff and defendant. He was employed to work, was assigned
a house, moved in, and the deductions from his wages were made as heretofore
stated. Other houses of the company were furnished at higher rates, because
they were better or larger. While the plaintiff says his lease was from month
to month, that is a mere legal conclusion and we must look to the facts to
determine the nature of the tenancy, if it be a tenancy. The houses were built
by the company solely for the use of its employees at its mines. They form a
material and necessary part of its plant and equipment. When those who lived
in company houses went on strike, the company had to rent other houses for
other miners who were engaged to mine coal; hence its counsel urges that the
plaintiff's occupancy of its house was subsidiary and necessary to its service;
or if not necessary, it was incidental or convenient to the service or so connected
therewith as to render his occupancy that of a mere employee or servant, and
not that of a tenant. A great number of authorities are cited for this
proposition.
For example, in Lane v. Au Sable Electric Co. (181 Mich. 26, 147 N. W. 546,
Ann. Cas. 1916-C, 1108), plaintiff was employed to operate a station house at
a monthly wage, and was furnished as part of his compensation a dwelling
house valued at from $5 to $10 per month; he quit work, whereupon the com-
pany removed his furniture. In an action for eviction the court held that
plaintiff was an employee and not a tenant; that when he quit work his right
to occupy the house ceased. The opinion quotes with approval from Bowman v.
Bradley (151 Pa. St. 351, 24 Atl. 1062, 17 L. R. A. 213): "It is not necessary
that the occupation of a house or apartments should be a necessary incident
to the service to be performed in order that the right to continue in possession
should end with the service." It is enough if such occupation is convenient for
the purposes of the service and was obtained by reason of the contract of
hiring. (Ital'cs ours.)


===== [扫描序号 1132] =====
2136
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Another well-considered case and one which illustrates the importance of
correctly determining the relation of the parties is that of Kerrains v. People
(60 N. Y. 221, 19 Am. Rep. 158). Kerrains was convicted of assault with a
deadly weapon with intent to kill. He had been employed in operating a paper
mill and was paid a daily wage, and furnished a house and garden. They
disagreed, his employer discharged him, paid him up, and told him to vacate
the house or he would employ force and throw his goods out. Kerrains refused
to leave and the employer, with two men, began removing the goods.
Kerrains was then absent, but his wife sent for him, and returning, he saw
what was going on, went to the woodshed, got an ax, went to the house, and
ordered the men out. The employer, Son, refused and drew h´s pistol; an
altercation ensued, during which Kerrains hit Son with the ax, inflicting a
serious injury. His indictment followed. The important question was, “What
was the character of the holding under the contract? If that was a tenancy.
then the party holding over would be a tenant at will, and the landlord would
not be justified in entering with strong hands;" but if defendant's occupancy was
that of a servant only, then a tenancy at will or at sufferance did not spring
up immediately upon determination of his service, but to have that effect, the
holding over must be sufficiently long to warrant an inference of consent to a
different holding; that under the facts shown, the original relation was that of
employer and employee, and the defendant having held over but a few days
after his discharge, his holding was not converted from that of servant to
tenant. If he was a mere servant, and the court held he was, the employer had
the right of possession and the right to remove the defendant with his effects
and to use the force necessary to accomplish that purpose.
In People v. Annis (45 Barb. (N. Y.) 304), where the defendant was hired
by the realtor Hubbard to work one year on his farm, for the sum of $270, and
was to furnish him houseroom for himself and family, a garden, and pasture
for a cow, it was held that this was not a demise in the nature of a lease,
creating the relation of landlord and tenant, but that of employer and employee,
the house, garden, and pasture being a portion of the consideration for the
service. There is a multitude of cases to the same effect, among them: Mead v.
Owen, 80 Vt. 273, 67 Atl. 722, 12 L. R. A. (N. S.) 655, 13 Ann. Cas. 231; Davis v.
Long, 45 N. D. 581, 178 N. W. 936, 14 A. L. R. 796; Davis. v. Williams, 130 Ala.
530, 30 So. 488, 54 L. R. A. 749; MacKenzie v. Minis, 132 Ga. 323, 63 S. E. 900;
State v. Hoover, 107 N. C. 795, 12 S. E. 451; Chatard v. O'Donovan, 80 Ind. 20,
41 Am. Rep. 782.
In all the foregoing cases there was no reservation of rent, no actual pay-
ment of rent by that name; the occupant merely performed service for its use;
no rent account or charge was kept. This is a material circumstance to be
considered, and has an important bearing in the present case.
There is another class of cases where the employee was furnished a house
and deduction from his wages was made for its use. In Eichengreen v. Appel
(44 Ill. App. 19) Appel was employed at $10 per week by Eichengreen, a whole-
sale milk dealer; he was furnished certain "downstairs" rooms in the em-
ployer's house, and $1 per week was to be deducted from his wages for the rent.
He was not hired for any special period nor was there any agreement that he
was to occupy the rooms for any definite time. He moved in, worked five
months, and quit work. During this period his employer deducted $4 a month
from his wages for rent. After Appel quit work Eichengreen hired another man
to take his place and told Appel to vacate; upon his refusal to do so he carried
his goods to a warehouse. Appel sued for damages for dispossession and for
injury to his goods. It was held that when Appel quit the service he became
a mere tenant at sufferance and might be put out on reasonable notice, no
unnecessary force being used.
In McGee v. Gibson (1 B. Mon. (Ky.) 105) a farmer employed a laborer
for a year, at a certain price per month, agreeing to furnish him a house, for
which he was to pay $2 per month, and to keep his cow. at $1 per month, both
sums to be paid monthly. The laborer quit work before the end of the year,
and the farmer evicted him. It was held that there was no independent lease
for a year or any other period, but that his right of occupancy was incident to
his contract of hire, and ceased when he quit work; that from that time he
was in no better position than a mere tenant at will, who by his own act ter-
minated his tenancy, and at most was entitled only to a reasonable time to
remove his goods.


===== [扫描序号 1133] =====
