2137
In Graniteville Manufacturing Co. v. Renew (113 S. C. 171, 102 S. E. 18),
Renew was a worker in a cotton mill. According to the custom common in
the mills in that State, he was furnished a company house and was paid wages,
from which deductions were made for his rent. The company discharged him,
paid him his wages, less the rent due, and notified him to vacate the house
he occupied within three days. This he declined to do. The company sued
for possession. Renew defended on the ground that he was not a tenant at
all, but merely an occupier of the house as an incident to his employment; but
that to dispossess him he should have had 10 days' notice instead of three.
There were two statutes relating to dispossession in force in that State, one
requiring 10 days' notice to tenants at will, domestic servants, and common
laborers (3508 Civil Code, 1912), and the other providing that "In all
cases where tenants hold over after the expiration of their lease or contract
for rent, whether the same be in writing or by parol, or shall fail to pay
the rent when the same shall be due, the landlord is hereby authorized * *
to demand possession thereof, and in case of refusal or resistance
apply to a magistrate, whose duty it shall be to have a notice served upon
the person or persons so refusing to be dispossessed to show cause, before
him, if any he can, within three days from the date of said personal service of
such notice, why he should not be dispossessed" (3509, Civil Code). The court
held he was not a tenant at will, and not therefore to be dispossessed under
the statute reqiring 10 days' notice; but that he was a tenant holding over
after the expiration of his lease, which expired when he quit work, and
therefore the three-day statute, quoted above in part, applied; that if he
was merely an incidental occupier of the house he could be dispossessed under
the statute, or summarily without notice, the employer using such force as
might be necessary to put him out. In our view he was a tenant at will.
* *
to
Counsel for plaintiff relies upon the English case of Smith v. Overseers of
Seghill (10 Q. B. 422) which he claims is very like the instant case. There
Smith was a coal miner, employed by the Seghill colliery to mine coal at so
much per ton. The colliery had 340 houses which it kept for its workmen.
Sometimes there were more workmen than houses, but whether a miner lived
in a colliery house or not he received the same rate per ton, just as in the
present case. If there were not sufficient houses for the married men, the
colliery gave them an allowance to assist them in paying their rent else-
where. If a house became vacant, the colliery could call upon a married miner
to occupy it, and if he refused, his allowance for rent ceased. The single
miners got no allowance for rent. Smith with his family occupied one of the
colliery's houses. It was conceded that he had no right to notice to vacate
and that his right to occupy the house ceased when he quit work. His right
to occupy the house was only incidentally involved in the particular case; the
question was whether he was a tenant or a mere employee. It arose under
the poor rate assessment act (32 and 33 Vict., c. 41), which provided that:
"The overseers in making out the poor rate shall in every case, whether the
rate is collected from the owner or occupier, or the owner is liable to the pay-
ment of the rate instead of the occupier, enter in the occupier's column of the
weight book, the name of the occupier of every ratable hereditament, and such
Occupier shall be deemed to be duly rated for any qualification or francise as
aforesaid." Smith sought to compel the overseers to enter his name in the
rate book, probably for the purpose of enabling him to vote, though the reason
is not mentioned in the opinion. The colliery contended that he was a mere
employee; he contended that he was a tenant. The court held that he was a
tenant at will so long as he resided in the house under the arrangement
between him and the colliery owners, and was entitled to have his name entered
in the rate book under the statute.
Applying the principles announced in these cases to the facts in the present
case, where do the parties stand? It is conceded that plaintiff was not em-
ployed for any definite time nor did he enter defendant's house for any definite
term. We think that from the nature of the agreement between them it was
necessarily implied that when he ceased to work his right to occupy the house
ceased also. He made no offer to pay rent after he quit work, but, according
to his own testimony, claimed the right to occupy the house without payment
of rent or performing work for the company-a position that could not be
properly maintained for a moment. Whatever his rights to the dwelling were,
he was not the legal owner. Now, if he was a mere employee, then his posses-
sion was not in law his own, but that of his employer; and he could not, if an


===== [扫描序号 1134] =====
2138
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
employee only, bring anyone into the house to live with him, such as a lodger
or roomer, without his employer's consent; if he did, the employer-owner might
eject the lodger, because he would be a trespasser. (Tipsword v. Potter, 31
Idaho 509, 174 Pac. 133.) But in this case the parties treated the deductions
from plaintiff's wages as rent. Both call it by that name, and so long as the
plaintiff worked for defendant, we think the circumstances show that the de-
fendant treated the plaintiff as having an independent right to the possession,
and that necessarily their relation was that of landlord and tenant. But for
what term? Of wholly uncertain duration, dependent upon the will of both
parties. Either party could terminate their relation at any time; therefore
it was a tenancy at will. "An estate at will in lands is that which a tenant
has by an entry made thereon under a demise to hold during the joint wills
of the parties to the estate." (24 Cyc. 1036 and cases cited.) Such was the hold-
ing of the court in the case of Smith v. Overseers of Seghill, supra, relied on by
counsel for the plaintiff. Being a tenancy at will, plaintiff chose to terminate
it by quitting work. His tenancy then ended. But he remained in possession
from March 15 to October 1 without any demand by the company to vacate.
Whether he was during this period a trespasser, a tenant at will, or a tenant
at sufferance is unimportant. He was notified on October 1 to vacate.
This demand was renewed October 20 in writing. It was his duty then
to remove his family and his goods from the company's premises. Indeed, we
have heretofore held that an estate at will may be terminated without notice.
unless notice is required by the terms of the lease. (Hinton Foundry &
Machine Co. v. Lilly Lumber Co., 73 W. Va. 477, 80 S. E. 773.) If his holding
over after he quit work, without objection by the company, made him a tenant
at will, or by sufferance, that tenancy was terminated October 1.
The tenancy being terminated, the company had a right to reenter the
premises and take possession, without legal process, provided it did so peace-
ably and without violence or breach of the peace. (Bachinsky v. Federal
Coal & Coke Co., 78 W. Va. 721, 90 S. E. 227.) The defendant's employee en-
tered peaceably; they committed no violence; there was no breach of the peace;
they violated no law, and plaintiff could not claim that he was unlawfully
evicted because he had no legal right to possession.
The court gave the following instruction on behalf of the plaintiff :
"The court instructs the jury that if you believe from the evidence in this
case that at the time plaintiff's property was removed from defendant's house,
the plaintiff was renting said house from the defendant from month to month.
and if you further believe from the evidence that the defendant through its
agents and servants and without process of law, evicted the plaintiff from the
said house and removed plaintiff's household and kitchen furniture and prop-
erty from said house and placed the same out in the open and in a place
where it was damaged, then you are instructed that the defendant is liable for
whatever damage plaintiff sustained by reason of such damage to said furniture,
not to exceed the sum sued for in the declaration, and you should find for the
plaintiff in whatever amount you believe has been proven by the evidence, pro-
vided you further believe from the evidence that plaintiff used due diligence to
protect the said property and to reduce his loss to a minimum after he had
been so evicted."
Plaintiff was not a tenant from month to month; therefore it was error to
give this instruction.
Defendant's instructions Nos. 2, 3, and 6 were based upon the theory that
the plaintiff was an employee only and not a tenant; they were therefore
properly refused.
Defendant's instruction No. 4 reads as follows:
"The court instructs the jury that under the evidence in this case when
the plaintiff refused to work for the defendant, it was his duty to leave the
house and premises and remove his personal goods therefrom, and for the
plaintiff to insist upon retaining possession of the house made him a trespasser,
and the defendant had the right to eject him and remove his goods and
property therefrom, using as much force as was necessary."
Had the defendant evicted plaintiff immediately or soon after the plaintiff
quit work this would have been a proper instruction so far as that point was
concerned; but he remained in the house for more than six months after he
had quit work and it might be a reasonable inference that from March
15 to October 1, when the first notice to vacate was given, he was there with
defendant's consent, hence a tenant at will; he therefore would not be a


===== [扫描序号 1135] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2139
trespasser until his tenancy was terminated. But after it was terminated, he
became a trespasser by remaining and the defendant had a right to remove his
goods. The instruction ignores this distinction; it should have been directed,
not to the character of the occupancy on March 15, when plaintiff quit work,
but to the character of the occupancy when he was evicted. Had it been so
modified it would have been proper on that point.
Defendant's instruction No. 6 was properly refused because it told the jury
that the relation between the company and the plaintiff was not that of land-
lord and tenant, but merely that of master and servant. We have already
shown that both relations are not inconsistent, and may exist between the same
parties at the same time. At the time of the eviction neither evisted.
The only question remaining relates to the quantum of damages. The verdict
was for $300. No attempt has been made to prove damages for the eviction,
but only for injury to the goods removed. Plaintiff filed an itemized list of
the furniture owned by him, with what he claims were the approximate prices
paid for each item. These aggregate more than $1,000. He then says the prop-
erty was damaged $500 from frost. His wife says the damage was that
much partly caused by frost while the furniture remained out of doors, and
partly by careless handling, whereby it was scratched; some of the parts got
soiled on the ground, and some of her fruit jars were turned upside down and
the contents lost. No witness details any particulars of loss, except the wife.
She testifies to scratches on the furniture, but does not specify any piece nor
go further into detail. Among the articles listed were one canned fruit and
jar and one stone jar, valued at $5 each, and groceries valued at $25. It may be
true that the canned fruit was destroyed, but that could not have amounted
to more than $5. All plaintiff's witnesses claimed the greater part of the
damage was caused by the frost. For that damage the defendant can not
be held liable in this case.
The record shows that defendant very carefully removed all the goods
and piled them up near the railroad, about 50 feet from the house, covered
them with two tarpaulins, and placed a guard over them. This was done
in daylight, in mid afternoon. Plaintiff, instead of taking care of them as
it was his right and duty to do, immediately left for Charleston to consult
an attorney. He was looking for a lawsuit and got this one started before
he attempted to find a place for his goods. Neither he nor his wife nor
anyone for them tried to preserve the goods while they remained out of
doors during the four days and nights. They say the furniture was not
wholly covered with the tarpaulins; then it was their duty to do what they
could to cover it, if that would help, or they should have used more diligence
to secure a place of storage. We do not think that plaintiff is entitled to
any damage to his goods occasioned by the frosts; and upon the present
record the proof of damage by scratches or soiling of his goods is insufficient.
The evidence is wholly insufficient to sustain the amount of the verdict.
We therefore reverse the judgment, set aside the verdict, and grant a new
trial.
Reversed and remanded.
STATEMENT OF R. TEMPLETON SMITH, SECRETARY-TREASURER
LOWBER GAS COAL CO., PITTSBURGH, PA.
Mr. SMITH. I represent the Ontario Gas Coal Co., of Washing-
ton County and the Lowber Gas Coal Co. of Fayette County in
western Pennsylvania, investments totaling several million dollars.
These companies were signatories to the Jacksonville agreement and
kept the agreement to the letter, asked for no concessions from the
United Mine Workers of America and received none whatever.
Our reasons for appearing before this committee are these:
We want to show you what has happened to coal companies in
western Pennsylvania who have dealt in good faith with the United
Mine Workers of America.
We want to call your attention to the condition of the coal busi-
ness in the earlier days in western Pennsylvania and show what has
happened to change that condition.

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
We wish to present a picture of the present coal freight-rate struc-
ture, and we would like to offer some suggestions as to action the
Senate can take toward settlement on a sound economic basis of the
fundamental causes of the present collapse of the soft-coal industry.
First, just a word about our mines and our dealings with the
union, because they are typical of many smaller companies from
whom you have not heard.
The Ontario mine is thoroughly equipped with modern machinery
for producing and cleaning coal. The Fayette mine of the Lowber
Co. is a slope mine with particularly good working conditions and
unusually thick coal. Both of these mines are in the heart of the
Youghiogheny gas coal belt. The coal is the highest quality gas
coal produced in Pennsylvania. During the three-year life of the
Jacksonville agreement, Fayette mine was operated a total of 122
days, Ontario mine 270 days.
During the period these mines have been shut down such union
miners as chose to remain in the company houses have been per-
mitted to do so without paying rent, which rent, if collected, would
have amounted to over $19,000. These men have worked and are
working now in mills, on the roads, and in nonunion mines else-
where.
It costs several thousand dollars a month each to keep these mines.
idle, in addition to interest on the money invested. It is perfectly
apparent that no business men would have sustained losses of this
magnitude if they could have been avoided or turned into profits by
operating.
The record now contains a history of the negotiations with the
United Mine Workers of America and a repetition of it at this time
is not necessary. Our companies were represented at the conference
at Miami held in February, 1927, six weeks before the expiration of
the Jacksonville agreement. We pointed out to Mr. Lewis the eco-
nomic difficulties we face, as will be shown you in this statement, and
we heartily agree with his reply to us that we are up against a tough
proposition.
We believe a very great mistake was made at that conference in
ignoring the economic factors that have a bearing on the determina-
tion of wages. It was a mistake that has cost our men and our
companies dearly.
We believe that if men who work in the mines so desire they
have a right to be collectively represented in their relations with
their employers.
It should be developed from the information gathered in these
hearings and in subsequent consideration by the committee, in
collaboration with the best brains in the industry, just how far, if
at all, beyond the individual companies this collective representation
should extend.
Certain it is that the grouping together of sections of the country
which do not compete with each other, such as Illinois and Indiana
with western Pennsylvania, leaving out of account West Virginia
with whom western Pennsylvania does compete, has not worked
either to the advantage of the miners, the operators, or the public in
western Pennsylvania.

2141
We stated at the outset that we wanted to show something about
the coal business in western Pennsylvania in the earlier days and the
things that have changed those conditions.
First, may we point out that the western Pennsylvania coal fields
are in the heart of the great coal-consuming territory of the country.
Millions of dollars were invested in the coal industry here, because
of the geographic location close to the great markets. We did ship
coal to the Northwest by cheap water transportation via our lake
ports only 178 miles away. We did supply the Michigan peninsula
with coal, which moved by rail through Toledo, and we shipped into
New York State and by rail to Canada. Our high-grade gas coal
formerly supplied the public utilities in New York City, Baltimore,
Philadelphia, and other eastern cities and we shipped to New
England via tidewater.
There was enough coal available and developed here to supply
these markets at reasonable prices. The coal was developed in
western Pennsylvania because these markets existed close by.
What's been happening to change this reasonably prosperous con-
dition of the coal industry in the heart of the consuming territory
into a condition of chaos and bankruptcy?
People, seeing the speculative possibilities, went down into West
Virginia and eastern Kentucky and bought coal lands distant from
railroads at nominal prices. They gradually had the railroads ex-
tended to them. The freight-rate groupings, were continuously in-
creased and the haul on the same rates lengthened until to-day we
have the rate structure I wish to show you. Railroads in those
districts were glad to extend their lines into the new coal fields on
account of their then corporate relations with the coal companies
and to get new revenue from hauling coal. We know this committee
can not investigate rates, but we think it is necessary for you to
have a clear picture of the present rate structure in order to under-
stand the whole coal problem.
The map I hand you shows the Michigan peninsular and adjacent
territory. Fifty million tons of coal per year are used within the
area surrounded by the dotted line. Most of the coal moving into
this territory enters via Toledo. Coal mined in all the territory
colored pink, extending from the Pittsburgh district down to Ken-
tucky moves on identical freight rates into this outlined territory.
Please note that the northern districts secure no advantage what-
ever in these rates on account of their natural location, hundreds of
miles nearer the market.
The chart accompanying the map shows that the distance from
McRoberts, Ky., district to Toledo is 195 miles farther than from
Pittsburgh to Toledo. That means they get the 195-mile haul for
nothing.
Last year the Pittsburgh district, only 281 miles from Toledo,
shipped only 34,000 tons to Michigan, while southern West Vir-
ginia and Kentucky, from 100 to 200 miles farther away, shipped
over 18,000,000 tons to Michigan. The reason is obvious. While
we have been paying the Jacksonville scale the South has paid less
wages, so their costs were less than ours, resulting in the loss to
us of practically all the business in the great territory outlined on


===== [扫描序号 1138] =====
2142
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
the map. The coal is now hauled from 100 to 200 miles farther past
our mines to this former market of ours.
Consider the situation east, as shown by the tidewater chart.
Kanawha, W, Va., district gets its coal to its tidewater port of
Hampton Roads, 24.6 miles more than our distance to our port of
New York, for 57 cents less than we pay. Big Sandy, Ky., district
gets its coal to tidewater 141.2 miles farther than our distance to
New York for 47 cents less than we pay. The grades over the
mountains in both instances are less in the North than they are in
the South. So you see here again, instead of having a freight
advantage on account of being closer to our ports, we are placed at
a disadvantage through the payment of higher rates for less distance.
While we were trying to pay the Jacksonville wage scale and
they were paying less, they have been taking this eastern market
away from us and again transporting coal needlessly great distances.
With the southern rates lower than ours, as they are here, we couldn't
even expect to compete on an even wage basis, and nobody in the
North wants to sink to their wage level.
Consider the much discussed Lake cargo business. In 1913 Pitts-
burgh shipped 12,000,000 tons up the Lake; in 1927, 2,500,000.
Southern districts shipped 6,000,000 in 1913 and 24,000,000 in 1927.
While West Virginia and eastern Kentucky paid a differential of
only 25 cents a ton over Pittsburgh for excess distances ranging
as high as 282 miles as shown by the chart, we tried to pay $7.50
per day wages against their $5 per day and down to $2.68 per day,
and this market nearly disappeared.
Last summer, too late to affect the situation in 1927, the Inter-
state Commerce Commission granted a cut of 20 cents per ton to
the northern districts, making the differential 45 cents and fixing
the Pittsburgh rate at $1.46 for 178 miles, while, as the chart shows,
under that decision, districts in the South still were permitted a
282-mile excess haul for 45 cents. When this decision came out,
people who did not know what they were talking about announced
that now our troubles in western Pennsylvania would be over and
we could pay the Jacksonville scale.
Let's see.
In the first place this Lake market, if we had it all.
only amounts to 25,000,000 or 30,000,000 tons, or about one-third
of our easy production. It was developed pretty clearly in the
Lake cargo-case testimony of the consumers in the Northwest that
the 20 cent cut would shift possibly two and one-half million tons
of the business from the South to western Pennsylvania, giving us
a total of 5,000,000 tons. They are the buyers. They ought to know
what they are going to buy. When we were operating on the Jack-
sonville scale the Southerners got into our markets at Youngstown
on a differential against them of $1.05 per ton, so you see the 45-
cent differential, if it had been allowed to stand, would have been no
guarantee that the northern districts were going to get a great per-
centage of this business back. But even this 45-cent differential
which, compared with the ore rate for the same haul over the same
tracks for the same distance, is still 40 cents too high was knocked
out by three Southern judges April 14 when they granted an injune-
tion which results in restoring the differential existing before the
case was ever brought to the commission and completely nullifies
the decision of the Interstate Commerce Commission.

Commissioner Esch understood this Lake case. He is an honest

become mixed with politics. We recommend that the members of the

Another handicap which we can not avoid altogether in our more
highly developed communities is the extra tax burden. Our taxes
per acre, according to testimony in the Lake Cargo case, average
10 times those paid in eastern Kentucky. We are proud of our good
roads, our country parks, our educational system. Our expenditures
per pupil have been 333 per cent higher than West Virginia's and
more than double Kentucky's annual expenditures per pupil.
These things make better living conditions for our men. At the
same time the coal operators of western Pennsylvania are watchful
of extravagance of expenditures by public officials, and through
taxpayers' associations, which they support, keep experts in the field
who give their services to country school boards, road supervisors,
and anyone who has to do with the spending of money, to the end
that constructive improvements may be carried on, but that waste
may be eliminated.
To offset this handicap progressive companies which dominate the
industry here have been diligent in their efforts to modernize their
mines and introduce machinery, where possible, to cut production
costs.
In short, we have not been asking the wage earners to bear all
the brunt of our difficulties as we have been accused of doing.
You have had many suggestions for eliminating the troubles of
the coal industry, some of which it is within the power of the Senate
to adopt and others beyond your jurisdiction.
May we suggest one thing you can do which we believe gets at
the fundamental underlying cause of overproduction. Your com-
mittee is convinced that overproduction is wrecking the industry and
that any effective remedy must curb overproduction. To cut out
overproduction it is necessary to shut down some mines. Then you
get into the difficulty of deciding which mines to shut down and
play fair in doing it.

CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
We believe that the permanent prosperity of the coal industry
depends upon a scientific freight-rate structure. Rates on coal must
be fixed on a basis of service rendered by the railroads, ton-mile
rates, if you please, modified by terminal charges and transportation
conditions. All other factors should be secondary. When this is
done the uneconomic unnecessary long hauls and cross hauls will be
eliminated. Coal will move from the district adjacent to the various
markets until those districts can not supply the demand and then the
outlying districts will begin to ship.
If this had been done 15 years ago, we would not have had the
tremendous overproduction we now have and the spectacle could
not exist of hauling coal hundreds of miles to pass idle mines almost
at the destination of the long haul.
Waste is always paid for. If a railroad isn't paid any more for
hauling coal 476 miles than it is for hauling it 281 miles, either
the consumer at the end of the 281-mile haul pays too much for
his coal or the farmer or shipper of other goods pays excess freight
on those goods, so that the buyer of the coal at the end of the 476-
mile haul can get the cheap rate.
This new basis of figuring rates would not work such a hardship
on even the outlying districts as might occur to you at first.
Kentucky would be assured of its markets west and Missouri would
get cheaper coal. Kentucky would increase its business in southern
Indiana because the rates would be lowered. It's not fair to the
consumers in Indiana now to maintain a rate of $2.52 for a 343-mile
haul from Harlan, Ky., to Indianapolis, so that the same rate
can be maintained for a 100-mile-longer haul from Pittsburgh
to Indianapolis. The low volatile and smokeless coals of southern
West Virginia will always retain their markets. They have no real
competition. Northern West Virginia's markets would be widened.
Maryland coal could move into its natural markets and the residents
of Washington, D. C., would have a lower coal bill. New York
State and City would benefit. Connecticut and Rhode Island would
get their coal cheaper. Naturally Ohio would be benefited and
Michigan would pay less freight on coal.
This principle of rate making if followed out would not make
Idaho and Montana pay more freight on goods from Chicago than
does California.
The people of this country have a right to demand a freight-rate
structure that will eliminate wasteful hauls, with the consequent
shifting of the burden to certain districts, and the raising of rates
on the farmers' products and other freight. We might as well face
the facts now and do the scientific thing. Delay will only make the
situation worse.
True, under this system, some of the newer mines in the South
who have come into the business recently might have to cease
operation for a time and conserve their coal, their capital assets.
But they will be better off if they do. They testify in the rate cases
before the Interstate Commerce Commission that they are losing
money now, that the coal is given away for less than cost. Because
this coal is mined and sold for less than cost, needlessly hauled
hundreds of miles, mines near the markets must shut down. It has
been manifestly unfair to the districts close to the markets to make


===== [扫描序号 1141] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2145
possible by favorable freight rates the opening and maintenance of
far distant mines, which must depend for their markets on cross
hauling the mines which represent long prior investments.
The only advantage possessed by western Pennsylvania mines
over West Virginia is their geographical location. This very loca
tion makes some costs higher, so it is unjust to deny us the benefit
of the lower rates that our proximity to the markets justifies.
These rates are Government created or Government sponsored.
May we ask that your committee recommend to the Senate that the
Government which permitted this condition to grow up now remedy
it? Let us remove a Government subsidy which causes overproduc-
tion. It has been suggested to you that the laws be changed to per-
mit great combinations of coal operating companies, or to permit
the establishment of district selling agencies under Government
regulation. Something like this might tend to reduce the competi-
tion within the districts, but it would not go far toward preventing
overproduction unless these district sales agencies, or combined
operating companies, could also work together, with all it would
mean. I guess nobody believes that would be tolerated. If it were,
it opens the way for unlimited legislation and regulation in many
industries, which would be harmful to the country.
Suppose, for instance, right now we had one operating company
in the Pittsburgh district. There isn't local business enough, inde-
pendent of freight rates, to pay interest on the capital that would
be invested. That company would still have to get two-thirds of
its business in markets bringing it into competition with the south-
erners on an even freight rate basis, so that this big company
couldn't pay more wages than they do and the competition would be
just as keen.
However, if you first fix this freight rate structure so that long
hauls and cross hauls are eliminated and the country is thus divided
into its natural districts, then combinations in the districts would be
helpful.
This proposal points a way for the Government to promptly
relieve the deplorable condition of the bituminous coal industry in
a way that will make possible the payment of better wages in the
coal fields in the heart of the consuming territory and in curbing
the chief trouble, overproduction, acts to close those mines which
now pay the lowest wages and depend for their markets on waste-
ful, unnecessary, long hauls by the railroads.

The following figures show the necessity for such an adjustment.
In the year 1924 the mines of this association produced 3,079,196
tons. Notwithstanding this large tonnage, our loss for the year was
$900,422.08. As a result of this full year's operation we knew that
it was impossible to mine Cambridge coal, pay the Jacksonville wage
scale, and sell the coal in a competitive market at a profit.
Although we knew in advance that continued operation meant fur-
ther losses, yet there were important reasons that made is advisable
for us to maintain operation on a reduced production basis, namely:
Existing contracts covering a period of years on which we were
obligated, also other contracts where it was advantageous to fill the
tonnage requirements with Cambridge coal rather than permit these
customers to obtain their fuel from other districts. Then again, the
loss at certain mines while operating would be less than to maintain.
them during an extended idle period.
For these reasons the production of the district, in 1925, dropped
to 1,311,127 tons, and the total loss was $1,006,459.65.
In 1926, due to the market flurry in the fall of that year, production
and prices slightly increased. The year's tonnage being 1,468,974
tons and the total loss for the year $602,886.43.
During the three years named the mines in the district produced a
total of 5,859,297 tons; the total loss for the three-year period amount-
ing to $2,509,768.16.
At this point I desire to call your attention to this statement: Dur-
ing the life of the Jacksonville agreement there was no abrogation
of contract in the Cambridge district on the part of any operator;
all of the companies were operating in strict accordance with the
terms of the Jacksonville agreement during the month of March,
1927, and, furthermore, none of these companies own, operate, or have
interests in properties located in any nonunion district or State;
neither have they any affiliation with any company so located. Since
April 1, 1927, all of the mines in the Cambridge district have been
continuously idle, absolutely no effort having been made to open a
mine or mines on any open shop or nonunion scale.
Therefore, in addition to the tremendous losses during the life of
the Jacksonville agreement, amounting to over two and a half mil-
lion dollars, must be added the expenses incidental to maintenance of
idle properties from March 31, 1927, to the present date, a period of
more than one year.


===== [扫描序号 1146] =====
2150
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Operation of coal mines at a loss or their idle maintenance for
three successive years is a burden to the strongest company and
ruinous to those financially weaker. Of the six operating com-
panies in the district in 1924 one is now under a receivership and
another is in the hands of a bankers' committee. The other com-
panies still survive as independent corporations but manifestly their
financial position has been severely injured.
Thus briefly have we summarized the losses thrust upon the oper-
ators during the life of the Jacksonville agreement. Let us now
consider for a moment its effect upon the mine workers in the Cam-
bridge district.
The mines operated by the members of this association, when work-
ing full, give employment to around 5,000 men. At no time since
1924 have the mines of the district been operated at capacity, there-
fore at all times there have been hundreds of miners out of employ
ment. Since March 31, 1927, they have all been out of employment.
If they remained in the Cambridge district they have had to depend
upon odd jobs of work for their livelihood. As a result many of
them have left their homes and gone to neighboring large cities in
search of employment as unskilled laborers in shops, foundries, steel
mills, and factories. When so employed their wage has averaged
around 35 to 45 cents per hour, out of which they had to pay room
and board for themselves, the meager remainder going for the sup-
port of their families back home. If employed in road construction
work they received probably 40 cents per hour. For farm work they
received even less. We are assured that hundreds of our Cambridge
miners have quietly departed from their homes and that they are
now working and for months past have been working in the non-
union mines of West Virginia, Pennsylvania, and eastern and
southern Ohio.
It is natural to ask: Is this condition necessary? The operators of
the Cambridge district, so far as their own mines are concerned, are
in position to answer: It is not.
In our effort to end this deadlock we have gone from the highest
union official to the workers themselves. All of our efforts have been
fruitless.
The late Mr. Albert A. Augustus, then president of the largest coal
company in the district, had a personal interview with Mr. John L.
Lewis.
In June of 1927, Mr. Augustus together with Mr. George M. Jones
endeavored to arrange a meeting with the Ohio officials of the United
Mine Workers. For a time it looked as though a meeting of miners
and operators could be arranged but after long preliminary negotia-
tions call for the contemplated meeting was not issued because at the
last moment the miners' officials then, and not until then, declared
that they were not authorized and did not have the right to enter
such a conference unless the Jacksonville agreement should be the
basis. To substantiate this statement, I quote two paragraphs of a
letter written by Mr. Lee Hall, president of the United Mine Work-
ers for Ohio, to Mr. R. M. Allison, chairman of the Joint Service
Club's committee, Cambridge, Ohio. Mr. Hall's letter is dated June
27, 1927.
After some little discussion on the general coal situation Mr. Augustus and
Mr. Jones, representing the operators, asked myself and Mr. Savage if the


===== [扫描序号 1147] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2151
mine workers of Ohio had authority to negotiate a wage scale on a basis
less than the Jacksonville agreement.
To this inquiry the mine workers' representatives on the committee stated
that in line with the action taken by the policy committee of the interna-
tional organization of the United Mine Workers of America, at its meeting
held in Indianapolis on March 28, 1927, we were only auhorized to enter
into district wage negotiations with our respective operators, upon the basis
of the existing agreement, which was then in effect-the Jacksonville agree-
ment.
At that time, before the conference was broken up, Mr. Augustus
and Mr. Jones made a direct offer to join with Mr. Hall in calling
a joint conference for the purpose of negotiating a scale of wages
"on the basis of and not less than the November, 1917, agreement."
This offer was refused by Messrs. Hall and Savage as representatives
of the Ohio miners.
For fear that the miners of the Cambridge district would not be
advised of this offer the Cambridge Coal Operators Association
caused to be inserted in the daily Jeffersonian, published at Cam-
bridge, Ohio, on June 18, 1927, a prominent advertisement setting
forth the offer of $5 per day for inside labor and 70 cents per ton for
cutting and loading.
When it became clearly evident that a competitive wage scale
could not be obtained from either the international or Ohio officials
of the United Mine Workers, two separate efforts to deal direct with
our own employees were made.
In November, 1927, the following notice was posted at the mines
of the Akron Coal Co.:
To the employees of the Akron Coal Co.:
On account of the deadlock over the wage question which has existed since
last March, the representatives of the Akron Coal Co. desire to meet with you
for the purpose of trying to work out a plan to put the mines in operation.
At such a meeting we could discuss the percentage plan and explain its
working and answer questions on same.
This method would be open and any other method could be discussed as to
some plan of starting the mines.
We believe it is worth while to try and end this deadlock which has and
is causing so much suffering on account of the mines being idle.
We could explain why we can not pay the Jacksonville scale. Would suggest
that the meeting be held at the Murray Hill and Senecaville mines and that
you notify a representative of the above company your intentions in this
matter.
Hoping for a favorable reply and that the meeting will be arranged as soon
as possible, I beg to remain,
Yours very truly,
AKRON COAL Co.,
WM. RIGBY, Sr., President.
Actions which will be fully described later on prevented acceptance
of this invitation and a meeting was not held. The men remained
idle, winter ensued, the union could not provide relief funds for the
miners and their families. Soup kitchens were established in the
schools for children, and supplies for miners' families were fur-
nished by charitable organizations. In the midst of the winter the
operators of the district issued the following letter:
President.
Secretary.
CAMBRIDGE, OHIO, January 28, 1928.
GENTLEMEN: We respectfully request you to call a meeting of the men who
were employed at
mine as of March 31, 1927, for the purpose of selecting
one or more delegates from said mine to meet in joint conference with the

2152
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
operators of the Cambridge district at Cambridge, Ohio, February 8, 1928, at
10 a. m.
We are requesting this meeting for the specific purpose of considering and if
possible agreeing on a wage scale that will permit mines of the Cambridge
district to resume operation.
Yours very truly,
COAL CO.
The publication of this invitation created a tense situation in the
district. Hundreds of our former employees privately and publicly
stated that they were in favor of meeting the operators on February
8, 1928, agreeing upon a scale and going to work. It was an open
secret that the scale the operators were prepared to offer was one
that would return a living wage to those accepting employment there-
under.
All of the mines in the district had been idle since April 1, 1927.
Some of them had also been idle for extended periods during the
years 1925 and 1926, due solely to the fact that nonunion mined coal
from West Virginia and Kentucky, sold at a low price, was replac-
ing Cambridge coal which was union mined and therefore had to be
sold for a higher price. The operators knew, and the large majority
of the miners knew, that the mines of the Cambridge district could
not again be placed in operation until our mining scale and working
conditions had been established on a parity with nonunion States,
and the open-shop districts of Ohio and Pennsylvania, which fields
furnish our market competition.
As soon as our invitation was made public, miners' officials and
radical union miners began earnest and open effort to prevent the
men, or any part of them, accepting our invitation. We are credibly
informed that there was a meeting of the State board of the United
Mine Workers in the city of Columbus, Ohio, on Monday, January
30, 1928, and that instructions were sent to the union officials in
charge of the Cambridge district and to local officials at the various
mines in the district that they were not to call meetings or give the
men any opportunity to meet and accept the operators' invitation.
On the morning of February 8, 1928, a large number of miners were
in the city of Cambridge, but the miners' officials, Mr. Lee Hall,
State president, Mr. David Watkins, State vice president, Cambridge
district officials and officers of the mine locals were present, mingling
with the miners in the public square and on the sidewalks, and these
officials by their presence, comment, and admonition influenced and
prevented attendance of the miners; therefore, there was no meeting
and the operators, assembled at the appointed time and place, did not
have an opportunity to present our proposition. As a result, the
mines of the district remain idle and the miners are either unem-
ployed or are working at poorly paid odd jobs.
The wage scale that we would have offered was approximately
the same as was paid at our mines in the year 1918 and I desire to
offer a schedule showing the average earnings of various classes of

We offer the above figures, which are actual earnings, as being
indicative of the approximate annual wage that miners in the Cam-
bridge district ought to enjoy if the mines were operating on a wage
scale which is competitive and which would permit us to sell our
product in the open market and keep our mines in operation.
We have another condition in the Cambridge district that is
rather unusual for mining communities, namely, there are compara-
tively few "company" houses. The large majority of our miners
live in the city of Cambridge, and in towns and villages scattered
throughout the district, in houses that are privately owned. Also
a large munber of miners own their own homes in the country,
having garden patches and small farms of 1, 2, and 3 acres, and
even larger farms. The Cambridge miner, as a rule, is a good
workman, thrifty, saving, English-speaking; their homes are com-
fortably furnished; they own radios, phonographs, automobiles, and
in general they share in the comforts of modern life. Their children
attend the county high schools-there being about 25 schools in the
two counties teaching high-school grades-and often these miners'
children are the best students in their respective classes. There
are, of course, families that are representative of the class that is
always to be found everywhere-the spendthrift, the poor home
manager, the shiftless worker, the man who no matter how plentiful
the work or how high the rate of pay, is always broke and in debt.
Of the company houses in the district many are vacant. Those
that are occupied are the homes of miners who have paid no rent
since April 1, 1927, but notwithstanding this nonpayment of rent
there has not been a single eviction of a miner's family from a
company house in the Cambridge district. Also there are no com-
pany stores in the district.
During the periods of idleness caused by our inability to operate
under the Jacksonville agreement and meet market competition, as
well as the recent and continuing idleness due to the insistence
of the officials of the United Mine Workers upon renewal of an
unworkable agreement, many valuable contracts have been rendered
void because of our inability to supply the tonnage. Several of
these contracts are permanently lost to the mines of the Cambridge
district, even should we get our mines again in operation. In addi-
tion to the huge losses in money, described herein, and the loss of
valuable contracts, we have also suffered large losses in acreage and
recoverable coal.


===== [扫描序号 1150] =====
2154
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
This loss is due to natural causes, and when mines in the Cam-
bridge district stand idle for long periods of time such loss is
inevitable. Mine timbers decay, the roof falls in, slate, water, and
gas accumulate in working places, particularly in territories that
are far removed from the shaft. In such cases when the mine
resumes operation the expense of clearing up the haulageways, re-
pairing timbering and tracks, pumping water, and clearing out gas
is so large that the amount of recoverable coal in that particular
territory will not justify the expense.
Therefore, laying aside for the moment the question as to whether
the operator or the miner is right or wrong in this contention or
is to blame for the idleness that exists, it is clearly apparent that
strikes and suspensions are wasteful in the extreme and destroy
the natural resources of the country which would have been recovered
had the strike not taken place.
Permit me to give you some startling figures in connection with loss
of time and earnings due to strikes that have been recently called in
the mines of the Cambridge Collieries Co. During the years 1918
to 1924, both inclusive, the men employed at the mines of this com-
pany lost a total of 4,165,957 man-days. The rates of pay during
these years varied but it is fair to assume that the miners lost about
$25,000,000 from their pay envelopes because of these strikes. The
time lost by the other companies in the district would at least equal
the record of the collieries, therefore it is safe to say that during
these years the miners in the Cambridge district lost $50,000,000 be-
cause of strikes called by their own officials. These figures do not
include the wage loss by reason of mines being idle during the life
of the Jacksonville agreement or the losses incurred by the miners
since April 1, 1927.
The operators of the Cambridge district have earnestly endeavored
to end this deplorable and destructive condition. We have met with
the international officials, the State officials and other officers of the
United Mine Workers. We have tried to deal with our own employees.
All to no effect. The miners' officials are unwilling to negotiate a
competitive wage agreement; the men are afraid to respond to our
offer of employment. Furthermore we do not believe that the Fed-
eral Government will be able to grant the coal industry any relief,
at least no immediate relief, and our mines must be placed in opera-
tion or we can not continue to survive or hope to retain our business
connections. Therefore it would seem that it will be necessary for
the operators of the Cambridge district to adopt a policy that is
alike fair to the miner and the operator, and place our mines on a
competitive basis.

and we let them go out and buy their coal themselves from districts
where they could secure an adequate supply at the market price.

Mr. TYTUS. I have been engaged in the coal business since 1919,
all of the time with the Sunday Creek Coal Co.
Sunday Creek Coal Co. operates in the Hocking and Crooksville
districts. The Hocking district consists of Athens and Hocking
Counties and part of Perry County, and the Crooksville district is
situated northeasterly of the Hocking district and consists of part
of Perry County, Muskingum County, and Morgan County. These
districts are served by the New York Central, Hocking Valley, Penn-
sylvania, and the B. & O. Railroads.


===== [扫描序号 1178] =====
2182
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
The maximum capacity of these combined districts is about 17,000,-
000 tons, and these districts should mine from 10,000,000 to 12,000,000
tons annually. Since the Jacksonville agreement went into effect the
production has greatly decreased. In 1924 the district produced
6,000,000 tons; in 1925, 5,400,000 tons, and in 1926, 5,600,000 tons.
The great reduction during these years was due to two general con-
ditions; first, the labor situation growing out of the high wage scale
of the Jacksonville agreement and second, the discriminatory freight
rates.
In past years Hocking coal was sold throughout all of the State of
Ohio excepting the extreme eastern portion, in the northern half of
Indiana, northeastern Illinois, and in the entire State of Michigan.
In addition, we used to ship over a million tons annually to the lake
trade. Under the Jacksonville scale we have lost all of our busi-
ness in southern Ohio, practically our entire market in Indiana and
Illinois, at least two-thirds of our market in Michigan, and our lake
business has dwindled from over a million tons to a paltry 75,000 or
100,000 tons a year. Practically all of this business has been lost
to the nonunion fields of West Virginia and Kentucky.
Hocking coal is suitable for steam and domestic purposes only. It
is not a special-purpose coal. It has always been very satisfactory
for steam, being not too high in ash and comparatively low in sul-
phur. It has had considerable success as a domestic fuel. It mines
in large blocks, is free from soot, and does not degrade too much in
handling. It has always had an excellent reputation for domestic
purposes throughout both our all-rail territory and in the Northwest.
Prior to the war, when our wages were only slightly higher than
those of the operators in West Virginia and Kentucky, Hocking coal
sold actively in competition with the coals from those two States.
In the Hocking district the tendency is for our miners to live in
towns or villages instead of a little settlement immediately surround-
ing the mines. When our mines last worked, perhaps half of our
employees lived in towns or villages. The building of good roads
and the use of automobiles has made it possible for them to drive 8
or 10 miles easily to work, and in the last five years there has been
a marked tendency toward making their homes in towns.
When the Sunday Creek Coal Co. last operated there were many
vacant houses at its camps, for example, at Mine No. 10, where we
employed about 300 men, there were only 75 houses. Two-thirds of
the men working at that mine lived in Glouster, which is only a mile
or a mile and a half from this operation.
None of the mines of the Sunday Creek Coal Co. have been oper-
ated since April 1, 1927, and none of the larger operators in the
Hocking and Crooksville districts have conducted any operations
during that period. The only mines which have been operated in
this district since April 1 are a few of the smaller operations. Some
of these in isolated localities have operated nonunion.
Mr. BELDEN. Mr. Tytus, let me ask you right there if during the
period of the Jacksonville agreement your company continued to
operate under that agreement?
Mr. TYTUS. We did.
Mr. BELDEN. All through.
Mr. TYTUS. All through the Jacksonville agreement; yes, sir.

2183
Mr. BELDEN. You may go ahead with your statement.
Senator GOODING. Mr. Chairman, I turn the chair over to you.
The CHAIRMAN. I should be glad to have you continue presiding.
Mr. TYTUS. There were probably 11,500 miners altogether em-
ployed in the Hocking and Crooksville districts during 1924, 1925,
and 1926, when the production was about 5,000,000 tons. This num-
ber is at least 50 per cent in excess of the men actually required to
produce this tonnage. Because of the scarcity of work and the
number of miners in the Hocking district, the operators agreed
to permit the men to double up so that each could get a share of
what work was available, this in spite of the fact that it made our
operations considerably more expensive than they would have been
otherwise. This was done at the request of the United Mine Workers
of America, but now the officials of this organization are offering
the low annual earnings of the Ohio miners during the Jacksonville
scale period as an argument for the maintenance of a high wage
scale, when, as a matter of fact, these low earnings were brought
about by crowding the mines with unnecessary labor at their request.
Business conditions in the towns and villages of the Hocking
district are desperate. The local merchants are doing nothing, and
credit has been extended to the point where they face bankruptcy.
Deposits in the banks have fallen off to far below normal. Many local
business men have already been forced to liquidate and leave the
communities, and it is only a question of a short time until a great
many others follow suit.
Less than half of the miners of the Hocking Valley have remained
in the district. Most of the younger and more industrious men have
found work elsewhere, either in the nonunion mines in West Virginia
and Kentucky, or in the large manufacturing centers, such as Cleve-
land, Toledo, Detroit, etc. These men are, of course, sending a por-
tion of their earnings home to support their families and dependents,
and have been of much assistance to the district.
Since the middle of November I have been spending three to four
days a week in the Hocking Valley, and on my trips to the district
I have visited continuously most of the larger communities. I am
acquainted with, and have talked to, many of the local merchants,
bankers, and business men, and know how serious their situation is.
There is, unquestionably, suffering in the district among the families
of the idle miners. Many of the men, particularly those who own.
their own homes, have been unable to leave and seek work elsewhere.
A great many of the older men have exhausted their lifetime sav-
ings. They are too old to seek other employment. While there has
been, and still is, considerable suffering in the valley, I believe that
the statements recently made in the press are considerably exagger-
ated. As a matter of fact, there has been a great deal of want and
privation in the Hocking district for the past four years during the
entire period that the mines operated under the Jacksonville scale,
because so many of the mines were idle and others worked only a
small percentage of full time. In 1923, 1924, 1925, and again in
1926 Governor Donahey issued proclamations urging Ohio citizens
to burn Ohio coal in order to help relieve the desperate situation in
the mining districts of this State.

Soup kitchens have been established in practically every commu-
nity, both large and small, in the Hocking district. I believe there
are now about 70 in operation. These are operated at the various
schools by local people under the supervision of National Guard of-
ficers, and they feed all of the pupils at these schools, regardless of
whether they come from needy families or not.
In Nelsonville, prior to the establishment of soup kitchens by the
governor, the Parent-Teachers Association had been carrying on this
same work and feeding the needy children a meal at noon. The Nel-
sonville superintendent of schools made the statement that, with the
exception of probably six children, the same ones were being fed this
year that have been fed every year since 1924.
There have been no evictions of miners from company-owned
houses in the Hocking and Crooksville districts since April 1, 1927,
except in a few isolated instances for law breaking, such as boot-
legging or for destruction of property; and, as I have said, some-
thing like half of the miners in those districts do not live in company
houses anyway.
"
At various times in the last two months, I have talked to two or
three hundred of our former employees. I think I am safe in saying
that over 90 per cent of these men would be glad to return to work
on the $5 scale offered them, and would do so if the officials of the
United Mine Workers of America would permit them. I base this
opinion upon the statements made to me by numerous of our former
employees with reference to their desire to go to work. Their hesi-
tation to do so is in some instances, due to their loyalty to the union,
but in more instances is, I believe, due to the fear that some harm
will come to them or their families in case they resume work in
opposition to the desire of the unions.
Unquestionably, the policy of the United Mine Workers has had a
blighted effect on the Hocking district. The men as a whole certainly
realize this, and criticism of the international organization and its
officers is practically universal. This criticism is freely expressed by
individuals and also in groups. I, likewise, have attended meetings
with groups of from 15 to 25 men where such opinions were very
frankly expressed. Furthermore, Dougherty, president of the Hock-
ing subdistrict, has criticised Lewis and the international policy bit-
terly in open meeting.

Mr. TYTUS. Efforts have been made to resume operations in the
Hocking district on a cooperative basis. A plan, known as the Morris
plan, which provided a base wage scale of $5, to be adjusted every
three months in accordance with the average selling price of coal, was
proposed. This plan was worked out so as to give the miners ap-
proximately 60 per cent of the gross sales prices and the operators
the remaining 40 per cent. Mr. Page Morris, vice president of the
New York Coal Co., called a meeting of the operators at Nelsonville
in January, which was attended by practically all the operators in
the Hocking district, and they almost unanimously agreed to adopt
this plan and propose it to their men. Each operator agreed to try
to open up a mine, and did so. However, the officials of the United
Mine Workers immediately became active in opposition to this plan
and sent representatives around the district to urge the men not to go
to work on this basis. As a result, those men who wanted to accept
the operators' proposition were driven from their jobs as soon as they
appeared. Large crowds assembled at the mines that attempted to
operate, and those men who desired to work were threatened with
severe bodily harm or death if they persisted in working under this
Morris plan.
The entire controversy in the Hocking district results from the un-
willingness of the officials of the United Mine Workers to permit their
men to resume work at a wage scale which the operators can afford
to pay. All coal produced in the Hocking district must be sold in
competition with the nonunion fields of West Virginia and Kentucky.
In years past, when our wages were only slightly above those in the
fields south of the river, the Hocking operators were able to sell their
coal freely in their normal markets. This condition continued until
1923 when the southern fields began to reduce their wage scales and
break away from the union. Soon after the signing of the Jackson-
ville scale in April, 1924, the mines in Kentucky and southern West
Virginia which had previously operated on a union basis became non-
union and were able to reduce their wage scales, and consequently
their operating costs to a point which has practically eliminated the


===== [扫描序号 1182] =====
2186
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
Ohio fields from competition. The wage scales in these two States
will now average less than two-thirds of the Jacksonville scale.
While conditions in the entire coal industry are so bad that any
hope of profitable operation is negligible, the Sunday Creek Coal Co.
would like to get its properties back in operation, as it realizes that
every additional month's idleness is injuring any prospects it may
have of ever regaining its place in the markets. This company has
large coal reserves, some 40,000 acres, the taxes and overhead are tre-
mendous, and this enforced idleness is very burdensome for the com-
pany, as well as detrimental to the communities. We would like to
begin opening our mines at once and increase our operations as fast
as market conditions will permit, and are entirely willing to pay to
our men the highest wage scale possible, consistent with general con-
ditions in the industry. The so-called Ohio $5 base wage scale repre-
sents the extreme limit that the operators can afford to pay at the
present time, and even with this scale, any operator who attempts to
run his properties during the coming 12 months will face staggering
losses while he is endeavoring to regain his lost markets.
On the other hand, the resumption of operations on this basis, even
by a few mines, would be most helpful in the Hocking district, and
would tend at once to relieve the suffering and produce a better feel-
ing among business men. It must be borne in mind that the annual
pay roll from the mining industry in the Hocking district used to
exceed $15,000,000. During recent years, due to the Jacksonville
scale, this was cut to about $8,000,000. For the past 13 months, it has
been practically nothing.
The responsibility for this situation is directly due to the unwill-
ingness of the officers of the United Mine Workers to recognize the
economic conditions under which the Ohio coal mines must be oper-
ated and to their unwillingness to adapt themselves to them. The
suffering and want in the Hocking district might largely have been
avoided if they had been willing to permit their men to continue to
work on a wage scale which would permit the industry to compete
with West Virginia and Kentucky, and unless and until the Ohio
mines can be operated on a basis which will permit them to meet
this competition, there is no hope for the Ohio industry.

years. The elimination of car shortage has eliminated the bulges.

Mr. JONES. I do not know why the charge was made. Bone coal

years. During the war, owing to the miners' organization objecting
to our punishing our men when they loaded dirty coal, all over the
United States, or wherever the United Mine Workers of America
were in control, there was a let down in the quality of coal. While
we endeavored to clean our coal as clean as possible, we could not
clean it at that time as we should for the reasons stated.
Mr. LEWIS. Do you not know that certain mining companies issued
orders to their miners to load everything black in the mine?
Mr. JONES. I do not know of any reputable company doing that;
in fact, I do not know of any other kind of company doing it.
Mr. LEWIS. You say the mine workers would not let you penalize
your miners for loading impurities. Don't you know that the con-
tract provided for penalties for loading dirty coal, all over the United
States?
Mr. JONES. Yes, sir; it provided for that, all right; but it was one
of the rules that was set aside by your organization at that time.
Mr. LEWIS. Are you speaking of the whole country or for the
Hocking district?
Mr. JONES. I am talking for the Hocking district now.
Mr. LEWIS. And you have never penalized your men in the Hock-
ing district for loading dirty coal?
Mr. JONES. We penalize them now. But there was a while that it
was very hard for us to penalize them, during the war. Our super-
intendents did the best they could to have loaded only clean coal, by
coaxing and talking to the men; but we were not able to enforce any
rigid fines or discharges.

that did.

Mr. JONES. The organization did not do it, but the men did, and

Mr. JONES. I do not understand that question.

Mr. LEWIS. As a general commercial policy, do you think it desir-
able, advantageous, or justifiable for the coal industry to sell its
coal to railroads and other consumers below cost of production?
Mr. JONES. Not as a continual thing, because it would lead to

Mr. LEWIS. Well, then, why do the operators as a rule not refrain

Mr. JONES. They were in hopes that by selling their coal below

wait for the demand for coal to improve, which did not take place,
however.
Mr. LEWIS. Now, that it has been demonstrated that the selling of

think the policy of selling coal below cost should be continued or
discontinued?
Mr. JONES. I think it should continue until some of the high-
cost mines are put out of business and the production and consump-
tion of coal can be brought closer together.

TESTIMONY OF EZRA VAN HORN, VICE PRESIDENT OF THE
CLARKSON COAL MINING CO.
(The witness was duly sworn by Senator Gooding.)
(Direct examination by Mr. Belden. attorney for Ohio Coal
Operators' Association :)
Mr. BELDEN. Have you prepared a statement of what you want to
say?
Mr. VAN HORN. I have.
Mr. BELDEN. Which of the Ohio districts are you interested in?
Mr. VAN HORN. Eastern Ohio No. 8.
Mr. BELDEN. I wish you would read that statement before I begin
asking you questions.
Mr. VAN HORN. I am vice president of the Clarkson Coal Mining
Co., which operates mines in the eastern Ohio district.
The eastern Ohio district, as the term is used, includes Harrison.
Belmont, and Jefferson Counties, which constitute the Ohio portion
of the No. 8 seem of coal. These counties, when the mines are in
operation, produce something like 60 per cent of all the coal pro-
duced in Ohio.
No. 8 coal is used for steam and domestic purposes and is largely
purchased for railroad fuel.
The coal fields of Ohio are located chiefly in the eastern and south-
eastern portions of the State so that they adjoin the coal fields of
Pennsylvania and are not far distant from the coal fields of West
Virginia. The Ohio coal fields operate under conditions more or
less similar to those in the other States, serving to a large extent the
same markets and are lagely govened by the same conditions so that
it is impossible for Ohio to operate on a union wage scale when
West Virginia and Pennsylvania operate on a lower scale.
The Jacksonville scale went into effect on April 1, 1924, and was
in fact a continuation of the wage scale which had been in effect
prior to that time.
It is impossible to correctly understand the situation to-day with-
out reviewing briefly conditions during the years of the Jackson-
ville wage scale.
The Clarkson Coal Mining Co. continued operations through the
period of the Jacksonville scale but with a decreasing production.
In 1924 we produced 1,147,262 tons; 1925, 894,285 tons: 1926.
858,782 tons; but our operations in all these years resulted in sub-
stantial losses. We had to choose between losses resulting from
idleness and those resulting from operation and we chose the latter.
because it allowed us to retain markets which had been established
with much effort and which our company was particularly equipped


===== [扫描序号 1241] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2245
to serve. Our people have coal docks at Ashland, Wis., and
Duluth, Minn., and have a large trade in the Northwest, especially
with railroad companies which have been accustomed to use our coal
for locomotive purposes for many years. It takes a long time to
establish such business and when once lost it is difficult to regain,
and we felt it better to sustain some losses in operation than to run
the risk of losing this business to our competitors; and we were still
living in the hope that our difficulties with the union would be
smoothed out by negotiations and that the wage scale would be
modified to conform to existing business conditions. On that point
I desire to state that we did everything we could to convince the
principal officers of the United Mine Workers of America that the
Jacksonville wage scale must be modified so as to permit the Ohio
coal mines to compete with West Virginia and Kentucky and that
if this were not done the mines of our district would have to close.
In June, 1927, I went to Chicago with the late Mr. A. A. Augustus,
president of the Cambridge Collieries Co., one of the largest pro-
ducers in Ohio; we presented the Ohio situation to John Lewis and
Lee Hall, and urged them to consent to negotiations for the modi-
fication of this wage scale. We told them that if they would consent
to a reasonable modification of the wage scale we would reopen our
mines at once and by reason of our railroad customers would have a
regular market so that we could give their men continuous employ-
ment. They refused to consider any modification. It was not until
after all efforts to secure an adjustment had failed that we under-
took any other course.
The Clarkson Coal Mining Co. was confronted, like the other
companies of that district, with the alternative of having their mines
remain closed with their houses occupied by strongly antagonistic
tenants, unwilling to work, or to open the mines on an open-shop basis
employing men who were willing to work.
Before describing what we did in this connection, I want to say
that the Clarkson Coal Mining Co. determined, on its own responsi-
bility, to resume operations on the open-shop basis. This was not
done at the instigation of any customer, railroad or otherwise, and
was solely for the purpose of mining coal to supply our markets
as far as we could.
We have always had difficulty at the coal mines in this district in
securing the regular attendance of workmen. Even when operating
under arrangements with the union, the number of absentees without
leave has seriously interfered with our operations. I have kept a
record at our mines for a number of years on this subject. I have
hereto attached a statement of wages earned by employees of the
Clarkson Coal Co. for the period extending from January 1, 1921,
to August 27, 1921, inclusive, during which period this company
operated full time on a wage scale equal to the Jacksonville scale,
and was desirous of producing the greatest tonnage possible. This
statement shows that the number of days lost by our regular em-
ployees was 24,893, and that the wages which they would have re-
ceived for those lost days aggregated $189,842.72. During this
period our company was forced to go into the open market and to
purchase more coal to fill our orders than we could have produced
had our men worked 100 per cent of the time. We have records


===== [扫描序号 1242] =====
2246
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
extending over a period of several years, and they show that as a rule
our men do not work more than 80 per cent of the time, even when
an opportunity for regular employment is given them.
There have been more men trying to work in coal mines during the
last few years than there have been places for them, and at our mines
the union requested that the work be divided among our employees,
thus increasing the number of employees and reducing the yearly
earnings of each man.
Before I leave this subject I want to call attention to the fact that
during the years when the Jacksonville wage scale was in effect,
there had been considerable suffering and hardship in some of the
Ohio districts, and this occurred in 1925 and 1926. I have with me
a set of newspaper clippings taken from Cleveland papers in Febru-
ary and March, 1926, when the Jacksonville wage scale was in effect.
The suffering in the mining district had become so general at that
time that the newspapers were sending special writers to investigate
and write up the situation such as has been done during the present
winter. I want to read a paragraph from a signed article written by
Robert W. Hughes and published in the Cleveland Press on Febru-
ary 17, 1926:
The coal-mining industry, which but three years ago ranked second only
to agriculture as the greatest industry of the State, has collapsed until in
1925 it ranked as the fifth industry of the State. Steel, rubber, clay, and
brick products have passed it.
To-day more than 34,000 Ohio coal miners are out of work. Most of them
have not done a day's work for more than six months. Some have not had
work for two years.
Most of these 34,000 idle miners have families. Suffering and privation
among these people in the Hocking Valley and Cambridge fields has been the
worst ever known this winter.
Senator GOODING (presiding). What winter was that?
Mr. VAN HORN. The winter of 1925-26.
Mr. BELDEN. When the Jacksonville scale was in effect, Mr.
Chairman.
Senator GOODING. All right.
Mr. BELDEN. You may go on with your statement.
Mr. VAN HORN. I continue quoting:
Of 1,500 mines in the State, less than 300 are operating to-day. They
are losing money every day, and it is simply a question with the operator
whether he will suffer a smaller loss by operating the mine than from the
upkeep and deterioration if it was idle.
Yet there is no strike or lockout in Ohio.
Operators and union officials are
on the best of terms and are cooperating desperately in attempts to keep

Of the 70,000,000 tons of coal used in Ohio last year, only 12,000,000 tons was
Ohio mined. The rest was shipped in from West Virginia and Kentucky and
sold right under the noses of Ohio operators.
Senator GOODING. That is a most remarkable statement, it seems

Ohio's production dropped from 45,878,191 tons a year in 1920 to 23,000,000
in 1925. This year's production, unless there is a radical change in conditions.
may not reach 12,000,000 tons.
This, despite the fact that Ohio has the coal, the mines, and the miners to
furnish all its own 70,000,000 tons a year consumption.
On February 18, 1926, the Cleveland Press published a further
article by the same writer in which he told how John Collins, the
owner of the Beaumont Mine near Athens, had offered to give his
coal mine to the men if they would work it. In doing so he showed
them his operating statement for the previous month from which
it appeared that the mine was operating at a large loss.
Another article published by the Press is entitled: "Idle miners
of Ohio face starvation," and gives the details of the suffering of
the women and children in the coal districts.
Another article published in the Cleveland Press on February 23,
1926, is entitled: "Many miners out of work go barefoot," and
describes conditions in the Crooksville and Cambridge fields. This
article tells how one large coal company was forced into receiver-
ship; how some of the others were operating on a part-time basis;
and how all the mines of the Cambridge Collieries Co. had been
obliged to shut down. There are pictures of the cabins in which
the miners were living, their destitute condition being due to the
fact that the mines were not operating. In fact, the newspaper
articles written at that time rivaled those which have been written
during the present winter.
The situation in Ohio became so serious that on March 2, 1926,
Governor Donahey issued a proclamation calling upon State agencies,
chambers of commerce, civic and fraternal bodies to assist in a cam-
paign to get Ohioans to burn Ohio coal. He said: "The miners'
pay roll in Ohio dropped from $82,000,000 in 1920 to $35,000,000 in
1925. No State can afford to lose $50,000,000 a year in wages to its
workmen." Governor Donahey pointed out "that if the 70,000,000
tons of coal consumed in Ohio this year were all mined in Ohio there
would be no such disaster facing the industry as exists."
Senator GOODING. Did the governor's campaign do you any good
at all?

Mr. VAN HORN. Very little. The people continued to buy coal
where they could buy it cheapest, as I have stated in my statement
here.
Senator GOODING. All right, you may go on.
Mr. VAN HORN. It is well known that at that time many munici-
palities and school districts in Ohio, as well as railroads and private
consumers were purchasing coal from West Virginia and Kentucky
because such coal could be bought at lower prices than Ohio coal,
and they continued to purchase coal on competitive prices even after
the governor's proclamation.
Everything which I have said thus far relates to conditions hap-
pening while the Jacksonville scale was in effect. It was this record
of hardship to our employees, of money losses to the operators, and
the disappearance of our markets that forced us to begin operations
on an open-shop basis, and about August 1, 1927, our mines were so
opened.
As soon as this became known the peaceful condition existing at
our mines entirely changed. When we began to send in supplies and
material to put the mines in operation our trucks were interfered
with by large crowds. The first truck delivering supplies to our
mines was turned back and the driver stoned and abused. Large
crowds of men, women, and children gathered along the highways
and around the entrance to our mines and threatened with injury
the drivers of the trucks and also threatened men seeking employ-
ment, and in many instances threw stones and rotten eggs and struck
them with clubs. This intimidation became so general as to make
it impossible to begin operations without protection.
For this protection we joined with other coal companies in com-
mencing suit in the Federal court at Columbus on the 15th of August,
1927, setting forth the acts of violence which had been committed,
and the danger to our men and property, and Judge Hough of that
court granted us a restraining order. My office has kept a record of
newspaper clippings from the Martins Ferry Times, a daily news-
paper which has the widest circulation of any newspaper in the
eastern Ohio field. I have 176 pages of these clippings, beginning
with April 1, 1927, and it is worth while to note that not a single
act of violence is recorded in these clippings prior to the issue of
August 1, 1927, which coincides with the time when we announced
we were going to resume operation on an open-shop basis.
I have prepared and attached hereto a list showing the headings of
clippings referring to violence, etc., from that day forward. I have
omitted all items which refer to other districts, and this list relates
solely to the eastern Ohio field. It begins with the burning of the
Sommers tipple at Adena on August 1; includes the throwing of eggs
at nonunion men at Webb mine on August 2; stoning of nonunion
miners at our mine August 13 and 16; the attack on the Smithsville
mine crew August 18; stoning of officials of the Y. & O. Coal Co.,
Martins Ferry, August 22, and shooting affrays on the 29th and
30th, also numerous instances including the dynamiting of houses
and mine structures, fires, riots, injuries to employees, marches on
mines, and other activities down to date.
