After the restraining order was issued additional United States deputy
marshals were appointed by Judge Hough and placed at the different mines.
These deputies, together with deputy sheriffs, assisted in giving protection
to the open-shop workmen who were brought into the mines.
In September our application for a preliminary injunction was granted
and copies of the injunction were posted in English, Italian, and Polish
and pamphlets containing the injunction were served upon all the leaders of the
mobs.
There is no doubt whatever as to where the responsibility rests for these
disturbances. Officials of the United Mine Workers were frequently at our
property in conference with the men and directing their activities.
John Cinque, president of the subdistrict, testified in court at Steubenville
that he had charge of the strike and personally appointed the pickets which
were posted at our mines and also at the other properties operating open shop,
and that he received daily reports from them.
Mr. Clinque visited our properties from time to time and many lesser officials
were also there, and the officials of the local union were constantly with the
crowds.
There is no doubt that a concerted effort was made by the United Mine
Workers to stop our operations and the operations of all the other mines
operating open shop in that district.
The protection given us by Judge Hough was not only reasonable, but was
necessary under the circumstances to protect our properties and the lives of
our men.
At first we had to bring in men from the outside, and the labor turnover
was large as they did not like to endure the taunts, shouts, and threats of
the union men.
Our men were perfectly satisfied with working conditions and the money
they could earn. After a while we began to receive applications from some
of our former employees and also from men who came to the office seeking
work. As a matter of fact, more than one-half the men now employed at our
mine are either our old employees or men living in the surrounding territory.
These men either walk to our mine or come by automobile to work.
Under the injunction the United Mine Workers are permitted to have two
picket posts in the vicinity of our property with three men on duty at each
post all the time, and are permitted to use peaceful persuasion in getting our
men to leave. These picket posts are an annoyance, both to us and our men.
so much so that a majority of the men who walk to our mines come in over
the hills to avoid passing the regular picket posts on the highway.
On February 16 our men, of their own volition, prepared a petition to the
trustees of Richland Township, Belmont County, Ohio, which was signed by
220 of our employees. It is as follows:
ST. CLAIRSVILLE, OHIO, February 16, 1928.
To the Trustees of Richland Township, St. Clairsville, Ohio.
GENTLEMEN: We, the undersigned, who are residents and taxpayers in Bel-
mont County, earnestly request the removal of two so-called picket posts
occupied by members of the United Mine Workers of America on roads lead-
ing to the Clarkson No. 1 mine.
These buildings are a menace to those who are compelled to travel the public
highways in performance of their duty.
WILL PATRICK
(And 219 others).
This will show you what our workmen think of the efforts being made to
try to prevent them from earning a living. There is hardly a day passes but
that some of our workmen go to our superintendent and repeat to him their


===== [扫描序号 1247] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2251
5
satisfaction with working conditions and wages and ask him to use his influence
to secure the removal of these picket posts.
I want to say a word about hardship and suffering in our district. There
is no hardship or suffering in the vicinity of our mines except on the part
of those men who have not been working since April 1, 1927, and who will
not go to work. It is quite natural that the families of men who have not
worked for almost a year should be living in difficult conditions, but we have
not been responsible in any way for such hardship.
We have at the Provident mine approximately 100 houses. When the mines
were closed on April 1, 1927, nearly all of these houses were occupied by
our employees. These houses were built solely for use at our mines to provide
homes for our workmen and constitute just as much a part of our mine
equipment as the tipple itself. We need these houses to take care of our
present employees and are handicapped because we can not get them. We
made application last fall to Judge Hough for these houses. He decided, on
December 17, 1927, that we were entitled to the houses but because of the
winter season gave the occupants until April 1, 1928, to get out. None of
those occupants have paid any rent since April 1, 1927, except a few employees
who are on our official staff and are now and have been continuously working.
These occupants not only retain possession of our houses, in which they live,
but make it as unpleasant as possible for open-shop families which we put in
adjoining houses.
I want to say in that connection that they have all moved out.
Those houses are not occupied at the present time by our former
employees.
I give you a good illustration of their attitude. Here is an anonymous letter
which I received dated February 16, 1928.
CLARKSON COAL Co.,
Provident, Ohio.
DER SIRS: This is not a trittor or any bunk; this is a worning to the coal co
it self and the Wheeling Railroad Co. We are here to worn you personali
that if you people kep going lod coal aney longer you well se what hapens
not only to the Clarkson Coal Co. but to the Wheeling Railroad Co. the same
because we are fighting our rights and not only ours but thousands of others.
We are ready to go to work almost at aney time but not for nothing, so if
you please stop loading coal we bage you and save troble (— unless you stop
working we weel not bother nothing) we are giving you the time until the 1st
of April to stop loading coal. If you refuse this speckt your property and the
Wheeling R. Ry bridges the same one or the other you know what tat mean
this no bunk at all cause you know we can do it esie cause we have all the
material we want and there lots of us to it weel take onley few minutes to
do it cous we know how your or W. L. E. guards dont amount to nothing
in this matter at all.
KWICK LITE.
This letter shows the kind of threats that are being made.
We are now producing about 1.200 tons per day at our Provident mine, and
by the 1st of May we expect our mine to be up to its normal capacity.
Exhibit A which is attached shows the time which is lost, which
I referred to in the earlier part of my statement.

Mr. BELDEN. Tell the committee what your experience has been and

Mr. VAN HORN. Well, I want to say that in the vicinity of our

Mr. BELDEN. What is the situation around your mines as to schools
and churches, Mr. Van Horn?
Mr. VAN HORN. We have public schools in the vicinity of our
mines where the children go until they get up to the eighth grade
and then they go to high school in the towns near by. Of course, if the
high school are close enough so they can live at home they go to
school every day.
The church facilities are about as good as in any mining com-
munity. We have churches in the small towns. We also have one
church at our mine; and, so far as our nonunion fellows are con-
cerned and the colored boys who live at the mine, that church service
is conducted in that camp. Along that line I want to say that the
colored quartette which sings in our nonunion camp has been singing
at St. Clairsville at the Sunday night services.
Mr. BELDEN. What wage scale is in effect at your mines?

apiece.

the average for every man working in that mine was $5.58.
In the month of March the 10 highest loaders averaged $6.53
apiece; our machine men averaged $8.20 apiece, and every man
working at that mine averaged $5.78.

ST. CLAIRSVILLE, OHIO,
1928.
EMPLOYMENT AGREEMENT
It is hereby agreed between the Clarkson Coal Mining Co., hereinafter called
"employer," and
hereinafter called "employee,"
as follows:
-
1. Employee is hereby employed by and agrees to work faithfully and effi-
ciently for employer while this agreement is in force under the classification
as a miner in employer's mine No. 1 at St. Clairsville, Ohio, but shall at the
request of the employer do work of other classification for which he may be
competent.
2. Employee shall be paid at the rate prescribed in the employer's wage
scale hereto attached, such pay to be for work of the classification which
employee shall be competent to perform and shall perform hereunder. He


===== [扫描序号 1253] =====
CONDITIONS IN THE COAL FIELDS
2257
shall be paid only for the time he actually works or for the work which
he actually performs, except as hereinafter provided. Employer shall operate
said mine during the term of this agreement whenever, in its judgment, said
mine can be operated at a profit and shall make use of employee's services
hereunder to the fullest extent possible consistent with the economical opera-
tion of said mine whenever said mine is in operation. Employer guarantees
to pay employee hereunder at least $35 each 30 days during the term hereof.
This agreement shall remain in effect for at least 30 days and thereafter until
terminated by notice from one party to the other.
3. Employer agrees that it will not operate its said mine as a closed union
shop during the term of this agreement with employee, and that it will not
during the term hereof enter into any agreement with any union affiliated
or connected with United Mine Workers of America. Employee agrees that
he will not while he is an employee of employer, make any effort amongst
its employees to bring about the unionizing of employer's said mine or of any
other mine owned, leased, or operated by the employer, or the unioniz.ng of
any of employer's employees, and that it will not at any time take an action
designed or tending to place said mine or any other mine owned, leased, or
operated by the employer upon the closed union shop basis, and that he will
not at any time foment, advocate, or take part in any strike of employer's
employees.
4. The reasonable rules and regulations of the employer not in conflict here-
with, as posted upon its bulletin board at said mine from time to time, shall
become and be a part of this agreement. Violation of the terms hereof by
either party shall be ground for the immediate termination hereof by the
other.
5. Employee understands that the United Mine Workers of America, or
unions or persons affiliated, associated, or cooperating with United Mine
Workers of America, or local unions thereof, may object to the operation of
said mine upon the open-shop basis and that there may be unlawful attempts
to interfere with the operation of said mine and with the performance by
employee of his duties hereunder. Any risk arising out of any such inter-
ference or attempted interference is voluntarily assumed by employee.
Advances of earnings will not be made and pay will be issued on regular
pay days only.
By
CLARKSON COAL MINING CO.

incentive to reduce your wages?
Mr. LEWIS. I certainly have, Mr. Van Horn, because I do not
believe, in the first place, that you can follow me down as far as
I can go in West Virginia; and, in the second place, I have no alter-
native than to reduce or leave my mine idle.
Mr. VAN HORN. That is exactly our position.
Mr. LEWIS. And I am dealing with my employees individually,
and I possess the power to deflate their wages at will by merely put-
ting a notice on our pit head.
Mr. VAN HORN. Are you going to if you know that we are going
to reduce wages?
Mr. LEWIS. Why not? Because I know that otherwise our prop-
erty will be confiscated.
Mr. VAN HORN. Then we have no alternative.

Mr. LEWIS. Do you not know that if the mining industry should

STATE OF OHIO,
Jefferson County, 88:
Personally appear before me the undersigned, a notary public, Joseph Sher
man and Homer Douglas, who being first duly sworn according to law depose
and say that on and for sometime prior to the 13th day of October, 1927.
they resided at No. 1452 Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh, Pa.; that on said date
affiants sought employment at the Hanna Employment and Commissary
Agency, located in the city of Pittsburgh, Pa., that they were informed in the
presence of agents of the Atlantic Contracting Co. that they were in need of
men at the Florence mine of said company, located near Martins Ferry, Ohio,
and were told that the work consisted in developing a new mine, that there
were no labor troubles in and around said mine; that working conditions were
good and wages high and were assured of at least a year's steady employment.
Affiants say that the first they knew that a strike was in progress at said
Florence mine was when they had traveled within 2 miles of said mine and
union pickets, stationed along said highway, attempted to peacefully persuade
them not to work in said mine because it was being operated nonunion.
Affiants say that had they known a strike was in progress at this mine
they would not have entered the employ of said company; that they sought
after their arrival in the camp of said mine, sufficient money to return to
Pittsburgh, Pa., but were refused and were told that they would be compelled
to work until the expenses of transporting them from Pittsburgh to said
Florence mine were "worked out " by their labor.


===== [扫描序号 1264] =====

Affiants say that they worked from the 14th day of October, 1927, each
and every day including Sundays, up to and including the 11th day of Novem
ber, 1927, and during that time they were housed in a brick dwelling on the
second floor thereof; that on the first floor thereof six company guards were
housed by said company; that on or about the 7th day of November, 1927,
at about the hour of 9.30 p. m., affiants retired; that at about the hour of 10
p. m. and while affiants were awake, one Nick Leonard, captain of the guards
employed by said company, together with several other guards, visited the
guards who were housed on the first floor of said building and there a con-
versation took place and that the conversation these affiants distinctly over-
heard in substance as follows: That General Manager Squibbs, in charge of
the operation of said Florence mine, ordered the said Nick Leonard to reduce
the force of guards by the 15th of said month and gave as his reason therefor
that quietness and order prevailed and that there were no disturbances caused
by union miners or their sympathizers, nor had there been any destruction of
property and that the present force was too large and expensive; that during
the course of said conversation said Nick Leonard said in substance as follows:
"I like you boys and I'd like to keep you on the force and I would suggest
that you or some of you do something or cause something to happen so that
I can have some good reason to influence Squibbs to retain all of you, and
if something is done we can place the blame on the striking miners."
That on the following morning, while affiants were preparing to enter the
mine affiants were informed that one of the company houses burned down to
the ground.
Affiants say that the following evening at about the hour of 10.30 p. m.
affiants overheard several of the guards on the first floor remark about the
fire in the following manner: "Well, it was a good job. I believe we have
accomplished something; they won't fire us now," and other like language,
expressing their extreme pleasure over the occurrence and confident that they
would be able to retain their jobs.
Further these affiants saith naught.
JOSEPH SHERMAN,
HOMER DOUGLAS

Mr. WARRUM. In your employment agreement you have this pro-
vision:
Employer guarantees to pay employee hereunder at least $35 each 30 days
during the term hereof. This agreement shall remain in effect for at least
30 days and thereafter until terminated by notice by one party to the other
Do you understand that your employees have the right to terminate
this service relationship at will and when they please, or that they
are under obligation to remain nonunion and work for you as non-
union men for 30 days?
Mr. VAN HORN. That is a legal question in there, sir, and I would
assume, as I recall the language of the agreement, that they would
have the right to terminate it at the expiration of 30 days.
Mr. WARRUM. I will ask you if you are not familiar with the in-
junction that you got based upon that employment agreement as
follows:
The peaceful persuasion herein referred to is peaceful persuasion directed
toward one who is not known to be an employee, in the effort to keep him from
becoming an employee, or directed toward one who is an employee, in the
effort to induce him to terminate his relation of employment upon the expira
tion of any employment contract he may be under, bu does not include peace
fully persuading one to break an existing employment contract.
I will ask you if you did not secure that injunction order, and
if you are not aware of the fact that it was based on the construction
I have given your service agreement, that you would employ these
men for 30 days, have an interest in their union status for 30 days.
and it should not be interfered with by peaceful persuasion during
that time.
Mr. VAN HORN. I think that is the wording of the agreement.
Mr. WARRUM. And is it not a fact that when these pickets in an
attempt to exercise the right that is apparently given them under
this decree they are met with the statement from your officers and
guards that, "You must not talk to these men as they are under
employment?"
Mr. VAN HORN. We take it for granted that they are under em-
ployment.
Mr. WARRUM. And having stated to them that they are under con-
tract of employment you insist that the pickets shall not talk to them
under this contract and the injunction, do you not?
Mr. VAN HORN. Yes, sir.
Mr. WARRUM. You also have this provision:
The employee agrees that he will not at any time foment, advocate, or take
part in any strike of employer's employee.
You understand that you have bound your employee up so that
while he might quit work individually, he could not talk with his
roommate in the mine or with anyone associated with him there
about striking on account of your wages, do you not?
Mr. VAN HORN. We just take the wording of that agreement, sir.
Mr. WARRUM. Yes; and that is exactly what you mean by it when
you put that into the agreement, that you could enjoin your
employees if they undertook to talk together about striking.
